abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pre-procedural nutritional status has been proposed as a prognostic marker in transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), although most studies rely on isolated nutrition scores. This study examined how multiple serum-based nutritional scores influence post-TAVR survival.
METHODS: Consecutive patients undergoing TAVR between December 2021 and December 2023 were retrospectively analyzed. Eight serum biomarker-based scores were calculated for each patient (GNRI, PNI, CONUT, PALBI, TCBI, PACI, AGR, ALBI). Associations with overall survival were assessed with Kaplan-Meier curves and adjusted multivariable Cox regression. Principal component analysis (PCA) evaluated relationships among scores.
RESULTS: A total of 459 patients were included (mean age 81.7 ± 7.1 years, 45.8% female, median STS 2.8 [1.8-4.4]). The eight scores frequently classified the same patients into different risk strata. Significant survival differences were observed for all scores' most severe stratification except CONUT (p = 0.083) and PNI (p = 0.133). In adjusted Cox models, most scores showed a statistically significant association with overall mortality, except for GNRI (p = 0.237), PALBI (p = 0.378) and TCBI (p = 0.125). PCA demonstrated substantial collinearity among several scores and highlighted a dominant first principal component (PC), PC1 = 54%, without improved discrimination compared to STS score. In the adjusted Cox model, PC1 was also significantly associated with overall mortality (p < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Despite capturing overlapping biological domains, serum-based nutritional scores inconsistently classify TAVR patients. PCA suggests that a single underlying biomarker dimension explains most of the variability among scores, highlighting overlap and inconsistency across them and supporting the need for a more integrated approach to nutritional assessment rather than single metrics.
title: Multidimensional profiling of serum biomarker nutritional scores in TAVR using principal component analysis.

abstract: The right heart is a crucial determinant of prognosis across a broad spectrum of cardiovascular diseases, including pulmonary hypertension, tricuspid regurgitation, and heart failure. In the contemporary era of transcatheter device-based therapies, accurate assessment of right ventricular (RV) and right atrial anatomical and functional remodeling is critical for clinical decision-making. Although echocardiography remains the cornerstone of right heart evaluation, its interpretation is often limited by complex geometry of the RV and the load dependency of some parameters. Recent advances in multimodality imaging have enabled more robust and quantitative characterization of right heart structure and function. Three-dimensional echocardiography and RV strain provide improved functional assessment beyond conventional parameters of RV function. Cardiac magnetic resonance offers reference-standard quantification of RV volumes and mass, enhancing reproducibility and risk stratification. Computed tomography contributes complementary anatomical, functional and volumetric information, particularly relevant in structural heart interventions and evaluation of systemic venous congestion. Importantly, imaging biomarkers reflecting RV-pulmonary arterial coupling, atrial remodeling, and systemic venous congestion have demonstrated incremental prognostic value. Integration of these quantitative metrics into clinical practice may refine risk stratification, optimize timing of intervention, and identify patients unlikely to benefit from invasive therapies. This review summarizes contemporary advances in right heart imaging and proposes a practical framework for integrating echocardiography, Cardiac magnetic resonance, and computed tomography into therapeutic strategy in patients with right heart disease.
title: Multimodality imaging of the right heart: Translating quantitative assessment into therapeutic strategy.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Dementia is associated with lower use of invasive therapies and poorer outcomes after acute myocardial infarction (AMI). However, its impact in AMI complicated by cardiogenic shock (AMICS), where timely invasive management is critical for survival, remains poorly characterized. We evaluated the association between dementia, treatment intensity, and in-hospital outcomes in AMICS.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the National Inpatient Sample (2016-2019). Adults hospitalized with AMICS were identified using ICD-10-CM codes and stratified according to pre-existing dementia. Outcomes were in-hospital mortality, major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), and use of invasive and supportive therapies. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for demographic, hospital, socioeconomic, presentation, and comorbidity characteristics estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We additionally performed 1:1 propensity score matching.
RESULTS: Among 226,570 patients with AMICS, 10,895 (4.8%) had dementia. Patients with dementia were older, more frequently female, had greater comorbidity burden, and fewer markers of acute disease severity. They underwent coronary angiography (50.2% vs. 70.4%), percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) (39.3% vs. 55.0%), coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) (5.2% vs. 17.5%), mechanical ventilation (34.1% vs. 45.5%), and circulatory support (23.7% vs. 46.4%) less frequently than those without dementia (all p < 0.001). Dementia was independently associated with lower odds of coronary angiography (aOR 0.50, 95% CI 0.48-0.52), PCI (aOR 0.58, 95% CI 0.55-0.61), CABG (aOR 0.31, 95% CI 0.28-0.34), and circulatory support (aOR 0.49, 95% CI 0.46-0.51), as well as higher odds of in-hospital mortality (aOR 1.17, 95% CI 1.12-1.22) and MACCE (aOR 1.13, 95% CI 1.09-1.18). Results were consistent in the propensity-matched pairs.
CONCLUSIONS: Among patients hospitalized with AMICS, dementia was independently associated with lower treatment intensity and worse in-hospital outcomes despite fewer markers of acute clinical severity. These findings highlight the importance of individualized, goal-concordant decision-making while avoiding unwarranted limitation of potentially life-saving therapies.
title: Dementia, Treatment Intensity, and Outcomes in Acute Myocardial Infarction with Cardiogenic Shock.

abstract:
AIMS: We examined the association between ticagrelor pretreatment and angiographic no-reflow in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), with in-hospital mortality as a secondary outcome and clinical phenotyping as an exploratory objective.
METHODS: In a retrospective multicentre registry (2018-2021), 623 patients referred for percutaneous coronary intervention were compared by loading strategy: pretreatment at first medical contact or deferred before PCI. Cohort-wide inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), using a clinical covariate-balancing propensity model and 50 imputations, estimated adjusted risk ratios (RRs). Outcome-blind latent class analysis preceded a treatment-weighted comparison of class-specific no-reflow risks.
RESULTS: No-reflow occurred in 28/464 pretreated patients versus 27/159 comparators (6.0% versus 17.0%); the crude RR was 0.36 (95% CI 0.22-0.58), and the IPTW-adjusted RR was 0.43 (95% CI 0.24-0.74; P = 0.003). Ten patients died (adjusted RR 0.46, 95% CI 0.13-1.67). Three classes comprised 328, 231 and 64 patients, but their pretreatment-standardised no-reflow risks did not establish prognostic separation.
CONCLUSIONS: Ticagrelor pretreatment was associated with lower angiographic no-reflow after propensity weighting. The adjusted mortality and exploratory class-risk findings did not reach statistical significance. Residual confounding and uncertain covariate timing limit causal interpretation, and prospective validation is required.
title: Ticagrelor pretreatment and angiographic no-reflow in STEMI: a multicentre observational study.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Integrated care based on the Atrial fibrillation Better Care (ABC) pathway improves outcomes in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), but whether treatment effects differ across older patients remains unclear.
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE) of ABC pathway-based care and assess its transportability across healthcare settings using causal machine learning (ML).
METHODS: Individual participant data from the cluster-randomised mAFA-II and MIRACLE-AF trials were analysed, including 3,209 patients aged ≥65 years. Three causal ML models were developed in mAFA-II and externally validated in MIRACLE-AF. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality, ischaemic stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, or major bleeding.
RESULTS: The uplift random forest demonstrated the best performance and identified meaningful HTE. In the mAFA-II testing cohort, ABC pathway-based care was associated with a lower risk of the primary outcome in patients predicted to benefit, whereas no benefit and possible harm were observed in those predicted to derive harm (P-interaction=0.002). In external validation, benefit was preserved in the predicted benefit group but not in the predicted harm group, although treatment discrimination was attenuated. Patients predicted to derive limited benefit had greater clinical complexity, including higher comorbidity burden and CHA2DS2-VASc scores. Sex, heart failure, and hypertension were the strongest predictors of treatment effect.
CONCLUSIONS: ABC pathway-based integrated care demonstrates clinically meaningful treatment heterogeneity among older patients with AF. These findings support more personalised implementation of integrated care and highlight the potential of causal ML to guide precision management in AF.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: MAFA-II trial (ChiCTR-OOC-17014138 || http://www.chictr.org.cn/, registered on 26 December 2017), MIRACLE-AF trial (NCT04622514 || https://clinicaltrials.gov/, registered on 10 November 2020).
title: Heterogeneity of Treatment Effect of ABC Pathway-Based Care in Older Atrial Fibrillation: Insights from the mAFA-II and MIRACLE-AF Trials Using a Causal Machine Learning Approach.

abstract:
AIM: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is increasingly performed in older adults with severe aortic stenosis, but there is limited evidence on their post-procedure changes in care needs, healthcare costs, and mortality risk.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used linked medical and long-term care (LTC) insurance claims data from 1361 patients aged ≥ 75 years who underwent TAVI in 13 Japanese municipalities. Patients were stratified into four groups by baseline certified care needs level: Independent (n = 725), Support Level 1-2 (n = 321), LTC Level 1-2 (n = 208), and LTC Level 3-5 (n = 107).
RESULTS: Among 532 patients in the 36-month observation cohort, 53% were independent at baseline, and approximately half of those remained independent at 36 months. Monthly total medical and LTC costs at 36 months were approximately 5 times higher in the LTC Level 3-5 group than the Independent group. The LTC Level 3-5 group also showed significantly higher all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 3.19, 95% confidence interval 2.18-4.67).
CONCLUSIONS: Higher baseline care needs are associated with poorer outcomes and higher costs after TAVI. Incorporating care needs levels into clinical assessments may inform clinical decision-making and resource planning in older populations.
title: Changes in Long-Term Care Needs, Healthcare Costs, and Mortality Risk After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation in Japan: The Longevity Improvement & Fair Evidence Study.

abstract: Importance It remains unclear if intraoperative hemodynamic therapy should be guided by cardiac index. Objective To evaluate whether individualized cardiac index–guided hemodynamic therapy vs routine hemodynamic therapy improves outcomes in high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter, single-blind, superiority randomized clinical trial enrolled high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery between October 8, 2023, and October 25, 2025, at 12 university medical centers in Austria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Germany, and Spain. The date of last follow-up was January 15, 2026. Interventions Patients were randomized to individualized cardiac index–guided hemodynamic therapy targeting the patient’s preoperative resting cardiac index vs routine hemodynamic therapy (with blinded cardiac index monitoring). Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was a composite of acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, severe infectious complications, nonfatal cardiac arrest, or death within the first 7 postoperative days. Secondary outcomes included the individual components of the primary outcome within the first 7 postoperative days. Results Of the 1128 patients enrolled, 1111 were randomized and 1095 were included in the primary analysis (median age, 67 years [IQR, 59-74 years]; 49.4% were female). The primary outcome occurred in 243 of 549 patients (44.3%) in the individualized cardiac index–guided hemodynamic therapy group vs 256 of 546 patients (46.9%) in the routine hemodynamic therapy group (relative risk, 0.94 [95.1% CI, 0.83-1.08]; P = .38). There were no between-group differences for the incidence of the individual components of the primary outcome within the first 7 postoperative days. Conclusions and Relevance Among high-risk patients undergoing elective major abdominal surgery, individualized cardiac index–guided hemodynamic therapy targeting the patient’s preoperative resting cardiac index did not reduce the incidence of a composite outcome of acute kidney injury, acute myocardial injury, severe infectious complications, nonfatal cardiac arrest, or death within the first 7 postoperative days compared with routine hemodynamic therapy. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05648279
title: Individualized Cardiac Index–Guided Hemodynamic Therapy in High-Risk Patients Undergoing Elective Major Abdominal Surgery

abstract: ABSTRACT Background Frailty is highly prevalent among elderly patients with coronary heart disease (CHD) undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and is associated with adverse clinical outcomes and impaired health‐related quality of life. However, different frailty assessment tools vary in their conceptual frameworks, assessment domains, and predictive performance, and their applicability in elderly PCI populations remains unclear. Aims To compare four commonly used frailty assessment tools, including the Frailty Phenotype (FP), FRAIL scale, Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI), and Frailty Index (FI), and to investigate their associations with quality of life in elderly patients with CHD undergoing PCI. Methods This cross‐sectional study included 244 elderly patients with CHD undergoing PCI at a tertiary hospital in Shanghai from August to December 2024. Frailty was assessed using the Frailty Phenotype (FP), FRAIL scale, Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI), and Frailty Index (FI), and quality of life using the 12‐Item Short Form Health Survey (SF‐12). Agreement was evaluated using the Kappa statistic. Associations with physical component summary (PCS) and mental component summary (MCS) scores were assessed using correlation and multivariable linear regression, while discriminatory performance was examined using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and Bayesian discriminant analyses. Results Mean PCS and MCS scores were 40.08 ± 11.23 and 52.30 ± 7.82, respectively. Frailty prevalence was 40.6% by FP, 8.6% by FRAIL, 28.3% by TFI, and 22.1% by FI. Agreement was fair to moderate (Kappa = 0.242–0.496). Higher frailty scores were independently associated with lower PCS and MCS after adjustment for age, sex, education, smoking, and comorbidity burden. FP and FI showed comparable discrimination for PCS, whereas TFI had the highest AUC for MCS. Classification accuracy was highest for FP in PCS and TFI in MCS (both 79.51%). Conclusion Frailty was consistently associated with poorer quality of life. FP and FI performed similarly for physical health, whereas TFI showed the most favorable performance for mental health.
title: Application of Four Frailty Assessment Tools in Elderly Patients With Coronary Heart Disease PCI and Its Relationship With Quality of Life

abstract: ABSTRACT Failure of true‐lumen re‐entry after subintimal wire passage is a well‐recognized limitation of endovascular treatment for external iliac artery (EIA) chronic total occlusions (CTO). We report a 73‐year‐old woman with severe limb ischemia and a prior failed endovascular attempt who underwent hybrid left common femoral artery (CFA) endarterectomy with patch angioplasty, followed by trans‐patch retrograde access and dedicated device‐assisted re‐entry (Outback Elite) after antegrade and retrograde wires repeatedly tracked subintimally without reaching the true lumen. Controlled re‐entry preserved hypogastric artery flow and allowed drug‐eluting stent reconstruction of the EIA. At 12‐month follow‐up, ABI improved from 0.36 to 0.50, and TBI improved to 0.37. Duplex ultrasound at 6‐month follow‐up confirmed patency of the reconstructed segment without evidence of hemodynamically significant restenosis. This technical report illustrates the use of an endarterectomized CFA as a retrograde re‐entry platform and reviews contemporary strategies for managing subintimal crossing failure in iliac CTOs.
title: Trans‐Patch Retrograde Re‐Entry During Hybrid Revascularization of an External Iliac Artery Chronic Total Occlusion: A Technical Note and Review of Re‐Entry Strategies

abstract: ABSTRACT Background Real‐world data after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) using drug‐coated balloons (DCBs) in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) are limited. Aims We compared 1‐year clinical outcomes after PCI with paclitaxel DCBs between the ACS and non‐ACS patients. Methods The ALLIANCE is a prospective, multicenter registry of PCI using paclitaxel DCBs. Primary endpoint was target lesion failure (TLF), defined as a composite of cardiac death, myocardial infarction (MI), or clinically driven target lesion revascularization. Secondary endpoints included all‐cause mortality at 1 year. Adverse events were adjudicated by an independent committee. Propensity score matching was performed to adjust for baseline differences between the ACS and non‐ACS patients. Results From July 2023 to February 2024, 1794 patients with de novo lesions (ACS 513 [28.6%] and non‐ACS 1281 [71.4%]) were enrolled at 57 medical institutions in Japan. Mean age was 71 years, and 76% were male. Among ACS patients, 34.7% had ST‐segment elevation MI, 33.9% non–ST‐segment elevation MI, and 31.4% unstable angina. Intracoronary imaging was used in 88.5% of lesions. Bailout stenting after DCB angioplasty was required in only 1.1% of 1984 lesions. Technical success, defined as post‐procedural residual stenosis < 40% and absence of flow‐limiting coronary dissection, was significantly lower in patients with ACS than those with non‐ACS. At 1 year, TLF occurred in 7.0% of ACS and 3.8% of non‐ACS patients (adjusted HR 1.83; 95% CI 1.06–3.17, p = 0.03). All‐cause mortality was 6.4% and 3.3%, respectively (adjusted HR 2.06; 95% CI 1.13–3.75, p = 0.02). Conclusions One‐year TLF and all‐cause mortality were significantly higher in ACS than non‐ACS patients treated with paclitaxel DCBs in real‐world clinical settings. Registration: Japan Registry of Clinical Trials ( https://jrct.mhlw.go.jp ); unique identifier: jRCT1032230218.
title: One‐Year Clinical Outcomes of Paclitaxel‐Coated Balloon Angioplasty in Patients With and Without Acute Coronary Syndrome: The ALLIANCE Registry

abstract: ABSTRACT Systemic atrioventricular valve (SAVV) regurgitation contributes importantly to systemic right ventricular deterioration in adults with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (ccTGA) and dextro‐transposition of the great arteries ( d ‐TGA) after atrial‐switch repair. Transcatheter edge‐to‐edge repair (TEER) has emerged as an option for selected patients at high or prohibitive surgical risk, and prior congenital series have established the feasibility of transseptal, transbaffle, and alternative access strategies. However, procedural execution remains highly anatomy‐dependent because systemic venous pathways, atrial baffles, ventricular topology, cardiac orientation, and access‐to‐valve geometry can substantially alter guide‐catheter support and device coaxiality. We report a single‐center Interventional Rounds experience of four consecutive high‐risk adults undergoing SAVV‐TEER across four distinct transposition anatomies: ccTGA with dextrocardia, d ‐TGA after Mustard atrial‐switch repair, Mustard anatomy with severe iliofemoral tortuosity, and ccTGA with interrupted inferior vena cava and azygos continuation. Transfemoral access was used in two patients, and right internal jugular access in two. Three procedures were performed with PASCAL ACE and one with MitraClip. Device implantation was successful in all four patients, with SAVV regurgitation reduced from severe (3+) to mild (1+). Final mean SAVV gradients were 1.5, 2.1, 1.9, and 1.8 mmHg, respectively, and no major acute procedural complications occurred. The principal technical message is that access selection should be guided not only by anatomic patency but by the anticipated mechanical trajectory of the delivery system. Right internal jugular access may be selected prospectively as the preferred primary route when inferior venous anatomy is absent or expected to provide unfavorable curvature, support, or device alignment. Dextrocardia and atrial‐switch baffle anatomy may additionally require specific steering and traversal adaptations. These observations represent focused procedural refinements within the evolving congenital TEER experience rather than evidence of comparative efficacy or safety.
title: Anatomy‐Driven Transcatheter Edge‐to‐Edge Repair of the Systemic Atrioventricular Valve in Complex Transposition Anatomy

abstract: ABSTRACT Background In‐stent restenosis (ISR) after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in true bifurcation coronary lesions can lead to repeat revascularization and adverse outcomes. Aims To identify independent risk factors for ISR in patients with coronary bifurcation lesions undergoing PCI and to develop a predictive model for ISR‐free survival. Methods Patients with coronary artery disease and Medina coronary bifurcation lesions was analyzed. Baseline characteristics, laboratory values, bifurcation anatomy, and PCI details were collected. Cox proportional hazards models were used to identify independent predictors of ISR and its performance was evaluated Model interpretability was explored with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), and a nomogram was constructed for clinical use. Results Univariate analysis showed lesion/procedural factors were strongly predictive. Multivariable Cox analysis identified use of a drug‐coated balloon in the side branch and side‐branch stenting with a drug‐eluting stent as the top independent predictors of ISR. Lesion location in the left circumflex was associated with higher ISR risk The Cox model Calibration plots showed close agreement between predicted and observed ISR probabilities. A SHAP analysis confirmed the direction and relative importance of each predictor, enhancing the model ' s interpretability. Conclusions In true bifurcation PCI, Side‐branch interventions are associated with higher ISR risk, whereas a simple single‐stent approach confers lower risk. The developed Cox‐based nomogram demonstrated robust ability to predict ISR, which can aid clinicians in risk stratification and personalized management. Early identification of high‐risk patients may enable closer surveillance or preventive measures to improve long‐term outcomes after bifurcation PCI.
title: Risk Factors and Predictive Model for In‐Stent Restenosis After PCI in Coronary Bifurcation Lesions: A Retrospective Study

abstract: ABSTRACT As life expectancy in patients with congenital heart disease continues to increase, coronary artery disease and acute coronary syndromes are encountered more and more in this population, with a higher level of complexity, especially in the acute setting. We present a case of acute thrombotic occlusion of the left circumflex coronary artery in a patient with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries. This case highlights several challenges from ECG and computed tomography interpretation to coronary angiography and PCI performance. Key pre‐procedural and procedural steps are revised to guide toward prompt and successful revascularization.

abstract: Abstract Background Acute decompensated severe aortic stenosis may preclude waiting for elective treatment, and evidence for non-elective transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is limited. We assessed 12-month mortality, 30-day safety, and recovery after urgent, emergency, or salvage TAVI. Methods We prospectively enrolled patients undergoing urgent, emergency, or salvage TAVI at one centre in 2022–2025. The primary endpoint was 12-month all-cause mortality; secondary endpoints included device success, 30-day safety, and functional and echocardiographic recovery. Results Among 53 patients, 36 underwent urgent, 14 emergency, and 3 salvage TAVI. Device success was 52/53 (98.1%). Thirty-day mortality was 1/36, 0/14, and 0/3; 12-month mortality was 2/36, 1/14, and 0/3 (3/53). Kaplan–Meier 12-month survival was 94.3% (95% confidence interval 83.5–98.1%). New atrioventricular block was detected in 2/53 on postoperative day 2; by 30 days, haemofiltration or renal replacement therapy occurred in 1/53 and permanent pacemaker implantation in 0/53. At 12 months, cardiovascular mortality was 2/53, heart-failure readmission 4/53, stroke 1/53, a separate Valve Academic Research Consortium-3 type 2 bleeding event 1/53, and permanent pacemaker implantation 0/53. Paired analyses showed improved New York Heart Association class, Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire-12, left ventricular ejection fraction, and transvalvular gradients at 30 days and 12 months (all P&lt;0.001). Conclusions Selected patients had high device success and low early event rates after non-elective TAVI; paired data showed sustained functional and haemodynamic improvement. These findings support timely Heart Team assessment and consideration of non-elective TAVI, when appropriate, at experienced centres; comparative benefit over alternative strategies warrants prospective study.

abstract: Abstract Aims Mechanical Circulatory Support (MCS) remains limited in advanced heart failure due to blood-contact complications and the absence of biventricular support. We report the first prospective clinical trial of a novel soft-robotic, biventricular, pulsatile technology placed externally around the heart without blood contact, designed to deliver individualized cardiac assistance (reBEAT®, AdjuCor GmbH, Munich, Germany). Methods and Results The system was temporarily applied in 10 end-stage heart failure patients immediately before elective LVAD implantation. Devices were custom-manufactured using preoperative CT scans to match individual cardiac anatomy. Safety, feasibility, and effects on haemodynamics were evaluated. Implantation was rapid (3±2 min), demonstrating procedural feasibility. We observed two procedure-related adverse events while no device- or procedure-related severe adverse events occurred. Absence of new ECG abnormalities, and no tissue injury confirmed safety. An iterative assessment on haemodynamics provided key insights into individualized cardio-circulatory support. While device presence reduced preload dependent haemodynamics in some patients, low average support pressures of 65–66 mmHg produced variable improvements towards baseline, predominantly on the pressure signal: mean arterial pressure (MAP; 67.5 ± 10.6 vs. 76.2 ± 11.7 mmHg, p&lt;0.01), stroke work (SW; 347.8 ± 118.2 vs. 434.1 ± 131.0 mJ, p&lt;0.01), and cardiac power output (CPO; 407.9 ± 108.2 vs. 503.7 ± 116.2 mW, p&lt;0.01). Additionally, effects were observed on atrioventricular valve function and interventricular balance, which were not significant. Conclusion This soft-robotic biventricular MCS platform provides short term evidence of a safe and feasible approach to pulsatile biventricular support without blood contact. Significant increases in MAP, CPO, and SW towards baseline indicate functional effects. Continuous device-driven workflow improvement is mandatory and further data are required to refine individualized optimization strategies. This technology may offer a novel biventricular assist modality. Its reduced complexity may enable broader adaption for both temporary and durable support. Avoiding blood contact and enabling balanced biventricular assistance will be central drivers of its continued clinical development.
title: Short-term safety, feasibility, and performance of a novel soft robotic biventricular mechanical circulatory support device avoiding blood contact – The MISSION reBEAT trial

abstract: Abstract Acute heart failure (AHF) represents a major cause of emergency medical care worldwide and continues to carry a substantial burden of morbidity and mortality despite advances in chronic heart failure management. Most patients with AHF present to emergency departments (EDs), where the first hours of care are critical to determine prognosis. Of these, some have been previously evaluated and treated by prehospital emergency medical services before ED arrival. This consensus document summarizes the current evidence and provides practical advice to emergency physicians for the diagnosis, treatment, and disposition of patients with AHF in these emergency settings (emergency medical services and ED). It emphasizes the importance of a rapid phenotypic classification into acute decompensated heart failure, acute pulmonary oedema, isolated right ventricular failure, or cardiogenic shock, as a key tool to guide early management and triage decisions. It reviews evidence on prehospital and ED management, including the use of biomarkers, imaging, ventilatory support, diuretic and vasodilator strategies, and early initiation or continuation of guideline-directed medical therapy. It also discusses risk stratification and disposition decisions supported by validated tools. Finally, it identifies major knowledge gaps and future research priorities, including pragmatic trials to assess prehospital interventions, biomarker-guided therapy, and early initiation of disease-modifying treatments. Ultimately, this consensus document is aimed to contribute to the improvement of outcomes in AHF.

appraisal.design_and_n: Consensus document; no sample size.
appraisal.main_limitation: Expert consensus with practical advice rather than new comparative evidence; cardiogenic shock is one of four phenotypes covered.
appraisal.one_line: Consensus document on diagnosis, treatment and disposition of acute heart failure in prehospital and emergency department settings, including cardiogenic shock phenotyping.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: The abstract does not report an effect estimate.
appraisal.why_it_matters: Sets out early phenotypic triage and research priorities that bear on shock recognition and escalation in the emergency pathway.

title: Acute heart failure in emergency settings

abstract: Abstract Background Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is an established treatment for severe, symptomatic aortic stenosis, often used in older patients and those at increased surgical risk. Assessment of left ventricular (LV) diastolic function in this population is challenging, and available data on diastolic changes following TAVI remain inconsistent. Purpose To investigate changes in diastolic function over time after TAVI according to the 2025 American Society of Echocardiography (ASE) guidelines and to determine whether left atrial reservoir strain (LASr) a newly recommended parameter, provides incremental diagnostic value. Methods Diastolic function was assessed using transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) before and at follow-up after TAVI in 109 consecutive patients treated between 2019 and 2021. Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) were excluded. All TTE measurements were performed on retrospectively stored image datasets by a single experienced operator in accordance with the 2025 ASE guidelines. The following diastolic parameters were analysed: E- and A-wave velocities, medial e’ velocity, tricuspid regurgitation (TR) velocity, left atrial volume index (LAVi), and LASr. LV ejection fraction (LV-EF) and global longitudinal strain (GLS) were also assessed. Changes between baseline and follow-up were analyzed using the paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test, as appropriate. Results Of the 109 included patients, 70 (64%) were included in the final analysis after exclusions due to atrial fibrillation, missing data, or death prior to follow-up. Median age was 80 years (interquartile range 77-85), and 49% were women. Pre-procedural TTE was performed a median of 164 (118-218) days before TAVI, and follow-up TTE at 423 (382-463) days after the procedure. LAVi decreased significantly after TAVI (41 mL/m2 vs. 37 mL/m2, p = 0.003). LASr was reduced at baseline and showed a non-significant increase at follow-up (18.8% vs. 20.5%, p = 0.22). Conventional diastolic parameters - including E/A ratio (0.75 vs. 0.69, p = 0.27), TR velocity (2.7 m/s vs. 2.5 m/s, p = 0.63), and E/e´ ratio (16.0 vs. 15.7, p = 0.59) - remained largely unchanged, although A-wave velocity increased significantly (102 cm/s vs. 109 cm/s, p = 0.0008). LV end-diastolic volume (LV-EDV) decreased significantly (95 mL vs. 87 mL, p = 0.008). LV-EF and GLS remained unchanged in the overall cohort. Conclusion At 14 months after TAVI, patients demonstrated significant structural reverse remodeling, reflected by reductions in LAVi and LV-EDV, as well as improved late diastolic filling evidenced by increased A-wave velocity. However, LASr showed only a non-significant increase and did not provide incremental value in the assessment of diastolic function in this cohort.Graphical Abstract
title: Changes in diastolic function after TAVI: trends in conventional parameters and the role of left atrial reservoir strain

abstract: Abstract Background Current guidelines emphasize reverse remodeling as a therapeutic goal in Heart Failure with reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF). However, the influence of the specific non-coronary vs ischemic clinical history (ST-elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) vs. Non-ST-elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) vs. Chronic Ischemia) on long-term myocardial recovery in HFrEF remains poorly defined. Methods Retrospective study following 357 HFrEF patients (Left Ventricle Ejection Fraction (LVEF) &lt;40%) over a 60-month period, categorized into four groups: Non-ischemic (G1), Chronic Ischemic (G2), nSTEMI (G3), and STEMI (G4). Serial echocardiography assessed LVEF, ventricular diameters, and diastolic function (lateral E/e'). Statistical differences in final and absolute changes among the four phenotypes were assessed using One-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni post-hoc test for multiple comparisons. Results Left Ventricle Ejection Fraction: At 5-year follow-up, LVEF recovery was significantly asymmetrical (p=0.030). Non-ischemic G1 achieved the highest functional improvement (+14.3%), whereas STEMI (G4) and nSTEMI (G3) patients showed the most blunted responses (+4.2% and +4.9%, respectively). Left Ventricle (LV) End-Diastolic Diameter: Paradoxically, the STEMI group exhibited the most pronounced reduction in LV end-diastolic diameter (-7.31 mm vs. -4.42 mm in non-ischemic G1, p=0.001), suggesting a pattern of structural remodeling without functional recovery. Right Ventricular Function and Diastolic Function: Furthermore, STEMI was the only group where right ventricular function (TAPSE) failed to improve (-0.2 mm vs. +2.2 mm in non-coronary G1, p=0.001) and diastolic filling pressures significantly worsened (lateral E/e' +5.6% vs. -11.6% in G1, p=0.013). Conclusions Long-term ventricular recovery in HFrEF is highly phenotype-dependent. Post-STEMI patients exhibit a "Remodeling Paradox," where significant reduction in ventricular size does not translate into functional LVEF recovery, likely due to fixed myocardial fibrosis with persistent microvascular dysfunction, reduced contractile miocardiocitic reserve due to ischemic cell apoptosis and reduced exposure time to prognosis modifying pharmacotherapy through reduced survival. Inversely the greatest reduction in Left Ventricle telediastolic diameter was observed in this particular STEMI subgroup reflecting the positive effects coronary revascularization and optimal prognostic pharmacotherapy can have on cardiac ventricular remodeling. The increased lateral E/E’ ratio observed in group 3 and 4 acute ischemic cardiomyopathies (diastolic dysfunction) could be related to impaired aerobic pathaways with reduced Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) regeneration and deficient myosin and actinine interaction at the myocardiocite level; reflecting the myocardium’s reduced capillarity and increased need of non oxygen related pathaways to create and destroy actin-myosine cross-bridges.Table 1Baseline CharacteristicsTable 2Echocardiography
title: The remodeling paradox in ischemic HFrEF: dissociation between left ventricular cavity reduction and functional recovery according to ischemic phenotype

abstract: Abstract Background Right ventricular-pulmonary arterial (RV–PA) coupling reflects the interplay between RV contractility and afterload, and serves as a potential prognostic marker in aortic stenosis. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) reduces left-sided filling pressures and pulmonary pressures, which may enhance RV–PA coupling. However, impact of baseline left atrio-ventricular (LA–LV) coupling on how RV–PA coupling responds after TAVI is not yet fully understood. Purpose To assess: (1) extent of improvement in RV–PA coupling after TAVI; and (2) relation between LA–LV coupling and improvement in RV–PA coupling following TAVI. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 88 patients who underwent transfemural TAVI and had good quality pre- and early post-procedural echocardiographic studies. RV–PA coupling was assessed using TAPSE/sPAP ratio, Fractional Area Change (FAC)/sPAP ratio, RV lateral S’/sPAP ratio, and RV free-wall longitudinal strain (RVFWLS)/sPAP ratio. Post vs pre-procedural changes (Δ) were calculated. Baseline LA–LV coupling was assessed using left atrial coupling index (LACI), calculated as the ratio of LA end-diastolic volume to LV end-diastolic volume. Linear regression models assessed the relationship between baseline LACI and ΔRV-PA indices. Results Early post-TAVI, after a median of 2.5 (2-5) days, sPAP decreased significantly (from 31.1±12.4 to 24.5±13.4 mmHg; p&lt;0.001). Among isolated RV functional parameters (TAPSE, FAC, RV lateral S', and RVFWLS), only FAC and RV lateral S' showed significant improvement post-TAVI. However, when incorporated into the RV–PA coupling indices, significant post-TAVI improvement was observed in all these indices (all p&lt;0.001) (Figure 1). Restricted cubic spline analyses demonstrated linear associations of LACI with all ΔRV-PA coupling indices, with no evidence of non-linearity (all p for non-linearity &gt;0.7). Higher pre-TAVI LACI was independently associated with smaller improvements in all RV-PA coupling indices, even after adjustment for baseline values of indices and for sPAP: ΔRVFWLS/sPAP (β −0.013, 95%CI −0.02 to −0.005; p=0.006), ΔTAPSE/sPAP (β −0.009, 95%CI −0.016 to −0.002; p=0.01), ΔFAC/sPAP (β −0.016, 95%CI −0.032 to −0.0003; p=0.04), ΔS’/sPAP (β −0.004, 95%CI −0.008 to −0.00006; p=0.04) (Figure 2). Adjustment for sPAP was deemed mandatory given the independent association of LACI with ΔsPAP (p&lt;0.001). Conclusion RV–PA coupling significantly improves early after TAVI, predominantly due to decrease of the systolic pulmonary arterial pressure, rather than to the intrinsic RV functional changes. However, advanced pre-TAVI LA–LV uncoupling identifies patients less likely to achieve right heart hemodynamic recovery early after TAVI. These results support earlier referral to TAVI, before decline of the left heart hemodynamics. This might improve patients selection and optimize timing for TAVI.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Baseline left atrio-ventricular coupling predicts early improvement of right ventricular–pulmonary arterial coupling after TAVI: potential implications for patients selection

abstract: Abstract Background Relief of left ventricular afterload after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) may induce rapid changes in diastolic function. However, the extent of these changes, and which diastolic parameters are the main drivers of these changes after TAVI remain unclear. The 2024 British Society of Echocardiography (BSE) algorithm1 evaluates diastolic function hierarchically: first-line BSE triad (E/e′, TR velocity, LAVi) combines surrogates of filling pressure and pulmonary pressure with a marker of LA remodeling, followed by an intermediate adjudication stage (LA strain, e' velocities) and supplementary parameters. Purpose To assess early changes in diastolic function after TAVI, according to the sequential BSE 2024 algorithm, and the diastolic parameters that primarily drive these changes. Methods We retrospectively analyzed patients who underwent transfemoral TAVI, who had full echocardiographical acquisitions before and early after TAVI. Diastolic function was graded according to the BSE 2024 algorithm. Improvement of diastolic function was defined as transition to a lower diastolic dysfunction grade. Parameter normalization was defined as abnormal pre-TAVI values becoming normal post-TAVI, according to guideline cut-off values. Results Eighty-eight patients were included (mean age 77±5 years; 57% women; 85% in sinus rhythm; median NT-proBNP 730 pg/mL). After a median of 2.5 days post-TAVI, diastolic function improved in 45% of patients. Most transitions occurred from impaired diastolic function with elevated filling pressures to impaired function with normal filling pressures (Figure 1). Among improved patients, E/e′ decreased from 17.3±7.6 to 11.1±3.1 (p&lt;0.001) and TR velocity from 2.32±0.69 to 2.07±0.52m/s (p=0.031), while changes in myocardial functional and structural parameters did not reach statistical significance (LAVI: 51.3±12.8 vs 48.6±14.9 mL/m²; LVEF: 61.5±9.5 vs 58.7±8.5%; GLS: −21.6±5.8 vs −20.3±5.8%); first-line BSE triad shifted importantly towards normal values: TR velocity normalized 100% patients, elevated E/e′ normalized in 88.9%, while LAVi normalized in 30.3%, compared with lower normalization rates of 71.4%, 10%, and 15.8%, respectively, in patients without diastolic improvement. Downstream parameters shifted similarly, irrespective of diastolic improvement for LA reservoir strain (70% vs 59%), but differently for e' velocities (82 vs 44%; p=0.02) (Figure 2). Overall, normalization of E/e′ showed the strongest association with diastolic grade improvement (OR 32.0; p&lt;0.001), followed by TR velocity (OR 2.73; p=0.047). Conclusions Early diastolic improvement after TAVI is common, and is predominantly driven by rapid normalization of markers of filling pressure and pulmonary pressure (first-line BSE 2024 diagnostic pathway), while myocardial and structural parameters demonstrate limited short-term change.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Early changes in diastolic function after TAVI: a guideline-based analysis of diastolic improvement patterns

abstract: Abstract Background Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) effectively relieves valvular obstruction in patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS); however, long-term outcomes remain heterogeneous. While procedural success is high, many patients continue to experience an excess risk of death, suggesting that factors beyond the valve itself may determine prognosis. Global myocardial performance, reflecting integrated systolic and diastolic function, may capture residual heart failure biology after TAVI. Methods and Results In this retrospective single-center cohort study, consecutive patients undergoing transfemoral TAVI between 2016 and 2022 were screened. Patients with permanent atrial fibrillation (AF) or inadequate echocardiographic data were excluded. Global myocardial performance was assessed pre-procedurally using the myocardial performance (TEI) index. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality at 3 years. A total of 412 patients (mean age 82.1 ± 5.1 years; 47.1% male) were included. Higher TEI index values were associated with increased 3-year mortality in a graded manner. In multivariable Cox regression, each 0.1-unit increase in the TEI index was independently associated with a higher risk of death (HR 1.49, 95% CI 1.19–1.87; p &lt; 0.001). A pre-specified TEI index threshold of 0.45 effectively stratified patients into distinct long-term risk groups, with early and persistent separation of Kaplan–Meier survival curves. The TEI index provided incremental prognostic value beyond established clinical and echocardiographic parameters and demonstrated consistent associations across clinically relevant subgroups. Restricted cubic spline analyses supported an approximately linear relationship between the TEI index and mortality risk. Conclusions In patients undergoing TAVI, impaired global myocardial performance assessed before intervention is an independent predictor of long-term survival. The TEI index provides incremental prognostic value beyond established parameters, highlighting myocardial dysfunction as an important determinant of outcomes beyond valvular obstruction.Overview of Study Design & ResultsRestricted Cubic Spline Analysis
title: Global myocardial performance and long-term mortality after TAVI: prognostic value of the TEI index

abstract: Abstract Background Left ventricular (LV) longitudinal function is a major prognostic determinant in aortic stenosis (AS) and is typically assessed using speckle-tracking echocardiography. Mitral annular plane systolic excursion (MAPSE) is a simple and widely available surrogate of longitudinal function; however, its prognostic value has not been prospectively validated. Purpose To evaluate the prognostic value of MAPSE in patients with moderate-to-severe AS. Methods We prospectively enrolled 203 patients with moderate (aortic valve area [AVA] 1.0–1.5 cm²) or severe AS (AVA &lt; 1.0 cm²) and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) &gt; 50%. MAPSE was calculated as the average of septal and lateral mitral annular excursion in the apical four-chamber view. Patients were stratified according to MAPSE (&lt; 1.18 cm vs. ≥ 1.18 cm) and LVEF (&lt; 60% vs. ≥ 60%), defining four systolic phenotypes: Group A (MAPSE ≥ 1.18 cm and LVEF ≥ 60%), Group B (MAPSE &lt; 1.18 cm and LVEF ≥ 60%), Group C (MAPSE ≥ 1.18 cm and LVEF &lt; 60%), and Group D (MAPSE &lt; 1.18 cm and LVEF &lt;60%).The primary endpoint was a composite of aortic valve replacement (AVR) or all-cause mortality. Results Mean age was 71.8 ± 10.7 years, and mean LVEF was 64.4 ± 6.9%. Median MAPSE was 1.30 cm (IQR 1.09–1.44), and severe AS was present in 61.6% of patients. During a median follow-up of 24.3 months (IQR 13.8–36.5), the primary endpoint occurred in 32.5% of patients, while all-cause mortality was 11.3%. MAPSE &lt; 1.18 cm was strongly associated with the primary endpoint (p &lt; 0.001; HR 3.0 [1.84-4.87] Fig. 1A), as was LVEF &lt; 60% (p &lt; 0.001; HR 2.67 [1.62-4.40] Fig. 1B).Regarding to systolic phenotype, Group D exhibited the worst event-free survival compared with all other phenotypes (p &lt; 0.001 vs. Group A; p = 0.008 vs. Group B; p = 0.007 vs. Group C; Fig. 1C). Compared to group A, group D has an HR of 5.78 (3.10-10.7). Notably, MAPSE &lt; 1.18 cm was significantly associated with all-cause mortality (Fig. 2A; p = 0.003; HR 3.27 [1.41-7.56]), whereas LVEF was not (Fig. 2B; p = 0.251; HR 1.69 [0.69-4.07]). MAPSE remained predictive of the primary endpoint across LVEF strata (p = 0.004 for LVEF ≥ 60%; HR 2.39 [1.29-4.43] and p = 0.008; HR 3.23[1.29-7.58] for LVEF &lt; 60%; Fig. 2C and 2D, respectively). Conclusion MAPSE is a robust and clinically meaningful prognostic marker in patients with moderate-to-severe AS, providing incremental risk stratification beyond LVEF. These findings highlight the importance of longitudinal LV function for risk stratification, independent of the assessment modality.
title: Longitudinal function in aortic stenosis: prognostic value of mitral plane systolic excursion.

abstract: Abstract Objective Accurate assessment of mitral valve leaflet morphology is essential for patient selection and procedural planning in transcatheter mitral valve interventions. While transoesophageal echocardiography (TEE) and cardiac computed tomography (CT) are routinely performed prior to transcatheter mitral valve replacement, TEE remains the primary imaging modality for screening patients considered for transcatheter mitral edge-to-edge repair (TEER). As adequate leaflet length is critical for procedural success, potential systematic discrepancies between imaging modalities warrant further investigation. Methods Patients referred for comprehensive imaging prior to transcatheter mitral valve replacement using the Tendyne™ valve were screened for inclusion. All patients underwent both TEE and full-cycle cardiac CT as part of the standardized Tendyne™ screening protocol. The anterior (AML) and posterior (PML) mitral leaflets were measured in predefined anatomical segments (A1–A3, P1–P3). Corresponding segmental measurements obtained by TEE and CT were compared using paired t-tests. For each segment, mean differences (bias), standard deviations, and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated to assess inter-modality agreement. Results Thirty patients (16 women; mean age 75y) were analyzed. Mean PML lengths in segments P1, P2, and P3 were 11 mm, 13 mm, and 11 mm by TEE versus 12 mm, 13 mm, and 12 mm by CT. Mean AML lengths in segments A1, A2, and A3 were 24 mm, 27 mm, and 23 mm by TEE versus 25 mm, 28 mm, and 24 mm by CT (p &lt; 0.05). Across all segments, leaflet lengths measured by TEE were consistently shorter than those derived from CT. The overall bias was 0.9 mm for AML and 0.6 mm for PML (TEE &lt; CT; p &lt; 0.05). Statistically significant differences were observed in four segments (A1, A2, P1, and P3; p &lt; 0.05 for each). Conclusions Although segmental mitral leaflet measurements obtained by TEE and CT demonstrate strong correlation, TEE systematically underestimates leaflet length compared with CT. These findings may be clinically relevant in borderline cases where leaflet length is critical for TEER planning and patient eligibility assessment. CT may provide complementary anatomical information to support procedural decision-making.
title: Comparison of segmental mitral leaflet length assessment by TEE and cardiac CT in patients undergoing transcatheter mitral valve evaluation

abstract: Abstract Background Cardiogenic shock (CS) is a heterogeneous condition with high mortality, and valvular heart disease (VHD) represents an important underlying cause. Although valvular intervention has been proposed for patients with CS and severe VHD, its prognostic benefit remains uncertain, and long-term outcome data are scarce. Purpose This study aimed to evaluate the impact of severe VHD on long-term mortality in CS and to identify predictors of long-term mortality, including the effect of valvular intervention in patients with CS and severe VHD. Methods Consecutive patients admitted to our institute with acute myocardial infarction or acute decompensated heart failure between January 2015 and December 2024 were retrospectively identified. Patients requiring vasopressors and/or mechanical circulatory support during hospitalization were defined as having CS and included. Time-dependent covariate analysis was performed to address immortal time bias related to valvular intervention among patients with CS and severe VHD. Results A total of 530 patients with CS were included in the analysis, of whom 94 (17.7%) had severe VHD. The median age was 77 years (interquartile range [IQR], 68–83), and 36.6% were female. At CS onset, 64.9% of patients were classified as SCAI stage C, 24.7% as stage D, and 10.4% as stage E. During a median follow-up of 395.6 days (IQR, 32.4–1191) from CS onset, 202 deaths (38.1%) occurred. Multivariable Cox regression analysis showed that severe VHD was an independent predictor of long-term mortality (Figure 1). Among patients with CS and severe VHD, severe mitral regurgitation was observed in 48 patients (51.1%) and severe aortic stenosis in 24 patients (25.5%). Overall, 28 patients (29.8%) underwent valvular intervention, including 14 surgical procedures (50.0%), 10 transcatheter aortic valve replacements (35.7%), and 4 transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repairs (14.3%). The median time from shock onset to valvular intervention was 17.4 days (IQR, 8.0–35.9). During a median follow-up period of 181.9 days (IQR, 21.28–2333) from the onset of CS, 51 deaths (54.3%) occurred. Multivariable Cox regression analysis identified older age, prior heart failure hospitalization, and higher serum creatinine as independent predictors of long-term mortality (Figure 2). In time-dependent Cox regression analyses, valvular intervention was not independently associated with long-term mortality after adjustment for hemodynamic severity or renal dysfunction (hazard ratio 0.46; 95% confidence interval 0.18–1.14; p=0.09). Conclusions Severe VHD independently predicted long-term mortality in patients with CS. Long-term outcomes were driven more by patient characteristics and organ dysfunction than by valvular intervention. Therefore, valvular intervention should be considered by a heart team based on individual patient characteristics.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Long-term outcomes and predictors of mortality in patients with cardiogenic shock and severe valvular heart disease

abstract: Abstract Introduction Patient selection for aortic valve replacement (AVR) in paradoxical LFLGAS (PLFLGAS) requires verification of aortic stenosis (AS) severity and symptoms attributable to the valvular lesion. Routine hemodynamic parameters (peak velocity, MG, and AVA) acquired during resting transthoracic echocardiograms (TTE) are unable to discriminate between pseudo-severe and true severe AS. Multislice computed tomography aortic valve calcium scoring (AVCS) is recommended as the adjudicator. However, current AVCS diagnostic thresholds were principally defined in cohorts of concordant AS, then extrapolated to PLFLGAS with limited validation, and may underestimate severity where valvular fibrosis predominates. The MG:AVA ratio of &gt;=25mmHg/cm2 has been demonstrated to correctly identify true severe AS in classical LFLGAS and was independently associated with increased risk of mortality or AVR. The role of MG:AVA in PLFLGAS has not been assessed. Purpose To determine the prognostic utility of MG:AVA as a surrogate marker for hemodynamically significant stenosis in PLFLGAS. Methods Patients with TTE findings of PLFLGAS (defined by AVA&lt;1.0cm2 or indexed AVA&lt;0.6cm2/m2, peak velocity&lt;4.0m/s, MG&lt;40mmHg, indexed stroke volume =&lt;35ml/m2, and left ventricular ejection fraction&gt;=50%) were identified from the echocardiography laboratory databases within our health service. Included patients were grouped according to a MG:AVA of &lt;25mmHg/cm2 and &gt;=25mmHg/cm2. Outcome data was obtained from the statewide cardiac registry. Primary outcomes were the composite of cardiac mortality or AVR at 3 and 5 years. Results 171 PLFLGAS patients (median age 77.0 years [Interquartile range (IQR): 69.0-82.0 years]; 56.7% female) were included in the study with 48 (28%) in the MG:AVA&lt;25mmHg/cm2 and 123 (72%) in the MG:AVA&gt;=25mmHg/cm2groups. Median follow-up was 8.9 years [IQR: 6.2-11.2 years] with 105 (61.4%) patients meeting the composite endpoint of cardiac mortality or AVR. Freedom from the primary outcome at 3 and 5 years was significantly higher in those with a MG:AVA&lt;25mmHg/cm2 (3 years: 88%, 95% confidence interval (CI): 79-97%; 5 years: 79%, 95% CI: 68-91%) in comparison to MG:AVA&gt;=25mmHg/cm2 patients (3 years: 50%, 95% CI: 42-60%; 5 years: 36%; 95% CI: 29-46%). On multivariable Cox proportional regression analysis, MG:AVA&gt;=25mmHg/cm2 independently predicted the composite endpoint at both 3 (Hazard ratio (HR):5.25, 95% CI:1.94-15.7; P=0.001) and 5 (HR:4.25, 95% CI:1.79-10.1; P=0.001) years. Conclusion MG:AVA ratio is a simple hemodynamic parameter that has prognostic value in undifferentiated PLFLGAS patients. MG:AVA&gt;=25mmHg/cm2 predicts a poorer outcome or need for AVR, implying prognostically significant AS, and may help guide decision-making for aortic valve intervention in PLFLGAS.
title: Prognostic value of mean gradient to aortic valve area ratio (MG:AVA) in paradoxical low-flow low-gradient aortic stenosis (LFLGAS)

abstract: Abstract Background Heart failure (HF) frequently occurs after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) for severe aortic stenosis (AS), even following an apparently successful procedure. Although angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) therapy improves outcomes in selected HF populations, its effects on cardiac function after TAVI remain unclear. Purpose To evaluate whether the addition of ARNI to conventional medical therapy improves echocardiographic parameters after TAVI. Methods This exploratory echocardiographic substudy was conducted within a prospective, single-center, open-label, randomized, parallel-group trial. Patients undergoing TAVI were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either conventional therapy alone (control group) or conventional therapy plus ARNI (ARNI group). In the ARNI group, medication was initiated on postoperative day 1 or 2, uptitrated as tolerated, and continued for at least the 6 months. Transthoracic echocardiography was performed at baseline and at 6 months after TAVI. Between-group differences in 6-month left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), LV mass index (LVMi), tricuspid regurgitation pressure gradient (TRPG), left atrial volume index (LAVi), and the ratio of early mitral inflow velocity to early diastolic mitral annular velocity (E/e') were assessed using analysis of covariance adjusted for the corresponding baseline value. Results A total of 77 patients were analyzed (control, n=39; ARNI, n=38). After adjustment for baseline TRPG, TRPG at 6 months was significantly lower in the ARNI group than in the control group (adjusted difference [ARNI minus control], -4.30 mmHg; 95% CI -7.83 to -0.82; p=0.017). Baseline-adjusted 6-month values of LVEF, LAVi, LVMi, and E/e' did not differ significantly between the 2 groups (Figure). Conclusions In this exploratory echocardiographic substudy, early initiation of ARNI after TAVI was associated with reduction in TRPG at 6 months after adjustment for baseline TRPG, whereas other echocardiographic indices did not show clear between-group differences.Figure
title: Echocardiographic effects of an angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor after transcatheter aortic valve implantation: a substudy of a randomized trial

abstract: Abstract Background Multivalvular heart disease (MVD) is frequently encountered in clinical practice, yet prognostic stratification remains largely based on individual valve severity rather than valve combinations. Whether distinct multivalvular phenotypes confer differential mortality risk remains unclear. Purpose To examine the phenotypes of different multivalvular diseases and their prognostic significance in relation to mortality. Methods We conducted a multicenter retrospective cohort study including 1,797 hospitalized patients with ≥2 clinically significant valvular lesions identified on echocardiography. Significant stenosis was defined as grade ≥3 (0-5 scale) and significant regurgitation as grade ≥4 (0-6 scale). Patients were categorized into seven prespecified multivalvular phenotypes based on valve combinations: mitral regurgitation (MR) and tricuspid regurgitation (TR), aortic regurgitation (AR) and MR, aortic stenosis (AS) and MR, AR and AR, AS and TR, AR, MR, and TR (3-valve disease) and AS, MR, and TR (3-valve disease). Long-term all-cause mortality was assessed using Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with log-rank testing. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models with multiple imputation were constructed to evaluate independent associations, adjusting for age, sex, heart failure, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, atrial fibrillation, arterial hypertension, coronary artery disease, acute decompensated heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, left ventricular ejection fraction, hemoglobin, and serum creatinine. Results MR-TR was the dominant phenotype (59.5%). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated significant survival differences across phenotypes (log-rank p&lt;0.0001) (Figure). The AR-MR phenotype exhibited the most favorable long-term survival, whereas AS-MR-TR showed the worst prognosis with early and sustained survival separation. In multivariable analysis, AS-MR-TR was independently associated with increased mortality (HR 1.61, 95% CI 1.26-2.06, p=0.00017), as was AS-TR (HR 1.31, 95% CI 1.00-1.70, p=0.048). Independent predictors of mortality included older age, CKD (HR 1.32, p=0.0076), lower LVEF (p&lt;0.001), lower hemoglobin (p&lt;0.001), and higher creatinine (p=0.042). Conclusions Multivalvular heart disease is prognostically heterogeneous. Valve combination, rather than valve count alone, defines distinct risk phenotypes. Triple-valve disease, including aortic stenosis, identifies a particularly high-risk structural substrate associated with excess mortality. Phenotype-based stratification may improve clinical risk assessment in multivalvular disease.Kaplan-Meier curves for MVD Phenotype
title: Clinical phenotypes and survival in multivalvular heart disease: differential prognostic impact of valve combinations

abstract: Abstract Background Comprehensive assessment of right ventricular (RV) function is pivotal in patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) undergoing tricuspid transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER). However, conventional echocardiographic parameters, including three-dimensional echocardiography (3DE) and speckle-tracking-derived markers, are inherently load-dependent and may not adequately reflect RV contractile reserve, particularly under the markedly altered loading conditions associated with severe TR and following T-TEER. Pressure-strain-volume (PSV) loop-derived myocardial work integrates preload, afterload, and chamber geometry within a unified hemodynamic framework and, therefore, may better reflect load-independent indices of RV contractility. Aims Accordingly, we aimed to determine whether RV PSV loop–derived myocardial work correlates with pressure-volume (PV) loop indices of contractility, and to assess acute changes in RV mechanics in patients undergoing T-TEER. Methods In 50 patients undergoing T-TEER, RV pressure waveforms were acquired intraprocedurally, immediately before and after device implantation, with simultaneous 3DE for RV volumes, to generate RV PV loops and to derive end-systolic elastance (Ees). Conventional echocardiographic metrics, such as tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) and ejection fraction (EF), were also obtained. Then, to obtain RV pressure-strain (PS) loops and global myocardial constructive work (GCW), RV pressure and 3DE-derived RV longitudinal strain tracings were combined. We further adjusted GCW to instantaneous RV volumes (GCWv) and constructed PSV loops. (Figure) Results Among the 50 patients with severe TR, T-TEER resulted in significantly lower RV volumes (end-diastolic volume from 183±59 to 143±51 mL, p&lt;0.001), RV EF (from 48±10 to 36±10%, p&lt;0.001, and TAPSE (from 18±4 to 16±5 mm, p=0.002). Conversely, RV contractility derived from PV loop analysis significantly increased after the procedure (Ees: from 0.38 [0.29-0.47] to 0.46 [0.36-0.55] mmHg/mL, p=0.008). While PS loop-derived GCW (from 615 [439-881] to 549 [394-756] mmHg%, p=0.007) showed significantly lower values after T-TEER, values of PSV loop-derived volume-adjusted GCWv (from 180 [106-275] to 180 [92-256] mmHg%/mL, p=0.295) remained similar after the procedure. Importantly, although TAPSE (r=0.21, p=0.049), RVEF (r=0.29, p=0.004), and GCW (r=0.37, p&lt;0.001) correlated modestly with Ees, volume-adjusted GCWv (r=0.62, p&lt;0.001) showed a stronger correlation with RV contractility. Conclusions In the setting of acute RV unloading following successful T-TEER, pressure-volume loop-derived Ees demonstrated improved contractility. Using our novel PSV loop approach, volume-adjusted global constructive work showed a stronger association with contractility and more accurately captured intrinsic RV mechanics than conventional, load-dependent echocardiographic indices.Figure
title: Right ventricular pressure–strain–volume loop–derived myocardial work as a marker of contractility before and after transcatheter tricuspid valve intervention

abstract: Abstract Background Although relative apical sparing (RAS) and apical sparing pattern of left ventricular (LV) longitudinal strain is a commonly used echocardiographic marker for diagnosing cardiac amyloidosis (CA), its diagnostic performance is limited in patients with aortic stenosis. In contrast, CA is also characterized by right ventricular dysfunction, including impaired right ventricular free wall strain (RVFWS). Purpose We investigated whether RVFWS provides superior diagnostic value for CA compared with RAS and other echocardiographic parameters in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Methods This single-center retrospective study included 274 consecutive patients who underwent TAVI between 2022 and 2025. After excluding 7 patients who underwent valve in valve, 43 patients who did not undergo endomyocardial biopsy (due to unstable hemodynamics, intracardiac device implantation, left bundle branch block, or physician’s decision) and 7 with inadequate echocardiographic images, 217 patients were included in the final analysis. All patients underwent echocardiography and endomyocardial biopsy before TAVI. RVFWS (Figure 1), LV RAS, and the Increased Wall Thickness (IWT) score, which has been reported to be useful for the diagnosis of CA in patients with increased LV wall thickness, were compared using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis for the diagnosis of CA. Results The mean age was 84 ± 5 years, and CA was diagnosed in 19 patients (8.8%). Compared with non-CA patients, those with CA had higher LV RAS (0.89 ± 0.22 vs 0.77 ± 0.23, p = 0.027) and significantly lower tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (17.5 ± 3.2 mm vs 19.9 ± 4.0 mm, p = 0.010), right ventricular fractional area change (37.7 ± 6.3% vs 44.0 ± 4.7%, p &lt; 0.001), and RVFWS (17.3 ± 3.7% vs. 21.6 ± 3.0%, p &lt; 0.001). On ROC analysis, RVFWS demonstrated a significantly higher area under the curve (AUC) for the diagnosis of CA compared with LV RAS and the IWT score (AUC 0.81 [95% CI 0.68–0.90] vs. 0.66 [0.52–0.78], p = 0.038; and AUC 0.81 [0.68–0.90] vs. 0.61 [0.49–0.72], p = 0.011, respectively) (Figure 2). Conclusions In patients undergoing TAVI, RVFWS may provide superior diagnostic accuracy for CA compared with LV RAS and the IWT score.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Diagnostic utility of right ventricular free wall strain for cardiac amyloidosis in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation

abstract: Abstract Background Contemporary matrix-array transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE) probes technically allow full 360° multiplane rotation; however, clinical imaging remains restricted to the conventional 0–180° range. This limitation may impair procedural efficiency during transseptal puncture (TSP) in mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER). Purpose To assess the frequency of mirrored four-chamber (4Ch) imaging (&gt;140°) during TSP in M-TEER and its association with procedural timing. A secondary objective was to evaluate the feasibility of unrestricted 360° multiplane imaging in a simulation environment. Methods We performed a retrospective analysis of 211 consecutive patients undergoing M-TEER. TOE recordings were reviewed to identify cases requiring mirrored 4Ch imaging during TSP. TSP time was defined as the interval from right atrial instrumentation to septal puncture. Additionally, a TOE simulator was modified to allow unrestricted 360° multiplane rotation, enabling negative-angle imaging (&lt;0°). Results Mirrored 4Ch imaging was required in 30 cases (14.2%). Median TSP time was 394 [291–560] seconds. Procedures requiring mirrored imaging were associated with significantly longer TSP duration compared with standard imaging (502 [326–745] vs. 383 [280–514] seconds; p = 0.039). Unrestricted 360° multiplane rotation was technically feasible in a simulator, enabling acquisition of mirrored and negative-angle views. Conclusion Mirrored 4Ch imaging during TSP is a frequent and clinically relevant phenomenon associated with prolonged transseptal access in M-TEER. Enabling optional unrestricted 360° multiplane rotation may facilitate more efficient transseptal guidance during structural heart interventions.
title: Unlocking 360° multiplane transoesophageal echocardiography for transseptal puncture guidance in mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair

abstract: Abstract Background Systemic follow-up after percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) with transoesophageal echocardiography (TEE) or cardiac computed tomography (CT) is mandatory to exclude device-related thrombosis or peri-device leaks. However, repeated CT scans entail cumulative radiation exposure, and conventional TEE requires sedation, with potential associated risks. TEE using a smaller probe performed under topical oropharyngeal analgesia could help to reduce procedure-related discomfort while preserving diagnostic accuracy. To our knowledge, this is the first study analysing the feasibility of this point of care focused TEE. Purpose Our objective was to evaluate the feasibility of using mini-probe TEE to detect device-related thrombosis or peri-device leaks after percutaneous left atrial appendage closure, and patient comfort during the mini-probe TEE without sedation. Methods We conducted a prospective, single-centre, observational study. Consecutive patients undergoing TEE for the detection of device-related thrombosis or peri-device leaks after percutaneous left atrial appendage closure were included. Mini-probe TEE with 3D capabilities (9VT, General Electric) was proposed as the first-line approach and patients undergoing conventional TEE due to the unavailability of the mini-probe during the same period of time were included as a comparison group. For left atrial appendage closure, both disc-based and plug-based devices were used. Results A total of 58 patients were included (50 in the mini-probe TEE group and 8 in the conventional TEE group). Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups and are presented in table 1. Mini-probe TEE was successfully performed in 98% of cases, with no need for venous access or intravenous medication (table 1 and 2). In the remaining case, mini-probe insertion was unsuccessful, and the procedure was converted to conventional TEE and completed uneventfully. No complications associated with the use of the mini probe were observed and overall patient satisfaction was very high. More than 90% of patients reported no or only mild discomfort, with no cases of severe anxiety or pain. Significant reductions in total procedure time (17.5 vs 48 min, p&lt;0.001), image acquisition time (3 vs 10 min, p&lt;0.001), preparation and recovery time (13 vs 39.5 min, p&lt;0.001) were observed. Image quality with the mini-probe was rated as good in 96% of cases and acceptable in the remaining cases. Device-related thrombosis was observed in 2 patients and significant peri-device leak in another 2, all in the mini-probe TEE group (p=NS). Conclusions Point of care TEE using a mini-probe under topical analgesia is a feasible and safe alternative to conventional TEE for follow-up after percutaneous left atrial appendage closure, enabling reliable detection of device-related thrombosis and peri-device leaks while reducing recovery time and overall procedural duration with good patient tolerance.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Point of care transesophageal echocardiography for thrombus surveillance after left atrial appendage occlusion: feasibility study

abstract: Abstract Background Left ventricular (LV) thrombus remains a clinically important complication following anterior acute myocardial infarction (AMI), associated with embolic risk and exposure to prolonged anticoagulation. Current risk stratification relies predominantly on left ventricular ejection fraction (EF), yet EF lacks specificity: many patients with reduced EF do not develop thrombus, while others with relatively preserved EF do. Given the bleeding risks associated with anticoagulation alongside potent dual anti-platelets, identification of patients truly at risk is required. Apical rotation (twist), reflecting the heart’s systolic wringing motion, may provide a mechanistic marker of regional stasis predisposing to thrombus formation. Purpose To determine whether apical rotation (twist) assessed by speckle tracking echocardiography predicts LV thrombus formation following AMI. Methods In a prospective registry of 200 patients with anterior AMI, apical twist (degrees) was quantified using speckle tracking echocardiography. Baseline imaging was performed prior to hospital discharge. Follow-up imaging (CMR or TTE) was conducted at a median of 1.5 months to assess for thrombus presence. Patients were categorised into two groups: those who developed LV thrombus (34.5%) and those without thrombus (65.5%). Results The baseline characteristics and echocardiographic parameters were comparable between groups. Peak apical twist was significantly lower in patients who developed thrombus [6.0° (IQR 3.4-8.1°)] compared to those who did not [10.5° (IQR 7.1-14.3°)], p&lt;0.001. Representing a marked blunting of apical rotation throughout systole. Univariate analysis confirmed an association between decreased apical twist and thrombus formation [OR 1.28, 95% Cl 1.17-1.39, p&lt;0.001]. After adjusting for EF, global longitudinal strain and LV end diastolic volume, apical twist remained an independent predictor of LV thrombus [OR 1.22, 95% Cl 1.11-1.34, p&lt;0.001]. ROC analysis identified an optimal twist cut-off of 8.6° for predicting thrombus development, with an AUC of 0.79. Conclusion In patients with anterior AMI, apical twist is an independent predictor of LV thrombus and provides better discrimination than conventional systolic indices. Integrating apical mechanical assessment into clinical workflows offers a targeted based approach to post-AMI surveillance and anticoagulation strategies. Large-scale validation is required to establish apical twist as a practical tool for LV thrombus risk stratification.Figure:Apical twist and LV thrombus
title: Apical mechanical dysfunction independently predicts left ventricular thrombus formation after anterior myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Sodium glucose Cotransporter-2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) have been recently administered efficiently in the acute phase of Acute Myocardial Infarctions (AMI) in patients without diabetes or heart failure. Purpose We aimed to address the effects of dapagliflozin in arterial wall elastic properties, thickness of endothelial glycocalyx and myocardial performance in STEMI participants. Methods We included participants hospitalized in the Cardiology Unit for STEMI without diabetes or heart failure. Patients were commenced on 10 mg dapagliflozin as an add-on to the standard of care treatment upon discharge for the index event. We also entailed a control group of STEMI patients with similar age, sex and risk factors by propensity score matching (1:1 ratio) who received standard of care treatment. We measured at enrollment and at 3 months: a) perfused boundary region (PBR) of the sublingual microvessels with a lumen diameter ranging from 4 to 25 μm, as a marker of endothelial glycocalyx integrity (Sideview Darkfield Imaging); higer PBR values reflect reduced thickness of endothelial glycocalyx layer b) carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (PWV- Complior SP ALAM), c) systolic blood pressure (SBP) and d) Left Ventricular Global Longitudinal Strain (LV GLS) and by echocardiography, as indicators of myocardial performance. Results We totally assigned (n=80) participants , aged 56±9 years, 61/80 (76.25%) were males, of which (n=40) received dapagliflozin and (n=40) served as controls. 32/80 (40%) were smokers, 28/80 (35%) had hyperlipidemia and 40/80 (50%) hypertension. The baseline PBR4-25 , PWV, SBP , LV GLS and LVEF did not differ between the two groups (p&gt;0.05). At 3-month follow-up assessment participants in the dapagliflozin arm displayed a greater improvement of PBR4-25, PWV and LVGLS compared to the control group (for PBR4-25: -8.40% vs 7.92% respectively, p=0.010; for PWV: -6.10% vs 12.30% respectively, p=0.004; for LV GLS: 9.90% vs -1.85% respectively, p=0.006) (Table). The percentage change of PWV was associated the percentage change of LV GLS (r=-0.581, p=0.001). No significant differences were observed in the change of SBP and LV EF between the two groups (p&gt;0.05). Conclusion STEMI patients without diabetes treated with dapagliflozin for 3 months show marked improvement of arterial stiffness, endothelial glycocalyx integrity and myocardial performance.Table
title: Dapagliflozin ameliorates arterial stiffness, endothelial glycocaclyx and myocardial performance in non-diabetic STEMI patients: a 3-month follow-up study

abstract: Abstract Background Left ventricular remodelling is a central mechanism driving disease progression and adverse outcomes in patients with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction. The extent to which coronary revascularisation promotes reverse remodelling beyond optimal medical therapy in routine clinical practice remains uncertain. Purpose To evaluate the impact of coronary revascularisation on left ventricular remodelling and functional recovery in patients with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and reduced ejection fraction. Methods This retrospective cohort study included 561 patients with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and left ventricular ejection fraction &lt;40% treated between 2014 and 2024. Patients were managed with percutaneous coronary intervention plus optimal medical therapy (PCI+OMT, n=281) or optimal medical therapy alone (OMT, n=280) according to clinical decision-making. Transthoracic echocardiography was performed at baseline and during follow-up using standardised protocols. Changes in left ventricular ejection fraction, left ventricular end-diastolic volume and functional mitral regurgitation were assessed. Reverse remodelling was defined as a reduction in left ventricular end-diastolic volume &gt;10%. Follow-up duration was 24 months.
