Results At 24 months, improvement in left ventricular systolic function was significantly greater in the PCI+OMT group compared with OMT alone (increase in ejection fraction +7.2±3.1 vs +1.9±2.8 percentage points; p&lt;0.001). A greater reduction in left ventricular end-diastolic volume was observed after PCI+OMT (−18±10 mL vs −5±12 mL; p=0.01), with reverse remodelling occurring more frequently (46.3% vs 25.0%; p&lt;0.001). The prevalence of functional mitral regurgitation ≥ grade II decreased markedly in the PCI+OMT group (from 62% to 24%) compared with OMT alone (from 28% to 21%; p&lt;0.001). Conclusion In this real-world cohort of patients with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and reduced ejection fraction, coronary revascularisation in addition to optimal medical therapy was associated with significant reverse left ventricular remodelling, improved systolic function and reduction of functional mitral regurgitation at 24 months. These findings support an individualised approach to coronary revascularisation aimed at promoting structural and functional recovery of the left ventricle.
title: Impact of coronary revascularisation on left ventricular remodelling in ischaemic cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction

abstract: Abstract Background & Objective Diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) is defined as myocardial remodeling and/or dysfunction attributable to diabetes in the absence of coronary artery disease, hypertension, or valvular disease, and it is a major cause of death in people with diabetes [1–3]. Its pathogenesis remains incompletely understood, and no disease-specific therapy is currently available. In recent years, excessive activation of the sympathetic nervous system has been shown to promote myocardial apoptosis, inflammation, and fibrosis, playing a critical role in the progression of DCM. Renal denervation (RDN), an emerging interventional therapy, has demonstrated certain efficacy in the treatment of hypertension and may exert protective effects against DCM by reducing sympathetic nervous activity. Nevertheless, its underlying mechanisms require further elucidation. This study aims to elucidate the molecular basis by which RDN improves cardiac structure and function in DCM through integrated multi-omics analysis and to identify key signaling pathways and potential therapeutic targets. Methodologies Eight-week-old male C57BL/6J mice were divided into control (CT), diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM), and renal sympathetic denervation (RDN) groups. Diabetes was induced by high-fat diet and STZ, followed by bilateral chemical RDN in the treatment group. After 22 weeks, assessments included glucose metabolism, cardiac function (echocardiography, exercise testing), and histological, ultrastructural, and molecular analyses. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic profiling of left ventricular tissue was performed to identify key targets and pathways. Result RDN partially improved glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity, and significantly enhanced cardiac function (increased LVEF, LVFS; reduced LVDd, LVDs, NT-proBNP; improved E/A ratio and exercise capacity). It alleviated cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, mitochondrial damage, and reduced IL-6 and IL-1β levels. Multi-omics revealed RDN-regulated changes enriched in pathways linked to MHC class I antigen presentation, T-cell activation, and DNA damage response, indicating suppressed immune activation and extracellular matrix remodeling. Conclusion RDN significantly improved cardiac function in DCM mice and reduced myocardial hypertrophy and fibrosis. These changes were accompanied by downregulation of inflammatory and immune pathways, suggesting a cardioprotective mechanism involving suppression of MHC-I/T cell–mediated autoimmunity and extracellular matrix remodeling.Graphical abstract
title: Integrated multi-omics analysis reveals the molecular mechanisms of renal denervation in alleviating diabetic cardiomyopathy

abstract: Abstract Background Prognostically important comorbidities such as diabetes, hypertension, and coronary disease are uncommon in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) secondary to chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy, yet these patients have worse outcomes, including worse survival, compared with other HF etiologies.1 N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is a well validated marker of myocardial wall stress and a strong predictor of morbidity and mortality in patients with HFrEF, while cardiac troponins, reflecting ongoing myocardial injury, are also independently associated with worse outcomes.2-4 The underlying mechanisms behind these findings have not been clearly delineated.4 Prior studies have demonstrated that reductions in NT-proBNP levels, particularly achieving concentrations below 1000 pg/mL, are associated with significantly improved clinical outcomes.5 Purpose To evaluate the effects of sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril on serial changes in NT-proBNP and high-sensitivity troponin T(hsTnT) concentrations in a subset of patients with HFrEF due to Chagas disease enrolled in the PARACHUTE-HF trial. Methods PARACHUTE-HF was a multicenter, randomized, open-label with blinded endpoint adjudication trial enrolling patients with chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy, left ventricle ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤40%, and elevated natriuretic peptides. Patients were randomized to sacubitril/valsartan or enalapril in addition to standard heart failure therapy. NT-proBNP was measured centrally at baseline, Week 12, and Month 8. hsTnT was measured at baseline and Month 8. Due to marked right skewness, NT-proBNP and hsTnT levels were logarithmically transformed before analysis, with results expressed as geometric mean ratios. Results Patients assigned to sacubitril/valsartan had a significantly greater reduction in NT-proBNP compared with enalapril at Week 12 (mean ratio 0.68; 95% CI 0.62-0.75), and this effect was sustained at Month 8 (0.76; 95% CI 0.66-0.88). The proportion of patients achieving NT-proBNP &lt;1000 pg/mL at Week 12 was higher with sacubitril/valsartan (41.3%) versus enalapril (34.5%), chi-square p=0.045. For hsTnT, there was no significant difference between study groups at month 8 (mean ratio 0.96; 95% CI 0.89–1.04). Conclusion In patients with HFrEF due to Chagas disease, sacubitril/valsartan led to a greater and sustained reduction in NT-proBNP compared with enalapril. A decrease in NT-proBNP likely reflects reduced cardiac filling pressures and myocardial wall stress, consistent with favorable hemodynamic effects of sacubitril/valsartan.
title: Effects of sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril on NT-proBNP and hs-troponin T in patients with heart failure due to Chagas disease: insights from the PARACHUTE-HF trial

abstract: Abstract Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) is a metabolically active depot located between the myocardium and pericardium. Under physiological conditions, EAT acts as a local buffer, absorbing excess circulating free fatty acids (FFAs) and protecting the myocardium from lipotoxic stress. In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), we hypothesize that EAT undergoes inflammatory remodeling that impairs this protective function. We analyzed EAT volume, density, histology, and radiomic features in HFrEF patients and healthy controls. Although EAT volume did not differ between groups, HFrEF patients showed increased CT density and reduced average adipocyte size in the innermost 2.5 mm layer adjacent to the left ventricle. Radiomic analysis revealed greater tissue heterogeneity in HFrEF, paralleled by a broader adipocyte size distribution- including both numerous small and abnormally large adipocytes-features absent in healthy EAT. These findings suggest a pro-inflammatory shift, with smaller adipocytes potentially reflecting diminished lipid storage capacity. As previously reported, NEFA levels were elevated in HFrEF, likely due to neurohormonal-driven lipolysis. EAT remodeling may further impair local buffering, increasing myocardial lipotoxic stress. Myocardial triglyceride (TAG) levels were not significantly increased in HFrEF. Interestingly, patients with denser EAT (≥ –80.5 HU) had lower myocardial TAG concentrations, suggesting that reduced adipocyte storage capacity may increase FFA flux into the myocardium and promote formation of bioactive, potentially toxic lipids. Our preliminary lipidomic data demonstrate a shift in lipid distribution, with increased accumulation of sphingomyelins and bioactive ceramides in the myocardium, lipid intermediates associated with apoptosis, inflammation, and mitochondrial dysfunction. These findings demonstrate that impaired EAT buffering may not lead to TAG overload within the myocardium but instead favor accumulation of bioactive, toxic lipids. Ongoing work includes expanded lipidomic profiling and assessment of mitochondrial function. Collectively, our findings suggest that in HFrEF, EAT loses its protective buffering role, contributing to myocardial injury through altered myocardial lipid handling.
title: Epicardial fat remodeling in HFrEF: loss of buffering capacity and lipotoxic risk

abstract: Abstract Introduction Heart failure (HF) with improved ejection fraction (HFimpEF) was recently defined as a distinct clinical phenotype within the HF spectrum. Despite increasing recognition, its prognostic determinants remain incompletely characterized. Right ventricular (RV) to pulmonary artery (PA) coupling is acknowledged as an important hemodynamic parameter quantifying the interaction between RV contractile performance and RV afterload. A practical, non-invasive indirect marker of RV-PA coupling is the echocardiographic ratio of the tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) to pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP). Purpose Our study aimed to assess the prognostic role of TAPSE/PASP alongside other biomarkers for left ventricular EF (LVEF) improvement after hospitalization for HF with reduced EF (HFrEF). Methods This is a retrospective cohort study including HFrEF patients previously hospitalized for HF and subsequently reevaluated between January 2024 - December 2025, with either improved or persistently reduced EF. HFimpEF was defined as baseline LVEF ≤40%, improved to &gt;40%, with a ≥10% increase. Results We included 202 HFrEF patients (mean age 68.76±10.57 years; 68.81% male); 32.67% developed HFimpEF. Rhythm control via atrial fibrillation cardioversion was a direct predictor of LVEF recovery (OR 9.28, p&lt;0.001). History of acute coronary syndrome (OR 0.25, p&lt;0.001), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (OR 0.14, p&lt;0.001), obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome (OSAS) (OR 0.20, p=0.005), peripheral arterial disease (OR 0.42, p=0.03) were inversely correlated with HFimpEF. Lower NYHA class (AUC 0.75, p&lt;0.001), PASP (AUC 0.79, cut-off ≤36mmHg, p&lt;0.001), NT-proBNP (AUC 0.66, p&lt;0.001) and higher LVEF at baseline (AUC 0.60, p=0.016), TAPSE (AUC 0.79, cut-off&gt;18mm, p&lt;0.001), and TAPSE/PASP (AUC 0.84, cut-off &gt;0.45, p&lt;0.001) were correlated with HFimpEF. The independent parameters associated with HFimpEF in multivariable analysis were used to build the baseline prediction model: successful cardioversion (HR 10.02, p&lt;0.001), NYHA class (HR 0.31, p&lt;0.001), COPD (HR 0.25, p=0.017), and OSAS (HR 0.11, p=0.024). When added to the model, TAPSE/PASP &gt;0.45mm/mmHg (HR 5.97, p&lt;0.001) outperformed and replaced TAPSE &gt;18mm (HR 2.88, p=0.018) and PASP ≤36mmHg (HR 3.46, p=0.06) as individual markers (Figure 1). The prediction model containing TAPSE/PASP &gt;0.45mm/mmHg, successful cardioversion, NYHA class, COPD and OSAS had the best association with HFimpEF in ROC analysis, outperforming all the significant individual variables (Figure 2). Conclusions RV-PA coupling, quantified in our cohort by a TAPSE/PASP &gt;0.45mm/mmHg, was an independent predictor of LVEF improvement in HFrEF patients. It outperformed individual assessments of PASP and TAPSE and improved the risk stratification model containing successful cardioversion, NYHA class, COPD, and OSAS as independent predictors of HFimpEF.Incremental predictive valueROC curves
title: Right ventricular to pulmonary artery coupling: an independent marker in a prediction model for heart failure with improved ejection fraction

abstract: Abstract Background In aortic stenosis (AS), left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) alone may not capture myocardial impairment, as some patients show heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)-like physiology. However, the prevalence and prognostic impact of this phenotype after aortic valve replacement remain unclear. Purpose This study aimed to classify patients undergoing surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) or transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) into three phenotypes by integrating LVEF with the HFA-PEFF score and to examine the prognostic implications of these phenotypes. Methods This multicentre registry included 2,811 consecutive patients who underwent SAVR or TAVR for severe AS from January 2016 through December 2021 at eight centres in Japan. After excluding 780 patients with ≥ moderate aortic regurgitation, ≥ moderate mitral regurgitation, ≥ moderate tricuspid regurgitation, or ≥ moderate mitral stenosis, and 292 patients with unavailable HFA-PEFF scores, 1739 patients (SAVR, n = 542; TAVR, n = 1197) with severe pure AS were included. Heart failure phenotypes were defined as follows: (1) non-HFpEF (LVEF ≥50% and HFA-PEFF score &lt;5); (2) HFpEF (LVEF ≥50% and HFA-PEFF score ≥5); and (3) HFrEF (LVEF &lt;50%). The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause death or heart failure rehospitalization. Results The median age was 82 years (interquartile range [IQR], 77–86), and 1,057 patients (60.8%) were female. The median follow-up duration was 3.9 years (IQR, 2.2–5.3). 610 patients (35.1%) were categorized as the non-HFpEF group, 892 (51.3%) as the HFpEF group, and 237 (13.6%) as the HFrEF group. Compared with the non-HFpEF group, both the HFrEF group (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 1.60; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.21–2.13; p = 0.001) and the HFpEF group (aHR, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.26–1.92; p &lt; 0.001) were independently associated with a higher risk of the primary endpoint. These associations were also observed in analyses conducted separately in the SAVR and TAVR cohorts. Among 188 asymptomatic patients, 84 (44.7%) were categorized as the non-HFpEF group, 97 (51.6%) as the HFpEF group, and 7 (3.7%) as the HFrEF group. In minimally adjusted analyses (age, sex, and procedure [SAVR/TAVR]), the HFpEF group was associated with a higher risk of the primary endpoint than the non-HFpEF group (aHR, 2.23; 95% CI, 1.14–4.37; p = 0.015). Conclusions HFpEF phenotype was associated with poor prognosis after SAVR or TAVR, similar to the HFrEF phenotype. This phenotyping approach may help guide the timing of aortic valve intervention and support the selection of appropriate pharmacological therapy.Overall cohortSAVR and TAVR cohort
title: Prognostic impact of heart failure phenotype based on left ventricular ejection fraction and HFA-PEFF score after surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement

abstract: Abstract Background Myocardial infarction (MI) remains one of the primary causes of heart failure (HF) due to myocardial injury. Left atrial (LA) mechanical dysfunction reflects impaired ventricular–atrial coupling following acute MI. While left ventricular (LV) systolic parameters are routinely used for risk stratification, strain-derived LA indices may provide incremental prognostic information for early heart failure (HF) development during hospitalization. Purpose To determine optimal cut-off values for left atrial reservoir strain (LASr) and left atrial contractile strain (LASct) in predicting new-onset HF after first acute MI. Methods Consecutive 105 patients (pts) with first acute STEMI/NSTEMI (81 males, 58 STEMI, 47 NSTEMI pts, mean age 61±11 years) undergoing successful primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) were prospectively studied. Comprehensive echocardiography including left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), LV global longitudinal strain (LVGLS), LASr and LASct assessed by speckle-tracking was performed between days 3-7 post PCI. The primary endpoint was new-onset HF, defined as the development of HF signs and/or symptoms after first MI in patients without prior chronic HF, confirmed by objective congestion, elevated NT-proBNP concentrations, and echocardiographic LV dysfunction. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was used to determine optimal thresholds based on maximal Youden index. Results New-onset HF developed in 34 patients (32%). Median time to HF onset was 10 days [IQR 8–13]. Patients who developed HF had significantly reduced LA strain parameters compared with those without HF (LASr: 19.8±6.7% vs 25.1±6.4%, p&lt;0.001; LASct: 10.2±4.0% vs 13.1±3.7%, p&lt;0.001). ROC curve analysis revealed good diagnostic significance of LASr and LASct for new-onset HF in acute MI. LASr &lt;19.7% predicted HF with an AUC of 0.728 (95% CI: 0.622–0.835; sensitivity 55.9%, specificity 83.1%; Youden index 0.390; p&lt;0.001; Figure 1). LASct &lt;11.5% was identified as the optimal cut-off for HF with an AUC of 0.720 (95% CI: 0.608–0.832; sensitivity 76.5%, specificity 67.6%, Youden index 0.441; p&lt;0.001; Figure 2). LA strain parameters identified high-risk individuals despite contemporary revascularization and standard medical therapy. HF patients exhibited also bigger impairment of LV systolic function (median LVEF 43% [38–49] vs 57% [51–60] and GLS −12.9±4.1% vs −16.8±2.9%, respectively: HF vs non-HF, p&lt;0.001). Conclusions Impaired LA mechanics are significantly associated with early HF development after first MI. Cut-off values of LASr &lt;19.7% and LASct &lt;11.5%, derived from ROC analysis with maximal Youden index, offer clinically balanced sensitivity and specificity and may improve early in-hospital risk stratification. LA strain assessment provides complementary information beyond conventional systolic parameters.ROC of LASr for new-onset HF in acute MI.ROC of LASct for new-onset HF in acute MI.
title: Left atrial strain predicts early in-hospital heart failure after first acute myocardial infarction: ROC-derived clinically relevant cut-offs

abstract: Abstract Background Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) multimorbidity is common in heart failure (HF) with mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction (HFmrEF/HFpEF) and contributes to adverse outcomes. However, whether the extent of CKM overlap in HF modifies the benefits or safety profile of finerenone in this population has not been rigorously evaluated. Purpose To evaluate clinical outcomes and treatment effects of finerenone according to the number and type of concomitant CKM components among FINEARTS-HF trial participants. Methods In this prespecified analysis of the FINEARTS-HF trial, cardiovascular disease (CVD) was defined as history of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or atrial fibrillation/flutter (per medical history or baseline electrocardiography). Chronic kidney disease (CKD) was defined as either a history of CKD, a baseline estimated glomerular filtration rate &lt;60 mL/min/1.73 m2, or a baseline urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio ≥30 mg/g. Metabolic disease was defined as either obesity (elevated body mass index or waist-to-height ratio ≥0.5), type 2 diabetes (history of type 2 diabetes or baseline glycated hemoglobin ≥6.5%), or history of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. Treatment effects of finerenone were examined according to CKM status. Results Among 6,001 participants, 5,977 (99.6%) had one or more concomitant CKM components; 619 (10.3%) had 0-1 overlapping CKM components, 2,170 (36.2%) had 2 overlapping CKM components, and 3,212 (53.5%) had 3 overlapping CKM components (Figure 1A). Participants with greater CKM overlap at baseline tended to be older and male, and had higher degrees of myocardial injury (troponin levels) and worse health status (KCCQ). When compared with participants with 0-1 CKM components, those with 2 (adjusted rate ratio [aRR], 1.32; 95% CI, 1.02-1.72) and 3 (aRR, 2.58; 95% CI, 2.01-3.32) CKM components experienced an incrementally higher rate of the primary composite outcome of cardiovascular death and total HF events over a median follow-up of 2.7 [1.9, 3.0] years (Ptrend&lt;0.001) (Figure 1B). Similar findings were observed when the number of unique CKM conditions was examined (Figure 1C-D). Benefits of finerenone on cardiovascular death and total HF events appeared consistent irrespective of the number of CKM components (Pinteraction=0.09) and CKM conditions (Pinteraction=0.35) at baseline. Risks of adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation were not enhanced with finerenone vs. placebo among participants with greater CKM multimorbidity. Conclusions In this analysis, we identified CKM multimorbidity in nearly all FINEARTS-HF trial participants, and the efficacy and safety profiles of finerenone did not appear to be modified by baseline CKM status. These findings underscore the importance of systematic identification and management of CKM conditions in persons with HFmrEF/HFpEF.
title: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic overlap and finerenone in heart failure: insights from the FINEARTS-HF Trial

abstract: Abstract Purpose Optimal beta-blocker selection in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) following acute myocardial infarction (MI) remains uncertain. While both carvedilol and metoprolol are commonly prescribed, comparative effectiveness data in HFpEF are limited. We evaluated 3-year cardiovascular outcomes associated with carvedilol versus metoprolol initiation within 1 month after MI in patients with HFpEF. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network (106 healthcare organizations). Adults ≥18 years with HFpEF (left ventricular ejection fraction ≥50% and ICD-10 I50), without atrial fibrillation, and with acute MI (ICD-10 I21) were included. Patients initiated on metoprolol (RxNorm 6918) or carvedilol (RxNorm 20352) within 1 month of MI were identified. The index date was defined as the first qualifying beta-blocker prescription after MI. Outcomes were assessed from 14 to 1,095 days post-index. Primary outcomes included all-cause mortality and acute heart failure (AHF). Secondary outcomes included recurrent MI (STEMI), hospitalization, stroke, ventricular tachycardia (VT), and cardiac arrest. Propensity score matching balanced demographics, cardiovascular comorbidities, and laboratory parameters, yielding 1,537 patients per group. Results After matching, the mean age was 70.7±13.3 years, with balanced comorbidities. Over 3 years, mortality did not differ significantly between metoprolol and carvedilol (15.1% vs 15.7%; hazard ratio [HR] 0.94, 95% CI 0.78–1.13; log-rank p=0.511). Recurrent MI risk was similar (4.8% vs 5.1%; HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.67–1.27; p=0.618). Hospitalization rates were comparable (27.1% vs 28.2%; HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.82–1.07; p=0.337). Notably, acute heart failure occurred less frequently in the metoprolol group (15.5% vs 18.2%; risk difference −2.7%; HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.68–0.97; log-rank p=0.019). Stroke (6.1% vs 6.1%; HR 1.00, p=0.979), VT (2.9% vs 2.9%; HR 1.01, p=0.969), and cardiac arrest (3.2% vs 3.3%; HR 0.95, p=0.789) were similar between groups. Conclusions In patients with HFpEF following MI, metoprolol and carvedilol were associated with comparable 3-year mortality, recurrent MI, hospitalization, and arrhythmic outcomes. However, metoprolol use was associated with a modest but statistically significant reduction in acute heart failure events. These findings suggest that in HFpEF patients post-MI, beta-blocker selection may not meaningfully impact survival or ischemic risk, but metoprolol may confer a lower risk of heart failure exacerbations. Prospective trials are warranted to clarify whether beta-1 selective versus nonselective beta-blockade differentially influences long-term outcomes in this population.
title: Clinical outcomes of carvedilol versus metoprolol in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction following myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Introduction In patients with acute myocardial injury and non-obstructive coronary arteries,differentiating myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) from myocarditis or Takotsubo syndrome is challenging. Although cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) is the diagnostic gold standard, it is often unavailable in the acute phase. Speckle tracking echocardiography (STE) can provide early diagnostic clues through longitudinal strain (LS) analysis. This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of LS parameters and their correlation with CMR findings. Methods Consecutive patients with acute myocardial injury and unobstructed coronaries from the AMIPE registry (2021–2023) were analyzed. All underwent 2D echocardiography with STE within 24 h and CMR within 14 days. Segmental longitudinal strain (SLS) was calculated using a 16-segment model. A coronary pattern (CP) was defined as two contiguous segments within the same coronary territory showing the least negative strain. Associations between LS and CMR findings were assessed, and predictors of ischemic pattern were identified by multivariable logistic regression. Results Among 189 patients, CP was found in 61 (32%). CP+ patients had lower LSmin (−4.6% vs −10.5%, p&lt;0.001) and greater LS difference (p&lt;0.001) than CP− subjects. All CP+ cases showed CMR abnormalities, mainly ischemic late gadolinium enhancement (54%), while 40% of CP− patients had normal CMR. CP independently predicted an ischemic pattern (OR 9.8, 95% CI 2.6–37.3, p&lt;0.001), as did LSmin (OR 1.4, 95% CI 1.1–1.6, p&lt;0.001), even when no visual regional wall motion abnormalities were detected. ROC analysis identified LSmin ≥ −7.6% as the optimal cutoff (AUC 0.73; sensitivity 85%; specificity 62%). Conclusions In suspected MINOCA, SLS adds diagnostic value beyond conventional echocardiography. CP and LSmin ≥ −7.6% independently predict ischemic injury on CMR. STE may represent a rapid, accessible, and cost-effective adjunct to CMR in this clinical setting.Boxplot
title: Diagnostic significance of myocardial longitudinal strain in patients with suspected MINOCA (myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries)

abstract: Abstract Background The cardiovascular disease continuum encompasses a progressive trajectory from risk factors to coronary artery disease, heart failure (HF), and end-stage cardiac dysfunction. Acute coronary syndromes (ACS)—including STEMI, NSTEMI, and unstable angina—are pivotal events in this progression. While secondary prevention post-ACS has traditionally focused on reducing recurrent ischaemic events and short-term mortality, the long-term development of incident heart failure (iHF) remains underexplored. Existing evidence is limited and often derived from outdated or small-scale studies. This study aimed to characterise the real-world incidence, risk factors, clinical outcomes, and healthcare burden of iHF following ACS in a large, population-based cohort. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study using data from the Catalan Health Surveillance System, encompassing all residents discharged alive after an ACS event between 2011 and 2021 in Catalonia (7,763,362 inhabitants), Spain. Patients with prior HF or in-hospital mortality were excluded. iHF was defined as the first post-discharge HF diagnosis in hospital or primary care (with concurrent loop diuretic prescription). Multivariable competing risk regression models (Fine and Gray) were used to identify predictors of iHF. Time-to-event analyses assessed major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and generalised linear models evaluated healthcare resource use and costs. Results Among 83,357 patients (mean age 66.8 years; 71.4% male), 23.3% developed iHF during follow-up. The 10-year cumulative incidence of HF was 33% (95% CI: 33–34%). Key predictors of iHF included older age (HR=1.03 per year), Killip class II–III (HR=2.16), and very low income (HR=2.08), while PCI during index ACS was protective (HR=0.72). Patients with iHF (Table 1) experienced significantly higher rates of all-cause death (48.8% vs 13.5%), recurrent ACS, stroke, atrial fibrillation, and MACE (71.3% vs 33.2%). Healthcare costs (Figure 1) rose sharply post-ACS, particularly among iHF patients, whose first-year costs nearly tripled compared to pre-ACS levels. iHF independently predicted increased use of primary care (IRR=1.63), unplanned hospitalisations (IRR=5.56), pharmacological treatments (IRR=1.97), and long-term care services (IRR=8.19), with a significant rise in overall healthcare expenditure (β=0.73). Conclusions In this large, real-world cohort, nearly one in four ACS survivors developed iHF, which was associated with markedly worse clinical outcomes and a substantial healthcare burden. Older age, ACS severity, and socioeconomic deprivation were key risk factors, while PCI was protective. These findings highlight the need for early risk stratification, targeted preventive strategies, and healthcare system planning to address the long-term impact of iHF in post-ACS populations.
title: Ten-year real-world incidence and prognostic impact of new-onset heart failure after acute coronary syndromes: a population-based analysis of 83,357 patients

abstract: Abstract Background Symptoms of heart failure (HF) often persist even after surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR). However, the prevalence and prognostic significance of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) after SAVR remain unclear. Objective This study aimed to assess the prevalence, long-term outcomes, and predictors of HFpEF after successful SAVR. Methods 320 patients were prospectively followed with a comprehensive clinical and echocardiographic evaluation before and after SAVR. Results One year after surgery 110 patients (34.4%) were not relieved of symptoms, presenting with NYHA class ≥ II (Figure 1). 63 patients (19.7%) met the diagnostic criteria for HFpEF, 36 patients (11.3%) had heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), and 221 patients (69.1%) were free from HF. Six year follow-up revealed that HFpEF was associated with an increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (unadj. HR 2.47, 95% CI 1.01–6.04; p = 0.048), primarily driven by HF-related hospitalizations (unadj. HR 4.49, 95% CI 1.21–16.74; p = 0.025). Independent predictors of HFpEF were age (aOR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01–1.07; p &lt; 0.001), body mass index (aOR 1.07, 95% CI 1.01–1.13; p = 0.018), smoking (aOR 2.33, 95% CI 1.20–4.53; p = 0.013), and a preoperative HFA-PEFF score ≥ 5 (aOR 2.76, 95% CI 1.41–5.42; p = 0.003). Conclusion This cohort study observed 20% HFpEF prevalence after successful SAVR and HFpEF was associated with adverse long-term outcomes. Age, obesity, smoking, and HFA-PEFF scores were found to be independent predictors of postoperative HFpEF, which may guide perioperative risk stratification and early postoperative management.Change in NYHA Classification
title: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction after surgical aortic valve replacement: prevalence, prognosis and predictors

abstract: Abstract Background and aim Since the original Sub-Saharan Africa Survey of Heart Failure (THESUS-HF) study (2008–2010), the HF landscape in Africa has evolved. However, contemporary epidemiological data, particularly on treatment availability and outcomes remain limited. This study describes the epidemiology, clinical presentation, and in-hospital, 30-day, and 6-month outcomes of acute HF in a large, representative cohort of patients across Africa. Methods and results THESUS-HF II is a prospective, multicentre, observational cohort study coordinated by the Pan-African Society of Cardiology. Overall, 1578 patients were enrolled during seven 24-hour periods within an 8-week window. Standardised data were collected on clinical characteristics and outcomes to discharge, 30 days, and 6 months across 17 SSA countries. Mean age was 54.2 years, 50.5% were female. A prior HF diagnosis was recorded in 35.8% of patients. The leading aetiologies of HF were hypertensive heart disease (HHD, 37%), cardiomyopathy (23%) and ischaemic heart disease (IHD, 23%), followed by valvular/congenital heart disease (VHD/CHD, 11%). Common modifiable risk factors included hypertension (62.7%), diabetes (20.3%), dyslipidaemia (15.8%), and current/past smoking (16.1%). AF was identified on admission ECG in 19.6% of cases. Most presented in NYHA class III (29.6%) or IV (57.7%). Echocardiography showed a mean LVEDD of 56 mm and a mean LVEF of 40.9%; patients with cardiomyopathy had the lowest LVEF (34%) compared to other groups (p&lt;0.001). Most (89.5%) were admitted to general wards (mean stay 8.1 days), while 10.2% required ICU care (mean 5 days). Among participating hospitals, 82.6% offered haemodialysis and 73.9% ventilatory support. However, advanced interventions were less accessible: valvular surgery (28.9%), PCI (23.9%), CABG (19.6%), ICDs (17.4%), and CRT (10.9%). At discharge, 87.8% of patients were prescribed loop diuretics, 76.9% beta-blockers, 42.3% ACEi, 30.8% ARBs, and 6.2% ARNIs. MRAs were used in 71.9%, SGLT2i in 54.7%, and digoxin in 26.7%. At discharge, 91.3% were alive. The 30-day mortality rate was 11.7%, with no significant variation by HF aetiology ( Kaplan-Meier, p=0.129, Figure 1) and a readmission rate of 2.7%. The 6-month overall mortality was 23.9% with substantial differences between the 5 groups, ranging from 16.5% for VHD/CHD, 18.4 % for IHD, 25.8 % for cardiomyopathy to 26.6% for HHD and 36.8% for other aetiologies (Kaplan-Meier, p= 0.006, Figure 1). The readmission rate was 12.2%. Conclusion THESUS-HF II (2024-2025) is the largest study of acute HF to date in SSA. It identifies HHD, cardiomyopathy and IHD as the leading contributors to acute HF presentations. Prescription of GDMT was better than expected but there are substantial gaps in access to advanced cardiac care. Acute HF was characterised by a high 30-day and 6-month mortality, underscoring the need to strengthen HF prevention and management across the continent.Graphical Abstract of THESUS-HF II StudyTHESUS-HF II Table
title: THe Sub-Saharan Africa Survey of Heart Failure (THESUS-HF II): Aetiology, 30- days and 6 months outcome

abstract: Abstract Background Severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) induces adverse ventricular interaction that may conceal left-sided diastolic dysfunction. Objectives Whether relief of TR by transcatheter tricuspid edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER) leads to true diastolic improvement or unmasks residual left-sided constraint remains unknown. We sought to define the longitudinal effects of T-TEER on left atrial (LA) remodeling and diastolic physiology. Methods We performed a single-center retrospective analysis of a prospectively enrolled cohort of 125 patients undergoing T-TEER between March 2021–December 2025. Serial transthoracic echocardiography was analyzed by a blinded core laboratory at baseline, pre-discharge, 6 months, and 12 months. LA volume index (LAVI), peak atrial longitudinal strain (PALS), E/e′ ratio, and left atrial stiffness index (LASI) were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Results T-TEER resulted in immediate LA volume reduction (−8.1 mL/m² at pre-discharge, Padj=0.033), without sustained reverse remodeling. In contrast, LA reservoir function declined early and remained persistently impaired at 12 months (PALS −1.2%, Padj=0.029). Left-sided filling pressure surrogates increased acutely (E/e′ +3.26, Padj&lt;0.001) and only partially normalized, with LASI remaining elevated at long-term follow-up. Forward flow indices were preserved. Early mitral regurgitation changes were common but transient and unrelated to diastolic indices. Conclusions Relief of severe TR by T-TEER induces early anatomical left atrial unloading but simultaneously unmasks latent left-sided diastolic constraint, evidenced by persistent atrial stiffness and impaired reservoir function. This dissociation highlights the limitations of volume-based assessment and positions LA strain as a key marker of diastolic reserve after tricuspid intervention.Central Figure
title: Left atrial remodeling and diastolic unloading after transcatheter tricuspid repair

abstract: Abstract Background High-sensitivity cardiac troponins are the gold-standard biomarkers for diagnosing myocardial injury. We have previously shown that elevated high-sensitivity troponin-T (hsTnT) is associated with both short- and long-term mortality in patients with acute pulmonary embolism (PE). However, it is unknown whether hsTnT may reflect concurrent or developing heart failure (HF) in this setting. Purpose To determine the early and late risk of HF in individuals with acute PE according to their hsTnT concentration at presentation. Methods Retrospective cohort study based on Danish nationwide administrative registries. We identified all patients discharged from the hospital with a PE from 2013 through 2020 (International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision diagnostic codes: I260, I269, and I269A) and merged them with all records of at least one hsTnT (Elecsys® Troponin T hs, Roche Diagnostics; 99th percentile upper reference limit, 13.5 ng/l) measurement obtained during the same hospitalization. Subjects with known HF were excluded. Persons were stratified into quartiles (Q1-Q4) based on their first hsTnT measurement. Standardized absolute and relative risks (RR) for HF at days 0-30 and days 31-365 were calculated through multivariable Cox regression with average treatment effect modeling. Models were standardized for demographic and clinical features, including hemoglobin concentration and estimated glomerular filtration rate. Results A total of 5,323 individuals were included. Median age (25th-75th percentile) was 70.2 (58.0-78.7) years, 2,651, (50.2%) were women, and 129 (2.4%) had a prior history of venous thromboembolism. Median baseline hsTnT was 27 (25th-75th percentile, 14-72) ng/l, and 3,996 (75.1%) had an elevated concentration. Seventy-one (1.3%) individuals had been diagnosed with HF at 30 days; 14 within the first day of admission, and 57 from days 2 through 30 (Figure 1). Only 2 HF events occurred in Q1, 16 in Q2, 26 in Q3, and 27 in Q4. Accordingly, the standardized absolute risk of early HF was negligible in Q1 (0.13%) and highest in Q4 (2.64%). The RR of developing HF within 30 days after acute PE was significantly higher in hsTnT Q3 and Q4 vs. Q1 and Q2 (RR: 3.17; 95% CI, 1.35-4.99; P=0.02). Seventy-two (1.5%) additional HF diagnoses were registered between days 31-365, with 5 events in Q1, 22 in Q2, 28 in Q3, and 17 in Q4 (Figure 2). The standardized absolute risk of HF was 0.52% in Q1, and 1.85% in Q4. The RR of HF 31-365 days after PE tended to be higher for individuals in hsTnT Q3 and Q4 vs. Q1 and Q2, but did not reach significance (RR: 1.72; 95% CI, 0.87-2.56; P=0.10). Conclusions The risk of HF in individuals with acute PE, without a history of HF, was very low. A large proportion of early HF cases appeared concomitantly with the PE event, and individuals with a hsTnT concentration &gt;=28 ng/l had a significantly higher risk of HF within 30 days of their acute PE.Figure 1Figure 2
title: High-sensitivity troponin-T concentrations and risk of heart failure in patients with acute pulmonary embolism

abstract: Abstract In NSTEMI with preserved ejection fraction, conventional echocardiography frequently fails to demonstrate overt regional wall motion abnormalities despite clinically relevant coronary stenosis, limiting early anatomical targeting. Two-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography (STE) quantifies myocardial deformation and may reveal subtle, predominantly subendocardial, ischaemia-related dysfunction. A rapid, pre-angiography strain “map” could therefore support culprit territory localisation when standard imaging appears unremarkable. To assess whether global longitudinal strain (GLS) and territorial/segmental longitudinal strain derived from STE identify the angiographic culprit vessel in NSTEMI with preserved ejection fraction, and to quantify the relationship between strain impairment and stenosis severity. We analysed 100 consecutive NSTEMI patients undergoing early coronary angiography at a single centre (January 2019–January 2020). NSTEMI was defined by serial high-sensitivity troponin I (hs-TnI) measurements demonstrating a rise/fall pattern alongside clinical evidence of myocardial ischaemia. Speckle-tracking echocardiography was performed approximately 1 hour before angiography using a standard 17-segment model. Two experienced readers, blinded to clinical and angiographic data, quantified GLS and territorial longitudinal strain assigned to LAD, LCx, and RCA perfusion territories. Angiography was performed within 24 hours. Two blinded invasive cardiologists determined culprit vessel and stenosis severity. We assessed associations between stenosis severity and GLS/territorial strain using linear models and reported model fit (R²). Mean age was 57.8±12.6 years; 66.3% were male; mean ejection fraction was 59.8±3.0%. GLS was −17.5±0.6%. Territorial strain demonstrated a clear gradient consistent with culprit-territory dysfunction: strain was most impaired in the LAD territory (−16.8±2.3%) compared with LCx (−17.8±1.8%) and RCA territories (−18.8±2.2%). Culprit lesions were located in LAD (56%), LCx (29%), and RCA (15%). Mean stenosis severity was 89.4±10.5%. Stenosis severity showed only a weak association with GLS (R²=0.125), whereas territorial strain exhibited substantially stronger associations, particularly in the RCA and LCx territories (R²=0.334 for LAD, 0.488 for LCx, and 0.638 for RCA). In NSTEMI with preserved ejection fraction, pre-angiography territorial strain mapping shows territory-specific impairment and relates to stenosis severity more strongly than GLS. Territorial/segmental strain analysis may enhance early culprit territory localisation and assist anatomical targeting when conventional echocardiography appears normal.table 1
title: The role of segmental and global longitudinal strain in identifying culprit lesion localization in NSTEMI patients with preserved ejection fraction

abstract: Abstract Background Coronary allograft vasculopathy (CAV) remains a leading cause of late graft failure after heart transplantation (HTx). Because CAV often develops silently, identifying circulating biomarkers and clinical parameters able to detect early vascular injury is of major clinical interest. Methods We analyzed 117 HTx recipients evaluated a median of 85.7 months after transplantation. Patients were stratified according to the presence of CAV. Clinical characteristics, echocardiographic parameters, and circulating biomarkers reflecting myocardial injury, heart failure, and graft damage—high-sensitivity troponin I (hs-TnI), N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), mid-regional pro-adrenomedullin (MR-proADM), and donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA)—were assessed. Univariate logistic regression identified variables associated with CAV. Multivariable logistic regression models were constructed, and model performance was evaluated using ROC analysis and confusion matrices. Results Fifty-seven patients developed CAV while 60 did not. Patients with CAV were older and had a significantly longer time since HTx. Mycophenolate therapy was more frequently used in patients without CAV. Echocardiographic indices of diastolic dysfunction were significantly altered in CAV (Table 1). Among circulating biomarkers, MR-proADM and dd-cfDNA were significantly elevated in patients with CAV (Table 1). Univariate analysis identified twelve variables associated with CAV, including time since HTx, age, BMI, diastolic function parameters, MR-proADM, and dd-cfDNA, whereas mycophenolate therapy was associated with reduced risk (Figure 1A). ROC analysis demonstrated the best discrimination for dd-cfDNA (AUC 0.766) and MR-proADM (AUC 0.736) (Figure 1B). Because several predictors reflected overlapping clinical or physiological domains, correlation analysis was performed to identify collinear variables before multivariable modeling (Figure 1C). Representative variables from each correlated cluster were then selected to avoid redundancy and improve model stability. In multivariable analysis, time since HTx and dd-cfDNA remained independent predictors of CAV, while mycophenolate therapy showed a protective association (Figure 1D). A parsimonious stepwise model including time since HTx, dd-cfDNA, E/e′ ratio, BMI, and mycophenolate demonstrated strong discrimination (AUC 0.856), comparable to the full model (Figure 1E,F). Conclusions Circulating biomarkers reflecting graft injury and vascular stress are strongly associated with coronary allograft vasculopathy after heart transplantation. dd-cfDNA emerged as an independent predictor of CAV, while mycophenolate therapy was associated with reduced risk. Integration of biomarkers with echocardiographic and clinical parameters enabled accurate discrimination of CAV, highlighting the potential of multimodal biomarker-based approaches for improving CAV risk stratification in transplant recipients.Table 1Figure1
title: Donor-derived cell-free DNA with clinical and echocardiographic data as independent predictors of Coronary Allograft Vasculopathy in heart-transplant recipients

abstract: Abstract Background Extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling is central to the pathogenesis of cardiovascular disease (CVD), yet clinically feasible tools to quantify ECM turnover remain limited. Versican, a central component for ECM remodelling after injury and inflammation, is cleaved by ADAMTS enzymes and ADAMTS enzyme activity is linked to pathological remodelling. Cleavage generates the fragment versikine, which may serve as a biomarker of pathological remodelling. Circulating versikine levels in human serum have not been characterized in CVD. Purpose We aimed to develop and validate a sandwich ELISA for quantifying versikine in human serum to determine its circulating levels in healthy individuals and in patients with CVD. Further, we examined the correlation between versikine and outcomes and clinical characteristics in the two patient cohorts. In one of the cohorts, we also examined correlation between versikine and markers of fibrosis. Methods A sandwich ELISA was developed using a neo-epitope capture antibody and a detection antibody targeting the G1 domain of versican. Analytical validation included assessment of repeatability, reproducibility, measuring range, linearity and spike and recovery. The assay was applied to three human cohorts: healthy individuals, patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). In the HCM cohort, in addition to clinical characteristics, versikine levels were compared with levels of known markers of fibrosis, including N-terminal propeptide of procollagen I and III (PINP and PIIINP) and C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CITP). Results The assay demonstrated acceptable results on linearity, repeatability (&lt;10%), reproducibility (&lt;15%) and recovery (&lt;±20%). The quantitative range was 0.2-166.7 ng/ml, and all measured serum samples fell within this range. Median (IQR) levels of versikine were lower in patients with HCM (15.2 (8.2–24.4) ng/ml) and STEMI (13.1 (9.6–19.4) at Day 1, 13.1 (9.9–19.2) ng/ml after 4 months), than in healthy individuals (24 (16.6–27.7)). Versikine demonstrated only weak associations with clinical variables, and no correlations with PINP, PIIINP and CITP. Conclusions We have developed and analytically validated a sandwich ELISA that quantify levels of versikine in human serum. In this initial clinical evaluation, versikine levels were lower in patients with CVD compared with healthy controls and were not associated with markers of collagen turnover. Further studies are warranted to clarify its biological and clinical relevance.Distribution of versikine levelsLevels of versikine, PINP, PIIINP and CITP
title: Development of an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for versikine detection and first analyses in human cardiovascular disease

abstract: Abstract Introduction Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is associated with increased risk for heart failure (HF). The underlying pathophysiology is complex and involves adipocyte-derived inflammation, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and neurohormonal activation. Together, these factors promote endothelial dysfunction, myocardial injury, and fibrosis, leading to adverse cardiac remodeling and HF. Composite cardiometabolic indices capture interactions among adiposity, lipid metabolism, and body composition. We evaluated whether these indices discriminate prevalent HF among adults with MetS using seven machine learning (ML) models capable of modeling complex and nonlinear cardiometabolic interactions. Methods We analyzed data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 1999-2016 and included adults aged ≥20 years, with ≥3 of the 5 MetS criteria, HbA1c &lt;6.5%, and with known HF status. HF was defined by self-reported physician diagnosis. Four cardiometabolic indices derived from anthropometric measures and laboratory values were evaluated: Atherogenic Index of Plasma (AIP), A Body Shape Index (ABSI), Body Fat Percentage (BFP), and Body Roundness Index (BRI). Missing data were imputed using random forest methods, class imbalance was addressed using SMOTE/SMOTEENN, predictors were standardized, and data were randomly split 70:30 into training and test sets. Seven ML models were compared with logistic regression. Performance was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, and calibration, including Brier score and recalibration. Results Among 9,738 adults with MetS, 486 had HF (5.0%). The mean age was 58.5±16.3 years, and 51.5% were female. Random forest achieved the highest discrimination (AUC 0.95) with favorable calibration after recalibration and improved Brier score, followed by XGBoost (AUC 0.88) and gradient boosting (AUC 0.86) (Figure 1). K-nearest neighbors showed high sensitivity (0.87) but lower specificity (0.64) (Table 1). Support vector machine demonstrated moderate discrimination, while the neural network showed lower performance. Traditional models showed modest discrimination, including logistic regression (AUC 0.64) and naïve Bayes (AUC 0.67) (Table 1). Calibration intercepts approached zero after recalibration, although Hosmer-Lemeshow tests remained significant (p&lt;0.05), reflecting large sample size effects. Receiver operating characteristic curves for all models are shown in Figure 1. Conclusion ML models incorporating composite cardiometabolic indices demonstrated superior discrimination of prevalent HF among adults with MetS compared with traditional models. These findings highlight the ability of ML to capture complex nonlinear cardiometabolic interactions and support the development of scalable screening tools for early HF phenotyping and risk stratification in high-risk MetS populations.Table 1.ML model performance for HF in MetSFigure 1.ML models ROC analysis
title: Machine learning-enabled cardiometabolic phenotyping for heart failure detection in metabolic syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Accurate assessment of diastolic dysfunction in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is crucial for guiding treatment strategies, yet conventional echocardiographic parameters often have limited sensitivity for estimating left ventricular filling pressure (LVFP). Left atrial reservoir strain (LARS) has recently emerged as a promising non-invasive indicator. Purpose To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of LARS for detecting elevated left ventricular end diastolic pressure (LVEDP) in STEMI patients after successful primary PCI, and to assess differences according to culprit vessel location. Methods This single-center observational cross-sectional study included 103 STEMI patients who underwent successful primary PCI. Invasive LVEDP was measured post-procedure, with elevated LVEDP defined as &gt;18 mmHg. Comprehensive echocardiography with speckletracking analysis for LARS was performed within 24 hours. Patients were stratified by culprit artery (LAD vs. non-LAD). Correlation analysis, ROC curves, and multivariate regression were used to assess diagnostic performance. Results LARS showed a strong inverse correlation with LVEDP (r = –0.58, p &lt; 0.001), outperforming E/e′ (r = 0.45). A LARS cutoff ≤22.5% identified elevated LVEDP with 78% sensitivity and 73% specificity (AUC = 0.79). Diagnostic accuracy varied by infarct location: LAD infarctions demonstrated excellent performance (AUC = 0.87; r = –0.71) with an optimal cutoff ≤23.0%, whereas non-LAD infarctions showed moderate accuracy (AUC = 0.70; r = –0.42). In multivariate analysis, LARS remained the strongest independent predictor of LVEDP (β = –0.45, p &lt; 0.001). Crucially, left atrial function was more impaired in the LAD group, as shown by a significantly lower LARS (21.2% vs. 23.5%, p=0.008). Conclusion LARS is a superior non-invasive marker for estimating elevated LVEDP in STEMI patients, with significantly enhanced performance in LAD-related infarction due to a tight pathophysiological coupling, and more moderate in non-LAD infracts. Our proposed diagnostic matrix and location-stratified algorithm provide a practical framework to implement this evidence, moving from a one-size-fits-all approach to personalized hemodynamic assessment. By multi-parametric algorithm that integrates LARS with conventional parameters, we provide a roadmap for translating this advanced echocardiographic measure into confident, evidence-based clinical decision-making.Multi-Parametric Interpretation Matrixwider dynamic range of pathology
title: From estimation to quantification: using left atrial reservoir strain to guide therapy in acute myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Introduction In up to 50% of patients, heart failure (HF) is first diagnosed at the time of hospitalization for acute HF, representing a missed opportunity for earlier treatment. Artificial intelligence–enhanced electrocardiography (AI-ECG) offers a rapid and scalable opportunity for HF detection and risk stratification. Two recently published AI-ECG models were developed using distinct proxy outcomes for HF: DeepECG, a Canadian model trained to detect left ventricular ejection fraction &lt;40% as a surrogate for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), and ECG2HF, a US model trained to predict incident HF using longitudinal electronic health record data. However, their performance for detecting heart failure in a pooled European cohort derived from five prospective studies remains unknown. Methods In this pooled external validation, we analyzed digital 12-lead ECGs from five prospective studies conducted at a single European center across diverse clinical settings, including outpatient diagnostic populations, perioperative inpatients at high cardiovascular risk, cardiac rehabilitation patients, and a national cohort undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation. HF was centrally adjudicated by two independent cardiologists according to guideline-recommended criteria, incorporating symptoms, natriuretic peptide levels with clinical adjustments, and structural and/or functional cardiac abnormalities. Model performance was assessed using discrimination and precision–recall analysis. The primary outcome was HF, and the secondary outcome was HFrEF. Findings Among 7124 patients with curated diagnoses (median age 70 years [IQR 61–78], 2279 [32%] women), 3153 (44%) had HF, including HFpEF in 1564 (21%), HFmrEF in 537 (7%), and HFrEF in 633 (9%). For the detection of HF, DeepECG and ECG2HF showed similar discrimination (AUC 0.72 [95% CI 0.71–0.73] vs 0.73 [0.71–0.74]) and comparable precision–recall performance (AUPRC 0.69 vs 0.68). For HFrEF, DeepECG demonstrated superior discrimination compared with ECG2HF (AUC 0.90 [0.89–0.91] vs 0.85 [0.84–0.87]) and higher precision–recall performance (AUPRC 0.52 vs 0.35). The combination of both models consistently improved performance, yielding higher discrimination and precision–recall metrics for HF (AUC 0.74, AUPRC 0.71) and HFrEF (AUC 0.91, AUPRC 0.54). Interpretation In this large European cohort spanning five clinical scenarios of heart failure detection, the performance of the deep learning models DeepECG and ECG2HF, which were developed to identify proxies of heart failure, was overall moderate. However, the improved performance observed with their combination suggests that each model captures distinct and complementary features related to heart failure. This highlights the potential limitations of relying on surrogate endpoints and supports the development of models trained directly on heart failure outcomes to improve risk stratification.AUC and AUPRC for HFAUC and AUPRC for HFrEF
title: External validation of artificial intelligence–based electrocardiographic models for heart failure detection across diverse clinical settings

abstract: Abstract Background Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is characterized by extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling and fibrosis, but clinically useful circulating biomarkers reflecting these processes remain limited. Purpose To assess whether circulating ECM-derived biomarkers (PRO-C3, PRO-C6 and endotrophin) are associated with HFpEF, key clinical HF features, and adverse outcomes. Methods In this prospective single-centre NETDiamond cohort analysis, plasma PRO-C3, PRO-C6 and endotrophin were measured using specific enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (Nordic Bioscience) in controls (n=15) and patients with HFpEF (n=78). Biomarker levels were compared between groups, and in HFpEF their associations with clinical, laboratory and echocardiographic variables, as well as a composite HF endpoint (cardiovascular death, HF hospitalization, or acute HF episode), were evaluated using Cox regression with adjusted models including age, sex, creatinine and BNP. Results Circulating endotrophin was higher in HFpEF versus controls (p=0.0046; exact p=0.0040), whereas PRO-C3 and PRO-C6 were not significantly different. In HFpEF, higher PRO-C6 and endotrophin tertiles were associated with a more adverse clinical profile, including higher high-sensitivity troponin I, worse renal function, and adverse remodelling/diastolic dysfunction indices (including higher LVMI and E/e′); PRO-C6 tertiles were also associated with lower LVEF and higher LAVI, while endotrophin tertiles were associated with higher pulse wave velocity. During follow-up in HFpEF (n=78), 28 HF composite endpoint events occurred. PRO-C6 and endotrophin were associated with higher event risk. In adjusted models, PRO-C6 (HR 3.41, 95% CI 1.22 to 9.53; p=0.019) and endotrophin (HR 2.74, 95% CI 1.20 to 6.22; p=0.016) remained significantly associated with the composite endpoint. Tertile analyses were concordant, with progressively higher risk across PRO-C6 and endotrophin tertiles. Conclusions In this prospective single-centre HFpEF cohort, PRO-C6 and endotrophin identified a higher-risk HFpEF phenotype characterized by myocardial injury and adverse remodelling, and were independently associated with adverse outcomes. These findings support the type VI collagen/endotrophin axis as a promising pathway for HFpEF risk stratification and may also help identify biologically relevant, potentially targetable mechanisms of disease.
title: PRO-C6 and endotrophin are associated with cardiac remodelling and adverse outcomes in HFpEF: data from the prospective NETDiamond cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis (LFLG AS) is associated with approximately 30% mortality at 2 years following transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). Contractile reserve (CR), assessed by dobutamine stress echocardiography (DSE), does not reliably predict mortality or ejection fraction (EF) improvement. Global longitudinal strain (GLS) has been shown to independently predict mortality in this population. Purpose Given GLS is load-dependent; Myocardial work (MW) is a novel echocardiographic parameter that integrates myocardial deformation and afterload and may help differentiate whether reduced GLS reflects intrinsic myocardial dysfunction or increased afterload. We evaluated the utility of baseline and 1-month post-TAVR MW parameters in predicting 1-year mortality in this population. Methods Baseline and 1-month post-TAVR GLS, global myocardial work index (GWI), global constructive work (GCW), global wasted work (GWW), and global work efficiency (GWE) were measured using automated function imaging software. MW parameters were derived from noninvasive left ventricular pressure–strain loops incorporating brachial systolic blood pressure and mean aortic valve gradient. A total of 43 patients (age 79 ± 7 years; 74% male; 81% coronary artery disease; EF 37% [27.5–45.0]; GLS −9.5% ± 3.5) who underwent DSE between 2017 and 2025 were included. Patients with &gt;10% absolute improvement in EF at 1 month were classified as responders. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to determine optimal cutoffs for prediction of 1-year mortality. Results At 1 month, 30% of the cohort were responders. Responders had significantly lower baseline EF compared with non-responders (p&lt;0.001) (Table 1). One- and two-year mortality was 16% and 30%, respectively. CR (present in 47%) as well as baseline and 1-month post-TAVR EF were not predictive of 1-year mortality (Figure 1). Baseline GLS (AUC 0.89, cut off &gt;–7%, p=0.002), GWI (AUC 0.87, cutoff &lt;1185 mmHg% p=0.001), and GWE (AUC 0.78, cutoff &lt;75%, p=0.02) showed high sensitivity and specificity for predicting 1-year mortality (Figure 1). Early (1-month) post-TAVR GWE demonstrated strongest discrimination (AUC 0.81, cut off &lt;77%, p=0.035), outperforming 1-month GLS (AUC 0.77, cutoff &gt;-8% p=0.045) for 1-year mortality. Responders demonstrated an increase in GWI and GWE, whereas non-responders exhibited a decline in these parameters despite comparable reductions in afterload at 1 month (Table 1). Conclusion Patients with LFLG AS undergoing TAVR have high mid-term mortality. Conventional measures including CR and EF were not predictive of 1-year mortality. In contrast, baseline and 1-month GLS and MW parameters demonstrated strong predictive value for subsequent mortality, supporting their role in early risk stratification in this population. Larger studies are warranted to confirm their independent prognostic value.Table 1Figure 1
title: Myocardial work assessment in low-flow low-gradient aortic stenosis

abstract: Abstract Background Heart failure (HF), valvular disease and cardiac amyloidosis are often underdiagnosed or detected late, particularly HF with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and cardiac amyloidosis due to phenotypic overlap and operator-dependent echocardiography. Aortic stenosis in HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) patients is frequently missed because of low flow. Early diagnosis improves prognosis in both aortic stenosis and cardiac amyloidosis. Purpose To evaluate whether automated AI-based echocardiographic analysis improves detection of cardiac amyloidosis and aortic stenosis in real-world hospital cohorts. Method Retrospective 2148 randomly chosen patients who underwent echocardiography for various clinical indications in 2024 were included. An AI model (US2AI) certified for HF and amyloidosis was employed to identify patients with either; 1) cardiac amyloidosis or 2) HFrEF and aortic stenosis. Data was manually validated via electronic health records to assess diagnostic accuracy, management and outcomes. Results Among 2,148 echocardiographic reports, findings suggestive of heart failure were identified in 50.6% (n=1,087). Patterns with EF ≥50% predominated (n=848, 78.1%), including HFpEF and HFimpEF (Heart Failure with improved Ejection Fraction), HFrEF (n=129; 11.9%) and Heart Failure with mildly reduced Ejection Fraction (HFmrEF) (n=110; 10,1%). In the HFrEF subgroup (n=129; 11.9% of), the AI model detected 8 cases (6.2%) of moderate to severe aortic stenosis including 6 moderate and 2 severe; Of these, 5 participants underwent valve intervention, whereas 3 died shortly after diagnosis. Within the group with EF ≥50% (n=848), the AI model flagged 34 patients (3.2%) with features suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis. Only 2 participants (7.4%) had a prior amyloidosis diagnosis. Among the 32 subjects flagged for amyloidosis; 40.7% presented conduction abnormalities including atrial fibrillation, atrioventricular block, or bifascicular block and 4 had died. Conclusion Systematic AI-phenotyping of routine echocardiograms identifies and may help with underdiagnosed conditions such as; cardiac amyloidosis and aortic stenosis among individuals with HF. Integrating AI into clinical practice could fundamentally improve the patient-tailored treatment and avoid the irreversible clinical deterioration.AI Echo Flowchart
title: AI-driven echocardiographic phenotyping in patients with heart failure – A help to identify amyloidosis and aortic stenosis in real word hospital cohorts

abstract: Abstract Background Global longitudinal strain (GLS) as assessed by echocardiography is a sensitive marker of left ventricular systolic function with established prognostic value in severe aortic stenosis. Artificial intelligence (AI)–based strain analysis may improve standardization and reproducibility. Purpose To evaluate agreement between physician- and AI-derived GLS measurements before and after surgical aortic valve replacement (AVR), and to assess their ability to detect functional recovery. Methods Sixty patients (66.3 ± 8.1 years; 58,3% female) with severe aortic stenosis undergoing surgical AVR were included. Pre- and 12-month post-operative transthoracic echocardiograms were assessed by physicians and by a CE-marked, commercially available AI-based strain analysis software. Agreement was evaluated using Pearson correlation, Bland–Altman analysis, and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC(3,1); two-way mixed-effects model, single measurement, absolute agreement). Proportional bias was assessed by regression of inter-method differences on measurement means. Longitudinal changes were analysed using paired testing. Statistical analyses were performed in Python using SciPy and pingouin. Results Pre-operatively, AI-derived GLS showed strong correlation with physician measurements (r = 0.72–0.79). For averaged GLS, agreement was good (ICC(3,1) = 0.77; 95% CI 0.65–0.86), with a mean physician–AI difference of 2.71% and Bland–Altman limits of agreement of approximately −6.4% to 11.8% (Figure 1). No significant proportional bias was observed. Post-operatively, correlation for averaged GLS remained moderate (r = 0.67), and inter-method bias increased to 3.65%, with a significant increase in the 3-chamber view (p = 0.003, Figure 2). The magnitude of inter-method differences was comparable to ranges reported for inter-observer variability in GLS assessment. Both methods detected significant GLS improvement at 12 months (physician +2.63%, p &lt; 0.001; AI +1.69%, p = 0.001). Conclusions AI-derived GLS demonstrates good agreement with physician assessment and reliably detects post-operative functional recovery after surgical AVR. Although a modest systematic offset was observed, the magnitude of inter-method differences was within ranges commonly reported for inter-observer variability in GLS assessment. These findings support the potential integration of AI-based strain analysis into clinical workflows.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Comparison of artificial intelligence and physician assessment of global longitudinal strain before and after surgical aortic valve replacement

abstract: Abstract Background Hyperkalaemia complicates heart failure (HF) and may limit guideline-directed therapy. Potassium binders differ in pharmacologic properties and sodium load, raising cardiovascular safety concerns. Real-world comparative evidence on cardiovascular outcomes associated with the different novel potassium binders in HF is limited. We aimed to compare cardiovascular outcomes associated with patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC), and sodium polystyrene sulfonate (SPS) using a target-trial emulation framework. Methods We conducted a retrospective comparative effectiveness study in the TriNetX network including adults with HF and hyperkalaemia initiating patiromer, SZC, or SPS (2019–2024). Three pairwise 1:1 propensity-matched comparisons were performed. Follow-up was up to 365 days (mean 0.7±0.4 years). Outcomes included death, HF hospitalisation, cardiovascular hospitalisation, myocardial infarction, incident atrial fibrillation (AF), pulmonary oedema/cardiogenic shock, end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), and ventricular tachyarrhythmia/cardiac arrest. Results After matching, 5,589 patients per group were included for patiromer vs SPS, 15,769 per group for SZC vs SPS, and 4,381 per group for SZC vs patiromer. Compared with SPS, patiromer was associated with lower risk of HF hospitalisation (HR 0.573, 95%CI 0.535–0.613) and cardiovascular-related hospitalisation (HR 0.737, 95%CI 0.697–0.779), but slightly higher mortality (HR 1.096, 95%CI 1.027–1.170). In contrast, SZC was associated with higher risks of death (HR 1.139, 95%CI 1.095–1.185), HF hospitalisation (HR 1.184, 95%CI 1.143–1.225), myocardial infarction (HR 1.132, 95%CI 1.018–1.260), ESKD (HR 1.137, 95%CI 1.082–1.196), and cardiovascular hospitalisation (HR 1.193, 95%CI 1.157–1.229) compared with SPS. Direct comparison showed SZC was associated with markedly higher HF hospitalisation (HR 2.735, 95%CI 2.519–2.969) and cardiovascular hospitalisation (HR 1.914, 95%CI 1.797–2.037) versus patiromer, with no significant difference in mortality. In stratified analyses according to HF phenotype, associations between SZC and patiromer were consistent across HFrEF and HFpEF. However, formal interaction testing demonstrated significant effect modification for cardiovascular hospitalization (p for interaction = 0.01) and pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock (p = 0.03), with stronger relative associations observed in HFpEF. Conclusions In patients with HF and hyperkalaemia, potassium binders demonstrated distinct cardiovascular outcome profiles. SZC was associated with higher risks of HF and cardiovascular hospitalisation compared with both patiromer and SPS, while patiromer was associated with lower HF hospitalisation compared with SPS. These findings highlight that potassium binders are not interchangeable from a cardiovascular perspective and underscore the need for randomised trials specifically powered for hard cardiovascular endpoints.
title: Cardiovascular outcomes with potassium binders in patients with heart failure and hyperkalemia

abstract: Abstract Background Systolic dysfunction after myocardial infarction (MI) is not uncommon, particularly in patients with ST-segment elevation MI (STEMI). Optimization of heart failure (HF) pharmacotherapy is essential for both symptomatic relief and prognostic improvement. Purpose We aimed to analyse the evolution of HF therapy in our local post-MI Cardiac Rehabilitation Program (CRP), focusing on treatment adjustments during Phase 2 and extended follow-up in Phase 3 (one year after MI). Methods Patients with MI and systolic dysfunction (defined as left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF] &lt;50%) between November 2021 and November 2024 who completed our Phase 2 CRP and at least a one-year follow-up visit in extended Phase 3 were included in a prospective registry. We evaluated the changes in HF therapy, including beta-blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEI), angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARB), neprilysin and angiotensin receptor inhibitors (ARNI), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), and other diuretics. Relative equivalent doses (ED, standardized to reference doses) and achievement of target doses were assessed for each drug class. Results Our cohort comprised 87 patients (mean age 63.83±12 years, 80.5% males, 46% previous smokers), mainly presenting with anterior (n=52, 59.8%) and inferior (n=24, 27.6%) STEMI. The mean LVEF was 40.34±4.43%, with 52.9% showing mildly reduced (40–49%), 36.8% moderately reduced (30–39%), and 10.3% severely reduced (&lt;30%) LVEF. HF therapy optimization was performed in 72 (82.8%) patients during Phase 2 and in 12 (13.8%) patients at one year. Beta-blocker therapy was nearly universal (n=84, 96.6% at one year) with no significant changes during follow-up. A trend toward reduced use of ACEI (32.2% to 25.3%) and ARB (28.7% to 23%) was observed, accompanied by a significant increase in ARNI use (25.3% to 41.4%) and ED (from 1 [0.5-1] to 1 [0.5-2] sacubitril-valsartan 24/26mg ED, p&lt;0.001). Both the use and ED of MRA increased (39.1% and 1 [0.5-1] to 73.6% and 1 [1-1] eplerenone 25mg ED, p&lt;0.001). Use of SGLT2i rose markedly (49.4% to 89.7%, p&lt;0.001), as did the use of other diuretics (26.4% to 36.8%, p=0.006). After one year, most patients had not achieved target doses for any drug class except SGLT2i (89.7%). NTproBNP levels decreased significantly from 2154 [1063.5-3796.5] pg/mL before Phase 2 to 375.5 [195.75-624.5] pg/mL after Phase 2 and 342.5 [170.25-661] pg/mL 1 year after MI (p&lt;0.001). Conclusion Substantial optimization of HF pharmacotherapy can be achieved during Phase 2 and Phase 3 CRP, particularly for MRA and SGLT2i. However, most patients do not reach guideline-recommended target doses, potentially due to symptomatic hypotension or LVEF recovery. The clinical implications of this treatment strategy warrant further investigation.Figure.HF therapy changes during CRPTable.HF therapy changes during CRP
title: Heart failure therapy optimization in myocardial infarction patients with systolic dysfunction during Phase 2 and 3 Cardiac Rehabilitation

abstract: Abstract Background Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) effectively relieves valvular obstruction in severe aortic stenosis, yet long-term cardiovascular outcomes remain heterogeneous. While structural remodeling may occur after valve intervention, adverse events are ultimately governed by baseline myocardial function. The prognostic importance of baseline atrial–ventricular mechanical integration, which determines ventricular filling efficiency and pressure transmission, has not been well defined. Objectives To determine whether baseline atrial–ventricular strain coupling and ventricular contractile reserve predict major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) after TAVR and enable clinically meaningful risk stratification. Methods We retrospectively studied 186 consecutive patients undergoing TAVR for severe symptomatic aortic stenosis. Baseline pre-procedural echocardiography assessed left atrial reservoir strain, left ventricular global longitudinal strain, atrial–ventricular strain coupling expressed as the left atrial–to–left ventricular (LA/LV) strain ratio, and left ventricular end-systolic elastance (Ees) as a measure of contractile reserve. Ees was estimated noninvasively as 0.9 × systolic blood pressure divided by left ventricular end-systolic volume. The primary outcome was MACE, defined as a composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, heart failure hospitalization, and stroke. Cox proportional hazards models were constructed using physiologically guided variable selection. Results Mean age was 80 ± 5 years; 54% male; atrial fibrillation 12%, coronary artery disease 68%. During a median follow-up of 3 years, 39 patients experienced MACE. Baseline atrial–ventricular strain coupling was the strongest independent predictor of MACE (hazard ratio [HR] 0.27, 95% CI 0.11–0.61; p = 0.001), exceeding the prognostic contribution of age, CAD, and AF. Greater baseline ventricular contractile reserve was independently associated with lower risk (HR 0.85 per unit increase in Ees, 95% CI 0.72–0.97; p = 0.012). Risk stratification using cutoffs of LA/LV strain ratio 1.26 and Ees 6.24 identified a high-risk phenotype characterized by impaired atrial–ventricular coupling and reduced contractile reserve, with graded separation of event-free survival (log-rank p = 0.0006). Conclusions Long-term outcomes after TAVR are determined predominantly by baseline myocardial physiology rather than by valvular obstruction alone. Atrial–ventricular strain coupling captures baseline myocardial vulnerability that may persist despite relief of valvular obstruction, while Ees reflects the heart’s adaptive contractile capacity. Together, these complementary measures provide a physiologically grounded framework for pre-procedural risk stratification in patients undergoing TAVR.Figure1
title: Baseline atrial–ventricular strain coupling and ventricular contractile reserve determine long-term outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve replacement

abstract: Abstract Background Myocardial infarction (MI) is caused by ischemia, leading to irreversible myocardial injury, chronic inflammation and collagenous scarring, i.e., fibrosis. Beta-blockers (BB) reduce the risk of heart failure progression in MI patients with reduced ejection fraction (EF), however their use and effects in patients with preserved (pEF) or mildly reduced (mrEF) EF is debated. Purpose To evaluate circulating levels of fibrillar collagen peptides in MI patients without heart failure, randomized to prolonged use of BB or not. Methods The BETAMI-DANBLOCK trial (beta blockers after myocardial infarction in patients without heart failure) randomized patients with MI and EF≥ 40% to BBs or not. Patients (n= 5574) were followed for 3.5 years for clinical endpoints. The biobank consisted of n=490 participants (median age 61, 19% women) recruited at four sites in Norway within 7 days of the index event, where n=65 had a primary endpoint. Procollagen has peptides at amino and carboxy termini that are cleaved off by proteases prior to fibril incorporation. They can reach the circulation, e.g. type I collagen C-terminal propeptide (PICP), which provides a stoichiometric representation of collagen type I synthesis. PICP was measured by ELISA (Microvue) in serum at baseline (n=436) and after six months (n=343). Cox proportional hazards regression was used to analyze time to primary composite endpoint, i.e., all-cause death and recurrent cardiovascular event. Results Median (IQR) of PICP was 76 (62, 100) ng/mL at baseline and increased to 97 (77, 126) ng/mL after six months (p&lt;0.001). Baseline PICP was higher in those with age&gt;median vs. those &lt;median (80 vs. 73 ng/ml, p=0.03), but not different in those with pEF (n=393; 76 (62, 99) ng/ml) vs. mrEF (n=44; 80 (61, 107) ng/ml), p=0.533. Baseline PICP was lower in those experiencing a primary endpoint vs. those without (median 70 vs. 77 ng/mL, p=0.043). ΔPICP was increased in both groups; BB users: n=116 up/30 down, and no users: n=122 up/28 down (both p&lt;0.001), with no difference in ΔPICP between BB users (+20 (+2, +41) ng/mL) vs. no users (+24 (+5, +40) ng/mL), p=0.371 (Table). In multivariable analysis, PICP was not associated with the primary composite endpoint (hazard ratio 0.842=[95% confidence interval, 0.074, 9.530]), p=0.889.
