title: Ivabradine for hemodynamic optimization and catecholamine weaning in cardiogenic shock: a retrospective cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background The management of cardiogenic shock (CS) and failure of catecholamine weaning is challenging, particularly in patients with concomitant atrial fibrillation (AF). Because ivabradine primarily acts on the sinus node, its role in patients with AF remains uncertain. We therefore specifically evaluated the hemodynamic effects of ivabradine in the atrial fibrillation subpopulation of patients with CS and unsuccessful catecholamine withdrawal. Methods This subgroup analysis included 12 patients with atrial fibrillation selected from a cohort of 39 individuals admitted to the Cardiology Department of our University Hospital, for cardiogenic shock with a failed catecholamine weaning study, between July 2024 and May 2025. All patients received ivabradine at a dose of 5 mg twice daily. Clinical, echocardiographic, and hemodynamic parameters were assessed at baseline and 48 hours after treatment initiation. Results In this atrial fibrillation subgroup, heart rate significantly decreased from 111.75 ± 31.06 bpm to 89.08 ± 20.09 bpm (p = 0.005). Importantly, this reduction was not associated with hemodynamic deterioration. Systolic arterial pressure increased from 101.75 ± 16.35 mmHg to 106.83 ± 10.63 mmHg, although not reaching statistical significance (p = 0.284). Mean arterial pressure rose modestly from 87.38 ± 12.66 mmHg to 92.69 ± 9.16 mmHg (p = 0.186), and diastolic pressure remained overall stable. Echocardiographic assessment demonstrated significant improvements. Velocity time integral increased from 7 (6–8) cm to 9.5 (8–10) cm (p &lt; 0.001), and stroke volume significantly improved from 21.98 (18.84–25.12) mL to 29.83 (25.12–31.4) mL (p &lt; 0.001). Cardiac output showed a slight, non-significant increase (2.56 ± 0.87 to 2.69 ± 0.76 L/min; p = 0.540), and cardiac power output rose modestly without statistical significance (0.44 ± 0.18 to 0.49 ± 0.16 W; p = 0.146). Systemic vascular resistance remained stable (p = 0.740). Notably, ventriculo-arterial coupling significantly improved from 6.55 ± 2.77 to 4.78 ± 1.61 (p = 0.002), reflecting enhanced cardiovascular efficiency even in the context of atrial fibrillation. Conclusions Among patients with cardiogenic shock and prior catecholamine weaning failure, the atrial fibrillation subpopulation demonstrated significant heart rate reduction and improvement in stroke volume and ventriculo-arterial coupling after ivabradine initiation, without deterioration of arterial pressure or vascular resistance. These findings suggest that ivabradine may be hemodynamically safe and potentially beneficial even in selected CS patients with atrial fibrillation, warranting further prospective investigationEvolution of hemodynamic parameters
title: Ivabradine in cardiogenic shock with catecholamine weaning failure: focus on the atrial fibrillation subpopulation

abstract: Abstract Background Recent research increasingly highlights the importance of extracorporeal veno-arterial membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) with (ECpella) or without Impella for the management of refractory cardiogenic shock (CS) resulting from acute myocardial infarction (AMI). However, there is a notable lack of large-scale, randomized trials that aim to head-to-head comparison of VA-ECMO versus ECpella for treating AMI-related CS. Purpose In order to assess this gap in the literature, we conducted a meta-analysis restricted to studies providing direct, head-to-head comparisons of these two mechanical circulatory support modalities to evaluate differences in 30-day mortality and device-related complications such as critical limb ischemia and major bleeding. Methods This meta-analysis included exclusively studies examining patients undergoing treatment with VA-ECMO with or without Impella for managing AMI-related CS. The primary outcome was the 30-day mortality rate, while secondary outcomes were major bleeding events and ischemic vascular complications. To estimate incidence rates, a random-effects model that used generic inverse-variance weighting for statistical aggregation was employed. The random effects Mantel-Haenszel method was utilized to calculate relative risks (RRs) and pooled mean differences (MDs), along with their respective 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for both categorical and continuous data. Results A total of 13 studies involving 8,288 patients were incorporated into this meta-analysis (Figure 1). The mean age of participants ranged from 56.31 ± 13.9 years in the ECMO cohort to 59.23 ± 10.77 years in the ECpella cohort without any statistically significant differences between the two groups. The results indicated that the ECpella strategy (2,652 patients) was associated with a significantly reduced 30-day mortality rate when compared to VA-ECMO alone (5,636 patients) (RR 0.88, CI 0.78 to 0.99, p=0.04), although the use of ECpella led to statistically significant higher bleeding (RR 1.44, C.I. 1.09 to 1.8, p=0.01) and ischemia complications (RR 1.63, C.I. 1.01 to 2.19, p=0.045). Lactate levels, available in 9 of the included studies, ranged from 4.5 to 12.7 mmol/l in the ECpella cohort and from 3.3 to 13.5 mmol/l in the VA-ECMO cohort, highlighting a serious state of shock. The comparison revealed no statistically significant differences in lactate levels between the two groups (SMD 0.07, CI -0.15 to 0.29). Accordingly age, pH were similar in both groups. Conclusions This meta-analysis indicates that the use of ECpella may be linked to a reduced mortality rate compared to VA-ECMO alone in ischemia-induced CS, despite the higher ischemic and bleeding complications associated with the combined use of these devices. Our findings may imply that Impella should serve as an early escalation therapy option for patients experiencing AMI-related CS treated with a VA-ECMO.Figure 1
title: Head to head comparison of ECPELLA versus venoarterial-ECMO in Myocardial Infarction associated cardiogenic shock: a meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Vasoactive therapy is central to the management of cardiogenic shock (CS). Although current guidelines recommend norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor, epinephrine remains used in clinical practice, particularly in advanced shock states. Comparative evidence on clinical outcomes remains limited and predominantly observational. Purpose To evaluate the association between epinephrine versus norepinephrine use and clinical outcomes in patients with cardiogenic shock. Methods A systematic search of MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane databases was performed to identify studies comparing epinephrine and norepinephrine in adult patients with CS. Randomised and observational studies were eligible. Eight studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Of these, four observational studies reported multivariable-adjusted mortality estimates suitable for quantitative pooling, and two studies reported outcomes related to continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Adjusted odds ratios (aORs) for mortality were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis with Hartung–Knapp adjustment. Risk ratios (RRs) were pooled for CRRT outcomes using random-effects models. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. Risk of bias was evaluated using validated tools appropriate to study design. Analyses were performed using R (RStudio version 2026.01.0, Build 392). Results Eight studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Across studies, epinephrine use was associated with greater metabolic derangement, higher vasoactive requirements, and increased markers of organ dysfunction. Four observational studies reporting adjusted mortality estimates were included in the quantitative analysis. Epinephrine use was associated with higher short-term mortality compared with norepinephrine (random-effects aOR 2.73; 95% CI 1.01–7.35; I² = 63.7%) (Figure 1). Two studies reported CRRT outcomes. Epinephrine use was associated with a higher risk of CRRT requirement (random-effects RR 3.22; 95% CI 1.78–5.82; I² = 0%) (Figure 2). Conclusion(s) In patients with cardiogenic shock, epinephrine use is associated with worse short-term clinical outcomes, including higher mortality and increased need for renal replacement therapy, compared with norepinephrine. These findings are consistent with current guideline recommendations favouring norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor in CS. However, given the limited number of studies and the observational nature of the available evidence, residual confounding cannot be excluded, and adequately powered randomised trials are warranted.Short-Term MortalityContinuous Renal Replacement Therapy

title: Epinephrine versus norepinephrine in cardiogenic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis of adjusted clinical outcomes

abstract: Abstract Introduction The Society for Cardiovascular Angiography & Interventions (SCAI) cardiogenic shock (CS) classification has been complemented by newer staging systems, including the Cardiogenic Shock Working Group classification (CSWG-SCAI) and the updated SCAI-2025 (1,2). The CSWG-SCAI focusses on selected ranges of non-invasive clinical parameters reflective of hypotension and hypoperfusion, whereas the SCAI-2025 classification recommends incorporation of invasive hemodynamic parameters for severity staging as hemodynamic profiling positively impacts prognosis. However, invasive metrics are often unavailable at heart failure related-CS (HF-CS) diagnosis, potentially hampering its clinical use in the early phase of CS. During this phase, rapid bedside staging is essential to guide escalation or de-escalation of CS therapy in attempt to improve prognosis. Purpose This study aims to compare the prognostic performance of the CSWG-SCAI and SCAI-2025 classifications at HF-CS diagnosis and after 24 hours. Methods This is a retrospective, multicenter study of patients admitted with HF-CS. HF-CS was diagnosed at the time of initiation of vasoactive–inotropic therapy. The primary endpoint was time-to-event 30-day all-cause mortality. Cox models were used to analyze the relationship between SCAI definitions and survival, adjusting for age, sex, body mass index, and chronic kidney disease, from both baseline and 24 hours. Discrimination was evaluated as the bootstrapped out-of-sample average time-dependent AUC over 30-day window (iAUC). Results In 469 HF-CS patients (mean age 70 ±14 years, 37% female) without available invasive hemodynamic data, 21% had de novo heart failure and 47% had LVEF &lt;30%. Both classifications were associated with 30-day mortality at the time of HF-CS diagnosis (P&lt;0.0001 for CSWG-SCAI and P=0.016 for SCAI-2025) and at 24 hours (P=0.01 for both). Discriminative performance of the models was moderate and comparable between the two scoring systems at both diagnosis (iAUC SCAI 2025 0.63, iAUC CSWG 0.65, DiAUC 0.02 (-0.04, 0.08) p = 0.44) and at 24 hours after HF-CS diagnosis iAUC SCAI 2025 0.64, iAUC CSWG 0.63, DiAUC -0.01 (-0.08, 0.05) p = 0.77). Conclusions Among patients with HF-CS, the CSWG–SCAI and SCAI-2025 classifications showed similar prognostic discrimination at HF-CS diagnosis and after 24 hours. However, the CSWG–SCAI 2025 classification appears to better prognosticate HF-CS patients as it demonstrated a clear, stepwise increase in mortality from Stage A to B at 24 hours. Additionally, the SCAI-2025 classification failed to stage patients as Stage D since it requires documented failure of CS therapy. Taken together, these observations suggest that CSWG–SCAI may be especially useful during the initial stages of HF-CS management. Alternatively, in more advanced trajectories in which hemodynamic indices are available, the SCAI-2025 may prove a superior a CS staging systemFigure 1.
title: The same, but different. 2025-SCAI and CSWG-SCAI shock classifications in heart failure-related cardiogenic shock

abstract: Abstract Background Women with infarct-related cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS) are underrepresented in randomised trials and may experience different clinical outcomes compared with men. Whether sex independently influences mortality in AMI-CS and whether treatment effects of extracorporeal life support (ECLS) differ by sex remain insufficiently defined. Purpose To investigate sex-specific differences in outcomes and treatment effects in patients with AMI-CS enrolled in the randomised ECLS-SHOCK trial. Methods This prespecified secondary analysis included 417 patients with AMI-CS randomised to early unselected ECLS plus usual medical treatment or usual medical treatment alone. The primary endpoint was 30-day all-cause mortality; the secondary endpoint was 12-month mortality. Hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were derived using multivariable Cox regression models adjusted for age, admission creatinine and lactate and multivessel coronary artery disease. Results Of 417 patients, 78 (18.7%) were women; median age was 63 years (IQR 56–70) in men and 65 years (IQR 58–72) in women (p=0.11). Women had lower serum creatinine (1.1 vs. 1.3 mg/dL; p&lt;0.001), less multivessel disease (58.1% vs. 68.7%, p=0.005) and fewer prior percutaneous coronary interventions (7.8% vs. 19%, p=0.018). Lactate levels on admission were comparable. Revascularisation strategy and cannulation techniques were similar, whereas mechanical ventilation was less frequent in women (85.5% vs. 93.3%; p=0.025). Thirty-day mortality was higher in women (57.7% vs. 46.3%). Female sex was not significantly associated with the unadjusted 30-day mortality (HR 1.38, 95% CI 0.98–1.92), but after adjustment (adjusted HR 1.69, 95% CI 1.18–2.42). In women, 30-day mortality was 56.4% with ECLS versus 59.0% with usual care (p=0.82); in men, corresponding rates were 45.9% and 46.7% (p=0.87), respectively. No sex-by-treatment interaction was observed (p=0.89), indicating no evidence of a sex-specific treatment effect. At 12 months, all-cause mortality was 61.5% in women and 54.0% in men (Figure 1). Although the unadjusted association between female sex and 12-month mortality was not statistically significant (HR 1.28, 95% CI 0.93–1.75), female sex remained independently associated with mortality after multivariable adjustment (adjusted HR 1.52, 95% CI 1.08–2.14). Conclusion In this secondary analysis of ECLS-SHOCK, female sex was independently associated with higher 30-day and 12-month all-cause mortality after adjustment for baseline characteristics in patients with severe CS. The treatment effect of early ECLS did not differ by sex. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the limited number of women (n=78) and the exclusion of 28 patients from adjusted analyses due to missing data.12-month all-cause mortality
title: Sex differences in infarct–related cardiogenic shock: a secondary analysis of the ECLS–SHOCK trial

abstract: Abstract Background Percutaneous microaxial flow pumps such as Impella are increasingly used in cardiogenic shock (CS) and complex high-risk indicated PCI (CHIP). Loss of pulsatility (LoP) during Impella support, defined as a transient reduction in pulse pressure &lt;20 mmHg for &gt;5 seconds, reflects ventriculo-arterial uncoupling and profound ventricular unloading. However, its clinical and prognostic implications remain poorly defined. Methods We analyzed data from the international multicentric IMMERGE registry including patients treated with contemporary Impella devices (CP, 5.0, 5.5) between January 2013 and January 2025. Among 1019 enrolled patients, LoP data were available in 593 cases. Patients were stratified according to the occurrence of LoP during support. Multivariable logistic regression assessed predictors of LoP and its association with 30-day mortality. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated long-term mortality (up to 1 year). Hemodynamic and biochemical trajectories were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Results LoP occurred in 170 of 593 patients (28%). It was more frequent in patients presenting with CS (64.1% vs. 37.8%, p&lt;0.001), cardiac arrest (40.8% vs. 12.8%, p&lt;0.001), and acute vessel occlusion (44.0% vs. 22.9%, p&lt;0.001). Independent predictors of LoP were cardiogenic shock (OR 1.62, p=0.01), cardiac arrest (OR 2.89, p&lt;0.001), and acute vessel occlusion (OR 1.56, p&lt;0.001). At 30 days, LoP was associated with significantly higher all-cause mortality (43.5% vs. 20.0%, p&lt;0.001), acute kidney injury, major bleeding, and sepsis. After adjustment, LoP independently predicted 30-day mortality (OR 2.2, 95% CI 1.2–3.8, p=0.007), together with CS (OR 9.5, p&lt;0.001). Hemodynamically, LoP patients exhibited lower SvO₂, higher lactate levels, lower systolic blood pressure, higher heart rate, and increased vasoactive support requirements. At a mean follow-up of 499±100 days, crude all-cause mortality remained higher in the LoP group (54.7% vs. 35.6%, p&lt;0.001), but LoP was not independently associated with long-term mortality after multivariable adjustment (HR 1.19, p=0.53). Age, CKD, cardiac arrest, and CS were independent predictors of long-term mortality. Conclusions Loss of pulsatility during Impella support is frequent and identifies a subgroup of critically ill patients with markedly increased short-term mortality and end-organ complications. LoP independently predicts 30-day mortality but not long-term mortality after adjustment. Recognition of LoP should prompt immediate hemodynamic reassessment and intensified clinical management. Further studies are warranted to clarify mechanistic pathways and evaluate targeted mitigation strategies.
