Conclusion This study demonstrates that T2DM modulates coronary atherosclerotic lesion severity by altering the differentiation phenotype of adipose-derived stem cells, revealing a novel mechanism underlying T2DM-related atherosclerosis.Fig.1
title: Empagliflozin attenuates coronary atherosclerosis by promoting the differentiation of pericoronary adipose-derived stem cells

abstract: Abstract Background Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) alleviates ischemic symptoms in stable coronary artery disease (CAD) but does not improve long-term cardiovascular outcomes. Recognizing lesions confer cardiovascular risk even after PCI is critical to optimize outcomes. Purpose This study aimed to assess whether coronary CT angiography (CCTA)-derived plaque parameters reflecting inflammation and component are associated with future risk after PCI Materials and Methods Patients with stable CAD who underwent CCTA followed by PCI within 30 days were included across three tertiary centers in 2021–2022. Pre-PCI fat attenuation index (FAI, a marker of local coronary inflammation) and plaque components (calcified, noncalcified, low-attenuation) were quantified from CCTA at PCI-treated lesions. The primary endpoint was the composite of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), including cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, repeat revascularization, or hospitalization for unstable angina. Periprocedural myocardial infarction (PMI) was evaluated as a potential mediator. Results Among 2,013 patients included, 226 (11.2%) experienced MACE over a median follow-up of 2.5 years. Higher FAI (adjusted HR per SD: 1.53, 95% CI: 1.34–1.74, P&lt;0.001) and greater noncalcified burden (adjusted HR per SD: 1.19, 95% CI: 1.04–1.36, P=0.012) were independently associated with increased MACE risk after PCI. The prognostic effect of FAI was stronger in patients with hyperlipidemia (P for interaction=0.006). PMI mediated 1.7% and 4.5% of the associations of FAI and noncalcified burden with MACE, respectively. Conclusion Plaque inflammation and noncalcified burden are associated with prognosis after PCI. These findings support the potential utility of these markers in guiding future investigations of treatment strategies.
title: Plaque inflammation and noncalcified burden predict adverse events after percutaneous coronary intervention

abstract: Abstract Background Current guidelines advocate physiology-guided revascularisation in stable ischaemic heart disease (SIHD), with the expectation that functional optimisation may standardise outcomes across coronary territories. Computational pressure-flow dynamics-derived fractional flow reserve (caFFR) is an angiography-derived index that determines FFR without invasive pressure wire or hyperaemic stimulus. However, whether physiological guidance fully accounts for the inherent risk associated with left anterior descending (LAD) artery lesions remains incompletely understood. Purpose To determine whether caFFR-concordant treatment mitigates the established prognostic disadvantage of LAD lesions in SIHD. Methods In this retrospective cohort study of 1679 SIHD patients, caFFR was analysed in 5037 vessels. Patients underwent revascularization at the discretion of the proceduralist according to the angiographic and clinical data available at the time. Treatment decisions were classified by concordance with caFFR (revascularisation for caFFR ≤0.80; deferral for &gt;0.80). The primary endpoint was the vessel-oriented composite endpoint, defined as vessel-related cardiovascular mortality, myocardial infarction (MI) and unplanned revascularisation at median 4.4-year follow-up. Results Among 3500 analysable vessels, 2720 (77.7%) were treated concordantly with caFFR, with 827 (30.4%) LAD and 1893 (69.6%) non-LAD vessels. Despite physiology-concordant management, LAD lesions demonstrated significantly higher event rates than non-LAD lesions (VOCE: 7.1% vs 4.8%, P=0.014; MI: 1.9% vs 0.8%, P=0.010). In multivariable analysis, concordantly managed LAD lesions remained independently associated with increased risk of VOCE (HR 1.49; 95% CI 1.08-2.07; P=0.016) and MI (HR 2.46; 95% CI 1.21-4.97; P=0.012). Notably, significant interaction was observed between LAD territory and ischaemic status (P-interaction=0.040): ischaemic LAD lesions (caFFR ≤0.80) exhibited heightened risk (HR 1.79; 95% CI 1.13–2.83), whereas non-ischaemic LAD lesions showed no excess risk (HR 0.90; 95% CI 0.56–1.46). Conclusion Even when revascularisation decisions are concordant with caFFR, LAD lesions continue to confer higher long-term risk of vessel-oriented events and myocardial infarction compared with non-LAD lesions. These findings suggest that physiological guidance, while essential, may benefit from integration with anatomical and vessel-specific considerations. Comprehensive risk stratification incorporating both functional assessment and coronary territory may further optimize decision-making in LAD disease.Kaplan-Meier Curves for VOCEKaplan-Meier Curves for MI
title: Left anterior descending artery lesions retain excess risk despite coronary angiography derived-fractional flow reserve concordant revascularisation

abstract: Abstract Background Real-world evidence comparing clinical outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) using different guidance strategies, particularly among patients with chronic coronary syndromes (CCS) in Thailand, is limited. Although advanced technologies, including intracoronary physiology and intravascular imaging, can improve lesion assessment and procedural optimisation, their impact on 1-year major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) outcomes remains uncertain. Purpose The aim of this study was to use a large real-world multicentre registry to compare 1-year MACE outcomes (myocardial infarction, stroke, death) among patients with CCS undergoing PCI guided by fractional flow reserve (FFR), intravascular imaging, or angiography alone, and to define the clinical outcomes associated with PCI revascularisation strategies in a real-world Thai population. Methods This study emulated a target trial using data from the Thai PCI registry, a nationwide multicentre prospective PCI registry. Among 19,701 patients, 8,135 with CCS were classified according to the use of angiography, FFR, or intravascular imaging, including intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) and optical coherence tomography (OCT). The primary outcome was 1-year MACE. Inverse probability weighting based on propensity scores was applied to balance baseline covariates and estimate comparative effects between strategies. Results At 1 year, MACE occurred in 858 patients (10.5%). Compared with angiography-only guided PCI, the estimated relative risk of MACE was 1.16 (95% confidence interval 0.98–1.35) with intravascular imaging (IVUS or OCT) guidance and 0.94 (95% confidence interval 0.22–1.67) with FFR guidance. Conclusion In patients with CCS undergoing PCI, FFR-guided and intravascular imaging-guided strategies were associated with similar 1-year MACE outcomes compared with angiography-only-guided PCI after adjustment for baseline differences. The results call for optimal utilisation of adjunctive intravascular technologies and proper operator training in real-world settings.Forest plot of Treatment effectCharacteristics of patients between group
title: Comparing the impact of intravascular imaging, fractional flow reserve, and angiographic guidance on one-year outcomes of PCI in patients with chronic coronary syndromes: an emulated trial

abstract: Abstract Introduction Refractory angina affects patients who remain symptomatic despite optimal medical therapy and for whom further revascularization is not feasible. Therapeutic options for this population are limited. The coronary sinus reducer (CSR) has emerged as a device-based treatment aimed at improving symptoms and functional capacity in this patient group. Evidence is growing, but real-world data remain scarce. Purpose To investigate whether Coronary Sinus Reducer (CSR) implantation is safe and efficient in a real-world cohort of patients presenting with refractory angina. Methods Twenty-six consecutive patients diagnosed with refractory angina, objective evidence of myocardial ischemia, despite receiving optimal medical therapy, in whom further revascularization was not feasible, were treated with CSR at our Institution between September 2023 and October 2025. The study endpoints, assesed at baseline and 3-months, were defined as changes in angina severity (Canadian Cardiovascular Society [CCS] class, the 7-item Seattle Angina Questionnaire [SAQ-7]), exercise tolerance (6-minute walking distance [6MWD]) and a change in pharmacological antianginal therapy together with safety outcomes (procedural success and complications). Results A total of 87,5% of the patients presented a reduction in angina severity reflected by a downgrade of at least one CCS class (P &lt; 0.0001) over the 3 months of follow up, as compared with the baseline. Angina control, quantified by the SAQ-7 summary score, improved from a mean (SD) of 15.95 (15.32) at baseline to 55.38 (27.74) at 3 months (P &lt; 0.0001). A similar pattern was observed in individual SAQ-7 domains. Physical limitation improved from 4.60 (2.68) to 10.08 (3.67) (P &lt; 0.0001), angina frequency decreased from 4.68 (2.04) to 8.72 (2.23) (P &lt; 0.0001), and quality-of-life scores rose from 3.20 (1.38) to 6.88 (2.52) (P &lt; 0.0001). The number of antianginal medications declined from a median of 3 (IQR 2–4) at baseline to 2 (IQR 1–3) at 3 months (P = 0.0046). The median 6-minute walk distance increased from 300 m (IQR 180-420) at baseline to 375 m (IQR 240-450) after 3 months (P = 0.0313). Procedural success was achieved in all patients, with no device related complications. Conclusions In this real-world, single-center experience, implantation of Coronary Sinus Reducer was safe and associated with marked improvements in symptom burden, quality of life, and functional capacity after 3 months. The procedure led to a significant reduction in CCS class, higher SAQ-7 scores across all domains, improved exercise tolerance, and decreased reliance on antianginal medication. These findings support the clinical benefit of the coronary sinus reducer as a safe and effective therapeutic option in patients with refractory angina unsuitable for revascularization.
title: Safety and efficacy of coronary sinus narrowing for treating refractory angina in real-world setting - single center experience

abstract: Abstract Background According to current guidelines for the care of chronic coronary syndromes (CCS), referral for invasive coronary angiography (CA) should be guided by a diagnostic approach based on clinical probability and non-invasive tests, without taking into account circulating biomarkers in this decision-making process. [1] Lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a), a well-known biomarker for atherosclerosis, is linked to a more severe presentation of coronary artery disease (CAD), yet its role in guiding invasive diagnostic evaluation in the chronic setting remains undefined. [2] Objectives The aim of the study was to examine the association of Lp(a) levels and significant CAD requiring coronary revascularization in a chronic setting. Methods The study included patients from the prospective CaRD registry who underwent CA at our facility between November 2019 and February 2026 and who had either an established or suspected CCS diagnosis (based on clinical presentation, available laboratory, and non-invasive test results). Logistic regression analysis was used to investigate the relationship between Lp(a) levels and the requirement for coronary revascularization (either percutaneous or surgical). Additionally, via Mann-Whitney test and χ2-squared test we compared baseline patients' characteristics, including age, sex, creatinine, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), Lp(a) levels, Synergy between Percutaneous Coronary Intervention with Taxus and Cardiac Surgery (SYNTAX) I score, prior known CAD, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, prediabetes/diabetes and smoking history, between the group that received conservative treatment and the group that underwent subsequent revascularization. A p-value of 0.05 was regarded as statistically significant. Statistical analysis was conducted in MedCalc Statistical Software version 14.8.1, Ostend, Belgium. Results Our observational registry-based study included 1315 patients with a median age of 68 years (IQR 61-74). Baseline characteristics of patients included in the study are displayed in Table 1. A total of 309 patients (23.5%) required revascularization based on angiographic findings. Logistic regression analysis demonstrated a positive association between higher Lp(a) levels and the subsequent coronary revascularization, p = .0009 (Figure 1). The positive link for Lp(a) levels remained significant after multiple regression analysis adjusted for age, sex, LDL, prior known CAD, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, prediabetes/diabetes and smoking history (p = .0014), and the model as a whole was significant (p&lt;.0001). Conclusion In this observational cohort, higher Lp(a) concentrations were associated with subsequent coronary revascularization, suggesting a possible role in refining risk assessment in CCS. Before Lp(a) is taken into consideration for incorporation into clinical decision-making algorithms, these exploratory findings need to be prospectively validated.
title: Can lipoprotein(a) predict the need for coronary artery revascularization in a chronic setting?

abstract: Abstract Background Subclinical dysglycemia contributes to atherosclerotic progression even in individuals without established diabetes mellitus. However, the relationship between composite dysglycaemic indices and coronary anatomical complexity in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remains insufficiently characterized. Purpose To evaluate the association between multiple dysglycaemic indices and coronary anatomical complexity assessed by the SYNTAX score in non-diabetic patients presenting with ACS and to compare their predictive performance. Methods This prospective observational study included 240 consecutive non-diabetic patients admitted with ACS who underwent coronary angiography. Patients with known diabetes, previous coronary revascularisation, chronic kidney disease, significant valvular disease or anaemia were excluded. Metabolic parameters measured within 24 hours of admission included fasting plasma glucose, glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), triglycerides and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. The triglyceride–glucose (TyG) index and atherogenic index of plasma (AIP) were calculated. Coronary anatomical complexity was quantified using the SYNTAX score by two blinded interventional cardiologists. High complexity was defined as SYNTAX score ≥22. Correlation analysis assessed associations between metabolic indices and SYNTAX score. Multivariable linear and logistic regression models were adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, hypertension, smoking status, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and C-reactive protein. Discrimination was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results Mean age was 58±9 years and 70% were male. High SYNTAX score (≥22) was observed in 86 patients (35.8%). Patients with high SYNTAX score had significantly higher HbA1c (6.0±0.5% vs 5.6±0.4%, p&lt;0.001), TyG index (9.0±0.5 vs 8.6±0.4, p&lt;0.001) and AIP (0.29±0.09 vs 0.21±0.07, p&lt;0.001). TyG index showed the strongest correlation with SYNTAX score (r=0.47, p&lt;0.001). In multivariable logistic regression analysis, independent predictors of high SYNTAX score were TyG index (odds ratio 2.62, 95% confidence interval 1.61–4.27, p&lt;0.001), HbA1c (odds ratio 1.98, 95% confidence interval 1.22–3.19, p=0.005), age (odds ratio 1.04 per year, p=0.003) and hypertension (odds ratio 1.76, p=0.04). Area under the curve values were 0.81 for TyG index, 0.74 for HbA1c and 0.76 for AIP. A combined metabolic model demonstrated an area under the curve of 0.87. Conclusion(s) In non-diabetic patients presenting with ACS, dysglycaemic indices are independently associated with increased coronary anatomical complexity. The TyG index demonstrated the strongest predictive performance. Assessment of subclinical metabolic dysfunction may enhance early identification of patients with complex coronary disease.Multivariate Linear RegressionROC Curve Analysis
title: Association of dysglycaemic indices with coronary anatomical complexity in non-diabetic patients presenting with acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background New therapies targeting different residual risk pathways have been shown to reduce recurrent events in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD). Plaque regression has been proposed as one mechanism underlying these benefits, but the comparative effects of these strategies on plaque regression remain unclear. Purpose To evaluate the comparative effects of different residual risk–targeted therapies, added to statin treatment, on coronary plaque regression as assessed by intracoronary imaging (intravascular ultrasound [IVUS] or optical coherence tomography [OCT]) or coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA). Methods Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies evaluating the effects of residual risk–targeted therapies, added to statin treatment, on coronary plaque regression assessed by intracoronary imaging (IVUS or OCT) or CCTA were included. A frequentist network meta-analysis was performed to estimate mean differences (MDs). The primary outcome was total atheroma volume (TAV), and the secondary outcome was percent atheroma volume (PAV). Additional analyses included a sensitivity analysis excluding studies not using high-intensity statin therapy and a subgroup analysis stratified by diabetes mellitus status (yes vs no). Statin-only therapy served as the comparator. Treatment strategies were ranked using P-scores, ranging from 0 (worst performance) to 1 (best performance). Results A total of 30 RCTs and 10 observational studies testing 7 treatment strategies (i.e., ezetimibe, eicosapentaenoic acid [EPA], glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists [GLP-1 RAs], icosapent ethyl [IPE], proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitors [PCSK9i], polyunsaturated fatty acids [PUFA], colchicine and sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors [SGLT2i]) were included in the network (Figure 1). Mean follow-up was 19 weeks. Compared with statin-only therapy, the greatest reduction in TAV was observed with IPE (MD -77.50; 95% CI -302.47; 147.47) followed by SGLT2i (MD -26.29; 95% CI -79.36; 26.78), PCSK9i (MD -17.90; 95% CI -29.66; -6.13) and colchicine (MD -15.90; 95% CI -52.02; 20.22), while other agents showed limited effects (ezetimibe = -4.53, PUFA = -0.87, GLP-1 RAs = 39.30)(Figure 2). Treatment ranking showed that PCSK9i (P-score = 0.739), IPE (P-score = 0.735), and SGLT2i (P-score = 0.717) performed best for TAV regression. Results were consistent across secondary analyses. For PAV, the greatest reductions were observed with SGLT2i and EPA, followed by PCSK9i, ezetimibe, and GLP-1 RAs. Conclusion Among patients with coronary artery disease receiving residual risk–targeted therapies on top of statin treatment, PCSK9i, IPE, and SGLT2i, were associated with the greatest degrees of plaque regression.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Effects of residual risk–targeted therapies on coronary plaque regression: a network meta-analysis of 40 studies

abstract: Abstract Background Thyroid hormones (TH) exert critical permissive effects on insulin and catecholamines, indirectly modulating lipid metabolism. While hypothyroidism is linked to increased cardiovascular risk, the impact of treated thyroid status on achieving ESC-mandated LDL-C targets (&lt;55 mg/dL) remains controversial. Methods We analyzed 368 consecutive post-Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI) patients stratified by thyroid status: Treated Hypothyroidism (on levothyroxine) vs. Euthyroid Controls. LDL-C levels were collected at 0, 6, 12, and 24 months. The primary endpoint was LDL-C goal achievement (&lt;55 mg/dL) at 6 months (2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines). Continuous variables (median [IQR]) were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test, and categorical outcomes using Fisher’s exact test. Adjusted multivariate logistic regression (age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, CKD) identified independent predictors of goal failure. Results Baseline LDL-C was comparable between groups (85.5 vs. 90.5 mg/dL; p=0.422).Temporal Dynamics: At 6 months, Treated Hypothyroid (H) patients showed a significant response lag compared to Controls (C) (62.5 vs. 56.5 mg/dL; p=0.008). However, this trend reversed long-term, with H patients achieving numerically lower LDL-C at 12 months (46.5 vs. 53.0 mg/dL; p=0.910) and 24 months (49.5 vs. 53.0 mg/dL; p=0.560).Multivariate Predictors: Despite the initial 6-month lag, treated hypothyroidism emerged as a potent independent protector against long-term goal failure (Adjusted OR: 0.106; 95% CI: 0.022–0.525; p=0.006). Conversely, Diabetes (OR: 3.13) and Male Sex (OR: 2.42) were confirmed as primary barriers.Clinical Safety: New coronary events showed no significant differences (21.7% H vs. 19.7% C; p=0.812). Safety profiles for NSTEMI, STEMI, and stent restenosis were comparable across all categories (all p &gt; 0.05). Conclusions A "Hypothyroidism Paradox" exists in post-PCI management, characterized by a critical 6-month response lag where treated hypothyroid patients underperform compared to euthyroid controls (p=0.008), creating a vulnerable metabolic window where suboptimal thyroid replacement therapy (TRT) directly hinders early LDL-C clearance. Thyroid hormones might enhance biliary cholesterol elimination, increase hepatic LDL-receptor expression, and boost cholesterol ester transferase activity. Clinical practice must prioritize aggressive thyroid optimization within the first 6 months post-PCI to eliminate this early barrier to lipid targets. However, once biochemical euthyroidism is stabilized, TRT acts as a long-term metabolic catalyst, yielding superior goal attainment (aOR: 0.106; p=0.006) through the described mechanisms. The relative lag in euthyroid patients suggests that undiagnosed subclinical hypothyroidism could be a hidden factor in "statin resistance," warranting systematic TSH screening.Table 1 Thyroid Paradox
title: The hypothyroidism paradox: treated thyroid status as a long-term catalyst for LDL-C target attainment post-percutaneous coronary intervention

abstract: Abstract Introduction Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is associated with a persistently high risk of recurrent ischemic events, particularly during the first year after discharge. The 2025 ESC Focused Update on Dyslipidaemias and the 2023 ESC Guidelines for ACS endorse a “strike early, strike strong” approach (STS), emphasizing rapid treatment intensification to achieve LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL and/or ≥50% reduction from baseline in very-high-risk patients. However, real-world data assessing the clinical impact of a structured “fire-to-target” strategy (using the full range of modern lipid-lowering agents) remain limited. Purpose To evaluate whether a structured “fire-to-target” strategy, consistent with the “STS” paradigm, improves achievement of the LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL target and reduces 12-month major adverse cardiovascular events compared with prior standard-of-care management. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort study including consecutive patients discharged alive after ACS (STEMI, NSTEMI, or unstable angina) between January 2022 and December 2023. Patients discharged in 2022 received a traditional stepwise lipid-lowering approach, whereas the 2023 group was managed with an early, proactive fire-to-target strategy based on upfront combination lipid-lowering therapy, including high dose statins, ezetimibe, bempedoic acid, PCSK9 inhibitors and inclisiran. Primary endpoints were achievement of LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL at follow-up (at 1, 6, and 12 months after discharge) and a composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, or stroke (3P-MACE) at 12 months.To minimize confounding, analyses were conducted using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW)-adjusted regression models accounting for clinical characteristics and cardiovascular risk factors. Results A total of 710 eligible patients (mean age, 66.0 ± 11.6 years; 51.4% men) were included (353 managed with a stepwise approach and 357 with the fire-to-target strategy). Baseline characteristics were broadly comparable between groups. During follow-up, treatment intensification was more frequent in the fire-to-target group, with greater use of non-statin lipid-lowering therapies. LDL-C levels were significantly lower in the intervention group at 1, 6, and 12 months, translating into a higher proportion of patients achieving the LDL-C target throughout follow-up. The multivariable analysis before IPTW, showed that all-cause mortality (1.7% vs 7.1%; HR, 0.23; 95% CI, 0.10–0.57; p=0.001) and the 3P-MACE (5.9% vs 11%; HR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.30–0.87; p=0.012) at 12 months were significantly lower in the fire-to-target group. After IPTW, the difference in all-cause death (aHR, 0.30; 95% CI, 0.10–0.87; p=0.026) and 3P-MACE (aHR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.26–0.91; p=0.023) between groups remained significant at 1 year. Conclusion In routine clinical practice, a personalized,“fire-to-target” lipid strategy improves LDL-C target achievement and significantly reduces short-term cardiovascular events.
title: Impact of a personalized, fire-to-target lipid-lowering strategy in patients with acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Infarct size is a key determinant of left ventricular remodeling and prognosis after acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) is the reference standard for infarct size quantification; however, its availability and contraindications limit routine clinical use. We developed a novel echocardiographic technique based on three-dimensional speckle-tracking area strain, Scar Imaging, which enables bedside visualization of infarct myocardium and estimation of its size. Purpose To evaluate the inter-modality agreement between Scar Imaging and CMR for quantifying infarct size in AMI. Methods We retrospectively analyzed AMI patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and received both Scar Imaging and CMR during the index hospitalization between June 2022 and December 2024. On CMR, infarct size was quantified from LGE as the percentage of left ventricular (LV) myocardium, using automated software-based analysis. Scar Imaging identifies LV regions with markedly reduced deformation as infarct according to a pre-specified area strain threshold and reports infarct size (Figure 1). Inter-modality agreement was assessed using Pearson correlation, Bland–Altman analysis, mean absolute error (MAE), intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC; two-way random-effects model, absolute agreement), and Deming regression. Results In 40 patients (median age 72 years; 33 men [82.5%]), the median time from PCI to CMR and to echocardiography was 7 and 8 days, respectively. Median CMR-LGE infarct size was 18.0% (IQR 8.69–25.46). Infarct size by Scar Imaging showed a strong correlation with CMR (r=0.755, p&lt;0.01). Bland–Altman analysis showed a small mean bias of −2.19%, with 95% limits of agreement from −19.91% to 15.52% (Figure 2). MAE was 7.56%, and ICC was 0.749, indicating good absolute agreement. Deming regression showed near 1:1 agreement (slope 0.999; intercept −2.18) and suggested no proportional bias. Conclusion Scar Imaging demonstrated good agreement with CMR for infarct size quantification in AMI, with minimal systematic bias and acceptable limits of agreement. It may serve as a practical alternative for infarct size assessment when CMR is unavailable or contraindicated.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Agreement between a novel echocardiographic “Scar Imaging” technique and cardiac magnetic resonance for quantifying infarct size in acute myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Frailty is increasingly prevalent among patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI), yet its impact on care delivery and long-term outcomes at a population level remains poorly characterised. We examined temporal trends in frailty, its association with evidence-based management, and its prognostic implications. Methods We analysed consecutive adults hospitalised with AMI in England and Wales between 2005 and 2019 using linked national registries. Frailty was assessed at index admission using the Secondary Care Administrative Records Frailty index and categorised as fit, mild, moderate, or severe. The primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included cardiovascular death, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), heart failure readmission, reinfarction, and major bleeding. Multivariable Cox and logistic regression models were used. Results Among 931,133 patients hospitalised with AMI, 29.4% were classified as fit, 36.2% had mild frailty, 21.8% moderate frailty, and 12.6% severe frailty. As shown in Table 1, increasing frailty was associated with older age, higher comorbidity burden, and a greater proportion of women. Median age increased from 61 years in fit patients to 80 years in those with severe frailty, while the proportion of females rose from 24.7% to 45.3%. Comorbidity burden increased markedly, with Charlson Comorbidity Index greater than 3 present in 0.5% of fit patients versus 55.6% of those with severe frailty. Patients with increasing frailty were more likely to present with NSTEMI, rising from 52.0% in fit individuals to 79.4% in severe frailty, and had worse haemodynamic profiles and left ventricular systolic function. The prevalence of moderate or severe frailty increased from 22.8% in 2005 to 42.1% in 2019, with severe frailty alone rising from 5.3% to 16.6% (Figure 1). Increasing frailty was associated with lower use of evidence-based care, including coronary angiography, dual antiplatelet therapy, and referral to cardiac rehabilitation. As shown in Figure 2, frailty demonstrated a strong graded association with adverse outcomes. Compared with fit patients, the adjusted hazard of 1-year all-cause mortality increased stepwise across frailty categories, with HR 1.65 (95% CI 1.61 to 1.70) for mild frailty, 2.33 (95% CI 2.27 to 2.40) for moderate frailty, and 3.01 (95% CI 2.93 to 3.10) for severe frailty. Similar dose–response relationships were observed for cardiovascular death, with HR 2.82 (95% CI 2.70 to 2.94), MACE, HR 2.56 (95% CI 2.51 to 2.60), heart failure readmission, HR 3.74 (95% CI 3.61 to 3.88), and major bleeding, HR 1.85 (95% CI 1.78 to 1.92), for severe frailty compared with fit individuals. Conclusion Frailty is increasingly common in contemporary AMI populations and is strongly associated with lower delivery of guideline-recommended care and substantially worse short- and long-term outcomes.Figure 2
title: Evolving burden and consequences of frailty in patients with acute myocardial infarction: evidence from a nationwide cohort

abstract: Abstract Background While cognitive impairment is prevalent in patients with stable coronary artery disease (CAD), its prognostic significance in stable CAD patients remains unclear. Purpose To investigate the impact of baseline cognitive impairment on the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and unplanned revascularisation in a large cohort of patients with stable CAD. Methods In this prospective cohort study of 6,130 stable CAD patients, baseline cognitive function was assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). The primary outcome was MACE, comprising all-cause death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and nonfatal stroke. Unplanned revascularisation was specified as a secondary outcome. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression were used to assess the prognostic impact of cognitive impairment. The robustness of the findings was tested via subgroup analyses, propensity score matching, and sensitivity analyses. Results During a median follow-up of 546 days, MACE occurred in 123 (2.0%) and unplanned revascularisation in 315 (5.1%) of the included patients (mean age 61.2 years, 75.8% male). Cognitive impairment (MoCA score &lt; 24) was highly prevalent among older adults (44.8%), females (50.6%), and patients with lower educational attainment or a high cardiometabolic burden. Patients with cognitive impairment exhibited a significantly higher cumulative incidence of MACE (Log-rank P=0.001), all-cause mortality (P=0.020), and the composite of nonfatal myocardial infarction and stroke (P=0.021), whereas no difference was observed for unplanned revascularisation (P=0.791). In fully adjusted multivariable Cox regression models, baseline cognitive impairment remained a strong independent predictor of MACE (hazard ratio [HR]: 1.58; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.06–2.37; P=0.026). The stability of these findings was confirmed across three sensitivity analysis strategies: using PSM to adjust for confounders, applying standard educational adjustments to MoCA scores, and excluding patients with baseline stroke. Subgroup analyses demonstrated consistent risks across most clinical strata, except in patients with low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) &lt; 1.8 mmol/L, where the adverse prognostic impact of cognitive impairment was attenuated (HR: 0.99; 95% CI: 0.45–2.17; P=0.973).Subgroup analyses demonstrated consistent risks across most clinical strata, except in patients with low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) &lt; 1.8 mmol/L, where the adverse prognostic impact of cognitive impairment was attenuated (HR: 0.99; 95% CI: 0.45–2.17; P=0.973). Conclusion Baseline cognitive impairment is a robust and independent predictor of MACE in patients with stable CAD.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Cognitive screening for cardiovascular risk stratification in stable coronary artery disease: a prospective cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background Non-ischaemic acute myocardial injury (NI-AMInj) carries high long-term mortality, yet no dedicated risk prediction tool exists. Existing scores developed for acute coronary syndromes inadequately capture the systemic pathophysiology of NI-AMInj. Purpose To develop and externally validate an interpretable machine learning model predicting 1-year all-cause mortality in NI-AMInj, and to identify key prognostic drivers. Methods NI-AMInj patients were identified from a regional multi-centre platform (development cohort, 2013–2022) and an independent critical care database (external validation, 2008–2022). NI-AMInj required troponin above the 99th percentile with &gt;20% dynamic change, excluding acute myocardial infarction. The development cohort was split 8:2 for training and internal validation. Feature selection used a consensus strategy across LASSO, Boruta, and recursive feature elimination. Nine algorithms were compared. Performance was evaluated by area under the curve (AUC), calibration, and decision curve analysis. Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) provided interpretability. Results 78,666 patients were included (development: 67,773; external: 10,893; 1-year mortality: 19.3% vs 34.7%). Eleven predictors were selected: age, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), white blood cell count (WBC), pulmonary infection, heart failure, malignancy, intensive care unit admission, cardiology admission, surgical procedures, reperfusion therapy, and statin use. Gradient boosting machine (GBM) achieved optimal performance (internal AUC: 0.783; external AUC: 0.773), with good calibration and positive net clinical benefit. SHAP analysis identified eGFR, WBC, pulmonary infection, age, and heart failure as top prognostic drivers. Statin use and reperfusion showed protective associations. A web-based calculator was deployed for individualised assessment. Conclusions An interpretable GBM model using 11 routine clinical variables accurately predicts 1-year mortality in NI-AMInj with good cross-population generalisability. Renal function and inflammatory markers are dominant prognostic determinants. This tool may support early risk stratification in this high-risk population.SHAP
title: An interpretable machine learning model for predicting 1-year all-cause mortality in patients with non-ischaemic acute myocardial injury: development and external validation

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Anomalous Aortic origins of coronary arteries (AAOCAs) occur infrequently in the adult population, with prevalence estimated at 0.3-2.3%(1). They have been specifically implicated in the occurrence of sudden cardiac death in cardiac arrest survivors and post-mortem studies(2,3). The clinical significance and burden of risk imposed on individuals by the presence of AAOCAs remain uncertain. Thus, we analysed the cardiovascular outcomes of adult patients diagnosed with AAOCAs at our institution. Purpose The 2020 ESC guidelines for the Management of Adult Congenital Heart Disease recommend surgical intervention for high-risk variants with risk defined by a combination of clinical, anatomical and functional frameworks. There is yet to be equipoise on where the burden of risk lies in all patients with AAOCAs, especially in patients diagnosed at an older age. Methods We conducted a retrospective review of all adult patients who had Cardiovascular Computed Tomography scans with contrast at our institution between January 2013 and January 2025. A total of 20292 scans were digitally reviewed using key search terms such as “coronary anomalies”, “anomalous coronaries”, and aberrant coronary”. A total of 188 scans that met the search term criteria were subsequently screened. The primary endpoint was a composite MACE of cardiovascular death, non-fatal stroke, transient ischemic attack (TIA), acute coronary syndromes (ACS) and non-ACS troponin positive events. A simple logistic regression model assessed the impact of coronary anatomy risk profile on the occurrence of MACE. Multivariable logistic regression models assessed the impact of coronary anatomy, CAD RADS class, age and ejection fraction on the occurrence of MACE. Kaplan Meier event-free survival curves were constructed stratified by CADRADS ≥ 3. Results We identified AAOCAs in 96 scans from 93 unique patients, resulting in a prevalence of 0.45% with a median age of 60.8years (IQR:52.8-70.3Y). The circumflex coronary artery origin was most frequently found to be anomalous (n=41, 44%). Of the 21 patients who had stress testing, just 1 of these was positive(4.8%), which occurred in a patient with CADRADS 4 CAD. MACE occurred in 9 patients, of which 3 were non-atherosclerotic events. On univariable analysis, CADRADS was strongly associated with MACE (OR 2.04, 95% CI 1.27–3.28, p=0.003), whereas high-risk inter-arterial anatomy was not (OR 1.75, p=0.43). In multivariable analysis, CADRADS remained independently predictive (adjusted OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.15–3.16). Kaplan–Meier analysis showed no significant survival difference between high- and low-risk anatomy (log-rank p=0.45). The overall discriminative performance of high-risk anatomy alone was poor (AUC 0.57). Conclusion In adults diagnosed with AAOCAs at our institution, obstructive coronary atherosclerosis is the strongest independent predictor of the occurrence of MACE.
title: Cardiovascular outcomes of adults diagnosed with anomalous aortic origin of the coronary arteries

abstract: Abstract Background Risk stratification in right anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery (R-AAOCA) remains challenging. Conventional diameter- and area-based stenosis metrics assume circular geometry and may underestimate hemodynamic relevance in the slit-like, elliptical lumens typical of R-AAOCA. Fluid-dynamics principles suggest that perimeter-dependent resistance may better capture flow limitation. We hypothesized that shape-aware geometric indices derived from coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) outperform conventional metrics for predicting invasive fractional flow reserve (FFR). Purpose To compare the ability of traditional versus shape-aware CCTA-derived geometric parameters to predict hemodynamically significant stenosis in R-AAOCA, using invasive FFR under both adenosine and dobutamine stress as reference standards. Methods Consecutive patients with R-AAOCA who underwent CCTA and invasive FFR during adenosine and dobutamine stress are included in the analysis. CCTA-derived geometric characterization included ostial and intramural lumen area (ILA) measurements, shape descriptors, elliptic ratio (ER = Dmajor/Dminor), circularity (C = 4πA/P²), shape-aware stenosis metrics, including effective and hydraulic diameter stenosis ratios (EDSR, HDSR), based on ED= and HD=4A/P (A = area, P = wetted perimeter). Resistance-based indices integrated geometric severity with lesion extent and angulation, including the resistance index (RI=L×P⁴/A⁴; L=stenosis length), ostial angulation penalty (OAP=Aostial/Aref×[1+tanθ]; θ=take-off angle), and a comprehensive stenosis score (CSS=RI×ER×[1+sinθ]). Hemodynamic significance was defined as FFR ≤0.80. Results A total of 81 patients with R-AAOCA were analyzed. Hemodynamically significant stenosis was present in 6.2% of patients during adenosine stress and 19.8% during dobutamine stress. Figure 1 shows top-performing parameters. Compared to adenosine reference standard, the RI demonstrated high discrimination (AUC=0.97) and achieved 100% sensitivity with 95% specificity at the optimal cutoff. Compared to dobutamine reference standard, overall discrimination was reduced; the ostial minor diameter showed the highest predictive performance (AUC = 0.85) with 100% sensitivity but lower specificity (57%). Resistance-based indices retained strong correlation with FFR under both stress modalities. Conclusion Shape-derived, physics-informed CCTA parameters demonstrate high discriminatory performance for identifying hemodynamically significant AAOCA. Resistance-based indices were among the top predictors when referenced to adenosine FFR, whereas minor diameter measurements showed the highest predictive performance relative to the dobutamine reference standard, suggesting that stress-related dynamic changes may contribute beyond static geometry. These findings support integrating shape-aware geometric assessment into R-AAOCA evaluation to enhance non-invasive risk stratification.Figure 1
title: Geometric shape-derived CCTA resistance metrics predict invasive FFR in anomalous right coronary arteries under adenosine and dobutamine stress

abstract: Abstract Background Cancer is common among patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and may influence management and outcomes. The prognostic impact of cancer status (active vs. past) and its anatomical site remains insufficiently defined. We evaluated the association between cancer and short- and long-term outcomes after AMI in a large population cohort. Methods Using linked administrative databases from Lombardy, Italy, we identified adults with a first AMI hospitalization from 2014–2022 (N=124,403). Patients were categorized by cancer history, cancer status (active vs. past), and cancer site. The primary endpoint was in-hospital mortality; secondary endpoints were 1-year all-cause mortality and 1-year rehospitalization for AMI or acute heart failure (AHF). Multivariable log-binomial, Cox, and Fine&Gray models were applied. Results Overall, 18,463 (14.8%) had a history of cancer. They were older and with higher comorbidity burden. Cancer history was associated with higher in-hospital mortality (adjusted risk ratio [RR] 1.06, 95% CI 0.99–1.13) and one-year mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 1.50, 95% CI 1.44–1.57). Active cancer carried the greatest risk (in-hospital RR 1.07, 95% CI 1.00–1.15; 1-year HR 1.64, 95% CI 1.57–1.72), whereas past cancer showed no excess mortality. Site-specific analyses identified lung (one-year HR 2.69, 95% CI 2.15–3.37) and haematological cancers (one-year HR 2.19, 95% CI 1.88–2.56) as highest risk. Elevated mortality with cancer was consistent in STEMI and NSTEMI. Competing-risk analyses showed similar risk of rehospitalization among cancer and non-cancer patients. Conclusions In a real-world, unselected AMI population, cancer worsens short- and long-term survival, especially when active and involving the lungs or the haematopoietic tissues. Incorporating cancer status into AMI risk stratification and strengthening cardio-oncology pathways in acute care are warranted to improve patient outcomes.
title: Prognostic impact of cancer in patients hospitalized for acute myocardial infarction: a population-based cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, closely correlated with high atherosclerosis burden and systemic endothelial dysfunction. While flow mediated dilation (FMD) is a validated prognostic marker for cardiovascular events, the drivers of endothelial recovery post-AMI still remain underexplored. It is currently unclear whether systemic endothelial repair is limited by the basic metabolic profile, coronary anatomical complexity, or intrinsic hemodynamic mechanisms. Purpose Our aim was to identify the independent clinical, metabolic, and hemodynamic predictors of the relative change in endothelial function, measured via brachial artery FMD, from the acute phase of AMI to a 6-month follow-up. Methods This sub-analysis of the prospective, single-center FLARE-ACS trial evaluated endothelial function via brachial artery FMD in patients with AMI during the acute phase (within 4 days) and at 6 months. The primary endpoint was the relative change in FMD% in diastole. Predictors identified through univariable regression (p&lt;0.10) were entered into a multivariable model. This model adjusted for baseline hemodynamics (flow volume, baseline FMD), clinical status [presence of heart failure (HF)], metabolic markers [HbA1c, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C)] and coronary anatomical complexity [three-vessel disease (3VD)]. Results The study analyzed 98 patients (60±11 years, 79% male). Most presented with STEMI (65.3%) or NSTEMI (33.7%), with 87.8% undergoing successful revascularization. Prevalent comorbidities were hypertension (44.9%), dyslipidemia (37.1%), and diabetes (17.3%), while 12.2% had prior coronary artery disease. Multivessel disease was common, including 27.6% with two-vessel and 6.1% with three-vessel involvement. Multivariate analysis showed that 6-month endothelial recovery was independently driven by baseline hemodynamics and clinical severity, whereas metabolic and anatomical variables lost significance. Relative FMD improvement was independently predicted by baseline branchial artery flow volume (β:0.330, p=0.013) and presence of HF (β:0.244, p=0.01), reflecting a lower baseline status and intensive medication-driven neurohormonal optimization. Notably, lower baseline FMD also predicted greater proportional recovery (β:-0.380, p&lt;0.001). Conversely, HbA1c (p=0.188), LDL-C (p=0.175) and 3VD (p=0.249) did not retain independent predictive value for functional recovery (Table). Conclusion Following AMI, 6-month endothelial repair is driven by blood flow and shear stress rather than metabolic or anatomical factors. While metabolic risks cause initial vascular damage, they do not seem to limit the vessel’s ability to recover once hemodynamics stabilize. Our findings indicate that FMD serves as a marker of shear-induced repair, demonstrating that responding to physical flow stress is fundamental for endothelial recovery post-AMI.
title: Predictors of systemic endothelial recovery post-acute myocardial infarction: a 6 month follow-up of the FLARE-ACS study

abstract: Abstract Background The circadian pattern of acute myocardial infarction (MI) onset is associated with subsequent clinical outcomes. We sought to examine the impact of age and sex on the association between time of symptom onset (TSO) in MI and 30-day mortality following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Methods Within the statewide Victorian Cardiac Outcomes Registry in Australia, we identified patients with MI who had documented TSO and underwent PCI between 2013-2023. Patients were stratified by age &lt; or ≥ 65 years. TSO as an outcome was summarized as circular means ± circular standard deviations and compared using circular-linear regression. TSO as a predictor was transformed using a periodic cubic B-spline with boundary knots at 00:00 and 24:00 and internal knots at 06:00, 12:00, and 18:00. Results The final study population comprised 26,459 patients (77.4% male; mean age 63.8 ± 12.5 years; 58.1% with ST-elevation MI presentation). Overall, 96.0% patients underwent successful PCI during the index admission. The mean TSO occurred later in patients aged &lt;65 years compared to those aged ≥65 years (12:07 ± 6:32 vs. 11:43 ± 6:25; p &lt;0.001). Mortality at 30 days varied significantly by TSO in patients aged &lt;65 years (OR 0.32, 95% confidence interval 0.14-0.71 at 12:00 compared to midnight), following adjustment for age, sex, diabetes, ST-elevation MI presentation, and history of coronary revascularisation. The same association was not observed in patients aged ≥65 years. In both age groups, males experienced an earlier TSO than females (p&lt;0.001), however the relationship between sex and 30-day mortality did not differ significantly by TSO. Conclusion TSO differs according to age and sex among patients presenting with MI, and is independently associated with subsequent 30-day mortality following PCI in patients aged &lt;65 years. This highlights potential differences in the effect of the circadian system on MI, and may in future help inform risk stratification and resourcing.
title: Age and sex differences in the circadian distribution of myocardial infarction and impact on outcomes

abstract: Abstract Background Arterial thrombotic events constitute the leading cause of mortality in hypertension. Gut dysbiosis induces endothelial dysfunction and systemic inflammation, contributing to hypertension and its associated cardiovascular complications. Whether these dysbiotic microbiota metabolites in hypertension directly regulate platelet hyperactivation and thrombosis remains unclear. Methods Fecal microbiota transplantation, 16S rRNA sequencing and untargeted metabolomics were performed using samples from hypertensive patients. In vivo FeCl3-induced mesenteric arteriole thrombosis model, ex vivo microfluidic whole-blood perfusion assay, and in vitro platelet functional studies defined the functional effects of acetate on platelet activation. Moreover, platelet-specific olfactory receptor 78 (Olfr78)-deficient mice were employed to explore the underlying mechanisms of acetate on platelet activation. Results Transplantation with fecal microbiota from hypertensive patients enhanced in vivo FeCl3-injured mesenteric arteriole thrombosis and ex vivo whole blood thrombus formation compared with fecal microbiota from healthy normotensive subjects. Untargeted metabolomics revealed gut microbiota-derived acetate was decreased in patients with hypertension, and plasma acetate concentration negatively correlated with integrin αIIbβ3 activation and P-selectin exposure. Acetate demonstrated superior antiplatelet efficacy against ADP-induced aggregation, dense-granule secretion, α-granule secretion and integrin αIIbβ3 activation than collagen or thrombin-induced platelet activation. Mechanistic studies using platelet-specific Olfr78-/- mice revealed that acetate bound to and activated Olfr78, a receptor not previously reported to express in platelets, to elevate cAMP level and activate PKA, thereby increasing p-VASP and decreasing Ca2+ mobilization as well as inactivating RhoA/ROCK2/MLC signaling to inhibit platelet activation. A high-fiber diet upregulated acetate/Olfr78 signaling in platelets to suppress microvascular thrombosis and protect against myocardial injury during myocardial infarction in mice. Conclusions Acetate is a negative regulator of platelet hyperreactivity and thrombus formation via Olfr78 receptor, and acetate deficiency contributes to platelet hyperreactivity in hypertension. Lifestyle modifications, particularly high-fiber dietary intervention and acetate supplementation, exhibit potent antithrombotic effects in hypertension.Plasma acetate linked to thrombotic potentialStructured graphical abstract
title: Hypertension-associated acetate deficiency enhances platelet activation and thrombosis via Olfr78

abstract: Abstract Background Subclinical liver fibrosis, assessed using the Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index, has emerged as a robust prognostic marker across cardiovascular conditions. Large prospective cohort studies and meta-analyses have shown that elevated FIB-4 values are associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular events and mortality in individuals, both with and without metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease. However, the biological mechanisms linking liver fibrosis to adverse outcomes in ischemic heart disease (IHD) remain incompletely understood. We hypothesize that platelet dysfunction, a key determinant of atherothrombosis and inflammation, may serve as a mechanistic link between liver fibrosis and cardiovascular risk. Methods This study is a post-hoc analysis of the prospective observational Endocrine Vascular disease Approach (EVA) study. Adults undergoing coronary angiography for acute coronary syndrome or stable angina were prospectively enrolled and included in this study, and the FIB-4 index for liver fibrosis was calculated. Platelet function was evaluated using platelet count–adjusted soluble P-selectin and mean platelet volume (MPV), biomarkers previously shown to reflect platelet activation in IHD. All-cause and cardiovascular death were recorded during follow-up. Results Among 462 individuals (mean age: 66.8±11.4 years; 30.9% females) with IHD included in the analysis, 54 (11.7%) patients showed a FIB-4 &gt; 2.67, indicating a high risk of advanced fibrosis. Patients with higher FIB-4 were older and had a higher prevalence of heart failure (HF). In the multivariable logistic regression analysis, C-reactive protein (OR 1.10, 95% CI 1.02–1.20, per mg/dL increase) and PLT-adjusted soluble P-selectin levels (OR 1.83, 95% CI 1.30–2.60, per increasing quartile) were independently associated with FIB-4 &gt; 2.67. Among the 440 (95.2%) individuals with available follow-up data, all-cause mortality was higher among patients with FIB-4 &gt;2.67 (Figure 1); similar results were observed for cardiovascular mortality. Higher FIB-4 values were independently associated with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in a multivariable Cox regression model. Conclusions In individuals with IHD, FIB-4 identifies a high-risk phenotype characterized by enhanced platelet activation and systemic inflammation; higher FIB-4 values are independently associated with adverse outcomes. These findings support platelet dysfunction as a potential biological link between subclinical liver fibrosis and cardiovascular risk.Figure 1
title: Platelet dysfunction, liver fibrosis and adverse outcomes in individuals with ischemic heart disease: a post-hoc analysis of the prospective observational EVA study

abstract: Abstract Background Layered plaques in epicardial coronary arteries are considered a signature of previous subclinical plaque destabilisation and subsequent healing; however, the mechanisms of their formation remain incompletely elucidated. Purpose We sought to investigate determinants of layered plaques in the infarct-related artery (IRA) with an emphasis on the coagulation system activity and endothelial and vascular dysfunction in patients after primary coronary angioplasty for ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Methods Ninety-four STEMI patients were enrolled, including 72 males, with a median age of 61 (interquartile range 54-69) years. In all patients optical coherence tomography (OCT) of IRA was performed twice, first after restoration of epicardial blood flow following aspiration thrombectomy to assess the naive structure of the culprit vessel, and second after stent deployment to assess the procedural result. On admission, thrombin generation was assessed ex vivo by calibrated automated thrombogram including peak thrombin generation and endogenous thrombin potential. Plasma fibrin structure/function was assessed ex vivo by fibrin clot permeability (Ks), reflecting fibrin pore size, and clot lysis time (CLT), reflecting fibrin clot susceptibility to lysis. Endothelial and vascular function were assessed within 3 days using brachial artery flow-mediated dilatation (FMD) and nitroglycerine-mediated dilatation (NMD), respectively. Results The layered plaques in IRA were identified in 67 (71.3%) patients. Patients with layered plaques in IRA versus those without did not differ in terms of age, body mass index, ischaemia time, previous angina, cardiovascular risk factors, lipid profile and enzymatic infarct size but had higher plasma fibrinogen (3.64 [3.21-3.71] versus 3.36 [2.96-4.14] g/L, P=0.024, respectively). Women were more frequent in the group with layered plaques than in the group without (28% versus 8%, P=0.032, respectively). There were no significant differences in OCT characteristics of IRA, FMD, or NMD between the two groups. The presence of layered plaques in IRA was associated with a lower Ks (3.70 [3.01-4.40] versus 5.31 [4.39-6.36] x10-9 cm2, P&lt;0.001) and a longer CLT (128 [107-165] versus 119 [97-141] min, P=0.019), but not with endogenous thrombin potential (P=0.157) or peak thrombin generation (P=0.258). Moreover, Ks correlated inversely with the number of layered plaques (Figure). On multivariable analysis, after adjustment for plasma fibrinogen, Ks (odds ratio [OR] 0.324, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.176-0.599, P&lt;0.001) was independently associated with the presence of layered plaques in IRA. Conclusions The layered plaques in IRA, identified in two-thirds of STEMI patients, were more common in women and were present irrespective of endothelial and vascular function. Layered culprit plaques in IRA were independently associated with a more compact fibrin network.Correlation plot
title: A dense fibrin network favours layered plaque formation in the infarct-related artery in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Introduction The Reduction of Cardiovascular Events with Icosapent Ethyl-Intervention Trial (REDUCE-IT) showed that icosapent ethyl (IPE) reduces major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in high-risk patients with hypertriglyceridemia. While IPE is approved as an adjunct to statins for triglyceride reduction, emerging data indicate additional cardioprotective actions beyond lipid modulation. As elevated baseline pro-coagulant activity is linked to higher cardiovascular (CV) risk, this analysis aimed to evaluate whether IPE, a highly purified ethyl ester of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), affects coagulation or fibrinolytic pathways. Methods This post hoc analysis examined a subset of high-risk patients from the REDUCE-IT (n=100 IPE; n=100 placebo) who had experienced myocardial infarction or unstable angina within the 12 months before randomization. Blood samples collected at baseline and after 2 years were analyzed using Luminex 200 technology to quantify circulating levels of tissue factor (TF), TF pathway inhibitor (TFPI), and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1). Group comparisons were performed using generalized linear models. For the time-to-event analyses, patients were stratified by the median baseline TF level (46.5 pg/mL) across the entire cohort, resulting in four subgroups: placebo-low TF, placebo-high TF, IPE-low TF, and IPE-high TF. Kaplan–Meier curves were generated to assess the first occurrence of the primary composite endpoint as defined in REDUCE-IT. Complementary in vitro experiments were conducted in primary human aortic endothelial cells (HAECs) treated with increasing EPA concentrations prior to stimulation with tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α. Protein expression of TF, TFPI, and PAI-1 were assessed by western blot. Results TF blood levels were reduced after 2 years in IPE-treated patients compared with placebo (median 49.4 and 55.8 pg/mL, p=0.046). Consistently, EPA (8×10-5 M) decreased TF protein expression in TNF-α–stimulated HAECs (p=0.032), whereas TFPI and PAI-1 levels were unaffected in patients or in vitro (Figure 1). Event-free survival varied across the four TF-stratified groups (log-rank p=0.022), with the placebo-high baseline TF group experiencing the highest incidence of events over time. This contrast was most evident when comparing placebo-high baseline TF patients with IPE treated-high baseline TF patients (red and gold curves, Figure 2). Conclusion IPE reduces circulating TF levels in a subset of high-risk CV patients of the REDUCE-IT; similarly, it reduces TF in HAECs exposed to TNF-α. Patients with higher baseline TF demonstrated more favorable event-free survival under IPE treatment, whereas the placebo-high baseline TF subgroup exhibites the greatest incidence of events. The findings herein offer an additional mechanistic explanation for the MACE reduction reported in REDUCE-IT and support an antithrombotic effect of IPE, especially among patients with high baseline TF.
title: Effects of icosapent ethyl on coagulation biomarkers and their association with event-free survival in high-risk cardiovascular patients: a post hoc analysis of the REDUCE-IT

abstract: Abstract Background Despite advances in the invasive treatment of acute myocardial infarction (MI) and the widespread use of guideline-based pharmacotherapy, long-term prognosis remains challenging. Many patients experience recurrent cardiovascular events and death within several years after acute coronary syndrome, reflecting a persistent residual risk, however the molecular determinants responsible for its maintenance remain insufficiently understood. Purpose We sought to identify fibrin clot-bound proteins and to assess their temporal changes between the acute phase of MI and six-month follow-up to better characterize the mechanisms contributing to the persistent prothrombotic risk. Methods Enrolled were 73 statin-naïve patients (median age 62 years, 55 males) with STEMI or high-risk NSTEMI undergoing primary PCI. On admission and at 6-month follow-up, peak thrombin generation and endogenous thrombin potential (ETP) were assessed ex vivo using calibrated automated thrombogram. Also ex-vivo fibrin clot structure and susceptibility to lysis were evaluated by clot permeability (Ks) reflecting fibrin pore size and clot lysis time, respectively. Qualitative and quantitative proteomic analysis of plasma fibrin clot-bound proteins was performed at both time points. Results A total of 231 clot-bound proteins were identified at both time points, clustering into distinct functional pathways. 43 proteins demonstrated significant changes over six months. 36 proteins, mainly involved in platelet and neutrophil degranulation, complement cascade, and positive regulation of immune response, decreased. 7 proteins, associated with plasma lipoprotein assembly, remodeling, and clearance, increased. Among 65 hemostasis-related proteins analyzed at follow-up, Ks negatively correlated with 9 proteins, with strongest associations observed for alpha-1-antitrypsin (r=-0.426, P&lt;0.001), alpha-1-antichymotrypsin (r=-0.357, P=0.002), and plasminogen (P=-0.462, P&lt;0.001). ETP positively correlated with 4 proteins, with the strongest association with apolipoprotein B-100 (r=0.321, P=0.006) and selenoprotein P (r=0.366, P=0.002). By multivariable analysis, after adjustment for fibrinogen, age and gender, Ks at follow-up was independently affected by clot-bound plasminogen (beta -0.359, confidence interval for beta -0.560 - -0.157, P&lt;0.001) Conclusions The fibrin clot-bound proteome undergoes significant remodeling within six months after MI. Reduced inflammation- and degranulation-related proteins suggests attenuation of acute thrombo-inflammatory activity, whereas increased lipoprotein-associated proteins may reflect statin influence on lipid-driven prothrombotic characteristics. The associations between clot-bound proteins and hemostatic parameters indicate their potential role in modulating fibrin architecture and thrombin-generating capacity beyond the acute phase. These findings provide new mechanistic insight into the residual thrombotic risk after MI.
title: Temporal remodeling of the fibrin clot-bound proteome after myocardial infarction and its association with persistent prothrombotic phenotype

abstract: Abstract Background P2Y12 inhibitors are a cornerstone of cardiovascular pharmacotherapy. However, bleeding events remain their leading complication and are frequently observed in patients with concomitant infection. We recently demonstrated that infection renders platelets hyporeactive toward agonist activation. We hypothesized that this inflammatory platelet dysfunction amplifies the pharmacodynamic response to P2Y12 inhibitors, resulting in an increased bleeding risk. Purpose We aimed to assess how the potency of P2Y12 inhibitor therapy is altered during infection and sepsis. Methods In this prospective study, we recruited two cohorts comprising (i) a discovery cohort (n=89 patients; n=38 sepsis, n=33 infection without fulfilling the sepsis criteria, n=18 healthy controls) and (ii) a validation cohort (30 patients with coronary artery disease (CAD); n=15 with infection, n=15 without infection). We determined platelet function comprehensively using flow cytometry (PAC-1 binding following ADP stimulation), light transmission aggregometry, a microfluidic system on a collagen/tissue factor–coated surface under high shear (1000 s⁻¹), and the VerifyNow point-of-care device. Results In our discovery cohort, ADP-induced GPIIb/IIIa activation was reduced in infection and blunted in sepsis patients. In healthy controls, cangrelor induced a dose-dependent inhibition with complete suppression of GPIIb/IIIa activation at 1 µM. In contrast, a 100-fold lower concentration (10 nM) fully abolished ADP-induced activation in infection patients. Baseline maximal aggregation upon ADP stimulation was only moderately reduced in infection (57% vs. 67% in controls). However, 10 nM cangrelor reduced aggregation to 22% in infection, whereas aggregation in controls remained largely preserved (51%). Under arterial shear, baseline thrombus formation was comparable (22% vs. 21%), yet 10 nM cangrelor reduced platelet surface coverage to 9% in infection versus 17% in controls, revealing a heightened sensitivity to P2Y12 inhibition under inflammatory conditions. We recruited a validation cohort comprising patients with established CAD receiving clopidogrel for P2Y12 inhibition. Concomitant infection was associated with near-absent ADP-induced activation, markedly reduced aggregation (10% vs. 39%, p&lt;0.0001), and impaired thrombus formation (8% vs. 16%, p&lt;0.0001) (Fig. 1A,B). Strikingly, VerifyNow testing demonstrated a profound shift toward "low platelet reactivity" (LPR) (&lt;94 platelet reactivity units (PRU)) in infection patients compared to non-infection CAD patients (93% vs. 13%), with values clearly falling below the established “optimal platelet reactivity” (OPR) window (95–208 PRU) for clopidogrel therapy (Fig. 1C), reflecting an increased pharmacodynamic response. Conclusion In infection, P2Y12 inhibitor therapy is frequently functionally overdosed. Infection represents a novel and clinically relevant determinant of P2Y12 inhibitor response.Figure1
title: Infection drives excessive platelet inhibition during P2Y12 inhibitor therapy in coronary artery disease

abstract: Abstract Background Stress hyperglycemia (SHG) frequently occurs in patients with acute myocardial infarction (MI) and is a strong independent predictor of poor clinical outcomes, even in individuals without pre-existing diabetes. Although stress-induced hyperglycemia has been closely linked to exaggerated cardiac inflammation, the molecular mechanisms by which acute hyperglycemic stress disrupts inflammatory resolution and myocardial repair remain largely unclear. Methods and Results In this study, we identify the transcription factor FOXK2 as a critical molecular sensor linking hyperglycemic stress to maladaptive inflammatory responses during MI. FOXK2 expression was significantly reduced in cardiac macrophages from hyperglycemic mice following MI and in peripheral blood mononuclear cells from MI patients with SHG, with FOXK2 levels inversely correlating with infarct severity and cardiac dysfunction. Macrophage-specific deletion of FOXK2 markedly exacerbated myocardial injury, enhanced inflammatory cytokine production, and impaired post-infarction cardiac repair. Mechanistically, hyperglycemia promoted the interaction between FOXK2 and O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT), leading to site-specific O-GlcNAcylation of FOXK2 at threonine 552. This modification triggered K11-linked polyubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation of FOXK2, thereby releasing a broad pro-inflammatory transcriptional program during MI. Integrated CUT&Tag and RNA-sequencing analyses demonstrated that FOXK2 normally restrains macrophage inflammatory activation by suppressing H3K27 acetylation at key inflammatory loci, with the IL-6/STAT3 signaling axis emerging as a prominently derepressed pathway in the absence of FOXK2. Mass spectrometry and functional validation further revealed that a FOXK2T552A mutant was resistant to hyperglycemia-induced degradation, confirming the functional importance of this modification site. To translate these mechanistic insights into therapeutic intervention, we developed a cell-penetrating peptide (Peptide-I) that disrupts the FOXK2–OGT interaction and stabilizes FOXK2 under hyperglycemic conditions. Administration of Peptide-I significantly attenuated cardiac inflammation, improved cardiac function, and enhanced myocardial repair in both acute SHG and chronic diabetic MI models. Conclusions These findings establish FOXK2 as a central molecular node integrating hyperglycemic stress with macrophage-driven inflammatory responses during MI and provide proof-of-concept that targeting FOXK2 O-GlcNAcylation may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for improving outcomes in MI complicated by stress hyperglycemia.
title: Macrophage FOXK2 promotes cardiac repair in myocardial infarction with stress hyperglycemia

abstract: Abstract Background Chronic inflammation and cellular metabolic stress often persist following an acute coronary syndrome (ACS) event despite guideline-therapy. SGLT2 inhibitors (gliflozins) exhibit potent cardio-protection, but their ability to modulate long-term systemic inflammation and monocyte function post-ACS is poorly defined. This work investigated systemic inflammatory markers and monocyte metabolic activity across coronary artery disease (CAD) spectrum and evaluated the long-term anti-inflammatory effect of gliflozin therapy post-ACS event. Methods Blood samples from healthy subjects (H; n=20), individuals with cardiovascular risk factors without coronary lesion (CVD, n=20), stable CAD and no history of ACS event (CAD, n=60), acute STEMI (n=30), 3-6 months post-STEMI (ACS, n=35), and 3-6 months post- STEMI treated with gliflozin for &gt; 4 weeks due to other clinical indication (n=25) were collected. Plasma IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1, ICAM-1, and VCAM-1 along with monocyte oxidative stress, glucose uptake and adhesion activity were assessed. Primary comparisons evaluated inflammatory progression from healthy to acute STEMI, post-ACS recovery and the impact of gliflozin therapy. Patient groups were comparable in age, sex distribution, BMI, smoking and cardiovascular risk profile, whereas healthy subjects differed. Results Across the CAD spectrum, a stepwise increase in systemic IL-6, TNF-α, MCP-1, ICAM-1, and VCAM-1 were observed, reaching peak levels during acute STEMI. In parallel, PBMCs metabolic activity increased progressively, with oxidative stress reaching 3.1-fold, glucose uptake reaching 2.9-fold and adhesion to endothelial cells reaching 4.7-fold increase in STEMI, compared to their activity in healthy state. At 3-6 months post-STEMI, TNF-α (13.5 ± 1.3 vs 8.5 ± 1.2 pg/mL) and ICAM-1 (397.3 ± 19.8 vs 241.1 ± 11.4 ng/mL) remained elevated compared to stable CAD patients with no history of ACS. Consistently, monocytes oxidative stress, glucose uptake and adhesion capacity remained significantly higher by 16.3%, 12.7% and 28.1% than in stable CAD. In patients treated with gliflozin, TNF-α (7.7 ± 0.9 pg/mL) and ICAM-1 (243.6 ± 15.6 ng/mL) were significantly decreased to levels no longer different from stable CAD, accompanied by a reduction in PBMC oxidative stress, glucose uptake and adhesion to endothelial cells by 20.6%, 20.8% and 53.7% respectively, restoring metabolic activity to levels comparable to stable CAD. Conclusion Inflammatory and endothelial activation markers increase progressively across the CAD spectrum and peak during acute STEMI. While most markers decline after the acute phase, TNF-α, ICAM-1 and monocyte metabolic activation remain persistently elevated months post-ACS. On the other hand, gliflozin therapy significantly attenuates persistent inflammation and monocyte oxidative/metabolic activation, restoring values to those observed prior to ACS.
title: Gliflozin therapy attenuates persistent systemic inflammation and monocyte metabolic dysfunction post-ACS: a comparative study across the CAD spectrum

abstract: Abstract Background Inflammation contributes to plaque destabilization and adverse outcomes in acute coronary syndromes (ACS). The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) is a low-cost marker available at presentation, but its independent prognostic value in contemporary, comorbidity-adjusted cohorts is not fully established. Purpose To determine whether admission NLR independently predicts post-discharge all-cause mortality, major in-hospital adverse events, and hospital length of stay (LOS). Methods We retrospectively analyzed adult patients from a large multicenter cardiovascular registry, hospitalized with ACS. NLR was derived from admission complete blood counts. Multivariable logistic regression tested associations between NLR and a major in-hospital composite (intubation, inotrope use, temporary pacemaker/defibrillator implantation, or cardiopulmonary resuscitation [CPR]) and each component. LOS was modeled as ln(LOS+1) using multivariable linear regression. Post-discharge all-cause mortality was evaluated with adjusted Cox models. Kaplan–Meier curves compared low, intermediate, and high NLR categories. Prespecified subgroup analyses were performed by sex, age (&lt;75 vs ≥75 years), and ACS type (STEMI vs NSTEACS). Results Among 5,628 patients (median age 67 years; 23.8% women), higher NLR independently predicted longer LOS (β=0.180 for ln(LOS+1), p&lt;0.001), higher post-discharge mortality (adjusted HR 1.030 per 1-unit increase, p&lt;0.001), and higher odds of the in-hospital composite (adjusted OR 1.076 per 1-unit increase, p&lt;0.001). Higher NLR was also associated with intubation (aOR 1.080), temporary pacing/defibrillation (aOR 1.061), inotrope support (aOR 1.057), and CPR (aOR 1.088) (all p&lt;0.001). Survival declined stepwise across NLR categories (log-rank p&lt;0.001 overall and within subgroups). Associations with in-hospital events were stronger in men, patients &lt;75 years, and STEMI. Conclusion Admission NLR provides an independent risk factor for in-hospital clinical deterioration, prolonged hospitalization, and post-discharge mortality in ACS, supporting its use for early risk stratification in practice.nlr esc hr and ornlr esc km
title: Prognostic value of neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio on acute coronary syndromes

abstract: Abstract Background Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Because circulating Lp(a) levels are largely genetically determined by the LPA gene, a single lifetime measurement has traditionally been considered sufficient. However, emerging evidence suggests that Lp(a) may fluctuate during the acute phase of acute coronary syndrome (ACS), with a possible peak around two weeks after onset. We aimed to identify clinical determinants of acute-phase Lp(a) changes and characterize its temporal pattern following ACS. Methods This single-center retrospective study included consecutive ACS patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention between January 2023 and January 2026. All received intensive statin therapy and had at least two Lp(a) measurements: at admission and within 30 days. Baseline Lp(a) was defined as the value within 72 hours of admission. ΔLp(a) was calculated as follow-up minus baseline Lp(a).Correlations between ΔLp(a) within 14 days and peak creatine kinase-MB (CK-MB), peak C-reactive protein (CRP), peak aspartate aminotransferase (AST), estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and baseline Lp(a) were assessed. Multivariable linear regression identified independent determinants. Linear and quadratic regression models were applied to evaluate the overall time-course pattern. Results Eighty-four patients were analyzed (mean age 69.4 years; 21.4% female). Baseline Lp(a) was 20.8 ± 19.0 mg/dL. Mean ΔLp(a) was 13.3 ± 14.1 mg/dL, with a maximum increase of 72 mg/dL at 12 days.ΔLp(a) within 14 days correlated with baseline Lp(a) (r = 0.42, p &lt; 0.001) and CRP (r = 0.27, p = 0.016), but not with CK-MB or AST. In multivariable analysis adjusting for age, sex, timing, CRP, and baseline Lp(a), CRP (β = 0.64, p = 0.001) and baseline Lp(a) (β = 0.33, p &lt; 0.001) remained independently associated with ΔLp(a). Quadratic regression demonstrated a significant non-linear trajectory (p for non-linearity = 0.012). Conclusions Lp(a) shows a transient, non-linear increase during the acute phase of ACS associated with inflammatory response. Early post-ACS Lp(a) measurements may not reflect steady-state levels and should be interpreted cautiously.Lp(a) Changes in the Acute Phase of ACSCorrelation of baseline Lp(a) and CRP
title: Dynamic and non-linear changes in lipoprotein(a) during acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Interleukin 6 (IL-6) has attracted attention as a key contributor to deleterious pro-inflammatory processes in patients after acute myocardial infarction (AMI). IL-6 may also worsen heart failure (HF) by disrupting iron metabolism. However, data about IL-6 in these settings remain incomplete. Purpose To assess the association of IL-6 with outcome, early markers of iron metabolism and HF in patients after AMI. Methods A case-control design of AMI patients within the prospective, multicenter SPUM-ACS cohort (n=4787) was used: 158 cases (all-cause death or reinfarction within 1 year) were matched 1:1 to controls (without events) by age, sex, AMI subtype, recruitment site and time from symptom onset to blood sampling (≤ 24h). All patients underwent successful primary percutaneous coronary intervention. Cytokines were analyzed by multiplex Mesoscale assays, iron biomarkers were measured as in routine practice. Linear mixed models (LMM) were used for the matched structure of cases and controls.
