The robustness of these findings was confirmed by the Rosenbaum sensitivity test, showing that the effect remained significant (p &lt; 0.001) even at a Gamma sensitivity level of 2.0, indicating the effect persisted despite potential unmeasured confounding factors. Conclusion Substantial sex-related disparities in ACS management and prognosis remain evident. The unfavourable outcomes observed in female patients underscore the necessity for individualised, equitable, and prompt care, with clinical guidelines evolving to consider the interplay between age, sex, and comorbidities. According to our analysis, these differences are largely attributable to older age, greater comorbidity burden, and reduced rates of revascularisation among women. When adjusted for these factors, the female sex was associated with a significant survival advantage. Enhancing access, raising awareness, and pursuing continued research are vital to optimise ACS care and address existing gaps.
title: Sex affects care and prognosis in acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background The prognostic role of baseline hemoglobin (Hb) levels in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remains uncertain, particularly over very long-term follow-up. The interaction between anemia and age may play a key role in determining outcomes. The aim was to evaluate the association between baseline hemoglobin and long term mortality Methods We analyzed 571 patients admitted with ACS and discharged alive from three Italian hospitals (1992–1998). Only three patients were lost to follow-up before death or 26 years. Patients were followed for up to 26 years. Cox regression models stratified by year of enrollment were used. Interaction between Hb and age was formally tested. In the fully adjusted models, covariates included were age, sex, heart failure, hypertension, prior myocardial infarction, antiplatelet therapy, and estimated glomerular filtration rate. Analyses were performed using Stata version 18 (StataCorp LLC, TX, USA). Results Mean age was 66±12 years and 30% were female. Over 26 years, 483/571 patients (85%) died. At univariable analysis, baseline Hb was not significantly associated with mortality (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.80–1.00; p=0.07). Despite this, a significant interaction between Hb and age was observed. Hb showed a positive association with mortality (HR: 1.5; 95% CI: 1.1–2.2; z=2.6; p=0.01), and a negative interaction with age (HR: 0.8; 95% CI: 0.7–0.9; z= -2.6; p=0.01). In models including the interaction term, lower Hb levels were associated with higher mortality in older patients, and lower in younger individuals. These findings remained consistent after multivariable adjustment, both with the negative interaction with age (HR: 0.8; 95% CI: 0.7–0.9; z=–2.5; p=0.01) and mortality (HR: 1.5; 95% CI: 1.1–2.1; z= –2.5; p=0.01). As illustrated in the predictive margins plot (Figure 1), lower Hb levels were associated with a higher relative hazard of global mortality in elderly patients (green line). In contrast, this risk-gradient was attenuated in the medium-age group (red line) and slightly reversed in younger participants (blue line), confirming that the clinical impact of Hb on survival is strongly modulated by age. Conclusions In this very long-term study, the prognostic impact of hemoglobin after ACS is strongly modified by age. Low Hb identifies a higher-risk subgroup among older patients, supporting the importance of considering anemia within an age-specific clinical context.Fully adjusted risk of global mortality
title: Hemoglobin levels and long-term mortality after acute coronary syndrome: a 26-year follow-up

abstract: Abstract Introduction and Purpose Despite advances in pharmacological and interventional treatments, acute coronary syndromes (ACS) remain a leading cause of death and high morbidity worldwide, particularly among the elderly. Due to age-related physiological changes, a greater burden of atherosclerosis, and a higher prevalence of cardiovascular and other comorbidities, elderly patients receive fewer guideline-recommended cardiovascular medications and invasive treatments. The aim of our observational study was to examine the baseline characteristics of our patients and intrahospital prognosis. Results We included 1036 consecutive patients aged 75 years or older (80.9±4.4) with ACS in our study. 488(47.1%) were female, and 548 were male (52.9%). Myocardial infarction with ST-segment elevation (STEMI) was diagnosed in 40.69% of patients; myocardial infarction without ST-segment elevation (NSTEMI) in 53.33%; and non-stable angina pectoris in 5.98%. Typical chest pain was present in 70.2% of patients. The average left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) was 46.24 ± 13.43%. The most common comorbidities were arterial hypertension (78.9%), dyslipidemia (44.9%), diabetes mellitus (35.8%), and chronic renal insufficiency (25%). 29.2% of patients previously experienced a myocardial infarction, 8.23% had a stroke, and 16.4% had a percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Angiography was performed in 62.7% of all included patients: 74.3% with STEMI, 54.4% with NSTEMI, and 50.9% with non-stable angina. 25.6% had multivessel coronary disease, and 6.37% had left main disease. PCI was performed in 320 patients. At discharge, 61.2% were on dual antiplatelet therapy and 69.1% on statins. Hospital stay was 5.57 ± 3.88 days. Laboratory parameters in Table 1. 178 (21.9%) patients died during hospitalization. Multivariable logistic regression analysis that included baseline clinical, laboratory, echocardiographic, and angiographic findings showed that independent predictors of intrahospital mortality were lower systolic blood pressure (OR = 0.99; p = 0.049), higher heart rate (OR = 1.01; p = 0.031), worse renal function, that is lower eGFR (OR = 0.97; p &lt; 0.001), higher levels of C-reactive protein (OR = 1.01; p = 0.011) and higher glycemia at admission (OR = 1.11; p &lt; 0.001). Conclusions Our patients had a high mortality rate; however, age was not associated with increased intrahospital mortality. Laboratory parameters at admission, suggesting the presence of uncontrolled comorbidities (diabetes, renal insufficiency, inflammation) and hemodynamic markers, were better predictors of mortality. This suggests that chronological age merely indicates the accumulated burden of comorbidities rather than being an independent factor influencing outcomes. Despite guideline recommendations, patients received suboptimal acute and chronic management, with PCI performed only in a third of patients and suboptimal antiplatelet and statin therapy at discharge.Table 1
title: The severity paradox in ACS: comorbidities define outcomes, not age

abstract: Abstract Introduction and aim Elderly patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and diabetes mellitus have a worse prognosis than non-diabetic counterparts, characterized by higher in-hospital mortality, adverse cardiovascular events, and complications such as extensive coronary disease and multimorbidity. The aim of our study was to investigate differences in intrahospital mortality rates between diabetic and nondiabetic elderly patients (75 years or older) with ACS, as well as differences in routinely measured biomarkers and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). Results We included 1036 consecutive patients, aged 75 years or older (80.9±4.4), with ACS in our observational study. 488(47.1%) were female, 548 (52.9%) were male, and 371 (35.8%) were diabetic. Myocardial infarction with ST-segment elevation (STEMI) was diagnosed in 40.69% of patients; myocardial infarction without ST-segment elevation (NSTEMI) in 53.33%; and non-stable angina pectoris in 5.98%. Typical chest pain was similarly distributed between patients with and without diabetes at admission (68.73 vs. 69.02%, p=0.9). Patients with diabetes had significantly higher glycemia levels at admission (11.34±5.32 vs. 7.87±3.49 mmol/L, p&lt;0.001). Troponin I levels (1.24 ± 10.195 vs. 1.18 ± 9.21 ng/mL) and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels (1208.08 ± 812.6 vs. 1350.15 ± 560.35 pg/mL) were not statistically different between patients with and without diabetes. LVEF was similar between diabetics and elderly nondiabetic patients (46.11±13.3 vs. 46.42±13.65%). 36% of diabetics and 25.3% of non-diabetics had a previous myocardial infarction (p&lt;0.001). Previous PCI was slightly more frequent in diabetics than in non-diabetics (18.7% vs. 15%, p=0.139). PCI was performed in 30.19% of diabetics and 31.28% of nondiabetic patients. 178 patients died during hospitalization, and mortality was slightly higher in diabetic patients (19.14% vs. 16.09%), p=0.213. In multivariable logistic regression analysis that included the aforementioned clinical, laboratory, and echocardiographic findings, as well as PCI status, we found that higher glycemia at admission (OR 1.096, CI: 1.045–1.150, p&lt;0.001) and lower LVEF (OR 0.952, CI: 0.924–0.981, p&lt;0.001) were significant predictors of in-hospital mortality in diabetic patients. In nondiabetic patients, glycemia at admission (OR 1.221, CI:1.138–1.310, p&lt;0.001), lower LVEF (OR 0.970, CI: 0.949–0.998, p&lt;0.01), and non-performing PCI (OR 0.308, CI: 0.197- 0.547, p&lt;0.001) were associated with increased mortality rates. Conclusion At age 75+, elderly diabetics with acute ACS have similar outcomes to non-diabetics. Hyperglycemia at admission and lower LVEF are strong predictors of worse outcomes in the elderly, irrespective of diabetes. Non-performing PCI is associated with 70% increase in mortality in non-diabetic elderly patients. Chronological age in ACS, when combined with or without diabetes, should not limit evidence-based interventions.
title: Does diabetes matter after 75? Mortality in the elderly with acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Hospitals operate with reduced staffing levels during weekends. Weekend admissions for acute myocardial infarction (MI) are fewer than weekday admissions, and the proportion of NSTEMI is lower. Prior studies have suggested increased mortality among patients admitted during weekends; however, the degree to which this reflects differences in case mix remains uncertain. Purpose To evaluate whether 30-day mortality is higher among patients admitted during weekends compared with weekdays, adjusting for MI type (STEMI/NSTEMI) and relevant clinical risk factors. Methods All Norwegian hospitals are mandated to report hospitalized cases of acute MI (ICD-10 I21–I22) to the Norwegian Myocardial Infarction Registry (NORMI). The registry includes detailed information on medical history, clinical presentation, diagnostic assessments, treatments, and discharge medications. Logistic regression models were used to estimate 30-day mortality associated with weekend versus weekday admission. Models were adjusted for age, sex, MI type (STEMI/NSTEMI), and the risk factors prior MI, diabetes and hypertension. Results From 2018 to 2024, 77 004 acute MI hospitalizations were recorded. The overall unadjusted 30-day mortality was 8.5%. In the age- and sex-adjusted model, weekend admission was associated with higher mortality (OR 1.10, p &lt; 0.01). Adjustment for MI type reduced the estimate (OR 1.08, p = 0.01), and further adjustment for risk factors produced an identical result (OR 1.08, p = 0.01). Mondays had, on average, a 12% higher number of admissions compared with Tuesday–Friday. In the full model excluding Monday admissions, the OR was 1.07 (p = 0.03). In the full model, only including STEMI, the OR was 1.12 (p=0.03). Conclusions Weekend admission for acute MI is associated with higher 30-day mortality compared with weekday admission. This association persists after adjustment for MI type and key clinical risk factors. Further analyses examining the association with time to treatment are warranted.Odds ratio with 95 % confidence intervalNumber of admissions per day of week
title: Increased 30 day mortality after weekend admission for acute myocardial infarction: results from the Norwegian Myocardial Infarction Registry

abstract: Abstract Background Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and is typically considered stable over time. However, the acute-phase dynamics of Lp(a) following an acute coronary syndrome (ACS) are not well understood. Purpose To define the longitudinal trajectory of Lp(a) levels following ACS. Methods In this observational longitudinal study, patients presenting with an ACS were enrolled and underwent serial measurements of Lp(a) at baseline (within 24 hours of MI), Day 1, Day 3, Days 4-7, Day 30, and late follow-up (≥6 months). Longitudinal changes in Lp(a) were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, with time modeled as a categorical fixed effect and participant-level random intercepts to account for repeated measurements. Lp(a) values were natural log-transformed prior to analysis to address right-skewness and allow interpretation of effects as relative changes. Model-based contrasts were used to compare each timepoint with baseline and Wilcoxon signed-rank test to compare the baseline and ≥6 months values. Results A total of 78 patients were enrolled; mean age was 61.4 ± 12.1 years, 39% were women, 31% were Black individuals, 63% presented with a non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), 37% with an ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), and 64% underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) during admission (Table). Median baseline Lp(a) was 61.5 (29.0; 184.0) nmol/L. Lp(a) demonstrated a significant overall time effect in linear mixed-effects modeling (p &lt; 0.001). Compared with baseline, Lp(a) did not change significantly at Day 1 (+1.5%, 95% CI -8.8% to +13.0 %; p = 1.00), but increased significantly by Day 3 (+18.5%, 95% CI +4.3% to +34.8%; p = 0.0007) and peaked during the early subacute phase (Days 4-7), increasing by 30.0 % relative to baseline (95% CI +8.7% to +54.8%; p = 0.0001). By Day 30, Lp(a) remained modestly but significantly elevated compared with baseline (+15.0%, 95% CI +2.2% to +29.3%; p = 0.0042). At late follow-up (≥6 months), Lp(a) was no longer significantly different from baseline (+6.5%, 95% CI -6.0% to +20.7%; p = 0.90). (Figure) A paired analysis of the 44 patients with both baseline and ≥6-month follow-up Lp(a) measurements demonstrated no statistically significant change in Lp(a) concentrations, with median values of 61.5 (31.75–187.8) at baseline and 86.0 (26.25–194.5) at ≥6 months (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.52). Conclusion(s) Lp(a) exhibits a dynamic but transient increase following an ACS, with a significant rise during the early subacute phase and returning near baseline at late follow-up. These findings highlight the importance of measurement timing when interpreting Lp(a) levels after ACS. The pronounced elevation during the early post-ACS phase suggests a potential window for therapeutic targeting of Lp(a), supporting further investigation of early Lp(a)-lowering strategies.
title: Temporal changes in lipoprotein(a) after acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Obesity is associated with cardiovascular disease (CVD) and mortality. In women with established CVD, less is known about prevalence of obesity and diabetes as concomitant comorbidities and their impact on prognosis. Purpose To analyse the burden of obesity in women in a modern cohort with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and the associated risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) stratified by diabetes status. Methods We included all women with AMI investigated with coronary angiography in Sweden between 2010-2021. Body mass index (BMI) at admission was grouped according to the WHO classification into low BMI (&lt;18.5 kg/m2), normal BMI (18.5-24.9 kg/m2), overweight (25.0-29.9 kg/m2), class 1 obesity (30.0-34.9 kg/m2), class 2 obesity (35.0-39.9 kg/m2) and class 3 obesity (≥40.0 kg/m2). Information on baseline characteristics and long-term adverse events was collected from national Swedish registries. Multivariate Cox proportional survival analyses were performed to assess outcomes where normal BMI without diabetes served as a reference. Results Of 39 881 women included, 21.9% (n=8721) had diabetes, 38.2% suffered a ST-elevation myocardial infarction and mean age was 72.0 years (SD 11.4). Obesity was twice as common if diabetes was present, 40.1% vs. 20.8%. Women with class 3 obesity were substantially younger than those with normal BMI regardless of diabetes status (66.7 vs. 74.0 in women with diabetes, and 62.3 vs. 72.7 years in those without). Previous diagnoses of hypertension and hyperlipidaemia were more common among patients with diabetes (76.8% vs. 53.1%, and 49.4% vs. 23.5% respectively) and such prevalence increased with obesity classes, regardless of diabetes status. On the contrary, smoking and previous myocardial infarction (MI) were more common in those with normal BMI, although prevalence of the aforementioned was twice as high if diabetes was present. Women with diabetes had a higher absolute one-year MACE rate (first of all-cause death, MI, stroke, or heart failure) compared to those without, 30.9% vs. 20.2%. After adjustments, diabetes increased the risk of future MACE regardless of obesity but was even higher if more severe obesity was present, associated Hazard Ratio (HR) with 95% Confidence Interval (CI) for diabetes and class 3 obesity 1.73 (1.50-2.00) vs. 1.25 (1.07-1.47) in those with only class 3 obesity and no diabetes. Corresponding figures for all-cause death was 1.84 (1.52-2.23) vs. 1.26 (1.00-1.59). Conclusion In women with myocardial infarction, where around one fifth of the women suffer from diabetes, obesity is common and present in 40% of the patients with diabetes and 20% in those without diabetes. The risk of future events and mortality was especially increased if diabetes or class 3 obesity was present. This strengthens the importance of a cardioprotective secondary preventive approach in women with obesity, diabetes and established cardiovascular disease.
title: Obesity and diabetes, two important modifiable prognostic risk factors after myocardial infarction in women

abstract: Abstract Background and aims Prediction of long-term mortality after acute myocardial infarction (AMI) remains challenging. Artificial intelligence (AI) may overcome the limitations of traditional statistical methods1.We aimed to establish an AI-based model for predicting long-term all-cause mortality after acute Myocardial Infarction (the AIMI model). Methods We consecutively enrolled AMI patients undergoing emergent coronary angiography and PCI within 24 hours of symptom onset. Five machine learning (ML) algorithms (RF, SSVM, CoxPH, GBSA and XGB) were employed2. We used recursive feature elimination (RFE) to select predictive variables. Individual predictions were visualized by SHAP plots. AIMI model was compared against GRACE and TIMI scores using time-dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, Brier scores, and Kaplan-Meier (K-M) analyses. External validation was also performed at the same way. (Figure 1) Results A total of 4825 patients were used to train and test the AIMI model and 723 patients for external validation. Model incorporated 15 variables achieved robust performance (C-index=0.81). As indicated by AUCs in test set, the model outperformed GRACE and TIMI risk scores across short-, mid- and long-term periods, especially for long-term prediction (1, 3 and 5 years). K-M curves confirmed precise discrimination between low-, median-, and high-risk groups (all p&lt;0.05). External validation confirmed AIMI model's good generalization and robustness (AUCs: 0.88, 0.91, 0.83, 0.75, 0.78 and 0.77 during hospitalization, at 30 days, half-year, 1-year, 2-years and 3-year follow-up; comparisons of K-M curves across three risk groups, all p&lt;0.05). Brier scores showed its good performance in individual level (mean value of internal validation cohort: 0.022; external validation: 0.021). (Figure 2) Conclusions AIMI model surpassed traditional methods in predicting all-cause death, especially for long-term prediction. AI/ML-based model demonstrated potential to enhance risk stratification, guiding clinical decision-making and personalized treatment3.Figure 1Figure 2
title: An artificial intelligence based model for predicting long-term all-cause mortality after acute myocardial infarction(the AIMI model)

abstract: Abstract Background Atrial fibrillation (AF) frequently occurs in patients presenting with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) but the prognostic implications of new-onset AF in first-time ACS patients are unclear. Purpose To assess the association between new-onset AF after a first ACS and outcomes. Material and Methods A nationwide cohort of patients with first time ACS was identified from a registry between 2007 and 2020 and linked to national patient, death, and prescription registers. The study included 139,961 patients with first-time ACS and no prior AF. New-onset AF was defined as AF diagnosed during the index ACS hospitalization or within 30 days. Fine–Gray competing-risk models were used to estimate crude and adjusted sub distribution hazard ratios (HRs) for all-cause mortality, cardiovascular death, stroke, recurrent myocardial infarction (MI), bleeding, and hospital readmission at 30 days, 1 year, and end of follow-up. Results Among 139,961 ACS patients without prior AF, 9,291 (7%) developed new-onset AF (mean age 77 years; 64% male), while 130,670 remained AF-free (mean age 68 years; 67% male). Mean follow-up was 6.7 years. New-onset AF was associated with a substantially increased risk of all-cause mortality, with adjusted HRs of 1.73 (1.43–2.08), 1.30 (1.20–1.40) and 1.09 (1.04–1.14) at 30 days, 1 year and end of follow up respectively. The corresponding adjusted HRs for cardiovascular death were 1.50 (0.95–2.37), 1.11 (0.98–1.26) and 0.87 (0.82–0.93). Stroke risk was markedly higher nearly threefold at 30 days and remained elevated throughout follow-up (HRs 1.33–1.87). Recurrent MI risk was approximately 30% higher, and bleeding risk increased with an HR of 1.55 (1.13–2.14) at 30 days. All-cause readmissions were consistently more frequent in the new-onset AF group. Conclusions New-onset AF during ACS is associated with substantially higher short-term mortality and persistently elevated stroke risk, recurrent MI, bleeding, and hospital readmission. These patients represent a high-risk group, requiring close monitoring and optimized long term management.
title: Long-term outcomes in patients with acute coronary syndrome complicated by new-onset atrial fibrillation: a nationwide cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background Data supporting percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) beyond the 12-hour cut-off are sparse and contradictory. Current guidelines provide inconsistent recommendations for stable late-presenters, representing a critical evidence gap for clinicians and policymakers, particularly in regions with delayed access to care. Purpose The study aimed to evaluate the effects of delay to hospital presentation on 30-day mortality following PCI versus routine medical treatment (RMT) in stable STEMI patients presenting 12 to 48 hours after symptom onset. Methods We identified 2,730 clinically stable patients with STEMI presenting 12 to 48 hours after symptom onset from the ISACS registry. The effects of PCI versus routine medical treatment (RMT) were assessed. Patients with cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, severe heart failure, persistent angina, or early revascularization were excluded. The primary endpoint was 30-day mortality. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) based on propensity scores was applied to adjust for baseline differences, and interaction testing was performed to evaluate effect modification by time of presentation. Results PCI was associated with lower 30-day mortality compared with RMT (3.1 % versus 5.5%; OR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.36 to 0.84) in the overall cohort. Yet, delay to hospital presentation influenced treatment outcomes (Pinteraction =0.001). Risk-adjusted 30-day mortality rate after PCI was higher in patients who underwent PCI between 12 to 24 hours (6.3%) compared with that of patients who underwent PCI between 25 to 48 hours (1.8%). PCI was associated with better survival compared with RMT only in patients undergoing PCI between 25 and 48 hours after symptom onset (OR: 0.30; 95%CI: 0.16–0.58; P &lt;0.001). Propensity score matching gave similar results. Conclusions In clinically stable STEMI patients presenting 12–48 hours after symptom onset, the benefit of PCI is highly time-dependent and suggests a "tailored" rather than "universal" approach. The survival advantage is specifically concentrated in the 25–48 hour window, challenging the assumption that earlier intervention is always superior and supporting a more tailored, time- and symptom-sensitive approach. Selective revascularization may improve outcomes without exposing all late presenters to unnecessary intervention.

appraisal.design_and_n: Registry cohort (ISACS) of 2,730 clinically stable STEMI patients presenting 12 to 48 hours after symptom onset; inverse probability of treatment weighting.
appraisal.main_limitation: Observational treatment comparison with possible residual confounding and immortal-time or selection effects in late presenters; congress abstract without full methods.
appraisal.one_line: Registry analysis of stable late-presenting STEMI (12 to 48 hours) suggests the association of PCI with lower 30-day mortality is concentrated in the 25 to 48 hour window.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: PCI was associated with lower 30-day mortality compared with RMT (3.1 % versus 5.5%; OR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.36 to 0.84); PCI was associated with better survival only at 25 to 48 hours (OR: 0.30; 95%CI: 0.16–0.58).
appraisal.why_it_matters: Guidelines are inconsistent for stable STEMI beyond 12 hours, so this bears on a recognised equipoise gap and on the Q-register topic of late reperfusion.

title: Time-dependent survival benefit of late PCI in stable STEMI: a propensity-weighted analysis of the 12–48 hour window

abstract: Abstract Introduction Left ventricular (LV) reverse remodeling (RR) can occur after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), but it remains incompletely understood. Pre-TAVR CT-derived extracellular volume (ECV-CT), a marker of extracellular matrix expansion (including both focal replacement fibrosis and diffuse interstitial fibrosis), has been correlated with worse outcomes, but its association with LV RR is ill defined. We aimed to assess the association between pre-TAVR ECV-CT and LV RR at 1-year post-TAVR. Methods Single-center retrospective study including consecutive patients with severe symptomatic AS undergoing TAVR between 2022-2024. Only patients with echocardiographic (TTE) data both before and 1-year after TAVR were included. All patients underwent a pre-TAVR-planning CT on a 192-slice dual-source scanner, using an additional post-contrast low-radiation-dose prospective acquisition. ECV-CT was calculated according to the equation and example in Fig1. Patients were grouped by mean ECV-CT, and TTE measures were compared before and after TAVR within each group using paired analyses. Results A total of 81 patients were included (median age 82 (IQR 78-87) years; 47% male). Pre-TAVR TTE showed a median transaortic gradient of 47mmHg (IQR 41–56), a mean aortic valve area of 0.75±0.19 cm², a median indexed LV mass (LVMi) of 138 g/m² (IQR 106–161) and a median indexed LV end-diastolic volume (LVEDVi) of 51mL/m² (IQR 41–68). The median LV ejection fraction (LVEF) was 56% (IQR 51–63) and mean global longitudinal strain (GLS) was -15 ± 4%. No patient had a clinical diagnosis of cardiac amyloidosis. The mean ECV-CT was 33.9 ± 8.0%. Patients with ECV-CT ≥33.9% had numerically higher LVMi (143 g/m² [IQR 107–161] vs 130 g/m² [IQR 106–161], p=0.481). At 1-year post-TAVR, TTE demonstrated a significant reduction in LVMi to 121 g/m² (IQR 98–148; p=0.018). No significant changes were observed in other parameters [LVEDVi 51 mL/m² (IQR 38–66), LVEF 56% (IQR 52–61) and GLS -16 ± 4%); p&gt;0.05 for all]. After stratification according to mean ECV-CT, patients with ECV-CT &lt;33.9% (n=42) showed a non-statistically regression in LVMi (130 g/m² [IQR 106–161] vs 121 g/m² [IQR 101–149]; p=0.333), whereas those with ECV-CT ≥33.9% (n=33) demonstrated a significant reduction in LVMi (143 g/m² [IQR 107–161] vs 122 g/m² [IQR 91–142]; p=0.023). Both groups achieved similar LVMi at 1-year after TAVR (p=0.717) (Figure 1). Conclusion In this preliminary study, patients with elevated ECV-CT showed a post-TAVR reduction in LVMi that brought them to levels similar to those with normal ECV. This pattern suggests that elevated ECV-CT, despite associated with poorer prognosis in previous studies, is not necessarily a marker of irreversible adverse remodeling in aortic stenosis.
title: The role of ECV-CT in left ventricular remodeling after TAVR

abstract: Abstract Background Management of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) has evolved substantially over the past decade, particularly with widespread adoption of radial access and contemporary mechanical circulatory support (MCS). Whether these changes have translated into sustained improvements in outcomes in an aging population remains uncertain. Purpose To determine whether temporal changes in invasive strategies and reperfusion practice were associated with changes in in-hospital mortality over a 10-year period in a large multicenter ACS registry (K-ACTIVE). Methods We analyzed consecutive ACS patients enrolled between 2015 and 2024 across 58 centers. Temporal trends in patient characteristics, reperfusion metrics, procedural strategies, and in-hospital outcomes were assessed using trend analyses. Results A total of 18,762 patients were included. Over time, patients became significantly older (mean age 68±13 vs. 71±13 years; p for trend &lt;0.01), while the proportion of STEMI remained stable (~75%; p=0.38). Radial access markedly increased from 53% to 86% (p for trend &lt;0.01), and multivessel disease decreased (56% to 44%; p&lt;0.01). Door-to-device time remained stable (median 84 vs. 83 minutes), and the proportion achieving &lt;90 minutes did not substantially improve (~45%; p&lt;0.01), suggesting overall system maturity rather than further temporal shortening. Use of IABP declined (18% to 13%), whereas Impella was introduced after 2020. In-hospital mortality decreased from 9.4% in 2015 to 6.4% in 2016 and remained consistently around 6.5% thereafter (p for overall trend &lt;0.01). When excluding 2015, mortality remained stable without evidence of temporal increase despite progressive aging. Conclusion In this large 58-center registry of 18,762 ACS patients, in-hospital mortality remained consistently low over the past decade despite progressive aging and stable reperfusion metrics. The evolution of invasive strategies—particularly widespread radial adoption—may have contributed to maintaining favorable outcomes in an increasingly complex ACS population.10 year
title: Temporal trends in management and outcomes of acute coronary syndrome in an aging population: a 10-year multicenter registry

abstract: Abstract Background C-reactive protein (CRP) is a well-established marker of inflammation and is widely measured in the Danish hospital setting. Myocardial infarction (MI) causes an acute inflammatory response, including an increase in CRP, which is also an established risk factor for both incident and recurrent MI. Clinical trials are underway investigating the protective effect of targeted anti-inflammatory treatment in high cardiovascular disease-risk patient populations. While most previous studies have analyzed risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) using a single CRP measurement, we here model the risk using all available CRP measurements following acute MI. Purpose The aim of the present study was to identify trajectories of CRP following incident MI and investigate their association with the risk of recurrent MACE, including death. Methods In this nationwide Danish registry-based cohort study we identified patients with first-time MI in 2018-2021. To identify distinct inflammatory trajectories, latent class trajectory modelling was applied to repeated CRP measurements obtained during routine clinical care within the first 120 days following the incident MI. Individuals were assigned to the latent classes based on their posterior probability of latent class membership, reflecting shared patterns of CRP over time. The posterior probabilities served as exposure in the Cox proportional hazard regression analysis of recurrent MACE (stroke, recurrent MI or all-cause death) within 3 years of the incident MI, adjusting for sex, age STEMI/non-STEMI type, geographic region, calendar year of MI, education and comorbidity index (M3). Results Among 22,769 individuals who survived 120 days following hospitalization with incident MI, we identified three probable latent classes of CRP trajectory (Figure): A low CRP class (Class 1) characterized by a relatively modest rise in CRP during the acute MI followed by a gradual decline (41.3% of the cohort); An intermediate CRP class (Class 2) characterized by a large initial surge in CRP, followed by a steady decline although stabilizing at a higher level than the low CRP class (44.2%); And a high CRP class (Class 3) characterized by a large acute surge which remained high throughout the 120 days (14.6%). The high CRP class was older, had a longer duration of hospitalization, and had more comorbidities than the other classes (Table). In total, 15.4% (n=3511) individuals experienced MACE during follow-up. The probability of allocation to the high CRP class trajectory was associated with increased risk of MACE (adjusted hazard ratio [HR]: 2.00 [95% confidence interval: 1.80-2.22]) compared with the low CRP class trajectory, and for the intermediate CRP class trajectory the adjusted HR was 1.34 (1.20-1.49). Conclusion The present results demonstrated different trajectories of CRP after MI and corroborate that sustained inflammation following incident MI is associated with poor prognosis.Figure
title: Trajectories of C-reactive protein levels after incident myocardial infarction and its association with risk of recurrent cardiovascular events in Danish patients – a registry-based cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background Early-onset acute coronary syndrome imposes a heavy socioeconomic burden on the younger workforce. Although chest pain centers have expanded across China to standardize care, evidence regarding the interplay between regional economic levels and gender on the prognosis of these young patients remains limited. Purpose This study aimed to evaluate temporal trends in age standardized in hospital mortality and investigate the association of regional economic levels and sex with these longitudinal outcomes. Methods We conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study using the Chinese Cardiovascular Association Database Chest Pain Center. The 31 provinces were stratified into High GDP, Middle GDP, and Low GDP regions based on economic data. Weighted Generalized Linear Mixed Models adjusted for patient characteristics and provinces were employed to assess temporal trends in age standardized mortality rates and account for regional heterogeneity Results Among 1008673 patients included, the mean age was 47.0 years and 86.7% were male. Low GDP regions accounted for 40.1% of the study population. In the GLMM analysis, mortality rates in High GDP regions remained stable over the study period. Low GDP regions demonstrated a significant downward trend in mortality (Interaction P=0.025). Stratified analyses showed a significant interaction between study year and economic region among male patients (P=0.016), with a specific decline observed in Low GDP regions. For female patients, the interaction between year and economic region was not statistically significant (P&gt;0.05). At the national level, female patients exhibited a continuous decline in age-standardized mortality rate (EAPC: -3.39; 95% CI: -6.49 to -0.19), whereas for male patients, a decreasing trend was specifically observed only in the Low-GDP region (EAPC: -3.27; 95% CI: -5.15 to -1.35). Conclusion The mortality decline in low GDP regions confirms the effectiveness of standardized care promoted by Chest Pain Centers. Future health policies should prioritize gender specific care pathways and optimize resource allocation to eliminate these persistent health inequalities.Figure1Figure2
title: Bridging the regional gap: declining mortality trends in early onset acute coronary syndrome in low GDP region of China: findings from the Chinese Cardiovascular Association (CCA) database-chest pain

abstract: Abstract Introduction Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) represents a heterogeneous entity involving microvascular dysfunction, thrombosis, and genetic susceptibility. Although women are more frequently affected, sex-specific genetic determinants and cardiometabolic profiles remain insufficiently characterised. Objective To stratify MINOCA by sex and evaluate its association with traditional cardiovascular risk factors and CAD-related genetic variants in a Southern European population. Methods This prospective single-centre cohort included 1,633 consecutive patients admitted with myocardial infarction between 2000 and 2019. Coronary angiography was independently assessed by two interventional cardiologists using the Leaman Score; a score of 0 defined MINOCA. MINOCA patients were stratified by sex and compared with those with obstructive MI (MI-CAD). Thirty-three SNPs previously associated with CAD were genotyped using TaqMan assays. Associations between genetic variants, clinical risk factors, and MI phenotype were evaluated using bivariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses, Results MINOCA was diagnosed in 87 patients (5.3%): 29 women and 58 men. Women with MINOCA showed lower prevalence of type 2 diabetes (p=0.005) and metabolic syndrome (p=0.003) and reported higher physical activity (p&lt;0.0001) compared with MI-CAD women. Genetic variants PON1 rs854560 (p=0.040) and CDKN2B rs4977574 (p=0.036) showed significance, but after multivariate adjustment, only CDKN2B GG remained independently associated with MINOCA women (p=0.020), together with type 2 diabetes (p=0.025), age (p=0.012), and sedentary lifestyle (p=0.008). Men with MINOCA showed lower rates of hypertension (p=0.033), diabetes (p=0.021), and metabolic syndrome (p=0.042) versus MI-CAD men. Significant SNP associations included TCF21 rs12190287 (p&lt;0.0001), FTO rs9939609 (p=0.048), and PCSK9 rs562556 (p=0.038) in MINOCA men. When adjusted in multivariate logistic regression, TCF21 GC+CC (p&lt;0.0001) and PCSK9 GA+AA (p=0.042) remained independently associated with MINOCA men, along with age (p&lt;0.0001). Conclusion MINOCA patients exhibit a more favourable cardiometabolic profile compared with obstructive MI-CAD, irrespective of sex. However, distinct sex-specific genetic associations were identified: CDKN2B in women and TCF21/PCSK9 in men. These findings suggest divergent biological pathways underlying MINOCA and support the need for sex-specific risk-stratification strategies.MINOCA stratified by sex
title: MINOCA syndrome and obstructive coronary artery disease: does sex matter?

abstract: Abstract Introduction Type 2 myocardial infarction (MI) is common and associated with poor prognosis. There is major heterogeneity in the diagnosis and treatment of this condition, and a lack of prospective clinical trials to inform guidelines. Purpose To compare the characteristics and clinical outcomes of patients with type 2 MI who were enrolled and those screened but not recruited into the DEMAND-MI prospective observational cohort study. Methods DEMAND-MI was a prospective observational cohort study evaluating coronary artery disease and left ventricular impairment following type 2 MI. Consecutive patients with elevation in cardiac troponin concentration were adjudicated according to the Universal Definition, forming a prospective registry of consecutive patients with type 2 MI. Registry data were linked to routine health records to determine baseline characteristics, management and clinical outcomes from screening to date of last follow up (01/07/2025) stratified by recruitment status. The primary outcome was subsequent MI or cardiovascular death. Subdistribution hazard ratios (sHR) were estimated using a Fine-Gray competing risk model accounting for non-cardiovascular death and adjusted for age and sex. Results Between January 2018 and October 2020, 660 consecutive patients with type 2 myocardial infarction were identified with 4,045 patient-years of follow-up (median 6.12 years [IQR 5.54–6.69 years]). A total of 108 patients (16%, 108/660) were eligible and recruited, with 552 (84%, 552/660) not recruited, primarily due to severe frailty (41%, 224/552), renal impairment (20%, 110/552), hepatic impairment (4%, 23/552) or critical illness (23%,128/552). Excluded patients were older (78.6 years versus 64.5 years, P &lt; 0.001), had a longer median hospital stay (7 days versus 3 days, P &lt; 0.001) and a greater burden of cardiovascular comorbidity (hypertension [57% versus 44%; P = 0.021]; cerebrovascular disease [22% versus 8%; P = 0.002]; heart failure [23% versus 11%; P = 0.010]). Excluded patients were at higher risk of MI or cardiovascular death (sHR 2.12, 95% CI 1.32-3.42; P = 0.002) and non-cardiovascular death (sHR 3.59, 95% CI 1.96-6.60; P &lt; 0.001) relative to those recruited. Conclusion Patients with type 2 MI who were screened but not recruited into our cohort study were older, with a higher prevalence of co-morbidities and significantly worse clinical outcomes. Despite an excess in non-cardiovascular death, these patients were at two-fold increased risk of future MI or cardiovascular death. These findings highlight a high-risk population underrepresented in studies and underscore the need for careful consideration of inclusion criteria in future clinical trials.CIF_RecruitmentBaseline Characteristics by Recruitment
title: Recruitment status and long-term outcomes in consecutive patients with type 2 myocardial infarction: a prospective registry

abstract: Abstract Introduction Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is a highly prevalent pathology worldwide and in our country, being the leading cause of mortality and disability globally. Multiple scales have been developed to estimate the risk of complications and mortality associated with the development of ischemic heart disease; however, many of these require para-clinical tests, which in low-resource settings demand time that could potentially delay decision-making in patients at elevated risk of mortality. The modified shock index (MSI) is a widely used tool to predict the risk of mortality in patients with medical and surgical pathologies. Some observational studies have shown that the modified shock index could be useful in predicting in hospital mortality in patients with acute coronary syndrome; however, there are no studies in our population that evaluate its utility in this scenario. Purpose To evaluate the ability of the MSI to predict the risk of in-hospital mortality in patients with acute coronary syndrome. Methods A retrospective cohort study design was used, employing secondary data provided by a Tertiary care hospital in Colombia. Patients older than 18 years who were admitted to the emergency service with a diagnosis of acute coronary syndrome, underwent coronary arteriography, and had obstructive coronary artery disease were included. Patients with incomplete clinical records, other types of circulatory shock, or cardiogenic shock at emergency department admission were excluded. Results A total of 404 individuals were recruited, with an in-hospital mortality rate of 8.9%. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis showed that an MSI ≥ 0.99 had good performance for predicting in-hospital mortality, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.86 (95% CI: 0.81–0.92). The optimal cutoff point was 0.99, determined by a Youden index of 59.4, with a sensitivity of 72.2% (95% CI: 58–86) and a specificity of 86.9% (95% CI: 84–90). The positive predictive value (PPV) was 35.1% (95% CI: 25–45), while the negative predictive value (NPV) reached 97.0% (95% CI: 95–99). Conclusions The MSI showed good discriminatory ability to predict in-hospital mortality in the evaluated population, even after adjustment for potential confounding variables. This suggests that the MSI could be incorporated into the comprehensive risk assessment battery for patients with ACS, particularly to identify those at higher 12 risk of death who may benefit from early intervention. This single-center retrospective cohort study has limited external validity; therefore, new multicenter studies are needed to confirm the usefulness of the MSI in different populations.ROC CURVETABLE 1
title: Modified shock index as a clinical predictor of in-hospital mortality in patients with acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Introduction Type 2 myocardial infarction is common, and patients with this diagnosis are often older and comorbid. Therefore, determining the optimal treatment strategy can be complex. Whether frailty is associated with cardiovascular outcomes and could inform management is uncertain. Purpose To determine if frailty influences cardiovascular outcomes in patients with type 2 myocardial infarction after adjusting for non-cardiovascular death as a competing risk. Methods The DEMAND-MI registry was a prospective multi-centre study identifying consecutive patients admitted to a secondary or tertiary care hospital with an elevated cardiac troponin concentration and an adjudicated diagnosis of type 2 myocardial infarction. Registry data were linked to health record data to determine baseline characteristics, management and clinical outcomes from recruitment to date of last follow up stratified by frailty status. Frailty was scored using the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) and stratified into ‘fit’ (CFS 1-3), ‘mild’ frailty (CFS 4-5), ‘moderate’ frailty (CFS 6) and ‘severe’ frailty (CFS 7-9). The primary outcome was subsequent myocardial infarction or cardiovascular death. Subdistribution hazard ratios (sHR) were estimated using a Fine-Gray competing risk model accounting for non-cardiovascular death and adjusted for sex, recruitment status and mechanism of type 2 myocardial infarction. Results Between January 2018 and October 2020, 660 consecutive patients with type 2 MI were identified with 4,045 patient-years of follow-up (median 6.12 [5.54-6.69] years). In the cohort, 600 (91%) patients had documented clinical frailty scores: 211 (35%) classed as ‘fit’, 214 (36%) with ‘mild’ frailty, 113 (19%) with ‘moderate’ frailty, and 62 (10%) with ‘severe’ frailty. Higher clinical frailty scores were associated with longer length of hospital stay (P=0.001) and more co-morbidities (hypertension, cerebrovascular disease, atrial fibrillation, heart failure, and COPD; P&lt;0.01 for all). Higher clinical frailty scores were associated with an increase in the risk of subsequent myocardial infarction or cardiovascular death (mild frailty; sHR, 1.48 [1.00-2.20]; P=0.049; moderate frailty; sHR, 1.98 [1.28-3.07]; P=0.002; severe frailty; sHR, 2.13 [1.25-3.63]; P=0.005) and non-cardiovascular death (mild frailty; sHR 2.52 [1.53-4.14]; P&lt;0.001; moderate frailty; sHR, 2.97 [1.73-5.10]; P&lt;0.001; severe frailty; sHR, 3.15 [1.70-5.82]; P&lt;0.001) compared to ‘fit’ patients. Conclusion One-third of patients with type 2 myocardial infarction have moderate or severe frailty, which is an independent predictor of future cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular events. Incorporating frailty assessment into routine clinical evaluation may enhance risk stratification and support multidisciplinary decisions regarding investigation and treatment.CIF FrailtyBaseline Characteristics Frailty
title: Frailty is associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes in type 2 myocardial infarction: a prospective registry study

abstract: Abstract Background Elevated admission blood glucose is associated with higher mortality in acute myocardial infarction (AMI). However, it does not distinguish stress-induced hyperglycemia (SIH) from chronic hyperglycemia, particularly in diabetic patients. The stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR), calculated as admission blood glucose divided by estimated average glucose from glycated hemoglobin, offers a more accurate marker of stress hyperglycemia independent of baseline glycemic status. This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed the prognostic value of SHR for adverse outcomes in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Methods We systematically searched PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and Scopus from inception to January 2026. Observational cohort studies of ACS patients were included. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), cardiovascular mortality, recurrent myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, heart failure (HF), and revascularization. SHR was analyzed as both continuous and categorical variables. Hazard ratios (HRs) for the highest versus lowest SHR categories or per 1-unit increase were pooled using random-effects models with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Subgroup analyses were performed according to diabetes status. Results Thirty-five studies involving 167,575 participants (mean age 64.4 years, 73.6% male) were included. Higher SHR was strongly associated with increased all-cause mortality (HR: 1.68, 95% CI: 1.52–1.85, p &lt; 0.0001, I² = 0%). Similar association persisted in continuous analyses (HR: 1.39 per unit, 95% CI: 1.06–1.81, p &lt; 0.0001, I² = 86.3%). The highest SHR category was also linked to elevated risks of MACE (HR: 1.55, 95% CI: 1.34–1.79, p &lt; 0.00001, I² = 80.7%), cardiovascular mortality (HR: 1.74, 95% CI: 1.19–2.55, p = 0.004, I² = 84.6%), stroke (HR: 1.73, 95% CI: 1.15–2.60, p = 0.009, I² = 0%), and HF (HR: 1.71, 95% CI: 1.39–2.11, p &lt; 0.0001, I² = 6.6%). Risks of revascularization and recurrent MI did not differ significantly across SHR categories. Associations remained consistent in continuous analyses. The relationship between higher SHR and mortality was consistent across diabetes subgroups. Increased mortality risk was observed among patients with diabetes (HR: 1.52, 95% CI: 1.18–1.95, p = 0.0347, I2 = 61.4%) and those without diabetes (HR: 1.84, 95% CI: 1.45–2.34, p = 0.0846, I2 = 51.2%), with no significant subgroup differences (p for interaction = 0.27). Conclusion SHR offers incremental prognostic value in ACS patients and may serve as a simple, widely available tool for risk stratification independent of diabetes status. Further research is needed to clarify its clinical utility.
title: Prognostic value of the stress hyperglycemia ratio in patients with acute coronary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Recent studies suggest that warmer ambient temperatures at the time of conception may be associated with a reduced activity of brown adipose tissue (BAT) in healthy adults. Reduced BAT activity is linked to higher triglyceride (TG) and lower high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels. Purpose To investigate in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS), the association between periconceptional temperature and the Atherogenic Index of Plasma (AIP), a marker of established prognostic value in this context. Methods We analysed 967 consecutive Spanish patients admitted for ACS in our centre, with confirmed coronary disease and in-hospital TG and HDL-C measurements between July 2023 and January 2026. Individual data were linked with historical climatological records of our region (reference years: 1991-2020) to estimate the mean temperature and diurnal temperature range (DTR) during the month of conception (estimated as date of birth minus 266 days). The AIP was calculated as log10(TG/HDL-C). Multiple linear regression models were used to test whether summer conception or mean temperature and DTR were independent predictors of adult AIP. The models were adjusted for age, sex, diabetes, active smoking, body mass index (BMI), cholesterol lowering therapies (statin, ezetimibe or bempedoic acid), fibrates or eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) treatment and mean temperature on the day of admission. Results Patients conceived in summer (n = 236) had a higher AIP on admission compared to those conceived during the rest of the year, although the difference was not statistically significant (0.176 ± 0.312 vs 0.141 ± 0.263; p=0.085). A visually bimodal pattern was observed, with higher AIP values also in late winter (February - March), coinciding with a wide DTR (Figure). In the multivariate analysis, summer conception was independently associated with higher AIP (β=0.039; p=0.039). Furthermore, higher mean temperature (β=0.007 per ºC; p=0.018) and wider DTR (β=0.094 per ºC; p=0.019) during the conception month were significantly associated with a higher AIP at ACS admission. Other predictors of higher AIP were admission at younger age, male sex, diabetes, active smoking, higher BMI, and previous treatment with fibrates or EPA (Table). Conclusion Conception during periods of higher ambient temperature and wider diurnal temperature range is associated with a more pro-atherogenic lipid profile decades later in ACS patients. These findings support early metabolic programming as a potential determinant of lifelong cardiovascular risk and may have implications for risk stratification in the context of climate change, although residual confounding related to birth date cannot be excluded.FigureTable
title: Periconceptional ambient temperature and adult atherogenic lipid profile: a life-course study in patients with acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Advances in primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) have substantially reduced in-hospital mortality in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI). However, real-world data regarding mid-term post-discharge outcomes, particularly among Japanese patients treated in the contemporary era, remain limited. A precise assessment of post-discharge events is essential to optimize secondary prevention strategies after AMI. Purpose To elucidate 2-year post-discharge outcomes in Japanese patients with AMI in the contemporary era. Methods We analyzed 6,394 consecutive patients with AMI who were enrolled in the Mie ACS Registry between January 2013 and December 2022 and survived to hospital discharge. The study endpoints were all-cause death and major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), defined as cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, or non-fatal stroke occurring after discharge. Cumulative event rates up to 2 years were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method. Temporal comparisons were performed between the early period (2013–2017) and the late period (2018–2022). Event rates were also compared between the first year (0–365 days) and the second year (366–730 days) after discharge. In addition, outcomes were stratified according to Killip class at presentation. Results The 2-year cumulative incidence of all-cause death after discharge was similar between the early and late periods (7.0% vs. 6.3%; log-rank P = 0.58; Figure 1A). Likewise, the 2-year cumulative incidence of MACCE did not differ significantly between periods (5.2% vs. 5.3%; log-rank P = 0.95; Figure 1B). For both endpoints, event accumulation was steeper during the first year after discharge than during the second year, with significantly higher incidence rates in the first year (all-cause death: incidence rate ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.52–0.77, p &lt; 0.001; MACCE: incidence rate ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.44–0.69, p &lt; 0.001), indicating attenuation of risk beyond the first year. When stratified by Killip class, the cumulative incidence of all-cause death increased stepwise with increasing Killip severity (Killip I, Killip II/III, and Killip IV; log-rank P &lt; 0.001; Figure 2A). Similarly, MACCE incidence was significantly higher among patients with more advanced Killip class (log-rank P &lt; 0.001; Figure 2B). Conclusions In this contemporary Japanese cohort, no significant temporal improvement in 2-year post-discharge outcomes was observed over the past decade. The first year after discharge represents a particularly vulnerable period, and Killip class at presentation remains a strong determinant of long-term prognosis. These findings underscore the importance of early and intensive secondary prevention, especially in patients presenting with higher Killip class.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Two-year post-discharge outcomes after acute myocardial infarction in the contemporary era: Ten-year temporal trends from the Mie ACS Registry

abstract: Abstract Background Aortic valve stenosis (AS) severity in high gradient stenosis as assessed by transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) can remain inconclusive when flow velocity (VmaxTTE), mean pressure gradient (MPGTTE), and calculated effective valve area (eAVATTE) are noncongruent. To aid severity classification, we suggest AVA by computed tomography angiography (CTA)-planimetry (aAVACTA) as additional severity criteria marker as part of an integrated approach for heart team discussion. Methods Patients who presented to our institution with discordant high gradient (HG) TTE based stenosis findings (eAVATTE ≥1.0cm² despite severe indicative maximum velocity VmaxTTE≥4m/s and mean gradient MPGTTE≥40mmHg) and underwent a pre-TAVI-CTA-scan between 2013 and 2025 were included for analysis. aAVACTA as a 4th severity marker was assessed using recently published aAVACTA severity cut-offs for stratification to CTA planimetry based severe, indeterminate or non-severe stenosis. Invasive hemodynamic measurements (MPGCath) were included when available within 60days of CT-Scan. Results Screening yielded a total of 189 cases with discordant HG aortic stenosis of which 168 had additional invasive gradient availability (MPGCath). aAVACTA values indicated severe stenosis (TC&lt;0.95cm², BC&lt;1.08cm²) in 40.7% of total cases (n=77 of 189). This percentage was 43.1% (n=69 of 160) when excluding cases with more than mild Aortic Insufficiency; 39.4% (n=39 of 99) excluding TTE based Stroke Volume Index (SVI) &gt;58ml/m²; 39.6% (n=44 of 111) excluding low invasive MPGCath&lt;35mmHg; and 31.5% (n=23/73) at eAVATTE cut-off raised to ≥1.1cm². Conclusion Despite eAVATTE showing a valve area indicative of nonsevere stenosis, aAVACTA confirmed MPGTTE/VmaxTTE severe stenosis in &gt;30% of cases yielding added value to TTE based measurements.
title: CTA-based planimetry in discordant high-gradient aortic stenosis

abstract: Abstract Introduction Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMS) are recommended quality indicators to measure patients' perspectives of symptoms and quality of life. In ischaemic heart disease, the Seattle Angina Questionnaire (SAQ), Rose Dyspnoea Score and Patient Health Questionnaire are suggested. However, routine longitudinal measurements are under-utilised, due to lack of workflow integration, administrative burden and patient fatigue1. While recommended for 5-year collection after acute coronary syndrome (ACS)2, it is unclear if this is feasible and clinically meaningful. Purpose We investigated the feasibility and completeness of real-world PROMS collection in ACS patients for 5 years, analysing characteristics of those who did respond on follow-up. We compared PROMS across different interventions of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) and medical therapy only. Methods This was a prospective observational study. ACS admissions between Aug 2017-Jan 2021 were surveyed in-person, via phone or SMS. Due to manpower constraints, only SMS were used at 3-5 years. Intervention data was collected prospectively, mortality and readmissions via retrospective linkage to existing registries. Paired t-tests were used for PROMS and chi-square for binary variables. Results 1673 baseline PROMS were submitted. 902 patients responded to at least one follow-up. They were younger (62 vs 65y, p&lt;0.0001), had higher education (68.6% vs 58.2%, p&lt;0.0001), more likely employed (60.3% vs 53.5%, p=0.006), and able to self-care (50.5% vs 41.6%, p&lt;0.0001). Response rates peaked at 1 month (32.9%) and 1 year (32.0%), were 25-26% at 3 and 6 months, 13.5% at 2 years, and fell below 10% after 3 years, reaching 3% at 5 years. Among responders who were recommended PCI or CABG, we compared those receiving either with those who chose medical therapy alone. 5-year mortality was significantly higher in the latter (Fig.1). At baseline, patients on medical therapy instead of CABG had slightly better angina frequency scores, though still in the monthly frequency range. Changes in SAQ, computed between baseline and latest scores, reached minimally clinically important difference (MCID) thresholds across all groups. Summary scores suggest significant improvements that peaked in the initial months and largely plateaued over time (Fig.2). However, those on medical therapy had significantly smaller improvements in physical limitation compared to PCI and angina frequency compared to CABG. Conclusion SAQ appeared to differentiate some aspects of patient-reported quality of life amongst ACS patients receiving different therapies. While possible to collect PROMS over 5 years, attrition affects the long-term conclusions. Majority of PROMS improvements occurred in the initial months. As long-term collection after ACS is challenging, more real-world studies are needed to justify its collection for longer-term clinical management.Figure 1.PROMS and clinical outcomesFigure 2.5-year PROMS across groups
title: Measuring what matters: 5-years experience with patient-reported outcome measures in acute coronary syndrome patients

abstract: Abstract Background & Aims Left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD) and ventricular remodeling after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for acute myocardial infarction (AMI) are major predictors of long-term adverse cardiovascular events. Current evaluation tools such as B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and echocardiography are limited by high cost, professional operation, and insufficient dynamic monitoring. Electromechanical activation time (EMAT, ms) is a non-invasive indicator reflecting left ventricular electromechanical coupling, but its prognostic value in AMI patients after PCI remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the predictive value of EMAT measured by a wearable synchronous phonocardiogram-electrocardiogram (PCG-ECG) device for LVSD and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs) in AMI patients post-PCI. Methods This single-center prospective cohort study enrolled AMI patients undergoing emergency PCI between May 2024 and April 2025. Baseline EMAT was measured by a wearable synchronous PCG-ECG device. Baseline characteristics, comorbidities, medications, laboratory parameters, and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) were collected. Primary endpoints were 6- and 12-month MACEs. Secondary endpoints included all-cause death, unplanned readmission, and LVSD (LVEF &lt;50%). The correlation between EMAT and LVEF was analyzed using smoothing splines. Multivariate Cox regression was performed to evaluate the independent prognostic value of EMAT. Subgroup analysis was conducted according to age. Peri-procedural ΔEMAT was also assessed. P&lt;0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results A total of 375 patients completed 6-month follow-up and 152 completed 12-month follow-up. Baseline EMAT was negatively and linearly correlated with LVEF (Figure 1). With increasing EMAT tertiles, LVEF decreased significantly (52.00–75.00 ms: 56.01%; 76.00–86.00 ms: 53.02%; 87.00–129.00 ms: 51.32%, P&lt;0.001). At 6 months, 78 MACEs occurred; at 12 months, 31 MACEs occurred. In multivariable Cox regression, per 1 Z-score increase in EMAT was associated with higher 12-month MACE risk (HR=2.06, 95%CI:1.39–3.06, P=0.0003). The highest EMAT tertile conferred a 5.72-fold higher MACE risk compared with the lowest tertile (HR=5.72, 95%CI:1.63–20.13, P=0.0065; Table 1). The predictive effect of EMAT was stronger in patients &lt;60 years (P-interaction=0.0053). Peri-procedural ΔEMAT showed no significant prognostic value (P&gt;0.05). Conclusions Prolonged baseline EMAT is an independent predictor of LVSD and MACEs in AMI patients after PCI, especially in those younger than 60 years. The wearable PCG-ECG device provides a non-invasive, convenient, and low-cost strategy for risk stratification. Peri-procedural short-term ΔEMAT has no significant prognostic impact in this population.EMAT and LVEF in AMI patients post-PCIEMAT for MACE in AMI post-PCI (6-/12-mo)
title: ElectroMechanical Activation Time (EMAT) from wearable synchronous phonocardiogram-electrocardiogram device predicts left ventricular systolic dysfunction and prognosis in acute myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Despite improved outcomes in the overall acute coronary syndrome (ACS) population, older patients still have worse prognoses than younger patients. Patients aged ≥90 years (nonagenarians) represent a rapidly growing but underexplored subgroup. These patients often have morbidities and limited therapeutic options, resulting in unfavorable outcomes. However, there is limited data on diagnostic strategies, therapeutic management, and in-hospital outcomes for nonagenarians with ACS. To address this gap, we conducted an analysis focusing on age-stratified outcomes, particularly among the oldest old. Purpose This study aimed to evaluate age-specific trends in in-hospital outcomes following ACS and to clarify the clinical characteristics, treatment patterns, and prognoses of nonagenarians compared to those of younger patients. Methods The REVEIL-ACS registry is an ongoing, multicenter, prospective study that enrolled consecutive patients undergoing emergency coronary angiography for ACS at 25 Japanese centers between January 2024 and March 2025. Eligible patients were divided into four age groups: 20–69, 70–79, 80–89, and 90–99 years. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (MACCE) during hospitalization. The secondary outcomes were in-hospital death and major bleeding events. We used a parametric g-formula to estimate the marginal probabilities of in-hospital outcomes across age groups. Results Of 2,071 eligible patients, 828 (40%) were aged 20–69, 585 (28%) were 70–79, 559 (27%) were 80–89, and 99 (4.8%) were 90–99 years. The prevalence of elevated cardiac troponin, non-ST elevation myocardial infarction, and left main and multivessel disease increased in the higher age groups, while the proportion of patients undergoing emergent percutaneous coronary intervention and receiving mechanical circulatory support was similar across age groups. Of 1,822 patients with available post-hospitalization outcomes, those in the higher age groups were more likely to have comorbidities, including hypertension, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, and anemia. Approximately 90% of nonagenarians had a high bleeding risk based on the ARC-HBR criteria. Adjusted probability of MACCE was 5.1% (95% CI, 3.2%–6.8%) in patients aged 20–69 years, 9.2% (95% CI, 7.1%–12%) % in 70–79 years, 11% (95% CI, 8.4%–14%) in 80–89 years, 20% (95% CI, 10%–30%) in 90–99 years (Figure 1). Adjusted in-hospital mortality was lowest in the patients aged 20–69 years and highest in those aged 90–99 years (Figure 2A). However, this age-related trend was not observed for the adjusted probabilities of major bleeding (Figure 2B). Conclusions Even in nonagenarians, invasive treatment was frequently performed without an increase in major bleeding events. However, the incidence of in-hospital MACCE remained disproportionately high, underscoring the need for personalized medical strategies for nonagenarians.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Clinical characteristics, treatment pattens, and in-hospital outcomes in nonagenarians with acute coronary syndrome: insight from the REVEIL-ACS registry

abstract: Abstract Background Patients presenting with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) after prior coronary revascularization have traditionally been regarded as a high-risk population with poorer outcomes than those experiencing their first ACS event. Although many clinical trials have described this adverse prognosis, contemporary guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) may attenuate the clinical risk. This study evaluated current clinical characteristics and long-term outcomes of ACS patients with previous coronary revascularization in a real-world setting. Methods Our institution is the only hospital in the region providing 24-hour emergency percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), resulting in a high concentration of ACS referrals, including those with prior interventions. We retrospectively reviewed 502 consecutive ACS patients who underwent emergency PCI from January 2021 to July 2024. Patients were categorized into Prior Revascularization and First-time Revascularization groups. Baseline demographics, cardiovascular risk profiles, medication use, angiographic findings, and in-hospital outcomes were compared. The primary endpoint was 1-year major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as a composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, and target lesion revascularization. Results Among the 502 patients, 93 (18.5%) had prior revascularization, whereas 409 (81.5%) presented with their first ACS requiring PCI. Patients with prior revascularization were older and had higher rates of diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and peripheral artery disease. They more frequently received antiplatelet therapy, statins, and beta-blockers, resulting in lower LDL-cholesterol levels at presentation. The incidence of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) was markedly lower in patients with previous revascularization. Despite these differences, the incidence of 1-year MACE did not differ significantly, and survival analysis revealed no significant divergence in event-free survival. Conclusion ACS patients with prior coronary revascularization carried a higher burden of comorbidities yet were less likely to present with STEMI. Their 1-year outcomes were comparable to first-time ACS patients, suggesting that contemporary secondary prevention strategies and optimized therapy may mitigate the traditionally elevated risk of recurrent ACS. These findings highlight the impact of sustained GDMT in preventing total coronary occlusion and improving long-term prognosis in this high-risk population.Patient characteristicsMACE
title: Impact of prior coronary revascularisation on clinical presentation and one-year outcomes in acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Clinical manifestations of coronary heart disease (CHD) increase steeply with age and occur earlier in men than in women. Previous studies of first manifestations of acute coronary syndromes (ACS), defined as a first hospitalization for angina, acute myocardial infarction (AMI), ischemic heart disease (IHD), or death due to CHD have shown that women, compared with men of the same age, initially present with angina, whereas men more commonly present with AMI or CHD death. However, the advent of more sensitive biomarkers about 25 years ago may have caused a shift in the distinction between angina and AMI. Current data on the sex-specific distribution and incidence of different ACS manifestations is limited. Purpose to examine trends in occurrence and distribution of different forms of ACS in men and women aged 18-74 years in Sweden between 1997 and 2023. Methods Nationwide Swedish registers on hospital discharges and cause-specific deaths were used to calculate sex-specific trends for first coronary admissions or deaths in men and women aged 18-74 years during 1997 to 2023. Results A total of 416,572 individuals were identified with a first manifestation of ACS (29% women, 71% men). Marked declines in rates of CHD death, hospitalizations for AMI and for angina were noted in both men and women, with the most conspicuous decline seen for angina (Figure 1). Angina was the most common diagnosis in women during 1997-1999 (47% of all cases, followed, by AMI (36%) and coronary death (15%), with the corresponding proportions for men 35%, 41%, and 22%. By 2021–2023, the distribution had shifted substantially: among women, 19% presented with angina, 63% with AMI, and 12% with CHD death (Figure 2). The corresponding proportions in men were 20%, 61%, and 13%, indicating minimal sex differences in the distribution of first events. Conclusions The incidence of all first manifestations of CHD declined between 1997 and 2023, most notably for angina, likely at least partly reflecting the introduction of more sensitive biomarkers of myocardial injury. Whereas women were more likely than men to present with angina rather than AMI in 1997–1999, and less likely to present with AMI or CHD death, the clinical presentation was largely similar between sexes in 2021–2023. Notably, despite substantial reductions in coronary mortality over time, CHD death remained the first manifestation in 13% of men and 12% of women in 2021–2023.Figure 1Table 2
title: Trends in the distribution of first coronary events in men and women aged 18-74 years in Sweden 1997-2023 – women are becoming more like men

abstract: Abstract Background Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined and independent risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Current European and Indian guidelines recommend at least one lifetime measurement, with levels &gt;50 mg/dL associated with higher cardiovascular risk . However, data regarding the burden of elevated Lp(a) among Indian patients presenting with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) are limited. Purpose To determine the prevalence of elevated Lp(a) (&gt;50 mg/dL) in Indian patients hospitalized with ACS and to evaluate differences according to age groups. Methods This retrospective cross-sectional study included 1,540 consecutive patients admitted with ACS to a tertiary care center in India. Serum Lp(a) was measured using an immuno-turbidimetric method. Elevated Lp(a) was defined as &gt;50 mg/dL. Patients were stratified by age into younger (&lt;60 years) and older (≥60 years) groups. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± SD or median (interquartile range [IQR]) as appropriate. Prevalence estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Findings were interpreted in the context of a previously reported subset of 1,021 patients from the same cohort in which elevated Lp(a) showed significant association with angiographic severity (Gensini score). Results The cohort (n=1,540) had a mean Lp(a) of 44.7 ± 40.9 mg/dL and a median of 31.9 mg/dL (IQR: 14.4–64.3 mg/dL). Elevated Lp(a) (&gt;50 mg/dL) was present in 34.7% (535/1,540) of patients. Additionally, 22.7% (349/1,540) had Lp(a) levels &gt;70 mg/dL, representing a substantial very high-risk subgroup. When the patients were divided by age, high Lp(a) levels were common in both younger (&lt;60 years, n=749) and older (≥60 years, n=791) groups., with a numerically higher burden observed in patients &lt;60 years compared with those ≥60 years. This difference was statistically significant. Conclusion Approximately one-third of Indian patients presenting with ACS have elevated Lp(a), with nearly one-fifth exhibiting very high levels (&gt;70 mg/dL). The high prevalence of elevated Lp(a) in patients &lt;60 years highlights the possible contribution of inherited lipoprotein risk in younger individuals presenting with ACS. The high prevalence of elevated Lp(a) supports consideration of systematic Lp(a) assessment in patients with established ASCVD.
title: Prevalence of elevated lipoprotein(a) in Indian patients presenting with acute coronary syndrome: a large tertiary care cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background Premature myocardial infarction (MI) represents a major public health concern, particularly in transitional healthcare systems where risk factor control remains suboptimal. However, contemporary large-scale data on premature MI from Southeast Europe are limited. Aim To evaluate clinical characteristics, risk factor burden, management patterns, and in-hospital mortality among patients with premature MI in Kosovo over an 11-year period. Methods We analyzed 13,099 consecutive patients admitted with acute MI between 2014 and 2024 at our University Clinical Centre. Premature MI was defined as age &lt;55 years in men and &lt;65 years in women; very young MI as &lt;45 years. Baseline characteristics, invasive management, and in-hospital outcomes were compared with non-premature MI. Logistic regression identified predictors of in-hospital mortality. Results Premature MI accounted for 3,708 cases (28.3%), including 639 (4.9%) very young patients. Compared with non-premature MI, premature MI patients were more frequently male (100% men &lt;55; women &lt;65), active smokers (39–71%), and had a strong family history of cardiovascular disease (≈46–52%) (all p&lt;0.001). Very young MI patients had particularly high smoking prevalence (71%) but lower diabetes rates (14.6%). Hypertension (72.8%) and diabetes (40.4%) were highly prevalent among premature MI women, whereas smoking predominated in men (71%). STEMI presentation was common, particularly among very young patients (62.8%, p&lt;0.001). In-hospital mortality was significantly lower in premature compared with non-premature MI (6.1% vs. 11.1%, p&lt;0.001) and lowest in very young MI (2.0%). Independent predictors of mortality in premature MI included diabetes mellitus, left bundle branch block, reduced LVEF (&lt;50%), cardiogenic shock, and absence of PCI (all p&lt;0.001). Conclusions Nearly one-third of all AMI cases in Kosovo occur prematurely. Premature MI is characterized by an alarming burden of modifiable risk factors, particularly smoking and hypertension. Although short-term mortality is lower than in older patients, high-risk clinical features such as cardiogenic shock and LV dysfunction strongly determine outcome. These findings highlight the urgent need for aggressive primary prevention and early risk factor control in younger populations within transitional healthcare systems.Figure 1
title: Premature myocardial infarction in a transitional middle-income country: Clinical phenotype, risk burden, invasive management, and early mortality in an 11-year national cohort

abstract: Abstract Background and Aims The Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (UDMI) distinguishes type 1 from type 2 myocardial infarction (MI) but does not fully capture the heterogeneity of underlying mechanisms and prognosis. A causal endotype–based classification of MI has been proposed to better reflect pathophysiology and clinical risk. We evaluated the prognostic performance of this classification and its association with 1-year clinical outcomes. Methods Consecutive patients from the prospective, multicenter AMIPE registry with an adjudicated MI between 2017 and 2023 and ≥1-year follow-up were included.
