These findings suggest that distal embolic protection may mitigate microvascular injury during aggressive stent expansion and support selective use of filter devices in cases requiring large stent deployment.picture1
title: Saving myocardium: the protective role of filter devices during culprit overexpansion in STEMI

abstract: Abstract Background Drug-coated balloon (DCB)-based strategies are increasingly explored as an alternative or adjunct to drug-eluting stent (DES) implantation to reduce permanent metal burden. However, real-world data on the utilization and safety of DCB-based strategies in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remain limited. Purpose To evaluate real-world utilization and clinical outcomes of a DCB-based strategy compared with DES in patients undergoing PCI for ACS. Methods We performed a retrospective registry analysis of consecutive patients treated with PCI for ACS at a tertiary centre. Patients were stratified by revascularization strategy: DES-only versus DCB-based (DCB-only or hybrid approach). The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality at 1 year. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, prior coronary events, ACS presentation (ST-elevation myocardial infarction vs non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) or unstable angina), coronary complexity (SYNTAX score), and cardiogenic shock. Safety outcomes included in-hospital and 30-day mortality. Results A total of 2,684 patients were included, of whom 239 (8.9%) underwent a DCB-based strategy. Compared with DES-treated patients, those receiving a DCB-based strategy more frequently had diabetes (30.1% vs 22.6%, p=0.008), NSTEMI/unstable angina (59.8% vs 37.1%, p&lt;0.001), prior myocardial infarction (23.4% vs 10.9%, p&lt;0.001), and bifurcation lesions (15.3% vs 5.0%, p&lt;0.001). Rates of complete revascularization were comparable between strategies (61.9% vs 59.1%, p=0.417). One-year mortality was 5.9% in the DCB-based group and 7.1% in the DES group (p=0.503). After adjustment, a DCB-based strategy was not associated with higher 1-year mortality compared with DES (OR 1.08, 95% CI 0.56-2.09, p=0.81). Age, coronary complexity (SYNTAX score), and cardiogenic shock were independent predictors of mortality. There were no significant differences between DCB-based and DES strategies in in-hospital mortality (3.3% vs 3.1%, p=0.844) or 30-day mortality (4.6% vs 4.1%, p=0.718). Conclusion In this real-world ACS registry, a DCB-based, metal-minimizing revascularization strategy demonstrated comparable early and 1-year mortality to DES. These findings support lesion-tailored PCI strategies that minimize permanent metal implantation in contemporary ACS management.
title: Less metal, same outcomes: drug-coated balloon PCI in acute coronary syndrome - real-world registry data

abstract: Abstract Background Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients at high bleeding risk (HBR) are challenging because prolonged dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) after drug-eluting stent (DES) implantation increases bleeding complications, which are strongly associated with adverse prognosis in this population. Drug-coated balloons (DCB) offer a "leave nothing behind" strategy that may reduce bleeding risk by avoiding permanent metallic implants while maintaining efficacy, yet evidence in HBR ACS remains limited. Purpose To compare major bleeding outcomes between DCB and DES strategies in ACS patients meeting the Academic Research Consortium for High Bleeding Risk (ARC-HBR) criteria. Methods We retrospectively analyzed consecutive ACS patients with de novo lesions treated between January 2017 and March 2024 at a single center. HBR was defined by the Academic Research Consortium for HBR (ARC-HBR) criteria. Patients were stratified by revascularization strategy (DES vs. DCB) according to the operator’s discretion. The primary endpoint was BARC type 3–5 bleeding. To reduce confounding, 1:1 propensity score matching was performed using hemoglobin level, multivessel disease, Killip class, sex, left ventricular ejection fraction, use of oral anticoagulation, serum albumin level, age, presence of peripheral artery disease, and active malignancy as covariates. In the matched cohort, time-to-event outcomes were assessed using Kaplan–Meier analysis and compared using the log-rank test. Hazard ratios were estimated using unadjusted Cox proportional hazards models. Results Among 938 ACS patients, 414 met ARC-HBR criteria and were included (DES: 345; DCB: 67). After propensity score matching, 61 pairs (61 vs. 61) were analyzed. The median follow-up duration in the matched cohort was 13.7 months in the DCB group and 10.6 months in the DES group (p=0.963). DAPT duration in the matched cohort was significantly shorter in the DCB group than in the DES group (3.5 [1.0–7.0] vs. 6.0 [3.0–12.0] months; p=0.031). BARC type 3–5 bleeding occurred in 11 patients (18.0%) in the DCB group and 25 patients (41.0%) in the DES group. Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated a significantly lower cumulative incidence of bleeding in the DCB group (log-rank p=0.015). In the unadjusted Cox proportional hazards model, DCB treatment was associated with a lower risk of bleeding (HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.21–0.87; p=0.020). Conclusions In ACS patients meeting ARC-HBR criteria, DCB was associated with lower BARC type 3–5 bleeding in the propensity-matched analysis, together with substantially shorter DAPT duration. These real-world findings suggest that a DCB-based strategy may be a bleeding-sparing option for selected HBR ACS patients, although prospective studies are warranted to confirm safety and efficacy.BARC 3–5 bleeding in PS-matched cohort
title: Drug-coated balloon strategy and major bleeding in high-bleeding-risk acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Introduction Revascularization of patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is performed using drug eluting stent (DES). The introduction of devices that facilitate “stent-free” interventions, such as drug coated balloons (DCB), may allow similar performance in thrombotic outcomes, while requiring less intense antiplatelet treatment. As patients presenting with STEMI are considered higher risk, this meta-analysis aims to compare DCB versus DES PCI in this phenotype. Methods A systematic search was performed in three different databases. Following study selection, a meta-analysis was performed. For continuous outcomes, the mean difference (MD) from baseline along with the 95% confidence interval (95%CI) and for dichotomous outcomes, the risk ratio (RR) and the respective 95%CI, were calculated. Results A total of 7 studies and 4,510 patients reported separately event rates in patients with a STEMI diagnosis. In regard to outcomes, no difference was noted in either all-cause (RR: 1.11, 95%CI: 0.87-1.41) or cardiovascular mortality (RR: 1.17, 95%CI: 0.85-1.61). Moreover, patients undergoing DCB revascularization also had similar risk for MACE (RR: 0.85, 95%CI: 0.42-1.72), MI (RR: 0.88, 95%CI: 0.56-1.36), TLR (RR: 0.78, 95%CI: 0.43-1.40) and TVR (RR: 1.10, 95%CI: 0.39-1.37) as patients undergoing DES revascularization. Conclusion In patients presenting with STEMI, the use of DCB results in similar mortality and adverse cardiovascular events to DES. Further trials evaluating differences in presentation, thrombus presence, multivessel disease and pharmacotherapy to comprehensively assess stent-free interventions in this setting.
title: Drug coated balloon versus drug eluting stent angioplasty in patients presenting with STEMI: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Despite successful epicardial restoration via primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), microvascular obstruction (MVO) occurs in up to 40% of patients. While adjunctive intracoronary (IC) thrombolysis aims to dissolve distal micro-thrombi, clinical trials have yielded deeply polarized results, leading to fragmented guidelines. We hypothesized that this discrepancy is not a failure of the strategy, but a "specificity paradox" driven by the pharmacological properties of the agents used. Methods and results We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating IC thrombolysis during primary PCI. To address the primary hypothesis, trials were stratified into non-fibrin specific, moderately fibrin-specific, and highly fibrin-specific agents. The primary endpoint was major adverse cardiac events (MACE). Thirteen RCTs comprising 2,122 patients (including the recent STRIVE 2025 trial) were included. Overall, IC thrombolysis significantly reduced MACE (Risk Ratio [RR] 0.74; 95% CI 0.62–0.90; p=0.002). However, subgroup stratification revealed a highly significant interaction by drug class (p=0.003, I2=82.6%). Non-fibrin specific agents (RR 0.38; 95% CI 0.19–0.75) and moderately specific agents (RR 0.62; 95% CI 0.47–0.84) yielded robust clinical benefits. Conversely, highly fibrin-specific agents (e.g., alteplase) demonstrated no clinical benefit (RR 1.04; 95% CI 0.81–1.35). Statistical heterogeneity was entirely eliminated within all three defined subgroups (I2=0%). Conclusion The efficacy of adjunctive IC thrombolysis in STEMI is strictly dictated by a pharmacological class effect. While contemporary highly fibrin-specific agents demonstrate no clinical benefit, non-fibrin and moderately specific agents significantly improve outcomes. Future trials must prioritize the evaluation of non-fibrin restricted agents to address microvascular obstructionMace Intracoronary Thrombolysis
title: Unmasking the specificity paradox: why pharmacological class, not the strategy, defines success in intracoronary thrombolysis for stemi (role of fibrin specificity following the STRIVE trial)

abstract: Abstract Background With the COLCOT study demonstrating that colchicine can improve prognosis in myocardial infarction (MI) patients, anti-inflammatory therapy has become a major focus of current research. Mast cells (MCs), as key inflammatory cells, play a critical role in MI. MCs are rapidly activated in the early phase of MI and release multiple effector molecules, amplifying the inflammatory cascade1. Previous studies have shown that tryptase levels in the acute phase of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), a marker of mast cell activation, are an independent risk factor for long-term adverse outcomes2. Animal experiments suggest that stabilizing MCs or antagonizing their released products can alleviate I/R injury and reduce infarct size3. However, clinical evidence supporting this is still limited. Ketotifen, a classic mast cell stabilizer widely used in the treatment of allergic diseases, may have protective effects in myocardial infarction patients, which merits further investigation. Purpose This study aims to investigate the efficacy and safety of the mast cell stabilizer ketotifen in the treatment of STEMI patients. Methods This study enrolled STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI from September 2022 to September 2023, who were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio using block randomization: ① Control group: received standard treatment for STEMI; ② Ketotifen group: received standard treatment plus ketotifen (1 mg twice daily) for 3 months. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was performed at 3 months post-MI to assess infarct size as the primary endpoint. Results A total of 112 patients with STEMI were enrolled in this study and allocated to the ketotifen group (n = 56) and the control group (n = 56). The mean age was 56.74 ± 12.16 years, and 101 patients (90.18%) were male. At 3 months of follow-up, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was performed to assess infarct size. The ketotifen group had a significantly smaller myocardial infarct size than the control group (12.86 ± 5.63 g VS. 15.87 ± 4.87 g, P = 0.003) (Figure 1). This effect was consistent across different age groups, CKMB peak levels (≥100 U/L VS. &lt;100 U/L), and infarct locations (Figure 2). The ketotifen group had a lower extracellular volume fraction (27.27 ± 5.65% VS. 30.14 ± 5.14%, P = 0.006) and greater improvement in global longitudinal strain (3.24 ± 0.50% VS. 2.45 ± 0.73%, P &lt; 0.001) compared to the control group. Five patients in the ketotifen group experienced mild drowsiness, which resolved within approximately one week without affecting treatment adherence. Conclusion The mast cell stabilizer ketotifen reduces myocardial infarct size and fibrosis while improving myocardial strain in STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI, with a favorable safety profile. We are currently conducting a multicenter, randomized, event-driven clinical trial to evaluate whether ketotifen can reduce the incidence of adverse outcomes.figure--1.jpgfigure--2.jpg
title: Clinical study on the efficacy and safety of ketotifen in STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI

abstract: Abstract Introduction Multivessel coronary artery disease is widely common among patients presenting with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Percutaneous coronary intervention is deemed as the gold standard for the therapy of STEMI.1 This addresses the goal of revascularization of the infarct related artery as soon as possible. However, the optimal timing for complete revascularization of the non-infarct related artery is unclear. The aim of this study is to use evidence from published randomized controlled trials (RCT) to compare staged complete revascularization (SR) and immediate complete revascularization (IR) in terms of safety. Methods We followed the PRISMA statement guidelines. We searched multiple online databases. We included studies comparing SR to IR in terms of all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiac events (MACE), non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), spontaneous MI and unplanned ischemia-driven revascularization (UIDR). We conducted leave-one-out analysis and meta-regression according to timing of SR (in-hospital vs post-discharge). Results 7 RCTs (3,017 total patients) were included.2-8 The SR group was favored in terms of all-cause mortality (RR = 0.67, 95% CI = 0.48 - 0.93; t(6) = −2.97, p = 0.025). No statistically significant differences were found between the two groups in terms of MACE, UIDR and spontaneous MI. In terms of non-fatal MI, the IR group was favored (RR = 1.74; 95% CI = 1.03 - 2.95; p = 0.04). There was a significantly higher risk of procedure related MI in the SR compared to the IR group (RR = 3.77; 95% CI = 1.60 - 8.94; p = 0.02). In our meta-regression, no statistically significant difference was found between the early timing of the staged procedure and the IR group in all outcomes. However, late timing of the staged procedure was associated with worse outcomes in MACE (RR = 1.51, 95% CI = 1.10 – 2.07), non-fatal MI (RR = 2.74, 95% CI = 1.63 - 4.62; p = 0.004) and UIDR (RR = 1.75; 95% CI = 1.19 - 2.59; p = 0.015). Late timing of the staged procedure was not associated with a significant difference in all-cause mortality. Lastly, Bayesian meta-regression revealed that each doubling of the median duration of delay between PPCI and the staged procedure was associated with a 15% increase in the MACE risk ratio (RR per doubling = 1.15; 95% CrI = 0.91 - 1.43) with a &gt;90% posterior probability that longer delays worsen outcomes. Conclusion A significant difference was found favoring SR in all-cause mortality over IR. Early timing was associated with comparable to or better outcomes than IR. Late timing of the staged procedure was associated with a greater risk of events in nearly all outcomes.
title: Optimal timing of complete revascularization in patients presenting with STEMI and multivessel disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Right ventricular (RV) function has important prognostic implications across cardiovascular pathologies. However, its value after ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) remains poorly characterized. Purpose To determine the prevalence of RV dysfunction in a large STEMI cohort, assess its prognostic impact, and evaluate whether it differs by infarct location. Methods Using retrospective data from a large tertiary care center, we assessed routinely-measured echocardiographic parameters of RV function in STEMI patients, specifically tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) and tricuspid lateral annular peak systolic velocity (S'). The association between RV dysfunction and 30-day heart failure hospitalizations and all-cause mortality was evaluated in the entire STEMI cohort and according to infarct location (anterior vs inferior). Exclusion criteria included previous MI and factors which may affect RV function (implanted pacemaker, previous cardiac surgery, etc.). Results Included were 665 patients (79.7% men; mean age 62.5±12.9 years). Reduced TAPSE (&lt;1.7 cm) was present in 13.5%, was similar between anterior and inferior STEMI (14.6% vs 12.5%; p = 0.42), and was associated with worse prognosis (OR 4.30; 95% CI 2.40-7.55). Similarly, reduced S' (&lt;9.5 cm/s) was present in 16.1%, did not differ between anterior and inferior STEMI (16.0% vs 17.3%; p = 0.65), and was associated with adverse outcomes (OR 3.64; 95% CI 2.05-6.48). After adjustment for age, sex, and left ventricular ejection fraction, reduced TAPSE showed similar prognostic impact in both anterior and inferior STEMI (OR 1.74; 95% CI 0.38-7.92, p = 0.48), whereas reduced S' was prognostic only in inferior STEMI. Conclusions This is the largest study investigating RV dysfunction and its effect on prognosis across STEMI subtypes. RV dysfunction was prevalent following STEMI and was found to be associated with adverse outcomes across infarct locations. These findings may refine post-STEMI risk stratification and inform clinical decision-making.Prevalence of reduced TAPSE and S'30-day outcomes according to RV function
title: Prognostic impact of right ventricular function after ST-elevation myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Introduction The Stent for Life/Stent Save a Life (SFL/SSL) programme, launched in 2011, aimed to reduce delays in ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) treatment and increase access to primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PPCI). Momento 25 provides a new national assessment of the Portuguese PPCI network. This study compares key performance indicators from 2011–2025, identifies opportunities for improvement and highlights the importance of continuous monitoring of reperfusion times, including critical intervals, operational targets and regional variations. Methods Data from Moments 0–6 (M6, n=1652) and Moment 25 (M25, n=249) were analysed. Variables included patient delay (symptom-to-FMC), system delay (FMC-to-reperfusion), FMC-to-ECG, type of first medical contact (INEM vs self-transport), compliance with guideline targets (ECG ≤10 min; door-to-balloon ≤60 min; FMC-to-balloon ≤90 min; symptom-to-balloon ≤120 min) and initial admission to centres with and without PPCI. Results No significant differences were found for patient or system delay. Overall compliance with guideline-recommended timings also showed no significant changes, although Moment 25 recorded the highest door-to-balloon performance (59.6%). INEM activation increased steadily across study periods, from 35.2% in Moment 0 to 49.4% in Moment 25 (p&lt;0.001). Significant differences in target compliance were observed between patients with and without INEM activation (Table 1). A marked reduction in initial admission to non-PPCI hospitals was noted, from 54.5% in Moment 0 to 28.9% in Moment 25 (p&lt;0.001). Regional disparities persisted, with presentation to non-PPCI centres ranging from 36.5% in Lisbon and Tagus Valley to 54.3% in Alentejo. Conclusions Throughout the SFL/SSL initiative, sustained growth in INEM activation was observed, accompanied by improved network efficiency, reflected in higher proportions of patients reperfused within ≤90 min, and reduced admission to hospitals without interventional cardiology. However, significant delays and regional inequalities persist, compromising equitable access to PPCI. Strengthening cardiovascular emergency literacy, encouraging early INEM activation and reorganising regional networks are essential to improve and consolidate the gains achieved.
title: Primary angioplasty in Portugal during the stent for life / stent save a life initiative: where do we stand?

abstract: Abstract Background Early coronary reperfusion with primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) combined with dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) is the standard of care in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Although oral P2Y12 inhibitors are routinely administered, the optimal timing of pretreatment remains debated, with inconsistent evidence regarding ischemic benefit and bleeding risk. Purpose To evaluate the clinical impact of early oral P2Y12 pretreatment prior to primary PCI in patients with STEMI. Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library from inception through November 5, 2025, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cohort studies comparing early oral P2Y12 pretreatment versus no pretreatment in STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI. The primary outcomes were myocardial infarction (MI) and all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included post-PCI TIMI 3 flow and major bleeding. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were pooled using random-effects models. Risk of bias was assessed using ROB2 and ROBINS-I tools, and certainty of evidence was appraised using the GRADE framework. Results Twenty-four studies encompassing 110,326 patients (3 RCTs and 21 observational studies) were included. Pretreatment with oral P2Y12 inhibitors showed heterogeneous but overall favorable ischemic outcomes without a consistent increase in bleeding risk. Early P2Y12 pretreatment was associated with a significant reduction in recurrent MI at 30 days (RR = 0.84, 95% CI 0.73–0.96; p=0.01) with non-significant trends toward lower target vessel revascularization, mortality, stroke, stent thrombosis, MACE, and bleeding events. At 12 months, pretreatment was associated with a significant reduction in recurrent MI (RR = 0.73, 95% CI 0.57–0.95; p=0.02). No significant differences were observed in all-cause mortality or achievement of post-PCI TIMI 3 flow. Overall certainty of evidence was moderate. In prespecified subgroup analyses according to P2Y12 inhibitor type, differential treatment effects were observed across agents. Clopidogrel pretreatment reduced 30-day myocardial infarction (RR = 0.68, 95% CI 0.48–0.98; p=0.04), improved TIMI flow, and reduced bleeding risk (RR = 0.80, 95% CI 0.68–0.94; p=0.006). Ticagrelor pretreatment showed neutral effects across early and pooled follow-up analyses. Conclusions In patients with STEMI undergoing primary PCI, early oral P2Y12 pretreatment was associated with reduced recurrent myocardial infarction at short and long term follow-up, without a consistent increase in bleeding risk. No mortality benefit was demonstrated. Subgroup analyses suggested variability according to P2Y12 inhibitor type, with clopidogrel showing early ischemic and safety benefits. Further adequately powered randomized trials are needed to refine patient selection and optimal timing strategies.OutcomesINFOGRAPHIC
title: Timing matters: impact of early oral p2y12 pretreatment on ischemic outcomes and reperfusion in stemi patients undergoing primary pci

abstract: Abstract Background Despite advances in reperfusion, preventive medications, and guideline-directed medical therapies, patients presenting with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) continue to encounter significant but variable risk of heart failure (HF) and mortality. Defining the contemporary burden of this residual risk and the identification of high-risk profiles in routine practice could inform risk-guided management after myocardial infarction (MI). Purpose To characterize contemporary HF and mortality outcomes in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for STEMI and identify high-risk subgroups for targeted intervention. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study using Optum Market Clarity linked electronic health record and claims data (United States, July 2021–December 2023). Adults with STEMI undergoing PCI were identified. HF and mortality outcomes were assessed overall and in clinical subgroups, including anterior STEMI, anterior STEMI LAD/left main culprit vessel, and patients without prior HF or MI. Cox proportional hazards models were used to identify independent risk predictors. Results Among 63,276 STEMI patients, mean age was 64.2 years, 68.4% were male and cardiovascular risk burden was high (hypertension: 60.9%, type 2 diabetes: 32.5%, prior myocardial infarction: 6.9%). At 1 year, HF hospitalization (HHF) occurred in 8.21% (95% CI 8.00–8.43) and all-cause mortality in 8.50% (95% CI 8.29–8.72). Independent predictors of HHF included prior HF (HR 1.96, 95% CI 1.82–2.10), prior MI (HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.07–1.25), anterior STEMI (HR 1.54, 95% CI 1.47–1.63), and chronic kidney disease (HR 1.50, 95% CI 1.40–1.60). Mortality was strongly associated with cardiogenic shock (HR 2.95, 95% CI 2.77–3.14), cardiac arrest (HR 2.92, 95% CI 2.71–3.14), and anterior STEMI (HR 1.09, 95% CI: 1.04–1.15). Patients with anterior STEMI (n=25,088) represented a higher-risk group, with greater risks for HHF (10.36% [95% CI 9.98–10.74] vs 8.21%; relative increase 26%) and mortality (9.54% [95% CI 9.18–9.91] vs 8.50%; relative increase 12%) (Figure). In-hospital complications were more frequent among anterior STEMI patients, including cardiogenic shock (17.7% vs 14.5%) and HF (58.9% vs 44.5%). HF outpatient encounters were frequent, occurring in 37.5% of all patients and 50.3% of anterior STEMI patients within 1 year. Meaningful differences in event rates were observed across clinically relevant subgroups (Table). Conclusions Despite contemporary PCI and medical therapy, significant residual HF and mortality risks remain after STEMI, with anterior MI identifying a high-risk clinical group. These findings highlight the potential role of risk-guided surveillance strategies to mitigate downstream HF and mortality.
title: Contemporary heart failure and mortality burden after STEMI: insights from a real-world cohort

abstract: Abstract Background and Aims Despite advances in primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), uncertainty remains regarding the routine use of beta-blockers and potential heterogeneity among individual agents in the management of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). This study aimed to investigate the clinical outcomes associated with nebivolol versus bisoprolol in patients with STEMI undergoing primary PCI. Methods From Korea Acute Myocardial Infarction Registry between 2011 to 2020, 5,076 patients with STEMI who underwent successful primary PCI with second-generation DES were eligible for the final analysis. The primary endpoint was all-cause death. The secondary endpoints were stroke, stent thrombosis, cardiac death, and hospitalization for heart failure (HF), and major adverse cardiac events (MACE), a composite of all-cause death, recurrent myocardial infarction (MI), and any repeat revascularization. Results Among the study population, 2,027 patients received nebivolol and 3,049 received bisoprolol. After 1:1 propensity score matching, 1,605 patients were included in each group. During follow-up, clinical outcomes were comparable between the nebivolol and bisoprolol groups in the propensity score-matched cohort. At 1 year, the incidence of MACE did not differ significantly between groups [HR 0.877; 95% CI 0.639–1.204; P = 0.468]. Similarly, no significant differences were observed in all-cause death (1.7% vs. 2.1%; P = 0.605) or MI (0.7% vs. 0.8%; P = 0.838). At 3 years, rates of all-cause death (3.7% in the nebivolol group and 4.3% in the bisoprolol group, HR 0.864; 95% CI 0.607–1.230; P = 0.472) and MACE (10.1% of nebivolol users and 11.0% of bisoprolol users, HR 0.905; 95% CI 0.723–1.134; P = 0.421) remained comparable between the two groups. Conclusions Among patients with STEMI treated with primary PCI, nebivolol and bisoprolol were associated with comparable clinical outcomes.
title: Comparative clinical outcomes of nebivolol versus bisoprolol in patients with STEMI after primary PCI: a propensity-score matched analysis

abstract: Abstract Purpose This study aimed to explore the role of 18F-FAPI-04 PET/MRI in evaluating myocardial fibrosis in coronary heart disease (CHD) and its value in distinguishing the fibrotic status of myocardial segments. Methods A total of 47 CHD patients were enrolled in this retrospective bidirectional cohort study, including 32 patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), 11 patients with non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), and 4 patients with unstable angina (UA); the latter two were classified as the non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS) group. All the above patients underwent 18F-FAPI-04 PET/MRI examination, among which 19 STEMI patients received a second PET/MRI examination at an average of six months follow-up. Clinical, laboratory, and imaging data of these patients were collected. Differences in PET parameters between the STEMI and NSTE-ACS groups were compared; a prediction model of PET parameters for myocardial scar was constructed in STEMI patients who underwent serial PET/MRI examinations. Segmental myocardial fibrotic status was also analyzed by matching the 16-segment bullseye maps between PET and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) in these 19 STEMI patients. Results The standardized uptake value (SUV), target-to-background ratio (TBR), and myocardial FAPI uptake volume (MFUV) in STEMI patients were significantly higher than those in the NSTE-ACS group (P &lt; 0.05). In STEMI patients who underwent serial PET/MRI examinations, the model incorporating SUVpeak, left ventricular end-systolic volume index (LVESVI), and peak high-sensitivity troponin I (Hs-TnIpeak) showed the best predictive performance (adjusted R2 = 0.707). The segmental SUV (SUVseg), segmental TBR (TBRseg), and late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) in FAPI+LGE+ segments were higher than those in the other groups (P &lt; 0.001); the SUVseg and TBRseg in the FAPI+LGE- group were higher than those in the FAPI-LGE+ and FAPI-LGE- groups (P &lt; 0.001); the LGE in the FAPI-LGE+ group was higher than in the FAPI-LGE- and FAPI+LGE- groups (P &lt; 0.001). Conclusion 18F-FAPI-04 PET/MRI parameters can distinguish CHD subtypes, and the combined model can improve the accuracy of predicting myocardial scar. The matching analysis of 16-segment bullseye maps of PET and CMR can distinguish fibrosis stages, which provides a molecular imaging basis for CHD management.Inter-segmental Group Differences PlotCase pics
title: Multidimensional assessment of myocardial fibrosis in coronary heart disease using 18F-FAPI-04 PET/MRI

abstract: Abstract Background In the BRIGHT-4 trial, among 6,016 patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with a radial artery approach, procedural anticoagulation with bivalirudin plus a post-PCI high-dose infusion for 2-4 hours reduced the 30-day primary composite outcome of all-cause death or BARC (Bleeding Academic Research Consortium) types 3-5 bleeding, as well as death and bleeding individually, compared with heparin monotherapy. Purpose Whether the benefits of bivalirudin apply principally to patients who are at high bleeding risk (HBR) is unknown. Methods In a pre-specified analysis from BRIGHT-4, outcomes were examined by baseline bleeding risk, with HBR defined as a CRUSADE score ≥30. Results HBR was present in 1,435 (23.9%) randomized patients. HBR patients had higher rates of the 30-day primary endpoint (8.6% vs. 2.2%; hazard ratio [HR] 4.08, 95% CI 3.14-5.31), driven both by greater mortality and BARC types 3-5 bleeding. In HBR patients, the primary outcome occurred in 8.1% of patients randomized to bivalirudin vs. 9.2% randomized to heparin (difference -1.1%, 95% CI -4.0% to 1.8%; HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.62-1.26). In non-HBR patients, the primary outcome occurred in 1.4% of patients randomized to bivalirudin vs. 2.9% randomized to heparin (difference -1.5%, 95% CI -2.3% to -0.6%; HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32-0.75) (Pinteraction=0.04). Conclusions Among these patients, procedural anticoagulation with bivalirudin plus a high-dose post-PCI infusion for 2-4 hours reduced the 30-day primary composite outcome and all-cause death compared with heparin monotherapy at least as strongly in non-HBR patients as in HBR patients.Central Illustration

appraisal.design_and_n: Pre-specified analysis of the BRIGHT-4 randomised trial; HBR (CRUSADE score ≥30) present in 1,435 (23.9%) randomized patients.
appraisal.main_limitation: Subgroup analysis of a single trial with a borderline interaction P value; congress abstract without full methods.
appraisal.one_line: Pre-specified BRIGHT-4 analysis by baseline bleeding risk comparing bivalirudin with heparin in primary PCI for STEMI.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: In HBR patients the 30-day primary outcome occurred in 8.1% with bivalirudin vs. 9.2% with heparin (difference -1.1%, 95% CI -4.0% to 1.8%; HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.62-1.26). In non-HBR patients it occurred in 1.4% vs. 2.9% (difference -1.5%, 95% CI -2.3% to -0.6%; HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32-0.75) (Pinteraction=0.04).
appraisal.why_it_matters: Informs the choice of procedural anticoagulant in STEMI by bleeding risk and bears on the unresolved bivalirudin versus heparin question.

title: Bivalirudin versus heparin in high and low bleeding risk patients undergoing primary PCI for STEMI: pre-specified analysis from the BRIGHT-4 trial

abstract: Abstract Background To determine whether initial hospital level is associated with 5-year mortality after ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) in China and to identify factors underlying any differences. Methods The China Acute Myocardial Infarction registry enrolled 12,697 STEMI patients at 108 hospitals in 31 provinces from January 2013 through September 2014, with follow-up through January 1, 2020. Patients were classified by initial admission to provincial-, prefecture-, or county-level hospitals. The primary outcome was 5-year all-cause mortality. Kaplan–Meier and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess mortality risk across hospital levels, with competing risk models applied for cardiovascular deaths. Prespecified subgroup analyses tested effect modification. A multiple-mediation framework quantified contributions of patient characteristics and treatment differences. Results 5-year all-cause mortality was 19.8% at provincial-, 25.3% at prefecture-, and 36.2% at county-level hospitals. Compared to provincial-level hospitals, adjusted hazards for all-cause mortality were higher at prefecture (HR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.11–1.39) and county hospitals (HR, 1.54; 95% CI, 1.34–1.78; P for trend &lt;.001), with similar patterns for cardiovascular mortality. Disparities were most pronounced among patients with overweight/obesity, prior heart failure, cardiogenic shock on admission, or onset-to-arrival time &gt;12 hours. Mediation analysis implicated lower use of primary PCI, older age, and socioeconomic factors as major contributors. Conclusions In this nationwide cohort, initial treatment at lower-level hospitals was associated with substantially higher 5-year mortality after STEMI. Enhancing timely, evidence-based care and strengthening regional referral networks and capacity at lower-tier hospitals may reduce these disparities.Fig 1 K-M curves for all-cause mortalityTab 1.Mediated effect on mortality
title: Hospital-level disparities and long-term survival in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: evidence from a nationwide cohort study

abstract: Abstract Introduction Rapid and reliable detection of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) on 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) is essential for timely reperfusion and improvement of clinical outcomes. Artificial intelligence (AI)–enabled ECG interpretation may support early triage by automating STEMI recognition across heterogeneous clinical settings. Purpose To develop and validate an AI-enabled ECG model for automated STEMI detection and to assess its generalizability across multicenter external cohorts. Methods A retrospective single-center cohort comprising 1,226 patients and their corresponding 12-lead ECGs (34.91% STEMI cases) was used for model development. An AI model was trained to identify STEMI presence (cases) or absence (controls) using standard 12-lead ECG recordings. External validation was conducted on 604 ECGs derived from four independent public datasets (Chapman, Georgia, PTB_XL, and SPH) to assess generalizability across heterogeneous data sources. Additional preliminary evaluation was performed in an interim prospective multicentric cohort comprising 339 patients. Model performance was evaluated using Monte Carlo Cross-Validation (MCCV; 100 iterations) with repeated patient-level random subsampling for robust performance estimation. Performance metrics included the area under the curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and F1-score, and were reported as mean values across MCCV iterations with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results Dataset characteristics are summarized in Table 1, and performance metrics reported in Table 2. In internal validation, the model achieved an AUC of 0.963 (95% CI 0.962–0.965), with sensitivity of 91.96% (95% CI 91.46–92.47) and specificity of 90.72% (95% CI 90.27–91.17). External evaluation demonstrated preserved generalization across heterogeneous public datasets, with AUC values ranging from 0.819 (95% CI 0.815–0.823) to 0.926 (95% CI 0.923–0.929), despite differences in dataset composition and class distribution. Negative predictive value remained consistently high across external cohorts. In the interim prospective multicentric study cohort, the model achieved an AUC of 0.906 (95% CI 0.904–0.907), with specificity of 95.07% (95% CI 94.76–95.37) and sensitivity of 65.12% (95% CI 63.78–66.46). Conclusions This AI-enabled ECG model demonstrated strong discrimination in internal validation and consistent performance across heterogeneous external datasets, including a prospective multicentric cohort. These findings support the integration of automated STEMI detection within AI-ECG platforms for scalable clinical decision support, while highlighting the need for continued optimization in prospective real-world settings. Future research includes model optimization upon study completion to identify occlusive and non-occlusive myocardial infarction (OMI, NOMI) in addition to STEMI.
title: Augmenting an AI-ECG platform with automated STEMI detection: multicenter and prospective external validation

abstract: Abstract Background In ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is standard when performed early; however, many patients present ≥12 hours after symptom onset, and the role of PCI in this late-presenting setting remains controversial. Randomized trials in stable patients with persistently occluded infarct-related arteries failed to show clinical benefit, leading guidelines to recommend late PCI only in selected scenarios. Most prior studies have focused on clinical outcomes, with limited evaluation of angiographic reperfusion success—the mechanistic link between PCI and myocardial recovery. Whether angiographic success in late-presenting STEMI is driven by intrahospital timing or by clinical indication–based patient selection remains unclear. Purpose To evaluate the association between clinical indications for late PCI and angiographic reperfusion success in late-presenting STEMI, and to determine whether successful reperfusion is more strongly influenced by clinical selection than by intrahospital timing. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of consecutive STEMI patients presenting 12–72 hours after symptom onset who underwent PCI within 7 days of hospital arrival. Patients were classified according to the primary indication for late PCI: persistent angina, clinical deterioration, or myocardial viability/ischemia. The primary endpoint was angiographic success, defined as final Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) 3 flow with TMP ≥2. Secondary endpoints included epicardial failure (TIMI &lt;3), microvascular failure (TIMI 3 with TMP ≤1), and 30-day mortality. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for baseline TIMI flow and clinical covariates. Results Among 397 patients, 199 underwent PCI for persistent angina, 133 for clinical deterioration, and 65 based on viability or ischemia. Symptom-onset–to-presentation intervals differed across groups (p=0.044). Arrival-to-PCI time varied markedly (median 6 h, 17 h, and 132 h, respectively; p&lt;0.001). Baseline TIMI flow differed significantly. Angiographic success occurred in 90.8% of viability/ischemia patients, 75.9% of clinical deterioration patients, and 68.3% of persistent angina patients (p=0.001), despite the longest intrahospital delays in the viability/ischemia group. Thirty-day mortality was 1.5%, 23.3%, and 6.0%, respectively (p&lt;0.001). After adjustment for baseline TIMI flow and arrival-to-PCI time, clinical indication remained independently associated with angiographic success, whereas intrahospital timing was not significantly associated with effective reperfusion. Conclusion In late-presenting STEMI, angiographic reperfusion success is more strongly associated with clinical indication than with intrahospital timing. A selection-based strategy, particularly guided by viability or ischemia, identifies patients with the highest likelihood of effective reperfusion.
title: Selection matters: clinical indication, not timing, determines angiographic success in late-presenting STEMI

abstract: Abstract Background and aim ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) remains a major cause of mortality despite advances in reperfusion therapy, underscoring the need for improved risk stratification. This study investigated the interplay between clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP), a marker of age-related inflammation1, and stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR), an indicator of acute metabolic stress2, in STEMI patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention. Methods In a prospective cohort, we performed deep targeted sequencing to detect CHIP mutations (variant allele frequency ≥2%) and calculated SHR from admission glucose and HbA1c. Results We found that CHIP, particularly mutations in TET2, was significantly more prevalent in non-survivors. The adverse prognostic impact of CHIP was critically dependent on SHR levels. In patients with lower SHR (&lt;1.414), CHIP was independently associated with increased all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] = 1.70 for any-CHIP). Conversely, this association was absent in patients with higher SHR (≥1.414). Furthermore, elevated SHR itself was an independent risk factor for mortality, specifically in patients harboring common-CHIP or TET2 mutations (HR=1.84 and 1.83, respectively). Conclusion These results demonstrate that stress hyperglycemia modifies the mortality risk conferred by CHIP, with CHIP's effect being most pronounced in the context of lower acute glycemic stress. Our findings reveal a novel interaction between a somatic mutation-driven aging process and acute metabolic dysregulation, identifying a high-risk phenotype. This integrated approach paves the way for personalized risk assessment and suggests potential therapeutic targets for mitigating inflammation and metabolic stress in vulnerable STEMI populations.The distributions of CHIP mutationsCox regression analyses of CHIP prevalence
title: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential and stress hyperglycemia ratio among patients with STEMI---from a prospective cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background Patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) are at risk for malignant arrhythmias (MA), defined as sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) and ventricular fibrillation (VF). Over the past decades, advances in revascularization techniques and medical therapies have led to reduced mortality and improved outcomes following percutaneous coronary intervention. Nevertheless, the standard of care since the early 2000s has been hospital admission with continuous rhythm monitoring for at least 48 hours after an acute myocardial infarction. Taking these modern treatment strategies into account, the current incidence of MA may be lower than previously reported. Purpose This systematic review aims to describe the contemporary incidence and predictors of malignant arrhythmia in reperfused AMI patients, with the goal of identifying low-risk individuals who may benefit from shorter monitoring durations, thereby improving patient flow and reducing hospital bed occupancy. Methods Studies reporting the incidence of MA in hospitalized AMI patients (2000–2025) were identified through a systematic search, including ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Additionally, predictors of MA were identified. Results The medians (interquartile range) of study-level reported incidences of MA across studies were 2.8% (2.4–6.4%) in STEMI patients after primary PCI (13 studies), 1.7% (0.7–2.8%) in hospitalized NSTEMI patients (10 studies), and 5.2% (4.0–8.1%) in combined hospitalized STEMI/NSTEMI cohorts (18 studies). All three groups showed considerable heterogeneity (I2≥90%). No temporal decline in MA incidence from 2000 - 2025 could be identified. Most MA (82%) in STEMI patients occurred within 24 hours of admission. Multivariate regression analyses identified Killip class II-IV (4 studies) and peak creatine kinase (3 studies) as independent predictors of MA after reperfusion. Conclusions The incidence of malignant arrhythmia in reperfused AMI patients is not negligible, especially within 24 hours. Considerable heterogeneity was demonstrated, likely due to differences in populations and the duration of in-hospital monitoring. Predictors of MA include a worse clinical condition on admission and larger infarct size. Identifying AMI patients with low risk of MA could be proposed to prevent unnecessary hospitalization.Timing onset in-hospital malignant arrhythmiaIncidence of MA after PCI in STEMI patients
title: Current incidence and predictors of malignant arrhythmias in acute myocardial infarction. Reassessing the role of coronary care units in post-myocardial infarction monitoring

abstract: Abstract Background – Myocardial ischemia–reperfusion injury causes heart damage through oxidative stress and inflammation, and effective drug therapies are still lacking. Sodium thiosulfate (STS) is a strong antioxidant with anti-inflammatory and vasodilatory effects, partly through reducing reactive oxygen species and releasing hydrogen sulfide. STS may also help preserve circulating free thiols, which reflect the body’s redox balance and are associated with cardiovascular outcomes. Purpose – This study evaluates whether administration of STS increases free thiols (FTs), as a marker of systemic oxidative stress, and studies the associations of FT with outcomes after ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Methods – FTs were detected in archived plasma samples from 298 participants of a neutral randomized trial on STS after STEMI. FT levels were determined at presentation with STEMI and at 9 hours after reperfusion. Outcomes included infarct size and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), both determined with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging at 4 months follow-up. Results – A total of 256 patients were included (placebo n=131, STS n=125; mean age 62±11.7 years, 23% female). Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups, except for ethnicity. Serum free thiols were higher in the STS group at baseline and remained significantly higher after 9 hours of treatment; the increase from baseline to 9 hours was significantly greater with STS (all p&lt;0.001). Higher free thiol levels at 9 hours were independently associated with higher LVEF in univariable analysis and after adjustment for age, sex, STS treatment, angiographic variables, and cardiac biomarkers (β 0.048 per µmol/L increase, p&lt;0.001). Free thiols at 9 hours were not associated with infarct size at 4 months. Conclusions - STS treatment significantly increased circulating free thiol levels, reflecting an improved systemic redox balance. Elevated free thiols were independently associated with better left ventricular function on cardiac MRI 4-months post-STEMI, although no association with infarct size was observed. These findings support a role for STS-mediated redox modulation in functional recovery after myocardial ischemia–reperfusion injury.
title: Sodium thiosulfate treatments results in increased serum free thiol levels and improved cardiac function post ST-elevated myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Coronary artery ectasia (CAE) is a relatively rare phenomenon, characterized by a pathological, local or diffuse dilation more than 1.5 times the adjacent normal coronary artery segment. Echocardiographic assessment data in this patient population are conflicting, and risk factors associated with worse left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) in patients with CAE have not been studied. Purpose We explored treatment strategies, echocardiographic characteristics and their association in patients with CAE presenting with an ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Methods Data were analysed retrospectively from CAE and STEMI registries. Revascularization strategies and factors associated with LVEF in CAE patients are reported. Results 1926 patients were included; 158 (8.2%) had CAE. Significant differences in the types of revascularization were observed: while stenting was the final revascularization strategy in 1755 (99.3%) controls, in CAE patients a more varied approach was implemented: 129 (81.6%) received stents, 10 (6.3%) were treated by balloon angioplasty, 3 (1.9%) received no revascularization and 16 (10.1%) patients required urgent or emergency coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) (p &lt;0.001 for difference between the groups). No association between Markis class and revascularization strategy was observed (p=0.29; Figure 1). Suboptimal final Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) flow was more common in the CAE group, compared to controls (29 (18.4%) versus 106 (6.0%); p&lt;0.001). CAE patients had larger left atrial volume indices (30±9 ml/m2 versus 27±9 ml/m2; p=0.005), lower left ventricular (LV) filling pressures (9.6 (7.9; 11.8) versus 10.6 (8.5; 13.2); p=0.001) and worse LVEF (48±9% versus 50±8%; p&lt;0.001). In the CAE patient group on multivariate linear regression analysis only peak troponin levels and CABG were associated with worse LVEF (Figure 2). Conclusions Patients with CAE presenting with STEMI were treated with more varied revascularization strategies and had higher rates of suboptimal final TIMI flow. These patients also had worse LVEF and larger left atrial volume indices compared to controls, despite lower LV filling pressures. In patients with CAE, only peak troponin levels and CABG were associated with worse LVEF.
title: Impact of coronary artery ectasia on revascularization strategies and echocardiographic characteristics in patients presenting with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Very early discharge after successful primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been increasingly considered for carefully selected low-risk patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). However, prospective data from resource-limited settings remain limited. Objective To evaluate the safety and feasibility of very early discharge (≤48 hours) in low-risk STEMI patients treated with primary PCI. Methods We conducted a prospective, randomized, open-label, single-center study between June 2024 and June 2025. During this period, 544 consecutive patients were admitted with STEMI. Among them, 179 met predefined low-risk criteria based on preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, limited coronary artery disease burden, and successful radial-access PCI. These patients were randomly assigned to either very early discharge (≤48 hours) or routine discharge (&gt;48 hours). The primary endpoint was the occurrence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) at 3 months, defined as all-cause mortality, recurrent myocardial infarction, hospitalization for heart failure, or stent thrombosis. Results A total of 82 patients were allocated to the very early discharge group, with a median hospital stay of 25.8 hours, and 97 patients to the routine discharge group. At 3-month follow-up, the incidence of MACE was similar between the two groups, with with no statistically significant difference in MACE (2.4% vs 2.1%; p = 1.00). Conclusion In this prospective randomized study of carefully selected low-risk STEMI patients, very early discharge within 48 hours after primary PCI was not associated with an increased risk of adverse cardiovascular events at 3 months. These findings suggest that an individualized early discharge strategy may be safely implemented in selected patients.Consort study flow chartKaplan Meier curve
title: Safety and feasibility of very early discharge after primary pci in low-riskSTEMI patients : a prospective study

abstract: Abstract Background Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of mortality in Armenia. To address the lack of national real-world data on reperfusion practices and outcomes, the Armenian National Registry of Myocardial Infarction (ARMI) was established in December 2023 as the first nationwide prospective STEMI registry. Objectives The primary endpoint of the study was to determine in-hospital mortality rates in patients admitted with STEMI across all participating national centers. The secondary endpoints included assessing 30-day and 12-month cardiovascular mortality, all-cause mortality, and rehospitalization rates. Methods ARMI prospectively enrolled consecutive adults aged 18-93 years presenting with STEMI within 48 hours of symptom onset across 13 specialized hospitals nationwide. Trained investigators collected standardized clinical, procedural, and outcome data using a secure national REDCap electronic database. All patients were followed prospectively for 12 months, with structured assessments at 30 days and 12 months. Enrollment ran from 1 December 2023 to 1 July 2025. Results A total of 2,222 patients were enrolled across all 13 centers. The present analysis includes 1,392 patients with complete follow-up data. The cohort was predominantly male (81.1%; n=1,129), with 18.9% women (n=263). Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) was performed in 96.8% of patients (n=2,098), of whom 99.6% underwent primary PCI (n=2,090). Medical therapy alone was used in 2.7% (n=58), and 0.6% (n=12) required coronary artery bypass grafting. In-hospital reinfarction and recurrent ischemia occurred in 3.4% and 4.2% of patients, respectively. Overall in-hospital mortality was 3.1%. Cardiovascular causes accounted for 91.0% of all in-hospital deaths. Reduced systolic function was a major contributor, with 62.5% of deceased patients having LVEF ≤40%. Acute HF with Killip class 3-4 at presentation was identified in 8.0% of patients. In-hospital mortality in patients with Killip class 3-4 was substantially higher at 9.0% versus 3.1% for the overall cohort. At one year, all-cause mortality was 8% in the overall population and 32% in patients presenting with Killip class 3-4, confirming the powerful adverse prognostic impact of early HF severity. HF-related rehospitalization occurred in 13% of Killip class 3-4 patients versus 36% in the overall cohort, reflecting ongoing morbidity burden. Conclusions ARMI establishes the first national benchmark for STEMI care in Armenia, demonstrating near-universal primary PCI use and low in-hospital mortality (3.1%), comparable to that reported in European registries. Acute HF at presentation identified a high-risk subgroup with markedly higher in-hospital and 1-year mortality. Left ventricular ejection fraction ≤40% emerged as a key prognostic marker. The ARMI registry provides a foundation for future translational research and nationwide quality improvement initiatives.
title: ARMI registry: first nationwide prospective evaluation of STEMI outcomes in Armenia

abstract: Abstract Background Dense coronary calcification limits the use of conventional coronary CT angiography (CCTA) due to blooming artifacts that obscure the lumen and reduce its diagnostic accuracy. Ultra–high–resolution CT (UHR-CT), with improved spatial resolution, may mitigate this limitation and allow a more reliable assessment even in patients with high calcium score levels. Purpose To investigate the influence of coronary artery calcium score (CACS) in the diagnostic accuracy of UHR-CT for detecting hemodynamically significant coronary artery disease (CAD) at patient level using quantitative flow ratio (QFR) as the reference standard, and to explore whether a clinically meaningful CACS threshold exists beyond which UHR-CT accuracy declines. Methods In the CORE Precision study, participants with suspected obstructive CAD underwent non-contrast calcium scoring and UHR-CT prior to invasive coronary angiography. UHR-CT images were analyzed and stenosis ≥70% were deemed obstructive. Functional significance (reference standard) was defined by an abnormal QFR. CACS was analyzed both categorically (0–99, 100–399, 400–999, ≥1000) and as a continuous variable using a moving-threshold approach. Diagnostic accuracy was calculated across increasing CACS cutoffs, restricting analyses to thresholds where each subgroup comprised ≥10% of the cohort to ensure stability. Results A total of 118 participants (mean age 67±11 years, 75% male) were included. The mean calcium score was 1,004 (± 1,108). The global diagnostic accuracy of UHR-CT was 80.3%. Diagnostic accuracy declined progressively across increasing CACS categories, measuring 90.9% for CACS 0–99, 88.5% for CACS 100–399, 83.8% for CACS 400–999, and 76.7% for CACS ≥1,000. Performance attenuation at very high CACS values was primarily driven by reduced specificity, while sensitivity remained preserved. Detailed diagnostic performance metrics and confidence intervals are presented in Figure 1A. In the continuous analysis, no abrupt cutoff point was identified. The accuracy remained stable, especially in patients with CACS &lt;1,000, with a gradual decline with increasing calcium burden (Figure 1B). The histograms in Figure 1B illustrate correctly and incorrectly classified cases across CACS ranges. Conclusions UHR-CT maintains robust diagnostic accuracy across a wide range of coronary calcium scores, particularly in patients with CACS &lt;1000, with no evidence of a clear threshold for abrupt decline in diagnostic performance. The high accuracy for detecting obstructive CAD in patients previously considered unsuitable for the test suggests that UHR-CT may represent a noninvasive diagnostic alternative in this group.
title: Impact of coronary calcium score on the diagnostic accuracy of ultra-high-resolution CT for detecting obstructive coronary artery disease in the CORE PRECISION multicenter study

abstract: Abstract Background Ambulance use and delay times are critical components of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) care. Delays in managing STEMI patients are associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Foreign-born patients may face unique challenges in seeking timely care. Whether prehospital and hospital delays differ between foreign-born and native-born patients remains understudied. Purpose To assess possible disparities in ambulance use and delays in STEMI care, comparing foreign-born and native-born patients. Methods This retrospective study included all STEMI patients recorded in the SWEDEHEART MI registry in Sweden from 2008-2022. The exposure was country or region of birth, categorised into seven groups (Figure 1). Outcomes were: 1) ambulance use; 2) prehospital delay time (PHDT, defined as time from symptom onset to hospital admission) &lt;120 min; 3) hospital delay time (HDT, defined as time from hospital admission to initiation of reperfusion therapy) &lt;30 min; and 4) total ischaemic time (defined as time from symptom onset to initiation of reperfusion therapy) &lt;150 min. In crude and adjusted (age, sex, comorbidities, and socioeconomic variables) logistic regression models, the association between country or region of birth and outcomes was assessed. Results Of the 78,298 patients, 65,328 (83.4%) were native-born, and 12,970 (16.6%) were foreign-born. Patients born in the Nordic countries outside of Sweden comprised the largest group (n=3,823, 4.9%), whereas those born in the Americas comprised the smallest (n=475, 0.6%). The median age was 70 years (IQR 60–79); patients born in Africa were the youngest (56 y [IQR 50–65] ), and native-born patients were the oldest (71 y [IQR 62–79]). Compared with native-born patients, ambulance use was lower among patients born in non-EU countries (0.81 [0.73–0.90]) (Figure 1). Achieving PHDT &lt;120 minutes was more likely among patients born in non-Nordic EU countries (1.14 [1.03–1.26]), non-EU countries (1.19 [1.08–1.32]), Asia (1.21 [1.10–1.32]), and the Americas (1.45 [1.17–1.80]). Patients born in non-EU European countries were less likely to achieve HDT &lt;30 minutes (0.78 [0.70–0.87]). Total ischaemic time was shortest among patients born in the Americas (167 min [IQR 100–347]), with patients from the non-Nordic EU (1.14 [1.03–1.26]), Asia (1.20 [1.10–1.32]), and the Americas (1.31 [1.05–1.63) more likely to achieve the total ischemic time &lt;150 minutes. Conclusions We observed small differences in delay times and ambulance use between foreign-born and native-born patients. Some foreign-born groups had lower ambulance use or longer hospital delays, whereas prehospital delays were not prolonged and were shorter in several groups. Our findings suggest limited disparities in acute STEMI care.Main analysisTable 1.Ambulance use and delay times
title: Prehospital and hospital delays and ambulance use in foreign-born versus native-born patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction – a nationwide SWEDEHEART study

abstract: Abstract Introduction Unreperfused STEMI is frequent, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Late PCI in patients without myocardial viability remains controversial, with no specific randomized evidence available. Objective To evaluate whether late PCI reduces adverse left ventricular remodeling, measured by changes in indexed end-systolic volume (iESV) on cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), in patients with unreperfused STEMI and absent myocardial viability. Methods Prospective, single-center, randomized trial. Patients with STEMI between 24 hours and 30 days, without viability on CMR (transmural late gadolinium enhancement ≥50%), were randomized to PCI plus optimized medical therapy (OMT) or OMT alone. Follow-up CMR was performed at 6–12 months. A pre-specified subanalysis compared viable patients with STEMI between 24 hours and 30 days undergoing PCI with the non-viable PCI group. Results Between 2021 and 2024, 95 patients were enrolled; of these, 25 had myocardial viability and 70 did not. The 70 non-viable patients were randomized (34 PCI vs. 36 OMT). At 6–12 months, iESV did not decrease significantly in either group (PCI: -3.0 ml/m², p=0.295; OMT: -4.0 ml/m², p=0.147), with no difference between strategies (p=0.277). Ejection fraction improved significantly only in the OMT group (+2.96%, p=0.031). No difference in major adverse cardiovascular events was observed at 12 months. In the subanalysis, viable patients had lower iESV (45.0 [19.0–75.0] vs. 54.0 [26.0–136] ml/m²; p=0.009) and higher ejection fraction (50.7±10.0% vs. 40.5±11.1%; p=0.001) compared to non-viable patients who underwent PCI. Conclusion Late PCI conferred no structural or clinical benefit in patients without myocardial viability. Systematic viability assessment by CMR should guide therapeutic decisions in this population, avoiding unnecessary procedures and exposure to procedural risks without potential benefit.Table 1 PCI vs OMTTable 2 with viability vs without viability
title: Percutaneous coronary intervention in late-presenting acute myocardial infarction without myocardial viability: effects on left ventricular remodeling and function by cardiac magnetic resonance

abstract: Abstract Background A significant proportion of patients presenting with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) undergo emergent coronary angiography despite no obstructive culprit lesion can be identified. Data on their clinical profile, underlying diagnoses and early outcomes remain limited. Methods In this single-center retrospective sutdy, consecutive STEMI patients undergoing coronary angiography between 2015 and 2024 were analyzed. Patients without an identifiable culprit lesion were classified as MINOCA with ST elevation (STE-MINOCA) and categorized according to final discharge diagnosis. Clinical characteristics and in-hospital mortality were assessed across diagnostic entities. Results Among 1,403 STEMI patients undergoing coronary angiography, 105 (7.5%) had no identifiable culprit lesion. Compared with patients with culprit lesion, STE-MINOCA patients were younger (57.6 ± 18.5 vs. 65.3 ± 13.3 years, p&lt;0.001) and had higher left ventricular ejection fraction (48.3 ± 14.1% vs. 41.1 ± 10.9%, p&lt;0.001). The proportion of female patients did not differ significantly between groups (p=0.381). STE-MINOCA patients presented less frequently with cardiogenic shock (p&lt;0.001) or preceding CPR (p=0.024). Culprit lesion status was not independently associated with in-hospital mortality after adjustment for age and cardiogenic shock (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.45–2.29, p=0.982). Among STE-MINOCA patients, the most common diagnoses were inflammatory myopericardial syndrome (IMPS) (27%), Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (15%), and non-cardiac conditions including pulmonary embolism or aortic pathology (20%), non-ischemic cardiomyopathy (10%), and coronary vasospasm or embolism (11%) (Figure 1). Clinical profiles differed substantially across entities (Table 1). Patients with Takotsubo cardiomyopathy were predominantly female (87.5%) and had reduced LVEF (33.3 ± 12%). IMPS patients showed preserved LVEF (54.1 ± 11.5%) and no in-hospital deaths. In contrast, non-cardiac causes were associated with the highest rates of cardiogenic shock (21%) and in-hospital mortality (23.8%). Overall in-hospital mortality among STE-MINOCA patients was 9.5%, but ranged from 0% in inflammatory etiologies to 23.8 % in non-cardiac conditions (Table 1). Conclusion Approximately 8% of patients presenting with ST-segment elevation showed no identifiable culprit lesion on angiography. Although overall clinically less unstable than patients with a culprit lesion, STE-MINOCA patients represent a highly heterogeneous population with entity-specific clinical profiles and markedly different early outcomes. Particularly non-cardiac etiologies carry substantial short-term risk, underscoring the need for rapid differential diagnostic evaluation beyond coronary angiography.
title: MINOCA with ST elevation (STE-MINOCA) in contemporary practice: clinical profile and early outcomes

abstract: Abstract Background Risk stratification of patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) focuses primarily on left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and ischemic mitral regurgitation, whereas the prognostic role of tricuspid regurgitation (TR) remains poorly defined, particularly following LAD or LCX-related infarction. Purpose The purpose of this study is to investigate the association of TR in LAD and LCX-STEMI and to assess its short and long-term prognostic impact. Methods We conducted a retrospective, single-center cohort study of patients presenting with a first LAD or LCX-related STEMI (2000-2019) treated with primary percutaneous coronary intervention. Patients with prior myocardial infarction, revascularization, or significant valvular disease were excluded. Transthoracic echocardiography was performed during hospitalization and follow-up. Moderate-to-severe TR was considered clinically significant. The primary prognostic endpoint was time to all-cause mortality. Secondary endpoints included in-hospital mortality and 1-year major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Results Among 1,273 patients with LAD (n=981) or LCX (n=292) culprit lesions, moderate-to-severe TR was common and more frequently associated with LAD-related infarction (31.6% vs 24.7%, p = 0.02). Moderate-to-severe TR was consistently associated with higher all-cause mortality in both LAD (22% vs 9%) and LCX infarctions (21% vs 7%), as well as higher in-hospital mortality and 1-year MACE (all p&lt;0.01). In multivariable analysis, TR remained independently associated with mortality after adjusting for age, infarct size, and left ventricular systolic function (HR 1.81, 95% CI 1.29-2.53; p&lt;0.001). Among patients with TR, concomitant right ventricular dysfunction (RVD) identified a particularly high-risk phenotype, with more than two-fold higher mortality (risk ratio of 2.28, 95% CI 1.44-3.63; p=0.0052). Conclusions TR early after LAD or LCX-related STEMI is frequent and independently associated with adverse outcomes, particularly when accompanied by RVD, highlighting its importance in post-STEMI risk stratification.visual abstract
title: Prevalence and prognostic impact of tricuspid regurgitation following LAD and LCX related STEMI

abstract: Abstract Background Accurate detection of acute coronary occlusion (ACO) in patients presenting with chest pain remains challenging, as conventional STEMI criteria frequently fail to identify ACO—occurring in up to one in four non-STEMI cases. AI-enhanced ECG analysis has the potential to improve diagnostic precision, particularly in tachycardic patients, where ST-segment deviations may reflect artefacts, supply–demand mismatch, or true coronary occlusion. Distinguishing among these mechanisms is essential to guide appropriate decisions between emergency coronary angiography and primary arrhythmia management. Purpose To assess the diagnostic performance of an AI-enhanced ECG model for detecting ACO in chest pain patients with tachycardia on admission ECG, compared with conventional STEMI criteria, in a metropolitan chest pain unit (CPU) cohort. Methods All consecutive tachycardic patients (&gt;100 bpm) presenting with chest pain to the CPU (Nov 2018 to Jun 20221) were included. Clinical management followed current European Society of Cardiology guidelines. The endpoint was ACO, adjudicated by an independent physician blinded to the AI predictions, using coronary angiography, biomarker kinetics, and echocardiography. Diagnostic performance was assessed by ROC analysis and compared with STEMI criteria. A predefined subgroup analysis distinguished narrow (QRS &lt;120 ms) and broad (QRS ≥120 ms) complex tachycardias. The AI model itself based on a deep convolutional neural network. Results A total of 639 patients presented with tachycardia and were included (mean age 56.3 ± 19.3 years; 60.6% male). Tachycardia and tachyarrhythmia are summarized in table 1. Overall, 590 (92.3%) patients had narrow complex tachycardia, while 49 (7.7%) had broad complex tachycardia. The prevalence of ACO was 3.9% (n = 25). STEMI criteria identified only 7 of these 25 cases (28%). In contrast, the AI-ECG model correctly classified 19 of 25 (76%) ACO. The area under the curve was 0.987 (95% CI 0.978 – 0.996) for the AI-ECG model and 0.607 (95% CI 0.480 – 0.735) for STEMI criteria. Across all diagnostic metrics the AI model outperformed STEMI criteria, consistently across both tachycardia subgroups (figure 1). In the low-risk rule-out population, the AI-ECG model yielded seven false positives, potentially avoiding fifteen unnecessary emergency angiographies compared with strict application of STEMI criteria. Conclusion In tachycardic chest pain patients, conventional STEMI criteria inadequately guide the need for emergency coronary angiography, resulting in both missed occlusions and potentially avoidable interventions. AI-enhanced ECG analysis markedly improved ACO detection and may enable more selective, clinically guided triage. Its strong negative predictive value further highlights its potential to distinguish patients requiring primary arrhythmia management from those needing urgent coronary intervention, supporting prospective validation in independent cohorts.TableFigure
title: Artificial intelligence–enhanced detection of acute coronary occlusion in tachycardic patients using surface ECG

abstract: Abstract Background The detection of acute coronary occlusion (ACO) in patients presenting with chest pain remains challenging when relying solely on conventional ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) criteria on the electrocardiogram (ECG). Artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced ECG analysis may improve diagnostic accuracy, particularly in bradycardic patients, in whom ST-segment alterations may reflect either a demand–supply mismatch or true coronary occlusion. Accurate differentiation is crucial to appropriately guide emergency treatment. Purpose To evaluate the diagnostic performance of an AI-based ECG model for the detection of ACO in bradycardic patients presenting with chest pain on admission ECG, in comparison with conventional STEMI criteria, within a Chest Pain Unit (CPU) setting. Methods All consecutive bradycardic patients (&lt;60 bpm) presenting with chest pain to the CPU (Nov 2018 to Jun 2021) were included. Clinical management followed current European Society of Cardiology guidelines. The endpoint was ACO, adjudicated by an independent physician blinded to the AI predictions, using coronary angiography, biomarker kinetics, and echocardiography. Diagnostic performance was assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and compared with STEMI criteria. Results Among 4,440 patients treated in the CPU, 485 presented with bradycardia and were included in the analysis (mean age 57.7 ± 18.4 years; 71.8% male; mean heart rate 53.9 ± 4.8 bpm). Observed rhythms were sinus bradycardia (92.6%), atrial fibrillation (2.3%), idioventricular rhythm (0.4%), and other rhythms (4.7%). The prevalence of ACO was 2.3% (n = 11). Diagnostic metrics are illustrated in the accompanying figure. The area under the curve was 0.968 (95% CI 0.944 – 0.991) for the AI-ECG model and 0.607 (95% CI 0.411 – 0.792) for STEMI criteria. Conventional STEMI criteria identified 3 cases of ACO (27.3%), whereas the AI-ECG model detected 5 cases (45.5%). STEMI criteria yielded 33 false-positive findings (6.8%), compared with 6 (1.2%) using the AI-ECG model. Both approaches demonstrated high specificity. In the low-risk subgroup (“rule-out” according to the troponin-based algorithm), the AI-ECG model produced only one false-positive result and, compared with strict application of STEMI criteria, could potentially have avoided fifteen emergency coronary angiographies. Conclusion In bradycardic patients presenting with acute chest pain, a purely ECG-based strategy is insufficient for the reliable detection of ACO. Neither approach achieved sufficient sensitivity to safely exclude ACO; however, the AI-ECG model substantially reduced false-positive findings compared with conventional STEMI criteria. The low prevalence of ACO in the analyzed cohort warrants further prospective validation of the investigated AI-ECG model.Figure
title: Detection of acute coronary occlusion in bradycardic patients using ECG: comparison of STEMI criteria versus artificial intelligence–enhanced interpretation

abstract: Abstract Background Management of standard modifiable cardiovascular risk factors (SMuRFs) is central to secondary prevention after ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Paradoxically, “SMuRF-less” patients have been linked to higher long-term mortality in some studies, though findings are inconsistent. Data on in-hospital outcomes remain limited, particularly in German STEMI populations. Purpose To characterize SMuRF-less patients within a German metropolitan STEMI network and compare their outcomes with SMuRF-positive patients. Methods This multicentre STEMI registry included patients enrolled between January 2024 and October 2025. SMuRF status was defined by hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, or smoking; ≥1 factor classified patients as SMuRF-positive. Outcomes were in-hospital mortality, cardiogenic shock (CS), culprit lesion, and stent implantation. Unadjusted and adjusted logistic regressions were performed, adjusting for age (&lt;65/≥65), sex, infarction type, and pre-existing coronary artery disease. A two-sided p&lt;0.05 was considered significant. Results Of 1,128 recorded STEMI patients, 867 had complete SMuRF data and were included in analysis. Baseline characteristics were generally balanced between the groups, with notable differences observed in infarction type, pre-interventional resuscitation, and pre-existing coronary artery disease (Table). In unadjusted analyses, SMuRF-less patients exhibited higher odds of in-hospital mortality (OR 3.57, 95% CI 2.07–6.15, p&lt;0.001) and cardiogenic shock (OR 2.45, 95% CI 1.28–4.71, p&lt;0.01), but lower likelihood of culprit lesions (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.12–0.37, p&lt;0.001) and stent implantation (OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.19–0.56, p&lt;0.001) (Figure). These associations remained consistent after adjustment using binary logistic regression (Figure). Pre-interventional resuscitation emerged as the strongest independent predictor of mortality (OR 13.59, 95% CI 8.98–20.56) and was significantly more frequent among SMuRF-less patients. Sensitivity analyses excluding resuscitated cases showed that differences in mortality and cardiogenic shock were no longer significant, whereas the lower rates of culprit lesions and stent implantation in SMuRF-less patients persisted (Figure). Incorporating resuscitation status as a post-hoc adjustment in the regression model confirmed the robustness of these findings (data not shown). In final analysis, SMuRF-less STEMI patients less frequently presented with a culprit lesion and less often required urgent revascularization (71.3% vs. 92.1%, p&lt;0.001). Conclusion In-hospital outcome differences between SMuRF-less and SMuRF-positive STEMI patients were largely driven by higher pre-interventional resuscitation rates, suggesting potential survivorship or information bias. After adjustment, mortality and CS did not differ significantly. The consistently lower incidence of culprit lesions in SMuRF-less patients warrants external validation.TableFigure
title: The SMuRFs paradox in STEMI: insights from a metropolitan STEMI network

abstract: Abstract Introduction Accurate risk stratification in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is vital to identify early discharge candidates and optimize resources.
