The Zwolle Risk Score (ZRS) lacks contemporary prognostic markers like frailty and post-PCI left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), losing precision in ageing, complex populations. Objectives To evaluate the prognostic improvement of integrating frailty and post-PCI LVEF into the original ZRS (M-ZRS), and to compare this updated bedside tool against a machine learning Random Forest (RF) approach, seeking the optimal identification of low-risk candidates for safe early discharge. Methods A prospective, single-center, observational study of 585 STEMI patients who survived primary PCI (July 2023-January 2026) was performed. The sample was divided chronologically into derivation (n=449) and validation (n=136) cohorts. Frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale ≥4) and post-PCI LVEF were assessed. Independent predictors of in-hospital mortality were identified via multivariable logistic regression. M-ZRS was compared to ZRS and an RF model (trained via downsampling using age, KILLIP, anterior MI, 3-vessel disease, ischemia time, post-PCI TIMI flow, Clinical Frailty Scale, and categorical LVEF) using C-statistics and categorical Net Reclassification Improvement (NRI). Results In-hospital mortality was 6.5% (derivation 6.5% vs validation 6.6%, p=0.952). Multivariable analysis confirmed ZRS (OR 1.22 per point; p&lt;0.001), post-PCI LVEF &lt;40% (OR 2.71; p=0.029), and Frailty (OR 3.09; p=0.008) as independent predictors. Comparing B-coefficients, LVEF &lt;40% (B=0.996) and Frailty (B=1.129) were ≈5 and ≈6 times more impactful than a 1-point ZRS increase (B=0.199). Thus, 5 and 6 points were respectively added to ZRS to create the M-ZRS. In the validation cohort, discriminative capacity was highest for RF (C-statistic: 0.894), followed by M-ZRS (0.832) and ZRS (0.758); p&gt;0.05 by DeLong due to low event rate (Figure). Reclassification showed potentially great clinical value (Table), M-ZRS yielded an NRI of 22.2% vs ZRS (event NRI=22.2%, non-event NRI=0%). RF achieved an NRI of 36.4%, matching M-ZRS in identifying mortality cases (event NRI=22.2%) while correctly downgrading survivors to low-risk (non-event NRI=14.2%). With a ≤4 cut-off, M-ZRS identified 61.0% (83/136) as low risk (1.2% mortality; NPV 98.8%, Sensitivity 88.9%). Using its optimal threshold, RF safely expanded the low-risk pool to 74.3% (101/136) (1.0% mortality; NPV 99.0%, Sensitivity 88.9%). Conclusions Integrating frailty and LVEF into the ZRS substantially improves high-risk STEMI detection at the bedside. Furthermore, applying RF algorithms provides exceptional reclassification (NRI 36.4%), safely expanding the pool of true low-risk candidates for early discharge. Updating traditional scores and integrating AI modernizes and expedites safe discharge protocols.Figure 1.AUC of Predictive ModelsTable 1.Risk Reclassification Matrix
title: Safely expanding early discharge in STEMI: clinical and artificial intelligence tools for low-risk identification

abstract: Abstract Background Limitations persist in the literature regarding disparities in the management of patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), particularly when comparisons are made according to race/ethnicity and gender. Objective To compare clinical characteristics and to assess door-to-needle time (DNT) within 30 minutes and evaluate 180-day survival according to race/ethnicity (White, Brown [mixed race], and Black) and gender. Methods EQUITY-MI is a single-centre, prospective cohort study of patients diagnosed with STEMI in the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, who were referred to a single reperfusion centre. Continuous variables were analysed using the Kruskal–Wallis test and categorical variables using the chi-squared test. To estimate the effect of DNT within 30 minutes, logistic regression models were applied and odds ratios (ORs) were calculated. Survival analysis was performed using the Kaplan–Meier method with comparisons by the log-rank test. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate crude and adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) for 180-day mortality, adjusting for age, race/ethnicity, education level and household income. A significance level of 0.05 was adopted. Results Among 504 patients with STEMI, 27.2% were women and 67.8% self-identified as Black or Brown (mixed race). DNT within 30 minutes occurred in 27.2% of White patients compared with 12.5% of Black patients (p = 0.07). Race/ethnicity was an independent predictor, with Black patients having 2.86-fold lower odds of achieving DNT within 30 minutes compared with White patients (OR = 0.349, p = 0.023). Female gender was associated with 2.40-fold lower odds of DNT within 30 minutes compared with male gender (OR = 0.416, p = 0.015). Considering the interaction between race/ethnicity and gender, Black women had 5.49-fold lower odds of DNT within 30 minutes (OR = 0.182, p = 0.028). Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated significantly lower cumulative survival among women compared with men (log-rank p = 0.001), whereas no significant differences were observed across racial/ethnic groups (p = 0.304). In Cox regression, female gender was independently associated with higher 180-day mortality in both unadjusted (HR 4.63; 95% CI 1.68–12.75; p = 0.003) and adjusted models (HR 3.98; 95% CI 1.36–11.66; p = 0.012). Conclusion The EQUITY-MI study demonstrated inequities in both efficiency of care and clinical outcomes related to gender and race/ethnicity. Door-to-needle time frequently exceeded the recommended 30-minute target. Black patients and women had lower odds of timely thrombolysis, and female gender was independently associated with higher 180-day mortality. The interaction between race/ethnicity and gender revealed a pattern of intersectionality, with Black women experiencing the most unfavourable scenario compared with White men.Door-to-needle times stratifiedCox regression for survival at 180 days
title: Racial/ethnic and gender inequities in door-to-needle time among patients with STEMI: results from the EQUITY-MI cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Over the past decades, emergent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has substantially improved survival in acute myocardial infarction (AMI). However, contemporary long-term regional data examining whether expanding reperfusion strategies have translated into improved short-term outcomes across different clinical severities and age groups remain limited. Purpose To investigate 10-year temporal trends (2013–2022) in patient characteristics, reperfusion strategies, and 30-day mortality in a regional AMI cohort, with specific focus on Killip class and age-stratified outcomes. Methods We analyzed 6,890 consecutive patients with AMI enrolled in the ongoing multicenter Mie ACS Registry between January 2013 and December 2022. Temporal changes in emergent PCI use and reperfusion within 6 hours were evaluated overall and stratified by Killip class (I, II–III, IV) and age (&lt;65, 65–74, 75–84, ≥85 years). The primary endpoint was 30-day mortality. Age-adjusted mortality rates were calculated to account for temporal shifts in population aging. Annual trends were assessed using regression models and expressed as odds ratios (OR) per year with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results During the study period, the overall rate of emergent PCI use increased significantly from 84.0% to 90.5% (P&lt;0.001). The increase was most pronounced in Killip class IV (68.2% to 86.4%; OR 1.16 per year; P for trend &lt;0.001, Figure 1A), with a significantly steeper rise compared with Killip class I (interaction P=0.039). Reperfusion within 6 hours improved significantly in Killip IV but not in lower Killip classes. Correspondingly, age-adjusted 30-day mortality in Killip IV declined markedly from 46.3% to 28.4% (P=0.03, Figure 1B), whereas the overall reduction in 30-day mortality (8.8% to 6.7%) did not reach statistical significance (P=0.20). Across all age categories, PCI utilization increased significantly (Figure 2A). However, no significant temporal decline in 30-day mortality was observed within any age stratum, including patients aged ≥85 years (OR per year 0.96, 95% CI 0.90–1.02, Figure 2B). Conclusions Over the past decade, reperfusion strategies were increasingly extended to the highest-risk patients with AMI, particularly those with Killip class IV, resulting in substantial improvement in short-term survival in this group. In contrast, despite increased PCI use across all age strata, short-term mortality did not significantly improve among older patients. Optimizing outcomes in the rapidly aging AMI population remains a key challenge for the next decade.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Expanding reperfusion to the highest-risk patients: ten-year temporal trends in emergent PCI and 30-day mortality across clinical severity and age from the Mie ACS Registry

abstract: Abstract Background Comorbid alcohol use complicates the clinical profile of acute coronary syndromes, often serving as a proxy for polysubstance use and social vulnerability. However, its independent impact on survival and resource utilisation following STEMI remains poorly defined. Purpose To analyze the clinical impact of alcohol use in a nationwide STEMI cohort to determine survival, in-hospital complications, and readmissions compared to non-alcohol users. Methods We analyzed the Nationwide Readmissions Database (2019-2022) to identify adult STEMI hospitalizations. The cohort was stratified by comorbid alcohol use. We performed 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM) [nearest neighbor, caliper 0.2] to balance age, sex, payer status, hospital characteristics, and Elixhauser comorbidities. Doubly robust multivariable regression combining PSM with covariate adjustment was utilized to assess in-hospital mortality, 30-day readmission, length of stay (LOS), hospital charges, and routine home discharge. Results Of 569,574 weighted STEMI hospitalizations (median age 64; 30.4% female), 22,571 (4.0%) had comorbid Alcohol Use. Compared with controls, the Alcohol Use cohort presented with higher acuity, including significantly elevated rates of cardiac arrest (10.5% vs 8.0%), ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation (24.4% vs 19.9%), and sepsis (3.2% vs 2.3%; all P&lt;.05). In doubly robust multivariable analysis, Alcohol Use was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (aOR 0.86; 95% CI 0.77-0.95; P=.005). However, survival advantage was accompanied by prolonged length of stay (Ratio 1.14; 95% CI 1.11-1.17), increased hospital charges (Ratio 1.05; 95% CI 1.03-1.08), and reduced odds of routine home discharge (aOR 0.91; 95% CI 0.85-0.98; all P&lt;.05). Adjusted 30-day readmission risk showed an increased trend (aOR 1.09; 95% CI 0.99-1.21; P=.069), with heart failure being the leading cause of readmission (25.1%). Conclusion STEMI in the context of alcohol use lends a high-acuity phenotype associated with significantly elevated rates of cardiac arrest, ventricular arrhythmia, and sepsis/septic shock. While alcohol use in this population significantly increases hospital charges and length of stay, these patients demonstrate superior in-hospital survival. Increased resource utilisation and prolonged length of stay likely reflect intensive management required for this critical presentation, necessitating a comprehensive approach that addresses both clinical stabilization and complex discharge needs.
title: Alcohol use in STEMI patients: a complicated clinical course with paradoxically improved survival

abstract: Abstract Background The impact of cannabis use on ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) presentation and outcomes is often confounded by the younger demographic of cannabis users. We sought to separate these effects using propensity score matching (PSM) to evaluate whether cannabis use serves as a marker for unique clinical phenotypes regarding procedural complexity, arrhythmia burden, and readmission etiology. Purpose To evaluate the impact of cannabis use on in-hospital outcomes and readmissions in patients presenting with a STEMI compared to those who do not use cannabis. Methods We queried the Nationwide Readmissions Database (2019–2022) for index STEMI hospitalizations. We compared baseline characteristics, procedural utilisation, and outcomes between cannabis users (CU) and non-users (NU). A 1:1 propensity score matching (PSM) model balanced groups across age, sex, payer, hospital characteristics, and comorbidities (Van Walraven Elixhauser index). Doubly robust regression estimated adjusted odds ratios (aOR) for outcomes. Results Of 569,574 weighted hospitalizations, 2.4% (N=13,789) were CUs. In the overall cohort, CUs were significantly younger (median 53 vs 64 years; P&lt;.001) yet exhibited markers of accelerated disease and electrical instability, with higher rates of coronary atherectomy (14.9% vs 12.5%; P=.009) and ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation (22.3% vs 20.0%; P=.149). PSM yielded 7,519 balanced pairs (median age 53 vs 54). In the matched doubly robust analysis, cannabis use remained associated with significantly lower in-hospital mortality (aOR 0.57; 95% CI 0.48-0.68; P&lt;.001). However, this survival advantage was accompanied by higher resource utilisation, including increased hospital charges (Ratio 1.05; P&lt;.001) and length of stay (Ratio 1.03; P=.032). Readmission analysis revealed a distinct divergence with heart failure as the leading cause for NUs (25.3%) while recurrent acute MI (24.0%) and nonspecific chest pain (9.8%) were the primary drivers for CUs. Conclusion Cannabis use in STEMI is associated with lower adjusted mortality despite a phenotype of accelerated coronary complexity with higher rates of complex revascularization (atherectomy) and ischemic readmissions rather than heart failure. The associations with increased charges and length of stay suggest that cannabis use complicates the STEMI course, warranting aggressive secondary prevention for recurrent ischemia.
title: Cannabis use is associated with increased procedural complexity and need for atherectomy in STEMI despite younger age and lower mortality

abstract: Abstract Background Staging of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) based on tissue injury provides a robust framework for assessing myocardial damage via Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance (CMR). While universal CMR remains infeasible for all acute myocardial infarction patients, rapid blood-based biomarkers are needed to identify high-acuity Stage IV (hemorrhagic) injury, which carries the highest risk for adverse clinical outcomes. Intramyocardial hemorrhage (IMH) represents a critical therapeutic target in vulnerable revascularized STEMI populations. Purpose To evaluate whether serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTn-I) kinetics can reliably predict stages of myocardial injury and effectively triage reperfused STEMI patients for clinical trials and value-based imaging, with a specific focus on identifying hemorrhagic myocardial infarction. Methods We studied 267 consecutive reperfused acute MI patientsstaged according to myocardial injurycriteria using CMR for edema(T2-based) as Stage I, necrosis (Late Gadolinium Enhancement)as Stage II, microvascular obstruction (MVO) as Stage III, and IMH (T2*) as Stage IV. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTn-I) was sampled seriallypre-PCI, immediately post-reperfusion, and hourly up to 12 hours, then 16, 20, 24 and 48 hours. Peak hs-cTn-I was defined as the maximum concentration withinthe first 12 hours. Diagnostic performance and optimalthresholds for differentiating stages of myocardial injurywere determined using Receiver OperatingCharacteristic (ROC) curve analysis and Youden's J statistic. Results Peak hs-cTn-I levels demonstrated a clear stepwise increase correlating with the severity of tissue injury determined by CMR. Median (IQR) peak values in ng/ml were 9.0 (2.2–18.2) for Stage I, 39.1 (14.4–82.8) for Stage II, 73.3 (31.1–127.9) for Stage III, and 210.9 (115.9–415.1) for Stage IV. A threshold of peak [hs-cTn-I] &gt; 62.3~ng/ml separated Stage III or greater from Stage II injury with 81.7% sensitivity and 71.7% specificity (AUC 0.839). Importantly, a peak level &gt; 156.6~ng/ml identified Stage IV hemorrhagic injury compared to Stage III with 65.8% sensitivity, 90.0% specificity, and an AUC of 0.841. Analysis at 3 hours post-PCI yielded AUC values (0.806–0.876) that closely approximated the discriminatory accuracy of 12-hour peak values. Conclusion Post-reperfusion high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I kinetics allow for accurate staging of myocardial injury in reperfused STEMI patients. These findings demonstrate that blood-based biomarkers can effectively triage patients for value-based CMR and for clinical trials aimed at therapeutic interventions targeting specific stages of tissue injury, such as intramyocardial hemorrhage.CMR Phenotypes of Myocardial Injury StagesSerial hs-cTn-I Kinetics Post-Reperfusion
title: Hs-troponin-i kinetics enable rapid diagnosis of stages of injury and hemorrhagic MI in reperfused STEMI

abstract: Abstract Background Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have demonstrated cardioprotective effects in experimental ischemia–reperfusion models, including reduction of myocardial injury. Whether early administration before reperfusion can limit infarct size in ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) remains uncertain. Purpose We aimed to investigate the effect of pre-reperfusion dapagliflozin loading on myocardial infarct size measured by cardiac biomarkers and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) in STEMI patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Methods In this prospective, double-blind, randomized trial, 60 STEMI patients presenting within 12 hours of symptoms onset and eligible for primary PCI were randomized 1:1 to dapagliflozin (20 mg loading dose before wire crossing followed by 10 mg daily for 3 months) or placebo. The primary endpoint was infarct size quantified as the area under the curve (AUC) of cardiac troponin I (TnI) over 72 hours. The secondary endpoint was the infarct size change assessed by CMR at baseline and 3 months. Results Baseline clinical, angiographic, and procedural characteristics were comparable between groups (mean age 63.9±8.7 years; 66.7% male; baseline left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF] from echocardiography 50.8±11.2%). Pre-reperfusion dapagliflozin did not significantly reduce enzymatic infarct size. Median AUC TnI (0–72 h) was 2,812,946 in the dapagliflozin group vs 3,046,243 in placebo (p=0.57), with consistent findings in anterior and non-anterior infarctions. At 3 months, LVEF improved significantly in both groups without a between-group difference (dapagliflozin +5.4±10.1%, p&lt;0.001; placebo +3.6±14.2%, p=0.03). Among patients with serial CMR, infarct size reduction at 12 weeks was numerically greater with dapagliflozin, both in absolute infarct area (7.4±15.3 vs 0.7±8.7) and percentage change (24.6±50.3 vs 8.8±35.3), but differences did not reach statistical significance. Left ventricular volumes, mass, and microvascular obstruction were similar between groups. Conclusions Pre-reperfusion dapagliflozin loading in STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI did not significantly reduce infarct size assessed by cardiac biomarkers or CMR, although a consistent numerical trend toward infarct reduction was observed on follow-up imaging.Figure 1.Median AUC TnI (0-72 hrs)
title: Pre-reperfusion dapagliflozin does not reduce infarct size in STt-elevation myocardial infarction: a randomized controlled trial

abstract: Abstract Background In patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and multivessel coronary artery disease, complete revascularization improves outcomes, but the optimal timing of non-culprit lesion treatment remains uncertain. Diabetes mellitus is associated with more extensive coronary disease and higher ischemic and renal risk, raising the possibility that diabetes may modify the relative benefit of immediate versus staged complete revascularization. Methods The OPTION–STEMI trial enrolled 994 patients undergoing primary PCI for STEMI with multivessel disease. Patients were randomized to immediate or staged complete revascularization. Clinical outcomes at 1 year were compared according to diabetes status. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, or unplanned revascularization. Baseline clinical and procedural characteristics were evaluated across diabetes and treatment groups, and hazard ratios with interaction p-values were calculated to assess whether diabetes modified the treatment effect. Results Among the 994 patients, 416 (41.9%) had diabetes mellitus. Compared with non-diabetic patients, those with diabetes had a higher prevalence of hypertension (62.5% vs. 41.2%), dyslipidemia (63.9% vs. 53.5%), previous myocardial infarction (10.6% vs. 5.5%), and chronic kidney disease (10.3% vs. 4.8%). At 1 year, diabetic patients experienced higher rates of all-cause death (8.9% vs. 4.5%), cardiovascular death (7.0% vs. 3.5%), heart failure rehospitalization (7.0% vs. 2.9%), and contrast-induced nephropathy (7.8% vs. 4.3%). Within the diabetes subgroup, the primary endpoint occurred in 14.7% of the immediate group and 13.2% of the staged group (HR 1.10, 95% CI 0.66–1.85). In the non-diabetes subgroup, the primary endpoint occurred in 11.8% and 8.9%, respectively (HR 1.37, 95% CI 0.82–2.29). (Figure 1, 2) There was no significant interaction between diabetes status and treatment strategy for the primary endpoint (interaction p=0.555). Secondary outcomes—including all-cause death, cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and unplanned revascularization—did not differ significantly between immediate and staged strategies in either subgroup. Contrast-induced nephropathy showed a significant interaction (p=0.036), with staged procedures associated with higher incidence among non-diabetic patients. (Figure 1) Conclusion Among patients with STEMI and multivessel disease, immediate and staged complete revascularization resulted in comparable 1-year clinical outcomes regardless of diabetes status. Although diabetic patients exhibited higher overall risk, diabetes did not modify the relative effectiveness of the two revascularization strategies. These findings suggest that the timing of complete revascularization may be selected independently of diabetes status in clinical decision-making.
title: Diabetes and the timing of complete revascularization in STEMI with multivessel disease: insights from the OPTION–STEMI trial

abstract: Abstract Background Despite advances in reperfusion therapies, cardiogenic shock (CS) remains the leading cause of mortality in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). While early revascularization via percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the gold standard, the specific impact of total ischemia time (TIT) on in-hospital survival in this high-risk population requires further characterization. Methods We conducted a retrospective observational study at a tertiary cardiovascular center (2007–2025). A total of 512 adult STEMI patients complicated by CS who underwent PCI were analyzed. The primary objective was to assess the association between TIT (defined as symptom onset to wire crossing) and in-hospital mortality. Natural cubic splines and Cox proportional hazards models were utilized to identify risk thresholds and independent predictors. Results Of the 512 patients, 59% (n=302) had a TIT ≤402 minutes, while 41% (n=210) had a TIT ≥402 minutes. Patients with a TIT ≤402 minutes demonstrated a 32.5% lower risk of in-hospital mortality compared to those with longer delays (HR 0.68; 95% CI 0.50–0.91; p=0.010). In a continuous analysis, every 60-minute increase in TIT was associated with a 3.3% increase in the relative risk of death (adjusted HR 1.033; 95% CI 0.980–1.089). Other independent predictors of mortality included advanced age (HR 1.25 per 10-year increase), diabetes mellitus (HR 2.22), and higher SCAI shock stages (specifically stages D and E). Conclusion In STEMI patients presenting with cardiogenic shock, a total ischemia time exceeding 402 minutes is a critical independent predictor of in-hospital mortality. These findings emphasize the imperative need to optimize systems of care and minimize system delays, as every minute saved directly translates into improved survival for this critically ill population.Forrest plot of total ischemia timeHazard Ratio ischemia total
title: Total ischemia time and in-hospital survival in STEMI-related cardiogenic shock: the critical impact of reperfusion delay

abstract: Abstract Background Timely primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is central to STEMI management. Following the Heart Attack Ethiopia initiative, mission supported efforts enabled establishment of a structured STEMI care program to standardize rapid triage, catheterization laboratory activation, and guideline directed therapy. Purpose To evaluate the impact of STEMI program implementation on 1-year clinical outcomes. Methods we conducted a single center cohort study in 200 participants comparing consecutive STEMI patients treated before program implementation with patients managed after implementation of the program (prospectively followed cohort). Propensity score matching based on age and sex was performed. Baseline characteristics were summarized using means for continuous variables and proportions for categorical variables. The primary endpoint was 1-year major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: death, reinfarction, stroke, heart failure hospitalization, or unplanned revascularization). Follow up was administratively censored at 365 days. Kaplan Meier analysis and log rank testing were performed. This analysis represents a preliminary report; additional data will be incorporated into the final presentation. Results Seventy-seven patients were included (27 pre-program, 50 post program). Baseline characteristics were broadly comparable. MACE occurred in 6 patients (22.2%) in the pre-program era and 2 patients (4.0%) following program implementation. At 1 year, Kaplan Meier estimated cumulative incidence of MACE was 37.0% in the pre-program cohort versus 4.0% in the structured program cohort (absolute risk reduction 33.0%; log rank p=0.024). The post program era was associated with more consistent primary PCI delivery and improved adherence to guideline directed medical therapy. Conclusions Implementation of a structured STEMI care program supported by the Heart Attack Ethiopia initiative was associated with a significant reduction in 1 year MACE compared with the pre-program era, despite prior erratic PCI availability. These findings suggest that system level organization and protocolized delivery of care confer meaningful outcome benefits in resource constrained settings. Expanded prospective follow up will further define the durability and magnitude of effect.Kaplan Meier curves of cumulative MACETable for clinical characteristics
title: Impact of structured STEMI program implementation on 1 year outcomes in low middle income country: a propensity score matched cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PPCI) is the preferred reperfusion strategy for ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Pre-hospital administration of unfractionated heparin (UFH) is standard practice to ensure effective anticoagulation before arrival in the catheterization lab, yet evidence on the effect of pre-hospital UFH on Activated Clotting Time (ACT) upon catheterization lab arrival is limited. Purpose To assess ACT at catheterization lab arrival following a standardised pre-hospital bolus of 5000 IU UFH, and to evaluate associations with key time intervals, efficacy, procedural outcomes, and short-term clinical events. Methods This prospective, multicentre, observational pilot study included 100 STEMI patients transported by ambulance and treated with PPCI between April 2021 and June 2022. All patients received 5000 IU UFH pre-hospital, followed by an optional additional UFH dose at the catheterization lab. ACT was measured immediately upon arrival at the catheterization lab. Time intervals (symptom onset to administration of UFH (SO-UFH), administration of UFH to ACT measurement (UFH-ACT), SO-PPCI) were recorded and TIMI flow scale was used to assess patency in the infarct-related artery. Clinical, procedural, and 30-day outcomes were obtained retrospectively from electronic health records. Results The 100 STEMI patients had a mean age of 65 ± 13 years and 70% were male. Median ACT at arrival was 175 s (158-196), with 97% of patients below the therapeutic ACT target of 250 s. Median SO-UFH, UFH-ACT, and SO-PPCI intervals were 76 min, 45 min, and 121 min, respectively. Intervals were not significantly correlated with ACT values. No associations were observed between ACT levels and pre-procedural TIMI flow, peri-procedural complications, post-procedural complications, or 30-day MACE. However, SO-UFH was significantly associated with pre-procedural TIMI flow (OR = 0.994, p = 0.04). Conclusions A pre-hospital bolus of 5000 IU UFH resulted in subtherapeutic ACT levels in nearly all STEMI patients upon catheterization lab arrival. No associations were found between ACT and pre-procedural TIMI flow or short-term clinical outcomes. In contrast, the SO-UFH interval showed a significant association with pre-TIMI flow, suggesting that earlier pre-hospital anticoagulation may influence initial coronary patency. Larger, randomised studies with serial ACT monitoring are needed to define optimal pre-hospital anticoagulation strategies in STEMI.abstract visual
title: Subtherapeutic activated clotting time after pre-hospital unfractionated heparin in ST-elevation myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Despite mild-to-intermediate stenosis, deferred non-culprit vessels in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) remain at heightened risk of progression and subsequent revascularization. Angiography-derived coronary radial wall strain (RWS) is a novel approach for identifying vulnerable coronary plaque prone to future adverse events. This study aimed to investigate the prognostic utility of RWS in untreated mild-to-intermediate lesions in AMI patients. Methods Consecutive AMI patients who underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) from January 2009 to December 2018 had at least 1 coronary lesion with a percent diameter stenosis (DS%) of 30% to 70% in deferred non-culprit vessels were screened for enrollment. Patients were followed up until the occurrence of unplanned target lesion revascularization or the end of the study period (January 31, 2024). Patients were divided into two groups according to unplanned revascularization occurrence. A 1:3 propensity score matching was implemented. Results All together, 71 lesions with revascularization and 213 matched controls were enrolled. Baseline characteristics were generally well-balanced between the two groups. Maximal RWS (RWSmax) was significantly higher in the revascularization group compared to the control group [14.1 (12.3-15.5)% vs. 11.3 (10.1-13.35)%, P &lt; 0.001]. The area under the curve (AUC) for RWSmax to predict unplanned revascularization was 0.746 (95% CI: 0.685-0.807, p &lt; 0.001). Patients with at least one non-culprit lesion being RWSmax ≥ 13.0% had a significantly higher risk of unplanned revascularization compared to those without (risk ratio 7.463, 95% CI: 4.082-13.699, P &lt; 0.001). Conclusion Among patients with AMI, a high RWSmax of ≥ 13.0% in mild-to-intermediate lesions in non-culprit vessels was significantly associated with an increased risk of subsequent revascularization.FlowchartHigh RWSmax predicts more revascularization.
title: Angiographically derived radial wall strain predicts revascularization of mild-to-intermediate lesions in non-culprit vessels among patients with acute myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Despite contemporary reperfusion therapy, a subset of STEMI patients develops heart failure (HF) during follow-up, including those with preserved or mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), suggesting mechanisms beyond global systolic dysfunction. Purpose To evaluate whether integrative assessment of LV diastolic function and the left atrial (LA) strain-to-volume ratio provides incremental prognostic value for 6-month HF beyond conventional and advanced systolic indices, including LVEF and global longitudinal strain (GLS). Methods We analyzed 472 consecutive STEMI patients from the prospective registry who underwent comprehensive discharge echocardiography and completed 6-month follow-up (61±12 years, 26% women, LVEF 48±9%). The composite 6-month HF endpoint (HF hospitalization, emergency visit for HF, or NYHA ≥II) occurred in 59 patients (12.5%). Assessed parameters included LVEF, GLS, global work efficiency (GWE), post-systolic shortening (PSD), septal E′, LA strain-to-volume ratio (PALS/LAV), and TRVmax. Two multivariable logistic models were constructed: Model A (septal E′, PALS/LAV, GWE, PSD, TRVmax) and Model B (septal E′ and PALS/LAV). Internal validation was performed using 1000-sample bootstrap resampling; discrimination was assessed by ROC analysis. Results In univariable analysis, septal E′ (OR 0.69, p&lt;0.001), PALS/LAV (OR 0.04, p=0.001), PSD (OR 1.009 per ms, p=0.024), GWE (OR 0.96 per %, p=0.009), and TRVmax (OR 2.80, p=0.005) predicted 6-month HF, whereas LVEF and GLS showed modest discrimination (AUC 0.57 and 0.59). In multivariable analysis, only septal E′ and PALS/LAV remained independently associated with HF. Model A achieved AUC 0.72 (95% CI 0.63–0.81) and Model B 0.73 (95% CI 0.65–0.81). Model B outperformed LVEF (p=0.0287) and GLS (p=0.0338) (Figure 1). Conclusions Six-month HF after STEMI is primarily driven by discharge LV diastolic abnormalities and impaired LA structural–functional integrity rather than global systolic dysfunction, even in patients with preserved or mildly reduced LVEF. Early integrative diastolic–atrial assessment may enhance post-STEMI risk stratification beyond conventional, deformation-based, and myocardial work-derived systolic measures.Figure 1Graphical abstract
title: Discharge left ventricular diastolic abnormalities and left atrial strain-to-volume ratio predict 6-month heart failure after STEMI

abstract: Abstract Background Early reperfusion is the cornerstone of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) management, with treatment delays directly influencing mortality and haemodynamic complications. Although primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PPCI) is the guideline-recommended strategy, access limitations remain a major challenge in middle-income countries. The pharmacoinvasive (PI) strategy has been proposed as a pragmatic alternative, yet real-world comparative data remain limited. We evaluated in-hospital mortality and cardiogenic shock in patients treated with PPCI versus PI strategy. Methods In this multicentre observational study, 5,941 consecutive STEMI patients were included: 3,240 underwent PPCI (2014–2020) and 2,701 received PI strategy (2010–2020). Clinical characteristics, angiographic findings, and system delays (symptom-to-reperfusion and door-to-reperfusion times) were analysed. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for clinical and haemodynamic covariates was performed, with results expressed as adjusted prevalence ratios (aPR) and 95% confidence intervals. Results PPCI patients were older, whereas smoking was more prevalent in the PI group. Diabetes and hypertension were similarly distributed. Reperfusion times were significantly shorter with PPCI, which was also associated with higher rates of final TIMI 3 flow and myocardial blush grade 3(Table 1). In-hospital mortality was comparable between PPCI and PI strategy (5.8% vs 5.9%; p=0.94). However, cardiogenic shock occurred more frequently in the PI group (8.9% vs 2.6%; p&lt;0.001). After adjustment, age and diabetes independently predicted mortality. The PI strategy was not associated with increased mortality but remained strongly associated with cardiogenic shock (Figure 1B). Conclusion In this large real-world cohort, the pharmacoinvasive strategy achieved similar in-hospital mortality compared with PPCI but was associated with a markedly higher risk of cardiogenic shock. These findings reinforce the priority of timely PPCI and highlight the need for optimised regional STEMI networks in resource-limited settings.Figure 1- Mortality and cardiogenic shock
title: Reperfusion strategies in acute myocardial infarction: comparison between primary percutaneous coronary intervention and a pharmacoinvasive strategy in a real-world Brazilian setting

abstract: Abstract Background Pre-hospital triage strategies for ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) vary widely. Standard practices, such as autonomous paramedic activation or remote cardiology consultation, face evolving competition as artificial intelligence electrocardiogram interpretation develops. Evaluating this technology across distinctly different clinical pathways is essential to determine its real-world utility. Purpose This retrospective validation study assessed whether an artificial intelligence model [1] can accurately detect occlusive myocardial infarction (OMI) compared to both standard paramedic and cardiology triage. The primary aim was to determine if the technology could reduce false-positive pathway and emergency catheterisation laboratory activations without loss of diagnostic sensitivity. Methods The study retrospectively analysed 295 suspected STEMI cases collected consecutively in cohorts between 2024 – 2025 from two large regional heart attack centres in the UK. Centre A (177 patients) operated without pre-hospital cardiology review, relying on paramedic activation. Centre B (118 patients) used a nurse-led cardiology remote electronic electrocardiogram and clinical history review model. We compared the final clinical ground-truth diagnosis against the standard care decisions and the artificial intelligence predictions. True OMI was defined as Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction flow grade 0 to II, or grade III flow with a confirmed culprit vessel and troponin elevation. Blinded independent adjudication was performed of all clinical notes and angiography. Results Triage relying solely on paramedic activation resulted in high proportion of false-positive alerts (58% of total activations). In Centre A, applying the artificial intelligence electrocardiogram model yielded 94.7% sensitivity, 89.2% specificity, and 91.5% overall accuracy. This reduced false-positive activations (6% of total activations) without compromising patient safety. In Centre B, the existing cardiology remote review gatekeeper achieved 91.4% sensitivity and 91.6% specificity. The artificial intelligence model demonstrated comparable performance in this setting, achieving 94.3% sensitivity, 89.2% specificity, and 90.7% accuracy. Across both triage pathways, the artificial intelligence maintained a consistently low false-negative rate (5.5%). Conclusion The OMI artificial intelligence electrocardiogram model demonstrates broad clinical utility across diverse pre-hospital triage workflows. The model significantly improves specificity and overall diagnostic accuracy in paramedic-led pathways, safely reducing unnecessary laboratory activations. This matches the high diagnostic performance of a cardiology remote review pathway, but with opportunities for more effective resource utilisation. These findings suggest that artificial intelligence can effectively optimise STEMI pathway triage in a variety of underlying workflow structures.Flow diagramPerformance table
title: Multi-centre study of an artificial intelligence ECG model for the detection of occlusive myocardial infarction within the UK

abstract: Abstract Background GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) reduce cardiovascular events in patients with diabetes, but their impact on myocardial injury in acute myocardial infarction (MI) remains unclear. Purpose To our knowledge, no meta-analysis has evaluated the effect of GLP-1 RAs on infarct size. We performed a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials to quantify their effect on infarct size relative to the area at risk (AAR). Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Major databases (MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Google Scholar) were searched from inception through February 2026 for comparative studies evaluating the effect of GLP-1 RAs on infarct size. The goal was to identify studies comparing GLP-1 RAs (exenatide or liraglutide) versus placebo in patients with acute MI reporting infarct size. The primary outcome was infarct size as a percentage of AAR. Mean differences (MD) were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis (REML, Hartung-Knapp adjustment), with fixed-effect analysis performed as a sensitivity analysis. Heterogeneity was quantified using I². Forest plots were generated for visualization. Three RCTs were included (Lønborg et al., 2012; Bernink et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2016), totaling 205 patients. All studies focused on patients with ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Analysis was conducted using R version 4.5.2 software. Results Across the three RCTs, GLP-1 RAs significantly reduced final infarct size relative to the area at risk compared with placebo. The random-effects pooled mean difference was –10.14% (95% CI: –14.11% to –6.17%, p &lt; 0.001) (Figure 1). All studies favored GLP-1 therapy. Fixed-effect sensitivity analysis yielded similar results. Conclusions GLP-1 receptor agonists significantly reduce infarct size relative to AAR in acute MI, supporting a potential cardioprotective effect beyond glycemic control. These findings suggest that GLP-1 RAs may attenuate myocardial injury in MI, particularly in STEMI patients. Large-scale randomized trials are warranted to confirm these cardioprotective benefits and to assess clinical outcomes.Figure 1:Effect of GLP-1 RAs
title: GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce infarct size relative to area at risk in myocardial infarction: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

abstract: Abstract Background In ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) with multivessel coronary artery disease (MVD), the optimal timing of complete revascularization (CR)—whether during the index procedure, staged in-hospital, or deferred after discharge—remains debated, with implications for clinical practice. Methods We systematically searched PubMed and EMBASE through September 2025 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing outcomes of different CR timings in STEMI with MVD. Pairwise meta-analysis compared immediate versus staged CR, whereas network meta-analysis (NMA) evaluated immediate, staged in-hospital, and staged out-of-hospital CR. The primary endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Secondary endpoints included all-cause death, cardiovascular (CV) death, recurrent myocardial infarction (MI), and repeat revascularization. Results Eleven studies (9 RCTs and 2 prespecified sub-analyses; 5,483 patients) were included. In pairwise analysis, MACE did not differ between immediate and staged CR (OR 0.90, 95% CI 0.64–1.25; p= 0.54). Immediate CR was associated with higher all-cause mortality (OR 1.46, 95% CI 1.02–2.09; p= 0.039) but fewer recurrent MIs, including type 4a (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.43–0.94; p= 0.025). No differences were observed for exploratory endpoints. In the NMA, comparisons among the three strategies revealed no significant differences in MACE, all cause death and CV death. For recurrent MI, both immediate CR (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.32–0.85; p = 0.01) and staged in-hospital CR (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.48–0.98; p = 0.04) were associated with lower risk compared with staged out-of-hospital CR. Similarly, for repeat revascularization, immediate CR (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.35–0.82; p = 0.003) and staged in-hospital CR (OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.32–0.85; p = 0.01) showed significantly lower risks versus staged out-of-hospital CR. Bayesian ranking (SUCRA) identified staged in-hospital CR as the most effective strategy for reducing MACE, all-cause death, and CV death, whereas staged out-of-hospital CR ranked worst for MACE, recurrent MI, and repeat revascularization. Conclusions Staged in-hospital CR provides the most favorable balance of efficacy and safety in STEMI with MVD, outperforming staged out-of-hospital CR and demonstrating comparable outcomes to immediate CR. Larger, adequately powered RCTs are warranted to define the optimal revascularization timing.Results of Pairwise Meta-analysisResults of Network Meta-analysis
title: Immediate vs staged in-hospital vs staged out-of-hospital complete revascularization in STEMI patients with multivessel disease: a network meta-analysis of randomized trials

abstract: Abstract Background Clinicians increasingly use commercially available multimodal large language models (LLMs), without formal validation, to interpret 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs). ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) represents the highest-acuity ECG diagnosis: missed STEMIs delay reperfusion, whilst false positives trigger unnecessary catheterisation laboratory activation. Although recent studies have examined individual LLMs for myocardial infarction detection, no head-to-head comparison of current-generation models exists. Additionally, none has characterised which ECG pathologies most frequently trigger false-positive STEMI diagnoses. Purpose We hypothesised that current-generation multimodal LLMs lack sufficient diagnostic accuracy for STEMI detection to support safe clinical use. This study aimed to compare three LLMs head-to-head and identify which ECG pathologies most frequently trigger false STEMI diagnoses. Methods We presented 599 real-world 12-lead ECGs sourced from a published five-volume teaching case series to three multimodal LLMs (ChatGPT-5.1, Claude 4.5, Gemini 3) under minimalist and structured prompt conditions, generating 3,995 interpretive reports. Textbook-assigned expert interpretations served as the reference standard. Two authors independently classified each report as STEMI-positive or STEMI-negative; 87 of 599 unique ECGs (14.5%) were STEMI-positive. We evaluated sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and false-positive and false-negative rates by model and prompt condition, then cross-referenced false-positive reports against the true ECG pathology. Results All three LLMs demonstrated critically low STEMI sensitivity: 28.1% for ChatGPT, 30.4% for Claude, and 40.5% for Gemini (overall 33.2%), corresponding to a two-thirds miss rate (237/355 STEMI reports undetected). The overall false-positive rate reached 21.9% (798/3,640 non-STEMI reports), with a PPV of only 12.9%. Structured prompting shifted rather than resolved errors: for ChatGPT, it tripled the false-positive rate (12.6% to 38.3%) while raising sensitivity from 18.0% to 39.6%. False-positive STEMI calls clustered in normal ECGs (26.1%) and in recognised STEMI mimics: pericarditis (34.3%), old myocardial infarction (28.9%), ventricular strain (28.4%), and early repolarisation (27.1%) (Figure 1). No model achieved both sensitivity and specificity above 50% under any condition (Figure 2). Conclusion Multimodal LLMs missed two-thirds of STEMIs and fabricated the diagnosis in one-fifth of non-STEMI ECGs, with false positives concentrated in the very STEMI mimics and normal tracings where clinical discrimination matters most. These findings confirm our hypothesis and demonstrate that general-purpose LLMs cannot safely support STEMI triage. As these tools are readily accessible to clinicians at all training levels, prospective studies are urgently needed to define domain-specific safety thresholds.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Multimodal large language models miss two-thirds of STEMIs on electrocardiograms and concentrate false-positive diagnoses in STEMI mimics and normal tracings

abstract: Abstract Background Left ventricular (LV) diastole comprises active relaxation, chamber compliance, and filling pressure response. Whether these functional components reflect distinct patterns of myocardial injury early after ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) remains unclear. Methods We studied 258 STEMI patients (mean age 59.4 ± 11.1 years; 22.5% women) undergoing discharge cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) and comprehensive echocardiography. Markers of relaxation (e′), filling pressure (E/e′), chamber compliance (deceleration time of the E-wave, DT), and left atrial reservoir strain (PALS) were analyzed. CMR-derived infarct size, remote native T1 (NT1), microvascular obstruction (MVO), myocardial edema (T2), and LVEF were entered into multivariable linear regression models adjusted for age. Results Impaired relaxation (e′) was independently associated with age (β = −0.391, p &lt; 0.001), LVEF (β = 0.226, p = 0.003), infarct size (β = −0.216, p = 0.005), and remote myocardial injury (NT1) (β = −0.125, p = 0.029) (model R² = 0.311), indicating that early slowing of relaxation is associated not only with infarct-related myocyte loss but also with diffuse myocardial involvement beyond the infarct zone. Elevated LV filling pressure (E/e′) was independently associated with MVO (β = 0.271, p &lt; 0.001), age (β = 0.277, p &lt; 0.001), and remote NT1 (β = 0.131, p = 0.036) (R² = 0.142), suggesting that increased filling pressures early after STEMI are linked to infarct-zone microvascular injury on a background of global myocardial involvement. Chamber compliance (DT) was inversely associated with MVO burden (β = −0.183, p = 0.009) and infarct-related myocardial edema (T2) (β = −0.145, p = 0.026), while being positively associated with age (β = 0.167, p = 0.010), indicating reduced LV distensibility in the presence of acute microvascular and interstitial injury. PALS was independently associated only with LVEF (β = 0.290, p &lt; 0.001) and age (β = −0.311, p &lt; 0.001) (R² = 0.175), without association with CMR-derived tissue injury markers, supporting ventricular–atrial mechanical coupling rather than intrinsic atrial injury. Conclusions Early LV diastolic dysfunction after STEMI arises from distinct patterns of myocardial injury. Impaired relaxation is associated with infarct extent and remote myocardial involvement, whereas elevated filling pressures and reduced compliance are more closely linked to infarct-zone microvascular obstruction and myocardial edema. Multimodality imaging enables early differentiation of these mechanisms and may help identify patients with haemodynamic compromise not explained by infarct size alone. Figure 1 legend. Infarct-zone microvascular obstruction and edema translate into reduced compliance (DT) and elevated filling pressure (E/e′), whereas infarct extent and remote myocardial injury relate to impaired relaxation (e′). PALS reflects LVEF-driven ventricular–atrial coupling rather than tissue injury.Figure 1.
title: Diastolic dysfunction after STEMI: distinct mechanistic pathways revealed by CMR and echocardiography

abstract: Abstract Background Computational pressure-flow dynamics-derived fractional flow reserve (caFFR) enables FFR determination from angiography alone, without invasive pressure wire or hyperaemic stimulus. While its diagnostic accuracy is well-established, the clinical impact of adhering to caFFR-guided revascularisation strategies in patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS) remains to be fully elucidated. Purpose To determine whether caFFR-concordant revascularisation improves cardiovascular outcomes compared with discordant strategies in NSTE-ACS patients. Methods This retrospective cohort study analysed 283 NSTE-ACS patients (mean age 67.4±12.7 years; 65.7% male) with interpretable three-vessel caFFR who underwent revascularisation between 2014 and 2017. Patients underwent revascularisation at the discretion of the proceduralist according to the angiographic and clinical data available at the time. Concordant strategy was defined as PCI of all ischaemic vessels (caFFR ≤0.80) with deferral of non-ischaemic vessels (caFFR &gt;0.80); all other patterns constituted discordant strategies. To minimise indication bias, inverse probability of treatment weighting was used to balance baseline characteristics (standardised mean difference &lt;0.10). The primary endpoint was Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE; composite of cardiovascular mortality, myocardial infarction, and ischaemia-driven revascularisation) over median 4.3-year follow-up (IQR 4.0–4.6). Weighted Cox regression and Kaplan-Meier analyses assessed time-to-event outcomes. Results After IPTW adjustment, 157 patients (55.5%) received concordant and 126 (44.5%) discordant revascularisation. Among discordant cases, 72 (57.1%) were overtreated and 54 (42.9%) undertreated. While composite MACE rates and risk were similar (concordant 14.6% vs. discordant 19.0%; weighted HR 1.30, 95%CI 0.69—2.44, p=0.413), discordant strategy significantly increased the incidence rate and risk of myocardial infarction (10.4% vs. 1.2%; weighted HR 8.13, 95%CI 1.73–38.30, p=0.008). Sub-analysis of the discordant group revealed that this risk was predominantly driven by a significantly higher risk of MI for undertreatment compared to overtreatment (weighted HR 5.64; 95% CI 1.12–28.34; p=0.036). There was also a trend towards increased MACE in the undertreated group (weighted HR 2.32; 95% CI 0.97–5.51; p=0.058). Conclusion In patients with NSTE-ACS, a revascularisation strategy discordant with caFFR—particularly the undertreatment of physiologically significant lesions—is associated with a significantly higher risk of myocardial infarction. These findings suggest that integrating caFFR into the clinical decision-making process for NSTE-ACS may improve prognostic outcomes by ensuring haemodynamically significant stenoses are appropriately addressed.Kaplan-Meier Curves for all outcomesOutcomes according to caFFR concordance
title: Prognostic impact of coronary angiography-derived fractional flow reserve concordant versus discordant revascularization strategies in non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) encompasses a heterogeneous spectrum of clinical and electrocardiographic presentations. Diagnostic uncertainty is particularly pronounced in early presenters and in patients without overt ischemic ECG changes. Whether artificial intelligence–enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) maintains stable performance across this diversity remains unclear. Purpose To evaluate the robustness of AI-ECG across diverse NSTEMI phenotypes and to explore score distribution according to occlusion status. Methods In the prospective, multicenter ROMIAE cohort of 8,493 emergency department patients with suspected acute myocardial infarction, NSTEMI cases were analyzed. AI-ECG generated continuous probability scores from initial 12-lead ECGs using prespecified thresholds.1 Discrimination was assessed using AUROC. Prespecified subgroup analyses examined performance across age, comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes, coronary artery disease, prior myocardial infarction, heart failure), ischemic ECG features, rhythm abnormalities (atrial fibrillation, bundle branch block), and early presentation (≤3 hours). AI-ECG score distributions were compared between occlusive and non-occlusive NSTEMI. Results AI-ECG demonstrated stable discrimination for NSTEMI (AUROC ~0.80 range) without systematic degradation across clinical or ECG-defined subgroups. Performance remained consistent in early presenters, in patients without overt ischemic ECG features, and in those with rhythm abnormalities. (Figure 1) AI-ECG scores showed a graded distribution within NSTEMI phenotypes, with higher median values observed in occlusive compared with non-occlusive NSTEMI. (Figure 2) This gradient was evident despite absence of ST-segment elevation, suggesting that AI-ECG captures ischemic signal patterns beyond conventional criteria. Conclusion In a prospective multicenter cohort, AI-ECG maintained robust diagnostic performance across heterogeneous NSTEMI presentations and demonstrated graded signal distribution according to occlusion status. These findings support AI-ECG as a time-zero triage adjunct capable of reducing diagnostic uncertainty in NSTEMI while reflecting underlying ischemic burden.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Robust diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence–enabled electrocardiography across heterogeneous NSTEMI presentations: a prospective multicenter analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Cardiometabolic multimorbidity (CMM), defined as the coexistence of at least two cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs, including myocardial infarction, diabetes, and stroke), has been established as an important risk factor for adverse cardiovascular outcomes [1-2]. However, the differential impact of varying CMM burden on all-cause mortality following non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) has not been validated across multiple cohorts, and its value for clinical prognostic stratification remains unclear. Purpose This study aimed to investigate the association between different CMM burdens—stratified by the presence of diabetes and/or stroke—and the risk of all-cause mortality in patients with NSTEMI. Methods A total of 16,884 NSTEMI patients from two independent cohorts were included in this study: the TAMI cohort (n=14,880) and the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV (MIMIC-IV) cohort (n=2,004). Patients were categorized into hierarchical groups based on baseline CMM status: (1) non-CMM (NSTEMI only); (2) overall CMM; (3) NSTEMI with one CMD (diabetes or stroke); and (4) NSTEMI with two CMDs (diabetes and stroke). The primary endpoint was 10-Year all-cause mortality. Kaplan-Meier curves and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were employed to evaluate the association between CMM burden and all-cause mortality. Results In the TAMI cohort, 1,432 (9.6%) deaths occurred. In the MIMIC-IV cohort, 571 (28.5%) deaths occurred. The Kaplan-Meier curves demonstrated a significant upward trend in all-cause mortality risk for both cohorts as the CMM burden increased (log-rank P &lt; 0.001). In the TAMI cohort, compared to patients with NSTEMI only, CMM was significantly associated with a higher risk of mortality (HR: 1.390; 95% CI: 1.248–1.549). This risk increased incrementally with greater CMM burden: patients with one CMD had an HR of 1.309 (95% CI: 1.166–1.470), while those with both diabetes and stroke faced the highest risk (HR: 1.657; 95% CI: 1.423–1.929). When analyzed separately, diabetes alone conferred a higher risk (HR: 1.369; 95% CI: 1.206–1.555) than stroke alone (HR: 1.185; 95% CI: 1.001–1.403). Consistent trends were observed in the MIMIC-IV cohort, albeit with higher absolute event rates. The concordant findings across both cohorts validate the positive association between CMM burden and all-cause mortality in NSTEMI patients. Conclusion An increasing burden of CMM is associated with a higher risk of all-cause mortality in patients with NSTEMI, with the coexistence of both diabetes and stroke identifying the highest-risk subgroup. In clinical practice, systematic assessment of CMM burden in NSTEMI patients should be prioritized to optimize individualized prognostic stratification and to improve outcomes through comprehensive, multidisciplinary comorbidity management.
title: Cardiometabolic multimorbidity burden and all-cause mortality after non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: a multi-cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background The Geriatric Nutritional Risk Index (GNRI), derived from serum albumin and body weight, has demonstrated prognostic value in cardiovascular diseases. However, in patients with non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), its joint stratification effect with established clinical risk markers and the mechanisms linking GNRI to adverse outcomes remain incompletely understood. Purpose To evaluate the prognostic value of GNRI for long-term all-cause mortality in NSTEMI, to assess its combined stratification effect with established clinical risk markers, and to explore potential mechanisms underlying this association. Methods This single-center prospective cohort study enrolled 1,686 consecutive patients with NSTEMI admitted to our hospital from March 2016 to December 2020. GNRI was calculated at admission and categorized as ≤98 or &gt;98. The median follow-up was 5.36 years (IQR 4.17–6.57). The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality. Cox proportional hazards models assessed the association between GNRI and mortality. Restricted cubic spline analysis, joint stratification, and mediation analyses were performed to evaluate dose–response patterns, combined risk stratification, and potential mediating pathways. Results During follow-up, 249 deaths (14.8%) occurred. Restricted cubic spline analysis demonstrated a linear inverse association between GNRI and mortality risk. Compared with GNRI &gt;98, GNRI ≤98 was associated with higher mortality (HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.01–1.72; P=0.039). In fully adjusted models, lower GNRI remained independently associated with mortality (per 1 SD decrease: HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.06–1.37; P=0.005). The association was consistent across subgroups without significant interactions (all P for interaction &gt;0.05). Patients with low GNRI in combination with higher Killip class, elevated NT-proBNP, renal dysfunction, increased D-dimer, or obesity had the lowest long-term survival, indicating an additive risk pattern. Mediation analysis indicated partial mediation by NT-proBNP (28.26%), D-dimer (18.93%), and hs-CRP (15.66%). Conclusions Lower GNRI independently predicts long-term all-cause mortality in NSTEMI. The coexistence of low GNRI and high-risk clinical features identifies patients at particularly elevated risk. This association is partly explained by pathways related to cardiac dysfunction, inflammation, and coagulation, suggesting that nutritional risk reflects an integrated biological vulnerability.
title: Prognostic value of the geriatric nutritional risk index for all-cause mortality in patients with non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background/ Introduction Despite advancements in the treatment of acute coronary syndromes, patients with non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS) continue to experience significant morbidity and mortality. Current guidelines recommend early invasive management in high-risk NSTE-ACS patients. However, real-world data evaluating the effectiveness of early (≤24 hours) versus delayed (&gt;24 hours) percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), particularly in elderly patients, remains limited. Purpose To address this gap, we evaluated the difference in mortality among NSTE-ACS patients undergoing early PCI (≤24 hours from hospital admission) versus delayed PCI (&gt;24 hours), with a specific focus on those aged ≥75 years. Methods This retrospective observational cohort used prospectively collected data from the Netherlands Heart Registration and Dutch Hospital Data, including all NSTE-ACS patients who underwent PCI between 2018 and 2023. Results A total of 67,575 patients with complete follow-up were included. Early PCI was performed in 55% of the patients. Compared with delayed PCI, these patients were younger (67 versus 71 years) and had fewer comorbidities (higher eGFR, lower prevalence of diabetes, multivessel disease, prior myocardial infarction, PCI, and coronary bypass surgery). Early PCI was associated with a nonsignificant reduction in 30-day all-cause mortality in multivariable Cox regression (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77–1.01, p = 0.08) and in inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW-) weighted models (HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.76–1.01, p = 0.06). For 1-year all-cause mortality, early PCI was associated with lower mortality than delayed PCI in both multivariable Cox regression (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.75–0.87, p&lt;0.001) and IPTW-weighted models (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.76–0.87, p&lt;0.001). When stratified by age, early PCI conferred a clear survival benefit in patients &lt;75 years (30-day mortality: HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.52–0.82, p &lt; 0.001; 1-year mortality: HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.60–0.74, p &lt; 0.001), whereas no meaningful benefit was observed in those ≥75 years (30-day mortality: HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.91–1.30, p = 0.35; 1-year mortality: HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.85–1.02, p = 0.16). Interaction terms between PCI timing and age group were statistically significant for both 30-day and 1-year mortality. Conclusions In this Dutch cohort, early PCI was associated with a significant reduction in 1-year mortality compared with delayed PCI, whereas the 30-day mortality benefit was less pronounced and not statistically significant. This mortality reduction was consistently observed in patients &lt;75 years, in whom early PCI conferred a substantial survival advantage at both 30-day and 1-year follow-up. In contrast, among patients ≥75 years, early PCI did not significantly reduce mortality, underscoring the need for age-tailored timing strategies in invasive management.Forest plot: 30-day mortalityForest plot: 1-year mortality

appraisal.design_and_n: Retrospective observational cohort from the Netherlands Heart Registration, 67,575 patients with complete follow-up; early PCI in 55%.
appraisal.main_limitation: Observational with likely confounding by indication and immortal-time issues in timing comparisons; early PCI patients were younger and healthier.
appraisal.one_line: Dutch national registry comparison of early versus delayed PCI in NSTE-ACS, with an age interaction.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Early PCI was associated with 1-year all-cause mortality HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.75–0.87 (multivariable Cox) and HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.76–0.87 (IPTW); 30-day mortality HR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77–1.01. In patients ≥75 years, 1-year mortality HR was 0.94, 95% CI 0.85–1.02.
appraisal.why_it_matters: Large real-world signal on timing of invasive strategy in NSTE-ACS with a suggested age modification, relevant to a contested guideline decision.

title: Real-world outcomes of early versus delayed PCI in NSTE-ACS patients: insights from the Netherlands Heart Registration

abstract: Abstract Background There is currently a paucity of evidence on how to optimally treat elderly patients presenting with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) – especially regarding typical geriatric conditions. The EVALUATE-Pilot-Study was designed as a nonrandomized, prospective, single-centre study to evaluate the choice of treatment and 6-months-outcome of patients &gt; 75 years presenting with NSTEMI. Special attention was paid to the functional status, comorbidities and frailty. Methods Consecutive patients ≥ 75 years presenting with NSTEMI between 07/17 and 07/18 were included into the EVALUATE-study. Patients were asked to participate and sign informed consent within the first 48 hours after admission. Demographic data, past medical history and present medical condition were documented. Additionally, a geriatric assessment including clinical frailty scale, Barthel-Index, Charlson comorbidity index, “Timed up and go”-Test, Mini Mental Status Test, Geriatric depression scale, SF-36 (Quality of life), IADL, Killip-Score, Grace-Score and Euro-Score was performed. Follow-Up including a geriatric re-assessment was planned after 6 months either within a follow-up stay or by a visit at home. Functional decline was defined as a decrease in Barthel-Index by at least 20 points. Results Of 106 patients (mean age 81.9±5.3, 57% male), 68 were treated with intervention (64%) and 38 conservatively (36%). Patients treated with intervention were significantly younger (80.9±4.7 vs. 83.5±6.0; p=0.02) and had a lower Killip-Score (1.16±0.37 vs. 1.37±0.63, p=0.05). All other demographic variables as well as cardiovascular risk factors, functional status and laboratory parameters were comparable. Mean Barthel-Index at baseline was 85.9 ± 20.5 and showed no significant difference between patients treated with intervention and conservatively treated patients (88.0±19.9 vs. 82.2±21.4, p=ns). Patients were followed up after 33±12 weeks if alternate endpoints (death, severe cognitive impairment) had not already been reached. 22 patients (20.8%) were lost to Follow-Up. Mean Barthel-Index at follow-up was 84.9 ± 23.5. Functional decline was observed in 10 patients (17%). Grace Risk Score (OR 1.04, 95% CI: 1.00-1.08, NR2 0.125, p=0.04), Euro Score (OR 1.53, 95% CI: 1.12-2.23, NR2 0.189, p=0.01), CCI (OR 1.57, 95% CI: 1.15-2.32, NR2 0.223, p=0.01) and TUG (OR 1.14, 95% CI: 1.02-1.30, NR2 0.206, p=0.03) predicted functional decline. Age was no significant predictor of functional decline (OR 1.12, 95% CI: 1.00-1.26, NR20.096, p=ns). Conclusion In this prospective analysis, functional decline was observed in about every fifth patient, thus being a highly relevant problem for elderly patients with NSTEMI. Cardiac risk scores (Grace Score, Euro Score), comorbidity burden (CCI) and gait speed (TUG) predicted functional decline. More evidence on functional decline as a relevant outcome measure, its predictors and possible prevention is needed.
title: Predictors of functional decline after 6 months in elderly patients with NSTEMI

abstract: Abstract Background Mechanical circulatory support (MCS) is increasingly used in acute myocardial infarction–related cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS). In STEMI-CS, MCS has been associated with improved outcomes, yet whether similar benefit exists in NSTEMI-CS remains uncertain. Given important differences in comorbidity burden, coronary anatomy, and shock trajectory, treatment effects may differ by AMI phenotype. Purpose To evaluate whether the association between MCS use and in-hospital outcomes differs between STEMI-CS and NSTEMI-CS. Methods Adults with AMI-CS treated from 2016–2022 were stratified by AMI type (STEMI vs NSTEMI). The primary outcome was a composite of in-hospital mortality or in-hospital renal replacement therapy (RRT). The secondary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Multivariable logistic regression models were constructed separately within each AMI type to evaluate associations with the composite outcome. Results Among 1,375 patients (STEMI n=790; NSTEMI n=585), NSTEMI patients were older (71.7±12.0 vs 67.2±13.0 years; p&lt;0.001) and had greater comorbidity burden (CCI 6.3±3.2 vs 5.0±3.0; p&lt;0.001). NSTEMI presented with less severe admission SCAI stage but higher baseline and peak creatinine (both p&lt;0.001). In-hospital mortality was similar (34.6% vs 30.3%; p=0.09), though NSTEMI had longer length of stay (p&lt;0.001). MCS was used less frequently in NSTEMI (54.5% vs 71.6%; p&lt;0.001) and initiated later (median 1.0 vs 0.0 days; p&lt;0.001). Use of IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO, and multi-device support were all lower in NSTEMI (all p&lt;0.05). Despite these differences, rates of primary and secondary outcomes were similar between groups. In stratified multivariable models, MCS use was associated with lower odds of the composite outcome in STEMI (adjusted OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.41–0.97; p=0.04) but not in NSTEMI (adjusted OR 1.28, 95% CI 0.80–2.07; p=0.32). Consistent findings were observed for the secondary outcome of in-hospital mortality, with MCS associated with lower odds of death in STEMI (aOR 0.5, 95% CI 0.3–0.8; p=0.005) but not in NSTEMI (aOR 1.2, 95% CI 0.7–2.2; p=0.4). Mortality models were adjusted for the same covariates as the primary analysis, with haemodialysis treated as a covariate. Revascularisation was strongly protective against the primary outcome in both phenotypes (STEMI aOR 0.26; NSTEMI aOR 0.19; both p&lt;0.001). Conclusion In AMI-CS, the association between MCS and clinical outcomes differs by infarct phenotype. While MCS was associated with improved outcomes in STEMI-CS, no similar association was observed in NSTEMI-CS. These findings suggest potential effect heterogeneity and underscore the need for phenotype-specific evaluation of MCS strategies.In-Hospital-Mortality/Hemodialysis Predictors
title: Differential impact of mechanical circulatory support in STEMIversus NSTEMI cardiogenic shock

abstract: Abstract Background Conventional electrocardiogram (ECG) changes, such as ST elevation (STEMI) or non-ST elevation (NSTEMI), have long been the cornerstone for diagnostic categorisation of acute myocardial infarction. However, this has delayed timely interventions for patients with acute occlusive myocardial infarction (MI) with no ST- segment elevation, leading to prolonged hospitalisation and worsening outcomes1. Purpose The aim of this study is to identify correlations between specific ECG patterns, cardiac biomarkers, regional wall motion abnormalities (RWMA) on echo, and past medical history findings that could help distinguish between occlusive and non-occlusive MI, and predict one-year mortality for these patients. Methods Retrospective British Cardiovascular Intervention Society (BCIS) database analysis at a high-volume primary PCI centre in England, spanning 2015 to 2025.NSTEMI patients undergoing angiography were classified by pre-procedural infarct-related artery (IRA) flow (Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction [TIMI] 0 vs 1). Baseline characteristics were summarised by group. Univariate logistic regression evaluated associations with TIMI 0; peak troponin was log[x+1] transformed and sparse categories collapsed. A prespecified multivariable model (age, sex, diabetes, RWMA, and log-troponin) was fitted, and the model's sensitivity and performance were assessed. Results Of 3491 NSTEMI patients, 414 with TIMI 0/1 were recorded; 291 (70%) had TIMI 0, and 123 (30%) had TIMI 1. In univariate analyses, higher injury biomarkers were associated with complete occlusion: peak troponin (log[troponin+1]) increased the odds of TIMI 0 (OR 1.21, 95% CI 1.08–1.36, p=0.001, N=349), and peak CK (log[CK+1]) showed a similar association (OR 1.54, 95% CI 1.12–2.13, p=0.008, N=141). RWMA on echocardiography was also associated with TIMI 0. Presenting ECG changes (collapsed into no acute changes, ST depression, T-wave changes, and other) were not associated with complete occlusion (TIMI 0) on univariate analysis (ST depression p=0.911; T-wave changes p=0.258; other p=0.536, vs no acute changes). In the prespecified multivariable model, RWMA remained independently associated with TIMI 0 (adjusted OR 1.93, 95% CI 1.10–3.43, p=0.023). Log-transformed troponin was borderline after adjustment (p≈0.07). Adding BMI, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and 1-year mortality did not materially change results. Conclusion Many NSTEMI patients' angiography results showed complete artery occlusion despite non-ST-elevation presentation, highlighting limitations of the STEMI/NSTEMI paradigm. Presenting ECG patterns were non-discriminatory, whereas biomarker magnitude and regional wall motion abnormalities independently predicted TIMI 0 flow. These findings support a multimodal, physiology-based diagnostic approach and inform prospective studies aimed at developing a risk-stratification tool for acute occlusive myocardial infarction.
title: Prevalence and outcome of occluded coronary arteries in non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction patients in a high-volume primary percutaneous coronary intervention centre

abstract: Abstract Background Rapid identification of occlusive myocardial infarction (OMI) remains challenging in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) without ST-elevation. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted electrocardiography (AI-ECG) may enable early recognition before routine workup and allow access to timely reperfusion. Methods In this two-centre observational study, patients with suspected ACS were enrolled and managed according to current guidelines and underwent standard ACS pathway. ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) was excluded. Serial high-sensitivity troponin T measurements were collected. If needed, the patients underwent coronary angiography (CAG) and OMI was defined as acute culprit lesion with reduced TIMI flow or apparently normal flow with &gt;1000ng/l peak troponin. ECGs were analysed in a blinded core-lab using a commercially available, CE-certified AI-ECG algorithm to classify patients as AI-OMI or AI-NOMI (No signs of Occlusive Myocardial Infarction). Cardiovascular death was evaluated at twelve months using Kaplan–Meier analyses. Results Among 1,619 patients (mean age 69±17 years, 41% females) with suspected NSTE-ACS, 412 (25%) had confirmed NSTEMI and underwent CAG. Of those, 155 (37.6%) were classified as AI-OMI. AI-ECG reached a sensitivity of 83%, specificity of 99%, a positive predictive value of 98% and a negative predictive value of 89% for OMI detection. Baseline troponin levels were comparable among groups (61 [7; 205] vs 59 [8; 218] ng/L, p=0.8) with significantly higher peak troponin in AI-OMI patients (539 [122–1868] vs 219 [42–553] ng/L, p &lt; 0.001). At 12 months of follow-up, 7 (2.7%) AI-NOMI and 12 (7.7%) AI-OMI patients died (log-rank p=0.019). After adjustment for GRACE score &gt;140, AI-OMI was independently associated with increased 12-month mortality (HR 2.45; 95% CI 1.01–6.40; p=0.048). Conclusions Among NSTE-ACS, the prevalence of OMI is high and remains often clinically unrecognized. In this study, AI-ECG accurately identified OMI in a NSTE-ACS cohort. Compared to AI-NOMI, patients with AI-OMI are burdened with higher peak troponin values and with a higher 12-month cardiovascular mortality independently of GRACE score and may redefine NSTE-ACS early triage at first contact.Abstract illustration
title: Artificial intelligence–enabled ECG-identification of occlusive myocardial infarction in non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome and association with infarct size and survival

abstract: Abstract Background The optimal management of elderly patients with non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) remains uncertain, particularly among those with frailty. Purpose We aimed to evaluate the association between an invasive strategy and 1-year outcomes in patients aged ≥70 years, and whether frailty modifies the treatment effect. Methods We included 15,537 patients aged ≥70 years with NSTEMI from 2017 to 2021; 11,743 (75.6%) underwent invasive coronary angiography, while 3,794 (24.4%) were managed conservatively. Frailty was assessed using the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) and categorized as 1–3 (no-frail) 4 (vulnerable), 5–6 (mildly-moderately frail), and 7–8 (severely and very severely frail) . Outcomes included 1-year major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), all-cause mortality, and readmission for MI or stroke. To address confounding, we performed instrumental variable (IV) analysis using a two-stage residual inclusion Cox regression with the leave-one-out centre angiography rate as the instrument, and propensity score matching (PSM). Results In IV-adjusted models, an invasive strategy was associated with significantly lower risk of 1-year MACCE (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.44–0.64), mortality (HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.38–0.60), and MI (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.30–0.64), with no significant effect on stroke (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.41–1.72). PSM analyses confirmed these results (table 1).
