title: Upfront percutaneous coronary intervention versus conservative management in spontaneous coronary artery dissection: long-term outcomes from the Australian-New Zealand SCAD registry

abstract: Abstract Background Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) predominantly affects women, and endogenous hormonal influences are well recognised. However, the impact of exogenous sex hormone therapy on long-term cardiovascular outcomes remains uncertain, and current guideline recommendations are based on limited observational data. Purpose To evaluate whether exogenous sex hormone therapy at the time of SCAD, or after the index event, is associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Methods Female patients with core laboratory–adjudicated SCAD enrolled in the Australian–New Zealand SCAD registry1 (23 centres) were analysed. Exogenous hormone exposure included oral contraceptive pills (OCP), menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), and non-oral contraceptives (NOC). The primary endpoint was MACE (all-cause death, myocardial infarction, stroke/TIA, heart failure, unplanned revascularisation, or SCAD recurrence). Cox proportional hazards models assessed associations between baseline hormone use and MACE during follow-up. In prospectively recruited patients, post-SCAD hormone use was analysed as a time-varying covariate. Results Among 601 women (median age 53 years [IQR 45–60]), 10.8% were using exogenous hormones at the index SCAD event (MHT 40.0%, OCP 32.3%, NOC 23.1%, combined 4.6%). Baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics were similar between groups. Over a median follow-up of 13.7 months (IQR 2.5–35.6), MACE occurred in 54/601 patients (9.0%): 46/536 (8.6%) non-users and 8/65 (12%) hormone users in the unadjusted cohort. In the adjusted primary model (n=524), MACE occurred in 45 patients (8.6%): 37/470 (7.9%) non-users and 8/54 (15%) hormone users. After multivariable adjustment using LASSO variable selection (ACS type, revascularisation strategy, and coronary tortuosity), baseline hormone use was associated with an approximately twofold higher risk of MACE (adjusted HR 2.35, 95% CI 1.09–5.10; p=0.047). In a prospective subgroup (n=216), post-SCAD hormone therapy was not associated with recurrent MACE when modelled longitudinally (adjusted HR 1.27, 95% CI 0.37–4.38; p=0.712) [Figure1]. Hormone prescribing patterns shifted over time: by three years, 23.3% of women were using hormone therapy, predominantly lower-dose non-oral contraceptives (71.4%), mainly intrauterine devices [Figure 2]. Conclusion Exogenous sex hormone therapy at the time of SCAD was associated with an approximately twofold higher risk of MACE during follow-up. In contrast, initiation or continuation of predominantly lower-dose, non-oral hormone therapy after SCAD was not associated with recurrent events. These findings support a formulation-specific, individualised approach to hormonal management in SCAD survivors rather than universal avoidance.
title: Exogenous sex hormone therapy and long-term outcomes in spontaneous coronary artery dissection: insights from the Australian–New Zealand registry

abstract: Abstract Background Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is a non-atherosclerotic cause of acute coronary syndrome, predominantly affecting younger women. Optimal management, particularly the role of PCI, remains debated, with outcomes varying across angiographic subtypes. Methods We conducted a multicenter registry including 130 patients with angiographically confirmed SCAD from 14 PCI centers, followed during hospitalization, at 30 days, and at 1 year. Clinical presentation (STEMI/NSTEMI), SCAD type (1–4, including 2a/2b), management strategy (conservative vs PCI), TIMI flow, procedural details, low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) use, discharge therapy, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) were analyzed. Results Mean age was 47.8 years; 85% were female. STEMI occurred in 68%. Hypertension (49%), dyslipidemia (46%), and active smoking (42%) were common. Conservative therapy was applied in 63 patients (48%), while 67 (52%) underwent PCI, including stent implantation and/or balloon-only angioplasty (POBA). Among PCI patients, the most common angiographic patterns were type 2 (n=18, mainly 2a), type 4 (n=10), type 1 (n=7). Pre-procedural TIMI flow varied by subtype; TIMI 3 flow was not achieved in all patients after intervention. Among 62 patients who achieved TIMI 3 flow, 24% underwent PCI (stent and/or POBA), while 76% achieved TIMI 3 flow without any procedure. LMWH data were available for all 130 patients; 75 (58%) received therapy, mostly short-term (1–2 doses in 43 patients). Extended LMWH dosing (3–6 doses) was used in 11, 8–10 doses in 7, 12–16 doses in 3, and 22–28 doses in 2 patients. At discharge, therapy included DAPT (n=92, 73%), beta-blockers (n=53, 42%), statins (n=49, 39%), ACE/ARBs (n=38, 30%), aspirin (n=31, 25%), and P2Y12 inhibitors (n=3, 2%). In-hospital MACE occurred in 31 patients (24%), with 8% mortality; 30-day and 1-year MACE were 8% and 8%, respectively. Prior heart disease, previous coronary interventions, and statin therapy independently predicted in-hospital MACE. Namely, MACE occurred in 17% of PCI-treated patients at 30 days and in 8% at 1 year. Conclusions This first SCAD registry from an Eastern transitional country shows that PCI and DAPT were used more frequently than recommended by guidelines. Conservative management was associated with better short-term outcomes, emphasizing that invasive procedures are not always required. Timely and accurate diagnosis, along with judicious use of LMWH and other therapies, is crucial to optimizing outcomes.
title: Therapeutic approach to acute coronary syndromes caused by scad: insights from the serbian (RS) SCAD registry

abstract: Abstract Background Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is a potentially life-threatening cause of myocardial infarction (MI) mainly affecting young to middle-aged women. This study aimed to assess anxiety and depressive symptoms, perceived stress, and Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) in SCAD patients, in comparison to type 1 MI patients and healthy controls. Method A cross-sectional study of 188 SCAD patients, recruited from seven Swedish hospitals and the SWEDEHEART registry, 219 age- and sex-matched type 1 MI patients, recruited via SWEDEHEART and 94 age- and sex-matched healthy controls, recruited via the Swedish population registry. Validated questionnaires RAND-36, Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-14), and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) were used. Results Mean age±SD for SCAD patients, type 1 MI patients and healthy controls were 55.9±9.8, 60.9±9.4 and 55.5±9.1 years, respectively, and 86.2, 72.1 and 93.6% were women. Median years (IQR) since MI was 4.0(4.3) and 4.0(3.0) for SCAD and type 1 MI patients, respectively. Perceived stress was higher in SCAD patients in comparison with both type 1 MI patients and healthy controls, (mean±SD: 21.9±9.3 vs 18.5±8.7, p&lt;0.001; vs 17.7±7.9, p=0.001). A greater proportion of SCAD patients scored ≥8 points on the HADS-A subscale, indicating clinically relevant anxiety, in comparison with both type 1 MI patients and healthy controls (36% vs 20%, p&lt;0.001; vs 12%, p&lt;0.001). SCAD patients scored lower on the mental component summary (MCS) of RAND-36, than both type 1 MI patients and healthy controls (mean±SD 67.2±22.4 vs 73.7±22.0, p=0.004; vs 82.0±16.6, p&lt;0.001). Conclusions SCAD patients report significantly higher levels of perceived stress and anxiety, and poorer mental health aspects of HRQoL, in comparison with both type 1 MI patients and healthy controls. This is important to consider when forming future SCAD rehabilitation programs.Table 1
title: Psychological distress and health-related quality of life in spontaneous coronary artery dissection patients: a comparison with type 1 myocardial infarction patients and healthy controls

abstract: Abstract Background Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is a non-atherosclerotic cause of acute coronary syndrome that predominantly affects young to middle-aged women. Although physical activity is central to secondary prevention, evidence guiding exercise advice and cardiac rehabilitation after SCAD remains limited. As SCAD is often discussed in relation to physical or emotional stress, patients may receive cautious or inconsistent advice, potentially contributing to kinesiophobia and altered physical activity behaviour. Purpose To compare kinesiophobia, self-reported physical activity, and sedentary behaviour between patients with SCAD and type 1 MI; to examine associations between kinesiophobia, physical activity, and perceived physical capacity; and to explore factors associated with high kinesiophobia among patients with SCAD. Methods In this cross-sectional case–control study, 178 patients with SCAD and 279 patients with type 1 MI completed questionnaires. SCAD cases were identified through national registries and university hospitals; controls were recruited from a national myocardial infarction registry and matched as closely as possible for age, geographic region, and time since infarction. Kinesiophobia was assessed using the Tampa Scale of Kinesiophobia–Heart (TSK-Heart; ≥37 indicating high kinesiophobia). Physical activity, fulfilment of guideline recommendations, habitual activity level, sedentary behaviour, and self-perceived physical capacity were assessed using registry-based instruments and a visual analogue scale. Group differences were analysed using appropriate statistical tests and multivariable regression adjusted for age, sex, and time since infarction; associations were examined using Spearman correlations. Results Patients with SCAD reported higher kinesiophobia than patients with type 1 MI (median TSK-Heart 31 vs. 26) and a higher prevalence of high kinesiophobia (25.7% vs. 11.7%). SCAD was independently associated with high kinesiophobia after adjustment (adjusted OR 2.35, 95% CI 1.33–4.18). Habitual physical activity and sedentary behaviour did not differ between groups; however, fewer patients with SCAD met guideline-based physical activity recommendations (44.9% vs. 65.0%). Higher kinesiophobia was associated with lower habitual physical activity (ρ = −0.31) and poorer self-perceived physical capacity (ρ = −0.28). No demographic or clinical predictors of high kinesiophobia were identified among patients with SCAD. Conclusions Compared with patients with type 1 MI, patients with SCAD report higher kinesiophobia and are less likely to meet recommended physical activity levels despite similar habitual activity and sedentary time. These findings suggest that fear of movement may influence recovery after SCAD and highlight the need for targeted behavioural and rehabilitative strategies.Baseline characteristics
title: Kinesiophobia and physical activity after spontaneous coronary artery dissection: a comparison with type 1 myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Recurrent spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) has been reported in 10–30% of patients, yet the temporal patterns and clinical phenotypes of recurrence remain incompletely characterized. Most existing data originate from Western cohorts, and recurrence patterns in Asian populations are not well defined. Purpose To characterize the incidence, timing, and clinical phenotypes of SCAD recurrence in a Japanese multicenter registry. Methods This multicenter registry included 175 consecutive patients with SCAD enrolled at 15 participating centers in Japan between 2021 and 2025. Recurrent SCAD was defined as either: (1) a de novo lesion in a different coronary segment, (2) extension of the index SCAD lesion, or (3) unknown. Clinical characteristics, timing of recurrence, and discharge medications were evaluated descriptively. Results Among 175 patients (84.6% female; mean age 51.6 ± 10.0 years), 13 patients (7.4%) experienced recurrent SCAD. Recurrence patterns were classified as follows: de novo lesions in 6 patients (3.4%), extension of the index SCAD segment in 5 patients (2.9%), and unknown in 2 patients. A marked temporal difference was observed between recurrence phenotypes. Patients with de novo recurrence developed new lesions at a median of 939 [305–1564] days after the index event, representing late recurrence occurring years after initial presentation. In contrast, extension-type recurrence occurred at a median of 2 [0–3] days, and all cases developed during the index hospitalization, suggesting acute-phase lesion instability rather than late recurrence (Figure). Among patients with extension-type recurrence, escalation of antiplatelet therapy was frequently performed. In patients with de novo recurrence, discharge medications included renin–angiotensin–aldosterone inhibitors (83%), β-blockers (33%), calcium channel blockers (33%), and single antiplatelet therapy (83%). No significant association was observed between β-blocker therapy and recurrence in this cohort. No patients were clinically diagnosed with fibromuscular dysplasia. Conclusions In this Japanese multicenter registry, SCAD recurrence was less frequent than previously reported in Western cohorts and demonstrated two distinct temporal phenotypes: acute extension during the index hospitalization and late de novo recurrence years after the initial event. These findings suggest potential pathophysiological and ethnic differences in recurrence patterns and may have implications for surveillance strategies following SCAD.Figure
title: Clinical phenotypes and timing of recurrence in spontaneous coronary artery dissection: insights from a Japanese multicenter registry

abstract: Abstract Introduction Iatrogenic coronary artery dissection (ICAD) is a rare (&lt;0.2%) but potentially fatal complication of coronary angiography and may be particularly relevant in patients with spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) due to underlying arterial vulnerability. Material & Methods We analyzed patients enrolled in the Canadian SCAD Study with complete angiographic data and at least one follow-up visit. All included ICADs were catheter-induced and independently adjudicated by two cardiologists. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality and recurrent myocardial infarction (MI) during 1080 days of follow-up. Results Among 1141 eligible SCAD patients, 90.3% were female and 2.6% experienced additional ICAD. The right coronary artery was most frequently affected (56.7%) and there was no difference in access site (radial versus femoral; p=0.966) between patients with SCAD only and those with additional ICAD. Most ICADs occurred during the diagnostic part of an urgent angiogram for acute MI and were therefore induced by Judkins catheters (73.3%). Patients with ICAD required emergency revascularization more often than those with SCAD alone (PCI: 60% vs. 1.8%; CABG: 20% vs. 0.8%; both p&lt;0.001). Within the first 10 days, the cumulative incidence of the primary endpoint was markedly higher in the ICAD group (56.7% vs. 4.7%; p&lt;0.001), whereas event rates beyond the 10-day landmark were low and comparable (7.7% 5.2%; p = 0.723: Figure 1). Conclusion ICAD occurs with increased frequency in patients with SCAD despite an overall limited PCI exposure and is also associated with worse short-term outcome. This highlights the concepts of an underlying arterial fragility as potential shared mechanism predisposing to both spontaneous and iatrogenic dissections.Figure 1
title: Catheter-Induced Coronary Artery Dissection in Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection: Incidence, Procedural Characteristics, and Outcomes

abstract: Abstract Background Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is characterized by separation of the coronary arterial wall due to intramural hematoma, with or without an intimal tear, and is angiographically classified into four types (Types 1–4, Figure 1). Although this classification is widely used for diagnosis, its prognostic implications remain unclear, particularly in Asian populations. Purpose To evaluate the association between angiographic classification and clinical outcomes in Japanese patients with SCAD. Methods This multicenter registry included 175 patients with SCAD enrolled at 15 participating centers in Japan between 2021 and 2025. Patients were classified into four groups according to angiographic morphology. Baseline characteristics and in-hospital clinical outcomes were compared among angiographic types using appropriate statistical analyses. The primary endpoint was a composite of in-hospital adverse events including heart failure, cardiogenic shock, sustained ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation, recurrence of SCAD, and death. Results Among 175 patients, 148 (84.6%) were female, and the mean age was 51.6 ± 10.0 years. Angiographic classification revealed 17 patients (9.7%) with Type 1 lesions, 73 (41.7%) with Type 2a, 35 (20.0%) with Type 2b, 12 (6.9%) with Type 3, and 39 (22.3%) with Type 4 lesions (Figure 1). A composite of in-hospital adverse events occurred in 14.3% of all patients (Figure 2): 11.7% in Type 1, 20.5% in Type 2a, 8.6% in Type 2b, 16.7% in Type 3, and 7.7% in Type 4 lesions, which differed across angiographic types. Early recurrent SCAD due to extension of the original dissection occurred in 5 patients, of whom 4 (80.0%) had Type 2a lesions. Type 2a morphology showed a numerically higher rate of in-hospital composite events compared with other angiographic types (odds ratio 2.38, p=0.07). When stratified by TIMI flow grade, 76 patients had TIMI 3 flow and 93 had TIMI &lt;3 flow (6 classified as unknown or overlapping). The in-hospital adverse events occurred in 17.1% of patients with TIMI 3 flow and 9.7% with TIMI &lt;3 flow (odds ratio 1.93, p=0.23), indicating that preserved TIMI 3 flow did not confer a lower in-hospital risk. Conclusions Type 2a angiographic morphology may be associated with a higher propensity for lesion extension and in-hospital adverse events in patients with SCAD. Unlike acute myocardial infarction, preserved TIMI 3 flow in SCAD does not necessarily indicate a favorable in-hospital clinical course.Figure1Figure2
title: Angiographic classification and clinical outcomes of spontaneous coronary artery dissection in Japanese patients: Insights from a multicenter registry

abstract: Abstract Background Pregnancy-associated spontaneous coronary artery dissection (P-SCAD) is an uncommon but severe cause of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in women and is associated with extensive myocardial injury. P-SCAD often presents with left main involvement and rapid haemodynamic deterioration. Cardiogenic shock (CS) in this setting poses a time-critical management dilemma. SCAD pathophysiology may limit the reliability of standard ACS algorithms. Evidence guiding invasive and mechanical circulatory support (MCS) strategies in P-SCAD remains limited, underscoring the need for structured evaluation. Aim To evaluate the management strategies and outcomes of CS complicating P-SCAD, with focus on revascularisation and MCS utilisation. Methods Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched, on February 17th 2026, for original articles in PubMed, Embase, Scopus, EBSCOhost, and Cochrane from January 2006 onwards, using terms: ‘Spontaneous coronary artery dissection’ (OR ‘SCAD’ OR ‘coronary artery dissection’) AND (‘pregnancy’ OR ‘postpartum’) AND (‘cardiogenic shock’ OR ‘MCS’ OR ‘IABP’ OR ‘Impella’ OR ‘ECMO’ OR ‘LVAD’ OR ‘PCI’ OR ‘CABG’ OR ‘revascularisation.’). After screening 74 studies, 47 abstracts were reviewed, and 12 included; quality was appraised with the LEGEND tool. Results The majority of identified publications were narrative reviews, with few primary reports describing CS complicating P-SCAD. Included studies comprised 1 registry cohort, 8 case-reports , and 3 abstracts (included to minimise reporting bias if extractable clinical data present). Among 8 detailed cases, 63% occurred in the early postpartum period and 37% antepartum, consistent with registry data. Presentations frequently involved proximal territories and revascularisation strategies were heterogeneous with multiple reports of dissection propagation complicating PCI. Of the MCS therapies used, IABP was used in 3 cases, Impella in 6, and VA-ECMO in 3, with frequent escalation strategies. Devices were used sequentially or in combination. Registry data reported IABP use in 9.1% but did not disaggregate shock-specific management. Support duration ranged from 5-14 days. Maternal survival was reported in all cases however morbidity was substantial - including readmission, cardiac arrest, HFrEF and progression to cardiac transplantation (37%). Conclusion Management of CS in P-SCAD is highly individualized, often requiring escalating MCS strategies. While short-term maternal survival appears favourable, morbidity is considerable. The evidence is fragmented and largely observational with inconsistent reporting of revascularisation strategy, MCS selection, support duration and complications. This underscores the absence of structured registry-level data and standardised reporting of invasive and MCS pathways and highlights the need for dedicated multicentre registry evaluation.Cardiogenic Shock in P-SCAD PRISMA
title: Cardiogenic shock in pregnancy-associated spontaneous coronary artery dissection: a systematic review of invasive and mechanical circulatory support strategies

abstract: Abstract Background In extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) cases, whole-body CT is considered effective for evaluating complications associated with resuscitation and cannulation. Conventionally, aortic ring sign (ARS) on non-contrast CT has been reported as a characteristic finding of anaemia (!). However, ARS is frequently observed in post-resuscitation CT scans. Studies comparing post-mortem and clinical imaging have shown that a hyperattenuating aortic wall was detected in 100% of post-mortem CTs compared to only 2% of scans in living patients (2). In critical care setting, such as post resuscitation, mechanisms other than anaemia may contribute to the appearance of ARS. However, the prevalence and clinical significance of ARS specifically in post-resuscitation CT remain poorly understood. Purpose To investigate the prevalence and the factors associated with ARS in cases of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) undergoing ECPR. Methods We analysed 56 OHCA patients treated with ECPR at our institute between January 2015 and February 2026. A total of 52 patients who underwent non-contrast CT post-ECPR were enrolled. Data on patient backgrounds, CT findings (including ARS), and in-hospital outcomes were collected. Results ARS was detected in 36 patients (69.2%). The median haemoglobin level was 14.0 g/dL. ARS was observed significantly more frequently in older patients (67.5 vs 50.5 years, p&lt;0.01), those with prior coronary artery disease (40.0% vs 0%, p=0.04), and those with an initial non-shockable rhythm (44.5% vs 6.2%, p=0.03). The use of the Impella device was associated with a lower incidence of ARS (5.6% vs 37.5%, p=0.01). In-hospital mortality was 86.1% in the ARS group compared to 62.5% in the non-ARS group (p=0.07). Notably, haemoglobin levels were not significantly related to the presence of ARS (13.80 g/dL vs 14.70 g/dL, p=0.274). Conclusion ARS on non-contrast CT is frequently observed in OHCA patients undergoing ECPR, even in the absence of anaemia.
title: Prevalence and factors associated with the aortic ring sign in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation

abstract: Abstract Introduction Acute chest pain is a common reason for emergency department (ED) attendance. In patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS) but non-ischaemic electrocardiogram (ECG) and non-elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn), the optimal diagnostic approach remains uncertain. European guidelines support further non-invasive testing, whereas American recommendations suggest that additional testing may be unnecessary in selected low-risk patients. Randomised evidence in the hs-cTn era is limited. Purpose To determine whether exercise testing provides clinical benefit compared with a conservative diagnostic strategy based on clinical assessment in patients with acute chest pain, non-elevated hs-cTn and non-ischaemic ECG. Methods This prospective, single-centre, exploratory randomised controlled trial (1:1 allocation) enrolled adults presenting to the ED with non-traumatic chest pain within 24 hours of symptom onset between May 2019 and December 2024. Eligible patients had a non-ischaemic ECG and negative or inconclusive serial hs-cTnI (defined as &lt;5 ng/L or a 0/3-hour delta &lt;3 ng/L, with all values below the 99th percentile). Key exclusion criteria were typical angina, known coronary artery disease, left ventricular ejection fraction &lt;40%, severe valvular disease, or an alternative confirmed diagnosis.The primary endpoint was a composite of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE): cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, unstable angina requiring hospitalisation, or coronary revascularisation, assessed at 30 days, 3 months and 6 months. Secondary endpoints included index admission, additional cardiovascular testing (index visit or follow-up), ED reattendance for chest pain, and individual MACE components. Results A total of 153 patients were included (figure 1). Baseline clinical characteristics of the two groups are described in table 1. No MACE occurred in either group during 6-month follow-up. ED reattendance was low and similar between groups (2.6% vs 4.0%, p=0.68). In the intervention arm, 39% underwent exercise echocardiography and 92.2% of tests were negative; two false positives were identified. Four patients underwent additional testing at the index visit, and two required hospitalisation for coronary angiography. Additional downstream testing during follow-up was infrequent and similar between the groups (0% vs 4%, p=0.12). All final diagnoses were non-cardiac chest pain. Conclusion In low-risk patients with acute chest pain, non-ischaemic ECG and non-elevated hs-cTn, no major cardiovascular events were observed at 6 months. Routine exercise testing did not improve outcomes compared with a conservative approach. Larger studies are required to confirm these findings.
title: Conservative management VS. exercise testing in patients with acute chest pain and non-elevated troponin: a randomized clinical trial

abstract: Abstract Background In China, STEMI mortality is markedly higher in rural than urban areas, primarily due to prolonged pre-hospital diagnostic and reperfusion delays. A tele-electrocardiography (tele-ECG) network addressed this barrier by equipping primary healthcare facilities with portable ECG devices for real-time transmission to a central platform, enabling remote cardiologist interpretation, pre-hospital triage, and pre-activation of the catheterization laboratory. Purposes To assess the real-world effectiveness of the tele-ECG network in reducing reperfusion delays and in-hospital mortality among patients with STEMI. Methods Using data from the Chinese Cardiovascular Association (CCA) Database between January 2022 and May 2025, this retrospective cohort study included adult patients with a confirmed diagnosis of STEMI. Patients with in-hospital symptom onset were excluded. The tele-ECG cohort included patients with ECG records transmitted via the network from primary hospital, community health center or village clinic, and who presented to the chest pain center within 48 hours after ECG acquisition. Patients not enrolled in the ECG network were included in the standard care cohort. Propensity score matching (1:5 ratio) was performed based on demographics, vital signs, cardiovascular risk factors, comorbidities, and hospital characteristics. The primary endpoint was in-hospital all-cause mortality. Secondary endpoints included onset-to-ECG, door-to-wire, and door-to-needle intervals. Results A total of 15,072 patients (median age 67 years; 86.5% male) were included in the analysis, comprising 2,512 in the tele-ECG cohort and 12,560 in the standard care cohort. All baseline covariates were well-balanced after matching (standardized mean differences &lt;0.1). In-hospital all-cause mortality was lower in the tele-ECG cohort than in the standard care cohort (2.4% vs. 3.5%; HR 0.62; 95% CI 0.47–0.82; P&lt;0.001). Onset-to-ECG time was shorter in the tele-ECG cohort than in the standard care cohort (median 130 vs. 160 min; P &lt;0.001). Door-to-wire time (52 vs. 66 min; P&lt;0.001) and door-to-needle time (23 vs. 28 min; P&lt;0.001) were also reduced in the tele-ECG cohort. Conclusion In this large real-world cohort, the lower in-hospital mortality observed in the patients treated in the tele-ECG network may be attributable to more timely pre-hospital diagnosis and faster in-hospital reperfusion. These findings support the implementation of such networks to enhance STEMI care in resource-limited regions.Kaplan–Meier curves for in-hospital mortalityTreatment workflow in the tele-ECG network

title: Tele-ECG network reduces reperfusion deLay and mortality in STEMI patients in rural China: a real-world study

abstract: Abstract Background Early diagnosis of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in patients presenting with chest pain and normal high-sensitivity troponin remains challenging. Prothrombotic biomarkers may provide complementary diagnostic information in this setting. Objective To evaluate the diagnostic performance of plasminogen and other coagulation biomarkers for detecting ACS in patients admitted to a ER chest pain unit with initially normal high-sensitivity troponin T. Methods We conducted a prospective observational study including consecutive patients admitted to an emergency department chest pain protocol. High-sensitivity troponin T was measured at 0 and 3 hours. At admission, plasminogen, fibrinogen, fibrinogen degradation products, factor VIIIc, von Willebrand factor, and D-dimer were assessed. The serum samples collected and stored at -70°C and subsequently analyzed using IL coagulation systems and an ACL TOP 300 instrument VM. High-sensitivity troponin T was determined using a ROCHE ELECSYS analyzer. At the time of care, the researchers were blinded to the results of the thrombosis/thrombolysis markers.Patients receiving anticoagulation or heparin before sampling were excluded. The primary endpoint was in-hospital diagnosis of non-ST-elevation ACS. Multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses were performed in all patients. For data comparison, statistics and ROC curve analysis we used a SPSS version 26 software. Results One hundred fifty six patients were included (mean age 62±12 years, 42% women); 32% were diagnosed with ACS. Using the best cut-off value (66 % activity), serum plasminogen showed a LR+ of 1.70 and a LR - of 0.53 for ACS diagnosis. In multivariable analysis, plasminogen was independently associated with ACS (OR 1.04 per each unit increase; 95% CI 1.00–1.08; p=0.040), Plasminogen showed the best diagnostic discrimination (AUC 0.74; 95% CI 0.55–0.93) compared with fibrinogen 0.59 (95% CI: 0.39–0.79) , factor VIIIc 0.49 (95% CI: 0.22–0.76), von Willebrand factor 0.52 (95% CI: 0.28–0.75) , and fibrinogen degradation products 0.46 (95% CI: 0.25–0.67), multiple paired De Long Test comparisons p &lt; 0.05. .Serum plasminogen remained independently associated with ACS diagnosis after adjustment for age, sex, and ECG changes: OR 2.6 (IC 95% 0.849-8,406), p = 0.033 . Conclusion Our preliminary data demostrated that in patients presenting with suspected acute coronary syndrome and normal high-sensitivity troponin, serum plasminogen may be a useful tool for early risk stratification."
title: Serum plasminogen improves early detection of acute coronary syndrome in high sensitivity troponin t-negative chest pain patients

abstract: Abstract Introduction The management of patients presenting to the Emergency Department (ED) with chest pain is resource intensive and time critical. Timely identification of acute coronary syndromes (ACS) is essential for improving outcomes, while safe early triage is central to effective use of healthcare resources. Conventional risk-stratification tools depend on serial troponin testing and ECGs. In practice, this leads to prolonged ED stays and diagnostic lag due to time taken for investigations due to workflow pressures. There is a gap for a tool to support clinical decision making at the point of ED contact, before definitive diagnostic information is available. Purpose We developed and validated a workflow-aware System for Machine-Assisted Recommendation of Treatment in Acute Coronary Syndrome (SMART-ACS). We designed the tool to support sequential clinical decision-making support. First to support early triage (at initial assessment before ECG and troponin), second for definitive pathway selection (prediction of revascularisation). Methods We used a retrospective registry of 23,488 consecutive patients presenting with chest pain to three EDs serving a diverse population within the UK (2021–2023) for model development. Machine Learning XGBoost models were trained for two tasks: Triage (no treatment for ACS, medical management, or invasive management) and Revascularisation. Models were configured with two input stages: a "baseline" model using variables available within 10 minutes of arrival (demographics, medical history and observations) and a "full" model incorporating subsequent ECG and laboratory data as inputs. We externally validated the models on an independent Swedish cohort (n=1,200). Results The baseline triage model (without ECG or troponin input data) achieved a micro-AUROC of 0.843 (95% CI: 0.827 - 0.860) on internal validation and maintained good discrimination on external validation AUROC 0.805 (95% CI: 0.724 - 0.880). For definitive management and support with referral for invasive management, the full-variable Revascularisation model achieved an AUROC of 0.947 (95% CI: 0.932–0.962), significantly outperforming the conventional HEART score benchmark (AUROC 0.634; 95% CI: 0.622 - 0.647). External validation on the Swedish cohort demonstrated robust generalisability of the full Revascularisation model (AUROC 0.888). Conclusion The SMART-ACS framework provides good discriminative performance while aligning with real-world clinical workflows and providing management recommendations. The framework has potential to support earlier triage and resource allocation. Prospective evaluation of the models is needed to test real world clinical utility and compare model recommendations against clinician judgement. Model outputs are aligned with clinically meaningful decisions made at different stages of ED assessment. This approach offers a practical pathway to support early clinical decision-making and timely interventionModel performance (internal validation)Revascularisation model
title: A machine learning decision-support tool for the management of patients presenting to the emergency department with chest pain

abstract: Abstract Background According to the ESC hypertension guidelines, a hypertensive emergency is defined as a blood pressure of ≥180/110 mmHg associated with acute hypertension-mediated organ damage, often in the presence of symptoms. The standard operating procedures of the National Ambulance Service in our country align with the ESC guidelines enable the daily application of international recommendations. Purpose In this pilot study, we aimed to analyse the real-life, prehospital practices of medical treatment for hypertensive patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome or acute heart failure from the digital case report database of the National Ambulance Service in our country. Methods From January 1, 2023, to June 30, 2024, we collected data on 9,250 structured digital case reports of patients treated by advanced-level ambulance units. Inclusion criteria were an ICD code indicating acute coronary syndrome or heart failure, as well as a systolic blood pressure of 180 mmHg or higher or a diastolic blood pressure of at least 110 mmHg. We analysed key demographic and clinical variables, along with relevant drug therapies. Our analysis focused on identifying the most frequently used medications and combinations, as well as trends in medication indications based on different levels of elevated blood pressure. Results The median of the first measured systolic blood pressure was 190 mmHg (IQR 181-200), the last measured systolic blood pressure was 160 mmHg (IQR 149-175), and the difference is statistically significant (Wilcoxon rank-sum test p&lt;0.001). Patients frequently received only sublingual captopril (n=1,906, 20.6%) or nitroglycerin (n=1,750, 18.9%). For cases requiring intravenous drug treatment, the nitroglycerin-furosemide-morphine combination was the most preferred (n=1,411, 15.3%). In patients with the highest initial systolic blood pressure values (mainly above 200 mmHg SBP), urapidil was typically required, and no other monotherapy was used among the patients with the highest blood pressure. Conclusions Although guidelines for managing hypertensive emergencies primarily recommend intravenous medications, our observational study revealed that non-intravenous antihypertensive agents may also be valuable during prehospital care. If the initial therapy is ineffective, timely escalation of treatment is essential. Further targeted investigations and complex statistical analyses are necessary to determine the target blood pressure, taking into account the duration of the prehospital period, and whether sublingual antihypertensive medications can effectively manage some hypertensive patients presenting to ambulance care with chest pain or heart failure until hospital admission.Violin plots: blood pressure changesTable:Medical treatment strategies
title: Prehospital medical treatment of hypertensive emergencies in patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome or heart failure – a pilot real-world observational study

abstract: Abstract Background Accurate preoperative risk stratification is crucial among patients undergoing cardiac surgeries. Conventional measures such as left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and cardiac index (CI) have limitations in reflecting complex perioperative hemodynamics. Cardiac Power Output (CPO) is an integrative marker that combines flow (cardiac output) and mean arterial pressure (MAP), reflecting the true pumping power of the heart. Its prognostic value has been demonstrated in critical cardiac illnesses, but its role in the perioperative cardiac setting remains unclear. Purpose This study aimed to assess the accuracy of preoperative cardiac power output versus cardiac index based on 2D echocardiogram in predicting in-hospital outcomes among adult cardiac surgery patients. Methods This retrospective cohort study included adult patients who underwent cardiac surgery at two tertiary centers from April 2022 to October 2025. Preoperative CPO was calculated as (mean arterial pressure x cardiac output)/451. The primary outcome was the accuracy of CPO in predicting in-hospital all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital cardiovascular mortality and need for mechanical circulatory support (MCS). Optimal cutoffs were identified using Youden’s index. Diagnostic odds ratios, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, and accuracy parameters were computed. Subgroup analyses were performed according to preoperative LVEF. Results A total of 241 patients were included (median age 62 years; 77% male). Median LVEF was 57.7%, median CI was 2.2 L/min/m², and median CPO was 0.8 W. In-hospital all-cause mortality was 5.4%, while in-hospital cardiovascular mortality was 3.3%. MCS was required in 8% of the patients. Preoperative CPO did not demonstrate superior discriminative ability over CI for all-cause mortality (AUC 0.48 vs 0.49; p=0.829), with both parameters showing low sensitivity but high specificity and negative predictive value. CPO was significantly associated with cardiovascular mortality (diagnostic OR 13.17; p=0.014) and the need for MCS (diagnostic OR 6.63; p=0.003), whereas CI was not. CPO demonstrated acceptable discrimination for predicting MCS (AUC 0.70). In subgroup analyses, CPO retained a significant association with cardiovascular mortality and MCS among patients with LVEF &lt;50%. Conclusion Preoperative cardiac power output did not outperform cardiac index in predicting in-hospital all-cause mortality. However, CPO was significantly associated with cardiovascular mortality and need for mechanical circulatory support, particularly among patients with reduced preoperative left ventricular ejection fraction. These findings support the role of CPO as a complementary hemodynamic marker that reflects cardiac reserve. It also has a potential to enhance perioperative risk stratification beyond conventional indices.ROC curves: CI vs. CPOOptimal cutoffs of CPO and CI
title: Accuracy of preoperative cardiac power output vs cardiac index in predicting in-hospital outcomes among cardiac surgery patients: a retrospective cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background The use of catheter-based micro-axial flow pump, Impella, has progressively increased, and patient prognosis has improved following cardiogenic shock (CS). Notably, Impella 5.5 enables higher flow support and longer duration of use compared with Impella CP, and facilitates patient activity because of the cannulation approaches to the axillary or subclavian artery. However, the feasibility and safety of early mobilisation in this setting have not been well established. This study aimed to investigate mobility level trajectory and its safety and clinical outcomes in patients with CS supported with Impella 5.5 using a large amount of physiotherapy session data. Methods We reviewed consecutive patients with CS who underwent early physiotherapy while supported with Impella 5.5 in the intensive care unit (ICU) of a tertiary university hospital from 2022 to 2025. Daily mobility levels were determined through multidisciplinary discussions involving physiotherapists, cardiologists, intensive care nurses, and clinical engineers. We assessed mobility levels using the ICU Mobility Scale (IMS) as a primary outcome and recorded adverse events that led to physiotherapy termination during each session. Patient status after Impella 5.5 cessation was defined as follows: successful weaning from Impella 5.5; bridging to an implantable left ventricular assist device (iLVAD); death following transition to palliative care due to failure to wean from Impella 5.5; and death after weaning from Impella 5.5. The trajectories of IMS levels and their association with patient status were examined using a linear mixed-effects model, adjusting for age, adverse events, and prior mechanical circulatory support before Impella 5.5 implantation as covariates. Results A total of 876 physiotherapy sessions among 30 patients were included for analysis, with 550 sessions (63.3%) of out-of-bed mobilisation. Overall, IMS significantly increased throughout the clinical course, after adjustment for confounders (P &lt;0.001, Figure 1). IMS trajectories were higher in patients successfully weaned from Impella 5.5 compared with bridging to iLVAD, death following transition to palliative care due to failure to wean, and death after weaning (P for interaction = 0.064, 0.002, and 0.015, respectively). Adverse events leading to termination of physiotherapy were observed in 138 sessions (15.8%), including 43 events related to Impella device alarms (4.9%), 91 due to decreased arterial pressure (&lt; 60 mmHg) (10.4%), and 10 due to increased ventricular arrhythmia (1.1%), 5 of which were non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (0.6%); however, no life-threatening adverse events occurred during physiotherapy (Figure 2). Conclusions Early mobilisation trajectories increased progressively after Impella 5.5 implantation without severe adverse events. Higher mobility trajectories were associated with more favourable clinical status in patients with CS.
title: Trajectories of early mobilisation during Impella 5.5 support and associated outcomes in patients with cardiogenic shock

abstract: Abstract Background and aim Cardiogenic shock (CS) is increasingly recognized as a dynamic syndrome frequently complicated by vasodilatory components and secondary sepsis. The transition between cardiogenic and distributive phenotypes may affect therapeutic decisions, including vasoactive escalation and mechanical circulatory support (MCS). We aimed to characterize hemodynamic phenotypes and treatment trajectories in CS compared with septic shock, with particular focus on mixed shock states in contemporary real-world practice. Methods We conducted a retrospective single-center study including adults admitted with CS or septic shock (2015–2018). Advanced hemodynamic monitoring (AHM) was performed using transpulmonary thermodilution (PiCCO). CS severity was graded according to SCAI criteria. Mixed shock was defined as CS with SVRI &lt;2400 dyn·s·m²/cm⁵ or septic shock with CI &lt;2.5 L/min/m². PiCCO-derived CI, SVRI, extravascular lung water index and global end-diastolic volume index, fluid balance, vasoactive therapy, and outcomes were analyzed; primary endpoint was in-hospital mortality. Results We analyzed 132 patients (median age 66 years, 73% male), including 75 with CS (predominantly ischemic) and 57 with septic shock. Mixed phenotypes were frequent (79% of CS and 96% of septic shock). At AHM initiation, CI was lower and SVRI higher in CS, clearly separating cardiogenic from vasodilatory profiles (Figure A), whereas mean arterial pressure and lactate were similar. CS patients received more restrictive fluids and more frequent mechanical circulatory support, while septic shock patients underwent larger early resuscitation followed by de-resuscitation (Figure B); norepinephrine was the dominant vasopressor in both entities, with vasopressin mainly used in sepsis and inotropes (dobutamine, levosimendan) in CS. Over time, non-survivors with CS showed progressive deterioration of CI and SVRI, while hemodynamics remained relatively stable in septic shock; lactate clearance was more pronounced in survivors of both groups. Neither single AHM parameters nor mixed-shock definitions discriminated survivors from non-survivors. In-hospital mortality was 45% in CS and 58% in septic shock, with earlier mortality in CS and more protracted mortality in sepsis. Conclusions Cardiogenic shock frequently evolves toward mixed cardiogenic–vasodilatory phenotypes. Although AHM refines cardiovascular phenotyping and may support escalation strategies including MCS, single hemodynamic parameters are not prognostic. These findings support a trajectory-based cardiovascular approach to CS rather than static shock categorization.Figure A and B
title: Mixed cardiogenic–vasodilatory phenotypes in cardiogenic shock: insights from real-world advanced hemodynamic monitoring

abstract: Abstract Background Restrictive transfusion thresholds (haemoglobin [Hb] 7–8 g/dL) are widely implemented across acute care settings. However, acute coronary syndromes (ACS) represent a pathophysiological state characterized by impaired myocardial oxygen delivery and heightened ischemic vulnerability. Whether allowing Hb to fall to restrictive levels is biologically neutral in ischemic myocardium remains uncertain. Contemporary ACS guidelines state that transfusion to achieve Hb ≥10 g/dL may be reasonable in selected patients (Class IIb), underscoring persistent clinical equipoise. Importantly, most prior analyses have emphasized short-term outcomes without evaluating potential divergence over longer follow-up. Purpose To evaluate the impact of liberal versus restrictive transfusion strategies on both early (1-month) and mid-term (6–12-month) outcomes in patients with ACS and anemia. Methods We performed a systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing liberal (Hb trigger approximately 10 g/dL) versus restrictive (Hb trigger 7–8 g/dL) transfusion strategies in ACS or acute myocardial infarction populations. Early endpoints included all-cause mortality, death plus myocardial infarction (MI), and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) at 1 month. Mid-term endpoints were all-cause mortality and MACE at 6–12 months. Risk ratios (RR) were pooled using Mantel–Haenszel random-effects models. Results Five randomized datasets comprising approximately 4,500 patients were included for early analyses; four contributed to mid-term follow-up. At 1 month, liberal transfusion was not associated with a statistically significant reduction in all-cause mortality (RR 0.90;95% CI 0.57–1.41; I²=47.9%), death plus MI (RR 0.90;95% CI 0.55–1.46; I²=54.6%), or MACE (RR 0.91;95% CI 0.62–1.35; I²=48.8%). However, point estimates consistently favoured liberal transfusion across all early ischemic endpoints. At 6–12 months, liberal transfusion demonstrated a sustained directional reduction in ischemic events, with all-cause mortality RR 0.92(95% CI 0.82–1.04; I²=0%) and MACE RR 0.85(95% CI 0.69–1.04; I²=0%), with complete absence of heterogeneity. Conclusions Restrictive transfusion did not demonstrate superiority over liberal transfusion for early mortality or ischemic outcomes in ACS with anemia. However, a consistent signal toward lower mid-term ischemic events was observed with liberal transfusion, without evidence of excess harm. The pattern of early neutrality followed by mid-term divergence suggests that maintaining higher haemoglobin levels during the acute ischemic phase may improve myocardial oxygen delivery and influence longer-term cardiovascular outcomes. These findings indicate that transfusion thresholds in ACS may require disease-specific consideration rather than uniform extrapolation from general critical-care practice.1-month outcomes6-12 months outcomes
title: Is restrictive transfusion too restrictive in acute coronary syndromes with anemia? A meta-analysis of early and mid-term randomized outcomes

abstract: Abstract Background Micro-axial flow pumps are increasingly employed for temporary mechanical circulatory support in patients with acute myocardial infarction-related cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS) and during high-risk percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Despite hemodynamic benefits, device-related complications, including major access-site bleeding, limb ischemia and stroke, remain frequent and contribute substantially to morbidity and mortality. Access-site characteristics, particularly vascular anatomical features, may influence complication risk during mAFP therapy. Purpose To evaluate whether angiographic and computed tomographic access-site parameters, including vessel diameter, vascular length, calcification burden, tortuosity and stenosis of the common femoral artery (CFA), as well as level of the femoral bifurcation and epigastric zone, and angulation between the common iliac artery and aorta, are associated with an increased risk of clinically relevant access-site complications, defined as major bleeding at the access site (BARC ≥3), limb ischemia at the site of the mAFP insertion or stroke. Methods In this observational study conducted at a high-volume tertiary care center, consecutive patients undergoing mAFP therapy for AMI-CS or high-risk PCI were included. Procedural radiologic imaging (angiography or computed tomography) and procedural complications were independently analyzed by two blinded investigators. Logistic regression analyses were performed to evaluate associations between radiologic parameters and the primary endpoint (composite of any aforementioned access-site complication) as well as secondary endpoints (individual complications). Results A total of 202 patients receiving mAFP therapy were included, of whom 165 (82%) were male. Median age was 66 years (IQR 57-77). No radiologic parameter was significantly associated with the composite primary endpoint of any clinically relevant procedural complications. However, increasing CFA diameter was independently associated with a lower risk of limb ischemia: Each millimeter increase in CFA diameter was associated with a 45% risk reduction in limb ischemia (odds ratio 0.55; 95% confidence interval 0.33-0.91; p = 0.02). Receiver-operating-characteristic analysis identified a CFA diameter threshold of 7 mm or above as the optimal cut-off for minimizing limb ischemia risk. Other radiologic parameters were not significantly associated with secondary endpoints (Figure). Conclusion Radiologic access-site parameters show limited predictive value for major complications at the access site during mAFP support, with the exception of CFA diameter. These findings suggest that non-anatomical factors, such as patient-related risk profiles or puncture technique and the rate of mis-punctures, may play a more decisive role and warrant further investigation to improve complication risk stratification.Figure 1
title: Radiologic predictors of access-site complications during support with micro-axial flow pump support in infarct-related cardiogenic shock and high-risk percutaneous coronary intervention

abstract: Abstract Background Postoperative high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) elevation within 72 hours is common after non-cardiac surgery and is prognostically relevant even when non-ischemic. However, impaired renal function may confound hs-cTn interpretation and potentially modify its association with mortality. Purpose To evaluate (1) the correlation between creatinine and peak postoperative hs-cTn and (2) whether renal function modifies the prognostic impact of hs-cTn on long-term all-cause mortality. Methods We studied consecutive patients admitted to a postoperative ICU after non-cardiac surgery with systematic hs-cTn measurement within 3 postoperative days. Peak hs-cTn was normalized by the assay-specific 99th percentile upper reference limit (URL), generating a troponin-to-URL ratio. Creatinine was obtained from the same calendar day as the troponin peak. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) included any stage (dialysis or non-dialysis). Correlation between creatinine and troponin-to-URL ratio was assessed with Spearman’s rho. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality (time zero: surgery date). Cox proportional hazards models tested an interaction term log(troponin-to-URL) x log(creatinine), adjusting for age, sex, SAPS3, CKD, and surgery category. Results Cox analyses included 2,376 patients (median follow-up 6.7 years, IQR ~5.0–8.3); 25.0% died (n=594). Postoperative myocardial injury (MINS) occurred in 10.2% and CKD in 4.2%. Creatinine correlated moderately with troponin-to-URL ratio (rho=0.35, p&lt;0.001). In adjusted models, each doubling of troponin-to-URL ratio was associated with higher mortality (at creatinine 0.7, HR 1.08, 95% CI 1.04–1.11). The troponin x creatinine interaction was not significant (p=0.68), indicating a broadly consistent troponin–mortality association across renal function. CKD remained independently associated with mortality (HR 1.80, 95% CI 1.32–2.44). Conclusion Although creatinine and postoperative hs-cTn are correlated, renal dysfunction did not materially modify the long-term prognostic impact of postoperative hs-cTn elevation. A troponin-to-URL approach appears robust for long-term risk stratification after non-cardiac surgery.Central Figure
title: Interaction between creatinine and postoperative high-sensitivity troponin elevation for long-term mortality risk after non-cardiac surgery: a postoperative ICU cohort

abstract: Abstract Abstract Patients with refractory cardiogenic shock (CS) supported with percutaneous mechanical circulatory support (MCS) are exposed to prolonged intensive care unit (ICU) care, invasive central venous lines and immunological dysregulation. Bloodstream infections (BSI) may worsen outcomes, yet data on BSI burden and microbiology during Impella support are limited. Purpose To quantify confirmed BSI in Impella-treated refractory CS, describe microbiology, and explore etiology-specific differences. Methods This was a retrospective single-center cohort (Germany, 2013–2021) including adults with refractory CS treated with Impella 2.5/CP. Confirmed BSI was defined as positive blood cultures with clinical correlation; isolates were categorized into Gram-positive, Gram-negative and fungal pathogens and repeated cultures were considered per patient episode. Analyses were descriptive and stratified by CS etiology (acute coronary syndrome (ACS), dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) / myocarditis, aortic stenosis, sepsis-associated CS, other), survival comparisons were exploratory given confounding by duration of support/ICU exposure (confounding by indication and by duration). Results Among 409 Impella-treated patients, confirmed BSI occurred in 23.7% (97/409). Culture positivity was highest in sepsis-associated CS (75.0% (27/36). The microbiology spectrum included frequent staphylococcal species (including skin commensals and S. aureus) and clinically relevant Gram-negative organisms (Enterobacteria and non-fermenters such as Pseudomonas), with fungal isolates less common. This pattern is compatible with a mixture of catheter/device-associated and critical-illness-associated infections. Patients with sepsis-associated CS also demonstrated the highest early mortality in the overall cohort, highlighting a high-risk phenotype in which infection and shock mechanisms overlap. Interestingly enough, the incidence of BSI under Impella support was not higher compared to the CS group of patients treated for the same period without Impella or other MCS device. Conclusion Confirmed BSI is common during Impella support in refractory CS, particularly in sepsis-associated CS. These findings support stringent infection surveillance (early blood cultures, daily line/device review), prompt source control, and structured ICU prevention bundles in MCS patients. Key limitations include retrospective ascertainment and potential under-/over-detection depending on sampling intensity. Prospective studies with standardized sampling and time-dependent modeling are needed to disentangle BSI as a driver of deterioration versus a marker of prolonged critical illness and exposure.
title: Bloodstream infections during Impella support in refractory cardiogenic shock: incidence, microbiology and clinical implications

abstract: Abstract Background Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) provides haemodynamic support in severe cardiogenic shock (CS) but may increase left ventricular afterload and worsen pulmonary congestion. ECPELLA (VA-ECMO plus a microaxial flow pump) enables concomitant circulatory support and left ventricular unloading. Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) selectively reduces pulmonary vascular resistance and may facilitate VA-ECMO weaning by decreasing right ventricular afterload. Purpose To assess whether iNO initiated at the start of VA-ECMO weaning in ECPELLA-treated severe CS is associated with higher weaning success and improved 30-day outcomes, and to explore its haemodynamic effects. Methods In this single-centre retrospective study, 175 consecutive patients with severe CS treated with ECPELLA between August 2018 and December 2025 were screened. Since iNO became available from December 2021, groups were constructed according to iNO exposure at VA-ECMO weaning. During the iNO-available period, weaning was generally initiated when pulmonary artery catheter-derived cardiac output (PAC-CO) reached ≥1.0 L/min, and iNO was started at 40 ppm at weaning initiation (final decision by the treating physician). To minimise selection bias, patients who never achieved PAC-CO ≥1.0 L/min (n=34) and, in the iNO-available period, those not receiving iNO at weaning initiation (n=9) were excluded. The final groups were iNO (n=81) and non-iNO (n=51). Primary endpoints were VA-ECMO weaning rate, VA-ECMO duration, and 30-day survival. Secondary analyses assessed changes in oxygenation and haemodynamics from immediately before iNO initiation to 24 h after initiation in the iNO group. Results Baseline characteristics, including age, sex, cause of CS, comorbidities, and extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation, were similar between groups. VA-ECMO weaning was higher in the iNO group (91% vs 71%, p=0.004), while VA-ECMO duration was comparable (9.6 [6.9–10.3] vs 7.1 [5.5–10.8] days, p=0.27). In the iNO group, the PaO2/FiO2 ratio significantly improved 24 h after initiation, whereas other haemodynamic variables showed no significant change. Thirty-day survival did not differ (48% vs 55%, p=0.79). Among patients successfully weaned from VA-ECMO, survival was lower in the iNO group (53% vs 75%, p=0.03). Furthermore, landmark analysis after VA-ECMO weaning suggested a plateau of mortality hazard after almost 14 days in the non-iNO group, while risk persisted through 30 days in the iNO group. Conclusion In ECPELLA-treated severe CS, iNO at VA-ECMO weaning was associated with higher weaning success but not improved 30-day survival. Prospective studies are warranted to define optimal patient selection for iNO in this setting.Study flowchartKaplan-Meier Curve for 30-day Mortality
title: Evaluation of the utility of inhaled nitric oxide therapy in ECPELLA management

abstract: Abstract Background and purpose Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2-I) are associated with improved cardiovascular and renal outcomes in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and heart failure (HF). Whether pre-existing SGLT2-I therapy confers a prognostic advantage in patients presenting with cardiogenic shock, despite being paused during hospital stay, remains largely unknown. This study aimed to investigate the association between pre-existing SGLT2-I therapy and outcomes in patients with cardiogenic shock. Methods In this retrospective, single-centre cohort study, consecutive patients with cardiogenic shock presenting to a tertiary care hospital between 09/2021-09/2025 were included. Patients were stratified by pre-existing SGLT2-I therapy. Two comparisons were performed: (i) SGLT2-I users versus non-users, and (ii) SGLT2-I users versus patients with a guideline-based indication for SGLT2-I due to known HF (irrespective of LVEF) and/or CKD (G3-G5) but without such therapy (“indication non-users”). The primary endpoint was in-hospital all cause death. Secondary endpoints included 30-day and 90-day all-cause mortality, need for organ support at any time during hospitalization (renal replacement therapy, mechanical circulatory support [MCS], vasoactive or inotropic therapy), and occurrence of acute kidney injury (AKI). Results The study population comprised 650 patients (median 74 years, 38% women). Shock aetiology was ischemic in 30.2%, and non-ischemic in 69.8%. In-hospital all-cause death occurred in 305 patients (46.9%). In the overall cohort comparison, pre-existing SGLT2-I use showed no significant association with endpoints. Among patients with an indication for SGLT2-I (n=347), baseline characteristics were well balanced between SGLT2-I users (n=152) and indication non-users (n=195). The primary outcome occurred in 40.8% of SGLT2-I users versus 49.7% of indication non-users. After adjustment for age, sex, renal function, and known HF or baseline LVEF, pre-existing SGLT2-I therapy was independently associated with reduced in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.22-0.89; p=0.024). Model-based g-computation derived from the adjusted model estimated an in-hospital mortality of 45.3% without SGLT2-I versus 29.0% with SGLT2-I, corresponding to an ARR of 16.3% and a NNT of 6.1 to prevent one in-hospital death. SGLT2-I users also demonstrated improved 30-day (adjusted HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.31-0.89; p=0.017) and 90-day mortality (adjusted HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.35–0.93; p=0.023). No association was observed with the need for organ support or occurrence of AKI. Subgroup analyses suggested the strongest association in patients with known HF, baseline LVEF &lt;50%, and shock due to acute HF or valvular disease. Conclusion Pre-existing SGLT2-I therapy in patients with cardiogenic shock and a guideline-based indication for SGLT2-I due to HF or CKD was associated with improved survival during hospitalization and up to 90 days.

appraisal.design_and_n: 650 patients (median 74 years, 38% women); 347 with an indication for SGLT2 inhibitors.
appraisal.main_limitation: Retrospective, subgroup-driven finding with confounding by indication likely.
appraisal.one_line: Retrospective cohort: pre-existing SGLT2 inhibitor use in cardiogenic shock, associated with lower in-hospital mortality in patients with an indication.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Among indication patients, adjusted OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.22-0.89, p=0.024 for in-hospital death; no significant association in the overall cohort.
