title: Artificial intelligence-enabled cardiac CT for population-wide type 0-bicuspid aortic valve screening: a model development and validation study

abstract: Abstract Background Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) was initially developed for elderly patients and those at high surgical risk. As population’s annual aging and indications for TAVR expand to younger and lower-risk patients, longer lifetime management has become increasingly important. Accordingly, there is a growing need for risk stratification to predict longer-term outcomes after TAVR to guide treatment strategies; however, there is no established long-term prognostic indicator following TAVR. Recent studies suggest that phenotypic age, which serves as a surrogate marker of biological aging, may better reflect vulnerability and long-term prognosis than chronological age across a range of cardiovascular diseases. Nonetheless, the prognostic value of biological age in patients undergoing TAVR remains unclear. Purpose This study aimed to evaluate the utility of phenotypic age as a novel indicator for predicting long-term prognosis in patients undergoing TAVR. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 328 patients with severe aortic stenosis who underwent TAVR between October 2015 and December 2023 at our hospital. Phenotypic age was calculated from chronological age and nine biomarkers (albumin, creatinine, glucose, CRP, WBC, MCV, lymphocyte percent, RDW, and ALP), using baseline laboratory data upon admission. PhenoAgeAccel, which was defined as the residual from a linear regression model of phenotypic age on chronological age, was also calculated. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and heart failure hospitalization. A multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression model adjusted for PhenoAgeAccel, chronological age, sex, body mass index, LogBNP, LVEF and mitral regurgitation was performed to evaluate the association between the biological age and long-term outcome after TAVR. Results The median age of the entire cohort was 84.8 years, and 63.4 % of patients were female. Mean Phenotypic age was 85.2 years and PhenoAgeAccel was 0.05. Patients was categorized into three groups based on the degree of PhenoAgeAccel: Low-PhenoAgeAccel group (PhenoAgeAccel &lt;-5.64, n=109), Intermediate-PhenoAgeAccel group (-5.64≦ PhenoAgeAccel &lt;3.47, n=110), High-PhenoAgeAccel group (3.47≦ PhenoAgeAccel, n=109). Over a median follow-up of 595 days, the primary outcome occurred in 17 (15.6%), 42 (38.2%), and 50 (45.9%) patients in the Low-, Intermediate-, and High-PhenoAgeAccel groups, respectively (log-rank p&lt; 0.001: Figure). According to the multivariable Cox regression analysis, PhenoAgeAccel was independently associated with the primary outcome (Hazard ratio 1.04, 95 % Confidence Interval 1.02-1.06; p &lt; 0.001). Conclusion Biological age, assessed via PhenoAgeAccel, was a strong predictor of long-term outcome following TAVR. Incorporating biological age into determining TAVR eligibility and preprocedural assessment provides crucial insights for lifetime management strategies.Figure
title: Long-term prognostic value of biological age in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement

abstract: Abstract Background Aortic stenosis (AS) currently lacks pharmacological treatment to mitigate disease progression and heart failure (HF) development. Adverse myocardial remodelling in AS, characterised by left-ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction, parallels that in HFpEF. Since recent trials have demonstrated that SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP1RA) have clinical benefit in HFpEF patients, we hypothesized these agents may also improve clinical outcomes in patients with AS. Objectives To investigate the association between SGLT2i and GLP1RA-use and long-term clinical outcomes in AS patients, stratified by pre- and post-aortic valve replacement (AVR) status. Methods Using a global federated research network, we identified AS patients aged &gt;18 without prior HF from 2015 to 2026. Exposure was defined as SGLT2i or GLP1RA prescription within 6 months of AS diagnosis. Patients were further stratified by AVR status: pre-AVR cohort indexed at AS diagnosis and post-AVR cohort indexed at the time of surgical/transcatheter intervention. 1:1 propensity-score matching was performed across 18 baseline characteristics, including demographics, co-morbidities and concomitant medications. Primary outcomes included all-cause mortality, HF hospitalisation, time-to-AVR (surgical/transcatheter) and composite of death or HF - assessed via Kaplan-Meier and Cox models. Results 27,576 SGLT2i-users and 22,914 GLP1RA-users were equally matched with non-users (mean age 73 years, 39% female). Before matching, SGLT2i-users (31.1+6.8 vs 28.9+6.5 kg/m2) and GLP1RA-users (34.3+7.4 vs 28.7+6.3 kg/m2) exhibited higher BMI than non-users. Similarly, there was a greater prevalence of type 2 diabetes amongst the SGLT2i-users (73.6% vs 17.6%) and GLP1RA-users (76.8% vs 18.5%) compared to non-users. In the pre-AVR cohort, both SGLT2i (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.70-0.76, p&lt;0.001) and GLP1RA use (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.76-0.84, p&lt;0.001) were associated with reduced 10-year mortality. Reflecting this, SGLT2i-use (HR 1.33, 95% CI 1.25-1.43, p&lt;0.001) and GLP1RA-use (HR 2.16, 95% CI 1.98-2.35, p&lt;0.001) were both associated with increased likelihood of undergoing AVR. In the post-AVR cohort, SGLT2i was associated with a reduced 1-year risk of the composite outcome, death or HF hospitalisation (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.72-0.95, p=0.008), and mortality alone (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.80-0.93, p&lt;0.001). Conversely, GLP1RA-use was associated with reduced 1-year mortality (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.41-0.55, p&lt;0.001) but no significant benefit for composite endpoint (HR 0.92, 95% CI 0.78-1.08, p=0.29). Conclusions In aortic stenosis patients, SGLT2i and GLP1RA use was associated with improved outcomes prior to and after aortic valve replacement. SGLT2i use was associated with reduced incidence of HF following AVR. These findings provide a strong rationale for randomised controlled trials to evaluate these agents as potential disease-modifying therapies in valvular heart disease.Pre-AVR and Post-AVR Kaplan Meier Graphs
title: Association of SGLT2-inhibitor and GLP1-receptor agonist use with clinical outcomes in aortic stenosis: a large-scale propensity-matched study

abstract: Abstract Background Aortic stenosis (AS) is a common valve disease, with surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement (AVR) being the only treatment of proven benefit. Randomised controlled trials (RCT) have shown that sodium–glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA) reduce the risk of heart failure (HF) and cardiovascular (CV) death in HF by ~20%. However, these trials excluded individuals with AS undergoing AVR. Purpose Using routinely collected linked electronic health records and the target trial emulation (TTE) framework, we aimed to estimate the treatment effects of four HF therapy groups (Renin-Angiotensin-System inhibitors (RAASi); Beta-Blockers (BB); MRA; SGLT2i) in individuals with AS following surgical or transcatheter AVR. Methods We used linked primary care, hospital admissions, national cardiac disease and death registry data in England between April 2018 and March 2025 through the ‘Data Science Centre’s Cardiovascular Disease COVID-UK/COVID-IMPACT Consortium’. TTE is an approach to mimic hypothetical RCT using observational data, aligning eligibility, treatment assignment, follow-up and analysis to reduce bias and improve causal inference. We defined exposure as at least one prescription of a drug recorded in primary care data within 90 days post-AVR. The primary outcome was HF hospitalisation or CV mortality and secondary outcomes were all-cause mortality, CV mortality and hospitalisation. Inverse probability of treatment weighting was used to adjust for baseline confounders (demographics, medical history, AVR intervention, clinical biomarkers and prior prescribed medication), to balance the characteristics of those who were and were not prescribed medications. Weighted Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to estimate risk. Results We identified 57,676 AS individuals who underwent surgical (26,846, 46.5%) or transcatheter (30,830, 53.5%) AVR followed up for a median of 3 years (IQR: 1.6, 4.9). At 90 days post-AVR, 3,863 (6.7%) individuals had been prescribed an SGLT2i, 6,268 (10.9%) an MRA, 29,159 (50.6%) an RAASi and 37,495 (65.0%) a BB. We estimated lower risk of HF hospitalisation or CV mortality events in individuals prescribed RAASi (HR: 0.93 95% CI:0.89-0.98), BB (HR: 0.86 95% CI: 0.79-0.92) and SGLT2i (HR: 0.78 95% CI: 0.68-0.90), whilst MRA were associated with increased risk (Figure 1). These findings were largely consistent across endpoints and prespecified subgroup analyses (Figure 2). Conclusion In this national TTE study of 57,676 individuals with AS who underwent surgical or transcatheter AVR, pharmacotherapy with SGLT2i, RAASi and/or BB post-AVR significantly reduced the risk of CV mortality or HF hospitalisation. Although we used methods to reduce confounding inherent in observational data, residual confounding from unmeasured factors may remain. Efficacy of these drugs post-AVR needs to be confirmed in prospective RCT.
title: Pharmacotherapy in individuals post-aortic valve replacement (TAVI or SAVR) for severe aortic stenosis: a national target trial emulation study of 57,676 individuals

abstract: Abstract Introduction The rate of aortic stenosis (AS) progression is a major determinant of myocardial damage and adverse clinical outcomes. Sustained pressure overload drives diffuse myocardial fibrosis, which can be quantified non-invasively by computed tomography (CT)-derived extracellular volume (ECV). However, data on ECV changes and AS progression rate are limited. Methods Retrospective analysis of patients undergoing cardiac CT for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) planning (April 2024–April 2025). A standardized 5-minute delayed dual-energy acquisition was used for ECV quantification. AS progression was evaluated in patients with classical high-gradient severe AS and at least two echocardiographic examinations separated by ≥6 months. AS progression was defined as the annualized change in AS maximum velocity (ΔVmax/year). Rapid progression was defined as ΔVmax &gt; 0.30 m/s/year. Results Among 248 patients with available ECV quantification, 134 fulfilled criteria for AS progression analysis. Median age was 80 years [76–84], and 45.5% were male. The median annualized AS progression rate was 0.32 m/s/year [0.15–0.63], and the median ECV was 29.9% [27.0–32.3]. AS progression rate was significantly associated with ECV (Spearman ρ = 0.33, p &lt; 0.001). In linear regression, ΔVmax/year was associated with higher ECV (β = 2.60; p = 0.001). This association remained statistically significant after adjustment for baseline Vmax (β = 2.39; p = 0.009), for final Vmax (β = 2.79; p = 0.001), and after multivariable adjustment(β = 2.52; p = 0.001). Sensitivity analyses addressing non-linearity using inverse hyperbolic sine transformation and log-shifted progression confirmed consistent associations across all models (all p &lt; 0.001). When stratified by ECV quartiles, a stepwise increase in progression was observed, with median ΔVmax/year ranging from 0.23 m/s/year in the lowest quartile to 0.54 m/s/year in the highest quartile (p = 0.001). After categorizing patients as rapid (ΔVmax ≥ 0.30 m/s/year) or slow progressors, ECV remained independently associated with rapid progression (OR 1.20 per 1% increase in ECV, 95% CI 1.07–1.34; p = 0.001). Conclusion In patients with classical high-gradient AS, higher haemodynamic progression rates were consistently associated with greater myocardial fibrosis measured by CT-derived ECV. ECV identified patients with rapid haemodynamic progression across all approaches, supporting its role as a potential integrative marker of cumulative myocardial injury and a candidate for improving surveillance and timing of intervention.QuartilesREGLINEAR
title: Extracellular volume by cardiac CT and the haemodynamic progression of aortic stenosis

abstract: Abstract Background In severe aortic stenosis (AS) treated with transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), prognosis is strongly influenced by the extent of secondary cardiac damage, but echocardiographic staging is time- and resource-intensive and not universally available. Purpose We aimed to evaluate whether an AI-enhanced 12-lead ECG could reproduce multiparametric cardiac damage staging and support risk stratification along the cardiac damage continuum.​ Methods In this single-centre retrospective cohort, 280 baseline ECGs from severe AS patients scheduled for TAVI at the coordinating center and 88 healthy controls (stage 0) collected from a validated publicly available dataset were analyzed using a deep-learning app-based ECG model, consisting of a modified 16-layer convolutional neural network (CNN) with residual connections, trained on &gt;90,000 ECGs and externally validated, designed to extract quantitative digital biomarkers. Ten clinically selected biomarkers derived from this system were subsequently used as input features to train Random Forest models to predict echocardiographic secondary cardiac damage stages as binary (0 vs 1–4), three-class (0 vs 1–2 vs 3–4), and exploratory five-class (0–4) outcomes; a separate Random Forest model was developed to estimate the risk of post-TAVI permanent pacemaker implantation from baseline AI-ECG features. Performance was assessed by AUC with 95% confidence intervals, and explainability was evaluated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis. Results The binary model achieved an AUC of 0.99 (95% CI 0.99–1.00) for discriminating any cardiac damage (1–4) from stage 0. Three-class discrimination between no (0), early-to-intermediate (1–2), and advanced (3–4) damage yielded an AUC of 0.86 (95% CI 0.85–0.88), with SHAP analysis for stages 3–4 highlighting the AI-ECG biomarkers for atrial fibrillation probability and pulmonary oedema as the dominant drivers of advanced-stage assignment. In the exploratory five-class weighted model, AUC was 0.80 (95% CI 0.78–0.82), and the SHAP profile for stage 4 identified left- and right-ventricular dysfunction biomarkers as the principal contributors, consistent with the pathophysiology of end-stage biventricular damage. The dedicated pacemaker model achieved an AUC of 0.68 (95% CI 0.64–0.72). Conclusions An AI-enhanced ECG pipeline applied to a single baseline 12-lead ECG accurately reproduced echocardiographic secondary cardiac damage staging, with strong three-tier stratification that isolates high-risk stages 3–4 and biologically coherent SHAP profiles for advanced damage. These findings support AI-ECG staging as a scalable, low-cost surrogate for multiparametric imaging-based assessment of extravalvular damage in the TAVI work-up and warrant prospective multicentre validation.
title: Ai-enabled baseline ECG for staging secondary cardiac damage in severe aortic stenosis undergoing TAVIi: a retrospective study

abstract: Abstract Background Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) is a fat depot between the epicardial surface of the myocardium and the visceral pericardium and it has been proposed to play a crucial role in cardiac inflammation. Accumulating evidence links EAT to the development of various cardiovascular diseases, including coronary artery disease and atrial fibrillation. Aortic stenosis is one of the cardiovascular diseases that has gained increased attention in recent years due to the widespread adoption of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR); however, long-term mortality after TAVR remains substantial, highlighting the need for additional imaging biomarkers for risk stratification. Prior studies have demonstrated an association between EAT volume and prognosis after TAVR, whereas CT-derived EAT attenuation may provide complementary information by reflecting tissue composition and inflammatory activity. Nevertheless, evidence regarding the association between EAT attenuation and clinical outcomes after TAVR is limited, and its relationship with long-term prognosis remains unclear. Purpose We aimed to clarify the association between EAT attenuation and long-term clinical outcome in patients with severe aortic stenosis who underwent TAVR. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 496 patients who underwent TAVR at our hospital between October 2015 and June 2025. We excluded patients with unavailable CT data and those whose CT images were of insufficient quality for analysis. Finally, 415 cases were included. For analysis of EAT, we used REVORAS. Pre-TAVR CT images were reconstructed using REVORAS and EAT attenuation values were extracted. EAT was segmented from the level of pulmonary trunk bifurcation to the diaphragm, using a predefined attenuation threshold of -190 to -30 Hounsfield Units (HU). We utilized the dilated phase data of each pre-TAVR CT image. The primary outcomes were a composite of all-cause death, cardiovascular death, and heart failure hospitalization, and the secondary outcome was all-cause death. Results The mean age of entire cohort was 83.8±6.0 years and 258 patients (62.2%) were female. Balloon-expandable valves were implanted in 271 patients (65.3%). The mean follow-up duration was 882±650 days. The mean EAT attenuation was -74.6±6.7 HU, with a median of -75.0 HU. Based on a median value of EAT attenuation, patients were classified into two groups: High-attenuation EAT group (≥-75.0 HU) and Low-attenuation EAT group (&lt;-75.0 HU). Kaplan-Meier analysis revealed that primary and secondary outcomes were significantly higher in the High-attenuation group (both log-rank p &lt;0.01) (Figure). Conclusions In this single-center TAVR cohort, higher pre-procedural CT-derived EAT attenuation was associated with significantly worse long-term outcomes. These findings suggest that EAT attenuation may serve as a simple imaging biomarker for post-TAVR risk stratification and long-term prognostication.Kaplan-Meier Curve
title: Association between epicardial adipose tissue attenuation and long-term clinical outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve replacement

abstract: Abstract Background Diffuse coronary artery disease (CAD) is characterized by gradual, long-segment pressure loss, which may not be fully captured by anatomy-based stenosis severity alone. Computed tomography-derived fractional flow reserve (CT-FFR) provides noninvasive physiological assessment, but its performance in diffuse disease and its relationship with treatment strategy and outcomes remain incompletely defined. Purpose To evaluate the agreement and diagnostic performance of machine learning (ML)-based CT-FFR versus invasive pressure wire-based FFR in diffuse versus non-diffuse CAD, and to explore its associations with revascularization decisions and prognosis. Methods This multicenter retrospective study included consecutive patients from 3 hospitals in China. CCTA DICOM datasets and invasive FFR data acquired within 30 days were retrospectively collected. ML-based CT-FFR was centrally computed by offline post-processing in the Keya Medical core laboratory. Diffuse disease was defined as lesion length ≥20 mm (patient-level diffuse: ≥1 diffuse vessel). Vessel-level and patient-level analyses used invasive FFR ≤0.80 as the reference standard. Treatment-decision matching (0.80 threshold) was assessed against actual management, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) were analyzed using Kaplan–Meier and multivariable Cox models. Results Among 328 patients, 136 (41.5%) had diffuse CAD; 374 vessels were included for vessel-level analysis. CT-FFR showed strong correlation with invasive FFR at both vessel and patient levels (vessel: Spearman ρ=0.834, n=374, p&lt;0.001; patient: Spearman ρ=0.828, n=328, p&lt;0.001), with stronger correlations in diffuse than non-diffuse disease. Diagnostic discrimination was excellent overall (AUC 0.941 at both vessel and patient levels) and remained robust in diffuse CAD (patient-level AUC 0.971). Concordance between physiology-guided recommendations and actual revascularization was similar across diffuse and non-diffuse strata, with discordance predominantly driven by nonconcordant revascularization rather than nonconcordant deferral. In 208 patients with follow-up (48 MACE), Kaplan–Meier curves stratified by CT-FFR threshold did not separate significantly, and CT-FFR was not independently associated with MACE in adjusted Cox analysis (HR 1.33 per 0.10-unit change, 95% CI 0.90–1.94; p=0.15), likely reflecting attenuation of baseline physiological risk gradients by downstream revascularization. Conclusions ML-based CT-FFR closely agrees with invasive FFR and maintains strong diagnostic performance in both diffuse and non-diffuse CAD, with particularly favorable performance in diffuse disease. These findings support CT-FFR as a practical noninvasive physiological tool to inform revascularization planning, especially when anatomy alone may underestimate ischemic burden in diffuse lesions.Correlation analysis and AUC curve
title: Machine learning CT-FFR for physiologic decision-making in diffuse coronary artery disease

abstract: Abstract Background Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) predisposes to earlier aortic stenosis due to structural abnormalities. Although outcomes in BAV are often attributed to younger age, emerging evidence suggests prognostic differences beyond age alone. The mechanisms underlying differences between BAV and tricuspid aortic valve (TAV) remain unclear. As treatment options expand and life expectancy increases, clarifying these differences is important for optimal management. Purpose To determine whether BAV and TAV differ in clinical outcomes beyond age and whether such differences reflect distinct disease pathogenesis. Methods We retrospectively analysed 1349 consecutive patients undergoing isolated surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement for aortic stenosis at two cardiovascular centres. Patients aged 60–89 years were included; those without preoperative cardiac computed tomography were excluded. The final cohort comprised 988 patients (108 BAV, 880 TAV). Primary endpoints were all-cause mortality and major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE: death, heart failure, cerebrovascular events, reoperation, and endocarditis). Median follow-up was 37.1 months (22.9–51.9). Baseline characteristics were compared unadjusted. Postoperative variables were analysed using analysis of covariance, and clinical outcomes using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, sex, body surface area, aortic stenosis severity, and procedures. Results BAV patients were younger (74.8±8.2 vs 81.9±5.4 years) and more often in male (55.6% vs 33.9%). Hypertension, peripheral artery disease, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease were less prevalent in BAV. Echocardiography showed smaller left atrial diameter and less moderate-or-greater mitral and tricuspid regurgitation. Arterial characteristics differed between groups: pulse wave velocity was lower in BAV (1337 [1165–1535] vs 1588 [1401–1837] cm/s). Computed tomography demonstrated higher aortic valve calcification volume in BAV [766(498 – 1302) vs. 448(270 – 703) mm3), whereas mitral annular calcification (0(0 – 0) vs. 34(0 – 296) mm3) was lower compared with TAV. And then in BAV, systemic aortic calcification volumes (977(258 – 2497) vs. 3469(1725 – 6288) mm3) were lower compared with TAV. At 1 year, echocardiographic differences were no longer significant after adjustment. Unadjusted analyses showed lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.28–0.75) and MACCE (HR 0.36, 95% CI 0.24–0.56) in BAV. After adjustment, mortality differences were attenuated (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.44–1.25), while MACCE remained significantly lower (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.31–0.81). Conclusion After comprehensive adjustment, BAV remained associated with an approximately 50% lower risk of MACCE. Patients with bicuspid aortic valve demonstrated a greater propensity for intrinsic valvular calcification, yet tended to have less advanced systemic atherosclerosis than those with tricuspid aortic valve.BAV vs TAV Survival and MACCEBAV vs TAV CT imaging comparison
title: Bicuspid versus tricuspid aortic stenosis: differences in etiology and clinical outcomes

abstract: Abstract Background Multivalvular heart disease (MVHD) is highly prevalent among patients undergoing transcatheter valve interventions and is consistently associated with impaired clinical outcomes. However, comprehensive data on the prognostic implication in this complex population remain limited. The aim of this study was to assess outcomes of patients with MVHD undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) according to concomitant valvular heart disease. Methods The Multi-valve Intervention Registry and Analysis (MIRA) is an investigator-initiated, retrospective, international, multicentre registry of consecutive patients with MVHD undergoing transcatheter valve interventions at eight centres in Germany, France, and the United States (2008–2024). MVHD was defined as ≥1 severe valvular lesion treated by first transcatheter intervention (aortic, mitral, or tricuspid) and ≥1 additional lesion of at least moderate severity. This analysis included patients undergoing TAVI for severe aortic stenosis (AS) with concomitant mitral regurgitation (MR) ≥2+ (ASMR), tricuspid regurgitation (TR) ≥2+ (ASTR), or both (ASMR+TR). Baseline characteristics, changes in MR and TR after TAVI, and 5-year outcomes were assessed. The primary endpoint was 5-year all-cause mortality. Results A total of 10,075 patients with MVHD undergoing transcatheter valve interventions were included in the MIRA study. Among these, 6,805 patients with severe AS undergoing TAVI were identified (ASMR: n=2,032; ASTR: n=967; ASMR+TR: n=3,806; Figure 1). Baseline characteristics showed significant differences between the groups. In general, patients in the ASMR+TR group had higher estimated surgical risk, were more symptomatic, higher rates of AF, and higher sPAP compared to the other groups. Patients in the ASTR group showed the highest rates of chronic lung disease, prior myocardial infarction, and prior pacemaker. Following TAVI, MR improved from ≥2+ to ≤1+ in 21.9% of patients with ASMR and 17.4% of patients with ASMR+TR. Improvement of concomitant TR from ≥2+ to ≤1+ occurred in 31.7% of patients with ASTR, and in 24.2% of patients with ASMR+TR. Kaplan-Meier analyses (Figure 2) demonstrated significantly higher 5-year all-cause mortality in patients with ASMR+TR (66% vs. 59% in the ASMR, and 60% in the ASTR group, p&lt;0.001). Five-year mortality was not different between the groups of ASMR and ASTR (p=0.9). Conclusions This analysis of patients with MVHD undergoing TAVI highlights the impact of concomitant valvular lesions on outcomes after TAVI. The highest event rates were observed in patients with AS and combined MR and TR, in whom MR and TR improved less after TAVI, suggesting advanced myocardial damage and limited reversibility. In contrast, isolated MR or TR had a similar impact on 5-year outcomes. These findings support tailored management and careful preprocedural risk stratification in patients with MVHD.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Multivalvular heart disease and outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve implantation: updated results from the MIRA study

abstract: Abstract Background Over the past decades transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become an inevitable part of standard care of patients with severe aortic stenosis. With ageing population and expansion of TAVI applicability, waiting duration becomes of particular importance, as the natural course of the disease carries a poor prognosis without a timely definitive intervention. Purpose To assess how TAVI waiting times changed between 2009 and 2024 in a tertiary centre during a period of evolving practice. Methods A retrospective analysis of TAVI patient medical records during 2009 – 2024 was performed. Inclusion criteria were: i) confirmed diagnosis of severe aortic valve stenosis; ii) clear data points for the outcome variables. Primary outcome variable was total waiting time, starting with the date of the visit when indication for valve replacement was documented. Secondary outcomes were evaluation waiting time (from indication to the last pre-TAVI evaluation test) and procedural waiting time (from the last test to TAVI). Most recent cases during 2021 – 2024 were included in inferential analyses, for which only non-parametric tests were appropriate. Results Out of 866 TAVIs performed in the centre, 806 cases made up the final sample, of which 64.89 % were female and 85.36 % were 75 years or older. The total waiting time was a median of 237.5 (121.25; 501.75) days in 2009 – 2020 and a median of 173 (93; 310) days in 2021 – 2024. In 2021 – 2024, total waiting time differed significantly (p = 0.045), particularly between 2022 (153 days) and 2024 (238 days) (p = 0.046). Since 2021, procedural waiting time surpassed evaluation waiting time, at 70 and 66 days, respectively, and continued to increase (Figure 1), rising to 148 days in 2024 (p &lt; 0.001). On the contrary, evaluation waiting time declined (p = 0.037) from 66 days in 2021 to 41 days in 2022. In 2024, the rates of chronic kidney disease (49.6 %, n = 62, p = 0.034), dyslipidemia (96 %, n = 120, p = 0.002) and peripheral arterial disease (22.4 %, n = 18, p = 0.018) were significantly higher, compared to earlier years. Proportion of NYHA III class patients in 2024 increased as well (77.6 %, n = 97, p = 0.002). No significant differences in the prevalence of left ventricular ejection fraction groups, atrial fibrillation, diabetes and other comorbidities, sex, age, place of residence were observed during 2021-2024. Conclusions Despite the increase in cumulative TAVI volume and established pathways, waiting times remain excessive for many patients and in recent years showed an increasing trend, driven by prolonged procedural waiting. Chronic kidney disease, dyslipidemia, NYHA III class, peripheral artery disease were more common in those who underwent TAVI in 2024. It remains ambiguous if higher comorbidity prevalence could be causally linked to longer waiting.Fig 1.Waiting times and cumulative volume.
title: Temporal trends of TAVI waiting times in a tertiary centre: from initial implementation to contemporary practice

abstract: Abstract Background Surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) remains a standard therapy for severe aortic valve disease. Prosthesis–patient mismatch (PPM) occurs when the effective orifice area (EOA) of an implanted aortic valve is too small in relation to the patient’s body surface area. While PPM is known to impair outcomes, the prognostic impact of valve size in patients without PPM remains unclear. Purpose The aim of the current study is to investigate the association between prosthetic valve size and long-term mortality after primary isolated SAVR across ages and valve types in patients without PPM. Methods A nationwide retrospective cohort analysis was performed using the Netherlands Heart Registration aortic valve supplement (2007–2018). Adult patients undergoing primary isolated SAVR were included. Patients with prior surgery, concomitant procedures, endocarditis, or missing prosthesis data were excluded. Analyses were restricted to patients without any degree of PPM, as defined by the VARC-3 criteria. EOA reference values were derived from echocardiographic guidelines (1,2). Cox models were constructed to assess the association of prosthesis size and EOA, indexed EOA (iEOA) and absolute valve size with long-term mortality, adjusted for relevant available baseline characteristics (age, sex, BSA, LVEF, creatine, diabetes, chronic lung disease, neurological dysfunction, recent myocardial infarction, previous PCI, critical preoperative state, non-cardiac vasculopathy, prosthesis type, surgery year). To assess a potential non-linear relationship between prosthesis size and mortality, natural spline functions were used. Results Of 17140 SAVR patients operated in the Netherlands between 2007-2018, 7148 were free of PPM and met inclusion criteria (6084 bioprostheses; 1064 mechanical). Median follow-up was 7.3 years with 98.2% follow-up completeness; 1367 deaths occurred. Smaller prostheses (19–21mm) were independently associated with higher mortality versus larger sizes (Figure 1) in patients under the age of 74 (Figure 2), despite absence of PPM. In figure 2 values below 1 indicate a reduced mortality hazard of a size 27 (median EOA=2.1) valve compared to a 23 valve (median EOA=1.8). Increasing EOA was associated with lower mortality: an EOA of 2.5cm² was associated with a 23% lower adjusted hazard of death versus the cohort median of 1.8 cm². Conclusions In patients without PPM, under the age of 74 at time of primary isolated SAVR, smaller prosthesis size, EOA and iEOA are independently associated with increased mortality rates after SAVR, questioning whether current PPM definitions should be redefined. Surgical planning should prioritize maximizing prosthesis size, including consideration of annular or root enlargement, to optimize long-term outcomes and prospective valve-in-valve options. Future trials comparing SAVR with transcatheter options should be aware of this association in their inclusion process and analyses.Adjusted spline effect: EOA, iEOA, valve sizeAdjusted age-specific spline effect of EOA
title: Valve size matters: association of prosthesis size with mortality in patients without prosthesis-patient mismatch after surgical aortic valve replacement in a nationwide cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Aortic valve stenosis (AVS) is the most common valvular heart disease, characterized by a chronic inflammatory state and osteogenic differentiation of valvular interstitial cells (VIC). The cytokine IL-18 plays an important role in various inflammatory diseases, but its role in AVS is not yet clear. Methods The UK Biobank database was used to analyze the association between plasma IL-18 levels and the risks of AVS . Case-control analyses revealed elevated IL-18 expression in patients with AVS. Additionally, using single-cell RNA sequencing, we identified the cellular sources of IL-18 and the phenotypic states of VIC. Cellular and animal models were further employed to investigate the functional role and underlying mechanisms of IL-18 in AVS. Results Data from the UK Biobank revealed that elevated baseline plasma IL-18 levels were significantly associated with an increased risk of aortic valve calcification events and subsequent aortic valve replacement surgery. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards analysis demonstrated that this association remained independent after adjustment for traditional cardiovascular risk factors. ScRNA-seq of human aortic valve tissue identified macrophages as the primary source of IL-18, and the expression level of IL18 in macrophages from AVS was higher than that in macrophages from the control group.In vitro, stimulation of primary VIC with recombinant IL-18 protein directly promoted calcification in a dose-dependent manner. In DWI model mice and AopE-/- model mice, recombinant IL-18 was shown to exacerbate aortic valve flow velocity, increase leaflet thickness, and promote fibro-calcific remodeling. Furthermore, a macrophage-VIC co-culture system confirmed that macrophage-derived IL-18 is a key factor in VIC fibro-calcific remodeling. Conclusion These findings suggest that macrophage-derived IL-18 promotes AVS progression by directly inducing osteogenic differentiation of valvular interstitial cells, highlighting IL-18 as a potential therapeutic target for this disease.graphical abstract
title: Macrophage-derived IL-18 aggravates fibrocalcific remodeling of valvular interstitial cells

abstract: Abstract Background Heart failure is highly prevalent and a leading cause of hospitalisations and mortality in patients with aortic stenosis. Current clinical focus in aortic stenosis is largely limited to valvular factors. Risk factors and mechanisms associated with heart failure in aortic stenosis are incompletely understood. Objective To identify risk factors for heart failure in patients with aortic stenosis. Methods Patients with aortic stenosis were identified in the UK Biobank using ICD10 (I35.0, I35.2), ICD9 (4241) and OPCS4 (K26.1, K26.2, K26.3, K26.4) codes, excluding rheumatic disease (I06) and aortic insufficiency (I35.1). Heart failure was identified using ICD10 codes (I50, I11.0, I11.3, I13.2, Z94.1, T86.2). Patients with heart failure prior to aortic stenosis were excluded. Relevant diagnoses at aortic stenosis diagnosis and lab values at recruitment were obtained. An XGBoost Cox proportional hazards model was developed to predict heart failure development, with discrimination assessed by C-index and time-dependent AUROC at 2 and 5 years. SHAP values were used to assess feature importance. Patients were stratified into tertiles for risk based on the predicted risk scores and heart failure-free survival was compared between risk tertiles using Kaplan-Meier curves. Results A total of 6385 patients (median age: 72 [66;76], 37.1% female) with aortic stenosis were included, of which 1693 (26.5%) developed heart failure over a median follow-up of 3.93 years after aortic stenosis diagnosis. Patients who developed heart failure were more often male (p=0.003), obese (p&lt;0.001), smokers (p&lt;0.001), more commonly had atrial fibrillation (p&lt;0.001), hyperlipidaemia (p&lt;0.001), diabetes (p&lt;0.001), chronic kidney disease (p=0.004), COPD (p&lt;0.001), coronary artery disease (p&lt;0.001), and more often underwent aortic valve replacement (52.4% vs. 43.1%; p&lt;0.001). Of the patients who underwent valve replacement, 12.4% had already developed heart failure at the time of replacement and 18.1% developed heart failure after the procedure. The top predictors of heart failure development based on the machine learning model were age, markers of renal function, markers of obesity, atrial fibrillation, C-reactive protein, coronary artery disease, and type 2 diabetes (Figure 1). This model demonstrated good discrimination with a C-index of 0.81 and AUROCs of 0.839 and 0.899 at two and five years. Stratification into risk tertiles showed significantly divergent heart failure-free survival across groups (p&lt;0.001) (Figure 2). Conclusions Renal, metabolic, and inflammatory risk factors strongly predict heart failure development in aortic stenosis. Better risk factor identification and management beyond valvular features may lead to improved risk stratification and personalized treatment.Figure 1 - SHAP PlotFigure 2 - Risk-Stratified KM Curves
title: Cardio-renal-metabolic risk profile strongly predicts heart failure in patients with aortic stenosis

abstract: Abstract Background In severe aortic stenosis (AS), timely assessment for intervention is essential, while patients with advanced frailty, dementia, or limited life expectancy may benefit from conservative management and advance care planning (ACP). Although guideline-directed frailty assessment is recommended, implementation is inconsistent. At our centre, a consultant geriatrician supports the valve multidisciplinary team by assessing frailty and guiding treatment decisions. Purpose To develop and pilot an automated referral pathway for severe AS (“Red Alert Pathway”) and evaluate its impact on time to comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) and ACP compared with a traditional referral pathway. Methods We identified patients with severe AS who underwent CGA and ACP via the traditional pathway and analysed pathway timelines. The Red Alert Pathway was implemented using existing IT systems, automatically flagging patients aged ≥70 years with a peak aortic valve velocity ≥4.0 m/s at the time of diagnostic echocardiography, for consultant review. Suitable patients underwent telephone screening assessing symptoms, frailty, cognition, suitability for intervention, Katz score, and Clinical Frailty Scale. Patients were then triaged to surveillance, further investigation, or CGA. Reasons for not undergoing screening included inpatient echocardiography, inability to contact the patient, or patients already known to the valve pathway. Time intervals from diagnostic echocardiography to referral, screening, and CGA were analysed. Results From January 2025 to January 2026, 24 patients (M:14, F:10; median age 84.5) underwent CGA and ACP via the traditional pathway. Median time from diagnostic echocardiography to CGA was 375 days. Between October 2025 and February 2026, the automated pathway identified 116 patients (M:65, F:51, median age 81). Of these, 54 underwent telephone screening: 41 proceeded to further investigations and 7 to surveillance. 6 patients (M3, F3, median age 84.5) were referred for CGA, with 5 having to ACP and DNAR discussions and 1 undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (Figure1). Under the automated pathway, all 116 patients were referred within 1 day of diagnostic echocardiography, with consultant review within 1 day of referral. Telephone screening occurred a median of 2 days later, with a median of 6 days from echocardiography to screening. CGA occurred a median of 8.5 days after screening, giving a median of 22 days from diagnostic echocardiography to CGA (Figure 2). Conclusion An automated referral pathway enabled rapid identification and review of frail patients with severe AS, reducing time to CGA and ACP from a median of 375 days to 22 days. This pilot service redesign supports more timely, personalised, and guideline-aligned care for these patients, utilising specialist geriatric expertise efficiently. It may represent a scalable model for frailty-focused valve care.
title: Red alert – stop the clock: impact of an automated referral system for severe aortic stenosis on time to comprehensive geriatric assessment and advanced care planning

abstract: Abstract Introduction Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become standard of treatment for severe aortic stenosis patients with high or intermediate risk. Limited and controversial data are available on the impact of having a small aortic valve annulus (SAA) on left ventricular (LV) remodeling and clinical outcomes after TAVI. Purpose To evaluate the changes in LV remodeling and function after TAVI in patients with and without SAA and to compare their mortality after intervention. Methods Patients who underwent TAVI between September 2011 and December 2021 and had available CT-derived aortic valve annular area data, as well as both baseline and follow-up echocardiographic assessments, were included and divided into:SAA Group: AV annular area ≤430 mm²;No-SAA group: AV annular area &gt;430 mm². Baseline echocardiography was performed at a median of 1 day (range 1–73 days) before the TAVI procedure, while follow-up echocardiography was conducted at a median of 192 days (range 185–206 days) after the intervention. All-cause mortality was assessed during long-term follow-up. Results A total of 500 patients (46 % women; median age 81 years) were included, of whom 168 had SAA (34%). Patients with SAA were predominantly female (80%) and had lower prevalence of coronary artery disease and atrial fibrillation (Table). Balloon-expandable valves were less frequently used in the SAA group. At baseline, no difference in LV remodeling patterns were observed between the groups (p = 0.497). However, higher baseline LV ejection fraction (LVEF) (p=0.012) and global longitudinal strain (LVGLS) (p=0.031) were observed in the SAA group, along slightly smaller LV mass and volumes. At post-TAVI follow-up, residual mean AV pressure gradient was slightly higher in the SAA group (p=0.004), while stroke volume index was similar in both groups. Regardless of annular size, LVEF and LVGLS significantly improved, as also LV mass and end-systolic volume (p&lt;0.05). The group-by-time interaction was not statistically significant for LVEF (p = 0.092), LVGLS (p = 0.076), LV mass index (p = 0.906) or end-systolic volume index (p = 0.703), suggesting similar patterns of left ventricular reverse remodeling across the groups. During a median follow-up of 74 months, 200 patients (40%) experienced all-cause death. Long-term mortality was similar between the SAA and No-SAA groups (39% vs. 40%). Kaplan–Meier curve analyses showed no significant difference in all-cause mortality between groups (log-rank P=0.727, Figure). Conclusion Significant LV reverse remodeling and systolic functional improvement occur after TAVI regardless of aortic valve annular size. Comparable long-term survival was observed between SAA and No-SAA patients supporting the safety and effectiveness of TAVI in patients with SAA.
title: Left ventricular remodeling and outcome after transcatheter aortic valve implantation in patients with small aortic annulus

abstract: Abstract Introduction Randomized trials demonstrated that prognosis of asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS) is worse with conservative management compared to early intervention. Among those who are put on conservative management risk stratification is particularly important. Thus, we used data from the AVATAR trial to explore which parameter best predicts worse outcome in asymptomatic patients with severe AS and a normal left ventricular ejection fraction within the group of patients randomized to conservative management. Method AVATAR trial randomized total of 157 patients (79 to conservative management) with asymptomatic severe AS and normal LV systolic function to early surgical AVR or conservative management. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: the composite of death, acute myocardial infarction, stroke, or unplanned HF hospitalization). Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess predictors of MACE. Statistical significance was defined as p ˂ 0.05. Results The average age was 67 years, 57% were men, and the median Society for Thoracic Surgeons predicted risk of mortality score was 1.7%. Overall median follow-up in survivors was 68 months (IQR 58–79). During the follow up, 36/79 (44%) patients in conservative group underwent aortic valve replacement (AVR) due to AS-related indications. There was a total of 55 MACEs, 37/79 (46.8%) of them in the conservative treatment group. According to the univariate cox regression analysis brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) was found to be the only independent MACE predictor in patients randomized to conservative management.; Figure 1 The BNP value of 94 pg/ml was identified as the best (cut-off) predictive value for the occurrence of MACE, with a sensitivity 77.8% and a specificity 72.0% (AUC 0.784, p=0.001; Figure 2). Conclusion BNP is the best independent outcome predictor in asymptomatic patients with severe AS and a normal LVEF. Risk stratification with this parameter may help in optimal selection of asymptomatic patients considered to be at higher risk and who would additionally benefit from early AVRFigure 2Figure 1
title: Clinical outcome predictors in asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis and normal left ventricular systolic function initially managed conservatively: a subanalysis from the AVATAR trial

abstract: Abstract Background CCTA is increasingly used as a first-line test for suspected stable coronary artery disease, but anatomically “intermediate” findings often trigger invasive coronary angiography (ICA) despite uncertain haemodynamic relevance. In practice, the value of CT-FFR is to reduce nonactionable ICAs, improving system efficiency and minimising invasive diagnostics. However, real-world CCTA/CT-FFR implementation is frequently non-standardised (variable downstream decision ownership across radiology/cardiology), which may dilute clinical impact. Purpose To test the hypothesis that achieving the intended benefit of CT-FFR requires a structured pathway with competency-based clinical qualification, and to report interim results of a pragmatic implementation model supporting national reimbursement planning. Methods Prospective, pragmatic observational implementation at the National Institute of Cardiology. Consecutive patients were pre-screened; inclusion required: (1) eligibility by clinical criteria, (2) diagnostic-quality CCTA (minimum “good” quality; Likert ≥2), and (3) 50-90% stenosis in a potentially revascularisable coronary artery. Importantly, final qualification (conservative management vs ICA with intent to revascularise) was performed within a predefined algorithm by a cardiologist with the competence to qualify for PCI/CABG, integrating symptoms, CCTA anatomy and CT-FFR. Interim analysis: 01 Aug 2025–31 Dec 2025. Key outcomes: (i) proportion of ICA without revascularisation (primary), (ii) single-day discharge PCI rate, (iii) early safety in conservatively managed patients, and (iv) payer-perspective budget impact (NFZ tariffs). Results &gt;1000 patients were pre-screened; 229 met eligibility criteria and 174 underwent CT-FFR. Based on the structured algorithm, 88/174 (51%) were directed to an invasive strategy. At the time of interim analysis, 46/88 had undergone ICA (intent to treat): 29/46 proceeded to ad hoc PCI, and 16/29 (51%) of ad hoc PCI were performed with single-day discharge. ICA without revascularisation occurred in 11/46 (24%), representing a marked reduction versus the historically reported ~50% rate in the prevailing CCTA→ICA model in Poland. No unplanned revascularisations were observed among patients assigned to conservative management during early follow-up. A tariff-based model estimated a direct NFZ cost reduction of ≈3,465–3,695 PLN saved per patient. Conclusion In interim results, a structured, cardiologist-led CCTA+CT-FFR pathway—with explicit entry criteria (patient eligibility + diagnostic CCTA + revascularisable vessel with ≥50% stenosis) and ownership of downstream qualification—delivered the intended system-level benefit of CT-FFR, namely fewer non-therapeutic ICA procedures, with high feasibility, frequent single-day discharge PCI, and no early safety signal in conservatively managed patients. The full multicentre dataset and complete analysis will be presented at ESC Congress 2026.
title: Early clinical and economic impact of integrating FFR-CT into a coronary computed tomography angiography pathway: interim results from a pragmatic Polish implementation programme

abstract: Abstract Background Aortic stenosis (AS) is characterised by progressive fibrocalcific leaflet thickening. While computed tomography (CT) calcium scoring is an established discriminator of haemodynamic severity and outcomes, the independent haemodynamic and prognostic relevance of non-calcific leaflet thickening remains uncertain. Purpose To quantify the contribution of non-calcific leaflet thickening across the haemodynamic spectrum of AS and evaluate its diagnostic and prognostic significance relative to calcific burden. Methods In 1,505 patients undergoing contrast-enhanced cardiac CT, the aortic valve was segmented into calcific and non-calcific components using semi-automated software (AutoPlaque; Cedars-Sinai, Los Angeles, USA). Component volumes were indexed to annulus area and compared across concordant severe, concordant non-severe, and discordant AS defined by echocardiography. Associations with haemodynamic severity were assessed using correlation and receiver-operating characteristic analyses. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause death or aortic valve replacement evaluated using multivariable Cox regression. Results Non-calcific tissue constituted the major structural component of all haemodynamic strata. Indexed non-calcific volume increased modestly across severity strata (221.8, 232.7, 257.9 mm³/m²; p&lt;0.001) and correlated weakly with aortic valve area (r=−0.067) and peak velocity (r=0.147; both p&lt;0.001). Discrimination for concordant severe AS was poor (c-statistic 0.417). In contrast, calcific volume index increased markedly (41.8, 92.4, 205.1 mm³/m²; p&lt;0.001), correlated strongly with haemodynamic severity (r=0.697; p&lt;0.001), and demonstrated excellent discrimination for severe AS (c-statistic 0.940 in women; 0.921 in men). The fibro-calcific ratio declined across severity strata (5.3 to 1.2 p&lt;0.001), reflecting disproportionate calcium expansion. Women had higher non-calcific volume (253.7 [175.8–359.2] vs 227.3 [161.1–307.4] mm³/m²; p&lt;0.0001), but lower calcific volume than men (92.8 [32.4–188.3] vs 123.4 [59.1–224.9] mm³/m²; p&lt;0.0001), resulting in a higher fibro-calcific ratio (2.8 vs 1.8 p&lt;0.001). A progressive decline with increasing haemodynamic severity was observed in both sexes. Non-calcific volume failed to improve diagnostic performance beyond calcium volume overall or by sex. Over a median follow-up of 42 months, high calcific volume independently predicted the primary endpoint (HR 2.46 [1.89–3.22]; p&lt;0.001), whereas higher indexed non-calcific volume was independently associated with lower risk (HR 0.63 [0.48–0.82]; p=0.001). Conclusion Non-calcific leaflet thickening represents a fundamental structural substrate of AS, particularly in earlier disease and in women. However, its quantification does not enhance identification of severe AS or add diagnostic value beyond calcium. Further research is required to clarify the role of non-calcific thickening in disease progression.
title: Non-calcific leaflet thickening and calcific burden in aortic stenosis

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Some studies have shown that patients with aortic stenosis (AS) have a poor prognosis, even when the stenosis is moderate (1,2). Extravalvular staging has been shown to be a useful tool for assessing the short- and mid-term prognosis of these patients (3) Purpose To determine the long-term prognosis of a cohort of patients with asymptomatic moderate-to-severe aortic stenosis and to assess whether staging by cardiac damage (CD) is useful in this scenario. Methods We prospectively included 96 consecutive patients with asymptomatic moderate or severe AS in a dedicated registry in 2014. Baseline assessment comprised comprehensive echocardiography, cardiopulmonary exercise testing, blood biomarkers, cardiac magnetic resonance and computed tomography aortic valve calcium scoring. Patients were classified into 5 stages of cardiac damage (0-4)(3) at baseline, a classification in which stage 0 indicates no extravalvular involvement and stage 4 reflects right heart involvement. Stages 3 and 4 were merged for statistical purposes due to the small number of patients in each group. Follow-up was at the treating cardiologist’s discretion, and aortic valve replacement (AVR) was decided by the Heart Team according to current guidelines, using a watchful waiting strategy. Data on AVR, mortality, and heart failure hospitalization were collected retrospectively. Results The baseline characteristics of the cohort were: mean age 71 years; 72% male; 71% with hypertension; 55% with dyslipidemia; 55% with diabetes mellitus; mean aortic valve area (AVA) 1.04 cm²; and mean aortic gradient 39 mmHg. During follow-up, 20 patients (20.8%) developed symptoms within the first year and 68 (70.8%) became symptomatic at some point. 67 patients (69.8%) underwent surgical or transcatheter AVR, and 25 (26%) required hospitalization for heart failure before AVR, while heart failure occurred in 12 patients (12.5%) after AVR. At 10 years, 39 patients (40.6%) had died, of whom 15 died from cardiovascular causes; cancer was the most frequent cause of death. Of 11 patients (11.5%) that remained alive and free from AVR after 10 years of follow up, 9 were still asymptomatic; compared with the rest of the cohort, they were younger (71 vs 64 years. p= 0,04), had less severe baseline AS (mean gradient: 40 mmHg vs 30 mmHg. p= 0,008) and showed minimal or no extravalvular cardiac damage at baseline (9 of 11 patients were at stage 0). Statistically significant differences in 10-year all-cause mortality were observed according to baseline CD staging. Conclusions Ten-year mortality in patients with asymptomatic moderate/severe aortic stenosis managed with watchful waiting and Heart Team–guided intervention is high and mostly driven by non-cardiac causes. Extravalvular CD staging identified a small subset of patients with a markedly better long-term prognosis, with about 10% of the cohort remaining asymptomatic and free from valve intervention at 10 years.10 year Kaplan–Meier survival by stageMortality and intervention rates by stage
title: Long term follow up of patients with asymptomatic moderate–to-severe aortic stenosis in a real world cohort

abstract: Abstract Introduction Aortic valve stenosis (AVS) is the most prevalent valvular heart disease, characterized by chronic inflammation and progressive calcification. As transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) remains the only effective treatment, novel therapeutic targets are urgently needed. Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as key regulators of gene expression through epigenetics and post-transcriptional mechanisms, yet their roles in AVS remain largely unexplored. Our preliminary transcriptomic data from calcified human aortic valves identified a significant upregulation of MIAT and MEG3, lncRNAs implicated in fibrosis, atherosclerosis, and endothelial dysfunction. Purpose This study elucidates the functional roles and molecular pathways of MIAT and MEG3 in AVS pathogenesis to evaluate their potential as lncRNA-based therapeutic targets. Methods Primary human valvular interstitial (VICs) and endothelial cells (VECs) isolated from calcified and non-calcified valves were subjected to siRNA-mediated knockdown of MIAT and MEG3. To model AVS pathogenesis, endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) was induced in VECs using TGF-β and IL-1β stimulation. VICs calcification was induced using osteogenic medium, supplemented with dexamethasone, L-ascorbic acid, glycerol-2-phosphate, and separately by pro-calcifying NaH2PO4 treatment. Results Silencing either MIAT or MEG3 attenuated VEC migration and impaired angiogenic capacity, consistent with suppression of EndMT as shown by downregulation of mesenchymal marker ACTA2, while restoring endothelial marker CD31. In VICs, siMIAT and siMEG3 potently suppressed osteogenic drivers (BMP2, RUNX2) and reduced calcification, indicating an amelioration of core disease phenotypes. Furthermore, intercellular communication studies via extracellular vesicles (EVs) and co-culture models demonstrated that silencing MIAT or MEG3 in donor VECs diminished inflammatory signaling in recipient VICs as depicted by significant decrease of IL-6, TGF-β, ICAM-1, and VCAM-1 expressions. Bulk RNA sequencing on valvular cells following lncRNAs knockdown revealed significant dysregulation of pro-fibrotic genes COL1A1 and TAGLN. An integrated in silico and proteomic analyses identified caspase-3, p53, and HIF1α as potential downstream effectors mediating these lncRNA-driven inflammatory and calcification pathways. Conclusion MIAT and MEG3 are critical promoters of EndMT, inflammation, and calcification in AVS. Their silencing restores endothelial integrity and mitigates osteogenic differentiation, highlighting their potential as promising therapeutic targets. Ongoing mechanistic studies employing RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-seq), pulldown assays, and validation in valvular organoid and murine models will further delineate the specific molecular mechanisms and translate these findings towards clinical application.MIAT and MEG3 as crucial regulators in AVS
title: Long non-coding RNA MIAT and MEG3 are crucial regulators of inflammation and calcification in aortic valve stenosis

abstract: Abstract Background Aortic stenosis is typically associated with a progressive concentric hypertrophic response of the left ventricular (LV) myocardium. However, an asymmetric pattern of LV remodeling observed in some patients has been associated with earlier LV decompensation, more rapid progression to valve replacement, and an overall impaired prognosis. Purpose To evaluate the impact of computed tomography (CT)–derived asymmetric LV remodeling on the acute and long-term outcomes of patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Methods In this single-center retrospective study, contrast-enhanced ECG-gated CT scans of consecutive patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing TAVI between 2009 and 2021 were analyzed. Asymmetric LV remodeling was defined as a maximum LV wall thickness-to-opposite wall thickness ratio &gt;1.5, as measured on short-axis diastolic CT images. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes were major in-hospital complications, defined as a composite of major vascular complications, life-threatening or major bleeding, myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary occlusion, annular rupture, pacemaker implantation, or death Results A total of 803 patients (median age 82 years, 58% female) were analyzed. The median follow-up was 49 months. Patients with asymmetric LV remodeling (n = 435, 54.2%) were older than those without asymmetric LV remodeling (83 vs. 80 years, p &lt; 0.001), and had greater maximum LV thickness (14.3 vs. 12.5 mm, p&lt;0.01) (Figure 1). The incidence of major complications post TAVI was higher in patients with asymmetric LV remodeling compared with those without asymmetric LV remodeling (38% vs. 29%, p = 0.01). In multivariable logistic regression model asymmetric LV remodeling remained a predictor of major TAVI complications (OR 1.57, 1.1-2.2, p=0.01), independent of age, LV ejection fraction and maximum LV wall thickness. One-year (14% vs. 13%, p = 0.88) and three-year mortality (29% vs. 31%, p = 0.70) did not differ between patients with and without asymmetric LV remodeling (Figure 2). Conclusions Asymmetric LV remodeling is a common finding in the elderly population with severe aortic stenosis undergoing TAVI. Our data suggest that it might be associated with an increased risk of in-hospital post-TAVI complications but does not impact long-term prognosis.
title: Association of asymmetric left ventricular remodeling with outcomes in patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation

abstract: Abstract Introduction Echocardiography remains the first line imaging modality for aortic stenosis (AS); although discordant findings occur in around one third of patients.(1,2) Computed tomography derived aortic valve area (CT AVA) is larger than echocardiographic Aortic Valve Area (AVA), yet neither demonstrates improved correlation with transvalvular gradients nor greater specificity for severe AS.(3,4) We evaluated valve to annular ratio as anatomical reserve for its ability to improve the specificity for severe AS and obviate the effect of flow. Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted on 107 symptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS) being worked up for TAVI. Sub-groups were indentified: High Gradient (HG, N=69), Classical Low-Flow Low-Gradient (LFLG, N=16), Paradoxical LFLG (pLFLG, N=2), Bicuspid (BAV, N=7), and Mixed aortic stenosis/regurgitation (AS/AR) (N=13). Data was integrated from transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and ECG-gated computed tomography (CT). AVA was derived using: Echo-CE: Standard Doppler derived AVA using continuity equation, AVA-CT: Direct CT planimetry of the aortic valve systolic orifice, AVA-Hybrid: Integration of CT-derived annular area with Echo derived Doppler velocities. Spearman rank-order correlation (r) analysis assessed association between Echo-CE and AVA-CT within each subgroup. To quantify the Anatomical Reserve Valve to Annular Ratio (VA Ratio) was calculated as AVA-CT divided by the CT annular area. This dimensionless index was assessed across all phenotypes. Results The median age of the cohort was was 81 [IQR: 77–85] years with 70% males. Low correlation coefficients with large confidence intervals indicated significant discordance between measurement modalities (P &lt; 0.001 for HG and LFLG). Echo-CE consistently yielded lower values than AVA-CT (0.72 vs 0.93cm2 in HG), while AVA-Hybrid yielded higher values (1.18 cm2). Correlation between Echo and CT derived AVA was low to moderate across different flow states (HG: r=0.27; LFLG: r=0.43) and in the Mixed AR/AS group (r=0.43) (table 1). Despite this discordance, the VA Ratio (Anatomical Reserve) proved to be a robust biological constant for symptomatic severe AS, with a total cohort median of 0.22 [IQR: 0.18–0.26]. Phenotypic analysis confirmed the stability of this 22% threshold regardless of flow or gradient. Notably, Paradoxical LFLG patients exhibited the lowest anatomical reserve (Ratio: 0.18), while Mixed AR/AS patients possessed the highest (Ratio: 0.24) (figure1). Conclusion CT AVA demonstrated a weaker correlation to echo AVA by CE in high gradient and classical low flow low gradient AS. Anatomical reserve (valve to annular ratio) may represent a novel dimensionless anatomical index to grade severity of aortic stenosis. This has been shown to reveal limitations of CT aortic valve calcium score for grading severity of AS.(5) Larger studies are required to validate these findings prior to clinical implementationFigure 1.Table 1
title: Stability of the valve-to-annular ratio (anatomical reserve) as a biological constant in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis across clinical phenotypes

abstract: Abstract Background Better risk stratification in aortic stenosis (AS) for prognostication and decision for early valvular intervention purposes is in need. Complex relationships between various clinical parameters for risk stratification may not be easily delineated using conventional linear regression methods. A machine learning algorithm, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), is able to capture nonlinear relationships among parameters. Our study aims to utilise XGBoost to develop and validate an explainable model (ASNet) for predicting clinical outcomes in patients with AS using readily available clinical and echocardiographic data. Methods We conducted a retrospective, multicentre cohort study on 2759 patients with at least moderate aortic stenosis across three tertiary hospitals between January 2014 and February 2023. Moderate and severe aortic stenosis were defined as 1.0-1.5cm2 and &lt;1.0cm2 respectively by the continuity equation on transthoracic echocardiography. The primary outcome was defined as a composite of all-cause mortality and aortic valve intervention within 3 years from the date of index echocardiography. Patients from two hospitals were used for the ASNet model development and internal validation while external validation was performed on patients from the third hospital. ASNet was developed using various clinical and echocardiographic parameters, evaluated using discrimination, calibration, decision curve analysis, SHAP-based interpretability with subgroup analysis. Results 977 patients (35.4%) met the primary outcome with 641 deaths, 287 surgical valve replacements and 49 catheter-based interventions. The ASNet model demonstrated discrimination in the internal test cohort with area under the curve (AUC) 0.92 (F1-score 0.81–0.84) and maintained robust performance in the external validation cohort (AUC 0.83–0.84; F1-score 0.63–0.67) (Figure 1). SHAP analysis demonstrated that comorbidities of ischemic heart disease, hypertension, older age, echocardiographic parameters of lower left ventricular outflow tract stroke volume, higher aortic peak velocity were the strongest contributors to predicted risk of the primary outcome (Figure 2). Subgroup analyses have shown that ASNet maintained its performance in both moderate (AUC 0.815) and severe (AUC 0.818), elderly patients of age &gt;75 years (AUC 0.04), low left ventricular ejection fraction (&lt;40%) (AUC 0.842) and gender (male AUC 0.830; female AUC 0.846). ASNet risk stratified groups has also demonstrated poorer survival in the high-risk group in Kaplan-Meier survival analysis (log rank p&lt;0.001). Conclusion ASNet is an explainable and externally validated model which is based on readily available clinical and echocardiographic data. It has demonstrated ability to predict clinical outcomes in patients with at least moderate AS. This may allow earlier identification of high-risk patients with aortic stenosis, enabling timely interventions or closer surveillance.ROC curveSHAP analysis plot
title: ASNet: mortality and valve replacement prediction in patients with aortic stenosis using explainable artificial intelligence in a multi-ethnic asian cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Elevated Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is hypothesized to be associated with the pathophysiology of calcific aortic stenosis (AS), but the extent to which it influences disease progression and clinical outcomes has not been fully elucidated. Purpose The purpose of this meta-analysis is to analyse the association between elevated Lp(a) levels and haemodynamic progression of calcific aortic stenosis, rate of aortic valve replacement (AVR), major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and cardiovascular mortality in adults with existing calcific AS. Methods A literature search was performed to identify randomised controlled trials that analysed the association of elevated Lp(a) and haemodynamic progression of AS in adults with calcific AS, consistent with the enrolment criteria of the included randomised controlled studies. The primary endpoints of interest included MACE and cardiovascular mortality. The secondary endpoints included annualised change in peak aortic jet velocity and rate of AVR. Calcific AS was defined as peak aortic jet velocity greater than 2.0 m/s and non-rheumatic aortic valve calcification on echocardiography. Elevated Lp(a) was defined as ≥35 mg/dL or ≥125 nmol/L. The search engine included the following databases: PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science. TriNetX, registry, and post hoc analysis studies were excluded. Results A total of 2 randomised controlled studies were selected as there were not enough studies available in the current literature to perform analysis for our primary endpoints. However, there were 2 studies identified that allowed analysis of secondary endpoints and they included 2,107 patients (521 of which had elevated Lp(a) and 1,586 had normal Lp(a)). The median follow-up duration was between 30-60 months; mean age was 68.2 years and 53.8% were men. Patients with elevated Lp(a) demonstrated a significantly higher rate of AVR and cardiovascular mortality (OR 1.52, 95% CI 1.16-1.98; p=0.002). Heterogeneity regarding rate of AVR, cardiovascular mortality analysis was low (I² = 23%). Compared to patients with normal Lp(a), rate of increase in aortic valve peak velocity was faster in patients with elevated Lp(a) (mean difference 0.09, 95% CI 0.04-0.14; p=0.0002). Heterogeneity regarding rate of aortic valve peak velocity analysis was low (I² = 0%). Conclusions Elevated Lp(a) is associated with accelerated AS progression and worse clinical outcomes, supporting its role as a prognostic biomarker and possible therapeutic target in calcific AS.Rate of AVR and Cardiovascular MortalityRate of increase in AV peak velocity
title: Elevated lipoprotein(a) and progression of aortic stenosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cardiovascular outcomes

abstract: Abstract Background Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetic risk factor for the onset of calcific aortic valve stenosis (CAVS). However, whether elevated Lp(a) accelerates hemodynamic progression or independently predicts prognosis in Asian patients with established mild-to-moderate CAVS remains unclear. Purpose This study aims to investigate the association between baseline Lp(a) levels and both hemodynamic progression and clinical outcomes in a prospective Chinese cohort. Methods We conducted a prospective cohort study of mild-to-moderate CAVS patients defined as a peak aortic valve velocity (Vpeak) of 2.0–4.0 m/s. Patients with prior valve surgery, severe regurgitation, or significant comorbidities were excluded. Patients were stratified by baseline Lp(a) levels (cutoff: 30 mg/dL consistent with risk thresholds in Chinese populations). The primary endpoint was a composite of aortic valve replacement (AVR) or all-cause mortality. The secondary endpoint was hemodynamic progression, calculated as the annualized change in Vpeak [ΔVpeak/year]. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards and linear regression models were used to assess independent effects of Lp(a), adjusting for age, sex, hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, significant valve calcification and baseline Vpeak. Kaplan-Meier curves with log-rank tests compared event-free survival between groups. Results A total of 243 participants were included (mean age 67.5 ± 11.2 years, 60% male), 96 patients (39.5%) had elevated Lp(a) (≥ 30 mg/dL). During a mean follow-up of 5.5 years, 117 composite events (AVR or death) occurred. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed significantly lower event-free survival in the high Lp(a) group (Log-rank P &lt; 0.0001). In multivariable Cox regression, Lp(a) ≥ 30 mg/dL remained independently associated with a 2.5-fold increased risk of the primary outcome (adjusted HR 2.51, 95% CI 1.72–3.67, P &lt; 0.001). In patients with long-term follow-up (&gt; 5 years), elevated Lp(a) was identified as a significant independent predictor of an accelerated ΔVpeak/year (adjusted β = 0.059, P &lt; 0.05). This prognostic value was particularly pronounced in patients aged &lt; 65 years (adjusted HR 3.11) and those without significant baseline valve calcification (adjusted HR 2.63). Conclusion In this long-term prospective cohort of Chinese patients, elevated Lp(a) is a potent driver of AS progression and a strong independent predictor of adverse clinical events, especially in younger patients and early disease stages. These findings suggest that Lp(a) measurement should be integrated into risk stratification for mild-to-moderate AS and highlight Lp(a) lowering as a potential therapeutic target.The main results.
title: Prognostic value of lipoprotein(a) level in calcific aortic valve stenosis: insight from a prospective Chinese cohort

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Lesion-specific assessment of coronary ischaemia by non-invasive testing remains difficult, especially in patients with high plaque burden and calcification. Purpose To compare vessel-territory diagnostic performance of an artificial intelligence quantitative coronary computed tomography angiography ischaemia model (AI-QCT) with fractional flow reserve computed tomography (FFR-CT) across plaque volume strata. Methods This was a post-hoc pooled analysis of two prospective studies. Symptomatic patients with suspected coronary artery disease underwent coronary computed tomography angiography, FFR-CT, and invasive fractional flow reserve (FFR). Analyses were performed at the vessel-territory level. The reference standard was invasive FFR &lt;=0.80. Performance was evaluated overall and stratified by total plaque volume, calcified plaque, and non-calcified plaque (&lt;50, 50–150, and &gt;150 mm3). Accuracy and AUC were reported with 2-sided bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals using cluster sampling; AUC was estimated using Mann–Whitney statistics. Results The pooled cohort included 513 patients and 1,480 vessel territories. Overall, AI-QCT showed higher accuracy and discrimination than FFR-CT: accuracy 81.0% (95% CI 78.7–82.9) vs 75.4% (72.8–78.0); AUC 0.86 (0.84–0.88) vs 0.77 (0.74–0.80); p&lt;0.0001. Across total plaque volume strata (&lt;50/50–150/&gt;150 mm3), accuracy remained higher for AI-QCT: 90.2/79.6/74.8% vs 82.4/73.5/71.3%. In severe calcification (calcified plaque &gt;150 mm3), accuracy was 71.2% vs 68.5% (AUC 0.78 vs 0.68; p=0.010). In severe non-calcified plaque (non-calcified plaque &gt;150 mm3), accuracy was 77.1% vs 73.2% (AUC 0.89 vs 0.79; p&lt;0.0001). Conclusion(s) In a pooled dataset using invasive physiology as the reference standard, AI-QCT outperformed FFR-CT for detecting vessel-territory ischaemia and maintained performance across increasing total, calcified, and non-calcified plaque burden.ESC 2026 Table
title: Artificial intelligence coronary computed tomography angiography for lesion specific ischaemia: invasive physiology validation across plaque burden

abstract: Abstract Background and Purpose Severe aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with significant mortality, which is reduced with aortic valve replacement (AVR).1 Wait times for AVR have increased over the years and are associated with higher rates of mortality, making it crucial to identify patients at the highest risk who may benefit from expedited intervention.2 Individualized prediction tools to estimate 1-year mortality are imperative to improve clinical decision-making and timing of intervention. Methods Patients with a first diagnosis of severe AS (aortic valve area ≤ 1.0 cm², mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg, peak velocity ≥ 4.0 m/s) were identified from an institutional echocardiography database. The outcome variable of interest was all-cause mortality within 1 year of index echocardiography. The primary explanatory variable was AVR in the first year after diagnosis. Additional explanatory variables included age group (&lt;65, 65-74, 75-84, 85+), sex, chronic kidney disease (CKD), LVEF ≤ 50%, AVA ≤ 0.8 cm2, indexed AVA ≤ 0.5 cm²/m², transaortic mean gradient ≥ 45 mmHg, and LAVI ≥ 48 mL/m2. Univariable binary logistic regression models were fit for each candidate predictor. A multivariable model was then constructed using all predictors, followed by backwards elimination. Each regression coefficient within each selected model was divided by a common denominator to determine the points associated with each indicator variable in the final selected model. We computed a map from the minimum to the maximum number of points for each model to risk (probability of outcome) from model coefficients (including the intercept) and the inverse logit transformation. Results Full data comprised of N = 2559 subjects. Final variables in the multivariable analysis included receipt of AVR within 1 year, age ≥ 65 years, female sex, GFR &lt; 60 L/min/1.73 m, LVEF ≤ 50%, aortic valve area ≤ 0.8 cm², mean gradient ≥ 45 mmHg, and left atrial volume index ≥ 48 mL/m². The risk calculator risk-stratified the population from 0.8% to 75.7%. The strongest predictor of 1-year mortality was a reduced LVEF ≤50% (OR 3.25; 95% CI 2.44, 4.33; p-value&lt;0.001), followed by CKD (OR 2.29; 95% CI 1.73, 3.02; p-value &lt;0.001). LAVI ≥ 48 ml/m2 was associated with a two-fold increased risk of death at 1 year (OR 2.08, 95% CI 1.59, 2.73; p-value&lt;0.001). AVR within 1 year was independently associated with a 77% reduction of 1-year mortality (OR 0.23; 95% CI 0.16, 0.32; p-value &lt;0.001), offsetting the negative prognostic effects of high-risk clinical and echocardiographic features. Conclusion We developed a risk score predicting the likelihood of AS-related mortality within one year of diagnosis, incorporating clinical and echocardiographic factors, with consideration to receipt of AVR.Multivariable analysisRisk calculator
title: Development of a 1-year mortality risk calculator in severe aortic stenosis incorporating aortic valve replacement within the first year
