abstract: Abstract Background A novel classification has recently been proposed to characterize the clinical presentation of severe aortic stenosis (AS) and its independent association with clinical outcomes. This framework categorizes patients into three clinical phenotypes: silent (or stable) valve syndrome (SVS), progressive valve syndrome (PVS), and acute valve syndrome (AVS). Purpose To validate in a large Canadian cohort the prognostic utility of this classification for long-term all-cause mortality and to derive a multimarker score associated with AVS. Methods Consecutive patients with severe AS who underwent transcatheter aortic valve replacement at our institution between May 2007 and June 2025 were included and prospectively followed. Baseline demographic, clinical, and echocardiographic data were collected. Patients were stratified into SVS, PVS, and AVS, and survival analyses were performed to assess their association with all-cause mortality. In a predefined subgroup with complete baseline circulating biomarker data, the relationship between individual biomarkers and AVS was further evaluated. Results A total of 3366 patients were included in the study: 50 (1.5%) presented with SVS, 679 (20.2%) with PVS, and 2637 (78.3%) with AVS. Patients classified as AVS exhibited a greater burden of comorbidities, with higher prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, prior pacemaker implantation, history of myocardial infarction or coronary artery disease, stroke, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and renal failure. Although median left ventricular ejection fraction was 60% across categories, key measures of AS severity such as mean transvalvular gradient, indexed effective orifice area, and stroke volume index were lower in patients classified as AVS, who also showed impaired right ventricular function and a higher frequency of concomitant regurgitations. Over a follow-up period of up to 10 years, multivariable Cox regression analysis adjusted for relevant clinical covariates demonstrated that AVS was independently associated with a higher risk of all-cause mortality compared with PVS and SVS (HR [95%CI] 1.65, [1.42-1.92], p&lt;0.001). In a subgroup analysis including 362 patients, multivariable logistic regression identified CA-125, GDF-15, and creatinine as independently associated with AVS. A multimarker model showed that a greater number of elevated biomarkers was associated with AVS and added incremental predictive value to the clinical model. Conclusion In this large validation cohort within the Canadian healthcare system, the majority of patients with severe AS presented with AVS and showed a higher burden of comorbidities along with more adverse echocardiographic features, which translated into worse long-term all-cause survival. A multimarker strategy may facilitate the identification of patients at increased risk of developing AVS.Kaplan-Meier curves of long-term survivalMultivariable Cox Regression Analysis
title: Prognostic validation and biomarker characterization of acute valve syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is the treatment of choice for elderly patients or high-risk patients with severe symptomatic aortic valve stenosis with improved symptoms, morbidity and mortality in the follow-up. However, increasing attention is given to the role of frailty and cognitive dysfunction as risk factors, which may limit the therapeutic benefit of TAVR in certain patients. Cardiovascular guidelines recommend taking such comorbidities into account pre and post TAVR. By contrast, quantification of cognitive and neuromuscular function in patients with aortic stenosis before and after causal treatment is not well established. Purpose To validate a novel, easy to perform, standardized bio-feedback protocol testing four cognitive and neuromuscular domains using the CortexTrainer in patients with compensated symptomatic severe aortic valve stenosis before, shortly after and one month after TAVR. Methods N=120 patients consecutive patients scheduled for TAVR (81±1 yrs) were enrolled in a prospective monocentric observational registry. They were tested shortly before the procedure, shortly after as well as one month later as outpatients at the follow-up visit. Their test results were compared to N=70 healthy volunteers of different ages. The CortexTrainer was used to perform a standardized 10-minute supervised exam containing four distinct test domains: 1. postural stability test (sway way, in mm), 2. reaction test (hands vs. feet, in ms), 3. complex movement task (chasing a ball on screen, in % success), and 4. complex neurocognitive task (on-screen trail making test, TMT, in seconds). In addition, Barthel index, frailty scales, MMSE, paper-pen trail making test and clinical data were recorded. Results The 70 study control subjects without aortic valve stenosis showed a linear decrease of neuromuscular performance and postural stability with increasing age. Compared to age-matched control patients, TAVR patients were significantly worse with respect to sway way, reaction time, chase success and TMT, but also had a high inter-individual variability. After one month follow-up, TAVR was not associated with significant differences in Barthel index, Edmonton frailty scale, essential frailty scale, MMSE, handgrip strength and paper-pen TMT. However, in the CortexTrainer standardized assessment, stand stability (sway way 1263±227 vs. 1851±267mm, p=0.006), mean pedal reaction time (192±20 vs. 259±20ms, p=0.021), complex task success rate (p=0.029) and bio-feedback TMT (96±5 vs. 111±4 seconds, p=0.001) were improved. Data are mean±SEM, statistics are t-test and ANOVA for repeated measurements. Conclusion Standardized neuromuscular and cognitive performance measures of control subjects showed a decline with increasing age. Importantly, performance in TAVR recipients was even lower than in age-matched controls. Following TAVR, improved performance in all assessed tasks was seen after 1 month.
title: A novel standardized bio-feedback test for cognitive and neuromuscular performance with the CortexTrainer shows improvements within one month after TAVR in elderly severe aortic stenosis patients

abstract: Abstract Background Small aortic annuli (SAA) have long been recognised as a risk factor for patient-prosthesis mismatch (PPM) and a poor prognostic factor. However, while 430 mm², as analyzed by multi-detector computed tomography (MDCT), is frequently used to define SAA, a clear definition remains scarce. Furthermore, previous studies have often used the same 430 mm² definition for all individuals without considering regional variations in aortic valve anatomy. Purpose This study aimed to redefine SAA and to clarify the impact of SAA on outcomes following transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Methods The TOTO-TAVI study included patients who underwent TAVI in a university hospital and a clinic, from March 2024 to September 2025. The primary endpoint was the early safety. A subgroup analysis was performed to identify the independent risk factors of short-term outcomes using multivariate analysis. Results A total of 790 patients (385 from Japan and 405 from France) were included. When the definition of SAA in France was less than 430 mm², 189/405 (47%) cases met the criteria for SAA. Therefore, in this study, SAA was defined as less than 385 mm² to ensure that SAA patients constituted 47 % (180/385) in Japan. Overall, Japan and France showed differences in all patient background factors, with notable variations observed in age (83.9±6.1 vs. 82.8±6.2), gender (male: 42.6 % vs. 57.8 %), body mass index (22.3±3.8 kg/m² vs. 27.3±5.1 kg/m²), STS-PROM score (6.6 [3.7-10.3] % vs. 3.5 [2.3-5.7] %), and left ventricular ejection fraction (62.0±10.7 % vs. 59.1±11.6 %). Regarding anatomical differences by MDCT, patients in Japan demonstrated smaller anatomy than those in France in the annulus, left ventricular outflow tract, sinotubular junction, sinus of valsalva, both coronary arteries height, and both femoral arteries diameter (all p&lt;0.001). However, considering annulus-perimeter-derived diameter adjusted for height, patients in Japan showed larger than those in France (14.6±1.1 mm/m vs. 14.5±1.2 mm/m, p=0.024). The early safety was comparable between patients in Japan and in France, both overall and in the SAA group (overall: 81.3 % vs. 77.5 %, p=0.19; SAA: 76.7 % vs. 75.7 %, p=0.82). The other in-hospital outcomes, including mortality and the incidence of PPM, showed no significant differences between Japan and France, both overall and in the SAA group. For subgroup analysis, SAA was not significantly associated with independent risk factors for the early safety (odds ratio: 1.4; 95% confidence interval: 0.84-2.4, p=0.19). Conclusions Considering body size, the definition of SAA for patients in Asia should be used as less than 385 mm². Given that short-term outcomes after TAVI between Asia and France showed no significant difference, including safety endpoints and the incidence of PPM, TAVI has the potential for highly favourable results even in patients with SAA.
title: Definitions of small aortic annuli on transcatheter aortic valve implantation from the TOTO-TAVI study

abstract: Abstract Background Outcomes in low-gradient aortic stenosis (AS) are heterogeneous, and atrial fibrillation (AF) is linked to both adverse prognosis and altered transvalvular hemodynamics. Patients with AF more often present with a low-gradient phenotype, and gradients may vary by rhythm status, thereby unmasking true severity. In Asian populations, distinct features such as smaller body size, lower stroke volume, and differing prevalence of AS and AF may further influence hemodynamic assessment and prognosis. This study aimed to investigate the prevalence and outcomes of low-gradient AS in patients with AF using a large multicenter Asian cohort. Methods In this retrospective multicenter cohort study, 5,531 patients with moderate to severe AS diagnosed between 2008 and 2020 were stratified by rhythm at index echocardiography into rhythm (sinus rhythm vs. atrial fibrillation) and transvalvular mean pressure gradient (&lt; 40 mmHg vs. ≥ 40 mmHg). Patients with moderate or greater mitral valve disease, significant aortic regurgitation, left ventricular ejection fraction &lt;50%, or missing values for key variables, such as mean gradient, were excluded. After exclusion, 5,218 patients were included in the final analysis. Among them, 3,281 (62.9%) had severe AS defined as aortic valve area ≤ 1.0 cm2, and 2,910 (55.8%) were classified as low-gradient AS. By rhythm status, 4,723 (90.5%) were in sinus rhythm and 495 (9.5%) in atrial fibrillation. The primary outcome was defined as a composite of all-cause mortality and aortic valve replacement (AVR). Results Patients with AF were older and had a higher burden of comorbidities, including hypertension, diabetes, and prior cerebrovascular accident. They exhibited significantly higher left atrial volume index, higher E/e′, and higher estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure. Although aortic valve area (AVA) was similar between groups (0.93 ± 0.26 vs.0.92 ± 0.27 cm2, p=0.608), peak aortic jet velocity, and mean gradient were significantly lower (35.9 ± 17.2 mmHg vs. 42.0 ± 19.5 mmHg, p &lt;0.001) in the AF group. Thus, low-gradient AS was more prevalent in patients with AF than in those with sinus rhythm [66.3 vs. 54.7%, p &lt;0.001]. During a median follow-up of 44.6 months, 1,795 patients (34.4%) died, and 2,632 (50.4%) underwent AVR. All-cause mortality was higher, and AVR was less frequently performed in the AF group; AF remained independently associated with increased mortality after multivariable adjustment (adjusted HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.08–1.43). Among patients with low-gradient AS, the AF group and the sinus rhythm group (Figure). Conclusion In patients with moderate to severe AS, low-gradient AS was more common in those with AF, and transvalvular pressure gradients were lower despite comparable aortic valve area. AF was associated with worse clinical outcomes, particularly in patients with low-gradient AS, in whom prognosis was significantly poorer compared with those in sinus rhythm.K-M survival
title: Outcome of low-gradient aortic stenosis in patients with atrial fibrillation: insights from a multicenter cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) stenosis has been associated with challenging anatomical features for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Ascending aorta dilatation is frequently observed in patients with BAV stenosis and its implications for TAVI outcomes remain undetermined. Purpose To assess short and long-term clinical outcomes after TAVI for BAV stenosis according to ascending aorta diameter. Methods The study involved consecutive patients with computed tomography-diagnosed BAV who underwent TAVI due to symptomatic stenosis at 30 centres in Europe and North America with a long-time established interventional program and a systematic prospective collection of data. The primary outcome was a composite of death or stroke assessed from TAVI up to 3 years. Adjusted estimates were computed by binomial or linear multivariable mixed-effects models and semi-parametric shared frailty models accounting for multiple potential clinical, anatomical, and procedural confounders, transcatheter heart valve (THV) type, and centre. Results A total of 1815 patients with BAV treated by balloon- (1099, 60.6%) or self-expandable THV (716, 39.4%) were included. THVs were predominantly of newer generations (1439, 79.3%). The cohort was analysed according to the ascending aorta diameter, either &lt;40 mm (1231, 67.8%) or ≥40 mm (584, 32.2%). The median ascending aorta diameters were 35.0 [32.2-37.2] mm and 43.0 [41.4-45.2] mm, respectively. Both unadjusted and adjusted in-hospital outcomes did not significantly differ between patients with normal or dilated ascending aorta. Moderate-to-severe postprocedural aortic regurgitation was not significantly different between groups (6.1% vs 5.7%). After multivariable adjustment, this conclusion remained unchanged (odds ratio [OR]MVA 0.84, 95% CI 0.47-1.50, P=0.557). At 3 years, death or stroke was not significantly different between patients with normal and dilated ascending aorta (24.5% vs 25.6%; hazard ratio [HR] 1.03, 95% CI 0.80-1.33, P=0.833). After multivariable adjustment, this result did not change (HRMVA 1.02, 95% CI 0.73-1.42, P=0.944). The individual outcomes of death (HRMVA 1.00, 95% CI 0.68-1.48), stroke (HRMVA 0.92, 95% CI 0.51-0.68, P=0.996), repeat valve replacement (HRMVA 1.44, 95% CI 0.52-4.03, P=0.695), valve thrombosis (HRMVA 1.00, 95% CI 0.68-1.48, P=0.663), and pacemaker implantation (HRMVA 1.01, 95% CI 0.74-1.38, P=0.974) were not significantly different between groups. Landmark analyses (30 days, 1 year, and 2 years), and subgroup and sensitivity analyses did not reveal inconsistencies. Conclusion In patients with BAV stenosis, cardiovascular outcomes after TAVI are not affected by baseline ascending aortic diameter. Death or Stroke 3Y
title: Influence of ascending aorta diameter on short- and long-term clinical outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve implantation for bicuspid aortic valve stenosis

abstract: Abstract Aortic stenosis (AS), the most prevalent valvular heart diseases in developed nations, primarily affects elderly, multimorbid patients. With the increasing availability of valvular interventions, the proper evaluation of cardiac function remains a key question in both diagnosis and patient management. Conventional echocardiographic parameters, including ejection fraction (EF) and global longitudinal strain (GLS), are strongly influenced by loading conditions and may not accurately reflect left ventricular (LV) contractility in cases of hemodynamic overload. Although pressure–strain loop–derived myocardial work partially addresses these limitations, it does not account for preload and LV geometry. Data on dedicated AS subtypes, particularly paradoxical low-flow low-gradient (pLFLG) AS, remain limited. We aimed to introduce pressure–strain–volume (PSV) loop–derived, volume-adjusted myocardial work and to evaluate its diagnostic and prognostic value in patients with severe AS undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). We enrolled 300 patients with severe AS undergoing TAVR (age 78.7±6.3 years, 41% female). Preprocedural echocardiography and non-invasive blood pressure measurements were performed a day before the intervention. EF and LV volumes were assessed using the biplane Simpson method, and GLS was obtained by speckle-tracking. LV pressure curves were estimated from cuff blood pressure and the Doppler-derived transaortic gradient. Global constructive work (GCW) was calculated from pressure–strain loops and then further adjusted to instantaneous LV volumes to derive volume-adjusted GCW (GCWVi). Patients were classified as normal-flow high-gradient (NFHG), classical low-flow low-gradient (cLFLG), or pLFLG in accordance with current guidelines. The endpoint was all-cause mortality, reached by 62 patients during a median follow-up time of 25 months. GCW was comparable between NFHG and pLFLG but reduced in cLFLG (1583 ± 459 vs. 1378 ± 535 vs. 967 ± 470, p &lt; 0.001). In contrast, GCWVi was significantly lower in both cLFLG and pLFLG compared with NFHG (5.04 ± 2.03 vs. 5.79 ± 1.87 vs. 6.72 ± 2.35). Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated improved survival in patients with GCWVi above the median in the overall cohort (p = 0.017) and in those with preserved EF (p = 0.007). The novel PSV-loop derived myocardial work measure had shown a significant difference in subtypes of aortic stenosis and had prognostic value in patients undergoing TAVR. As such volume-adjusted global constructive work may have the potential to more accurately measure LV contractility in a hemodynamic overload state. This novel approach may improve functional assessment and risk stratification in patients undergoing TAVR.GCWVi bar graph
title: Volume-adjusted myocardial work, a novel diagnostic and prognostic tool in subtypes of aortic stenosis

abstract: Abstract Background Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) procedural volumes are increasing, and advances in technology have contributed to lower complication rates and shorter hospitalizations. After TAVI, routine transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is still performed before discharge and repeated at 3-month follow-up in Denmark. However, the clinical yield of discharge TTE has not been examined systematically. Purpose To examine the clinical yield of post-procedure, pre-discharge echocardiography in TAVI patients from a contemporary cohort. Methods We included all patients who underwent TAVI in Eastern Denmark in 2023–2024. The population was stratified by simple (tricuspid valve, transfemoral access) vs complex procedures (bicuspid valve, valve-in-valve, or alternative access). The discharge TTE was defined as clinically relevant if it led to one of the following: 1) additional early follow-up TTE; 2) new transoesophageal echocardiography for further valve assessment; 3) reintervention; 4) or if it revealed post procedural fall in LVEF to &lt;40%. Results A total of 894 patients were included (62.1% male; median age 80.0 years [IQR 76.5–83.7]), of whom 723 (80.9%) underwent a simple procedure and 171 (19.1%) a complex procedure. Patients who underwent a simple procedure were older than those who underwent a complex procedure (80.6 vs 78.0 years; P&lt;0.001). Overall, comorbidities were similar between groups. Clinically relevant findings were detected in 25 (2.8%) patients: 16 (2.2%) in the simple group vs 9 (5.3%) in the complex group (P=0.03). Among these 25 patients, TTE led to additional follow-up TTE in 12 (48%), transoesophageal echocardiography for further valve assessment in 6 (24%), referral to a heart failure clinic in 6 (24%) (due to LVEF drop to &lt;40%), and reintervention in one (4%) patient (Figure). Conclusion In a contemporary TAVI cohort, approximately 3% of patients had a clinically relevant TTE finding that prompted further investigation. Among these, 6 patients were referred to a heart failure clinic and one patient underwent reintervention. These findings suggest limited overall clinical yield of routine discharge echocardiography after TAVI.
title: Clinical yield of discharge transthoracic echocardiography in transcatheter aortic valve implantation patients from a contemporary cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Aortic stenosis (AS) commonly leads to myocardial hypoperfusion in the absence of obstructive epicardial coronary disease, a potential driver of irreversible myocardial scarring, associated with cardiac decompensation and death.(1,2) Long-term prognosis following aortic valve replacement (AVR) remains poor and the determinants of reverse remodelling remain poorly understood. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) can determine myocardial remodelling, quantification of scar burden and rest/stress myocardial blood flow (MBF). Purpose Using a multi-modal approach, we aimed to demonstrate the reversal of myocardial hypoperfusion and fibrosis burden one year following aortic valve replacement for AS and to understand the predictors of post-AVR myocardial perfusion. Methods Patients with severe symptomatic AS referred for AVR were recruited and underwent deep phenotyping (CMR including adenosine stress perfusion and multiparametric mapping; echocardiography; and cardiac biomarkers [NT-proBNP/HsTnT]) at baseline and 1-year following AVR. CMR quantified extracellular volume fraction (ECV%), late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), rest and stress MBF using automated in-line pixel-wise imaging. Multivariable linear regression models were fitted to assess baseline predictors of 1-year global stress MBF. Model fit and parsimony was assessed using Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC). Results 71 patients (age 69.6±8.6years, 70.4% male, Vmax 4.2±0.4 m/s, AVA 0.82±0.22cm2/m2) underwent paired stress perfusion imaging. At a median follow-up of 389 days post AVR (55 [77.5%] surgical AVR / 16 [22.5%] TAVI), indexed left ventricular (LV) volume (-6%), mass (-20%), diffuse and focal fibrosis significantly regressed and global stress MBF improved significantly (1.78±0.49 to 2.30±0.64 ml/g/min, p&lt;0.001) (Table 1, Figure 1). The greatest improvement in perfusion was seen in the subendo- than subepicardium (+0.55±0.64 vs +0.49±0.81 ml/g/min). On multivariable linear regression, baseline LV mass (b -0.13 [-0.024 to -0.002]; p=0.022) and baseline matrix volume (b -0.003 [-0.007 to 0.000]; p=0.049) were predictors of global stress MBF at 1-year post AVR in their respective models, along with age, sex, and concomitant hypertension, independently of BMI, the presence of coronary artery disease, AS severity and baseline global stress MBF. Both models demonstrated similar model fit and parsimony (AIC 121.1 vs. 122.7). Conclusions 1 year post AVR for severe AS, left ventricular mass regression is accompanied not only by improvement of stress myocardial perfusion but also regression in focal and diffuse fibrosis. Improvement in stress myocardial blood is independently predicted by the degree of myocardial hypertrophy and diffuse fibrosis. These therefore not only provide better post AVR outcome prediction but are also promising targets for post AVR pharmacological intervention.Table 1 changes 1-year post AVRFigure 1 CMR changes post AVR
title: Myocardial blood flow in aortic stenosis: predictors of recovery after aortic valve replacement

abstract: Abstract Introduction Coronary revascularization guided by physiological assessment improves outcomes versus angiography alone, and trials have shown iFR to be noninferior to FFR at 1 year. Yet 5-year results from DEFINE-FLAIR (higher mortality with iFR) and iFR SWEDEHEART (neutral) have created uncertainty about long-term differences. We analyzed a large clinical cohort to compare FFR and iFR, evaluate prognostic performance, and apply machine learning to identify high-risk phenotypes among patients with negative physiological measurements. Methods All patients undergoing FFR or iFR assessment from 2012–2022 were included. Clinical outcomes comprised 5-year all-cause mortality, acute coronary syndrome (ACS), and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or unplanned revascularization). Outcomes were evaluated with Kaplan–Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards models. In patients with negative iFR values, unsupervised machine-learning clustering identified subgroups, which were analyzed for 5-year outcomes. Results We analyzed 1,314 physiological measurements from 915 patients (349 FFR; 566 iFR) with a mean 5.9-year follow-up. Baseline characteristics were similar and comparable to DEFINE-FLAIR, though iFR patients more often presented with ACS and had less prior PCI. All-cause mortality was higher with iFR (HR 1.52; CI 1.17–1.98), while rates of ACS, MACE, and unplanned revascularization were similar. Survival curves separated between 12–24 months, mirroring DEFINE-FLAIR. Physiologically positive lesions were numerically lower with iFR. To identify high-risk individuals within the iFR-negative population, we applied machine-learning clustering based on features distinguishing true from false negatives, identifying three clusters. Since clusters 2 and 3 showed no outcome differences, they were merged as low-risk, while cluster 1 was classified as high-risk. In five-year survival analyses, excess adverse events occurred in the high-risk group, which had higher rates of death (HR 2.6; p=0.006) and MACE (HR 1.83; p=0.03). This group was older with worse renal function, more anatomical and clinical complexity, and heavier comorbidity burden. Using the strongest prognostic variables, we built software that automatically identifies high-risk patients through an integrated risk-classification interface. Conclusion In this large real-world cohort, iFR was associated with higher 5-year mortality despite similar rates of ACS, MACE, and revascularization, echoing divergence seen in DEFINE-FLAIR. Machine-learning identified a high-risk phenotype within the iFR-negative population that accounted for the excess events. These findings challenge the assumption that a negative iFR uniformly denotes low risk and highlight the need for closer follow-up and potentially intensified management in selected patients.
title: FFR vs iFR for clinical outcomes: insights from machine-learning risk stratification

abstract: Abstract Background Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is a leading cause of aortic stenosis (AS) in younger patients. Recently, the anatomical understanding of BAV has increased, and BAV subtypes are known to also be found in calcific aortic stenosis of the elderly. With the expansion of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) into lower-risk populations, the proportion of patients with BAV undergoing TAVR is expected to increase. However, robust long-term outcome data in this population remain limited. Objectives To determine the prevalence of BAV among patients undergoing TAVR and to evaluate procedural and long-term clinical outcomes compared with tricuspid aortic valve (TAV) anatomy. Methods We retrospectively analyzed all consecutive patients undergoing TAVR at our center between 2013 and 2022. BAV morphology was assessed by pre-procedural computed tomography and classified according to the Sievers classification. Patients with missing imaging, inadequate image quality, or relevant anatomical abnormalities were excluded. The primary endpoint was 3-year all-cause mortality. Secondary endpoints included VARC-3 composite endpoints technical failure and device failure. Multivariable Cox regression was performed to adjust for baseline differences. Results Among 3,961 screened patients, 3,816 were included in the final analysis. BAV was identified in 263 patients (6.9%), predominantly Sievers type 1 (90.1%), most commonly with a raphe between the left and right coronary cusps. Compared with patients with tricuspid aortic valves, those with BAV were younger (78.2 vs. 81.9 years, p&lt;0.01) and had a lower Society of Thoracic Surgeons risk score (2.1 vs. 3.4, p&lt;0.01), as well as fewer comorbidities, including diabetes mellitus, hypertension, coronary artery disease, and chronic kidney disease. At 3 years, all-cause mortality was significantly lower in the BAV group (25.1% vs. 37.7%; hazard ratio [HR] 0.53; 95% confidence interval [CI] [0.40–0.72]; follow-up rate 93%). After multivariable adjustment, BAV remained independently associated with lower mortality (adjusted HR 0.57; 95% CI [0.43–0.77]). Technical failure (4.9% vs. 4.1%), device failure (16.0% vs. 11.6%), and procedural mortality (1.5% vs. 0.6%) were numerically higher in patients with BAV, primarily driven by paravalvular regurgitation and higher post-procedural mean transvalvular gradients. Conclusions In this large single-center cohort, BAV was present in approximately 7% of patients undergoing TAVR. Although procedural complexity and device failure were slightly increased, TAVR was associated with favorable long-term survival in patients with BAV. The observed mortality benefit is likely attributable to their younger age and lower comorbidity burden. These findings support the feasibility of TAVR in selected patients with BAV, while underscoring the need for dedicated long-term evaluation in this anatomically distinct population.All-cause mortality after three years
