title: Outcomes of transcatheter aortic valve replacement in patients with bicuspid aortic valve

abstract: Abstract Background Paravalvular leak (PVL) following transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) remains associated with adverse outcomes and increased mortality. Current risk stratification relies primarily on anatomic features from cardiac CT, which incompletely capture the complex structural and functional remodelling influencing valve seating. The AccurKardia Aortic Valve Stenosis (AK-AVS) score is an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiographic (AI-ECG) biomarker validated to detect moderate-to-severe aortic stenosis by integrating electrical consequences of structural changes including left ventricular hypertrophy, fibrosis, and conduction abnormalities. Purpose To determine whether preoperative AK-AVS scores independently predict PVL. Methods We analysed 1,456 patients who underwent TAVR at our institution (2013-2024) after excluding patients with permanent pacemakers or missing preoperative AK-AVS scores. The AK-AVS score was derived from standard 12-lead ECGs obtained within 30 days prior to TAVR. PVL was graded according to Valve Academic Research Consortium-3 criteria as none, mild, or moderate-to-severe. Multivariable logistic regression models were adjusted for AK-AVS score (scaled per 0.10 increase) and established predictors: mean gradient, aortic valve area, aortic annulus diameter, valve size, aortic valve calcium score, device type (balloon-expanding [BEV] vs. self-expanding [SEV]), and STS risk score. Receiver operating characteristic curves were generated and area under the curve (AUC) values were compared using DeLong's test. Results Of 1,456 patients, 232 (15.9%) developed PVL. Patients with PVL had higher preoperative AK-AVS scores (0.71 vs. 0.67, p=0.011), lower ejection fraction (51.6% vs. 54.5%, p&lt;0.001), larger valve size (27.3 vs. 26.2mm, p&lt;0.001), higher calcium burden (2,743 vs. 2,413 Agatston units, p=0.001), and higher STS scores (6.4% vs. 5.4%, p=0.003) (Figure 1). Each 0.10 increase in AK-AVS score independently predicted PVL (OR 1.10, 95% CI 1.03-1.22, p=0.028) after adjusting for other predictors. Addition of AK-AVS to the base clinical model improved discrimination, increasing AUC from 0.643 (95% CI 0.609-0.677) to 0.686 (95% CI 0.653-0.719), p=0.007 (Figure 2A). In ordinal regression examining PVL severity, each 0.10 increase in AK-AVS score was associated with 12% higher odds of more severe PVL (OR 1.12, 95% CI 1.03-1.22, p=0.01). A clear dose-response relationship was evident: mean AK-AVS scores were 0.67 (SD 0.20) for no PVL, 0.71 (SD 0.19) for mild PVL, and 0.78 (SD 0.18) for moderate-to-severe PVL (Figure 2B). Conclusion Preoperative AK-AVS scores independently predict PVL development and severity following TAVR, providing incremental value beyond traditional clinical, echocardiographic, and procedural risk factors. This universally available AI-ECG biomarker may aid preprocedural risk stratification and guide valve selection or procedural planning to minimize PVL risk.
title: Preoperative AI-ECG analysis predicts paravalvular leak after transcatheter aortic valve replacement

abstract: Abstract Background Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is the standard treatment for severe aortic stenosis (AS). However, prolonged waiting times expose patients to substantial pre-procedural risk. Identifying predictors of adverse events during the waiting period may support risk-based prioritization. Purpose To assess incidence and predictors of death or heart failure (HF) hospitalization while awaiting TAVI. Methods In this multicenter registry across six Italian centers, consecutive patients listed for TAVI between March 2016 and November 2024 were included. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause death or HF hospitalization during the waiting period. Predictors were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models. Results Among 1074 patients (mean age 82±5 years; 49% women), median waiting time was 133 days. During waiting, 230 patients (21.4%) reached the primary endpoint, including 49 deaths (4.6%) and 144 HF hospitalizations (13.4%). Notably, a significant clustering of mortality occurred within the first 90 days. Independent predictors of adverse events included chronic kidney disease (HR 1.78; 95%CI 1.24–2.55; p=0.002), LVEF &lt;50% (HR 1.67; p=0.004), NYHA class III (HR 1.70; p=0.020), anemia (HR 1.46; p=0.025), and high-risk clinical presentation (HR 1.50; p=0.018). Conclusions One in five patients awaiting TAVI experiences death or HF hospitalization, with a critical early vulnerability window. Risk-stratified prioritization based on renal function, systolic dysfunction, and symptom severity may reduce avoidable pre-procedural morbidity and mortality.Table 1:predictors of events on waiting listFigure 1:death on waiting list
title: Incidence and predictors of deaht and heart failure hospitalization on TAVI waiting list: a multicenter italian registry

abstract: Abstract Background Patients with small aortic annuli undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) are at risk of higher residual transvalvular gradients. Evidence on the performance of new-generation intra-annular self-expanding valves in this anatomical setting remains limited. We evaluated the impact of annular size on procedural, hemodynamic, and clinical outcomes after TAVI with the Navitor valve. Methods Patients were stratified by annular area measured by multi-slice computed tomography, defining small annulus as ≤430 mm². Primary endpoints at 12 months were: (i) a clinical composite of all-cause death, disabling stroke, or heart failure rehospitalization and (ii) a composite endpoint of bioprosthetic valve dysfunction. Secondary endpoints included VARC-3–defined procedural and early outcomes and valve hemodynamic performance. Results The study population consisted in 218 patients, including 91 (41.7%) with a small annulus. VARC-3 technical success was high and comparable between small and non-small annuli (96.7% vs. 96.1%). Patients with small annuli had higher early post-procedural mean transvalvular gradients (7.7 ± 3.8 vs. 6.6 ± 3.0 mmHg; p=0.029) and smaller effective orifice areas index (1.1 ± 0.3 vs. 1.3 ± 0.2 cm²/m2; p=0.037), while the incidence of mean gradients ≥20 mmHg remained low (1.1% vs. 0.0%; p=0.432). At 12 months, the clinical composite endpoint occurred in 8.8% of patients with small annuli and 10.2% with non-small annuli (p=0.759). Bioprosthetic valve dysfunction was infrequent and similar between groups (6.6% vs. 6.3%; p=0.875). Conclusions TAVI with the Navitor valve was associated with high procedural success, favourable valve hemodynamics, and comparable mid-term clinical outcomes irrespective of annular size.12-months clinical and Haemodynamic Outcomes
title: Impact of aortic annulus size on clinical and hemodynamic outcomes of transcatheter aortic valve implantation with the navitor valve

abstract: Abstract Background New-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) and left bundle branch block (LBBB) frequently occur after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). Although both have been linked to adverse outcomes, prior studies are limited by residual confounding and time-dependent bias, leaving uncertainty as to whether these conditions represent independent prognostic factors or simply markers of higher baseline risk.1–3 Purpose To evaluate the association of NOAF and new-onset LBBB detected at 7 days post-TAVR by 12-channel ambulatory ECG or 24-hour Holter ECG with all-cause mortality using a propensity score–matched landmark analysis. Methods This retrospective observational cohort study included patients undergoing TAVR at a high-volume tertiary care center between January 2012 and December 2023 (n = 2,488). The population was elderly (mean age 82 years, 95% CI 79–83), with mean left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 53.3% (95% CI 52.7–53.8) and EuroSCORE II 6.1% (95% CI 5.8–6.3). Most were symptomatic at baseline, with 82% in NYHA class II–III. Mean follow-up was 39 months (95% CI 33–45). A 7-day landmark analysis was performed to mitigate immortal time bias; NOAF and LBBB were assessed at this time point, including only patients alive and event-free. Propensity scores were estimated using logistic regression (age, sex, body mass index, EuroSCORE II, NYHA class, baseline LVEF), and patients were matched 1:1 using nearest-neighbour matching without replacement. Covariate balance was assessed using standardised mean differences (&lt;0.1), yielding matched cohorts of 1,193 patients for NOAF and 916 for LBBB. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality. Survival was analysed using Kaplan–Meier estimates and Cox proportional hazards models. Results In landmark analyses, NOAF was associated with significantly higher mortality (log-rank p = 0.001; HR 1.46, 95% CI 1.23–1.75). This association persisted after multivariable adjustment in the unmatched cohort (adjusted HR 1.38, 95% CI 1.16–1.65; p &lt; 0.005). Addition of NOAF significantly improved model fit (likelihood-ratio χ² = 46.7, p &lt; 0.001), despite only a modest increase in discrimination (C-index 0.614 to 0.622). In contrast, LBBB at 7 days was not associated with mortality in the matched cohort (log-rank p = 0.712; HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.73–1.24) or after multivariable adjustment in the unmatched cohort, including among patients with LVEF &lt; 40% (p = 0.811). Furthermore, LBBB was not associated with new pacemaker implantation (adjusted OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.897–1.028; p = 0.694). Conclusions In an elderly TAVR population, NOAF at 7 days post-TAVR was independently associated with adverse long-term outcomes and provided incremental prognostic information beyond established risk factors. In contrast, LBBB at 7 days was not associated with adverse outcomes. Prospective randomised studies are warranted to determine whether targeted management of NOAF improves clinical outcomes.Kaplan-Meier Estimate for NOAFKaplan-Meier Estimate for New-LBBB
title: Prognostic impact of new-onset atrial fibrillation and left bundle branch block after TAVR: a propensity-matched landmark analysis

abstract: Abstract Background The introduction of a dedicated prosthesis for transcatheter treatment of patients with severe isolated aortic valve regurgitation (JenaValve Trilogy®) offers an interventional treatment option for patients unable to undergo surgical valve replacement. It is currently not known what proportion of all-comer patients with isolated aortic regurgitation unsuitable for surgery has appropriate valve anatomy for treatment with this transcatheter heart valve. Similarly, the specific reasons that preclude placement of the valve prosthesis have not been systematically explored. Methods An all-comer cohort of 107 consecutive patients with symptomatic aortic valve disease under consideration for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) using the Trilogy Valve (JenaValve®) was included in this analysis. A detailed echocardiographic and computed tomographic (CT)-based assessment of aortic root anatomy and dimensions was performed. Mechanisms of aortic regurgitation, screening failure rate, and reasons for unsuitability were identified and compared between eligible and non-eligible patients. Results Out of 107 consecutive patients who underwent diagnostic workup prior to TAVI using the Trilogy Valve, 57 were excluded due to previous valve replacement, mixed aortic valve pathology including stenosis, or indications for TAVI using the Trilogy Valve other than isolated aortic regurgitation. Consequently, 50 patients were included (77±9 years, 22 females (44%), left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 46±11%, vena contracta 6.5±1 mm, New York Heart Association (NYHA) class III in 50% and class II in 43%). Mechanisms of aortic regurgitation were as follows: 22% prolapse of the right coronary cusp, 20% prolapse of the non-coronary cusp, 16% annular dilatation, 34% degenerative disease, 4% bicuspid degenerative disease, 1 patient with prolapse of the left coronary cusp. Anatomy was suitable for implantation of the Trilogy Valve in 27 patients (54%), and unsuitable in 23 (46%). Reasons for screening failure included: large annular dimensions (61%), unfavourable aortic anatomy (22%), severe leaflet restriction (9%), bicuspid valve morphology (4%), and small annular dimensions (4%). Unsuitable patients had larger annular dimensions than suitable patients (mean diameter 27 vs 25.4 mm; area 588 vs 509 mm²; perimeter 87 vs 81 mm; all p&lt;0.05). Other CT parameters such as the presence and degree of aortic valve calcification, aortic root angle, eccentricity index, and aortic dimensions were not significantly different between both groups. Conclusion Among patients with isolated aortic valve regurgitation at high risk for conventional surgery, approximately 50% were eligible for transcatheter treatment with the currently available models of the Trilogy heart valve. The most frequent reasons for non-eligibility include large annular dimensions or unfavourable anatomy of the aortic valve cusps.
title: Aortic valve anatomy and feasibility of transcatheter bioprosthetic valve implantation in isolated aortic regurgitation

abstract: Abstract Objectives Aortic valve (AV) repair has emerged as an increasingly adopted surgical alternative to aortic valve replacement (AVR) in bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) patients. Although several favorable anatomic and functional predictors have been described, a standardized methodology for identifying patients with optimal characteristics for AV repair is lacking. This study aims to develop and internally validate a novel scoring system - the HOME score - based on routine transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) to assess the likelihood of successful BAV repair of BAV repair. Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of 203 consecutive patients who underwent surgery for isolated BAV regurgitation (2018-2024). Preoperative TEE parameters were systematically analyzed to identify factors associated with successful surgical repair. Results Four baseline TEE measurements emerged as powerful, independent parameters associated with BAV repair in multivariate analysis: geometric height≥18 mm (Odds Ratio [OR]: 8.05; 95% confidence interval (CI): 3.15 to 22.94; p=&lt;0.001), commissural orientation≥140° (OR: 8.29; 95% CI: 2.67-25.67; p=&lt;0.001), undamaged leaflets (OR: 20.4; 95% CI 6.59-63.53; p=&lt;0.001), and preserved leaflet mobility (OR: 11.1; 95% CI: 3.98-31.45; p=&lt;0.001). We integrated these findings into the simple, 9-point HOME score. The score demonstrated excellent discrimination for successful repair (Area Under the Curve = 0.89), effectively stratifying patients into groups with low (score 0 – 4), intermediate (5 – 6), and high (7 – 9) likelihoods of a valve-preserving surgery. Conclusions The HOME score may help identify BAV patients with a high probability of AV repair in a more standardized and reliable way. Its utility and accuracy require validation in larger, multicenter cohorts.
title: The HOME score: an echocardiographic scoring system for bicuspid aortic valve repair

abstract: Abstract Background Combined aortic regurgitation (AR) and mitral regurgitation (MR) is a relatively common multiple valvular heart disease. Current guidelines recommend intervention (AVI and/or MVI) when either lesion becomes severe in the setting of symptoms, left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction or dilation, as in isolated severe AR and MR, but no evidence has been generated specifically for this combination. Purpose To compare survival among patients with significant combined AR and MR (≥ moderate AR and ≥ moderate MR) and those with isolated severe AR in a multicenter setting. Methods A total of 421 patients (age 66 ± 15 years, 68% male) were included. Of these, 108 had isolated severe AR. Patients with concomitant AR and MR (n=313) were classified into 4 groups according to regurgitation severity: moderate AR with moderate MR (n = 145), moderate AR with severe MR (n = 70), severe AR with moderate MR (n = 46), and severe AR with severe MR (n = 52). Regurgitation severity was determined using a multiparametric approach, in accordance with current ESC/EACVI guidelines. The study endpoint was all-cause mortality, with valve intervention accounted as a time-dependent covariate. Results Over a median follow-up of 6 years (IQR 2-10), 147 (35%) patients died. A total of 221 (53%) patients underwent either AVI or MVI. Patients with isolated severe AR were younger, had more prevalence of bicuspid aortic valve (BAV), while patients with moderate AR and MR were older and more often female (Table 1). Patients with severe AR and MR had larger LV dimensions, and those with associated severe MR had more prevalence of atrial fibrillation (AF), primary MR and larger left atrial volume index (LAVI). After multivariable adjustment for age, New York Heart Association (NYHA) class, hypertension, diabetes, coronary artery disease, AF, BAV, LAVI, LV end-systolic diameter index, LV stroke volume index, tricuspid regurgitation and valve intervention, increasing severity of AR and MR was independently associated with progressively worse survival (Figure 1A). Adjusted survival curves (for the same variables, Figure 1B) showed that patients with combined moderate AR and MR, had survival comparable to patients with isolated severe AR. In contrast, severe AR with moderate or severe MR showed the worst survival (HR 2.98; 95% CI 1.21-7.33; p=0.017 and HR 3.30; 95% CI 1.36-8.04; p=0.009, respectively) (Figure 1B). Conclusion Among patients with combined AR and MR, severe degree of any regurgitation is independently associated with worse long-term survival. Interestingly, patients with combined moderate AR and moderate MR have adjusted outcomes comparable to those with isolated severe AR, suggesting the significantly increased risk also of a combined moderate valve disease.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Long-term outcomes of combined significant aortic regurgitation and mitral regurgitation versus isolated aortic regurgitation

abstract: Abstract Background In chronic severe aortic regurgitation (AR), left ventricular (LV) remodeling and prognosis differ by sex. However, sex-specific differences in LV remodeling patterns and their prognostic implications remain incompletely defined. Purpose We aimed to investigate the sex differences in the degree of LV remodeling and clinical outcomes among patients with chronic severe AR. Methods We analyzed a multicenter cohort from three tertiary centers, including 1,149 patients (754 men, 403 women) with chronic severe AR. LV remodeling was assessed by echocardiographic linear, volumetric, and functional parameters, including LV ejection fraction (LVEF) and LV global longitudinal strain (LVGLS). The primary outcome was a composite of cardiac death or heart failure hospitalization. Aortic valve replacement was treated as a time-dependent covariate. Results Women had smaller absolute LV dimensions and volumes but relatively larger indexed LV end-systolic diameters, while indexed LV volumes remained smaller than in men. Despite these geometric differences, LV systolic function was better preserved in women, with higher LVEF and more favorable LVGLS. During a median follow-up of 6.2 years, women underwent aortic valve replacement less frequently than men (35.4% vs. 56.4%, p &lt; 0.001), despite similar clinical outcomes. In sex-specific multivariable models, LV functional parameters demonstrated the robust prognostic performance in women, with LVGLS showing the highest discrimination (C-index, 0.78–0.79). In contrast, LV chamber size–related parameters were more predictive in men. Conclusions LV remodeling and its prognostic significance differ substantially by sex in chronic severe AR. In women, functional impairment assessed by LVGLS is particularly prognostic, even when conventional criteria are preserved. Incorporating LVGLS into a sex-specific approach may improve risk stratification and clinical decision-making in severe AR.Incremental prognostic value
title: Sex-specific prognostic value of global longitudinal strain beyond ventricular remodeling in chronic severe aortic regurgitation

abstract: Abstract Background At present, there is no comparative assessment of pooled clinical outcomes between patients with aortic valve regurgitation (AR) and those with aortic valve stenosis (AS) who underwent transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Purpose A systematic review to examine the clinical outcomes of TAVI in patients with AR compared to those with AS. Methods A meta-analysis was conducted according to the Cochrane Handbook and the PRISMA statement. A comprehensive systematic electronic literature search was conducted from inspection to June 11, 2025. RStudio software was used to calculate the pooled odds ratio (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). A Random-effects model was used to allow a more conservative approach. A p-value of &lt;0.05 was set as the statistical significance. Results Nine cohort observational studies were included. Overall, baseline characteristics did not differ between the comparison groups. In patients with AR, TAVI was associated with significantly higher rates of conversion to open heart surgery (OR 3.63, 95% CI: 2.23; 5.91), bleeding (OR 1.23, 95% CI: 1.01; 1.51), and all-cause death (OR 2.00, 95% CI: 1.25; 3.20) than those with AS post procedure before hospital discharge. There was no difference between the groups in terms of procedure success, presence of paravalvular leak, need for a second device or permanent pacemaker (PPM), stroke, or length of hospital stay. Outcomes at 30-days and longer-term follow-up did not differ between the groups in terms of the need for PPM, aortic valve re-intervention, stroke, and death (Figure 1). Conclusion TAVI in patients with AR was associated with worse post procedural outcomes but not at follow-up. Future investigations are warranted to identify potential risk factors in patients with AR to ensure post procedure safety.Procedural and clinical outcomes
title: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation in aortic regurgitation versus aortic stenosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background The prognostic significance of longitudinal change in CCTA derived fractional flow reserve (CT-FFR) in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) remains incompletely defined. We aim to investigate whether hemodynamic changes during serial CCTA examinations are associated with an increased risk of MACE. Methods We studied 949 patients who underwent two CCTA examinations with CT-FFR assessment (mean interval between scans: 2.5 years) and followed them for a mean of 4.5 years. MACE was defined as unstable angina, myocardial infarction, and cardiac death. CT-FFR analysis methods included: (1) Longitudinal change classification: stable (|ΔCT-FFR|&lt;0.03), improved (ΔCT-FFR≥0.03), and worsened (ΔCT-FFR≤−0.03); (2) State transition analysis using a 0.80 threshold: CT-FFR &gt; 0.80, CT-FFR ≤ 0.80 → &gt; 0.80, CT-FFR &gt; 0.80 → ≤ 0.80, and CT-FFR ≤ 0.80. Results Compared with the functional stability group (n=402, 42.4%), the functional deterioration group (n=277, 29.2%) exhibited a higher risk of MACE (aHR 2.3, 95% CI 1.32–3.96, P=0.003), while the functionally improved group (n=270, 28.5%) showed a non-significant trend (aHR 1.7, 95% CI 0.92–3.01, P=0.09). Compared with functionally stable patients (n=697, 73.4%), the functionally persistent abnormal group (CT-FFR ≤0.80; n=122, 12.9%) had the highest risk (aHR 4.6, 95% CI 2.73–7.66, P&lt;0.001); patients in the functional deterioration group (CT-FFR&gt;0.80→≤0.80; n=70, 7.4%) exhibited significantly higher MACE risk (aHR 3.4, 95% CI 1.73–6.72, P&lt;0.001). Patients in the functionally abnormal-to-normal group (≤0.80→&gt;0.80; n=60, 6.3%) exhibited residual risk that did not reach statistical significance (aHR 2.1, 95% CI 0.91–5.15, P=0.08). Conclusions In CAD patients, functional deterioration from CCTA is independently associated with an increased risk of long-term major cardiovascular events. Furthermore, persistent functional deterioration and progression from normal to abnormal levels can identify high-risk patients, supporting the value of risk stratification through repeated functional assessment using CT-FFR.CT-FFR
title: Predictive value of serial coronary CTA-derived fractional flow reserve in patients with coronary artery disease

abstract: Abstract Background Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) disease has long been considered a substrate for accelerated aortopathy, characterized by earlier valvular degeneration and progressive enlargement of the thoracic aorta. Whether this presumed intrinsic aortic vulnerability persists after aortic valve replacement remains unclear. Comparative data between BAV and tricuspid aortic valve (TAV) populations following valve intervention are heterogeneous and have not been comprehensively synthesized. Therefore, a systematic review and meta-analysis was performed to evaluate postoperative aortic growth and major aortic complications after valve replacement in BAV versus TAV patients. Methods A systematic search of MEDLINE, CENTRAL and Web of Science, covering the period from database inception to April 2025, was performed to identify prospective and retrospective cohort studies enrolling adult patients with BAV or TAV undergoing surgical (SAVR) or transcatheter (TAVI) aortic valve replacement. Eligible studies were required to report longitudinal measurements of aortic growth rate (mm/year) and/or the occurrence of aortic dissection or aortic reintervention. Studies involving concomitant aortic surgical repair were excluded. Random-effects meta-analytic models were applied to estimate mean differences (MD) and risk ratios (RR), along with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results Fifteen studies met inclusion criteria. Quantitative synthesis included 1,772 patients for aortic growth rate analysis, 2,307 for aortic dissection, and 2,598 for aortic reintervention. Across studies, annual aortic growth rate following valve replacement did not significantly differ between BAV and TAV patients (MD 0.15 mm/year; 95% CI −0.03 to 0.33; p = 0.09, I² = 82.6%). Meta-regression confirmed that age disparities between BAV and TAV cohorts were not associated with any modification of the overall neutral effect on aortic growth. Subgroup analyses yielded consistent results across study designs, although modest differences were observed according to procedure type (SAVR: MD 0.21 mm/year, p=0.07; TAVI: MD −0.04 mm/year, p=0.53; p=0.02 for interaction between SAVR and TAVI). Regarding clinical events, pooled analyses revealed no statistically significant differences in the risk of aortic dissection (RR 1.34; 95% CI 0.63–2.83; p = 0.44) or need for future aortic reintervention (RR 0.95; 95% CI 0.56–1.61; p = 0.84). Conclusions Aortic expansion and event rates after valve intervention were comparable between BAV and TAV patients. These findings challenge the long-standing assumption that bicuspid morphology–associated pathophysiological mechanisms intrinsically drive accelerated postoperative aortic disease across all patients.Figure 1
title: Ascending aortic growth and risk of aortic sissection or reintervention after valve replacement in bicuspid and tricuspid aortic valve disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Aims Because mixed aortic valve disease (MAVD) has complex hemodynamic characteristics, grading its severity remains challenging. We propose a new approach for grading MAVD based on the deviation of mean pressure gradient (PG) from the expected value, which may better reflect the overall hemodynamic burden. Methods and Results Between 2008 and 2020, a total of 7,075 patients with moderate to severe aortic stenosis (AS) (aortic valve area ≤1.5 cm2) were enrolled from three tertiary centers. MAVD was defined as the presence of concomitant mild or greater aortic regurgitation (AR). Patients with isolated AS were used as the reference population to estimate expected mean PG by modeling the relationship between aortic valve area and mean PG. The primary outcome was cardiac death or hospitalization for heart failure (HHF). Among the 7,075 patients with moderate or severe AS, 3,647 (51.5%) had isolated AS and 1,677 (48.5%) had MAVD. The incidence of cardiac death or HHF was higher in the MAVD group compared with the isolated AS group (log rank p=0.032). In the MAVD group, a greater measured mean PG relative to the expected value was associated with a lower risk of cardiac death or HHF (per +10%, adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.92–0.99; p=0.004) but with a higher risk of aortic valve replacement (AVR) (aHR 1.10; 95% CI 1.08–1.13; p&lt;0.001). These associations remained significant after adjustment for conventional AR grading. MAVD patients in the highest quartile of mean PG deviation had a risk of cardiac death or HHF comparable to those with isolated AS, but a higher risk of AVR. Conclusions In patients with MAVD, the directional deviation of mean PG from the expected value derived from isolated AS was independently associated with the risk of cardiac death or HHF, beyond conventional AR grading.Outcome by the deviation from ref. mean PGStratification by the mean PG deviation
title: Pressure gradient deviation predicts outcomes in mixed aortic valve disease: a novel stratification framework

abstract: Abstract Background Mitral regurgitation (MR) is a prevalent valvular disease, and mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER) is recommended for patients with severe MR who are inoperable or at high surgical risk. While M-TEER has shown comparable outcomes to conventional surgery, over 10% of patients experience mortality, and nearly 15% are rehospitalized for heart failure within the first year. This study aimed to assess the prognostic value of advanced right ventricular (RV) function parameters in predicting major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) following M-TEER using the MitraClip system. Methods This retrospective cohort study analyzed 60 patients who underwent M-TEER between March 2015 and November 2023. Echocardiographic assessments were performed at baseline, post-procedure (before discharge), and at 6-month follow-up. Advanced echocardiographic parameters, including tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion to pulmonary artery systolic pressure (TAPSE/PASP), TAPSE normalized to right ventricular end-diastolic area (TAPSE/RVAD), and TAPSE normalized to right ventricular end-systolic area (TAPSE/RVAS), were evaluated for their predictive value for MACE. Right ventricular myocardial work (RVMW) indices, including RV global work index (RVGWI), RV global constructive work (RVGCW), RV global wasted work (RVGWW), and RV global work efficiency (RVGWE), were also analyzed. MACE, including all-cause death, heart failure hospitalization, and stroke, were assessed at one year of follow-up. Results TAPSE/PASP, TAPSE/RVAD, and TAPSE/RVAS were significant predictors of MACE in both univariate and multivariate analyses. Pre-procedural TAPSE/RVAD (coefficient estimate: 0.697, 95% CI: 0.569–0.853, p=0.001) with a cut-off value of 1.1, and pre-procedural TAPSE/RVAS (coefficient estimate: 0.823, 95% CI: 0.731–0.926, p=0.002) with a cut-off value of 1.5, were strong independent predictors of MACE. TAPSE/PASP also remained an independent predictor (p=0.0247) with a cut-off value of 0.35. The AUC values from the multivariate models ranged from 0.76 to 0.80, indicating moderate to strong predictive performance (Figure 1). RVMW indices, however, showed limited prognostic value, with AUC values below 0.60 across all time points. Conclusion TAPSE/PASP, TAPSE/RVAD, and TAPSE/RVAS emerged as significant independent predictors of MACE in patients undergoing M-TEER, underscoring the importance of comprehensive RV assessment for risk stratification. Although RVMW indices did not demonstrate strong prognostic value in this cohort, their role in RV functional evaluation warrants further investigation in larger studies.
title: Advanced and novel echocardiographic right ventricular function parameters predict outcomes after percutaneous mitral valve repair

abstract: Abstract Background Patients undergoing transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) for severe functional mitral regurgitation (FMR) exhibit heterogeneous structural substrates reflecting atrial and ventricular phenotypes. The prognostic significance of phenotype and global cardiac damage burden remains incompletely defined. Purpose To characterize phenotypic and prognostic differences between atrial and ventricular FMR and assess the prognostic performance of cardiac damage staging. Methods We analyzed 225 consecutive patients undergoing mitral TEER (April 2018 - January 2025). Atrial phenotype (AFMR) was prespecified as LVEF ≥50%, left atrial volume index ≥40 ml/m², and LV end-diastolic volume &lt;159 ml; others were classified as ventricular phenotype (VFMR). Baseline cardiac damage stage (Genereux classification) was assessed. 1-year follow-up echo was available in 127 patients. The primary composite endpoint was all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalization. Results Mean age was 79.2 years and 78 patients (34.7%) met AFMR criteria. Patients were stratified according to cardiac damage stage as stage 1 (n=2), stage 2 (n=44), stage 3 (n=60), and stage 4 (n=119). For outcome analyses, stages were grouped as early (stages 1–2), intermediate (stage 3), and advanced (stage 4). Patients were highly symptomatic at baseline (NYHA 3.01±0.54; NT-proBNP 3211 pg/mL). Symptoms were similar between phenotypes at baseline, although NT-proBNP was higher in VFMR (p&lt;0.001). Median follow-up was 1025 days (IQR 477–1908). At 1-year, significant improvement occurred across the cohort, phenotypes, and damage stages with significant reductions in NYHA class and NT-proBNP(p&lt;0.001). The primary composite endpoint occurred in 18.7% at 1 year and 31.1% overall and was lower in AFMR than VFMR (9.0% vs 23.8% and 21.8% vs 36.1%). AFMR was associated with lower event risk (HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.33–0.98; p=0.043). Cardiac damage stage at baseline predicted outcome (HR 1.42 per stage, p=0.032) with stepwise reduction in 1-year event-free survival (89.1%, 85.0%, 80.7%). In baseline echocardiography, AFMR demonstrated less leaflet tethering with smaller tenting height (8.4 vs 9.9 mm, p=0.005), tenting area (2.23 vs 2.74 cm², p=0.001), anterior leaflet angle (24.0° vs 28.6°, p&lt;0.001), and posterior leaflet angle (24.9° vs 31.7°, p&lt;0.001). At 1 year, echocardiography demonstrated significant reverse remodeling, although phenotype-specific differences between AFMR and VFMR persisted. Conclusion In patients undergoing TEER for severe FMR, AFMR demonstrates less leaflet tethering and lower event risk, while cardiac damage stage provides prognostic stratification. Global cardiac damage burden and phenotype appear to be stronger determinants of outcome than MR severity alone.Figure 1:KM curves AFMR vs VFMRFigure 2:KM curves by cardiac damage stages
title: Prognostic implications of phenotype and cardiac damage stage in patients with severe functional mitral regurgitation undergoing transcatheter edge-to-edge repair

abstract: Abstract Introduction Primary mitral regurgitation (PMR) causes left atrial (LA) and left ventricular (LV) dilatation, with subsequent LV hypertrophy1,2. In treating PMR, MV repair (MVr) is recommended over MV replacement (MVR) if possible2. Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) is reserved for those at high surgical risk. MV intervention (MVI) causes significant reductions in LA and LV size, with cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) considered the gold standard to assess LA and LV size and function. Prior work shows similar reverse remodelling following MVr or MVR, but comparison with patients post-TEER has not been assessed before with CMR3. Purpose To assess reverse remodelling processes in patients with PMR undergoing MVr, MVR or TEER using CMR, to assess differences post MVI. Methods This was a prospective single centre study of patients with severe PMR listed for MVI. Severe PMR was confirmed on echocardiography prior to recruitment, and type of MVI decided by the local multidisciplinary Heart Team2. Patients with secondary MR, significant aortic valve disease, and New York Heart Association class IV were excluded. Participants underwent 6-minute walk test (6MWT) and CMR within 1-month prior to MVI, and 6-months after. CMR protocol included cine and phase contrast imaging. Results One hundred and one patients were recruited. Patients undergoing TEER were significantly older, with higher rates of diuretic use. TEER patients also had higher surgical risk scores, and worse baseline 6MWT (table-1). There were no significant differences between the groups in LV size or function, by indexed LV end-diastolic volume (LVEDVi) and effective forward LV ejection fraction (EF-LVEF) (table-1). There were no significant differences in LA size or MR severity in the three groups. Patients underwent MVR (n=40), MVr (n=43) and TEER (n=18). Patients post-TEER had significantly more residual MR compared to MVR or MVr (table-2). Despite this there were no significant differences in LVEDVi, indexed LV mass, or EF-LVEF between the three cohorts. LA and RA sizes were significantly larger in the TEER cohort, with significantly more TR at visit 2. All three cohorts had significant reductions in LVEDVi and EF-LVEF post-MVI (table-2). All three groups had significant reductions in MR severity, but only MVR and MVr cohorts had significant reductions in LA size. All groups had significant improvements in patient reported quality of life and 6MWT (table 2). The TEER cohort had significantly higher all-cause and cardiovascular mortality over a median 5.5-year follow-up. Conclusion This study demonstrates patients undergoing TEER had significantly more residual MR than with other MVI modalities. Despite higher levels of residual MR with TEER, LV reverse remodelling post-MVI is similar regardless of MVI. LA reverse remodelling was only seen after MVR or MVr. Whilst larger studies are required, these data may affect future TEER use.
title: Cardiac remodelling and clinical outcomes following surgical and transcatheter mitral valve interventions

abstract: Abstract Background Transvenous cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) leads across the tricuspid valve may present anatomical challenges for transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER). However, the safety and efficacy of T-TEER in these patients are unclear. Methods We conducted a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library from inception through November 2025 for studies comparing T-TEER in patients with versus without transvalvular CIED leads. Pooled risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using a random-effects model. Results Six studies comprising 4,891 patients (1,240 with and 3,651 without CIEDs) were included. Procedural success was comparable between the two groups (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.98–1.02, p=0.96; I2=0%). At discharge, successful TR reduction (≤ 2) was similarly achieved in both cohorts (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.94–1.04, p=0.60; I2=0%), with results remaining comparable for sustained TR ≤ 2 (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.90–1.02, p=0.20; I2=0%) and functional improvement to NYHA class ≤ II (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.89–1.01, p=0.12; I2=0%) at mid-term follow-up. CIED presence was not statistically associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, heart failure-related hospitalization, or tricuspid reintervention. Conclusion In this meta-analysis, procedural success, sustained TR reduction, and mid-term clinical outcomes were similar between patients undergoing T-TEER with and without CIEDS leads, supporting T-TEER as a feasible and safe option in selected patients.Graphical Abstractprevalence of TI regurgitation severity
title: Outcomes of tricuspid transcatheter edge-to-edge repair in patients with cardiac implantable electronic devices: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Right atrial (RA) remodeling is increasingly recognized as a determinant of status and outcomes in severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR), yet longitudinal RA structural, functional, and geometric trajectories after transcatheter tricuspid edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER) remain poorly defined. Objectives To characterize longitudinal RA remodeling after T-TEER and to identify determinants of late RA structural re-dilatation and acute and late changes in RA function. Methods We performed a single-center retrospective analysis of a prospectively enrolled cohort of 131 patients undergoing T-TEER between March 2021–December 2025. Serial transthoracic echocardiography was analyzed by a blinded core laboratory at baseline, pre-discharge, 6 months, and 12 months. RA volume index (RAVI) was measured by the area–length method; RA reservoir function was quantified as peak right atrial strain (PARS) by 2D speckle tracking; RA geometry was assessed by the RA sphericity ratio (RASR). Longitudinal changes were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models. Late structural remodeling was defined as %ΔRAVI from pre-discharge to 12 months. Associations between RASR and %ΔRAVI were tested using correlation and multivariable regression adjusted for baseline RAVI, rhythm, and residual TR. Results RAVI demonstrated a biphasic trajectory (χ²(3)=45.06, p&lt;0.001): 69.9 mL/m² (95% CI 64.8–75.1) at baseline, 58.7 (53.5–63.8) pre-discharge, 63.0 (57.7–68.3) at 6 months, and 68.8 (63.3–74.3) at 12 months. In contrast, PARS declined acutely from 11.3% (95% CI 10.3–12.4) to 9.6% (8.5–10.6) at pre-discharge (p=0.002) and showed no recovery through 12 months. In patients with durable procedural success, baseline right atrial geometry independently predicted late structural remodeling: for each +0.10 increase in baseline right atrial sphericity ratio (RASR), late right atrial re-dilatation (%ΔRAVI from pre-discharge to 12 months) decreased by 9.11% (95% CI −16.9 to −1.4; p = 0.022). Acute PARS reduction was independently associated with change in RV free-wall longitudinal strain (β=−0.17 per 1%, p=0.045) and baseline PARS (p&lt;0.001), whereas no variable predicted late PARS change (all p&gt;0.2). Conclusions After T-TEER, RA remodeling is characterized by a marked structure–function dissociation: biphasic volumetric unloading with late re-dilatation, alongside persistent functional impairment. Baseline RA geometry (RASR) identifies patients at risk for late structural failure, while RA functional recovery appears limited, supporting a dominant role of atrial myocardial substrate in shaping remodeling after valve intervention.Central FigureRight atrial geometry and RA re-dilatation
title: Right atrial phenotype determines structural reversibility after transcatheter tricuspid repair

abstract: Abstract Background Advanced imaging in tricuspid regurgitation (TR) has revealed substantial variability in tricuspid valve morphology beyond the classical tri-leaflet configuration, with many patients exhibiting additional or non-uniform leaflet segments. Such anatomical complexity may increase procedural difficulty during tricuspid transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER). The Hahn et al. classification provides a standardized framework for morphological assessment of the tricuspid valve (TV). Aims To evaluate the impact of tricuspid valve morphology on procedural efficacy and clinical outcomes following T-TEER. Methods This analysis is based on the multicentre, real-world EuroTR registry, including patients with relevant tricuspid regurgitation undergoing T-TEER between 2016 and 2025 at 20 European centres. Tricuspid valve morphology was systematically classified according to Hahn et al., and patients were stratified accordingly. Procedural efficacy was assessed by TR reduction at discharge using a cumulative link mixed model. Clinical outcomes were evaluated by Kaplan–Meier analysis, with a composite endpoint of all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalization. Results Among 726 patients with sufficient imaging quality for morphological stratification (median age 80 years [IQR 76–84]; 55% female), the distribution of TV morphologies closely mirrored that reported by Hahn et al., with Type I (52.9%) and Type IIIb (25.3%) being most prevalent. Baseline characteristics were well balanced across morphology groups. Baseline TR severity differed between morphology types, with Type II morphology associated with more severe TR, reflected by a larger effective regurgitant orifice area (p=0.012). Type I morphology was associated with the most pronounced TR reduction and superior procedural efficacy compared with Type IIIb (p=0.02; OR 1.86 [95% CI 1.10–3.13]) and with all other morphology types pooled due to smaller sample sizes (p=0.001; OR 2.63 [95% CI 1.53–4.53]) (Figure 1A). Despite more severe baseline regurgitation severity, TR reduction in Type II morphology was comparable to that observed in Type I (p=0.121; OR 1.78 [95% CI 0.89–3.57]). Kaplan–Meier analysis of the composite endpoint of all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalization at three years revealed no significant differences between morphology types (Figure 1B). Conclusion In this large real-world registry, the distribution of TV morphologies closely reflected that previously reported by Hahn et al. While Type I anatomy was statistically most amenable to T-TEER and achieved the greatest TR reduction, long-term clinical outcomes were comparable across morphology types.Figure 1
title: Impact of tricuspid valve morphology on outcomes after transcatheter edge-to-edge repair: insights from the euroTR registry

abstract: Abstract Background While transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR) improves quality of life and reduces heart failure hospitalization (HFH) in patients with symptomatic severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR), a considerable residual risk of cardiovascular events remains. Purpose We sought to evaluate whether estimated right atrial pressure (RAP) assessed by transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) after successful TTVR can stratify the risk of cardiovascular events and to identify the determinants of persistent RAP elevation. Methods A total of 119 consecutive patients underwent TTVR at our institution between 2018 - 2025. After excluding patients who died within 30 days (n = 9) or had unavailable TTE data (n = 2), 108 patients were included in the analysis. RAP was estimated with TTE 30 days after TTVR based on inferior vena cava diameter and collapsibility, classified as 3, 8, 15, and 20 mmHg. Patients were stratified into 2 groups: low RAP (3 or 8 mmHg, n = 47) and high RAP (15 or 20 mmHg, n = 61). Kaplan-Meier analysis with a 30-day landmark was performed for the composite of cardiovascular death or HFH, and event rate were compared using the log-rank test. Logistic regression was also performed to identify baseline predictors of high RAP following TTVR. Results Mean age was 74.8 years, and 57% were female. Patients with high RAP after TTVR was more likely to be male, have ascites, higher TRI-SCORE, higher dose of diuretics, lower albumin and hemoglobin levels, and a greater prevalence of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) &lt; 50%, and basal RV diameter &gt; 49 mm. On right heart catheterization, these patients exhibited higher RAP, higher mean pulmonary artery pressure, and higher post-capillary wedge pressure with lower pulmonary artery pulsatile index (PAPi), compared with those with low RAP after TTVR. The 1-year cumulative incidence of the composite of cardiovascular death or HFH was significantly higher in patients with high RAP compared with those with low RAP (23.9% vs. 6.1%, log rank P = 0.009) (Figure). Even after restricting the analysis to patients with baseline RAP of 15 or 20 mmHg, the results showed a consistent directional trend (19.0% vs. 9.7%, log rank P = 0.19). On multivariable logistic regression, LVEF &lt; 50% (Odds ratio [OR] 5.94), severe RV dilatation (OR 2.65), and lower PAPi (OR 0.62) were significant determinants of high RAP following TTVR. Conclusions More than half of patients had residual elevated RAP 30 days after successful TTVR. Reduced LVEF, severe RV dilatation, and lower PAPi at baseline were associated with residual elevated RAP. Patients with residual elevated RAP experienced significantly higher rates of cardiovascular death or HFH compared with those without residual RAP elevation. These findings may facilitate post-procedural risk stratification and guide therapeutic optimization after TTVR.Figure
title: Prognostic significance and determinants of persistent right atrial pressure elevation following transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement

abstract: Abstract Background Right ventricular–pulmonary artery (RV-PA) coupling assesses right ventricular function in relation to its adaptation to afterload and has emerged as an important prognostic marker. However, its potential role in identifying patients with tricuspid regurgitation (TR) who may benefit from transcatheter tricuspid valve intervention (TTVI) remains unclear. Objectives To evaluate the potential benefit of TTVI compared to conservative management (medical) according to a non-invasive RV-PA coupling surrogate in patients with severe isolated TR. Methods In TRIGISTRY, a multicenter international registry of patients with severe isolated TR, we identified 908 patients conservatively managed and 1054 patients who underwent a TTVI in whom a noninvasive surrogate of RV-PA coupling, tricuspid annular systolic plane excursion (TAPSE) divided by pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP), could be assessed. Patients were categorized according to TAPSE/PASP terciles defined by the medical group with lower tertile representing greater uncoupling: &lt;0.29 mm/mmHg, 0.29-0.43 mm/mmHg, and &gt;0.43 mm/mmHg. We assessed the impact of treatment modality on two-year survival within each TAPSE/PASP tercile after adjustment for comorbidities and the TRI-SCORE. Outcomes for terciles defined by the TTVI group as well as previously reported terciles of TAPSE/PASP, were also explored. Results Survival decreased significantly with lower TAPSE/PASP in both the medical and TTVI groups (both P&lt;0.0001). This was primarily driven by excess mortality in patients within the lowest tercile (Figure 1), whereas no significant difference in mortality was observed between the intermediate and highest terciles in either the medical group (P=0.76) or the TTVI group (P=0.52). Within each TAPSE/PASP tercile, there was no difference in survival between the medical and TTVI groups in low and high terciles (P=0.76 and P=0.79 respectively) whereas a significant survival benefit with TTVI was observed in the intermediate tercile (P=0.0003). Importantly, these findings remained consistent when tercile cutoffs were defined by the TTVI population distribution, (&lt;0.32, 0.32-0.475, and &gt;0.475 mm/mmHg) or based on the reported Euro-TR thresholds (&lt;0.32, 0.32-0.46, and &gt;0.46 mm/mmHg). Conclusions A non-invasive surrogate of RV-PA uncoupling, TAPSE/PASP, was associated with increased mortality irrespective of treatment modality. A potential survival benefit of TTVI was observed in patients within the intermediate RV-PA coupling tercile, but not in the lowest or highest terciles. These findings may help identify patients with severe, isolated TR who are most likely to have a survival benefit from intervention.
title: Impact of right ventricular-pulmonary artery coupling on outcomes in tricuspid regurgitation – insights from the international TRIGSTRY

abstract: Abstract Introduction Severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) is strongly associated with increased mortality, supported by robust clinical data. However, sex-related differences in the natural history and prognosis of TR remain inadequately characterized. Purpose To evaluate sex-related differences in outcomes among patients with varying degrees of TR severity. Methods Consecutive echocardiographic studies performed at a tertiary medical center between 2007 and 2025 were linked to clinical data. Patients were categorized into three mutually exclusive TR severity groups: mild, up to moderate, and significant (&gt;moderate) TR, and further stratified by sex. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) for all-cause mortality. Patients who underwent tricuspid valve interventions were excluded. Mediation analysis was performed to identify comorbidities that may account for sex-related differences in TR-associated risk. Results The final study cohort included 122,501 patients with a median age of 66 (IQR 53–77) years, of whom 43%were women. There were 61,191 (49.9%), 56,095 (45.8%), and 5,215 (4.25%) patients in the mild, up to moderate, and significant TR groups, respectively. Over a median follow-up of 10.2 (IQR 5.9–12.8) years, 32,796 (26.8%) patients died, with mortality increasing progressively with higher TR severity (all p&lt;0.001). In univariate analyses, significant sex-related differences in TR-associated mortality were observed, with men exhibiting a higher excess risk (HR 4.56 vs. 3.89 for significant vs. mild TR in men vs. women, p for interaction &lt;0.001). In contrast, after multivariable adjustment, TR-associated risk was similar in men and women (HR 1.57 vs. 1.50 for significant vs. mild TR in men vs. women; p for interaction not significant). Mediation analysis identified several comorbidities contributing to these sex-related differences, with the most prominent indirect effects related to chronic kidney disease (CKD; indirect OR 1.54) and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF; indirect OR 1.417). Conclusions Sex-related differences in mortality among patients with TR appear to be largely explained by differences in comorbidity burden rather than sex per se. The excess risk in men is mainly mediated by CKD and HFrEF, while TR severity remains an independent predictor of mortality in both sexes. These findings support risk stratification and management strategies focused on TR grade and comorbidity profile, rather than sex alone, and highlight CKD and HFrEF as key therapeutic targets in significant TR.Unadjusted mortality in men and women with TR
title: Sex, comorbidities, and mortality in tricuspid regurgitation: Reassessing risk beyond valve severity

abstract: Abstract Background Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) and transcatheter mitral valve implantation (TMVI) are established therapeutic strategies with expanding indications. Infective endocarditis (IE) remains a rare but serious complication associated with high morbidity, in-hospital mortality and diagnostic challenges related to prosthetic imaging. Purpose To evaluate the incidence, determinants, microbiological characteristics and prognosis of IE following TAVI and TMVI. Methods We conducted a single-centre retrospective observational study including all definite or possible IE cases, according to ESC criteria, occurring after TAVI or TMVI between October 2006 and February 2025. Determinants of IE were analysed using Fine and Gray competing risk models, with death as a competing event. Separate univariable and multivariable analyses were performed for the TAVI and TMVI cohorts. Kaplan–Meier analyses were performed to assess overall, endocarditis-free and post-IE survival in both cohorts. Results Among 2,545 patients who underwent TAVI and 237 who underwent TMVI, IE occurred in 72 TAVI patients (76 episodes; 2.8%) and 11 TMVI patients (4.6%). After TAVI, cumulative IE incidence was 1.3% at 1 year and 3.8% at 5 years. Younger age and atrial fibrillation were independently associated with IE, whereas elective procedures were protective. Enteric bacteria accounted for 47.4% of cases, predominantly enterococci (28.9%) and streptococci of gastrointestinal origin (18.4%), followed by staphylococci (19.7%) and oral streptococci (13.2%). The colon was the main portal of entry (22.4%). Embolic events occurred in 44.7% of cases. An intravenous-to-oral antibiotic switch was performed in 20 patients (26.3%), while surgery was performed in only 2 of the 27 patients with a surgical indication (7.7%). In-hospital mortality was 23.7%. After TMVI, cumulative IE incidence was 2.7% at 1 year and 5.1% at 5 years. Staphylococcus aureus predominated (36.4%), frequently associated with catheter-related infection (27.3%). Embolic events occurred in 27.3% of patients. No patient received oral antibiotic therapy, and surgery was performed in only one of the seven patients with a surgical indication (14.3%). In-hospital mortality reached 36.4%. Conclusion IE following TAVI and TMVI remains an uncommon complication but carries a poor prognosis. Microbiological profiles and portals of entry differ according to the procedure, supporting targeted preventive strategies, including antibiotic prophylaxis covering enteric pathogens, rigorous catheter management and screening for oral and dental infectious foci. Given the predominance of a colonic portal of entry, assessment of colorectal cancer screening status prior to TAVI implantation may warrant consideration.Kaplan-Meier curves of survival after IE

appraisal.design_and_n: Single-centre retrospective observational study; 2,545 TAVI and 237 TMVI patients, with IE in 72 TAVI patients (2.8%) and 11 TMVI patients (4.6%).
appraisal.main_limitation: Single centre with small TMVI numbers and no comparator, so determinants and prophylaxis implications are hypothesis-generating.
appraisal.one_line: Single-centre retrospective study of infective endocarditis after TAVI and transcatheter mitral valve implantation, describing incidence, organisms and poor outcomes.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Cumulative IE incidence after TAVI was 1.3% at 1 year and 3.8% at 5 years; in-hospital mortality 23.7%. After TMVI, incidence was 2.7% at 1 year and 5.1% at 5 years; in-hospital mortality 36.4%. Enteric bacteria accounted for 47.4% of TAVI cases.

title: Infective endocarditis following transcatheter aortic and mitral valve implantation: incidence, predictors and outcomes

abstract: Abstract Background and Aims Left-sided infective endocarditis (IE) is associated with high morbidity and mortality and frequently requires urgent valve surgery. Current guidelines recommend selective preoperative coronary angiography based on clinical risk profile, yet supporting evidence in real-world IE populations is limited and largely observational. Moreover, angiography may delay surgery and expose unstable patients to procedural and renal risks. We evaluated the association between preoperative coronary angiography and cardiovascular outcomes after surgery for left-sided IE using a large real-world cohort. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, a federated platform aggregating de-identified electronic health records from &gt;170 healthcare organizations worldwide. Adults undergoing open aortic or mitral valve surgery for IE were identified. Exposure was invasive coronary angiography within 1 month before surgery. A 1:1 propensity score–matched analysis was performed using 77 baseline variables including demographics, cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular comorbidities, medications, and laboratory parameters. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke or thromboembolism (TE), severe heart failure (cardiogenic shock or acute pulmonary edema), or end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). Follow-up was up to 3 years. Results Among 1,546 patients undergoing surgery for left-sided IE, 453 (29%) underwent preoperative coronary angiography. After matching, 353 patients remained in each group with excellent covariate balance. During a mean follow-up of 2.0±1.2 years, the primary composite outcome occurred in 178 (17.7%) patients in the angiography group and 186 (19.1%) in the no-angiography group (hazard ratio [HR] 0.92, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.75–1.14; p=0.44). No significant differences were observed for all-cause death (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.71–1.37), stroke or TE (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.60–1.97), ventricular arrhythmias or cardiac arrest (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.74–1.60), heart failure hospitalization (HR 1.14, 95% CI 0.93–1.39), or severe heart failure events (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.71–1.49). There was no interaction according to aortic versus mitral valve involvement. Conclusions In this large real-world cohort of patients undergoing surgery for left-sided IE, preoperative coronary angiography was not associated with improved cardiovascular outcomes. These findings question the routine use of invasive coronary angiography in this setting and support a more selective, risk-based approach pending randomized evidence.
title: Preoperative coronary angiography in patients with surgery for left-sided infective endocarditis. a study from a global federated research network

abstract: Abstract Introduction According to the European registry (ESC-EORP EURO-ENDO), embolic complications in bacterial endocarditis occur in a quarter of cases, while the length of vegetation &gt;10 mm is an independent predictor of death. Although European guidelines recommend surgical treatment for large vegetations, 25-30% of patients are unable to undergo surgery due to contraindications. This cohort exhibits the highest mortality rate, reaching up to 44%. Percutaneous aspiration, a less invasive alternative, may reduce the risk of embolic complications and mortality. Purpose We describe the clinical features, indications, procedural details, in-hospital outcomes of patients undergoing percutaneous aspiration of large vegetations for endocarditis at a single German high-volume center. Methods This retrospective, single-arm single-center registry included all patients with percutaneous treatment of probable or definite endocarditis within last 5 years. Results 17 patients with totally 18 procedures were identified and included in the registry. In one case, the procedure was repeated due to the recurrence of vegetation. The mean age was 64±16 years, with 53% female patients. In the most cases (70.6%) vegetations were present on the tricuspid valve, including 3 patients who also had vegetations on intracardiac electrodes; in one case, vegetations were found exclusively on the electrodes. The mitral valve was involved in 3 cases (17.7%), and floating structures were aspirated via transseptal access in 3 cases and retrograde transaortic in one procedure. Upon admission 41.2% of patients had sepsis, including 2 patients with septic shock; septic pulmonary embolism was present in 29.4%, and embolism at other sites was observed in 23.5% of cases. All cases were discussed in heart team and surgery was declined due to prohibitive operative risk. All procedures were done under transesophageal or transthoracic echocardiography guidance. The mean size of the floating structures was 23±9 mm. Two mitral valve procedures were performed via transseptal approach and one aortic and mitral valve procedure was done via transbrachial arterial access. Steerable sheaths (8.5-12F) or large bore catheter (20-24F) and vacuum aspiration pump were used to aspirate the vegetations. Following the procedure, 1 patient developed septic pulmonary embolism, 2 patients had a recurrence of vegetations and 2 patients experienced worsening tricuspid regurgitation. No procedure-related systemic embolism especially no stroke cases and no access site complications were observed. The mean duration of antibiotic therapy was 40±23 days. Hospital mortality rate was 11.8%. Conclusion Percutaneous vegetation aspiration represents a potentially effective alternative to surgery, particularly in selected patients with inacceptable surgical risk. Further studies are required to refine patient selection criteria and establish precise indications for the procedure.
title: Patient characteristics, procedural features and outcomes of percutaneous aspiration of large vegetations in patients with infective endocarditis

abstract: Abstract Objectives Endocarditis is a known complication after TAVI, but no data are published in the group of patients under hemodialysis, who are at high risk[1, 2]. We aimed to assess the short and long-term risk for endocarditis after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) in patients on hemodialysis based on German administrative claims data. Methods Administrative claims data of patients undergoing transvascular TAVI between 2013 and 2023 and follow up until 2023 derived from the largest provider of statutory health-care insurance (Allgemeine Ortskrankenkasse [AOK]) in Germany were used. Age, sex and risk adjusted odds ratios of endocarditis for chronic hemodialysis compared to no hemodialysis was calculated in the initial hospital stay and after 30 days and one year of discharge. Variables included for risk adjustment were age, sex, cardiac surgery, NYHA class, atrial fibrillation, acute myocardial infarction, acute stroke, cardiogenic shock, diabetes, COPD and arterial hypertension. Results A total of 71,450 patients were included in the analysis. Of those, 2,970 (4.2%) were on hemodialysis (see table for details). The raw frequency of endocarditis was 2.2% in hemodialysis patients compared to 1.0% in others within one year (see figure). The odds ratio for endocarditis in the full adjusted model was 4.52 (3.03-6.74) during index hospitalization, 3.29 (2.29-4.75) within 30 days after discharge and 1.70 (1.27-2.26) within one year. Sensitivity analyses including dialysis mode and vascular access did not change the results significantly. Conclusions Patients on hemodialysis have a significant elevated risk for endocarditis after TAVI, which is highest in the acute phase. Interventional studies are needed to evaluate prophylactic use of antibiotic treatment, i.e. during the first 30 days after TAVI.
title: Risk of endocarditis after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) in patients under hemodialysis

abstract: Abstract Introduction The use of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) is already the dominant treatment for severe aortic stenosis and is expected to increase following recent international guideline updates. By lowering the age threshold for TAVI, patients who previously would have undergone surgical replacement will instead live longer with a TAVI valve, thereby increasing their cumulative lifetime risk of TAVI-associated infective endocarditis (TAVI-IE), a serious complication. Echocardiography is essential for the diagnosis and follow-up of TAVI-IE. Purpose To assess associations between echocardiographic measurements of left ventricular (LV) systolic function, LV geometry, and mortality in patients with TAVI-IE. Methods We included 71 consecutive patients with TAVI-IE who had undergone TAVI at the same tertiary centre between 2012 and 2023. Transthoracic echocardiography was performed at baseline before TAVI, at routine postoperative follow-up, and shortly after admission for TAVI-IE. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Cox-regression models were used to evaluate predictors of mortality. Results Mean LV ejection fraction (LVEF) was 56±11% at baseline, 57±9% at first postoperative follow-up, and 53±12% at admission for TAVI-IE (p=0.008 for baseline versus TAVI-IE). From baseline to admission for TAVI-IE, LV stroke volume declined from 79±23 mL to 66±25 mL (p=0.005). LV end-diastolic diameter did not change from baseline to TAVI-IE. There were 42 (59%) deaths during a mean follow-up of 2.7±2.3 years of follow-up after admission for TAVI-IE. Reduced LVEF (&lt;50%) at baseline (HR 2.42, p=0.011), postoperative follow-up (HR 2.36, p=0.019), and at TAVI-IE diagnosis (HR 2.36, p=0.008) was associated with higher mortality. At admission for TAVI-IE, low LV stroke volume (&lt;60 mL, HR 3.04, p=0.006) and low indexed LV stroke volume (&lt;25 mL/m2, HR 2.30, p=0.043) were also associated with increased mortality. Development of clinical heart failure during admission further increased mortality risk (HR 3.95, p&lt;0.001). LV mass, LV dilatation, paravalvular leakage and valvular vegetations were not associated with mortality. Conclusion In patients with TAVI-IE, reduced LVEF and LV stroke volume during hospitalization for TAVI-IE are strongly associated with mortality, underscoring the prognostic importance of routine assessment of LV systolic function in this high-risk population.Visual abstract
title: Echocardiographic predictors of mortality in infective endocarditis after transcatheter aortic valve implantation

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction The coexistence of transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis and severe aortic stenosis (AS) is increasingly recognised, yet the underlying pathophysiology remains debated. Emerging evidence suggests that high shear stress across the stenotic valve may induce conformational changes in the transthyretin (TTR) tetramer, promoting its dissociation and subsequent myocardial infiltration. Purpose To investigate whether the relief of mechanical obstruction after an aortic valve replacement modulates circulating TTR levels. Methods In this prospective observational study (Sept 2025–Jan 2026), we enrolled patients with severe AS undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Serum TTR was quantified via Luminex xMAP technology at baseline (within one month pre-intervention) and at three months post-procedure. A non-AS control group was used for baseline comparison. Statistical analysis was performed using R-Studio (version 4.5.2), employing paired t-tests for longitudinal changes and independent t-tests for group comparisons, with p &lt; 0.05 considered significant. Multivariable analysis was employed to adjust for confounders, including nutritional status, albumin, and renal function. Results Thirteen AS patients treated with TAVI and 30 control subjects were enrolled. There was no difference between AS and control subjects in age (80.6 ± 6.9 vs. 79.6 ± 8 years), male gender, CRP, and creatinine levels. Baseline TTR levels in patients with AS were lower than those in the control group (96.8 ± 50.3 mg/L vs 152.0 ± 93.0 mg/L, p value 0.05) but did not reach statistical significance (Figure 1). In Patients with AS treated with TAVI, serum TTR concentration increased significantly from 96.8 ± 50.3 mg/L at baseline to 141 ± 61.5 mg/L at follow-up (p = 0.04) (Figure 2). Individual data inspection demonstrated that all patients with low baseline TTR levels (&lt; 50 mg/L) exhibited a marked post-procedural increase in concentration. Conclusions Patients with severe aortic stenosis present lower levels of circulating TTR. The relief of mechanical obstruction in patients with severe AS following TAVI is associated with an increase in circulating TTR levels. Elimination of valvular shear stress may promote TTR tetramer stabilisation and restoration of protein homeostasis.fig1fig2
title: Transthyretin levels increase in patients with severe AS following TAVI

abstract: Abstract Background Sex differences in coronary artery disease (CAD) are well recognized but remain poorly understood among symptomatic patients with a coronary artery calcium score of zero (CAC=0). Non-calcified coronary plaque (NCP), detectable by coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA), may be present despite CAC=0. Purpose To evaluate sex differences in coronary plaques and determine sex-specific associations with CCTA-derived CAD findings and outcomes in patients with stable chest pain and CAC=0. Methods PROMISE participants without known CAD who underwent CCTA and had CAC=0 (n=1,476) were evaluated for clinical characteristics, CCTA plaque measures, and outcomes stratified by sex. Multivariable regression models assessed baseline associations with NCP presence and CCTA measures. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated associations with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: death, non-fatal MI, unstable angina) over 26 months (IQR 18–34). Results In the overall trial, CAC=0 was more common in women (n=935, 63%) compared with men (n=541, 37%). Women with CAC=0 were older than men (60±7 vs 55±6 years) with CAC=0 and had more frequently hypertension (62% vs 56%), dyslipidaemia (65% vs 57%), family history of premature CAD (32% vs 27%), and sedentary lifestyle (52% vs 44%), while men were more often smokers (51% vs 40%). Symptom profiles and statin use were similar between sexes (Table 1). Despite a lower burden of risk factors, NCP was more prevalent in men than in women (16% vs. 10%), and men had more stenosis ≥50% (1.9% vs. 0.6%) and high-risk plaque features (HRP, 4.6% vs. 1.9%). Among those with NCP (n=177), men had higher total plaque volume (51 vs 40 mm3) and low-attenuation NCP burden ≥4% (LAPB, 3.7% vs 1.9%). Male sex was associated with NCP presence (aOR 2.2, 95%CI 1.5-3.2), adjusted for age, statin use, and risk factors (hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, family history of premature CAD, smoking, sedentary lifestyle, and obesity). Male sex further increased the odds of stenosis ≥50%, HRP and LAPB ≥4% (Figure 1). The likelihood of NCP increased with age, with 2.2x higher odds in men aged ≥50 years (95% CI 1.2-4.2) and 1.8x higher odds in women aged ≥60 years (95% CI 1.1-2.8), independent of statin use and risk factors. Any NCP was associated with a 6.7-fold MACE risk in men (95%CI 1.8-25.0; MACE rate: 5.8%) and a 4.8-fold MACE risk in women (95%CI 1.2-19.0; MACE rate: 3.3%) over a median follow-up of 26 months. Survival analyses were underpowered to detect sex differences (18 events). Conclusions Among stable chest pain patients with CAC=0, women had a lower prevalence of NCP (10% vs 16% in men), with lower plaque volumes and less frequent obstructive stenosis and HRP than men, despite more traditional risk factors. The odds of having NCP were higher in men ≥50 years and women ≥60 years, independent of risk factors. Any NCP conferred a similarly elevated risk of adverse events in both sexes.Table 1Figure 1
title: Sex differences in stable chest pain with zero coronary artery calcium score in the PROMISE trial

abstract: Abstract Background In transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), prognosis is primarily stratified using cardiac biomarkers reflecting myocardial injury and wall stress. Circulating transthyretin (TTR), beyond its role as the amyloid precursor protein, may reflect systemic biological reserve and metabolic integrity independently of cardiac injury pathways. Objectives To determine whether circulating TTR constitutes an independent systemic prognostic axis in ATTR, distinct from established cardiac biomarkers. Methods We analyzed 1,924 consecutive patients with ATTR enrolled in the French national HEAR registry and managed according to contemporary standards, with 172 patients with non-amyloid cardiomyopathy included as a reference group. Multivariable Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, CRP, creatinine, high-sensitivity troponin T (hsTnT), and NT-proBNP assessed the independent association of TTR with all-cause mortality. Restricted cubic splines evaluated dose-response relationships, and principal component analysis (PCA) explored the biological structure of circulating biomarkers. Results Circulating TTR was significantly lower in ATTR than in non-amyloid cardiomyopathy (230 [187–274] vs. 259 [222–304] mg/L; p&lt;0.001), indicating disease-specific systemic alteration. Within the ATTR cohort (median age 81 years, 79% male, 12% hereditary), 165 deaths occurred over a median follow-up of 23 months. TTR showed modest correlations with cardiac biomarkers (NT-proBNP ρ=−0.19; hsTnT ρ=−0.15) but a stronger association with albumin (ρ=0.34), supporting biological independence from myocardial injury pathways. Four-year mortality increased progressively across decreasing TTR quartiles (Q1: 47% vs. Q4: 23%; log-rank p=0.0023). After full adjustment, each 10 mg/L increment in TTR was independently associated with reduced mortality (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.94–0.99; p=0.01), with patients in the highest quartile carrying a 42% lower risk of death (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.36–0.95). Spline modeling confirmed a linear dose-response without threshold effect. PCA identified two orthogonal biological dimensions: a cardiac severity axis (NT-proBNP, hsTnT) and a systemic nutritional-biological axis (TTR, albumin), establishing their biological independence. Conclusions Lower circulating TTR identifies a systemic vulnerability phenotype in ATTR that is biologically and prognostically distinct from myocardial injury. The near-doubling of 4-year mortality across TTR quartiles, independent of established cardiac biomarkers, supports TTR as an autonomous risk dimension. These findings suggest that circulating TTR reflects global metabolic and inflammatory reserve, providing incremental prognostic stratification beyond conventional cardiac staging — and positioning TTR as both a complementary risk biomarker and a potential systemic therapeutic target in ATTR.Impact of TTR on survival
title: Circulating transthyretin as an independent systemic vulnerability signal in transthyretin amyloidosis: insights from the French HEAR Registry

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Myocardial injury is common in hospitalized COVID-19 patients and predicts acute adverse outcomes, but its long-term impact remains unclear. Purpose To evaluate the association of myocardial injury during hospitalization with one-year all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), persistent symptoms, and quality of life in COVID-19 survivors. Methods This prospective cohort study included 2,185 COVID-19 survivors discharged from a tertiary hospital in China (December 2022 – March 2023). Myocardial injury was defined as high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) &gt;99th percentile upper reference limit (&gt;26.2 pg/ml) during hospitalization. Patients were followed for one year after discharge. Primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and MACE (cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, or hospitalization for heart failure). Secondary outcomes included persistent symptoms and health-related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L, EQ-VAS) assessed by structured questionnaires. Propensity score matching (PSM) and multivariable Cox regression were used to adjust for confounders. Results Of 2,185 patients, 531 (24.3%) had myocardial injury. At one year, patients with myocardial injury had higher all-cause mortality (15.8% vs. 4.9%; adjusted HR 3.14, 95% CI 2.31–4.27) and MACE (25.6% vs. 5.1%; adjusted HR 5.22, 95% CI 3.97–6.86) compared to those without injury, with consistent results after PSM. Long-term use of ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ACEI/ARB) was associated with lower mortality (HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.23–0.85) and MACE (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.36–0.92) in the myocardial injury group. Among 2,020 survivors completing the questionnaire, 71.5% reported at least one persistent symptom; fatigue (25.3%) and sleep difficulties (16.4%) were most common. Myocardial injury survivors had higher symptom burden and lower EQ-VAS scores (median 80 vs. 85, P&lt;0.001) than those without injury. Conclusion(s) Myocardial injury during COVID-19 hospitalization is independently associated with increased one-year mortality, MACE, persistent symptoms, and reduced quality of life. ACEI/ARB therapy may improve outcomes in these patients.
