title: Dual antiplatelet therapy after CABG: does ticagrelor plus aspirin improve graft patency enough to outweigh major bleeding? an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of 9,659 patients

abstract: Abstract Background The surgical management of moderate ischemic mitral regurgitation (IMR) in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) remains controversial, with limited real-world evidence, particularly from Asian populations. Purpose To compare long-term clinical outcomes and echocardiographic changes between isolated CABG and CABG with concomitant mitral valve repair (MVr) in patients with coronary artery disease and moderate IMR. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 650 patients with moderate IMR who underwent isolated CABG (n=493) or CABG with MVr (n=157) between August 2009 and April 2024. Inverse probability of treatment weighting was applied to adjust for baseline differences. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality. The secondary endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), defined as a composite of all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, repeat revascularization, repeat mitral valve surgery, and rehospitalization for heart failure. Results During a median follow-up of 36.6 months, CABG with MVr was associated with lower all-cause mortality (multivariable HR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.22-0.79; weighted log-rank P=0.006) and fewer MACCE (weighted log-rank P=0.001), mainly driven by fewer deaths and rehospitalizations for heart failure. Findings were consistent across sensitivity and subgroup analyses. At echocardiographic follow-up (median, 11.6 months), CABG with MVr showed greater improvement in mitral regurgitation (75.4% vs 50.4%, P&lt;0.001) and a larger reduction in left ventricular end-diastolic diameter (4.0 [0.0, 7.8] vs 3.0 [-1.0, 6.0], P=0.026). CABG with MVr was associated with longer postoperative intubation, longer intensive care unit stay, and an increased risk of acute kidney injury, without increased early mortality. Conclusions In one of the largest Asian real-world cohorts, concomitant MVr during CABG for moderate IMR was associated with lower mortality, fewer MACCE, and greater echocardiographic improvement, but at the expense of increased perioperative morbidity.FigureFor image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.
title: Survival after coronary artery bypass grafting with or without mitral valve repair for moderate ischemic mitral regurgitation

abstract: Abstract Background Ethnic heterogeneity influences cardiometabolic risk in coronary artery disease, but whether it translates into different early outcomes after urgent CABG for acute myocardial infarction (AMI) in universal-access systems is unclear. Methods We retrospectively analysed 143 consecutive patients undergoing CABG for AMI (2015–2022) at a tertiary centre: South-Asian (n=86), Middle-Eastern (n=44), African (n=10), and Other-Asian (n=3). Primary outcomes were in-hospital mortality and postoperative length of stay (PLOS; operative-to-discharge days). Categorical variables were compared using chi-square tests. Given the non-normality of PLOS (Shapiro–Wilk p&lt;0.001 in most strata), PLOS was compared using Welch ANOVA. Results South-Asian patients presented younger than pooled non–South-Asian patients (52.8±8.0 vs 59.7±10.7 years; Δ −6.9 years, 95% CI −10.1 to −3.6; p&lt;0.001) and demonstrated higher metabolic burden (HbA1c 7.68±2.2%; LDL 124.5±51.2 mg/dL; LDL p=0.03). Marked sex imbalance was observed across groups (p&lt;0.001). Surgical approach was predominantly on-pump (136/143; 95.1%) without ethnic variation (p=0.794), and AMI phenotype (NSTEMI vs STEMI) was similar across ethnicities (p=0.604). In-hospital mortality was low (4/143; 2.8%) with no observed difference by ethnicity (0/10 African, 2/44 Middle-Eastern, 2/86 South-Asian, 0/3 Other-Asian; χ²=0.939, p=0.816). Mean PLOS was 14.5±5.9 (African), 16.6±19.9 (Middle-Eastern), 13.9±7.3 (South-Asian), and 17.3±5.5 days (Other-Asian), with no difference on Welch ANOVA (F=0.511, p=0.685). Conclusion Despite ethnic variation in age at presentation and cardiometabolic profile, early postoperative outcomes after CABG for AMI were similar in this single-centre cohort under a universal-access system. However, very small minority strata and low event rates limit power and preclude robust adjusted analyses; findings should be considered exploratory and warrant confirmation in larger multicentre studies.For image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.Visual AbstractFor image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.
title: Ethnic disparities and surgical outcome equity in CABG for acute myocardial infarction: a single-centre retrospective cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Stress perfusion cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) is widely used to assess myocardial ischemia, yet its prognostic evidence—particularly in patients without known coronary artery disease (CAD)—is less extensive than that of older imaging modalities. Purpose We aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of stress CMR in a contemporary cohort of patients without known CAD. Methods We conducted a single-center retrospective study including patients without known CAD who underwent adenosine stress CMR on a 1.5-T system between 2019 and 2023. Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), cardiovascular hospitalization and late coronary revascularization, were recorded as the primary endpoint. Secondary outcomes were defined as each individual component of the composite endpoint. The prognostic value of inducible myocardial ischemia (≥2 segments) and ischemic-pattern late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) (previously unknown myocardial infarction) was evaluated using survival and Cox regression analyses. Results A total of 558 patients were included (median age 68.7 years; 57.5% male). Patients showed a high cardiovascular risk burden, including hypertension (73%), dyslipidaemia (65%), smoking (31%), diabetes mellitus (27%), chronic kidney disease (27%), and atrial fibrillation (22%). Stress CMR was positive for inducible myocardial ischemia in 14.5% of patients and ischemic LGE in 15.8%, with 4.5% presenting both findings. Concomitant non-ischemic LGE was identified in 11.3%. Over a median follow-up of 2.9 years, the primary endpoint ocorred in 16.3%. Survival analysis showed a higher incidence of the primary endpoint in patients with inducible ischemia, ischemic LGE, or both (log-rank p&lt;0.001). Increase in event rates was also observed for all-cause mortality (log-rank p=0.005), non-fatal MI (log-rank p=0.018), cardiovascular hospitalization (log-rank p=0.013) and late coronary revascularization (log-rank p&lt;0.001) (figure 1). In multivariable Cox regression analysis, age (HR 1.03, 95% CI 1.01–1.04, p&lt;0.001), LV ejection fraction (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.96–0.98, p&lt;0.001), inducible myocardial ischemia (HR 1.67, 95% CI 1.25–2.23, p&lt;0.001), and ischemic LGE (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.24–2.23, p=0.001) were independent predictors of the primary endpoint. Conclusion Stress CMR offers robust prognostic information in patients without known CAD. Inducible ischemia and ischemic LGE were independently associated with an increased risk of MACE. Importantly, stress CMR also revealed a substantial number of previously unrecognized MI, a finding with direct implications for patient management.CMR_Figure_ESC_2026
title: Prognostic value of stress perfusion CMR in patients without known coronary artery disease: a real-world single-center experience

abstract: Abstract Introduction The TRI-SCORE was originally developed as a risk model for predicting 30-day mortality in patients undergoing isolated tricuspid valve surgery. Whether the TRI-SCORE retains prognostic value in a broader and more complex surgical population remains uncertain. Methods We conducted a retrospective, single-center cohort study of adults who underwent tricuspid valve repair for secondary TR performed concomitantly with other cardiac procedures between January 2018 and December 2024. The primary outcome was 5-year all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included 30-day mortality, 5-year heart-failure (HF) hospitalization or tricuspid reintervention, and 1-year postoperative TR severity. TRI-SCORE was calculated preoperatively for each patient. Results A total of 182 patients were included (mean age 65.2 ± 14.6 years; 65.4% female). Right-ventricular dysfunction was present in 19.8%, and mean TAPSE was 18.6 ± 4.1 mm. Mean LVEF was 56.2 ± 8.3% and estimated GFR 64.6 ± 26.7 mL/min. Median NYHA class was 3 (IQR 2–3), and the median daily furosemide-equivalent dose was 40 mg (IQR 20–60). Atrial fibrillation/flutter was present in 74%. Baseline TR severity was moderate in 40.0%, severe in 36.1%, and torrential in 10.0%. Concomitant procedures included mitral valve surgery (67.8%), left atrial appendage closure (34.3%), aortic valve intervention (27.1%), coronary artery bypass grafting (15.7%), and surgical AF ablation (14%). Median TRI-SCORE was 3 (IQR 1–4). Scores of 0–1 accounted for 33% of the cohort, intermediate scores of 2–4 for 44%, and high-risk scores ≥5 for 23%. The TRI-SCORE demonstrated strong and consistent prognostic performance across all evaluated endpoints. For 30-day mortality, each 1-point increase in TRI-SCORE conferred a hazard ratio (HR) of 1.45 (95% CI 1.15–1.82; p = 0.002), with excellent discriminatory ability (AUC 0.842, 95% CI 0.753–0.931). Over long-term follow-up, the TRI-SCORE remained independently associated with 5-year all-cause mortality (HR 1.56 per point, 95% CI 1.27–1.91; p &lt; 0.001). For the secondary composite of 5-year HF hospitalization or tricuspid reintervention, the risk also increased progressively with TRI-SCORE (HR 1.40 per point, 95% CI 1.24–1.59; p &lt; 0.001). Furthermore, higher TRI-SCORE values predicted greater residual TR at 1 year (ρ = 0.31; p &lt; 0.001), indicating increased TR recurrence in patients with worse baseline status. Conclusions In this contemporary cohort of patients undergoing concomitant surgery for secondary TR, the TRI-SCORE was strongly predictive not only of early postoperative mortality but also of long-term survival, HF-related events, and residual TR. These findings substantially extend the applicability of the TRI-SCORE beyond its original validation setting, highlighting its potential for preoperative risk stratification in non-isolated cardiac surgery involving the tricuspid valve.GraphsFor image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.
title: Prognostic value of the TRI-SCORE in concomitant surgery for secondary tricuspid regurgitation

abstract: Abstract Background Risk stratification after surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) relies mainly on clinical scores, while imaging-based markers are underutilized. Pulmonary artery dimensions can be easily obtained from routine preoperative computed tomography (CT) and may reflect right heart burden. We investigated their prognostic value for long-term mortality after SAVR. Methods In this single-center cohort, 476 patients undergoing isolated SAVR with available preoperative CT were analyzed. Truncus pulmonalis diameter (TP), TP indexed to body surface area (TP/BSA), and the TP-to-ascending aorta ratio (TP/AA) were assessed. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality during follow-up of up to 7 years. Cut-offs were derived using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Survival was analyzed by Kaplan–Meier estimates. Associations were evaluated using Cox regression and restricted cubic spline analyses. Multivariable models were adjusted for clinical variables (age, sex, eGFR, COPD, NYHA) and alternatively for EuroSCORE II. Incremental prognostic value was assessed by changes in C-index and likelihood ratio testing (LRT). Results Using ROC-derived cut-offs (TP ≥ 29 mm, TP/BSA ≥ 15.5 mm/m², TP/AA &gt; 0.75), higher values were associated with significantly reduced survival (all log-rank p &lt; 0.001). ROC analysis demonstrated good discrimination for 1-year mortality (AUC: TP 0.782, TP/BSA 0.808, TP/AA 0.746). In clinical adjusted Cox regression models, all parameters were independently associated with mortality (per 1 SD: TP HR 1.26 [1.08–1.47], p = 0.003; TP/BSA HR 1.28 [1.08–1.52], p = 0.005; TP/AA HR 1.24 [1.05–1.45], p = 0.009). Restricted cubic splines demonstrated a continuous increase in risk with increasing values, with the strongest association for TP/BSA (overall p &lt; 0.01). Addition of pulmonary artery parameters to the clinical model improved discrimination (C-index 0.647 vs. 0.674 for TP) and significantly improved model fit (all LRT p ≤ 0.011). Similarly, pulmonary artery parameters provided incremental prognostic value beyond EuroSCORE II (all LRT p &lt; 0.001), with only minor changes in discrimination. Conclusion CT-derived pulmonary artery dimensions are simple, reproducible markers that independently predict short- and long-term mortality after SAVR and provide incremental prognostic information beyond established clinical risk models. These findings support their integration into preoperative risk stratification.Kaplan-Meier CurvesFor image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.Restricted Cubic SplinesFor image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.
title: Routine CT-derived pulmonary artery dimensions independently predict mortality after surgical aortic valve replacement

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Carotid artery stenosis (CS) accounts for a substantial proportion of ischemic strokes (around 20%). Revascularization is recommended in symptomatic patients and in selected asymptomatic individuals with severe stenosis after multidisciplinary evaluation. However, prospective real-world data on carotid artery stenting (CAS), particularly in contemporary high-volume practice, remain limited. Purpose To evaluate the safety and short-term clinical outcomes of neuroprotected, patient-tailored CAS performed in a high-volume catheterization laboratory over a 4-year period. Methods This prospective cohort study included 76 consecutive patients undergoing elective CAS with systematic use of cerebral protection devices over a 4-year period. All patients underwent invasive angiographic assessment of both carotid and coronary arteries. The decision to perform CAS was based on symptomatic status, comorbidities, estimated surgical risk, anatomical considerations, and patient preference following multidisciplinary discussion. Procedural planning incorporated aortic arch anatomy, carotid tortuosity, calcification burden, prior carotid endarterectomy, and history of neck irradiation. Results The study population consisted predominantly of men (85%), and 70% had a history of prior ischemic stroke; 30% were asymptomatic. Procedural success was achieved in all cases (100%). The left internal carotid artery was treated in 51.7% and the right in 48.3% of patients. Periprocedural complications were infrequent. Vagal reactions occurred in 15.8% of cases and were managed with intravenous atropine; one patient (1.3%) required temporary trans-venous pacing. Periprocedural cerebrovascular events occurred in 3 patients (3.9%), including 2 symptomatic and 1 asymptomatic patient; all events were transient ischemic attacks without permanent neurological deficit. At 60-day follow-up, no major adverse cardiovascular events were recorded. Duplex ultrasound identified in-stent restenosis (≥50%) in 3 patients (3.9%), all asymptomatic. Conclusions In this prospective real-world cohort, neuroprotected, patient-tailored CAS was associated with high procedural success and low rates of periprocedural neurological events and short-term adverse outcomes. These findings, which are in accordance with the latest published data, provide contemporary observational insight on CAS performance in experienced centers and may alter clinical decision-making in selected patients with carotid artery stenosis, eventually contributing to stroke burden reduction.
title: Safety and clinical outcomes of neuroprotected, patient-tailored Carotid Artery Stenting: A prospective single-center cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Transfemoral access remains the primary route for transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), yet severe peripheral arterial disease and hostile iliofemoral anatomy may preclude this approach. Alternate strategies include non-femoral approaches such as extrathoracic (ET) and intrathoracic (IT) access, and facilitated transfemoral (TF) access enabled by percutaneous iliofemoral modification. There are no randomised controlled trials directly comparing these strategies, and contemporary observational data for relative safety and efficacy is inconsistent. This study aimed to compare safety and efficacy of non-femoral approaches and facilitated transfemoral access in TAVI. Methods This study was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and CENTRAL were searched through February 2026 for multivariable-adjusted or propensity-matched observational studies of facilitated TF (iliofemoral modification with angioplasty, stenting, and/or intravascular lithotripsy) versus non-femoral access (ET or IT). Three prespecified comparisons were performed: facilitated TF versus ET access, facilitated TF versus IT access, and ET versus IT access. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality at 30 days. Secondary endpoints included stroke, major vascular complications, and acute kidney injury. Risk ratios (RR) were pooled using a random-effects model. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses explored IVL-facilitated versus non-IVL facilitation and endovascular versus transthoracic alternative access. Results Eighteen studies (n=11,832; intrathoracic [IT] n=6,800; extrathoracic [ET] n=5,032) were included. IT access was associated with higher 30-day mortality versus ET access (RR 1.90, 95% CI 1.56–2.30) and higher 1-year mortality (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.21–1.42), with increased life-threatening bleeding (RR 1.71, 95% CI 1.41–2.07) and acute kidney injury requiring renal replacement therapy (RR 2.11, 95% CI 1.53–2.92), while risk of 30-day stroke was similar (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.55–1.93). Facilitated TF was associated with a trend towards reduced mortality compared to ET access, but this did not achieve statistical significance (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.39–1.27). Compared to IT access, facilitated TF was associated with reduced risk of major vascular complications (RR 0.45, 95% CI 0.35–0.60) and major bleeding (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.25–0.48). Conclusion IT access was associated with increased 30-day mortality, bleeding and AKI compared with ET access, while facilitated TF access demonstrated similar early mortality and reduced vascular complications compared to ET access in appropriately selected patients. Larger-scale prospective studies are needed to further refine patient selection criteria and define optimal alternative access strategies.30-Day Mortality by TAVI AccessFor image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.
title: Comparative outcomes of extrathoracic, intrathoracic and facilitated transfemoral access for transcatheter aortic valve implantation: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Severely calcified femoropopliteal (FP) lesions remain challenging. Jetstream atherectomy (JET) may improve lesion preparation before drug-coated balloon (DCB) angioplasty, but evidence in Japanese real-world practice, with a high comorbidity burden, is limited. Purpose To determine whether JET confers incremental clinical benefit over DCB alone in severely calcified FP lesions. Methods This was a single-center retrospective study of de novo or restenotic FP lesions with severe calcification (PACSS 3-4) treated with JET+DCB or DCB alone (April 2022-December 2024). The primary endpoint was 1-year primary patency assessed by Kaplan-Meier analysis. Secondary endpoints were post-procedural intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) minimum lumen area (MLA), freedom from target lesion revascularization (TLR), and freedom from major adverse limb events (MALE; major amputation or surgical reconstruction). An IVUS subgroup analysis stratified lesions by calcified nodules. Results Among 171 patients, 43.2% were on hemodialysis; mean lesion length was 156 ± 99 mm and chronic total occlusion (CTO) was present in 23.7%. Baseline hemodialysis rate, lesion length, and CTO prevalence were comparable between groups. One-year primary patency was similar with JET+DCB versus DCB alone (79.4% vs 75.0%, P=0.48). JET achieved a larger post-procedural MLA (16.0 ± 5.5 vs 13.8 ± 4.9 mm2, P=0.006). Freedom from TLR was comparable (84.1% vs 78.7%, P=0.38), as was freedom from MALE. In the calcified-nodule subgroup, JET resulted in greater acute luminal gain, but 1-year patency remained similar. Conclusion In this Japanese real-world cohort with frequent hemodialysis and long lesions, JET increased acute lumen area but did not translate into improved 1-year patency or limb-related outcomes versus DCB alone.
title: Clinical outcomes of drug-coated balloon angioplasty with or without Jetstream atherectomy for severely calcified femoropopliteal lesions: a Japanese real-world study

abstract: Abstract Background Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (V-A ECMO) is increasingly used during refractory cardiogenic shock (CS) but may impede myocardial recovery through increased left-ventricular afterload. Mechanical left ventricular unloading (LVU) with intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) or micro-axial flow pump (mAFP) may mitigate this effect; However, to date, no randomized trial has compared these strategies. We emulated a target trial to compare early LVU by IABP versus mAFP on myocardial recovery in refractory CS patients supported by V-A ECMO. Methods We analyzed adults with refractory CS from the international ELLIPSE registry (17 centers, 2010–2023) who received V-A ECMO plus mAFP or IABP within 24 hours of V-A ECMO initiation. Time zero was defined as initiation of unloading on top of V-A ECMO to avoid immortal-time bias. The primary endpoint was myocardial recovery at discharge (survival free from death, durable left ventricular assist device or heart transplantation) and at 1 year. Causal effects were estimated via inverse-probability-of-treatment weighting (IPTW). Results Among 1,112 screened patients with V-A ECMO and concomitant LVU, 747 met eligibilities (IABP n=379; mAFP n=368). Before weighting, patients in the V-A ECMO/mAFP group had higher lactate level (7.7 ± 5.6 vs 6.8 ± 5.3 mmol/L; P = 0.023) and lower acute myocardial infarction prevalence (63.0% vs 72.0%; P = 0.009). Myocardial recovery at discharge was significantly higher with V-A ECMO/mAFP (33.4% vs 26.9% %; absolute difference +6.6 percentage points, 95% CI, 3.3–12.8, p = 0.04) and this association remained significant after IPTW (weighted OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.56–0.96). At 1-year, myocardial recovery was significantly higher with V-A ECMO/mAFP, with longer restricted mean event-free survival compared with IABP (137 vs 110 days; absolute difference 26 days, 95% CI 5–52). Bleeding and ischemic complications were similar between groups, whereas renal replacement therapy was more frequent with V-A ECMO/mAFP. Conclusion In this international target-trial emulation, early LVU by mAFP during V-A ECMO was associated with higher myocardial recovery at discharge and sustained recovery at 1 year compared with IABP. These results support early active LVU and provide a rationale for randomized trials.Figure 1For image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.Figure 2For image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.
title: Early left ventricular unloading with intra-aortic balloon pump versus micro-axial flow pump in cardiogenic shock supported by VA-ECMO: an international observational target trial emulation

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction The International COSMOS Registry prospectively collects real-world data of hemoadsorption (HA) use in critically ill cardiac patients. In VA-ECMO patients, HA may reduce systemic inflammation, but its clinical benefit remains uncertain. Purpose To analyze the use of HA in VA-ECMO patients, focusing on timing, clinical effects, and safety. Methods The Registry protocol was approved by institutional Ethics Committees and all participants provided informed consent. Data were prospectively collected at screening, 24 hours pre and post HA, ICU discharge, and 90-day follow-up. Analyses followed a predefined statistical analysis plan. Results are reported as mean ± SD or median [IQR]. HA initiation relative to ECMO start was stratified into early (≤24 hrs) and late (&gt;24 hrs). Results 50 patients (mean age 57±13 years; 26% female) with median APACHE II score 25 [19, 31] from 10 centers (Germany, Portugal, Spain) were included. VA-ECMO indications were cardiogenic shock (62%), post-cardiotomy shock (5%), refractory ventricular tachycardia (8%), and periprocedural complications (11%); 57% had cardiac arrest before ECMO. HA was integrated into renal replacement therapy (80%), used as standalone hemoperfusion (12%), or connected to an ECMO bypass loop (8%). Median devices per patient were 4 [2, 7]; 30% received ≥6 devices, with 15 [9, 24] hours per device. Twenty-four hours after HA, interleukin-6 decreased (524 [187, 4,877] to 83 [49, 224] pg/mL; p&lt;0.0001), norepinephrine dose declined (0.13 [0.06, 0.29] to 0.04 [0, 0.14] µg/kg/min; p=0.0005), and fluid balance improved (+875 [-246, 2,549] to +190 [-849, 1,108] mL/day; p=0.011). Platelet counts were unchanged (p=0.058). SOFA scores improved from 14.5 [12, 16] to 12.5 [11, 15] (p=0.032). ICU mortality was 34% and 90-day mortality 44.7%. Early (n=27) versus late (n=23) HA initiation was associated with shorter ECMO duration (7 [4, 11] vs 14 [10, 29] days; p&lt;0.001). Among survivors, early HA was linked to shorter ICU stay (23 [18, 26] vs 35 [25, 57] days; p=0.024) and hospital stay (23 [19, 40] vs 49 [28, 68] days; p=0.017). No HA-related adverse events were reported. Conclusion In VA-ECMO patients, concomitant hemoadsorption was associated with reduced vasopressor needs, lower inflammatory markers, and improved organ dysfunction within 24 hours. Early initiation (≤24 hrs) was linked to shorter ECMO support and faster recovery. Controlled prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings.Key parameter relative percentage changeFor image description, please refer to the figure legend and surrounding text.
title: Hemoadsorption during VA-ECMO: results from the international prospective COSMOS registry

abstract: Abstract Background Refractory cardiogenic shock (CS) remains highly lethal despite contemporary intensive care and revascularization strategies. Percutaneous left-ventricular (LV) unloading with Impella is widely used, yet real-world outcomes across distinct CS etiologies and their clinical implications remain incompletely characterized. Purpose To assess in-hospital and 12-month survival in refractory CS treated with Impella 2.5/CP and compare outcomes across etiological phenotypes. Methods This was a retrospective single-center cohort study (2013–2021). Adults with refractory CS treated with Impella 2.5/CP were included. Patients with cardiopulmonary resuscitation on admission and those receiving additional mechanical circulatory support (e.g., VA-ECMO/IABP/other Impella systems) were excluded to obtain an Impella-focused cohort and reduce confounding by combined support strategies. Etiology groups were predefined as: acute coronary syndrome/coronary artery disease (ACS/CAD), dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)/myocarditis, aortic stenosis, sepsis-associated CS and other causes. The primary endpoint was in-hospital mortality. Secondary endpoints was 12-month survival (estimated with Kaplan–Meier, log-rank), and device-related complications (bleeding, limb ischemia, pseudoaneurysm, stroke). Group comparisons using Fisher’s test for categorical variables with two-sided p&lt;0.05 was considered significant. Results A total of 409 patients were analyzed (male 75.6%, mean age 70 years). The etiology distribution was as follows ACS/CAD n=269 (66%), DCM/myocarditis n=53 (13%), aortic stenosis n=32 (8%), sepsis-associated CS n=36 (9%), other causes n=19 (4%). Overall in-hospital mortality was 48.9% (200/409) and differed by etiology (p=0.048): ACS/CAD 46.9%, DCM/myocarditis 49.7%, aortic stenosis 56.3%, sepsis-associated CS 80.6%, other causes 31.6%. Twelve-month Kaplan–Meier curve separated significantly (log-rank p&lt;0.01), driven by early mortality in sepsis-associated CS. Overall complication rates were clinically relevant: transfusion-requiring bleeding 14.9%, limb ischemia 11.7%, pseudoaneurysm 4.9%, and stroke 1.0%. Conclusion In refractory CS treated with Impella 2.5/CP, outcomes are strongly etiology-dependent. Sepsis-associated CS has markedly worse early and 12-month survival, suggesting that LV support alone may be insufficient in this phenotype and highlighting the need for phenotype-guided selection and prospective validation of tailored support strategies.
title: Etiology-specific outcomes in refractory cardiogenic shock treated with Impella 2.5/CP: a 8-year real-world cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Microvascular obstruction after reperfused ST-elevated myocardial infarction (STEMI) predicts adverse prognosis on cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). The incremental risk associated with persistent microvascular obstruction on late or follow up imaging is less well defined. Methods We searched the literature through January 2026 for cohort studies of adults with STEMI treated with primary PCI who underwent CMR and reported outcomes by persistent microvascular obstruction status. Persistent microvascular obstruction (MVO) was defined on late gadolinium enhancement or follow up scans and was compared with transient microvascular obstruction or no microvascular obstruction. Random effects models pooled risk ratios and mean differences, and heterogeneity was assessed using I². Results Seven cohort studies including 2,180 patients with follow up from 1 month to 5 years were included. Compared with transient MVO, persistent MVO was associated with higher MACE (RR 2.40, 95% CI 1.51–3.81, p=0.0002) (Figure A) and higher death (RR 3.51, 95% CI 1.69–7.29, p=0.0008), with lower LVEF (MD −5.81%, 95% CI −9.04 to −2.58, p=0.0004) and larger infarct size (MD 7.26%, 95% CI 2.98–11.53, p=0.0009). Compared with no MVO, persistent MVO was associated with higher MACE (RR 3.72, 95% CI 2.48–5.60, p&lt;0.0001) (Figure B), higher death (RR 5.90, 95% CI 2.65–13.15, p&lt;0.0001), and higher heart failure readmission (RR 4.80, 95% CI 2.66–8.66, p&lt;0.0001), with lower LVEF (MD −11.33%, 95% CI −17.67 to −4.99, p=0.0005) and larger infarct size (MD 12.75%, 95% CI 6.34–19.17, p&lt;0.0001). Recurrent MI was not significantly different in either comparison, and heart failure readmission did not differ versus transient MVO. Conclusion Persistent microvascular obstruction identifies a high-risk STEMI phenotype with worse long-term outcomes and adverse remodeling markers.MVO Figure 1MVO Figure 2

appraisal.design_and_n: Systematic review and meta-analysis (random effects) of seven cohort studies including 2,180 patients, searched through January 2026.
appraisal.main_limitation: Pooled observational cohorts with few studies and variable definitions of persistent MVO and follow-up (1 month to 5 years).
appraisal.one_line: Persistent microvascular obstruction on CMR after reperfused STEMI was associated with higher MACE and death than transient or no obstruction.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Compared with transient MVO, persistent MVO was associated with higher MACE (RR 2.40, 95% CI 1.51–3.81) and higher death (RR 3.51, 95% CI 1.69–7.29). Compared with no MVO, persistent MVO was associated with higher MACE (RR 3.72, 95% CI 2.48–5.60) and higher death (RR 5.90, 95% CI 2.65–13.15).
appraisal.why_it_matters: Supports persistent MVO as a risk marker and possible enrichment criterion for trials of adjunctive therapy after primary PCI.

title: Prognostic impact of persistent microvascular obstruction on cardiac magnetic resonance after STEMI: a systematic review and meta analysis

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Lower extremity ischemia remains a frequent and serious complication of percutaneous mechanical circulatory support. Despite current approaches that rely on antegrade perfusion driven by systemic blood pressure or a cardiopulmonary support (CPS) circuit, many patients suffer significant morbidity including limb amputation. We report the first-in-human experience with a novel extracorporeal limb perfusion system that sources arterial blood and autonomously regulates pressurized perfusion via a distal perfusion catheter to the ischemic limb. Purpose The primary endpoint was technical feasibility, defined as successful device deployment, ability to deliver therapy, and successful device removal. The secondary safety endpoint was freedom from device or procedure-related major adverse events through 24 hours of follow-up. The secondary efficacy endpoints included an increase in SFA-MAP and treatment-limb near infrared spectroscopy during active perfusion. Methods After informed consent, adult patients undergoing arterial cannulation for cardiopulmonary support (CPS) were enrolled. A sheath for the Tulyp pump was placed into a donor artery and the outlet connected to a distal perfusion catheter in the superficial femoral artery of the ischemic limb. The Tulyp device was programmed to deliver a fixed mean arterial pressure in the limb for the duration of CPS therapy and removed at decannulation. Results are reported as medians with interquartile ranges. Results The Tulyp extracorporeal system was successfully deployed in all 6 patients (100% technical success). After cannulation, the Tulyp system was programmed to achieve an SFA-MAP of 80mmHg. Within 10 minutes of activation, SFA mean arterial pressure increased significantly to 81.0 (80.0–85.8) from 62.5 (56.8–66.8) mmHg, p=0.04 in the target limb. SFA-MAP was maintained by Tulyp at 80mmHg for an average duration of 133.2±26.8 min across all 6 subjects. Near infrared spectroscopy correlated directly with SFA-MAP across all subjects (R=0.60; 95% CI, 0.41–0.74; p &lt; 0.001). No device-related adverse events, vascular complications, or limb ischemia events were observed within 24 hours of Tulyp activation. Conclusion First in human experience with Tulyp demonstrated excellent technical feasibility and early safety data. The device autonomously delivered pressurized perfusion to the treatment limb and enhanced markers of tissue perfusion without adverse events. Prospective studies to evaluate the impact of this device on limb ischemia outcomes are in development.
title: First-in-human experience with Tulyp: a novel extracorporeal perfusion system for acute limb ischemia

abstract: Abstract Background The Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathways have been developed to optimize perioperative care and accelerate recovery. However, structured implementation in cardiac surgery remains limited. The present study evaluated the feasibility, adherence, and early perioperative outcomes of an ERAS program during its implementation phase. Methods The present prospective observational study included the initial n = 30 consecutive patients who underwent minimally invasive cardiac surgery during the period from September to December of 2025. The surgical interventions included fully endoscopic mitral valve replacement in combination with concomitant procedures (n = 25) and minimally invasive direct coronary artery bypass (n = 5). The ERAS protocol incorporated standardized perioperative care, encompassing patient education, opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia with routine PECS I/II blocks, early extubation, mobilization, and enteral nutrition. The observed adherence to established protocols was 100%, and the procedure was technically successful in all cases. Results The median age of the cohort was found to be 61 years (35–79 years), with a EuroSCORE II of 1.7 (0.7–4.2). The recovery metrics exhibited a swift rehabilitation process, with ventilation requiring an average of 5 (2–24) hours, mobilization requiring an average of 8 (4–26) hours, and oral nutrition requiring an average of 9 (4–26) hours postoperatively. The transition to the normal ward occurred after an average of 1 (1–5) days, and the removal of drainage tubes took an average of 1 (1–3) days. The median pain score was 2 (0–4), and the hospital stay was 5 (3–11) days. The absence of delirium, MACCE, infections, and in-hospital mortality (all 0%) is indicative of a successful clinical outcome. New-onset atrial fibrillation occurred in 3.3% of the patients, and 60-day rehospitalization occurred in 10% of the patients. Conclusion In this preliminary implementation cohort, the use of ERAS with opioid-sparing regional anaesthesia was found to be feasible, with full adherence, rapid recovery, and excellent safety, thereby supporting broader integration into perioperative cardiac care.
title: Enhanced recovery after cardiac surgery implementation enables rapid postoperative recovery with excellent safety: results from an initial minimally invasive cohort

abstract: Abstract Background and aim Adenosine stress perfusion cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) has high diagnostic accuracy for detecting obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD), but its prognostic value remains less well established than other imaging modalities. This study evaluated the prognostic utility of stress CMR in a contemporary cohort of patients with known CAD. Methods This single-center retrospective study included patients with documented CAD who underwent stress CMR (1.5-T) between 2019 and 2023. Patients were followed for major adverse events: all-cause mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), cardiovascular hospitalization, and late coronary revascularization (&gt;12 months post-CMR). The primary endpoint was the composite of all-cause death and non-fatal MI. Survival analysis assessed the prognostic value of inducible ischemia (≥2 segments) and ischemic late gadolinium enhancement (LGE). Results A total of 485 patients (75%male; mean age 68 ±11years) were included; 62% had prior MI, 63% prior percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), and 25% prior coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). Inducible ischemia was present in 147 patients (30%) and ischemic LGE in 338 (70%); both were present in 93 (19%), and non-ischemic LGE in 89 (18%). During a median follow-up of 2.9 years,126 events (26%) were recorded, including 92 primary outcomes (60 deaths, 32 non-fatal MIs), 70 cardiovascular hospitalizations, and 16 late revascularizations. Survival analysis showed that the presence of both inducible ischemia or LGE was associated with a significantly higher risk of the primary composite endpoint (log-rank p&lt;0.001), consistent across individual outcomes (all p&lt;0.01). Ischemic LGE predicted the primary endpoint overall (p=0.001) and when combined with ischemia (p=0.04), whereas ischemia alone was not (p=0.24) but was associated with higher rate of late revascularization(p=0.01). In multivariable analysis, with age (HR1.03, 95% CI 1.01–1.06; p=0.006), left ventricular ejection fraction (HR0.97; 0.96–0.99; p&lt;0.001) and chronic kidney disease (HR1.47, 0.93–2.03; p=0.10), LGE or ischemia independently predicted the primary endpoint (HR2.52, 1.08–5.89; p=0.03). In other models, ischemic LGE with concomitant ischemia (HR4.44, 1.62–12.21;p=0.004), was also an independent preditor, while ischemic LGE (p=0.07) was not. Inducible ischemia independently predicted late revascularization (HR 2.79, 1.01–7.66; p=0.047). Conclusion In patients with known CAD, stress CMR findings of ischemic LGE and/or inducible ischemia were associated with increased risk and were independent preditors of the primary endpoint while inducible ischemia was not, however it was associated with a higher rate of late revascularization. These findings highlight the prognostic value of stress perfusion CMR in risk stratification and support the routine assessment of myocardial scar, suggesting that inducible ischemia alone may have limited prognostic value.Freedom from primary outcome in years
title: Prognostic value of stress perfusion CMR: a real-world single-center experience in portuguese patients with known coronary artery disease

abstract: Abstract Background Patients with prior coronary artery disease (CAD) and recurrent angina are guideline-recommended to undergo non-invasive functional imaging to evaluate for the presence of myocardial ischemia. [1] A novel non-contrast cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) technique, stress T1 mapping reactivity (∆T1), has been proposed as a method for ischemia detection. ∆T1 is based on myocardial T1 relaxation times at rest and during vasodilator stress, and prior studies have suggested that ∆T1 can distinguish between normal, ischemic and infarcted myocardium. [2-4] However, validation studies assessing the diagnostic performance of ∆T1 against [15O]H2O PET and fractional flow reserve (FFR) in patients with prior CAD are lacking. Purpose The aims of this study are: (a) to assess the correlation between ∆T1 and [15O]H2O PET–defined myocardial blood flow (MBF); (b) to evaluate the diagnostic performance of ∆T1 for the detection of [15O]H2O PET-defined myocardial ischemia and FFR-defined significant CAD. Methods This PACIFIC-2 sub-study included patients with prior CAD (prior myocardial infarction and/or percutaneous coronary intervention) and recurrent angina, who underwent both rest and adenosine-induced-stress CMR T1 mapping (ShMOLLI) at midventricular level and [15O]H2O PET, preceding invasive coronary angiography with FFR measurements in all major coronary arteries. T1 mapping analysis was performed per vascular territory using cvi42. Pearson's correlation analysis was used to evaluate the association between ∆T1 and MBF per vascular territory. The diagnostic performance of ∆T1 on a per-patient basis was assessed by calculating the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) using stress MBF and FFR as reference standards. Results Of the 189 patients enrolled in the PACIFIC-2 trial, 70 were excluded: due to missing T1 mapping (n= 61), T1 mapping artifacts (n= 7), and incomplete PET data (n= 2). Consequently, 119 patients (mean age 64 ± 10 years; 23 [19%] female) were included. A weak correlation was observed between rest T1 and rest MBF (r = 0.116; p = 0.031) and between ∆T1 and stress MBF (r = 0.109; p = 0.043), whereas no correlation was observed between stress T1 and stress MBF (r = 0.025; p = 0.638). ∆T1 demonstrated an AUC of 0.591 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.489 – 0.693; p = 0.088] for the detection of PET-defined myocardial ischemia. For the detection of FFR-defined significant CAD, the AUC was 0.497 [95% CI: 0.381 – 0.613; p = 0.960] for ∆T1. Conclusion In patients with prior CAD the correlation between ∆T1 values and [15O]H2O PET-defined MBF is weak. Furthermore, ∆T1 demonstrated poor diagnostic performance for the detection of PET-defined myocardial ischemia and FFR-defined significant CAD in these patients. Consequently, CMR-derived ∆T1 does not appear to be a suitable diagnostic tool for patients with prior CAD and recurrent angina.
title: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance stress T1 mapping for the detection of myocardial ischemia and significant coronary artery disease: validation against [15O]H2O PET and fractional flow reserve

abstract: Abstract Background Myocardial edema is a key marker of acute myocardial injury and plays a central role in clinical decision-making. Conventional T2-mapping requires dedicated acquisitions and breath-holds, increasing examination time and motion artifacts. Oxygenation-sensitive (OS-CMR), a needle-free technique, contains intrinsic tissue information that may reflect myocardial relaxation properties [1]. We investigated whether advanced deep learning could generate clinically reliable quantitative T2-maps directly from OS-CMR without additional imaging sequences. Methods Consecutive patients (n = 2,189) who underwent OS-CMR and T2-mapping were included for model development. A residual generative deep learning framework was trained to synthesis quantitative T2-maps directly from OS-CMR images. Physiological fidelity was assessed by comparing T2 decay curves from regions of interest. For clinical validation, eighteen patients with confirmed myocardial edema who underwent were analyzed. Synthetic T2 maps were generated from OS-CMR images in approximately 40 seconds per case and reconstructed in CVI42 for standardized evaluation. Segmental T2 values were extracted using the AHA polar map model (n = 107 segments). The primary endpoint was segment-level agreement between synthetic and reference T2 values, assessed using Pearson correlation, two-way random intraclass correlation (ICC 2,1), and Bland–Altman analysis. The secondary endpoint was patient-level agreement, defined as the mean T2 value across segments. Discriminatory performance for edema detection was evaluated using a predefined clinically established T2 threshold appropriate for the acquisition protocol. Results The novel R-GAN consistently outperformed Pix2Pix (PSNR: 21.56–24.95 vs. 18.80–19.20 dB; SSIM: 0.672–0.739 vs. 0.055–0.659; PCC: 0.862–0.923 vs. 0.800–0.905). Segment-level analysis demonstrated strong quantitative agreement between synthetic and reference T2 values (r = 0.74, ICC = 0.73). Bland–Altman analysis showed minimal bias (+1.1 ms), with limits of agreement (–16.3 to +18.6 ms) within the expected physiological variability of clinical T2 mapping (Figure 1). Mean myocardial T2 values were nearly identical between synthetic and reference maps (51 ± 15 ms vs. 52 ± 9 ms), with preserved spatial distribution of edema on polar and colour maps. For segment-level edema detection, synthetic maps achieved 81.2% sensitivity and 74.1% accuracy. ROC analysis demonstrated strong discriminatory performance (AUC = 0.80) for identifying edema segments (Figure 2), supporting preservation of clinically relevant diagnostic information. Conclusion Advanced deep learning enables rapid (~40 seconds) quantitative T2 mapping from needle-free OS-CMR with strong agreement to conventional T2 and preserved edema detection. This strategy may streamline CMR workflows while maintaining diagnostic integrity. Prospective validation is needed.
title: Advanced ai–enabled rapid quantitative T2 mapping from needle-free CMR: clinical implications for myocardial edema detection

abstract: Abstract Background Renal denervation has re-emerged as a device-based therapy for hypertension, yet durability of effect versus sham over long follow-up remains debated. We synthesized sham-controlled evidence using each trial’s longest available follow-up. Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar from inception to 1 June 2025. Eligible studies were randomized, sham-controlled trials reporting change from baseline in office blood pressure and/or 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure. The primary outcomes were mean differences in office systolic and diastolic blood pressure and 24-hour ambulatory systolic and diastolic blood pressure at the longest follow-up. Random-effects inverse-variance meta-analyses were performed. Heterogeneity was quantified with I² and τ². Results Across 18 sham-controlled trials, using each study’s longest follow-up, renal denervation consistently lowered blood pressure versus sham. On average, office systolic pressure fell by 15.54 mmHg 95%CI (−18.56 to −12.52) and office diastolic by 8.19 mmHg 95 percent confidence interval (−9.89 to −6.50). The 24-hour ambulatory readings showed smaller but still meaningful drops: systolic −9.21 mmHg 95%CI (−11.19 to −7.23) and diastolic −5.39 mmHg 95% CI (−6.50 to −4.28). While the amount of benefit varied between studies I² about ninety seven percent across outcomes, the direction of effect was uniformly in favor of renal denervation at short and longer follow-up windows, indicating a durable reduction in both office and ambulatory blood pressure. Conclusions Using the longest available follow-up from sham-controlled randomized trials, renal denervation is associated with durable reductions in both office and 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure. Despite substantial heterogeneity, the pooled effects suggest a clinically meaningful benefit that persists beyond the short term. Future work should standardize outcome reporting, explore sources of heterogeneity, and determine which patient subgroups derive the greatest long-term benefit.Renal Denervation1Renal Denervation 2
title: Long-term impacts of renal denervation on office and 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure: a systematic review and meta-analysis of sham-controlled studies

abstract: Abstract Background Blood pressure variability (BPV) is increasingly recognized as a prognostic marker in cardiovascular disease. However, the combined impact of short-term and mid-term BPV on acute, in-hospital outcomes following acute myocardial infarction (AMI) remains insufficiently characterized. Methods In this prospective, single-center cohort study, both short-term and mid-term BPV were evaluated in patients hospitalized with AMI. Short-term BPV was assessed using average real variability (ARV) derived from 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), while mid-term BPV was calculated as the standard deviation (SD) of daily in-hospital blood pressure measurements. Associations with in-hospital outcomes, including mortality and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression models. Results Among 441 AMI patients, increased mid-term systolic BPV (SBP-SD) was strongly associated with in-hospital MACE, with each 1 mmHg increase conferring a 24% higher risk (OR 1.24, 95% CI 1.17–1.31). Patients in the highest quartile (Q4) of SBP-SD demonstrated a markedly elevated risk of in-hospital MACE compared with Q1 (OR 28.89, 95% CI 8.58–97.28). Short-term systolic BPV assessed by ABPM (SBP-ARV) independently predicted in-hospital mortality (OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.21–2.07) and MACE (OR 1.35, 95% CI 1.23–1.48). Elevated diastolic BP-ARV was significantly associated with in-hospital myocardial infarction, malignant arrhythmias, and cardiogenic shock. All associations remained significant after adjustment for mean blood pressure and established clinical risk factors. Conclusion Both short-term and mid-term systolic BPV independently and synergistically predict adverse in-hospital outcomes in AMI patients. BPV assessment during hospitalization may enhance early risk stratification beyond conventional blood pressure metrics.
title: Short- and mid-term blood pressure variability as predictors of in-hospital outcomes in acute myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Resistant hypertension (RHTN) remains a major clinical challenge. Purpose This systematic review/meta-analysis evaluated the blood pressure (BP)-lowering efficacy and hypertension control rates achieved after the addition of pharmacological or device-based interventions (renal denervation, RDN) in patients with true RHTN. Methods A systematic search of MEDLINE/PubMed was performed to identify studies assessing the antihypertensive effects of adding a single pharmacological or device-based intervention in patients with true RHTN. Primary analyses were conducted using a single-arm framework. Results Sixty-eight studies were included (n=6,297; weighted mean age 60 years; males 60%; diabetes 35%; smoking 16%; cardiovascular disease 27%). Participants received an average of 4.8 antihypertensive medications, with baseline office BP 164/92 mmHg and 24-hour ambulatory BP 148/85 mmHg. The median follow-up was 6 months. Meta-analysis of 58 studies (n = 4,579; 52% RDN) demonstrated a pooled mean 24-hour systolic ambulatory BP reduction from baseline -11.3 mmHg (95% CI: -12.3, -10.2). Meta-analysis of 15 studies (n = 2,700; 15% RDN) showed a pooled hypertension control rate during follow-up 35% (95% CI: 28, 42). No significant differences were observed between RDN and pharmacotherapy or between randomized and non-randomized studies. Conclusion(s) Single intervention (pharmacological or RDN) on top of guideline-directed background therapy resulted in clinically meaningful BP reduction in patients with true RHTN, but only one-third achieved BP control. Combination treatment strategies integrating optimized pharmacological regimens with device-based interventions may offer more effective and durable BP control in this particularly challenging patient population.Figure
title: Blood pressure lowering effects of pharmacological and device-based interventions for resistant hypertension: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Previous trials have demonstrated that intensive blood pressure (BP) control reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease and mortality at the expenses of kidney-related adverse events. Whether the net benefits outweigh the net harms in patients with different KDIGO risk class or vice versa remain unknown. Methods Patients with high cardiovascular risk were randomized to intensive treatment (targeting SBP below 120 mm Hg) or standard treatment (targeting SBP below 140 mm Hg). We categorized participants into low, moderate, and high/very high KDIGO risk according to KDIGO heatmap. Treatment responses were assessed according to KDIGO risk class. The primary outcome of the study was a composite of myocardial infarction, coronary or non-coronary revascularization, hospitalization or emergency room visit for heart failure, stroke, or death from cardiovascular causes. Safety outcomes included kidney outcomes, and other serious adverse events of special interest. Results Among 11,196 (99.5%) participants with classifiable KDIGO risk class at baseline, 7936 (70.9%), 2628 (23.5%), and 632 (5.6%) were low, moderate and high/very high risk, respectively. Higher KDIGO risk was associated with higher risk of primary outcome (moderate risk: HR 1.45, 95% CI: 1.27-1.65; high/very high risk: HR 2.09, 95% CI: 1.72-2.55, with low risk group as reference). Relative benefits of intensive BP control vs standard BP control on primary outcome and cardiovascular mortality were consistent across KDIGO risk class (P interaction = 0.12; P interaction = 0.16). However, in absolute terms, patients with greater KDIGO risk experienced greater risk reductions on primary outcome and cardiovascular mortality (P interaction = 0.047; P interaction =0.028). Risks of safety outcomes with intensive BP control were not enhanced among participants with high KDIGO risk. Conclusions Intensive BP control provides similar relative protection across the spectrum of KDIGO risk class studied, but progressively greater absolute risk reductions as baseline KDIGO risk increases. These data support the use of KDIGO heatmap to inform intensive BP control decisions.
title: Effects of intensive blood pressure control across the spectrum of renal impairment: a post hoc analysis from ESPRIT

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Hypertension is a major cardiovascular risk factor. While SPRINT supported systolic blood pressure (SBP) &lt;120 mmHg, ACCORD showed no similar benefit in diabetes. Recent trials raised safety concerns, leaving optimal SBP targets and the benefit-harm balance uncertain. Purpose To evaluate the efficacy and safety of intensive versus standard SBP targets for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and serious adverse events (SAE), including in diabetic patients. Methods This PRISMA/PROSPERO systematic review searched five databases up to Jan 2026. We included 12 trials. Bias was assessed via Cochrane RoB 2. Random-effects meta-analyses estimated risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence and prediction intervals (PI). Risk differences and numbers needed to harm (NNH) were calculated for SAEs. Analyses used Stata 19.0. Results Across 12 trials (50,070 patients; follow-up 2.0–4.7 years), intensive SBP control reduced MACE (RR 0.82; 95% CI 0.77–0.87; I²=40.9%; post-sensitivity RR 0.81; 0.76–0.87; I²=16.5%). Consistent reductions (I²≤13.0%) occurred in cardiovascular (CV) mortality (RR 0.71; 0.61–0.83), heart failure (RR 0.71; 0.61–0.83), myocardial infarction (MI) (RR 0.83; 0.73–0.94), and stroke (RR 0.80; 0.73–0.87), but not acute coronary syndrome (RR 0.93; 0.83–1.04). Benefit was independent of measurement method (automated vs. observed, p-int=0.646). Stroke decreased in diabetic (RR 0.72; 0.54–0.97) and non-diabetic (RR 0.82; 0.73–0.92) patients; however, MI (RR 0.80; 0.69–0.94) and CV mortality (RR 0.63; 0.52–0.76) reductions were exclusive to non-diabetics (p-int=0.641). Safety: intensive therapy increased hypotension (RR 2.34; 1.47–3.72; PI 0.91–5.99; NNH 94), renal failure (RR 1.67; 1.24–2.24; PI 1.08–2.58; NNH 240), syncope (RR 1.71; 1.28–2.28; PI 1.10–2.65; NNH 289), hyponatraemia (RR 1.44; 1.03–2.00; PI 0.81–2.56; NNH 184), and hypokalaemia (RR 1.30; 1.09–1.54). Overall SAEs (RR 1.01; 0.98–1.04; PI 0.98–1.04), arrhythmias (RR 1.13; 0.76–1.69), and falls (RR 0.98; 0.87–1.11) did not significantly increase. Conclusion(s) Intensive SBP targets offer substantial cardiovascular protection, mainly for non-diabetics, but require a clinical trade-off. While overall SAEs remain stable, elevated risks of hypotension, syncope, and renal failure mandate personalised, closely monitored treatment
title: Efficacy and safety of intensive versus standard systolic blood pressure treatment: A systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Ideal blood pressure control encompasses sustained 24-hour control, a normal circadian rhythm, and appropriate blood pressure variability to reduce cardiovascular events. The mechanism of renal denervation (RDN) may be well suited to achieving consistent 24-hour blood pressure control. Percutaneous catheter-based intravascular renal denervation (iRDN) has gained continued scientific and clinical interest for reducing blood pressure and has also revealed interesting new insights into the 24-hour profile of blood pressure reduction associated with the therapy. Purpose We evaluated the effects of an extravascular RDN (eRDN), an emerging alternative to iRDN, on 24-hour blood pressure patterns in patients with resistant hypertension. This eRDN approach is intended to enable more circumferential and complete ablation of renal sympathetic nerves. Methods In this open-label, single-arm first in human pilot study, patients (20 ~ 80 years) with resistant hypertension despite three or more antihypertensive drugs (including a diuretic) were enrolled. Eligible patients had an office blood pressure ≥ 140/90 mmHg and a 24-hour daytime ambulatory systolic blood pressure (ASBP) ≥ 135 mmHg. All patients underwent eRDN. Twenty four hour ABP was assessed using a validated device at baseline and 3 months after eRDN. Results Between November 2023 and December 2025, 10 patients were enrolled; 9 completed 3-month follow-up as of now. After eRDN, median 24-hour ASBP decreased from 146.0 mmHg (interquartile range [IQR] 140.0–161.0) at baseline to 124.0 mmHg (IQR 116.0–131.0) at 3 months. Corresponding reductions in nighttime ASBP (142.0 [132.0–154.0] to 116.0 [106.0–133.0]) and daytime ASBP (151.0 [145.0–158.0] to 128.0 [120.0–140.0]) were found. Median 24-hour ambulatory diastolic blood pressure (ADBP) also declined, from 95.0 mmHg (IQR 89.0–99.0) at baseline to 81.0 mmHg (IQR 72.0–87.0) at 3 months. Nighttime and daytime ADBP showed similar decreases (91.0 [87.0–99.0] to 75.0 [67.0–83.0] and 98.0 [90.0–99.0] to 85.0 [75.0–92.0], respectively). The changes in ABP measurement by 3 months following eRDN were evident over the 24-hour monitoring period, including an effect during the time of the morning BP surge (Figure 1 and 2). All these ABP changes were significant (p&lt;0.05) except daytime ADBP changes (p=0.054). Conclusion(s) eRDN produced substantial 3-month BP reductions, with ABP improvements sustained throughout the 24-hour period. Ongoing 12-month follow-up will determine the durability of this approach.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Effect of extravascular renal denervation on 24-hour blood pressure patterns in resistant hypertension

abstract: Abstract Background Renal denervation (RDN) has re-emerged as a complementary therapeutic option for patients with difficult-to-control hypertension; however, real-world evidence regarding patient selection, safety, and blood pressure (BP) response remains limited. Purpose To assess patient characteristics, procedural safety, and mid-term changes in BP and antihypertensive treatment burden in a real-world cohort undergoing RDN. Methods Single-center retrospective study including consecutive patients undergoing RDN. Baseline characteristics, procedural data, and outcomes were collected. BP was assessed by ambulatory monitoring when available or home monitoring otherwise. Primary endpoints were procedural safety and systolic BP (SBP) change; secondary endpoints included diastolic BP (DBP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), antihypertensive burden, and renal function. Paired comparisons used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results Thirty-one patients were included (61.3% male; mean age 52.9 ± 9.1 years). Hypertension was essential in 25 (80.6%) and secondary in 6 (19.4%), most frequently associated with obstructive sleep apnea. The cohort exhibited a high cardiometabolic burden, including obesity (38.7%), dyslipidemia (67.7%), type 2 diabetes (16.1%), chronic kidney disease (12.9%; median eGFR 92 [55–115] mL/min/1.73 m²), and obstructive sleep apnea (25.8%). Very high cardiovascular risk was present in 22.6%. Resistant hypertension was the main indication for RDN (38.7%), followed by shared decision-making, drug intolerance, and uncontrolled hypertension with high cardiovascular risk. Hypertension-mediated organ damage was present in 32.3%, mainly cardiac and renal. At baseline, patients were treated with a mean of 3.3 antihypertensive agents, with 71.0% receiving ≥3 drugs. All procedures were performed using the Simplicity Spyral system via femoral access with bilateral radiofrequency ablation. Median procedure time was 45 [39–49] minutes and hospital stay 1.5 [1–2] days. No procedure-related complications occurred. Median follow-up was 11.8 months (IQR 5.9–17.8), with paired BP data available in 11 patients. Median SBP decreased by −11.0 mmHg (IQR −17.0 to −4.0), mean reduction −12.0 ± 14.1 mmHg (p = 0.014). MAP decreased significantly (median −8.7 mmHg; IQR −14.3 to −4.0; p = 0.041). DBP showed a non-significant reduction (median −8.0 mmHg; IQR −11.0 to 1.0; p = 0.266). Antihypertensive treatment burden decreased significantly (3.3 to 3.0 drugs per patient; p = 0.012). Renal function remained stable, with no significant change in serum creatinine (median −0.05 mg/dL; p = 0.19) or eGFR (median +2.0 mL/min/1.73 m²; p = 0.29). Conclusions In this real-world cohort, RDN was safe and associated with clinically meaningful SBP and MAP reduction, lower treatment burden, and preserved renal function. Variability in response highlights the need for careful patient selection and further research on predictors of benefit.
title: Renal denervation in contemporary clinical practice: patient profile and early outcomes

abstract: Abstract Background and Aims Sympathetic nervous system overactivity is a key pathophysiological mechanism in hypertension and is closely associated with adverse metabolic alterations, including dyslipidaemia and impaired glucose metabolism. Renal denervation (RDN) is an established adjunctive treatment for uncontrolled hypertension with proven blood pressure-lowering efficacy. Emerging evidence suggests that sympathetic modulation by RDN may also influence metabolic pathways. This study aimed to evaluate metabolic changes following RDN and to assess estimated cardiovascular risk in a primary prevention subgroup. Methods This single-centre post-hoc analysis included 122 patients with uncontrolled hypertension who underwent radiofrequency-, ultrasound-, or alcohol-based renal denervation. Fasting glucose, HbA1c, and lipid parameters (total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and non-HDL cholesterol) were assessed at baseline and 6 months after the procedure. In a predefined primary prevention subgroup (n=61), 10-year cardiovascular risk was calculated using SCORE2 (Systematic COronary Risk Evaluation 2)). Results At 6-month follow-up, fasting glucose decreased significantly compared with baseline (14.9 ±47.3 mg/dL; p=0.031), whereas HbA1c remained unchanged. Significant improvements were observed in lipid parameters, including reductions in total cholesterol (10.3 ± 26.3 mg/dL), LDL cholesterol (7.0 ± 20.4 mg/dL), triglycerides (30.7 ± 69.4 mg/dL), and non-HDL cholesterol (all p&lt;0.01). Blood pressure was significantly reduced at follow-up, both for office measurements (13.5 ± 19.5/7.0 ± 11.7 mmHg) and 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure (7.0 ± 15.0/4.5 ± 9.2 mmHg; both p&lt;0.001). In the primary prevention subgroup, median 10-year SCORE2 risk decreased significantly from 14.1% at baseline to 11.3% at 6 months (p&lt;0.001), predominantly driven by systolic blood pressure reduction. Among 29 patients initially at High or Very High SCORE2 risk, 12 (41%) were reclassified to a lower risk category. Conclusion Renal denervation was associated with significant improvements in metabolic parameters and blood pressure in patients with uncontrolled hypertension. In patients without prior cardiovascular events, these changes were accompanied by a significant reduction in calculated SCORE2 risk, reflecting an overall improvement in cardiovascular risk factor profile.
title: Renal denervation improves metabolic parameters and reduces SCORE2-estimated cardiovascular risk in uncontrolled hypertension

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Renal denervation (RDN) is recommended for the management of arterial hypertension. Purpose The aim of this study was to assess the cost-effectiveness of RDN. Methods A systematic review/meta-analysis was conducted to identify RDN cost-effectiveness studies. The Incremental Cost-Effectiveness Ratio (ICER) per one Quality-Adjusted Life Year (QALY) gained (the extra cost needed for one additional year of good quality life) were compared to the respective country-specific Willingness to Pay (WTP) Thresholds (the maximum ICER/QALY gained that is considered acceptable by a healthcare system or organization for an intervention to be deemed cost-effective). Results Nineteen studies (16 countries) were included, all in favor of RDN cost-effectiveness. Most studies (n=12/19, 63%) were conducted after 2024, half in the context of European economic/healthcare systems. All studies implemented decision-analytic Markov models and compared RDN (mainly radiofrequency) plus standard of care (SoC) vs SoC alone. Meta-analysis of 7 studies indicated a pooled ICER/QALY gained 22209 €, compared to WTP Threshold 50000 €, thereby indicating the cost-effectiveness of RDN. Meta-analysis of 19 studies indicated a pooled ICER/QALY gained to WTP Threshold ratio of 0.31 (0.20, 0.44) (Figure). In sensitivity analyses RDN was shown to be cost-effective in both resistant and uncontrolled hypertensive patients especially in those with high cardiovascular risk and considering longer time horizons. Most studies were deemed to have low risk of bias. Conclusion(s) In line with guidelines recommendations, RDN appears to be a cost-effective intervention across a variety of clinical scenarios, both for patients with resistant or uncontrolled hypertension and especially in young and/or high cardiovascular risk patients.Figure
title: Cost-effectiveness of renal denervation: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Renal denervation (RDN) has been approved in recent guidelines as the third pillar for the management of resistant or uncontrolled hypertension. Purpose The aim of this study was to evaluate the long-term outcomes of radiofrequency (RF) RDN in a cohort of patients treated at an ESH center of excellence, with a mean follow-up of 8 years. Methods From a pool of patients with uncontrolled hypertension who had previously undergone RF RDN, we included those with a follow-up longer than 3 years (n=97). Baseline and follow-up data were collected for each patient, including office blood pressure (OBP), ambulatory blood pressure (ABP), use of antihypertensive medication, and markers of renal function. A propensity-matched control group of patients with resistant hypertension managed conservatively (without RDN) was selected for comparison. All-cause mortality and non-fatal cardiovascular events were recorded. Results A total of 76 patients (mean age 61.4±10.5 years, 25% female) had follow-up data over a mean of 8.3±3.4 years. OBP decreased significantly from baseline by 21.8±16.9 mmHg systolic and 13.1±9.6 mmHg diastolic (p&lt;0.001 for both). In 41 patients with ABP data, systolic ABP decreased by 19.4±13.1 mmHg and diastolic ABP by 12.7±10.0 mmHg (p&lt;0.001 for both). The number of prescribed antihypertensive medications was reduced by 0.54±1.2 (p&lt;0.01). By the end of follow-up, 9 of the 97 RDN patients (9.3%) had died, compared with 5 of 44 control patients (11.4%) over a mean follow-up of 8.1±2.3 years. Twelve patients were lost to follow-up. Estimated glomerular filtration rate declined significantly in the RDN group from 83.0±14.4 to 75.5±19.2 mL/min/1.73 m² (p&lt;0.001). Conclusion(s) RDN is a safe procedure that provides durable antihypertensive effects lasting for at least 8 years.Figure
title: Long-term effects of renal denervation on hypertension management: insights from a center of excellence

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Renal denervation (RDN) has been approved in Europe and the US and is recommended by the ESH, ACC/AHA and ESC hypertension guidelines as a therapeutic option for patients with resistant or uncontrolled hypertension. Purpose The aim of this study was to perform a systematic review and meta-analysis of current evidence to evaluate the long-term durability and safety of the procedure. Methods A systematic literature search was conducted to identify relevant studies reporting long-term outcomes of RDN beyond 3 years of follow-up. Data of interest (baseline characteristics, BP data, eGFR) were extracted and tabulated in order to be used in the context of a meta-analysis. Results Eight studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria and were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis. Most studies were conducted in Europe, one in Brazil, one in China and one in Australia. Follow-up duration ranged from 5 to 10 years. Meta-analysis of 8 studies (N=384, weighted mean age 61 years, 25% females) indicated a pooled follow-up minus baseline systolic and diastolic 24h ABP mean difference of -15.7 mmHg (-18.4, -13.0) and -9.2 mmHg (-10.5, -7.9), respectively, over a period of 8.7 years. Meta-analysis of 5 studies (N=187, weighted mean age 64 years, 34% females) indicated a pooled follow-up minus baseline eGFR mean difference of -8.9 ml/min/1.73 m2 (-11.1, -6.7) over a period of 8.5 years. Conclusion(s) The RDN procedure has a favorable efficacy and safety profile, with minimal peri-procedural and long-term vascular complications and no clinically meaningful effects on renal function. The lasting benefits of the intervention enhance its appeal as a supplementary approach for the management of hypertension.Figure
title: Long-term effects of renal denervation on hypertension management: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Treatment-resistant hypertension remains a significant clinical challenge and a major risk factor leading to adverse cardiovascular events. Importantly, it leads to cardiovascular remodeling, causing organ damage, such as left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and diastolic dysfunction. Among the patients with heart failure, increasing levels of NT-proBNP are associated with worsening of the disease. Renal artery denervation (RDN) has emerged as a novel therapeutic approach for hypertension patients by targeting the sympathetic nervous system to achieve better blood pressure (BP) control. Additionally, some studies suggested RDN might have a positive impact on cardiac remodeling assessed by echocardiogram, especially on diastolic dysfunction. Purpose Our study aims to evaluate the RDN impact on blood pressure and heart failure progression in resistant hypertension patients. Methods Our study included patients who failed to reach optimal BP control, defined by ESC guidelines as &lt;140/90 mmHg, despite optimal medical treatment for more than 1 year. All patients received at least 4 different classes of anti-hypertensive drugs, including beta-blockers. Patients were assigned for renal artery denervation after secondary causes of hypertension were ruled out. The procedure was done using a Symplicity Spiral Catheter. BP results were obtained using office measurements and 24-hour BP monitoring at baseline, 3 months, and 1 year after the denervation procedure. All patients had NT-proBNP analysis at baseline and 1 year after the procedure, and patients who voluntarily agreed had a preformed echocardiography. Results 40 patients were enrolled in the study. The mean patient age was 58 years, and 55% (N-22) were females. At the baseline, patients received 5.8 different medications for BP control, and mean BP was 167/89 ± 18.75/13.45 mmHg, with 73 ± 10.7 PBM. After 3 months mean systolic BP was 156 ± 21.5 mmHg (p = 0.030) and 89 ± 15.22 mmHg for diastolic (p=0.701). During 1-year follow-up, mean results for systolic blood pressure were 151 ± 9.9 mmHg (p = 0.008) with diastolic blood pressure 88 ± 11.1 mmHg (p=0.67). The mean NT-proBNP at index was 314.3± 301.9 pg/mL and 167.30± 184.1 pg/mL after RDN (p=0.026). In the echocardiogram group (N-17), left ventricular mass showed a positive reduction: from 132.4 ± 23.65 g/m2 to 122.5 ± 20.78 g/m2 (p = 0.026). Among the diastolic dysfunction parameters, deceleration time improved from 236.5 ± 44.70 ms to 213.6 ± 44.70 ms (p = 0.013), E/E’ changed from 14.18± 3.66 to 12.67± 2.43 (p = 0.065), E/A relation changed from 1.1± 0.28 to 1.13± 0.26 (p = 0.664), Edelta 6.52± 1.42 cm/s to 6.69± 1.85 cm/s (p = 0.720). Conclusion Renal artery denervation showed statistically significant systolic BP reduction after 3 months and 1 year, and additionally, a reduction in NT-proBNP levels in 1 year follow-up. After 3 months, positive changes were observed in myocardial function assessed by echocardiography.
title: Breaking resistance: impact of renal denervation on blood pressure control and heart failure development

abstract: Abstract Background Renal denervation (RDN) has demonstrated short-term blood pressure (BP) reduction in randomized trials; however, very long-term durability data beyond 10 years are scarce. Purpose To assess 13-year efficacy and safety of RDN in patients with resistant arterial hypertension (RAH). Methods Among 1,146 patients with RAH treated with ≥3 antihypertensive drugs, 16 met eligibility criteria; 8 underwent RDN. Mean age was 52.1 ± 3.9 years; hypertension duration 16.8 ± 2.2 years; baseline medication burden 5.5 ± 0.2 drugs. After therapy optimization, office BP was 156.9/95.0 ± 3.0 mmHg and 24-hour BP 149.2 ± 5.4/87.0 ± 5.1 mmHg. Follow-up included office and ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM), heart rate (HR), Computer Tomography (CT), renal function (GFR), medication burden, and cardiovascular outcomes over 13 years. Results RDN resulted in early BP reduction that was sustained throughout follow-up. Maximal office BP reduction reached −30/−17 mmHg at long-term assessment. Twenty-four-hour BP decreased significantly at all time points (p &lt; 0.05), confirming persistent ambulatory BP control. All treated patients (100%) achieved target BP by year 2 and maintained control through year 13 (office and ABPM). Medication burden decreased by 36% (from 5.5 to 3.5 drugs at 5 years and 3.7 at 10 years) and remained reduced at 13 years. Renal function remained stable over time (p &gt; 0.05). During 13 years, no cardiovascular events or cardiovascular deaths occurred; one non-cardiovascular death (thyroid cancer) was recorded. Conclusion In this long-term observational cohort, RDN demonstrated sustained BP reduction, significant medication burden reduction, preserved renal function, and absence of cardiovascular events over 13 years, supporting durable efficacy and safety in carefully selected RAH patients.
title: Durable 13-year outcomes after renal denervation in patients with resistant arterial hypertension in Ukraine

abstract: Abstract Background Uncontrolled hypertension is a key determinant of aortic dissection progression and recurrence. However, optimal blood pressure (BP) control remains challenging despite intensive medical therapy. Renal denervation (RDN) has demonstrated significant BP-lowering effects in randomized trials, but its feasibility and safety in patients with aortic dissection are not well established. Aims To evaluate the feasibility, safety, and antihypertensive efficacy of RDN in hypertensive patients with aortic dissection. Methods This prospective, single-center observational study enrolled hypertensive patients with prior aortic dissection who underwent RDN between 2017 and 2023. Pre-procedural aortic computed tomography angiography (CTA) was performed to assess renal artery perfusion using the Nagamine classification and to guide vascular access. The safety outcome was the occurrence of major adverse events (MAE) at 12 months. The efficacy outcome was change in office BP and antihypertensive medication burden at 12 months. Results Nine patients were included. All RDN procedures achieved technical success without periprocedural complications. No MAE, including death, myocardial infarction, stroke, aortic disease progression, or acute kidney injury, were observed at 12 months. Office systolic BP was significantly reduced (−23.6 ± 12.8 mmHg; p &lt; 0.001), whereas the reduction in diastolic BP was not statistically significant (−5.2 ± 11.7 mmHg; p = 0.218). Antihypertensive medication burden remained unchanged (+0.18 ± 1.16; p = 0.698). Conclusion In this small cohort, RDN was feasible and appeared safe in hypertensive patients with aortic dissection, achieving significant BP reduction without evidence of aortic disease progression. Larger, controlled studies are warranted to validate these findings.Graphic abstract
title: Clinical feasibility and efficacy of renal denervation in hypertensive patients with aortic dissection

abstract: Abstract Background Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) is a metabolically active visceral fat depot with paracrine inflammatory properties implicated in coronary plaque instability. While cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) enables detailed myocardial tissue characterization in ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), quantitative in vivo mapping of EAT has not been systematically explored. We aimed to assess EAT tissue characteristics using T1 and T2 mapping in acute STEMI and evaluate associations with myocardial injury and systemic inflammation.
