Methods We prospectively studied 12 patients with acute STEMI undergoing CMR in the acute phase and 9 patients with stable coronary artery disease as controls. The CMR protocol included LV volumes and ejection fraction (EF), late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), native myocardial T1 and T2 mapping, and extracellular volume (ECV). EAT thickness was measured in the 4-chamber view, and native T1 and T2 mapping were performed within EAT regions of interest. Serum IL-6 and NT-proBNP levels were obtained. Group comparisons were performed using Mann–Whitney U test and correlations using Spearman analysis. Results STEMI patients demonstrated higher myocardial T1/T2 and ECV compared with controls (p≤0.04). Within the STEMI cohort, EAT T1 mapping correlated inversely with EF (ρ=−0.62, p=0.031) and positively with LGE burden (ρ=0.64, p=0.023), infarct segment number (ρ=0.60, p=0.033), and ECV (ρ=0.57, p=0.048). EAT T2 mapping showed similar associations with EF (ρ=−0.60, p=0.038) and LGE (ρ=0.62, p=0.028). EAT thickness demonstrated weaker correlations compared with mapping parameters. IL-6 correlated with LGE (ρ=0.69, p=0.014), ECV (ρ=0.60, p=0.036), and EF (ρ=−0.65, p=0.023), and showed moderate positive associations with EAT mapping values, supporting a link between epicardial tissue remodeling and systemic inflammatory activation. Conclusions CMR-based quantitative characterization of epicardial adipose tissue is feasible in acute STEMI. Increased EAT T1 and T2 values are associated with myocardial injury severity and inflammatory activation, beyond simple volumetric assessment. These findings suggest that EAT mapping may provide incremental insight into myocardial–epicardial inflammatory interplay following STEMI. Larger studies are warranted to validate these exploratory observations.CMR Assessment of Epicardial Adipose TissueQuantitative CMR Parameters
title: Cardiovascular magnetic resonance tissue characterization of epicardial adipose tissue in acute STEMI: association with myocardial injury and systemic inflammation – exploratory pilot study

abstract: Abstract Background Diabetes mellitus confers a 2–5-fold higher risk of heart failure, yet the tissue-level substrate linking chronic hyperglycaemia to myocardial injury remains incompletely defined.1 Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) T1 mapping and extracellular volume (ECV) quantify diffuse interstitial fibrosis non-invasively, but their behaviour across normoglycaemia, prediabetes,2 type 1 and type 2 diabetes, and their quantitative relationship with HbA1c, remain uncertain. Purpose To characterise diffuse myocardial fibrosis and early ventricular remodelling across the glycaemic spectrum, and to quantify their association with HbA1c using CMR tissue mapping. Methods We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review and meta-analysis of adult cohorts undergoing CMR T1/ECV mapping with glycaemic stratification. Twenty-two studies (4,708 participants) contributed 28 ECV and 27 native T1 contrasts. Three-level random-effects models (restricted maximum likelihood) were used as primary analyses to account for clustering of contrasts within studies. Hartung–Knapp two-level models, cluster-robust variance estimation, and Bayesian random-effects models were prespecified sensitivity analyses to assess robustness. Moderator analyses evaluated technical (field strength, mapping sequence, region-of-interest, haematocrit correction) and clinical (diabetes type) sources of heterogeneity, and multilevel meta-regression assessed associations between mean cohort HbA1c and fibrosis indices. Results Compared with normoglycaemia, prediabetes and diabetes were associated with higher ECV (three-level SMD 0.78, 95% CI 0.48–1.07) and native T1 (SMD 0.43, 95% CI 0.20–0.66), with substantial residual heterogeneity (I² &gt;70%) that did not materially alter effect magnitude across modelling approaches. Global longitudinal strain was impaired (SMD 0.67, 95% CI 0.38–0.95) and left-ventricular mass index increased (SMD 0.34, 95% CI 0.10–0.58), consistent with early structural and functional remodelling. Each 1% higher HbA1c corresponded to 0.35 SD higher ECV and 0.19 SD higher native T1, although slopes were statistically imprecise after accounting for clustering and between-study variability. Effects were directionally consistent across technical subgroups and most pronounced in overt type 2 diabetes. Conclusions CMR-derived ECV and native T1 identify a diffuse fibrosis phenotype that scales with glycaemic burden and parallels early ventricular remodelling. These findings reinforce chronic hyperglycaemia as a mechanistic driver of heart failure–relevant myocardial injury and support CMR tissue mapping as a robust imaging biomarker and candidate surrogate endpoint for cardiometabolic trials.
title: Cardiometabolic myocardial remodelling across the glycaemic spectrum: a multi-level meta-analysis of CMR T1 mapping and extracellular volume

abstract: Abstract Introduction – Haemophilia A is a congenital bleeding disorder, which can be treated with factor VIII (FVIII) products and emicizumab, a bispecific monoclonal antibody mimicking endogenous factor VIII. These advances in prophylactic and on-demand haemostatic therapies have dramatically increased life expectancy in haemophilia patients, exposing them to age-related comorbidities including atherosclerotic cardiovascular (CV) disease. Despite the partial normalisation of haemostasis by emicizumab, it has historically been associated with thrombotic adverse events. Therefore, there is a need to better characterise CV risk factors and events in the ageing haemophilia patients in general, including those being treated with emicizumab. Purpose – This cohort study aims to characterise CV comorbidities and events in haemophilia A patients treated with emicizumab or FVIII therapy. Methods – This retrospective multicentre study included 105 patients with severe haemophilia A, aged 40 years or older during the study period from January 2020 till December 2024. We collected patient characteristics, subclinical CV markers, number of bleeding and CV events (atrial fibrillation, ischaemic stroke, myocardial infarction, venous thromboembolism), and antithrombotic practices post-events. CV risk factor prevalence was compared with the general Belgian population using Sciensano epidemiological data via a Fisher exact test. Results – Within this cohort, 99 (94.3%) patients were treated with emicizumab. The median age was 57 (IQR 49-65). Smoking was significant more prevalent in haemophilia patients than in the general Belgian population (current smokers 27.4% vs 15.6% [p=0.001], former smokers 32.6% vs 28.3% [p=0.001]). Individuals with haemophilia were more likely to have arterial hypertension (AHT) and dyslipidaemia compared to the general population and these differences were most pronounced in the age group of 40-65 years (AHT 70.4% vs 23.6% [p&lt;0.001], dyslipidaemia 50.0% vs 34.8% [p=0.005]). The mean body mass index (BMI) was 26.5 (95% CI 25.6-27.4), which was not different from the general Belgian population. During the study period, there were 4 CV events (2 atrial fibrillation cases, 1 subsegmental pulmonary embolism case and 1 acute anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction [STEMI] case). Conclusion – This retrospective cohort study represents the largest available source of information on real-world emicizumab use in Belgium and enables granular CV risk profiling under therapeutic emicizumab using an unbiased approach by evaluating all patients with haemophilia above 40 years. More prospective research is needed to further unravel the prevalence of CV risk and disease in the haemophilia population and to identify tailored antithrombotic therapy regimens following a CV event.
title: Cardiovascular risk and disease in haemophilia a patients: the comor-HA cohort study

abstract: Abstract Introduction Respiratory viral infections are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular events during hospitalization. However, it remains unclear whether this risk differs according to the specific viral etiology and whether these associations persist after adjustment for clinical severity. Purpose The objective was to compare the risk of in-hospital cardiovascular events among adults hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, influenza, or a negative viral test. Methods An observational study was conducted in hospitalized adults, classified into three groups according to respiratory viral etiology: RSV, influenza, or virus-negative controls. The latter were defined as patients presenting with febrile syndrome or acute respiratory infection and testing negative for RSV, influenza and SARS-CoV-2, including those with alternative identified etiologies. The primary outcome was a composite of in-hospital cardiovascular events, including ischemic stroke, acute coronary syndrome, heart failure, and venous thromboembolic disease. To reduce confounding by severity, a multinomial propensity score based on SOFA was estimated, and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) with stabilized weights was applied. In the weighted cohort, univariable and multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for age and SOFA were performed, including an interaction model with SOFA. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the estimates, including additional adjustment for the Charlson Comorbidity Index, estimation with robust variances, and analyses with truncation of extreme weights (p99 and p95), with adjustment for SOFA . Results A total of 666 patients were included: 234 virus-negative, 205 with RSV, and 227 with influenza. Adequate balance between groups was achieved after IPTW weighting. In the weighted multivariable analysis adjusted for age and SOFA, RSV infection was associated with a higher risk of in-hospital cardiovascular events compared with virus-negative patients (OR 1.98; 95% CI 1.20–3.28), whereas influenza was not significantly associated (OR 1.10; 95% CI 0.68–1.80)(Graphical abstract). Moreover, RSV was associated with a higher risk compared with influenza (OR 1.80; 95% CI 1.13–2.88). No significant interaction was observed between viral group and SOFA. Findings remained consistent across sensitivity analyses (figure 1). Conclusion Among hospitalized adults, RSV infection was associated with a higher risk of in-hospital cardiovascular events compared with both virus-negative patients and those with influenza, independently of clinical severity. These findings suggest a differential cardiovascular risk profile according to respiratory viral etiology, with potential implications for clinical risk stratification and in-hospital management.Graphical abstractforest_sensivity_analyses
title: Risk of in-hospital cardiovascular events according to type of respiratory viral infection: comparison between RSV, influenza and virus-negative patients

abstract: Abstract Background The C-Reactive protein-triglyceride glucose index(CTI), a reliable surrogate indicator of inflammatory and insulin resistance, is independently associated with coronary artery disease of various clinical manifestations. This study aimed to investigate the prognostic value of the CTI index in predicting in-stent restenosis (ISR) in chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Methods A total of 2147 participants were enrolled and divided into groups according to the tertiles of the CTI index. The primary endpoint was the incidence of ISR. Log-rank tests and Kaplan-Meier methods were performed to explore differences in event rates between CTI tertiles and plot time-to-event curves. The associations between the CTI index and the primary endpoint were assessed by multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression analysis with restricted cubic splines (RCS). The predictive performance of the models was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, with the area under curve (AUC) metric quantifying the model’s discriminative ability. The value of the CTI was defined as the Ln (fasting triglycerides (mg/dL)×fasting plasma glucose (mg/dL)/2) + 0.412 × ln [CRP (mg/L)]. Results Over a median follow-up of 60 months, 449 (20.91%) patients had experienced at least one primary endpoint event. The follow-up incidence of the primary endpoint increased with the CTI index tertiles. After adjusting for potential confounders, the CTI index was independently associated with the primary endpoint in CCS patients (HR, 1.17; 95% CI 1.02-1.34; P=0.025). Additionally, the highest tertile of the CTI group was correlated with a 1.35-fold risk of the primary endpoint compared with the lowest tertile of the CTI group (HR, 1.35; 95% CI 1.06-1.72; P=0.016). Furthermore, a linear and dose-response relationship was observed between the CTI index and the primary endpoint (non-linear P=0.119, P overall=0.019). CTI index, age, gender, BMI, diabetes, hypertension, previous PCI, previous MI, Lp(a), HbA1c, presence of multivessel CAD, presence of lesion length≥20 mm, number of stents, and stent length can be used as independent variables to construct a clinical prediction model. The ROC analysis demonstrated that this multivariate prediction model had moderate predictive accuracy for the primary endpoint, with area-under-the-curve estimates of 0.68 (95%CI 0.65-0.71) at 3 years and 0.70 (95%CI 0.67-0.73) at 5 years. Conclusions An increased CTI index was associated with elevated risk for ISR. Our study suggested that the CTI index could be a potent predictor in evaluating the prognosis of CCS patients undergoing PCI.
title: Inflammatory and insulin resistance indicators for predicting in-stent restenosis in patients with chronic coronary syndrome undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention

abstract: Abstract Background The Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction Risk Score for Secondary Prevention (TRS2P) is a well-validated score for predicting recurrent CV events among patients with recent myocardial infarction (MI). The TRS2P design does not account for coronary anatomy or disease complexity, which may provide additional prognostic insight following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Purpose We aimed to evaluate the prognostic performance of TRS2P in a contemporary PCI cohort and determine whether coronary artery disease complexity (c-CAD) addscomplementary risk information. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 22,534 consecutive patients who underwent elective or emergent PCI at a single center between 2004 - 2022. TRS2P was calculated using all 9 components and was categorized into low (0-1), intermediate (2) and high (≥3). To assess the potential incremental value of coronary anatomy, an extended TRS2P-based model (e-TRS2P) was constructed by incorporating c-CAD, defined angiographically as the presence of at least one of the following: left main intervention, multivessel disease including the proximal leftanterior descending artery, chronic total occlusion intervention, implantation of ≥3 stents, or treatment of long lesions requiring a total stent length ≥60 mm. The resulting e-TRS2P was categorized into low (0-1), intermediate (2-3) and high (≥4). Model performance was evaluated using C-statistics and net reclassification improvement (NRI), and associations of TRS2P and e-TRS2P with all-cause mortality and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; death, MI, stroke or unstable angina) were evaluated using Cox regression models. Results Overall, 9,855 (44%) and 6,380 (28%) were classified as high TRS2P and high e-TRS2P, respectively. Median follow up was 7.4 years (IQR 3-12). High TRS2P was associated with a greater risk for MACE (HR 3.9, 95% CI 3.7–4.2; p &lt; 0.001) and all-cause mortality (HR 5.6, 95% CI 5.2–6.0; p &lt; 0.001) compared to low TRS2P. Similarly, high vs low e-TRS2P was associated with greater risk of clinical outcomes (HR 5.0, 95% CI 4.7–5.4; p &lt; 0.001, and HR 7.3, 95% CI 6.6–7.9; p &lt; 0.001 for MACE and all-cause mortality, respectively). Incorporation of c-CAD into the TRS2P framework was associated with a modest but statistically significant improvement in discrimination (ΔC = 0.004, 95% CI 0.001–0.007 and ΔC = 0.007, 95% CI 0.004–0.01 for MACE and all-cause mortality, respectively). NRI analysis demonstrated an incremental prognostic value, with correct reclassification of 40% of patients (95%CI: 0.36–0.4, P&lt;0.001 and 95%CI: 0.38–0.5, P&lt;0.001 for MACE and all-cause mortality, respectively) compared with the TRS2P-based model. Conclusions The incorporation of coronary artery disease complexity into the established TRS2P framework was associated with additional improvement in discrimination and risk stratification, correctly reclassifying nearly 40% of patients for both MACE and all-cause mortality.
title: Risk Stratification Following Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Using the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction Risk Score for Secondary Prevention and a Novel Extension

abstract: Abstract Background Relative myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) with single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is widely used for evaluating coronary artery disease but may underestimate ischemia in multi-vessel disease or microvascular dysfunction. Absolute myocardial blood flow (MBF) quantification enhances diagnostic assessment, yet its clinical use is limited by restricted availability of positron emission tomography and cadmium-zinc-telluride systems. Whether widely available conventional sodium iodide (NaI) SPECT can provide clinically meaningful flow quantification against invasive physiological reference standards remains uncertain. Purpose To determine whether MBF and myocardial flow reserve (MFR) quantified by dynamic conventional NaI SPECT improve detection of hemodynamically significant coronary stenosis compared with relative MPI, using invasive coronary angiography (ICA) and fractional flow reserve (FFR) as reference standards. Methods In this prospective single-center study, 202 patients with suspected or known stable coronary artery disease underwent rest–adenosine stress dynamic SPECT using a conventional NaI camera. Stress MBF and MFR were quantified with a one-tissue compartment model. Relative MPI was assessed using a 17-segment visual scoring system. All patients subsequently underwent ICA with FFR for intermediate lesions. Hemodynamically significant stenosis was defined as diameter stenosis &gt;90% or FFR ≤ 0.80. Diagnostic performance was evaluated per vessel using receiver-operating characteristic analysis and generalized estimating equations. Results Among 580 vessels, 175 (30.1%) showed hemodynamically significant stenosis. Diseased vessels had lower stress MBF and MFR than non-significant lesions (1.47±0.63 vs. 2.05±0.64 mL/min/g and 1.95±0.79 vs. 2.58±0.75; both P&lt;0.001). Stress MBF (AUC 0.778; 95% CI 0.734–0.822) and MFR (AUC 0.774; 95% CI 0.729–0.820) outperformed relative MPI (AUC 0.637; 95% CI 0.598–0.676; both P&lt; 0.001), with no difference between quantitative indices (P=0.718). Sensitivity was higher for stress MBF and MFR (70.9% and 69.7%) than MPI (38.3%; both P&lt;0.001), with greater negative predictive values (86.5% and 86.2% vs. 77.0%), whereas MPI showed higher specificity (89.1% vs. 80.5% and 81.7%). In intermediate stenoses, quantitative parameters maintained superior discrimination (AUC 0.750 and 0.758 vs. 0.535; both P&lt;0.001). Adding stress MBF or MFR to MPI significantly improved discrimination (AUC 0.786 and 0.783) and yielded significant reclassification gains. Conclusions MBF quantification by widely available conventional NaI SPECT significantly enhance detection of hemodynamically significant coronary stenosis compared with relative MPI, maintaining advantage in intermediate lesions. These findings support broader clinical implementation of dynamic flow quantification using conventional SPECT and warrant multi-center validation.ROC: Quantitative Flow vs. MPI
title: Myocardial blood flow quantification by widely available conventional nai SPECT improves detection of hemodynamically significant coronary stenosis

abstract: Abstract Introduction Several indices have been developed for the clinician to estimate insulin resistance (IR), an important contributor to major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). One such novel tool taking obesity, dyslipidemia and hyperglycemia into consideration is the metabolic score of insulin resistance (METS-IR). METS-IR has shown great promise in IR estimation as well as prediction of type 2 diabetes, MACE and mortality. Nonetheless, there is a paucity of studies investigating its relation to MACE risk in European prospective cohorts. Moreover, the mechanisms underlying the association to the newly developed METS-IR have not been sufficiently investigated. Purpose To assess the relationship between METS-IR and prospective MACE in a Swedish cohort. The study also sought to explore potential mechanisms cross-sectionally using circulating biomarkers of metabolism, inflammation and extracellular matrix (ECM) turnover in a subset of the cohort. Methods Between 2012-2015, individuals from the general-population aged 40-75 years were randomly recruited from primary healthcare centers in southeast Sweden. Baseline data were obtained through clinical examinations, questionnaires and fasting venous blood sampling. METS-IR was calculated according to the original published formula. Follow-up was completed at the end of 2023 through linkage to national health registers, with ICD-10-based data on myocardial infarction, PCI, CABG, cardiovascular death and ischemic stroke comprised into a composite MACE endpoint. A dedicated subset of participants with available fasting EDTA-plasma was used for quantification of biomarkers related to metabolism (3), inflammation (3) and ECM turnover (6) using the Luminex assay. Uni- and multivariable Cox regressions, Spearman correlation analysis and multivariable linear regression were used. Results Among 6070 participants with calculated METS-IR at baseline (mean age 54±9.9 years, 43% men), 270 had developed MACE at follow-up. For biomarker analysis, the plasma of 196 MACE participants and 440 controls were available (mean age 63±7.4 years, 33% men). Following stepwise adjustment for potential confounders (Table 1), METS-IR remained a significant predictor of MACE: participants in the highest tertile had a 51% higher event risk than those in the lowest (p=0.027), with risk increasing 16% per SD (p=0.018). In correlation analysis against cardiovascular risk factors and biomarkers, METS-IR showed several significant (p&lt;0.001) correlations (Table 2). Of these, HOMA-IR, sex, age, SBP, lipid-lowering medication, sRAGE and leptin remained significantly correlated to METS-IR. Conclusions METS-IR was independently associated with prospective MACE in the Swedish middle-aged general population. Its significant and independent correlations to leptin and sRAGE even after accounting for HOMA-IR might be suggestive of mechanisms relevant for the role of METS-IR in the context of MACE.
title: The metabolic score for insulin resistance (METS-IR) predicts MACE and is correlated to plasma levels of leptin and sRAGE: validation and mechanistic insights from a Swedish population-based cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Genetic risk affect prognosis of coronary heart disease. High platelet reactivity(HPR) under antiplatelet treatment is associated with increased risks of adverse cardiovascular events. Purpose Our study aims to explore whether combining polygenic risk and HPR can provide incremental predictive value for acute myocardial infarction(AMI) risk in patients with 10-year follow-up after percutaneous coronary intervention(PCI). Methods Our study included patients who underwent PCI in 2013 and both had Thromboelastography(TEG) platelet function test results and coronary heart disease risk genes genotyping results. HPR was defined as adenosine diphosphate induced platelet-fibrin maximum clot strength(MAADP) &gt; 47mm in TEG test. The risk genes included test were according to the “polygenic risk score model(metaPRS) of coronary artery disease in Chinese cohort” which containing 540 single nucleotide polymorphism sites[1]. Patients were grouped based on the percentiles of metaPRS, evaluated the prognostic value of metaPRS alone or combined HPR in predicting 10-year AMI risk. Results A total of 2615 patients were included, among them 760 (29.1%) had HPR, 243(9.3%) occurred AMI. The results showed that metaPRS was independently associated with 10-year AMI risk, and the risk increased with higher percentiles of metaPRS. When grouped as quintiles of metaPRS, the patients of top quintile compared to patients of bottom quintile, the hazard ratio(HR) of AMI were 1.96(95% CI 1.28-2.99, P = 0.001). While other HR of AMI in different percentiles of metaPRS were 1.37 (median), 1.74 (tertiles), and 1.86 (quartiles), respectively. There was no significant association between HPR and 10-year AMI risk (P=0.254). However, when combined with HPR based on metaPRS, the prediction efficiency of AMI risk significantly improved, with HR increasing to 1.58 (median), 1.76 (tertiles), 2.38 (quartiles), and 2.64 (quintiles), respectively. After adjusting for clinical confounding factors by Cox regression analysis, the predictive power was further enhanced. Further dividing patients into six groups according to metaPRS (quintiles) and HPR status (Figure 1), Kaplan-Meier analysis showed significant differences in 10-year cumulative incidence of AMI between six groups (P=0.034). Compared with patients with non-HPR and lowest metaPRS(bottom quintile of the metaPRS), patients with both highest metaPRS (top quintile of the metaPRS) and HPR had the highest risk of myocardial infarction (HR=2.71, 95%CI 1.44-5.07, P=0.002). Notably, regardless of whether with HPR, patients with the lowest metaPRS (bottom quintile of the metaPRS) had lower 10-year AMI risk. Conclusions Polygenic risk scores are independent predictors of 10-year AMI risk after PCI in patients with coronary heart disease, and the risk increases with higher scores. Based on polygenic risk scores, combining high platelet reactivity status provides significant incremental prognostic value.
title: Combining polygenic risk score and high platelet reactivity for incremental predictive value of acute myocardial infarction in patients with coronary artery disease with 10-year follow-up

abstract: Abstract Background Acute Coronary syndrome (ACS) is becoming more prevalent in younger population but risk estimation in young adults remains difficult, as short-term absolute risk was studied in older population. We sought to examine how SCORE2 classifies patients who presented with premature myocardial infarction. Methods The YMIR (Young adults with Myocardial Infarction in Reunion Island) registry included all patients younger than 45 years admitted for ACS in Reunion island between 2016 and 2021. Among those 517, SCORE2 could be calculated in 228 individuals aged 40 years or older without prior cardiovascular disease nor diabetes. Risk categories were interpreted according to ESC 2021 age-specific thresholds. Results Using age-adapted cut-offs for individuals under 50 years-old, 58.8% of patients were classified as high risk (2.5–7.5%), and 0.4% as very high risk (≥7.5%). However, 40.8% were considered low-to-moderate risk (&lt;2.5%) despite subsequently experiencing MI before age 45. (Figure 1) The overall cohort (n = 517) displayed a substantial burden of modifiable risk factors: 68% were active smokers, 35.5% had obesity, 60% had HDL cholesterol below 0.4 g/L, and nearly 20% had diabetes. Overall, 51.6% of patients had LDL-C levels above 1.16 g/L, indicating that more than half exceeded recommended primary prevention thresholds despite their young age. Only 9.4% were receiving statin therapy prior to the acute coronary event. Conclusions Although SCORE2 identifies half of young adults who develop premature MI as high risk, a significant proportion remains classified as low risk despite significant cardiometabolic exposure with the limit that it can only be used for patients ≥40 years old. Implications These findings suggest that reliance on 10-year absolute risk alone may be insufficient in young adults and support complementary strategies such as earlier risk factor screening.Flowchart and SCORE2 of YMIR patientsPrevalence of cardiovascular risk factors
title: Young adults with premature myocardial infarction: are current SCORE2 thresholds sufficient?

abstract: Abstract Background Serum uric acid (sUA) has been associated with cardiovascular (CV) morbidity and mortality; however, its relationship with complex coronary artery disease (c-CAD) and long-term outcomes following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains inconclusive. Purpose To assess the association of sUA with c-CAD and to determine its prognostic value for long-term outcomes in a real-world cohort of patients undergoing PCI. Methods We analyzed 17,271 consecutive patients who underwent elective or emergent PCI at a single center between 2004 - 2022. c-CAD was defined as PCI involving at least one of the following: left main intervention, multivessel disease including the proximal left anterior descending artery, chronic total occlusion intervention, implantation of ≥3 stents, or treatment of long lesions requiring a total stent length ≥60 mm. sUA levels were categorized into sex-specific tertiles, comparing the highest tertile with the lower tertiles. Associations with c-CAD, all-cause mortality, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) were assessed using multivariable logistic and Cox proportional hazards models. Results Mean age was 66 ± 12 years, and 24% of participants were women. Mean sUA levels were 6.2 ± 2.0 mg/dL in men and 5.8 ± 2.0 mg/dL in women. c-CAD was identified in 4,632 patients (27%). Multivariable model found higher odds for c-CAD with upper tertilte of sUA (OR 1.15, 95% CI 1.1–1.2; p &lt; 0.001). Over a median follow-up of 7 years, 34% of patients died and 48% experienced MACE. Restricted cubic spline analyses demonstrated a non-linear U-shaped association between sUA and MACE (p &lt; 0.001). sUA upper tertilte was independently associated with increased risks of all-cause mortality (HR 1.3, 95% CI 1.2–1.3) and MACE (HR 1.2, 95% CI 1.1–1.2), with stronger associations observed among women and patients aged ≥75 years. Incorporation of sUA resulted in statistically significant improvement in discrimination for MACE, with a ΔC-statistic of 0.002 (95% bootstrap percentile CI 0.0006–0.0025). Conclusions Elevated sUA levels were associated with c-CAD and adverse long-term outcomes following PCI, particularly in women and older patients. sUA may serve as a simple and clinically useful marker for risk stratification in this population.
title: Sex specific serum uric acid is associated with complex coronary artery disease and cardiovascular outcome following percutaneous coronary intervention-a single center registry

abstract: Abstract Introduction Remnant cholesterol (RC) is increasingly recognized as a key driver of residual cardiovascular risk. However, its prognostic significance specifically within the heterogeneous population of patients with acute myocardial injury remains largely underexplored. Although these patients face a poor long-term prognosis, the specific metabolic risk factors driving these adverse outcomes remain poorly understood. Purpose To investigate the association between baseline RC levels and 1-year all-cause and cause-specific mortality in patients hospitalized with acute myocardial injury. Methods This retrospective cohort study utilized data from a large-scale electronic medical record database between January 2013 and December 2022. The study included 60,969 patients hospitalized with acute myocardial injury, defined by cardiac troponin elevation ( &gt; 99th percentile upper reference limit) with a dynamic rise and/or fall of ≥ 20%. Patients were categorized into quartiles (Q1 - Q4) based on baseline RC levels (calculated as TC minus HDL-C and LDL-C). The primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included cardiovascular death and cancer death. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models and restricted cubic splines (RCS) were employed to estimate hazard ratios (HR) and assess dose-response relationships, adjusting for demographics, comorbidities, and baseline medication use. Results During the 1-year follow-up, 11,106 deaths were recorded. In the fully adjusted model, elevated RC levels were significantly associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality. Patients in the highest quartile (Q4) had a 13% higher risk of death compared with those in the lowest quartile (Q1) (HR: 1.13, 95% CI: 1.07 - 1.19). Regarding cause-specific mortality, high RC was independently associated with cardiovascular death (HR: 1.11, 95% CI: 1.03 - 1.20) and cancer death (HR: 1.50, 95% CI: 1.24 - 1.81). RCS analysis revealed that while the unadjusted relationship was U-shaped, the association became linear and positive after full adjustment. Notably, the increased mortality risk associated with high RC persisted even among patients with low LDL-C ( &lt; 70 mg/dL) and those with lower magnitude of troponin elevation. Conclusion In this large-scale cohort of patients with acute myocardial injury, elevated RC levels were associated with an increased risk of all-cause, cardiovascular, and cancer mortality. These findings highlight the importance of RC assessment for risk stratification and potential therapeutic targeting in this high-risk population.Graphical Abstract
title: Remnant cholesterol and mortality in patients with acute myocardial injury: a retrospective cohort study

abstract: Abstract Introduction Single-photon emission computed tomography myocardial perfusion imaging (SPECT-MPI) is validated for ischemia detection and risk stratification; however, long-term prognostic data derive predominantly from North American and European cohorts. Evidence from Latin America remains limited, particularly regarding the prognostic impact of combined ischemia and infarction. Objective To evaluate the association between SPECT-MPI findings and 8-year MACE risk in a Latin American cohort with suspected myocardial ischemia, incorporating hierarchical analyses of individual components. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults undergoing SPECT-MPI for suspected myocardial ischemia at a national referral center in 2017. Of 1,998 patients, 789 met inclusion criteria and were followed for a median of 8 years (Figure 1). Perfusion was categorized as normal, ischemia, infarction, or combined defects. The primary endpoint was MACE, defined as cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or late coronary revascularization. Adjusted Cox models accounted for age, sex, trivessel disease, and cardiovascular risk factors. Kaplan–Meier, standardized incidence, inverse probability weighting, and hierarchical Win Ratio analyses were performed. Results Among 789 included patients, median age was 62 years, and 65% were male. Perfusion was normal in 38% of patients, while 15% had ischemia, 17% had infarction, and 29% had combined defects. Over 8 years, 94 patients (12%) experienced MACE, predominantly late revascularization. Standardized MACE incidence increased stepwise from 11.3 events/1,000 person-years in normal studies to 90.5 in patients with combined ischemia and infarction, paralleled by progressively reduced event-free survival across perfusion categories on IPTW-adjusted Kaplan–Meier analysis (Figure 2). In multivariable Cox models, ischemia (HR 4.36), infarction (HR 3.83), and combined defects (HR 7.66; p&lt;0.001) independently predicted MACE, with consistent hierarchical Win Ratio results (WR 4.62; p&lt;0.001). Conclusion In this Latin American referral cohort, SPECT-MPI abnormalities were strongly and consistently associated with long-term MACE, particularly when ischemia and infarction coexisted. Hazard ratios exceeded those reported in international cohorts. These findings support the integration of imaging and clinical parameters and underscore the need for local validation in high-risk populations.Figure 1.Patient selection flowchartFigure 2.Long-term outcomes by SPECT-MPI
title: Risk of major adverse cardiovascular events based on myocardial perfusion SPECT in patients with suspected ischemia: an 8-year retrospective cohort study from a reference cardiology center

abstract: Abstract Background Young patients with premature coronary heart disease (PCHD) are at high lifetime cardiovascular risk, yet existing risk scores are poorly calibrated for this population. Although inflammation and lipid accumulation are central to PCHD pathogenesis, the predictive value of LDL-C and hs-CRP for short-term adverse events in patients under 45 remains unclear. As a prelude to our ongoing National Science and Technology Major Project-funded cohort study, we aimed to develop a prediction model using existing multicenter data to establish a methodological framework and identify key predictors. Purpose To develop and validate a 2-year MACCE prediction model for PCHD patients aged ≤45 years and evaluate the incremental value of adding LDL-C and hs-CRP to conventional clinical factors. Methods We derived a 2-year MACCE prediction model from the multicenter PROMISE study (2015–2019; n=1091; PCHD patients aged ≤45 years) and validated it in an independent single-center cohort (2013; n=840). MACCE included all-cause death, myocardial infarction, revascularization, or stroke. Predictors included age, sex, BMI, hypertension, diabetes, prior revascularization, SYNTAX score, lipoprotein(a), uric acid, eGFR, LDL-C, and hs-CRP, selected by clinical consensus. Cox and Lasso-Cox models were developed with 10-fold cross-validation; hyperparameters were tuned via nested cross-validation. Model performance was assessed using the C-index with bootstrapped 95% CIs. Analyses used R 4.5.2. Results The derivation cohort included 1,091 patients (mean age 40.4±4.2 years; 94.4% male), with 86 MACCE cases (7.9%) during 2-year follow-up. The validation cohort included 840 patients (40.9±4.0 years; 94.5% male), with 86 MACCE cases (10.2%). The clinical-only Cox model achieved a cross-validated C-index (CV-Cindex) of 0.614 and external C-index of 0.659. The Lasso-Cox model demonstrated improved stability (CV-Cindex: 0.653; external C-index: 0.660). Adding LDL-C or hs-CRP individually yielded modest improvements: for the Cox model, CV-Cindex increased to 0.624 (LDL-C) and 0.627 (hs-CRP), with external C-indices of 0.654 and 0.662, respectively. The combination of both biomarkers yielded the highest performance in both the Cox model (CV-Cindex: 0.634; external C-index: 0.656) and Lasso-Cox model (CV-Cindex: 0.652; external C-index: 0.661) (Table 1). All models demonstrated statistical significance (p &lt; 0.001). Conclusion In young PCHD patients lacking validated risk tools, a simple model with routine LDL-C and hs-CRP improved 2-year MACCE prediction. These findings support combined biomarker–clinical stratification in this understudied high-risk population and will inform variable selection for our ongoing National Science and Technology Major Project-supported cohort study.Table 1.Model PerformanceFigure 1 C-index of Prediction Models
title: Development and validation of a 2-year MACCE prediction model incorporating routine biomarkers in young patients with premature coronary heart disease: a multicenter study

abstract: Abstract Background Myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) is widely used for risk stratification and guidance of coronary revascularization in patients with suspected or known coronary artery disease. However, real-world concordance between MPI findings and invasive coronary intervention remains incompletely defined. Objective To evaluate the real-life concordance between positive myocardial perfusion imaging and subsequent coronary revascularization, and to assess the clinical implications of concordant versus discordant findings. Methods We conducted a retrospective single-center study including consecutive patients referred for invasive coronary angiography (CAG) following a positive MPI between January 2020 and October 2024. Patients with prior coronary artery bypass grafting were excluded. The primary endpoint was the degree of concordance between ischemic territories identified on MPI and the coronary vessels treated during angiography (full, partial, none, or “matching plus”). Secondary endpoints included repeat angiography within one year and characterization of recurrent procedures. Descriptive and comparative statistical analyses were performed. Results A total of 523 patients were included (mean age 69±11 years; 74% male). Of these, 313 (60%) underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), 35 (6.7%) underwent CABG, and 175 (33.3%) had no obstructive lesion requiring intervention. Among PCI patients, full concordance between MPI findings and the treated vessel was observed in 61.3%, partial concordance in 6.8%, no concordance in 14.4%, and “matching plus” in 17.6%. Notably, approximately one-third of patients with positive MPI had no target lesion identified at angiography, indicating a substantial false-positive rate. Lower double product (DP) values were observed in discordant and no-intervention groups, suggesting suboptimal stress intensity during MPI. One-year follow-up demonstrated low rates of missed revascularization and clinically driven repeat angiography across all groups. Conclusions In this real-world cohort, concordance between positive myocardial perfusion imaging and subsequent coronary revascularization was moderate, with a substantial proportion of false-positive results. Suboptimal stress intensity, reflected by low double product values, may partially explain diagnostic discordance. These findings highlight the importance of careful interpretation of MPI parameters—including stress adequacy, ischemia burden, and clinical/ECG correlation—before proceeding to invasive coronary angiography.
title: Coronary revascularization guidance by myocardial perfusion imaging- retrospective real-life data from single center study

abstract: Abstract Introduction Despite optimal LDL cholesterol (LDL-C) control, genetically determined lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] remains a major source of residual cardiovascular risk1-2. Epidemiologic studies consistently link elevated Lp(a) to coronary events; however, whether this risk is mediated by a distinct calcific plaque phenotype in vivo—particularly one associated with adverse outcomes and procedural complexity—has not been clearly demonstrated3. Purpose We sought to determine whether elevated Lp(a) independently identifies a severe calcific coronary phenotype assessed by intravascular ultrasound (IVUS), and to define a clinically actionable threshold relevant to risk stratification and interventional planning. Methods We performed a retrospective analysis of 235 consecutive patients undergoing coronary angiography at a single tertiary center. Among them, 151 patients with both IVUS assessment and Lp(a) measurement were included. Coronary calcification was quantified using an IVUS-derived calcification score (CAC 0–4), and severe calcification was defined as CAC ≥3. Associations between Lp(a) and calcification severity were evaluated using correlation analysis and multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age, sex, LDL-C, diabetes, renal function, and acute coronary syndrome (ACS) presentation. To depict potential nonlinearity and clinical risk gradients, restricted cubic spline functions were fitted within the logistic model to generate adjusted probabilities of severe calcification across the range of Lp(a) and LDL-C. Discrimination for severe calcification was assessed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, with the optimal cutoff determined by the Youden index. Results The mean age was 72.4±11.6 years, and 77% were male. Median Lp(a) was 19.0 mg/dL and median LDL-C was 88.0 mg/dL. Lp(a) increased stepwise across CAC categories and demonstrated a strong positive correlation with calcification severity (Spearman’s r=0.60, p&lt;0.001; Figure 1). In multivariable analysis, Lp(a) remained independently associated with severe calcification after adjustment for LDL-C and other clinical covariates (adjusted OR 1.78 [1.42–2.22] per 10 mg/dL, p&lt;0.001). Spline-derived adjusted probability curves showed a progressive increase in the probability of severe calcification with higher Lp(a), whereas the corresponding LDL-C curve remained essentially flat (Figure 2). ROC analysis showed good discrimination for severe calcification (AUC 0.81), with an optimal Lp(a) threshold of 30 mg/dL. Conclusions Elevated Lp(a) independently identifies a high-risk calcific coronary phenotype beyond LDL-C levels. These findings provide in vivo structural insight linking genetically mediated lipoprotein biology to plaque remodeling. Lp(a) identifies a distinct calcific coronary phenotype independent of LDL-C, providing structural mechanistic support for Lp(a)-targeted therapy.
title: Lipoprotein(a) defines a calcific coronary phenotype independent of LDL cholesterol in the Lp(a)-lowering era

abstract: Abstract Background and Aim Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet its pro-atherogenic potency in the absence of acute inflammation remains debated. We aimed to investigate whether the impact of Lp(a) on subclinical atherosclerosis and adverse clinical outcomes is dependent on systemic inflammation (hs-CRP). Methods We analyzed participants from the Athens Angiometabolic Cohort (AAC), n=784, excluding patients with acute coronary syndromes. The final population consisted of individuals with no known coronary artery disease (non-CAD) and patients with stable CAD. Subclinical atherosclerosis was quantified using carotid and femoral ultrasonography (Sum of Wall Thickness - SumWT) and arterial stiffness via Pulse Wave Velocity (PWV). Participants were stratified into four phenotypes based on Lp(a) (cut-off 125nmol/) and hs-CRP (cut-off 2.0 mg/L). Findings were prospectively validated in the ATTICA study (n=2,126) over a 20-year follow-up for MACE and 10-year CV death using Cox proportional hazard models adjusted for SCORE2. Results In the AAC study, elevated Lp(a) alone (Group 3: High Lp(a)/Low hs-CRP) was not significantly associated with increased carotid SumWT (OR: 2.85, p=0.15) or femoral SumWT (OR: 0.79, p=0.85) (Table 1). Conversely, elevated hs-CRP alone (Group 2: Low Lp(a)/High hs-CRP) was associated with both carotid (OR: 2.77, p=0.024) and femoral (OR: 2.94, p=0.027) atherosclerosis. However, a potent synergistic effect was observed in the "Double Hit" phenotype (Group 4: High Lp(a)/High hs-CRP), which conferred the highest risk for carotid SumWT (OR: 4.1, p=0.041) and femoral SumWT (OR: 3.6, p=0.037) (Table 1). Most notably, the coexistence of high Lp(a) and high hs-CRP was the only significant predictor of polyvascular disease (simultaneous involvement of ≥2 vascular beds), demonstrating a six-fold increase in risk (OR: 6.26, 95% CI: 1.91–20.5, p=0.002) (Table 1). No significant associations were found with PWV &gt;10 m/s. In the prospective ATTICA validation, Group 4 exhibited a significant and sustained risk for CV death at 10 years (HR: 2.17, p=0.009) and MACE at 20 years (HR: 1.90, p=0.004) (Table 2). Notably, Group 3 (High Lp(a)/Low hs-CRP) showed no increased risk at any time point (p&gt;0.05). Kaplan-Meier curves confirmed early divergence for Group 4 for 20 year MACE (Figure 1). Conclusions Our findings suggest that systemic inflammation acts as a significant modifier of Lp(a)-associated cardiovascular risk. While elevated Lp(a) is a known risk factor, its pathogenicity is markedly amplified in a pro-inflammatory environment, leading to accelerated polyvascular atherosclerosis and increased long-term mortality. These data support a more integrated approach to risk stratification, suggesting that patients with the "Double Hit" phenotype may represent a priority group for aggressive preventive interventions targeting both lipid and inflammatory pathways.Figure 1
title: Lipoprotein(a) and hs-CRP interplay as a driver of polyvascular atherosclerosis and cardiovascular events

abstract: Abstract Background Small-dense low-density lipoprotein (sdLDL) is more atherogenic than larger LDL particles, but its measurement in routine clinical practice has not been validated. Recent evidence reports good agreement between measured and estimated sdLDL levels using a readily applicable formula, which includes standard lipoprotein fractions. We evaluated the clinical value of estimated sdLDL (esdLDL) in primary and secondary prevention settings for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Methods Analysis was conducted across three cohorts: an outpatients ASCVD primary and secondary prevention cohort (Athens Angiometabolic Cohort, n=1,327, (AAC)), a general population cohort (ATTICA study, n=1,590) and an acute coronary syndrome cohort (GREECS study, n=1,296). We examined the association between esdLDL and markers of subclinical atherosclerosis in AAC [carotid and femoral artery wall thickness (WT) and Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI)] and assessed its predictive value for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) including a composite of CV death, acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, revascularization and stroke in all cohorts after adjustment for established risk scores recommended in ESC guidelines. esdLDL was calculated using the formula: [esdLDL=LDL-C- 1.43*LDL-C+ 0.14*(LN(Triglyceride)*LDL-C) + 8.99.] Results esdLDL levels in the highest quintile were significantly associated with increased carotid (OR 1.60, p&lt;0.001), and femoral WT (OR 1.37, p=0.043), with ABI&lt;0.9 (OR 2.37 p=0.04) and number of diseased coronary artery vessels (OR: 0.606 95% CI: 0.309, 0.804, p&lt;0.001) (Table 1). esdLDL associated with MACE in all three cohorts independently of SCORE2 or SMART2 risk scores based on presence of ASCVD (AAC, HR: 2.07 per highest vs lower quintiles of esdLDL95% CI 1.17–3.67, p=0.012, median follow-up 2.5 years, ATTICA, HR:1.31 95%CI: 1.07, 1.61, P=0.008, median follow-up 20 years, GREECS HR: 1.27, 95% CI: 1.07, 1.52, P=0.008, , median follow-up 14 years). Adding esdLDL to SCORE2 and SMART2 risk model improved the C-statistic (AUC: 0.629 to 0.655 for SCORE2 and AUC: 0.613 to 0.624 for SMART2) and yielded a significant Net Reclassification Improvement (NRI) of 0.360 (p&lt;0.001) in the ATTICA study and NRI 0.115 (p=0.036) in the GREECS study. While esdLDL provided incremental value over LDL-C in ATTICA study ΔAUC 0.011, P=0.011, NRI: 0.148, p=0.003), this improvement was not significant in the ACS population (ΔAUC 0.002, P=0.497, NRI 0.08, P=0.12) Conclusion Estimated sdLDL calculated by a readily available formula, is associated with subclinical and clinically overt atherosclerosis and incrementally predicts long-term adverse cardiovascular events in 3 independent cohorts representative of the general population, outpatients assessed in ASCVD prevention clinics and ACS population. These findings should trigger further investigation regarding its utility in risk stratification in primary and secondary prevention.
title: The clinical value of estimated small dense LDL in primary and secondary prevention

abstract: Abstract Introduction The triglyceride to high density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio (TG-HDL-C ratio) has emerged as a clinically available proxy for insulin resistance (IR). It has also been found to be independently associated with the development of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Despite intense research on the subject, prospective cohort studies in European general populations are sparse. Also, few studies have taken abdominal obesity into account. Finally, from a clinical perspective, markers of IR and future MACE risk would be of specific interest among individuals without obvious IR in the form of diabetes or elevated fasting glucose. Purpose To examine the fasting TG-HDL-C ratio in relation to prospective MACE amongst normoglycemic non-diabetics from a Swedish general-population. Methods Individuals from a population-based cohort in southeast Sweden (n=6870; data collected 2012-2015) with baseline clinical and questionnaire data along with fasting glucose and lipid panels were enrolled. Participants with known diabetes (n=241) and/or high fasting glucose levels (≥6.1 mmol/L) (n=839) were excluded. The development of myocardial infarction, PCI, CABG, ischemic stroke and cardiovascular death was recorded during follow-up and used in a composite MACE endpoint based on ICD-10 codes from Swedish registers. Uni- and multivariable Cox regression models were used. TG-HDL-C ratios were analyzed as log-transformed Z-scores and in quartiles. Results At baseline, the study cohort consisted of 5601 normoglycemic non-diabetics with available TG-HDL-C ratios. Apparent from TG-HDL-C ratio quartile comparison (Table 1), individuals with higher TG-HDL-C ratio were more often men, smokers and users of antihypertensive and lipid-lowering medication (p&lt;0.001 for all). This group also exhibited a more adverse risk-profile, with higher waist-hip-ratio, blood pressure, glucose and lipid levels (p&lt;0.001 for all). During a median follow-up of 9.8 (IQR 1.6) years, 209 individuals developed MACE. In univariable analysis, higher TG-HDL-C ratio was generally associated with MACE, mainly driven by an association in the highest quartile (HR=3.18, 95% CI=2.06-4.90, p&lt;0.001). With stepwise introduction of covariates (Table 2) in the multivariable models, the association was attenuated but remained significant in the final model for the highest quartile when compared to quartile 1-3 (HR=1.41, 95% CI=1.03-1.94, p=0.031). Conclusions Higher fasting TG-HDL-C ratio is associated with incident MACE in a Swedish population-based cohort without diabetes or hyperglycemia. The relationship seems independent of traditional cardiovascular risk factors including waist-hip-ratio as a measure of abdominal obesity. The findings propose the TG-HDL-C ratio as a potential indicator of MACE risk among individuals without overt IR. Future studies should evaluate if this translates into added clinical value beyond traditional risk prediction tools.
title: The TG-HDL-C ratio is associated with incident MACE in normoglycemic individuals without diabetes: findings from a Swedish population-based cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Elevated levels of lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is considered to be an established and independent risk factor for coronary artery disease (CAD) and has been shown to be associated with worse outcomes amongst patients with already established CAD. Association status of baseline Lp(a) levels with prognosis of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), especially with respect to incidence of restenosis, however, still remains contentious. Purpose We conducted a systematic review and study-level meta-analysis to evaluate the relationship between pre-PCI Lp(a) levels and the incidence of coronary restenosis. Methods Online databases of PubMed, EMBASE, MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Knowledge were systematically searched for relevant articles published until November 11th, 2025. Qualifying studies had to have: (i) an angiographically determined restenosis group, (ii) an angiographically or clinically determined no-restenosis group, and/or (iii) published summary pre-PCI Lp(a) levels for both groups. Data was extracted from included studies, was transformed (if needed) and further synthesized for summary effect measures of standardized mean difference (SMD), mean difference (MD), and incidence rate ratio (IRR). Study level results were pooled using Z-test employing appropriate effects for analysis. Begg’s funnel plots and Egger’s test were used to detect publication bias. Results From 307 unique records retrieved, 24 studies were included for SMD based analysis (n= 4,596), 13 for MD based analysis (n= 2,016), whilst 17 for IRR based analysis (n= 9,633). Cases with coronary restenosis overall, were found to have significantly higher pre-PCI Lp(a) levels, demonstrating small-moderate effect size (SMD= 0.25), whilst the mean difference in Lp(a) levels between the restenosis and no-restenosis groups was found to be 5.87 mg/dl (SMD= 0.25, 95% CI= 0.11-0.38, p= 0.0003 and MD= 5.87, 95% CI= 1.78-9.96 mg/dl, p= 0.005 respectively). In addition, the risk of coronary restenosis was demonstrated to be 37% higher in patients with clinically elevated pre-PCI Lp(a) levels as compared to the rest (IRR= 1.37, 95% CI= 1.14-1.64, p= 0.0007). A graphical abstract showcasing aims, methods and main results of the present analysis is displayed as Figure 1. We found no evidence of publication bias amongst the analysed study groups and our leave-one-out sensitivity analyses further confirmed the robustness of our findings. Conclusions The present systematic review and meta-analysis confirms the association between elevated pre-PCI Lp(a) levels and angiographically confirmed coronary restenosis. Our findings underscore the potential of Lp(a) as a biomarker for risk stratification at the time of index PCI, helping to identify patients who may benefit from closer clinical monitoring and intensified secondary prevention strategies.
title: Pre-percutaneous coronary intervention lipoprotein (a) levels and its association with angiographically confirmed restenosis – a study level meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract According to the ESC/EAS guidelines, elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] levels (&gt;105 nmol/L) are considered a risk factor for cardiovascular events. However, Lp(a) levels vary across ethnicities and are lower in East Asian populations, for whom an appropriate risk threshold has not been established. This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic significance of Lp(a) and to identify a population-specific Lp(a) cutoff value in Japanese patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), using the CLIDAS-PCI database. The CLIDAS-PCI database is a multicenter registry in Japan. Among 9,690 registry patients, we analyzed 474 patients who underwent PCI between April 2014 and March 2019 and had Lp(a) levels measured prior to PCI. A conditional inference tree–based machine learning approach was applied to estimate an optimal Lp(a) cutoff, and patients were stratified into low and high Lp(a) groups according to the derived threshold. The primary endpoint was major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events plus (MACCE+), defined as a composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke, and coronary revascularization. In the overall cohort, the median age was 70 years, 75% were male, and the median Lp(a) concentration was 64.7 [30.1–128.5] nmol/L. During a median follow-up of 2.5 years, MACCE+ occurred in 26%. Conditional inference tree analysis identified a data-driven Lp(a) cutoff of 22.5 nmol/L. Based on this cutoff, patients were stratified into a low Lp(a) group (n = 97) and a high Lp(a) group (n = 377). Baseline clinical characteristics were largely comparable between the two groups stratified by this cutoff; however, the high Lp(a) group exhibited lower estimated glomerular filtration rates (eGFR) and more frequent statin use. Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated that patients in the high Lp(a) group experienced significantly higher MACCE+ event rates compared with those in the low Lp(a) group (log-rank p = 0.047; Figure 1). Importantly, in a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, blood pressure, eGFR, hemoglobin A1c, LDL cholesterol, and statin use, elevated Lp(a) remained independently associated with an increased risk of MACCE+ (hazard ratio, 2.00; 95% confidence interval, 1.08–3.72). Furthermore, a significant interaction was observed between Lp(a) category and renal function status (p for interaction = 0.02), indicating that the prognostic impact of elevated Lp(a) was more pronounced among patients with preserved renal function (eGFR &gt;60 mL/min/1.73 m²). A machine learning–derived cutoff of 22.5 nmol/L stratified cardiovascular risk, well below current guideline thresholds, particularly in patients with preserved renal function. These findings suggest that ethnicity-specific Lp(a) thresholds may improve risk identification in Japanese populations.
title: A machine learning–derived Lp(a) threshold far below current guideline levels predicts cardiovascular events in japanese PCI patients

abstract: Abstract Background Biological aging (BA) is a comprehensive marker reflecting systemic physiological aging, offering critical context for individual variability based on chronological age. A series of studies have demonstrated that BA is associated with the prognosis of cardiovascular diseases and outcomes following percutaneous coronary intervention. However, the predictive ability of various BA indicators calculated from clinical biochemistry biomarkers for outcomes in aortic stenosis (AS) patients after transcatheter aortic replacement (TAVR) remains unknown. This study aimed to To evaluate the role of BA indicators for prognosis of AS patients post-TAVR. Methods This study included a retrospective cohort and a multicenter prospective cohort who underwent TAVR for AS. We estimated biological age using the Klemera–Doubal method (KDM) and homeostatic dysregulation (HD) method, both involving biomarker selection through correlation analysis, machine learning based feature selection, and explainability analysis. And we calculated PhenoAge and ProBNPAge using well-established algorithms. Multivariable-adjusted Cox proportional hazards models incorporating restricted cubic splines were applied to evaluate the association between accelerated biological age and adverse clinical outcomes. Results A total of 937 patients (mean age 72.6±7.8 years) and 470 patients (mean age 71.6±7.3 years) were included. Five biomarkers were selected for HD and KDM calculation. In the retrospective cohort, a 1-SD increase in HD, log(HD) and PhenoAge, and accelerated aging, showed positive associations with 3-year mortality and MACE (HR &gt; 1.0; p &lt; 0.05) in four adjusted models. In the prospective cohort, HD was associated with higher 2-year mortality and readmission (HR &gt; 1.5; p &lt; 0.05) in four adjusted models. Restricted cubic splines demonstrated a linear dose-response relationship between BAs and adverse outcomes (p for non-linearity &gt; 0.05). Conclusion Biological age indicators particularly HD, demonstrate high prognostic utility for predicting post-TAVR mortality and adverse events. Incorporating these comprehensive markers provides a systemic physiological aging perspective, enhancing risk stratification and treatment selection for aortic stenosis patients.
title: Prognostic value of biological aging in TAVR for aortic stenosis: a combined prospective and retrospective cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background Accurate cardiovascular risk prediction in the general population is crucial for early identification of high-risk individuals. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) has emerged as a promising circulating biomarker by indicating early, subclinical end-organ damage and thereby providing incremental prognostic utility beyond traditional risk factors. Until recently, this was largely limited to hs-cTnI, as the available hs-cTnT assay lacked sufficient low-end analytical sensitivity. A next-generation hs-cTnT assay with markedly improved analytical performance now enables reliable quantification of hs-cTnT in the general population. Purpose To compare the prognostic utility of a novel hs-cTnT with an established hs-cTnI assay in a population-based cohort. Methods We analyzed participants aged 45-79 years. Baseline hs-cTn concentrations were measured using the next-generation hs-cTnT assay (6th Generation) and an established hs-cTnI assay in blood samples collected at time of study inclusion. Co-primary outcomes were all-cause mortality (ACM) and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), including incident myocardial infarction, coronary revascularisation, stroke and ACM. Prognostic associations of log-transformed hs-cTnT and hs-cTnI values were evaluated using Cox proportional hazard models unadjusted, adjusted for age and sex and additionally adjusted for traditional cardiovascular risk factors. Discriminative performance of hs-cTnT and hs-cTnI was assessed using time-dependent ROC analysis. Results A total of 14,361 individuals (median age 60 years, 48.9% female) with available follow-up information were included. Hs-cTnT was detectable above the assay-specific limit of detection in 98.9% of individuals, compared with 81.6% for hs-cTnI. During a median follow-up time of 4.4 (IQR, 3.0-5.8) years, 322 deaths and 730 MACE occurred. Both, hs-cTnT and hs-cTnI were identified as strong and independent predictors of ACM and MACE, even after adjustment for age, sex and traditional risk factors (Table 1). Standardized effect estimates (hazard ratio per 1 standard deviation of log-transformed hs-cTn) were consistently higher for hs-cTnT than hs-cTnI. Time-dependent AUC demonstrated superior discrimination of hs-cTnT compared with hs-cTnI for ACM and MACE up to five years. (Figure 1). For ACM, AUCs at 1 year were 0.795 for hs-cTnT versus 0.719 for hs-cTnI (p=0.042), and at 5 years 0.742 versus 0.703 at 5 years (p=0.0037). Conclusion In the general population, both the next-generation hs-cTnT and the established hs-cTnI assays provide strong, independent prognostic information beyond traditional risk factors. In direct comparison, hs-cTnT seems to offer superior risk discrimination for mortality and cardiovascular events than hs-cTnI. Future risk-prediction models should incorporate circulating biomarkers such as hs-cTn to enhance predictive accuracy.
title: Prognostic utility of a next-generation high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T assay compared to an established high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I assay in the general population

abstract: Abstract Background The stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR) has emerged as a robust predictor of adverse outcomes in acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Though accumulating evidence suggests that its prognostic value may be modified by systemic inflammatory status, commonly reflected by high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), it remains unknown whether integrating these pathways into a unified index improves risk prediction. Purpose This study aimed to develop and validate an integrated inflammatory-hyperglycemic stress index (IHSI) for mortality prediction in ACS patients. Methods We analyzed 6,149 ACS patients from a derivation cohort and 5,218 from a multicenter external validation cohort. The novel index was developed using a LASSO-based covariate selection approach followed by multivariable Cox regression, integrating hsCRP and the absolute deviation of SHR from its optimal value (identified by restricted cubic spline analysis) as: IHSI = 0.0277×hsCRP+0.6289×|SHR - 0.76|. Results The mean age was 58.4±10.4 years in the derivation cohort and 60.4±11.6 years in the validation cohort; 76.8% and 77.9% were male, respectively. Time-dependent ROC analyses showed that SHR achieved higher AUC values among patients with elevated hsCRP compared with those with lower hsCRP levels (e.g., 1-year AUC: 0.67 vs. 0.42). In the derivation cohort, IHSI demonstrated superior discrimination compared with hsCRP and SHR (1-year AUC: 0.72 vs. 0.66 and 0.60), with consistent findings in the validation cohort (0.72 vs. 0.68 and 0.65). IHSI also provided significant net reclassification improvement (derivation: 26.9% vs. hsCRP; 32.5% vs. SHR). Furthermore, in adjusted Cox models, each standard deviation increase in IHSI was independently associated with higher mortality, with HRs of 4.33 (95% CI 2.14-8.76) for 5-year mortality in the derivation cohort and 2.46 (95% CI 1.96-3.09) for 2-year mortality in the validation cohort. Conclusion The IHSI was independently associated with mortality and improved risk discrimination beyond individual biomarkers. Its robust performance across independent cohorts supports its potential utility as a risk assessment tool derived from routinely available metrics.
title: An inflammatory–hyperglycemic stress index predicts mortality in acute coronary syndrome: development and external validation in two large cohorts

abstract: Abstract Background The glucose-to-potassium ratio (GPR) is an emerging metabolic biomarker that has demonstrated prognostic value in several acute conditions, including intracerebral hemorrhage and heart failure. However, its prognostic significance in patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) remains undetermined. Purpose This study aimed to investigate the association between GPR and long-term adverse outcomes in patients with CAD after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Methods A total of 10,724 consecutive CAD patients undergoing PCI in 2013 were screened, and 9,585 with complete data were included in the final analysis. The primary endpoint was the occurrence of major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), and the secondary endpoint was all-cause mortality during the 5-year follow-up. GPR was analyzed as a continuous variable. Results Among the 9,585 patients, mean age was 58.4±10.3 years and 77.2% were male. Restricted cubic spline analyses indicated a linear association between GPR and both endpoints, with all tests reaching statistical significance (P &lt; 0.05) and no evidence of nonlinearity (P for nonlinearity &gt; 0.05). Cox proportional hazards models showed that elevated GPR was significantly associated with increased risks of MACCE and all-cause mortality across all adjustment models. In the fully adjusted model (Model 3), GPR remained an independent predictor of MACCE (hazard ratio [HR]: 1.123; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.029–1.225) and all-cause death (HR: 1.355; 95% CI: 1.125–1.631). Conclusion GPR is an independent predictor of long-term adverse outcomes after PCI and may serve as a simple, accessible marker for residual risk stratification in routine clinical practice.
title: Glucose-to-potassium ratio independently predicts long-term adverse outcomes in patients with coronary artery disease after PCI

abstract: Abstract Background The fibroblast activation protein inhibitor-04 (FAPI-04) specifically binds to the FAP of activated myocardial fibroblasts, which makes [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 positron emission tomography (PET)/magnetic resonance (MR) a new potential imaging technique for the evaluation of myocardial fibrosis. However, the long-term prognostic value of FAPI PET during the early phase of STEMI remains unclear. Aims This study aimed to evaluate the potential value of [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 PET/MR in predicting major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with STEMI. Methods A total of 164 patients with STEMI were enrolled. All patients underwent [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 PET/MR imaging within 45 days post-infarction. The primary endpoint was MACE, defined as a composite of cardiac death, heart failure, stroke, and reinfarction. Cox proportional hazards regression and two distinct machine learning algorithms were used for feature selection. Results Among the enrolled cohort (median age 65 years, 86.6% male), 12 patients (7.3%) experienced at least one MACE over a median follow-up of 17.8 (IQR: 12.3–25.7) months, comprising a total of 14 adverse events (2 cardiac deaths, 4 heart failures, 5 strokes, and 3 reinfarctions). [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 uptake volume (UV), but not maximum and mean target-to-background ratio (TBRmax and TBRmean), was significantly correlated with left ventricular end-systolic volume (r=0.684), end-diastolic volume (r=0.586), and ejection fraction (r=-0.506) (all P&lt;0.001). FAPI UV was a significant predictor of MACE (HR 1.01 per 1-cm³, 95% CI 1.01-1.02,P&lt;0.001), with the hazard increasing by 76% per 1-SD (+63.4 cm³; HR 1.76, 95% CI 1.23-2.52, P=0.002) and 56% per 50-cm³ increment (HR 1.56, 95% CI 1.17-2.08, P=0.002). All PET/MR parameters were further ranked based on their predictive importance for adverse outcomes, using two distinct machine learning (ML) algorithms (random forest and gradient boosting; Figure 1). In both Cox regression and ML analyses, FAPI UV emerged as the most important predictor of MACE. Compared to MR imaging and cardiac function parameters, UV demonstrated better predictive ability (AUC = 0.870, P &lt; 0.001) for MACE, with sensitivity of 66.7% and specificity of 98.1%. Finally, scatter visualization of an LVEF-UV quadrant (Figure 2A) revealed the highest MACE incidence (10.8%) in the high-risk zone (LVEF&lt;50% and UV≥ median). Conversely, patients with a low UV burden showed consistently low event rates (~6%) regardless of LVEF. A logistic regression-based heatmap (Figure 2B) further confirmed that predicted MACE probabilities escalated predominantly along the UV axis rather than the LVEF axis. Conclusion [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 PET/MR is an effective tool to non-invasively quantify myocardial fibroblast activation, and FAPI UV assessed in the early post-infarction period demonstrates potential predictive value for adverse outcomes.Figure 1.Importance rankingFigure 2.Risk mapping
title: Prognostic value of [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 PET/MR for major adverse cardiovascular events after acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction After percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), clinicians and patients are often reassured that coronary risk has been “treated”, yet substantial residual atherosclerosis may persist in non-coronary vascular beds. Polyvascular disease defines an extreme-risk phenotype for which guidelines recommend more aggressive LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C) lowering (target &lt;40 mg/dL) than for other patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (target &lt;55 mg/dL). Systematic non-coronary vascular assessment after PCI could therefore reclassify risk and highlight opportunities to intensify secondary prevention. Purpose To quantify the prevalence of ultrasound-detected polyvascular atherosclerosis after PCI and to test whether greater extra-coronary plaque burden is linked to more intensive LDL-C lowering and attainment of risk-adapted LDL-C targets. Methods We analysed a prospective registry of consecutive patients attending a post-PCI clinic ≥1 month after the index procedure (n=889). All underwent a routine ultrasound of the bilateral carotid and common femoral arteries. Atherosclerotic plaque was defined as a focal structure encroaching into the lumen or intima–media thickness ≥2.0 mm, using a stricter adaptation of Mannheim criteria. Patients were classified as CAD only (no extra-coronary plaque), CAD + 1 extra-coronary bed, or CAD + ≥2 beds (polyvascular extreme-risk). Baseline characteristics and lipid metrics (LDL-C, LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL, LDL-C &lt;40 mg/dL, combination lipid-lowering therapy) were compared with one-way ANOVA and chi-square tests.​ Results Of 889 patients, 361 (40.6%) had CAD only, 314 (35.3%) CAD + 1 extra-coronary bed, and 214 (24.1%) CAD + ≥2 beds, so nearly one in four had an otherwise unrecognised extreme-risk polyvascular phenotype detected only by routine vascular imaging. Age, male sex, and BMI &gt;25 kg/m² increased with plaque burden (all p≤0.001), whereas diabetes and hypertension were similarly prevalent. LDL-C management was not risk-aligned: mean LDL-C was 50.1, 51.1, and 52.8 mg/dL in the CAD only, CAD + 1 bed, and CAD + ≥2 bed groups (p=0.35), with comparable proportions achieving LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL (69.5%, 63.4%, 64.4%; p=0.20) and &lt;40 mg/dL (31.1%, 31.5%, 24.8%; p=0.19). Combination lipid-lowering therapy also did not increase with plaque burden (70.9%, 64.9%, 63.5%; p=0.12). Conclusion(s) Routine carotid and femoral ultrasound after PCI uncovers a substantial hidden subgroup with polyvascular extreme-risk anatomy, yet their LDL-C levels, LDL-C target attainment, and use of combination lipid-lowering therapy are indistinguishable from those with CAD only. This treatment–risk paradox underscores that reassurance after PCI can mask residual polyvascular risk; embedding systematic non-coronary vascular assessment into post-PCI pathways offers a practical means to refine risk stratification and trigger intensification of secondary prevention in patients who stand to benefit most.Table.Baseline characteristics
title: Beyond the stent: routine vascular ultrasound after PCI reveals polyvascular extreme risk without intensified LDL-cholesterol lowering therapy

abstract: Abstract Background Intracoronary optical coherence tomography (OCT) enables high-resolution visualization of lipid-rich plaque structures. Established OCT-based prognostic markers include thin-cap fibroatheroma (TCFA) and lipid arc. Previous studies have demonstrated the capability of artificial intelligence (AI)-based models to quantify plaque characteristics using the outer boundary of lipid pools, enabling metrics such as plaque burden. However, the prognostic value of these boundary-based OCT-derived metrics remains unknown. Purpose To investigate the association of AI-derived plaque characteristics on OCT with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients after myocardial infarction (MI). Methods Using our validated AI segmentation model (OCT-AID), 488 non-flow-limiting, non-culprit lesions were analyzed from 415 MI-patients enrolled in the PECTUS-obs study. OCT-pullbacks were automatically segmented by OCT-AID, focusing on frames within the predefined, core-lab selected lesions. We introduce the focal lipid-to-cap ratio (LCRf), a novel version of the lipid-to-cap ratio (LCR), defined as the AI-estimated lipid plaque thickness divided by the AI-estimated FCT at each of 360 circumferential degrees, measured from the centroid of the lumen. LCRf was designed to capture lipid-intima ratios at a more focal level, using automated AI-based calculation of the outer boundary of the lipid pool in every angle. The prognostic value of LCRf was compared to other metrics. The following metrics were calculated: TCFA, total number of frames with TCFA, and the maximum lipid arc, plaque burden, LCR and LCRf. Continuous metrics were split into tertiles, with patients with at least one lesion in the highest tertile being assigned to the “high” group, and remaining patients to the “low” group. Primary outcome measure was MACE at 2 year follow-up, defined as the composite of death from any cause, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and unplanned revascularization. Cox proportional hazard models were used to assess prognostic value. Results At two-year follow-up, MACE occurred in 34/415 cases (8.2%). Both binary TCFA and the number of TCFA frames were a significant predictor of MACE (HR 2.10, 95% CI 1.07-4.11, p=0.031 and HR 2.04, 95% CI 1.04-4.01, p=0.037, respectively). The new metric LCRf was associated with MACE (HR 2.39, 95% CI 1.21-4.70, p=0.012). No statistical association with MACE was found for lipid arc (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.59-2.33, p=0.640), OCT-derived plaque burden (HR 1.22, 95% CI 0.61-2.41, p=0.572 ) and LCR (HR 1.55, 95% CI 0.79-3.05, p=0.204). Conclusions We found that established markers such as TCFA and the number of TCFA frames were associated with cardiovascular events.
