Also, the novel LCRf metric was significantly associated with MACE, suggesting that AI-enabled lipid plaque quantification using OCT-estimations of lipid plaque thickness may be worth exploring further.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Artificial intelligence-based analysis of novel and established lipid plaque measures in relation to clinical outcome

abstract: Abstract Abstract 18F-sodium fluoride (18F-NaF) positron emission tomography (PET) has shown hope in refining risk stratification in patients with established coronary artery disease (CAD). Computed tomography is increasingly being employed for assessments of body composition, with this novel application providing additional prognostic value across a wide range of CAD manifestations. To date we lack data on the influence of body composition on outcomes in the challenging population of patients with established CAD. Purpose We aimed to elucidate the complex interplay between body composition, plaque activity and outcomes. Methods Patients with known CAD (with a history of either myocardial infarction or coronary revascularization) underwent 18F-NaF PET. Coronary 18F-NaF uptake was determined by the coronary microcalcification activity (CMA). Body composition quantification was performed with deep learning on low dose computed tomography acquired for attenuation correction purposes. Tissue types were differentiated using Hounsfield unit (HU) ranges. Adipose tissue within the intrathoracic space was considered visceral adipose tissue, unless segmented as epicardial adipose tissue. Four tissues (subcutaneous adipose tissue, skeletal muscle, intramuscular adipose tissue (IMAT), and bone) were segmented in the extrathoracic space. Non-fatal myocardial infarction and cardiac death served as the composite primary endpoint. Results The study population included 759 patients (age 64±8.0, 117 [15%] women) with a history of coronary revascularization and a high disease burden with a median coronary artery calcium score of 190 [52-571] Agatston units. On 18F-NaF PET overall 461 (61%) patients showed 18F-NaF coronary uptake (CMA&gt;0). The median CMA was 0.27 [0.0-2.32] with 288 (38%) patients presenting with 1 or 2 vessels with CMA&gt;0 and 173 (23%) with triple-vessel 18F-NaF increased uptake. Over a median of 4.5 [4.0 to 6.0] years and 3573 patient-years of follow-up 64 patients experienced the composite primary endpoint. Among all the baseline clinical and imaging characteristics only IMAT volume (250.0±121.7 vs 218.6±98.2, p=0.015) and CMA (1.6 [0.9-2.5] vs 0.6 [0.0-1.6], p=0.04) were significantly higher in those with an event. Indeed on cox proportional hazard modelling IMAT volume &gt;221.1 (HR 1.7; 95% CI 1.0-2.8, p=0.04) and CMA greater than 0 (HR 2.4; 95% CI 1.3-4.3, p=0.004) emerged as predictors of the composite primary outcome. These associations were independent of age and the coronary artery calcium score and persisted on multivariable cox regression modelling - HR 1.6; 95% CI 1.0-2.8, p=0.049 and HR 2.4; 95% CI 1.3-4.5, p=0.004; for IMAT volume and CMA, respectively). Conclusions While 18F-NaF coronary PET remains the strongest predictor of the composite endpoint of myocardial infarction or cardiac death, body composition analysis has the potential to enhance risk stratification in the challenging cohort of patients with established CAD.Fig 1
title: Body composition and atherosclerotic plaque activity in patients with established coronary artery disease

abstract: Abstract Background Early detection of coronary artery disease (CAD) through non-invasive comprehensive cardiovascular ultrasound in asymptomatic subjects represents an opportunity to concentrate maximal preventive therapy on higher-risk individuals. Objectives This study aims to assess the potential incremental value of an innovative but simple cardiac/carotid ultrasound (CCU) screening protocol for predicting outcome in asymptomatic individuals. CCU is based on the assessment of carotid plaques, myocardial global longitudinal strain (LV GLS) and Doppler coronary flow velocity in the mid tract of the left anterior descending coronary artery (V-LAD) at rest. Methods This prospective, observational, single-center study enrolled asymptomatic apparently healthy volunteers. Clinical data, blood tests, treadmill ECG and standard echocardiography data were collected on top of CCU variables. The primary combined end point was the occurrence during follow-up of a) hospital admission for acute coronary syndrome or angina (in this case requiring confirmatory CT detection of at least 50% coronary stenosis or an abnormal functional cardiac imaging test), b) cardiovascular death, c) hospital admission for heart failure, d) hospital admission for atrial fibrillation, e) elective coronary revascularization procedure. A secondary end point, corresponding to the primary end point without the e) component (coronary revascularization procedure), which is potentially increased in subjects with abnormal screening results (work-up bias) was also analysed to confirm robustness of the associations. Results We enrolled 1033 subjects (median age 59 years, 50% females). During a mean follow-up of 23 months, 150 primary combined endpoints (and 84 secondary end points) were recorded. In the overall population the mean mid-tract V-LAD was 41.5cm/sec, mean LV GLS was -20.6% and 327 subjects (32%) had a carotid plaque detected. Figure shows the Receiver Operating Curves (ROC) for both the primary and secondary end points based on V-LAD. Table shows the multivariable analysis of clinical and imaging variables for the association with the secondary end point. Only age, the presence of at least one carotid plaque, and V-LAD remained significant. While the analyses were conducted using continuous variables, the best V-LAD cut-off for the prediction of either primary or secondary end points resulted &gt; 44cm/sec; using this cutoff, abnormal V-LAD was present in 274 subjects (26.5%), while 759 (73.5%) had normal V-LAD. Conclusions A simple, low-cost, ultrasound screening strategy is capable to predict combined cardiac outcome significantly better than comprehensive evaluation of clinical risk factors and standard echocardiography variables. Twenty-four percent of study subjects who on initial screening showed increased V-LAD (274 subjects), i.e. higher than 44cm/sec, had a secondary end point over a mean 23-month follow-up, versus 2% of subjects showing normal V-LAD.Figure ROC curve V-LAD velocity vs endpointsTable Multivariable association with endpoint
title: Simple ultrasound parameters-carotid plaque and coronary Doppler velocity at rest- predict cardiovascular events better than clinical risk factors: the PENSIAMOCI-PRIMA screening study.

abstract: Abstract Introduction Revascularization of chronic total occlusions (CTO) aims to reduce myocardial ischemia and improve functional capacity. However, it remains unclear which CTO patients derive the greatest objective functional benefit from percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Purpose To evaluate whether baseline ischemic burden measured by [13N]NH3 PET-CT predicts functional benefit after CTO-PCI and whether ischemia reduction correlates with changes in cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET). Methods Thirty-two CTO patients were prospectively evaluated with [13N]NH3 PET-CT and treadmill CPET before and after PCI. Ischemia was quantified using summed difference score (SDS), both globally and within the CTO territory. CPET parameters included peak VO2, % predicted peak VO2, O2 pulse, VE/VCO2 slope, and exercise duration. A maximal effort (RER &gt;1.10) was achieved in 59% at both evaluations; however the full cohort was analyzed to reflect real-world response. Pearson correlations and multivariable linear regression adjusted for age and baseline CPET values were performed. Results CTO-PCI reduced global SDS (−5.6±5.9; p&lt;0.001) and regional SDS (−4.4±4.0; p&lt;0.001), indicating marked ischemia reduction. This was accompanied by improvements in peak VO2 (Δ1.6±2.7mL/kg/min; p=0.001), % predicted peak VO2 (Δ9.7±11.4%; p&lt;0.001), O2 pulse (Δ1.2±1.8mL/beat; p&lt;0.001), and exercise duration (Δ70.1±151.4s; p=0.016), with a trend toward lower VE/VCO2 slope (p=0.070). Reduction in global ischemia (Δ global SDS) correlated with improvement in peak VO2 (r=−0.454; p=0.009) and % predicted peak VO2 (r=−0.509; p=0.003), remaining independently associated after multivariable adjustment (peak VO2: β=−0.24, 95% CI −0.37 to −0.10; p=0.002; % predicted peak VO2: β=−1.09, 95% CI −1.63 to −0.54; p=0.001). Baseline global SDS showed a modest, non-significant correlation with Δ peak VO2 (r=0.342; p=0.055), which was not retained after adjustment (p=0.342). In contrast, baseline global SDS independently predicted change in VE/VCO2 slope (β=−0.32, 95% CI −0.59 to −0.04; p=0.036). Regional ischemia (baseline or Δ SDS) was not independently associated with peak VO2 gain. Conclusion In CTO patients, PCI resulted in marked global ischemia reduction and objective improvement in exercise capacity. Importantly, functional gain in peak oxygen consumption was independently linked to the magnitude of global - rather than territorial - ischemia relief. These findings suggest that the benefit of CTO revascularization extends beyond simple reperfusion of the occluded vessel and may reflect restoration of balanced global myocardial perfusion, potentially through attenuation of coronary steal phenomenon. By linking global ischemia reduction to improvements in exercise capacity, our results provide mechanistic insight into how ischemia relief translates into functional recovery and support an ischemia-guided approach to CTO revascularization.CPET and PET-CT parameters pre and post-PCIGlobal ischemia and improvement in peak VO2
title: Association between PET-derived ischemic burden and cardiopulmonary functional gain after CTO revascularization

abstract: Abstract Background Global longitudinal strain (GLS) reflects subclinical left ventricular dysfunction and has been linked to adverse outcomes in selected populations. Mechanical dispersion (MD), reflecting mechanical heterogeneity, adds prognostic value in cardiac disease, but its prognostic relevance in the general population remains uncertain. Purpose To investigate associations of GLS and MD with incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and all-cause mortality in a population-based cohort. Methods The ACE1950 Study enrolled 3,706 individuals born in 1950 between 2013 and 2015. Among these, 2,495 participants with complete strain and covariate data were analyzed. GLS and MD were assessed by speckle-tracking echocardiography. Participants were followed until December 31 st , 2022, for incident MACE (myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure, or coronary revascularization) and all-cause mortality. Multivariable Cox regression models adjusted for cardiovascular risk factors and left ventricular ejection fraction were applied. Non-linearity of GLS was assessed using restricted cubic splines. Results Over a median follow-up of 8.3 years, 180 MACE and 118 deaths occurred. GLS demonstrated a non-linear association with MACE, with increased risk confined to lower strain values. MD was independently associated with MACE (HR 1.16 per SD increase, 95% CI 1.01–1.33; p=0.034) and improved model fit beyond risk factors, ejection fraction, and GLS (likelihood-ratio p=0.016). Associations were weaker after adjustment for prevalent coronary artery disease. Neither GLS nor MD were associated with all-cause mortality. Conclusion In this middle-aged general population, lower GLS values were associated with incident cardiovascular events. MD provided incremental prognostic information beyond conventional risk markers and ejection fraction.Association between GLS and MACE
title: Global longitudinal strain and mechanical dispersion predict cardiovascular events in a middle-aged population: the ACE1950 study

abstract: Abstract Background Myocardial flow reserve (MFR) assessed by ¹³N-ammonia PET is a strong prognostic marker in ischemic heart disease (IHD). Although both heart failure (HF) and reduced MFR are associated with adverse outcomes, whether the prognostic value of MFR differs according to HF status across the spectrum of IHD remains unclear.Therefore, this study aimed to compare MFR distribution between HF and non-HF patients with IHD and to assess whether HF status modifies the prognostic value of MFR. Methods We conducted a single-center, retrospective, observational study including consecutive patients who underwent ¹³N-ammonia PET between 2013 and 2024. Patients with prior heart transplantation, non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, or unknown HF status were excluded. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, ischemic stroke, heart failure hospitalization, and unplanned revascularization ≥90 days after PET. Patients were stratified by HF status and MFR (cutoff 2.0). Cox regression and restricted cubic spline analyses were performed. Results A total of 675 patients were included (non-HF: n=573; HF: n=102). HF patients had lower stress myocardial blood flow and MFR compared with non-HF patients (both p&lt;0.001).Reduced MFR (&lt;2.0) was associated with higher event rates regardless of HF status (log-rank p&lt;0.001). In multivariable analysis, global MFR was an independent predictor of adverse events, whereas HF status was not. Patients without HF but with reduced MFR had significantly increased risk compared with those without HF and preserved MFR (HR 2.13, p=0.005). The association between reduced MFR and adverse outcomes was consistent across all subgroups, with no significant interactions. Conclusion MFR is reduced in HF patients but retains its prognostic value independent of HF status. Functional assessment of coronary microvascular dysfunction using MFR may provide consistent risk stratification across IHD patients regardless of heart failure status.Cumulative incidence of the primary endpoint
title: Reduced myocardial flow reserve on ¹³N-Ammonia PET predicts adverse outcomes independent of heart failure status

abstract: Abstract Background Effective secondary prevention is essential to reduce morbidity and mortality after acute coronary syndrome. However, adherence to comprehensive secondary-prevention strategies remains suboptimal, despite strong guideline recommendations. Aim To evaluate one-year cardiovascular risk-factor control and guideline-directed medical therapy within a structured intensive secondary-prevention program after ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Methods Consecutive STEMI patients were enrolled in the intervention group at four PCI centres in Slovakia. Participants attended four structured outpatient visits within the first year after discharge, focusing on clinical assessment, pharmacotherapy optimization, and comprehensive risk-factor management. The present analysis reports prespecified secondary objectives related to cardiovascular risk-factor control and pharmacotherapy during one-year follow-up in the intervention cohort. Analyses comparing clinical outcomes with standard care are ongoing and will be reported separately. Results Among 1,031 STEMI patients, significant improvements in risk-factor control were observed. Mean LDL-cholesterol decreased from 3.5 ± 1.1 mmol/L at index hospitalization to 1.8 ± 1.0 mmol/L at one year (p &lt; 0.001), with 67% of patients achieving &lt;1.8 mmol/L and 39% reaching the recommended target of &lt;1.4 mmol/L. Systolic and diastolic blood pressures declined significantly over study period (p = 0.047 and p &lt; 0.001, respectively), with 77% of patients attaining systolic BP &lt;140 mmHg and 51% reaching &lt;130 mmHg. Active smoking decreased from 49% at baseline to 13% at one year (p &lt; 0.001), and fasting plasma glucose levels improved significantly over the follow-up period (p = 0.013). BMI remained unchanged (p = 0.43). Use of recommended medications demonstrated high adherence to guideline-directed therapy. Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) was prescribed in 95% of patients at discharge and remained above 89% during follow-up. Statins were prescribed in 99% of patients at discharge and continued in 96% throughout the study. Combined hypolipidemic therapy with ezetimibe was used in 75% of patients, and PCSK9-targeted therapies in 16%. Beta-blockers use increased from 87% at discharge to 91% at one year. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) were used in 76% at discharge and 79% at one year. Conclusion Structured secondary prevention program delivered during the first year after STEMI was associated with significant improvements in lipid levels, blood pressure, fasting plasma glucose, and smoking cessation, as well as high utilisation of guideline-recommended medical therapy. Further outcome analyses will determine whether this novel approach translates into improved clinical outcomes.
title: Achievement of secondary prevention targets after STEMI: results from the IMPACS Study

abstract: Abstract Background Early identification of dysglycaemia and dyslipidaemia is essential for optimising secondary prevention after acute coronary syndrome (ACS). National guidance mandates HbA1c and lipid profile testing during admission; however, real-world adherence and inter-site variation remain suboptimal. Purpose To evaluate compliance with guideline-directed metabolic screening in ACS admissions and determine whether a structured system-level intervention improves adherence and reduces variation across two hospital sites. Methods A quality improvement project was conducted across two acute hospital sites within one healthcare Trust. Two audit cycles included 200 consecutive ACS admissions (100 per cycle; 50 per site). Baseline compliance was assessed against a 100% standard. Gaps included absence of pathway integration and inter-site practice variation. A structured intervention comprising multidisciplinary education, visual prompts, audit feedback, and pathway reinforcement was implemented. Re-audit occurred three months later. Proportions were compared using Fisher’s exact test. Results Baseline compliance was low, with HbA1c testing performed in 20% and lipid profile testing in 48% of ACS admissions. Following intervention, HbA1c testing increased to 74% (+54% absolute increase; p=1.21×10-12) and lipid testing to 79% (+31% absolute increase; p=1.02×10-5), demonstrating statistically robust improvement in guideline adherence. Conclusion Failure to embed metabolic screening within ACS pathways represents a modifiable secondary prevention gap. A structured, low-cost intervention produced statistically robust improvement and reduced variation. Closing this gap at the point of ACS admission provides a scalable model for system-level cardiovascular risk optimisation.Lipid profile, Hba1c test
title: Closing the secondary prevention gap in acute coronary syndrome through system-level metabolic risk standardisation

abstract: Abstract Background Beta-blockers are routinely prescribed after acute coronary syndromes and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), yet much of the supporting evidence comes from historical trials in patients with reduced systolic function. In contemporary practice, most patients have preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), and the survival benefit of routine beta-blocker therapy across the full LVEF spectrum remains uncertain. Purpose To assess the association between discharge beta-blocker therapy and all-cause mortality following a coronary event and PCI, stratified by LVEF. Methods We conducted a state-wide nested case-control study within a cohort of adults (≥18 years) discharged alive after a coronary event managed with PCI, using data from the Victorian Cardiac Outcomes Registry linked to the Australian National Death Index (2014–2022). Patients were stratified by LVEF (preserved ≥50%, mildly reduced 41–49%, moderately reduced 35–40%, severely reduced &lt;35%). Within each stratum, decedents (cases) were matched 1:1 to survivors (controls) on index discharge date. The exposure was beta-blocker prescription at discharge versus no prescription. Propensity scores incorporating 15 clinical and procedural covariates were used for 1:1 matching within time-matched sets. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Associations were estimated using conditional logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors. Missing LVEF (10.7%) was addressed using multiple imputation. Sensitivity analyses included complete-case models and 30-day cardiovascular mortality. Results Among 71,053 eligible patients, 67.3% received beta-blockers at discharge. After propensity score matching, beta-blocker therapy was associated with higher odds of all-cause mortality in patients with preserved LVEF (odds ratio [OR] 1.46, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.29–1.65) and mildly reduced LVEF (OR 1.48, 95% CI 1.15–1.91). No significant association was observed in moderately reduced (OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.92–1.58) or severely reduced LVEF (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.73–1.34). Sensitivity analyses were consistent with the primary findings: complete-case models produced similar estimates, and beta-blockers remained associated with increased 30-day cardiovascular mortality in preserved LVEF (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.10–1.73). Conclusions In this large contemporary state-wide cohort of adults discharged alive after PCI for coronary events, beta-blocker therapy was associated with higher all-cause mortality in patients with preserved and mildly reduced LVEF and showed no survival benefit in those with more severe systolic dysfunction. These real-world findings question the generalisability of historical evidence and support a more individualised approach to beta-blocker use after PCI based on LVEF.

appraisal.design_and_n: Nested case-control study within the Victorian Cardiac Outcomes Registry linked to the Australian National Death Index (2014-2022); 71,053 eligible patients, propensity score matched within LVEF strata.
appraisal.main_limitation: Observational nested case-control design with a conference abstract level of detail; confounding by indication and the direction of the association make a causal reading unsafe, and discharge prescription alone was the exposure.
appraisal.one_line: In a Victorian state-wide registry nested case-control analysis, discharge beta-blocker therapy after PCI was associated with higher odds of all-cause death in patients with preserved or mildly reduced LVEF and with no survival difference at lower LVEF.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Beta-blocker therapy was associated with higher odds of all-cause mortality in preserved LVEF (odds ratio [OR] 1.46, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.29-1.65) and mildly reduced LVEF (OR 1.48, 95% CI 1.15-1.91); no significant association in moderately reduced (OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.92-1.58) or severely reduced LVEF (OR 0.99, 95% CI 0.73-1.34).
appraisal.why_it_matters: Routine beta-blocker use after PCI with preserved LVEF is a common, contested decision in post-MI secondary prevention, and this adds a large contemporary signal of harm or confounding to be tested by trial emulation or randomised data.

title: Beta-blocker therapy and all-cause mortality after percutaneous coronary intervention: a state-wide propensity score matched analysis stratified by left ventricular ejection fraction

abstract: Abstract Background Beta-blockers remain central to post-myocardial infarction (MI) management, but their benefit in patients with midrange or preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) in the reperfusion era remains unclear. Purpose To synthesise evidence on the effectiveness, time-dependent effects, and role of LVEF in long-term beta-blocker use post-MI, stratified by study design. Methods We conducted an umbrella review and meta-analysis. MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library were searched (Jan 2019 - Dec 2025) for systematic reviews and meta-analyses of adults (≥18 years) receiving beta-blockers for ≥1-year post-MI. Outcomes were all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, and recurrent MI. Beta-blocker use was compared with no use. Unique primary studies were pooled using random-effects meta-analyses stratified by study design: randomised controlled trials (RCTs), propensity score matched (PSM) observational studies, and non-PSM studies. Meta-regression assessed follow-up duration; subgroup analyses examined midrange (40–49%) and preserved (≥50%) LVEF. Sensitivity analyses excluded converted effect estimates and validated findings using aggregate estimates from included reviews. Results Nineteen systematic reviews encompassing 52 primary studies (n = 495,827) were included. In RCTs (7 studies; n=24,191), beta-blockers were not associated with all-cause mortality (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.78–1.01) or cardiovascular mortality (HR 0.94, 95% CI 0.74–1.19) but reduced recurrent MI risk by 20% (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.66–0.97). Observational studies showed mortality benefits but no significant effect on recurrent MI. In RCTs, cardiovascular mortality and recurrent MI benefits attenuated over longer follow-up; no time effect was observed for all-cause mortality. PSM studies showed no duration effect, while non-PSM studies demonstrated attenuation of mortality benefits over time. RCT subgroup analyses were limited to preserved LVEF, showing no outcome benefit; observational data suggested greater benefit in midrange LVEF for all outcomes. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robustness and indicated that prior larger pooled effects were driven by observational studies. Conclusions Contemporary RCT evidence indicates that long-term beta-blocker use post-MI does not reduce mortality but lowers recurrent MI risk, with effects diminishing over time and seemingly absent in preserved LVEF. Observational studies suggested potential benefits in midrange LVEF, though these findings are prone to confounding. High-level evidence questions universal long-term beta-blocker use and supports an individualised, LVEF-stratified approach.
title: Beta-blocker therapy after myocardial infarction: an umbrella review

abstract: Abstract Background Premature coronary artery disease (CAD) is increasingly recognized as a distinct clinical entity with substantial long-term burden. However, data differentiating very early-onset CAD (≤35 years) from early-onset CAD (35–45 years) remain limited. A better understanding of baseline phenotypic differences may inform tailored prevention and management strategies. Purpose To compare baseline clinical characteristics, risk factor profiles, and angiographic features between very early- and early-onset CAD in a large multicentre prospective cohort. Methods This cross-sectional baseline analysis included 1,559 patients aged ≤45 years with imaging-confirmed CAD. Participants were categorized into very early-onset CAD (≤35 years, n=253) and early-onset CAD (35–45 years, n=1,306). Baseline assessments comprised sociodemographic characteristics, cardiovascular risk factors, medical history, lifestyle behaviors, anthropometric measures, laboratory biomarkers, and coronary angiographic findings. Results Overall, 94.2% (1468/1559) were male and 58.8% (898/1526) presented with acute coronary syndrome, with no significant difference in clinical presentation between groups. Very early-onset patients were characterized by pronounced central adiposity, exhibiting greater body mass index (28.35 [25.41-31.61] vs. 27.09 [24.99-29.77] kg/m², P&lt;0.001) and waist circumference (95.00 [88.00-105.00] vs. 94.75 [88.00-102.00] cm, P=0.004). This group demonstrated a highly pro-thrombotic and inflammatory baseline milieu, with elevated uric acid (412.45 ± 98.73 vs. 388.84 ± 99.85 μmol/L, P&lt;0.001), white blood cell counts (7.55 [6.41-8.37] vs. 7.24 [5.98-8.48] x10⁹/L, P=0.03), and platelets (250 [211-297] vs. 232 [197-272] x10⁹/L, P=0.003). In contrast, traditional atherosclerotic drivers were less prevalent in the ≤35 cohort, including diabetes (20.9% [53/253] vs. 28.4% [370/1,302], P=0.02) and hypertension (45.5% [115/253] vs. 52.5% [684/1,301], P=0.04). Angiographically, very early-onset CAD was heavily focal, featuring higher rates of single-vessel disease (38.7% [84/217] vs. 26.5% [304/1,147]) and significantly lower rates of three-vessel disease (35.5% [77/217] vs. 41.2% [473/1,147]). Despite this limited anatomical spread, very early-onset patients suffered a higher prevalence of prior myocardial infarction (38.7% [98/253] vs. 29.7% [387/1,300], P=0.005). Lipid profiles and statin use were comparable between groups. Conclusion(s) Very early-onset CAD is not merely premature disease but a distinct and potentially more aggressive phenotype marked by central obesity and systemic inflammation, with early myocardial infarction occurring despite limited angiographic extent. This challenges conventional metabolic paradigms and underscores the need for age-tailored prevention and management strategies.Table 1.Baseline CharacteristicsTable 1.Baseline Characteristics (Continued)
title: Distinct phenotype of very early-onset coronary artery disease (≤35 years): baseline findings from a multicentre prospective cohort

abstract: Abstract Background COVID-19 vaccination has been shown to reduce the risk of long COVID, but its role in preventing major post-COVID cardiovascular disease (CVD), particularly when administered before or after SARS-CoV-2 infection, remains unclear. Purpose To evaluate whether pre- and post-infection COVID-19 vaccination reduces the risk of post-COVID CVD and whether protection varies according to vaccine dose. Methods We included 496,338 COVID-19 positive and 1,537,275 COVID-19 negative individuals. Using a causal mediation framework, we evaluated the effects of pre-infection COVID-19 vaccination on post-COVID CVD, considering SARS-CoV-2 infection and reinfection as mediators. The effect of post-infection vaccination was examined using a target trial emulation framework, and dose-dependent associations were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models. Modes were adjusted for age, sex, Charlson Comorbidity Index, and the Index of Relative Socioeconomic Disadvantage (IRSD). Outcomes included total CVD, stroke, heart failure (HF), acute myocardial infarction (AMI), and acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Result Vaccination before infection reduced the absolute risk (ARR) of post-COVID CVD by 2.00% (95% CI: 1.92–2.04%), with most of this effect due to direct protection (ARR 1.73% [1.64–1.80%]) and a smaller portion mediated through prevention of SARS-CoV-2 infection (ARR 0.27% [0.23–0.29%]). Significant reductions were observed for stroke (ARR 0.26%), HF (ARR 0.38%), AMI (ARR 0.23%), and ACS (ARR 0.33%). Vaccination administered after infection was also protective, with total CVD ARR 1.40% (number needed to treat 71), and consistent reductions in stroke (ARR 0.26%), HF (ARR 0.25%), AMI (ARR 0.18%), and ACS (ARR 0.06%). Dose-response analyses showed increasing protection with additional vaccine doses, and influenza vaccination alone or combined with COVID-19 vaccination provided further cardiovascular benefit. Conclusion COVID-19 vaccination, administered either before or after SARS-CoV-2 infection, is associated with notable reductions in post-COVID CVD. Vaccination prevented approximately 1-2 post-COVID CVD events per 100 individuals at the population level. The protective effect increases with the number of vaccine doses, is driven primarily by direct effects, and is further enhanced through prevention of infection and reinfection.Graphical_Abstract
title: COVID-19 vaccination confers long-term cardioprotection against post-COVID cardiovascular disease: &gt;5-year evidence from causal mediation and target trial emulation

abstract: Abstract Background Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is widely used in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) undergoing early percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). However, its impact on short-term adverse outcomes in frail patients with AMI undergoing early PCI remains unclear. Purpose This study aimed to evaluate the effect of LMWH on short-term adverse outcomes in frail patients with AMI undergoing early PCI. Methods Data were sourced from the Coronary Artery Disease specialized database, comprising a retrospective multicenter cohort of patients discharged from 82 hospitals between 2010 and 2024. Patients were stratified into the LMWH group and control group (no LMWH, fondaparinux, or bivalirudin). Baseline covariates, including the use of unfractionated heparin, were balanced between the two groups through propensity score matching (PSM). Multivariable cox regression analyzed the association between LMWH use and outcomes in this cohort. Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank tests compared endpoint risks between groups.The primary endpoint focused on major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (MACCE, composite of cardiac death, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke) and net adverse clinical event (NACE, composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, BARC type 3 bleeding) within 30 days.The secondary endpoints were the components of MACCE and NACE. Results After 1:6 propensity score matching, 8,248 frail patients with AMI undergoing early PCI were enrolled, including 7,004 who received LMWH and 1,244 who did not. Post-matching balance was satisfactory, with absolute standardized mean differences below 0.1 for all covariates(Table 1). Cox regression analysis revealed that LMWH reduced MACCE (aHR = 0.51, 95% CI = 0.39-0.66, P &lt; 0.001) and NACE (aHR = 0.48, 95% CI = 0.38-0.62, P &lt; 0.001) at 30 days. These findings remained consistent in the secondary outcomes (cardiac death: aHR = 0.43, 95% CI = 0.32-0.58, P &lt; 0.001; all-cause death: aHR = 0.40, 95% CI = 0.30-0.53, P &lt; 0.001)(Figure 1). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated a significantly lower risk of MACCE and NACE in the LMWH group (log-rank P&lt;0.001, Figure 2A, B). Conclusions In frail patients with AMI undergoing early PCI, the use of low molecular weight heparin demonstrates benefits in short-term cardiovascular, cerebrovascular and net adverse clinical events.Table 1.Baseline Characteristics

appraisal.design_and_n: Retrospective multicentre cohort from 82 hospitals (2010-2024); after 1:6 propensity score matching, 8,248 frail patients with AMI undergoing early PCI, 7,004 who received LMWH and 1,244 who did not.
appraisal.main_limitation: Retrospective observational comparison with a control group mixing no LMWH, fondaparinux and bivalirudin, with a strongly unbalanced group size and a risk of residual confounding and immortal-time or selection effects; the effect sizes are implausibly large for a causal reading.
appraisal.one_line: In a propensity-matched multicentre cohort of frail patients with AMI undergoing early PCI, low molecular weight heparin use was associated with lower 30-day MACCE and net adverse clinical events.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: Cox regression revealed that LMWH reduced MACCE (aHR = 0.51, 95% CI = 0.39-0.66, P < 0.001) and NACE (aHR = 0.48, 95% CI = 0.38-0.62, P < 0.001) at 30 days; cardiac death aHR = 0.43, 95% CI = 0.32-0.58; all-cause death aHR = 0.40, 95% CI = 0.30-0.53.
appraisal.why_it_matters: Parenteral anticoagulant choice in frail older patients with AMI is poorly covered by randomised trials, so the signal identifies a population-specific question for a registry-based comparison.

title: Low molecular weight heparin for AMI with frailty: short-Term outcomes after early PCI

abstract: Abstract Background Polygenic risk scores (PRS) are widely used to predict long-term outcomes, but their value in secondary prevention remains unclear. Biological age (BA) may enhance risk stratification. This study investigated BA acceleration (BAA) as a dynamic complement to static PRS in post-PCI patients and examined whether BA provides additional prognostic value when genetic risk alone fails to differentiate mortality outcomes. Methods We included 3,484 patients undergoing PCI. PRS for coronary artery disease was categorized into low (bottom 20%), intermediate (20–80%), and high (top 20%) groups. BA was estimated using KDMAge, Light BioAge, and PhenoAge, and BAA was defined as the residual from regressing BA on chronological age. BA acceleration was analyzed as continuous, binary, and quartile-based variables. Multivariable Cox models were used to assess associations with all-cause mortality within each PRS stratum, and interaction terms were tested to evaluate effect modification by genetic risk. Results During a median follow-up of 10 years, the cumulative incidence of all-cause mortality did not differ significantly across the three genetic risk groups (P &gt; 0.05). In multivariable Cox regression analyses, neither the intermediate-risk group (HR = 1.03, P = 0.804) nor the high-risk group (HR = 1.14, P = 0.839) showed a significant independent association with all-cause mortality. These findings suggest that, in patients undergoing PCI, traditional genetic susceptibility stratification has limited discriminatory ability for long-term survival outcomes. Interaction analysis of genetic modulation effects demonstrated a significant statistical interaction between KDM-defined BAA and PRS (P for interaction = 0.024). Stratified analyses further showed that in the low genetic risk group, BAA was consistently associated with a significantly increased risk of all-cause mortality (HRcontinuous = 1.26; HRbinary = 1.81; HRQ4 vs. Q1 = 2.00; all P &lt; 0.05). Similar associations were observed in the intermediate genetic risk group (HRcontinuous = 1.22; HRbinary = 1.44; HRQ4 vs. Q1 = 2.05; all P &lt; 0.05). However, in the high genetic risk group, the predictive effect of BAA was completely attenuated (all P &gt; 0.05). Although analyses based on LightBioAge and PhenoAge did not demonstrate statistically significant interactions, their trends were consistent with those observed for KDM, with all three forms of BAA showing significant predictive value for all-cause mortality in the low- to intermediate-risk groups (Table 1). Conclusion In patients undergoing PCI, traditional PRS showed limited ability to discriminate mortality risk. In contrast, biological age acceleration provided significant prognostic value, particularly in low- to intermediate-genetic risk groups. These findings support integrating biological aging assessment with genetic risk to improve post-PCI risk stratification.
title: Beyond the genome: the dominant role of biological age over polygenic risk in post-PCI mortality prediction.

abstract: Abstract Background Residual cardiovascular risk reflects a complex interplay of lipid, inflammatory, thrombotic, and cardio-kidney-metabolic (CKM) pathways. In patients with acute coronary syndromes (ACS), this risk remains substantial despite intensive low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) lowering therapy.1,2 A more holistic understanding of ACS patient phenotypes is required to allow for more targeted interventions.3,4 Purpose To identify ACS phenotypes by machine learning (ML) and determine their individual contributions to residual cardiovascular risk. Methods We analysed 4,787 Swiss statin-treated acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients from the Special Programme University Medicine Acute Coronary Syndrome (SPUM-ACS) study and 15,283 French statin-treated ACS patients from the obseRvatoire des Infarctus de Côte-d’Or (RICO) study. By using the Davies–Bouldin index and silhouette coefficient, unsupervised ML identified four patient clusters (k = 4) across lipid, inflammatory, and CKM domains. One-year major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) were compared across phenotypes using Kaplan–Meier and multivariable Cox analyses. Results In SPUM-ACS, four patient clusters were identified by unsupervised ML, namely HDL-, LDL-, HbA1c-, and CRP-creatinine-dominant patient phenotypes. In RICO, similar clusters were identified. Risk of 1-year MACE differed significantly across clusters (log-rank p &lt; 0.001) in both Swiss and French patients, resulting in a 2.45- (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 2.45, 95% CI 1.64–3.66) and 2.40-fold (aHR, 2.40, 95% CI 1.60–3.59) higher MACE risk for HbA1c- and CRP-creatinine-dominant phenotypes in Swiss patients, respectively, while LDL- (aHR, 1.07, 95% CI 0.68–1.69) and HDL-dominant (reference) phenotypes showed the best outcomes among all patient clusters, with similar results in French patients (Figure 1). Importantly, the proportion of patients exceeding guideline-recommended risk thresholds differed significantly across the identified clusters, irrespectively whether Swiss or French patients were analyzed (Figure 2). Conclusions ML-derived unsupervised clustering identifies reproducible CKM phenotypes with distinct risk profiles, providing a foundation for phenotype-guided secondary prevention strategies in the contemporary era.
title: Unsupervised machine-learning identifies cardio-kidney-metabolic phenotypes and determines residual risk after acute coronary syndromes

abstract: Abstract Background High-intensity statins and antithrombotic therapy are Class I, Level A recommendations for secondary prevention in patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease according to ESC guidelines. Whether ther real- world implementation differs across vascular territories remains insufficiently characterized. Methods We conducted a prospective, multicenter registry across 30 cardiology centers in Argentina between April 2023 and October 2024. Among 2,937 patients hospitalized for cardiovascular conditions (emergency or elective), those classified as secondary prevention were included in this analysis. Secondary prevention was defined as prior coronary artery disease (CAD), including acute coronary syndrome, percutaneous coronary intervention, or coronary artery bypass grafting, or prior cerebrovascular disease, including ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attack, or carotid revascularization. Patients were categorized into mutually exclusive vascular territories. In cases of overlapping disease, patients were classified within the CAD group. We assessed the use of statins, high-intensity statins (rosuvastatin ≥20 mg or atorvastatin ≥40 mg daily), ezetimibe, aspirin, and any antithrombotic therapy (antiplatelet or oral anticoagulant). Multivariable logistic regression models were adjusted for age, sex, hypertension, diabetes, smoking status, and dyslipidemia. Results Among 1,151 patients classified as secondary prevention, 83.3% had CAD and 16.7% had cerebrovascular disease. Mean age was 70.5 ± 10.3 years, and 26.2% were women. Baseline characteristics are detailed in Table 1. Compared with patients with CAD, those with cerebrovascular disease were significantly less likely to receive statins (66.1% vs 81.3%, p&lt;0.001) and high-intensity statins (31.2% vs 53.2%, p&lt;0.001). Similarly, any antithrombotic therapy was less frequently prescribed in the cerebrovascular group (70.3% vs 86.4%, p&lt;0.001). Patterns of secondary prevention strategies are summarized in Table 2. After multivariable adjustment, CAD remained independently associated with a higher likelihood of receiving statins (OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.33–2.75; p=0.001), high-intensity statins (OR 2.34, 95% CI 1.67–3.28; p&lt;0.001), and any antithrombotic therapy (OR 2.60, 95% CI 1.70–3.99; p&lt;0.001). Notably, most patients (86.0%) had at least one outpatient visit in the previous year, 47.4% were followed by a cardiologist, 27.9%, 15.1% exclusively by an internist, and 27.9% by both a cardiologist and an internist. Conclusion Despite robust evidence supporting intensive lipid-lowering and antithrombotic therapy in secondary prevention, patients with cerebrovascular disease were consistently less likely to receive these treatments compared with patients with CAD. These findings identify a consistent implementation gap in secondary prevention across vascular territories, which likely contributes to residual cardiovascular risk in cerebrovascular patients.
title: Implementation gaps in secondary prevention between coronary and cerebrovascular disease: a multicenter real-world study

abstract: Abstract Background The increasing complexity of managing patients with ischemic heart disease requires the development of integrated hospital–community care models. In this context, secondary prevention clinics may represent an organizational strategy capable of improving clinical outcomes and healthcare quality indicators. Methods We performed an observational analysis of patients enrolled in a secondary prevention clinic for ischemic heart disease, with data updated to July 31, 2025. Demographic characteristics, cardiovascular risk factors, angiographic findings, clinical outcomes, and healthcare quality indicators were evaluated. A total of 1,093 patients were included: 899 men (82.2%) and 194 women (17.7%), with a mean age of 65.46 years. Territorial outpatient activity involved 85 patients between January 1 and April 30, 2024. Results Major cardiovascular risk factors included hypertension in 745 patients, dyslipidemia in 784, diabetes in 296, current/former smoking in 392, and family history in 438 patients. Angiographic characteristics showed incomplete revascularization in 212 patients, multiple stent implantation in 364, and multivessel disease in 435. Clinical outcomes dimostrate:total rehospitalization rates of 2.4% at 6 months and 3.2% at 12 months.overall mortality of 0.6%;rehospitalizations for CABG/PCI of 0.73% at 6 months and 1.9% at 12 months, with procedure-related mortality of 0.13%. Compared with patients managed exclusively by general practitioners, those followed in the clinic showed fewer medical-therapy rehospitalizations (6% vs 28%), fewer unchanged angiographic findings (34% vs 48%), and higher rates of appropriate revascularization (60% vs 24%). The 12-month rehospitalization rate was lower in clinic-managed patients (4.34%) compared with historical cohorts (7.21% in 2010 and 8.01% in 2014). Quality indicators showed first follow-up visits within 30 days in 45–73% of cases and LDL cholesterol target achievement in 74–89%, with improvement after the 2019 guideline update. Among territorially managed patients, LDL target achievement reached 89.2%. Conclusions A structured secondary prevention clinic represents an effective hospital–community integrated care model for ischemic heart disease, associated with low rehospitalization rates (3.2% at 12 months), low mortality (0.6%), and high cardiovascular risk-factor control. Continuous monitoring through quality indicators supports the role of structured secondary prevention in improving clinical outcomes and healthcare appropriateness. Inizio modulo
title: Secondary prevention clinic as a hospital–territory integrated care model in ischemic heart disease: analysis of quality indicators and clinical outcomes.

abstract: Abstract Background Obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD) and angina without obstructive coronary arteries (ANOCA) caused by coronary vasomotor dysfunction (CVDys) are distinct ischemic entities, yet comparative data on their cardiovascular risk profiles are limited. Purpose Understanding potential differences may improve risk stratification and inform tailored preventive strategies in patients with ischemic symptoms. Methods This observational study included patients with chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) from two prospective, multicentre all-comer registries in the Netherlands: the south-east Netherlands Heart Registry (ZON-HR), comprising patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for obstructive CAD, and the Netherlands registry of invasive Coronary vasomotor Function Testing (NL-CFT), including ANOCA patients who underwent a clinically indicated coronary function test (CFT). The prevalence of risk factors in CCS patients with obstructive CAD were compared with the prevalence in ANOCA patients with CVDys, defined as an abnormal CFT outcome. Results ANOCA patients with CVDys were younger (60 vs 69 years) and predominantly female (83% vs 27%) compared with patients with obstructive CAD. Traditional cardiovascular risk factors and prior atherosclerotic diseases were markedly more prevalent in obstructive CAD (table 1). Mean low density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels were comparable between groups (2.4 ± 2.2 vs 2.4 ± 0.9 mmol/L), despite substantially higher use of statins and ezetimibe in obstructive CAD (80.7% vs 48.5% and 16.5% vs 11.2%, respectively) (table 2). Conclusion Obstructive CAD and ANOCA caused by CVDys represent clearly distinct clinical phenotypes with evidently different cardiovascular risk profiles and treatment patterns. Although lipid-lowering therapy was more intensively prescribed in obstructive CAD, LDL-C levels remained above ESC guideline recommended targets (&lt;1.4 mmol/L), suggesting a potential treatment gap in secondary prevention. In contrast, ANOCA appears less driven by traditional atherosclerotic risk factors, underscoring the heterogeneous mechanisms underlying ischemic symptoms.Table 1.Risk factorsTable 2.Cardiac medication
title: Differences in cardiovascular risk profiles between patients with obstructive coronary artery disease and ANOCA patients with coronary vasomotor dysfunction: insights from two multicentre registries

abstract: Abstract Background Residual cardiovascular risk remains substantial in patients with established coronary artery disease despite contemporary secondary prevention strategies. Conventional approaches focused on isolated risk factors may fail to capture the multidimensional heterogeneity of this population. Purpose We aimed to identify distinct clinical phenotypes using an unsupervised analytical approach and to explore their association with recurrent cardiovascular events. Methods We conducted a multicenter observational study based on the INTERASPIRE registry, including 592 Latinamerican patients with prior acute coronary syndrome or coronary revascularization. Variables collected during a standardized face-to-face interview were grouped into demographic, clinical, metabolic and psychosocial domains. After systematic variable selection, clustering was performed using Partitioning Around Medoids with Gower distance. The change in mean silhouette width was evaluated after iterative exclusion of each variable to assess its contribution to cluster stability. Subsequently, factor analysis of mixed data (FAMD) was applied to identify variables with the greatest contribution to the principal latent dimensions of the data structure. Associations between derived clusters and 12-month cardiovascular events were assessed using Kaplan–Meier survival analysis and Cox proportional hazards models. Results Three clinically meaningful phenotypes were identified (Figure 1). Cluster 1 (42%) comprised predominantly younger patients with lower comorbidity burden and lower psychosocial vulnerability, representing a lower-risk profile. Cluster 2 (27%) was characterized by greater psychosocial vulnerability and an adverse lipid profile—including higher LDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein B—defining a psychosocial–atherogenic residual risk phenotype. Cluster 3 (31%) mainly included older patients with multiple comorbidities and greater renal dysfunction, defining an age-associated cardiorenal phenotype (Graphical abstract). During 12-month follow-up, 7% of patients experienced a cardiovascular event. Event rates differed across clusters (3%, 10%, and 9% in clusters 1, 2, and 3, respectively; log-rank p = 0.02). Compared with cluster 1, clusters 2 and 3 were associated with a higher risk of events (HR 3.03, 95% CI 1.22–7.54 and HR 3.11, 95% CI 1.27–7.63, respectively). Conclusions In this contemporary secondary prevention cohort, unsupervised phenotyping identified three multidimensional clinical profiles with distinct prognostic implications. Residual cardiovascular risk appears to arise from the interaction of lipid-related, renal and psychosocial domains beyond traditional risk factors. Integrating these dimensions into clinical assessment may support more personalized secondary prevention strategies.Graphical abstractFigure1
title: Residual risk in coronary artery disease: identification of cardio–reno–metabolic and psychosocial phenotypes in a Latinamerican cohort of the INTERASPIRE registry

abstract: Abstract Background Remnant cholesterol (remnant-C) is an emerging contributor to residual cardiovascular risk, particularly in patients with diabetes mellitus (DM). Purpose To evaluate the prognostic impact of remnant-C levels in diabetic patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). Methods We identified 15,824 patients with coronary artery disease and DM among 525,646 individuals who underwent PCI or CABG between 2011 and 2020 based on the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) database. Remnant-C was calculated as total cholesterol minus low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. The primary endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), defined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, repeat revascularization, or non-fatal stroke. Results Patients were stratified into tertiles according to remnant-C levels: T1 (&lt;18.5 mg/dL; n=5,014), T2 (18.5–28.5 mg/dL; n=5,515), and T3 (≥28.5 mg/dL; n=5,295). After adjustment for demographic factors, comorbidities, and lipid-lowering therapies, the risk of MACCE increased stepwise across tertiles compared with T1:T2 (hazard ratio [HR] 1.12; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.04–1.12; p=0.001), and T3 (HR 1.19; 95% CI 1.12–1.23; p&lt;0.001). The cubic spline curve demonstrated a linear correlation between remnant-C levels and MACCE incidence. Conclusions Elevated remnant-C levels were independently associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes in diabetic patients undergoing coronary revascularization, supporting remnant -C as a potential therapeutic target in this high-risk population.OutcomeCupic Spline Curve
title: Remnant cholesterol and residual cardiovascular risk in diabetic patients undergoing coronary revascularization: insights from a nationwide ohort

abstract: Abstract Background Socioeconomic inequalities are strongly associated with cardiovascular disease. However, whether socioeconomic status (SES) independently influences outcome after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains unclear. Purpose To investigate the association between SES and 1-year cardiovascular outcomes after PCI, and to determine whether observed disparities are explained by differences in cardiovascular risk burden. Methods Data were derived from the Southeast Netherlands Heart Registry (ZON-HR), an ongoing multicentre PCI registry. SES was determined through linkage of residential postal codes to national socioeconomic data from Statistics Netherlands (CBS). Patients with available SES score and complete 1-year follow up were included. SES was analysed as a continuous variable. Associations between SES and baseline characteristics, and between SES and 1-year outcomes were assessed using logistic regression. The risk of major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), defined as a composite of myocardial infarction, stent thrombosis, unplanned revascularisation, ischemic stroke, or cardiovascular mortality, was evaluated after multivariable adjustment. Results A total of 6,424 patients were included. Lower SES was strongly associated with a less favourable cardiovascular risk profile, including higher odds of acute coronary syndrome (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.07–1.75), peripheral artery disease (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.13–2.44), hypertension (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.35–2.23), obesity (OR 1.80, 95% CI 1.37-2.36), diabetes (OR 2.35, 95% CI 1.77–3.13), and active smoking (OR 4.00, 95% CI 2.96–5.39). Furthermore, lower SES was associated with higher unadjusted risk of MACCE (OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.01-2.04), mainly driven by ischemic stroke and cardiovascular mortality. After multivariable adjustment, SES was no longer independently associated with MACCE (adjusted OR 1.51, 95% CI 0.86-2.65). Conclusion In a contemporary PCI cohort, lower SES was associated with a substantially higher cardiovascular risk burden and worse unadjusted 1-year outcomes. However, the association with MACCE was attenuated after adjustment for traditional risk factors, suggesting that socioeconomic disparities in post-PCI outcomes are predominantly mediated by modifiable cardiovascular risk profiles. These findings highlight the importance of intensified primary and secondary prevention strategies targeting socially vulnerable populations.Figure 1 Forest plot baseline characteristicsFigure 2 Forest plot outcomes
title: Socioeconomic disparities in 1-year outcomes after PCI.

abstract: Abstract Background Despite achievement of guideline-recommended LDL cholesterol targets, substantial residual cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk persists. Inflammation is a recognized contributor to this risk, yet upstream modifiable determinants remain incompletely defined. Sleep insufficiency has been associated with cardiometabolic dysfunction, but its role in residual inflammatory risk among statin-treated individuals is unclear. Purpose To investigate whether sleep insufficiency is associated with residual systemic inflammation and incident major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) among statin-treated individuals achieving LDL targets, and to evaluate the mediating role of inflammation. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study within the Mass General Brigham Biobank. Adults on statin therapy who achieved LDL ≤70 mg/dL (established CVD) or ≤100 mg/dL (no CVD) between 2010–2020 were included. Sleep insufficiency was defined as self-reported sleep &lt;7 hours/night or documented insomnia; individuals with other sleep disorders were excluded. C-reactive protein (CRP) values were averaged over the observation window. The primary outcome was incident MACE (myocardial infarction, unstable angina, coronary/peripheral revascularization, stroke, or heart failure). Multivariable linear and Cox regression models adjusted for demographics, traditional cardiovascular risk factors, obesity, history of malignancy, and common inflammatory conditions were used. Mediation analyses quantified the indirect effect of CRP. Results Among 3,631 statin-treated participants (median age 68 years; 56% male), sleep insufficiency was present in 55%. Despite LDL control, median CRP was 3.9 mg/L. Sleep insufficiency was independently associated with higher CRP in the primary adjusted model (β=5.44; 95%CI 1.55–9.33; p=0.006, Table 1), remaining significant after further adjustment for obesity, inflammatory conditions, cancer, and prevalent CVD. Over follow-up (457 MACE events occurred), sleep insufficiency was associated with higher incident MACE risk (adjusted HR 1.50; 95%CI 1.23–1.83; p&lt;0.001, Figure 1). Residual inflammation was also independently associated with MACE (standardized HR per SD CRP 1.26; 95%CI 1.18–1.35; p&lt;0.001). Mediation analysis demonstrated that CRP partially mediated the sleep–MACE association (indirect effect β=0.032; 95%CI 0.005–0.071), accounting for 5.9% of total risk, while a substantial direct association persisted. Conclusion Among statin-treated individuals achieving LDL targets, sleep insufficiency is common and independently associated with residual systemic inflammation and increased long-term cardiovascular risk. Inflammation partially mediates this relationship, suggesting both inflammatory and non-inflammatory pathways. These findings identify sleep health as a potentially actionable target to reduce residual cardiovascular risk beyond lipid lowering.
title: Sleep Insufficiency as a Determinant of Residual Inflammatory Risk and Major Cardiovascular Events in Statin-Treated Individuals

abstract: Abstract Background Despite marked reductions in in-hospital mortality after advances in reperfusion and guideline-directed therapy, the burden of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) has shifted towards long-term risk management, making precise residual mortality stratification a major challenge. The rate–pressure product (RPP), reflecting myocardial workload, is prognostic at rest in ACS, yet its significance under stress and its dynamic change from rest to peak exercise remain unclear. Moreover, peak RPP may be influenced by exercise capacity, warranting fitness-adjusted assessment. Purpose To evaluate the prognostic associations of cross-state and fitness-adjusted RPP indices with residual mortality risk in ACS and their utility for long-term risk stratification. Methods ACS patients undergoing CPET in three hospitals (January 2018–December 2024) were included. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Multivariable Cox models assessed associations of resting RPP, peak RPP, haemodynamic gain index (HGI), and fitness-adjusted RPP (RPPpeak/METpeak) with mortality. Kaplan–Meier and restricted cubic spline analyses were performed. Combined HGI and RPPpeak/METpeak phenotypes were also evaluated. Results Among 6,644 patients, 134 deaths occurred over a median 24 months (IQR 12–41). Resting and stress-derived RPP indices showed divergent associations with mortality. Each 1-SD increase in resting RPP was associated with 19% higher risk (aHR 1.19, 95% CI 1.00–1.41), whereas peak RPP and HGI were associated with 29% ((aHR=0.71, 95% CI: 0.59–0.86) and 46% (aHR=0.54, 95% CI: 0.43–0.67) lower risk. Fitness-adjusted RPP was associated with 33% higher mortality per 1-SD increment (aHR=1.33, 95% CI: 1.14–1.55). Associations were predominantly linear. Mortality risk increased stepwise across combined phenotypes, with the low HGI–high RPPpeak/METpeak group showing the highest risk (aHR=5.00, 95% CI: 2.75–9.08). These associations remained consistent across predefined clinical subgroups. Conclusions RPP exhibited state-dependent prognostic associations in ACS patients. Higher resting and fitness-adjusted RPP were associated with increased mortality risk, whereas higher peak RPP and greater HGI were associated with lower risk. Integrated cross-state and fitness-adjusted assessment was independently associated with residual mortality risk, with combined phenotypes demonstrating clear graded risk patterns. These findings provide robust evidence to support more refined residual risk stratification during long-term management of ACS.KM Survival Curves for HGI–RPPpeak/METpeak
title: Cross-physiological and fitness-adjusted assessment of rate–pressure product for residual mortality risk stratification in acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Early intensive lipid-lowering therapy is recommended after acute coronary syndrome (ACS), and current guidelines recommend assessing attainment of lipid-lowering targets within 4–6 weeks; however, the prognostic significance of achieving a more than 50% reduction in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) shortly after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains unclear. Purpose To elucidate the prognostic value of achieving a more than 50% reduction in LDL-C at 6 weeks after PCI in ACS. Methods This retrospective study analyzed 1,505 consecutive patients with ACS who underwent PCI. LDL-C levels at 6 weeks and 1 year were estimated by linear interpolation using all available post-procedural measurements to calculate values at 42 and 365 days after PCI, respectively (Figure 1). The primary clinical outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke. Results The mean age was 71.0 years, and 74.1% were men. ST-elevation myocardial infarction accounted for 49.3% of cases, and a total of 32.0% had a history of prior cardiovascular events. The mean baseline LDL-C level was 2.95 ± 1.02 mmol/L. At 6 weeks, 574 patients (38.1%) achieved an LDL-C reduction greater than 50%. Over a median follow-up of 944 days (interquartile range: 554–1,430 days), the 6-year incidence of MACE was significantly lower in patients who achieved an LDL-C reduction greater than 50% at 6 weeks compared with those who did not (11.5% vs. 21.7%; adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 0.69; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.48–0.99; P=0.047) (Figure 2). Each 10% greater LDL-C reduction at 6 weeks from baseline was independently associated with lower MACE risk (adjusted HR, 0.92; P=0.003), whereas absolute LDL-C level at 6 weeks (per 1 mmol/L increase) and attainment of LDL-C &lt;1.4 mmol/L at 6 weeks were not (adjusted HR, 1.26; P=0.140 and adjusted HR, 0.84; P=0.298, respectively) (Figure 3). Of note, restricted cubic spline analysis demonstrated a monotonic inverse association between LDL-C reduction at 6 weeks and MACE risk, with no significant nonlinearity (P for nonlinearity = 0.37) (Figure 4). Interestingly, a shorter time to achieving an LDL-C reduction greater than 50% was significantly associated with a lower risk of MACE (per 10-day delay: adjusted HR, 1.01; 95% CI, 1.00–1.01; P=0.045). Furthermore, compared with patients who did not achieve an LDL-C reduction greater than 50% within 1 year, those who achieved this reduction within 6 weeks had a significantly lower risk of MACE (adjusted HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.45–0.99; P=0.048), whereas those achieving it between 6 weeks and 1 year did not (P=0.089). Conclusions Achievement of an LDL-C reduction of more than 50% at 6 weeks after PCI was associated with a lower long-term risk of MACE in patients with ACS. These findings support current guideline recommendations emphasizing an early and intensive lipid-lowering strategy.
title: Clinical impact of more than 50% reduction in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol at 6 weeks after percutaneous coronary intervention for acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Cumulative low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) exposure ("cholesterol burden") is causally linked to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and is increasingly recognised as a lifetime determinant of risk. (1) Contemporary concepts of coronary artery disease emphasise atheroma burden and prevention rather than ischemia alone. (2) However, real-world evidence directly relating measured cumulative LDL-C after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to subsequent clinical events remains limited, partly because calculating cumulative exposure requires dense longitudinal LDL-C data. Purpose To evaluate whether higher cumulative LDL-C exposure during secondary prevention after index PCI is associated with major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (MACCE). Methods We studied consecutive PCI patients at a single tertiary centre. Eligible patients had ≥1 year of follow-up and ≥3 LDL-C measurements, with no interval between measurements &gt;400 days. Cumulative LDL-C was calculated as the area under the LDL-C–time curve (AUC, mg/dL·year). Using a matched nested case–control design, MACCE cases were matched 1:1 to event-free controls on follow-up duration (matched population: 544 pairs; 1,088 patients). Group distributions were compared using paired non-parametric testing and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic. Dose–response was explored using conditional logistic regression with a restricted cubic spline. LDL-C targets and treatment intensity during follow-up were guided by contemporary European dyslipidaemia recommendations for secondary prevention. (3) Results Among 544 matched pairs (1,088 patients), median follow-up was 4.7 years (interquartile range, 2.5 to 7.5), and matching on follow-up was tight (median absolute difference, 9 days). Median cumulative LDL-C exposure was 490 mg/dL·year in MACCE cases and 180 mg/dL·year in controls (P&lt;0.001); the Hodges–Lehmann median paired difference was 261 mg/dL·year, and 79% of pairs had higher exposure in cases (Figure 1). The distribution of cumulative LDL-C exposure was right-shifted in cases (Kolmogorov–Smirnov D=0.369; P&lt;0.001). In restricted cubic spline conditional logistic regression, MACCE risk increased nonlinearly; at 400 mg/dL·year, the odds ratio was 2.80 (95% confidence interval, 2.32 to 3.39, Figure 2). Sensitivity analyses with follow-up time-truncation yielded qualitatively similar paired associations. Conclusions Among PCI patients with serial LDL-C measurements, higher measured cumulative LDL-C exposure during follow-up was strongly associated with MACCE. These findings support cumulative LDL-C as a practical risk marker and reinforce the need for sustained LDL-C lowering in secondary prevention. An AUC-derived cumulative LDL-C threshold near 400 mg/dL·year may help refine risk stratification and guide long-term lipid-lowering strategies beyond conventional LDL-C targets.Distribution of cumulative LDL-CCumulative LDL-C Exposure and MACCE
title: Cumulative LDL-cholesterol exposure after Index percutaneous coronary intervention and subsequent major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events

abstract: Abstract Background Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a causal, largely genetically determined risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and residual risk after LDL-cholesterol lowering. Contrary to the traditional assumption of lifelong stability, several recent studies suggest that Lp(a) may rise after acute myocardial infarction, and that peri-infarct values may not reflect subsequent steady-state levels. However, the temporal profile and persistence of these changes beyond 6 months after acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remain poorly characterized. Purpose To characterise individual and categorical trajectories of Lp(a) from index ACS admission to 1 month and 12 months, and to determine whether post-ACS Lp(a) elevations persist over time. Methods We retrospectively included consecutive ACS patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention at a tertiary cardiac centre (2022–2025) with Lp(a) measured at index admission, 1 month, and 12 months. Lp(a) was quantified in mg/dL and categorised as &lt;30, 30–50, 50–70, and &gt;70 mg/dL. Individual longitudinal trajectories were visualised with alluvial plots, and changes in median Lp(a) and risk-category distribution were assessed using paired non-parametric tests. Results Among 338 patients (mean age 61.3 ± 10.6 years, 81.3% male), median Lp(a) increased from 31.9 mg/dL at baseline to 64.3 mg/dL at 1 month, followed by partial decline to 53.2 mg/dL at 12 months (p&lt;0.001 for trend). The proportion with Lp(a) &gt;70 mg/dL almost doubled from 22.5% at baseline to 46.2% at 1 month and remained markedly elevated at 38.8% at 12 months. Conversely, patients with Lp(a) &lt;30 mg/dL fell from 47.9% at baseline to 22.2% at 1 month, with only partial recovery to 29.6% after 12 months. Alluvial plots revealed substantial interindividual heterogeneity but showed that a large subset transitioned from low to persistently high Lp(a) categories. Conclusions Lp(a) rises sharply after ACS, peaks around 1 month, and shows only incomplete normalisation at 12 months, indicating that peri-infarct measurements substantially underestimate the proportion of patients with sustained high Lp(a). These data support a paradigm in which ACS unmasks genetically mediated Lp(a) risk through an acute-phase response that only partially wanes over time, with potential implications for timing of Lp(a) testing, risk stratification, and selection for emerging Lp(a)-lowering therapies.Figure.Alluvial Plot
title: Transient surge, persistent risk: longitudinal changes in lipoprotein(a) following acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Cardiac involvement is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in Fabry disease, progressing from early myocardial injury to fibrosis, arrhythmia, and chronic heart failure. While cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can reliably detect myocardial oedema and fibrosis in Fabry disease, there is a need for a more sensitive imaging marker for distinguishing early active inflammation driving disease progression. Purpose To evaluate the use of hybrid somatostatin receptor 2 (SST2) positron emission tomography (PET)/MRI using 68Ga-DOTATATE for imaging myocardial inflammation in Fabry disease. Methods Consenting participants with genetically confirmed Fabry disease and established cardiac involvement underwent prospective 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/MRI of the heart. PET imaging was analysed visually by expert readers and quantified using maximum standardized uptake values (SUVmax) in each of the 17 myocardial segments and the right ventricle. Associations with clinical, biochemical, and MRI markers of disease activity and severity were assessed using non-parametric tests and mixed-effects models accounting for within-patient clustering. Results A total of 12 patients (mean age 62 [IQR 57–70] years; 42% female) were enrolled, of whom 6/12 (50%) had classical Fabry disease. All were receiving disease-specific treatment. Myocardial 68Ga-DOTATATE PET imaging showed focal left ventricular uptake in all patients with heterogeneous regional distribution. PET uptake occurred most often in the inferolateral segments, where late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) also frequently occurred (Fig.1A, arrows). PET signal was higher in segments with T2-weighted oedema and/or LGE on MRI (p&lt;0.05 for both, Fig.1B). There was right ventricular PET uptake with corresponding LGE in 2/12 (17%) patients. Global PET signal was also positively correlated with age, NT-pro-BNP, serum C-reactive protein, and the proportion of left ventricular segments with T2 oedema (p&lt;0.05 for all). PET signal often extended beyond areas of established scar, and 5/12 (42%) patients had focal PET signal in segments without structural MRI abnormality. Conclusion In this first study of SST2 PET/MRI in cardiac Fabry disease, 68Ga-DOTATATE detected focal myocardial inflammation associated with clinical, biochemical, and MRI markers of disease severity. PET uptake beyond areas of established scar, including in segments without structural MRI abnormality, suggests potential sensitivity for earlier active disease. Given that cardiac disease progression may continue despite current enzyme-targeted Fabry therapies, imaging myocardial inflammation may improve disease characterization and help identify novel therapeutic targets.
title: Myocardial inflammation imaging in fabry disease of the heart using somatostatin receptor PET/MRI

abstract: Abstract Background and aims High lipoprotein(a) is a causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and therapies lowering lipoprotein(a) by up to 98% are in phase 3 trials. However, the clinical benefit of lipoprotein(a) reduction remains uncertain. We estimated the effect of lipoprotein(a) lowering on major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in the context of ongoing trials and in hypothetical primary prevention trials. Methods Using real-world data from two large general population based cohorts (n=522,494), we constructed sub-cohorts mimicking Lp(a)HORIZON, ACCLAIM-Lp(a), and OCEAN(a), and hypothetical primary prevention trials across combinations of conventional cardiovascular risk factors and lipoprotein(a) inclusion thresholds (≥70, ≥82, or ≥94 mg/dL). High lipoprotein(a) was compared with 80% or 98% lower levels to simulate pharmacologic reduction. The outcome was 5-year MACE (myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, coronary revascularization, or coronary death). Results In ongoing trials, 5-year absolute risk reductions were 2.3%(95% CI -0.5%-5.1%; p=0.16) in Lp(a)HORIZON, 3.4%(1.0%-5.9%; p=0.0003) in ACCLAIM-Lp(a), and 3.7%(1.0%-6.5%; p=0.008) in OCEAN(a), with corresponding hazard ratios 0.86(0.69–1.07), 0.74(0.63–0.87), and 0.76(0.61–0.93). In primary prevention trials, absolute risk reductions ranged 1.1%–4.2%, increasing with additional baseline risk factors and with more potent lowering, while hazard ratios were similar across lipoprotein(a) inclusion thresholds and number of baseline risk factors, ranging 0.53-0.71 for 80% lowering and 0.43-0.57 for 98%. Conclusion Using real-world data, lipoprotein(a) lowering was associated with clinically meaningful reductions in 5-year MACE risk in both ongoing trials and in hypothetical primary prevention settings, supporting ongoing trials and informing design of future primary prevention trials.
title: Lipoprotein(a) lowering and risk of cardiovascular disease in primary and secondary prevention

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Cardiology inpatients represent a unique population in whom lipid management can meaningfully reduce recurrent events. However, data describing European Society of Cardiology (ESC) cardiovascular risk stratification and lipid target attainment in real-world cardiology hospitalizations are limited. Purpose To describe the distribution of ESC cardiovascular risk categories, the burden and timing of ASCVD, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) target attainment based on the 2019 ESC/EAS dyslipidaemia guidelines among patients admitted in cardiology departments. Methods Adult patients hospitalized in a tertiary cardiology centre from 2011 until 2022 were analyzed, as part of the retrospective CARDIO study. ASCVD was defined as established coronary, cerebrovascular, peripheral, or aortic atherosclerotic disease, and classified as prior or newly diagnosed during index hospitalization. ESC cardiovascular risk categories (low, moderate, high, very high) were assigned according to guideline criteria. LDL-C levels and ESC-recommended target attainment were assessed overall and according to ASCVD timing. Results Overall, 12,863 patients were included (mean age 68.9 ± 14.6 years, 64.4% male), of whom 7,357 (57.2%) had established ASCVD, predominantly coronary artery disease (93%). Approximately two thirds had documented prior ASCVD and one third were newly diagnosed during the index hospitalization. According to ESC criteria, 61.4% of patients were classified as very high cardiovascular risk, 14.5% as high risk, 15.7% as moderate risk, and 9.0% as low risk. Very-high-risk classification was more frequent among males than females (69.8% vs 46.1%, p &lt; 0.05). Although acute coronary syndromes (ACS) accounted for 26% of admissions, most very-high-risk patients were hospitalized for non-ACS indications (58%). Mean LDL-C was 94.2 ± 37.7 mg/dL and decreased with increasing risk category (p &lt; 0.001). Overall, 72.9% of patients were not at their ESC-recommended LDL-C target, including 84.1% of very-high-risk and 75.5% of high-risk patients; notably, 24.0% of very-high-risk patients had LDL-C ≥116 mg/dL (Figure 1). Compared with patients with prior ASCVD, those with newly diagnosed ASCVD had higher LDL-C levels (108.7 ± 39.8 vs 83.0 ± 34.3 mg/dL, p &lt; 0.001) and a greater prevalence of LDL-C target non-attainment (93.0% vs 79.8%, p &lt; 0.001). Conclusion(s) In this large real-world cardiology inpatient cohort, more than half of patients had established ASCVD and nearly two thirds were classified as very high cardiovascular risk. Approximately three out of four patients did not meet their ESC-recommended LDL-C goals. Almost one-third of ASCVD was newly diagnosed during hospitalization and was associated with significantly poorer LDL-C control compared with patients with known ASCVD. These findings highlight cardiology hospitalization as a critical opportunity for ASCVD detection and optimization of preventive strategies.LDL-C distribution and targets
title: Cardiovascular risk and LDL-C target attainment in cardiology inpatients: insights from the CARDIO study
