abstract: Abstract Background There is growing recognition that lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] increases cardiovascular risk through atherogenic, thrombogenic, and inflammatory properties. Conventional risk factors of smoking and diabetes may also convey risk through these mechanisms. The degree to which Lp(a), smoking, and diabetes are additive or interactive risk factors is uncertain. Purpose We determined whether Lp(a), smoking, and diabetes are additive or interactive risk factors for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in a post hoc analysis of the placebo group of the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial. Methods ODYSSEY OUTCOMES compared the effects of alirocumab or placebo in patients with recent acute coronary syndrome on optimized statin therapy. Baseline Lp(a) was measured by immunoassay in mass units and categorized by quartile. Smoking was categorized as current versus prior or never. Presence of diabetes was determined from history, laboratory, and prescription data. MACE (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, hospitalization for unstable angina, and ischemia-driven coronary revascularization) were determined over median (Q1, Q3) follow-up of 2.8 (2.3, 3.4) years. Cox regression models were adjusted for age, sex, geographic region, LDL-C, and systolic blood pressure and evaluated the association of Lp(a) with MACE, without and with further adjustment for smoking and diabetes. Results In 9462 patients assigned to placebo, median (Q1-Q3) Lp(a) was 21.6 (6.6-60.1) mg/dL, 24.1% were current smokers, and 29.1% had diabetes. The 4-year Kaplan-Meier cumulative incidence of MACE was 19.7% (1474 events). Lp(a) ≥median was associated with greater risk of MACE than Lp(a) &lt;median. In both Lp(a) categories, risk of MACE increased when active smoking, diabetes, or both were present (Figure). In Cox models without adjustment for either smoking or diabetes, Lp(a) quartile was significantly associated with MACE (hazard ratio Q4 vs Q1 1.26 [1.09-1.46; quartiles Ptrend=0.0006]). When adjusted for smoking Lp(a) quartile remained associated with risk of MACE without Lp(a) x smoking interaction (hazard ratio Lp(a) Q4 vs Q1 1.27 [1.10-1.47; Lp(a) quartile Ptrend 0.0004; Pinteraction 0.86). Similarly, when adjusted for diabetes, Lp(a) quartile remained associated with risk of MACE without Lp(a) x diabetes interaction (hazard ratio Lp(a) Q4 vs Q1 1.29 [1.12-1.49; Lp(a) quartile Ptrend=0.0002; Pinteraction=0.31). When adjusted for both diabetes and smoking Lp(a) also remained a significant predictor of MACE (hazard ratio Lp(a) Q4 vs Q1 1.30 [1.13-1.51; quartile Ptrend=0.0001). Conclusions Lp(a), smoking, and diabetes are additive but not interactive risk factors for MACE after ACS. Lp(a) remains an independent risk factor for MACE after adjustment for both smoking and diabetes.
title: Lipoprotein(a), smoking, and diabetes are additive, but not interactive risk factors for major adverse cardiovascular events after acute coronary syndrome: An analysis of the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial

abstract: Abstract Background To estimate the prevalence of elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] in patients with familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) diagnosed using Dutch Lipid Clinic Network (DLCN) criteria and to assess the correlation of variables (age, gender, diabetes mellitus, hypertension etc.) with elevated Lp(a) in FH patients. Purpose Coronary artery disease (CAD) is a leading cause of mortality worldwide, presenting at an earlier age and with increased severity among South Asian population. Premature CAD (i.e. diagnosed before the age of 55 years for men and 60 years for women) is two to three times more prevalent in Indian population, not fully explained by conventional risk factors, thus, highlighting the role of non-conventional risk factors like Lp(a) in aggravating the CAD risk especially among South Asian population. FH is genetically inherited disorder predisposing to premature coronary artery disease. Elevated Lp(a) i.e., plasma levels of more than 50 mg/dL, is also an independent risk factor for premature CAD. There is no data from Indian population regarding the prevalence of elevated Lp(a) in FH patients. Methods Study included 229 patients diagnosed as potential FH (probable and definite) using DLCN criteria (score ≥6). Demographic details, CAD risk factors, and complete lipid profile were noted. Pre-treatment levels of LDL-C was obtained after calculating correction factor for patients on lipid lowering therapy to calculate DLCN score. Patients with premature CAD with DLCN criteria score of ≥6 were included. Lp(a) estimation was done using immuno-turbidimetric method. Results A total of 229 potential FH patients [Males-176 (76.8%); females-53(23.1%)] with definite FH- 58 (25.3%); probable FH- 171 (74.6 %) with mean age- 46.75±9.2 years were included. Mean LDL-C was 154.07±67.18 mg/dL. Combined prevalence of elevated Lp(a) in potential FH patients was 49.3%. No significant correlation of variables was seen with elevated Lp(a). Conclusion Prevalence of FH in young acute coronary syndrome in our country is more than 15%. Prevalence of elevated Lp(a) in general population is 25% and in CAD is 35%. Combined prevalence of FH and elevated Lp(a) in premature CAD patients is 49.3% in Indian population. Thus, elevated Lp(a) is more common in FH patients and has synergistic role in severity and early onset of CAD.
title: Prevalence of elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] in patients with familial hypercholesterolemia (FH)

abstract: Abstract Background Refractory and recurrent in-stent restenosis (RISR) remains a major clinical challenge following percutaneous coronary intervention, with an incompletely understood pathophysiology. Beyond traditional mechanical and neoatherosclerotic mechanisms, accumulating evidence suggests an immune-inflammatory etiology; however, reliable assessment of local vascular inflammatory activity is lacking. Although [18F]-FAPI PET/CT has emerged as a promising noninvasive approach for imaging fibro-inflammatory processes, its value in characterizing RISR and its association with inflammatory signatures have yet to be established. Purpose To determine whether [18F]-FAPI PET/CT can identify a distinct inflammatory endotype in patients with RISR through principal component analysis (PCA). Methods Fourteen patients with angiographically confirmed RISR (defined as ≥2 episodes at the same stented segment), in whom common ISR mechanisms were excluded by intracoronary imaging, underwent [18F]-FAPI PET/CT. A panel of inflammatory and clinical variables was integrated using principal component analysis (PCA). PCA-derived component scores were compared between FAPI-positive and FAPI-negative patients, and their discriminatory performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. Results Four principal components (PC1–PC4) accounted for 85% of the total variance. Only PC2 differed significantly between FAPI-positive and FAPI-negative groups (P &lt; 0.05). PC2 was dominated by a strong positive loading of hsCRP (+0.790) and a strong negative loading of monocytes (–0.711), reflecting a CRP-associated inflammatory axis. FAPI-positive patients exhibited markedly higher PC2 scores, whereas FAPI-negative patients showed a monocyte-dominant profile. ROC analysis showed that PC2 discriminated FAPI positivity with an AUC of 0.80 (95% CI, 0.52–1.00). PC1, PC3, and PC4 showed no significant group differences or discriminatory performance. Conclusion [18F]-FAPI PET/CT identifies a biologically distinct inflammation–dominant RISR endotype, characterized by elevated hsCRP and reduced monocytes. These findings support the feasibility of integrating molecular imaging with inflammatory phenotyping to improve risk stratification and guide personalized therapeutic strategies in RISR.FAPI_PETCT_RISR_Positive_vs_NegativePC2_ROC_Curve_for_FAPI_Status
title: Identification of inflammation-dominant endotypes in refractory and recurrent in-stent restenosis by [18F]-FAPI PET/CT

abstract: Abstract Introduction The interplay between apolipoprotein B (apoB) and Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] in determining atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) severity remains complex, particularly under the influence of lipid-lowering therapy (LLT). Purpose To evaluate the association of apoB and Lp(a) with severe ASCVD in patients hospitalized for acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Methods An observational study was conducted in ACS patients, in whom fasting lipid profiles, including apoB and Lp(a) levels, were obtained. Severe ASCVD was defined as a prior multiterritory ASCVD and/or three-vessel coronary disease on index angiography. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of severe ASCVD, including the interaction between apoB and prior LLT, and log-transformed Lp(a) levels to account for skewed distribution. Stratified analyses were performed according to LLT status. Results 815 ACS patients were included. Severe ASCVD was present in 47.5% of the cohort, and 50.9% were on prior LLT. In the overall multivariable model (table), female sex was independently associated with a lower likelihood of severe ASCVD. Conversely, diabetes, hypertension, Lp(a) levels, and prior LLT emerged as independent factors associated with severe ASCVD. A significant apoB × LLT interaction was also identified. Stratified analyses revealed divergent patterns (figure): in LLT-naive patients, apoB was a significant determinant of severe disease, while Lp(a) showed no significant association. Conversely, in patients on prior LLT, Lp(a) emerged as a strong independent predictor of severe ASCVD, whereas lower apoB levels were paradoxically associated with higher disease burden, likely reflecting more intensive therapy in high-risk individuals. Conclusions In ACS patients, the predictive value of lipid biomarkers for disease severity is fundamentally modified by prior LLT. Lp(a) is a key driver of residual risk and disease burden in patients already on therapy, while apoB remains the primary marker in untreated individuals. Recognition of these patterns is essential to identify very high-risk individuals who may benefit from emerging Lp(a)-targeted therapies.TableFigure
title: Association of apolipoprotein B and lipoprotein(a) with severe atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease in patients with acute coronary syndrome: the modifying effect of prior lipid-lowering therapy.

abstract: Abstract Introduction Risk-weighted apoB (RW-apoB) is a novel marker of lipid risk that accounts for both particle concentration and specific atherogenicity, potentially providing a more accurate reflection of the total atherogenic burden than standard apoB measurement alone. However, its evaluation has been largely limited to populations without prior atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Purpose Our objective was to analyze the discordance between RW-apoB and measured apoB in patients admitted for acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Methods An observational cross-sectional study of 814 ACS patients was performed. RW-apoB was calculated using the formula: RW-apoB = 11.65 × TG (mmol/L) + 0.215 × lipoprotein(a) (nmol/L) + 0.736 × apoB (mg/dL). Patients were stratified by percentile difference between RW-apoB and apoB: concordant (&lt;10) and discordant (≥10 percentile increase in RW-apoB relative to apoB); clinical history, angiographic severity, and lipid profiles were compared. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between RW-apoB discordance and multivessel coronary artery disease, adjusting for age, sex, renal function, traditional cardiovascular risk factors, apoB levels and prior lipid-lowering therapy (LLT). Results RW-apoB/apoB discordance was identified in 49.4% of the population hospitalized for ACS (figure). Discordant patients were younger, more frequently female, and had a higher prevalence of smoking, dyslipidemia, lower creatinine clearance, prior LLT, and prior ASCVD (table). They also exhibited a more unfavorable lipid profile. Angiographic severity was higher in the discordant group, with increased rates of multivessel disease and in-stent restenosis (table). In multivariable logistic regression analysis, RW-apoB/apoB discordance was independently associated with multivessel coronary artery disease (OR 1.494; 95% CI 1.080-2.068; p=0.015). Conclusions In patients hospitalized for ACS, RW-apoB/apoB discordance identifies a high-risk phenotype. Despite more frequent use of LLT, these patients exhibit a more severe atherosclerotic burden. Integrating RW-apoB into clinical assessment could refine risk stratification and improve the identification of patients at high atherogenic risk who may otherwise be underestimated by conventional measures.TableFigure
title: Risk-weighted apolipoprotein B in patients hospitalized for acute coronary syndrome: characteristics associated with discordance with measured apolipoprotein B levels.

abstract: Abstract Background Following epicardial reperfusion after ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction, no-reflow phenomenon from myocardial microvascular obstruction is a major clinical problem. The underlying mechanisms are unclear but have been proposed to include vasoconstriction and tissue oedema. Platelet activation may contribute through distal embolisation and plugging of the microcirculation, although direct in vivo evidence linking platelet activation to myocardial microvascular obstruction is lacking. The radiotracer, [¹8F]GP1, binds activated glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors expressed on activated platelets, enabling targeted non-invasive imaging of platelet activation and thrombosis. Methods In a single centre observational study, 100 patients with acute anterior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction underwent hybrid [¹8F]GP1 positron emission tomography (PET) and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) at a median of 13 days after infarction. Myocardial uptake was assessed qualitatively and quantified using target-to-background ratio (TBRmax) and percentage myocardial uptake. Associations with infarct size and microvascular obstruction on CMR were examined using regression analyses. Patients with myocardial [¹8F]GP1 uptake underwent repeat imaging at 3–6 months. Results Myocardial [¹8F]GP1 uptake occurred in 44% of participants and co-localised with infarcted myocardial territories (Figure 1A, 1C and 2B). Microvascular obstruction on CMR was fully concordant with myocardial [¹8F]GP1 uptake. Myocardial PET [¹8F]GP1 burden exceeded CMR-defined burden by a mean of 18%. Microvascular obstruction burden correlated strongly with myocardial [¹8F]GP1 uptake intensity (Spearman ρ = 0.78; p&lt;0.001) and burden (Spearman ρ = 0.84; p&lt;0.001) independent of infarct size. Angiographic no-reflow was the strongest independent association with microvascular obstruction (adjusted odds ratio 16.15; p&lt;0.001) (Figure 2A). In patients with follow up imaging, 7/32 (22%) had persistent myocardial [¹8F]GP1 uptake at 6 months which was associated with lower left ventricular ejection fraction. (Figure 1B). Conclusions We provide the first direct in vivo evidence that microvascular obstruction following ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction is universally associated with microcirculatory platelet activation, suggesting the predominant mechanism is microcirculatory thrombosis. Importantly, myocardial [¹8F]GP1uptake extended beyond regions of CMR defined microvascular obstruction and enables serial quantification of uptake intensity and burden over time. Persistent [¹8F]GP1 uptake was associated with lower left ventricular ejection fraction at follow up, implicating the role of sustained platelet activation in ongoing functional impairment. This approach may enable mechanistic stratification and serve as a pharmacodynamic imaging biomarker for therapies targeting platelet activation, microvascular thrombosis, and thrombo-inflammatory pathways.
title: Myocardial platelet imaging with [¹8F]GP1 positron emission tomography identifies a platelet-dominant microvascular injury phenotype after ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Remnant cholesterol is emerging as residual lipid risk factors of coronary heart diseases supported by substantial evidence. Nevertheless, studies on the association between remnant cholesterol levels and prognosis in patients with STEMI are insufficient, and they were conducted in small sample size. Purpose The objective of this study was to investigate the relationship between remnant cholesterol levels and the risk of in-hospital and long-term mortality in STEMI patients in a large prospective cohort, the CAMI registry. Methods In this study, patients with STEMI enrolled from the CAMI registry were categorised by the quartile of remnant cholesterol distribution. remnant cholesterol was calculated by the equation: total cholesterol minus LDL cholesterol minus HDL cholesterol. The primary endpoints were in-hospital mortality and 24 months all-cause mortality. Cox-regression models were used to estimate the association between remnant cholesterol and risk of mortality. Results A total of 14928 patients with STEMI were included in the main analysis and divided by the inter-quartile of remnant cholesterol. The lower quartile, median and upper quartile of remnant cholesterol were 0.42mmol/L, 0.64mmol/L and 0.94mmol/L, respectively. We observed a U-shaped association between remnant cholesterol levels and in-hospital and long-term mortality. The in-hospital mortality was 5.8% in lowest quartile, 4.1% in the second quartile, 4.3% in the third quartile and 4.5% in the highest quartile(P=0.0020). After multivariable adjustment, the decrease in in-hospital mortality was still observed in the second quartile[HR (95%CI): 0.764 (0.620-0.942), P=0.0118]. In the 24-month follow-up, the all-cause mortality rate was 13.0% in the first quartile, 10.5% in the second quartile, 10.2% in the third quartile and 10.4% the fourth quartile (P=0.0003). After multivariable adjustment, we found a lower risk in the second and the third quartile[Q2: HR (95%CI): 0.835 (0.727-0.958),P=0.0103;Q3: HR (95%CI): 0.858 (0.747-0.987), P=0.0319]. Conclusions The analysis of STEMI patients demonstrates that both very low and elevated remnant cholesterol levels were associated with higher risk of in-hospital mortality and long-term mortality. A better prognosis was observed in the second and third quartiles of remnant cholesterol, ranging from 0.42mmol/L to 0.94mmol/L. Comprehensive assessment of the lipid profile, including remnant cholesterol, may play a relevant role in the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease. Enhanced lifestyle management alongside developed lipid-lowering therapy is highly underscored in the STEMI patients to improve prognosis.
title: Association between remnant cholesterol levels and the in-hospital outcomes and long-term prognosis in ST-segment elevated myocardial infarction patients

abstract: Abstract Introduction Women generally exhibit higher lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] levels than men, particularly after menopause. However, the influence of sex on the relationship between Lp(a) and the risk of coronary artery disease (CAD) remains controversial. While some studies suggest this association is sex-independent, others indicate that CAD characteristics may differ between men and women with high Lp(a) levels. Objectives Our objective was to analyze potential sex-based differences in Lp(a) levels among patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and to evaluate their association with the extent of CAD. Methods Prospective, observational, single-centre study of a cohort of patients admitted for ACS with angiographicaly proven obstructive coronary lesions by angiography. Fasting lipid profiles including plasma Lp(a) levels were obtained. Variables associated with elevated Lp(a) were analyzed using multivariable linear regression, with the natural logarithm of Lp(a) as the dependent variable. Subsequently, binary logistic regression was used to identify clinical and analytical predictors of extensive CAD (defined as severe three-vessel disease), including a Lp(a)*female sex interaction term. Results The study included 931 patients (mean age 66.6 ± 12.0 years), of whom 24.2% (n=225) were women. Female sex was associated with a higher prevalence of dyslipidemia (70.2% vs. 62.0%; p=0.026), but a lower prevalence of prior smoking (48.4% vs. 74.9%; p=0.004) and prior CAD (16.0% vs. 27.1%; p=0.001). No differences were found in other clinical variables. Women presented higher levels of total cholesterol (164 [138-199] vs. 156 [126-188]; p=0.003), HDL cholesterol (43 [36-54] vs. 37 [32-45]; p&lt;0.001), and Lp(a) (76 [31-204] vs. 59 [25-137]; p=0.002), as well as lower creatinine clearance (67 [48-91] vs. 87 [66-112]; p&lt;0.001). The proportion of patients with Lp(a) &gt;105 nmol/L was 44.0% (n=99) in women vs. 33.0% (n=122) in men (p=0.003). In the multiple linear regression analysis, higher Lp(a) levels were independently associated with female sex, prior CAD, and elevated apolipoprotein B levels (Table 1). In the analysis of independent predictors for extensive CAD, only diabetes mellitus (OR 2.020 [95% CI 1.402–2.911]; p&lt;0.001), creatinine clearance (OR 0.992 [95% CI 0.985–0.999]; p=0.029), and Lp(a) (OR 1.003 [95% CI 1.001–1.005]; p=0.013) reached significance. Neither female sex nor the Lp(a)*female sex interaction showed a statistically significant association with extensive CAD (Table 2). Conclusions In patients with ACS, women have significantly higher Lp(a) levels than men. In this population, extensive CAD is associated with traditional risk factors such as diabetes and reduced creatinine clearance, as well as Lp(a) levels. The association between Lp(a) and the extent of CAD is not influenced by sex.Table 1.Predictors of lipoprotein(a) levels.Table 2.Predictors of extensive CAD
title: Sex-specific differences in lipoprotein (a) levels and their shared impact on coronary artery disease extent in ACS

abstract: Abstract Introduction Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) target attainment can mask residual atherogenic particle burden when Apolipoprotein B (ApoB) remains elevated, particularly at very low LDL-C levels where cholesterol-depleted, ApoB-rich particles (remnant/VLDL-related) may predominate. The prevalence of LDL-C-ApoB discordance at contemporary very high and extreme-risk LDL-C thresholds (&lt;55 and &lt;40 mg/dL) and its association with PCSK9 inhibitor–based intensification in routine care is not well defined. We therefore aimed to quantify LDL-C-ApoB discordance across lipid-lowering therapy intensities at these LDL-C thresholds and assessed associations with PCSK9i-based intensification. Methods We analyzed a prospective tertiary lipid-clinic registry using a cross-sectional patient-level approach. Triglycerides, ApoB, non–HDL-C, and Lp(a) were measured on fasting blood samples, and LDL-C was calculated using the Friedewald equation. Discordance was defined as LDL-C &lt;40 mg/dL with ApoB ≥65 mg/dL or LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL with ApoB ≥80 mg/dL. Lipid-lowering therapy was categorized as statin monotherapy, statin plus ezetimibe, or statin plus ezetimibe plus a PCSK9 inhibitor; non-PCSK9i therapy (statin ± ezetimibe) was pooled and compared with triple therapy including PCSK9i. Group differences in discordance prevalence were assessed, and standardized mean differences (pooled SD) for ApoB, triglycerides, non–HDL-C, and Lp(a) were calculated within each LDL-C target stratum (&lt;40 and &lt;55 mg/dL). Results At LDL-C &lt;40 mg/dL, LDL-C-ApoB discordance was common with non-PCSK9i therapy (statin ± ezetimibe: 17.6%, 13/74) but was rare with triple therapy including PCSK9i (1.7%, 2/119; Δ −15.9%; p&lt;0.001). At LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL, discordance occurred in 6.9% (14/204) under statin ± ezetimibe and in 0.0% (0/141) under triple therapy (Δ −6.9%; p&lt;0.001). Discordant patients showed a consistent atherogenic phenotype with higher triglycerides and non–HDL-C across both LDL-C thresholds, whereas Lp(a) was only modestly higher. Conclusion In a real-world tertiary lipid clinic cohort, achieving LDL-C &lt;55 and &lt;40 mg/dL did not reliably indicate ApoB control under statin ± ezetimibe, with clinically relevant discordance persisting in a meaningful proportion of patients. Intensification with PCSK9i-based triple therapy was associated with near-elimination of discordance and a lower residual atherogenic signature. Phenotype profiling further indicated that discordance at target LDL-C predominantly clustered with higher triglycerides and non-HDL-C. These findings support incorporating ApoB assessment, particularly when triglycerides or non-HDL-C remain elevated and suggest that PCSK9i-based intensification can effectively resolve LDL-C-ApoB discordance among LDL-C target achievers.Fig. 1:Prevalence of DiscordanceFig. 2:Discordance Phenotype
title: Apolipoprotein b discordance at very low low-density lipoprotein cholesterol thresholds: a patient-level analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is a primary therapeutic target in coronary artery disease (CAD); however, residual cardiovascular risk persists despite LDL-C control. Remnant cholesterol (remnant-C) has emerged as a potential contributor to this residual risk. Purpose To evaluate clinical outcomes according to combined LDL-C and remnant-C phenotypes in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). Methods Using the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) database, we identified 63,119 patients who underwent underwent PCI or CABG between 2011 and 2020. Patients were stratified into four groups according to LDL-C (cut-off 70 mg/dL) and remnant-C (cut-off 22.5 mg/dL): Group 1 (both low), Group 2 (low LDL-C/High remnant-C), Group 3 (high LDL-C/low remnant-C), and group 4 (both high). The primary endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (MACCE), defined as cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, repeat revascularization, or non-fatal stroke. Multivariable Cox models sequentially adjusted for demographic factors, comorbidities, lipid-lowering therapy, and antithrombotic medications. Results During follow-up, group 4 demonstrated the highest risk of MACCE compared with group 1 (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 1.15; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.11–1.20; p&lt;0.001). Notably, patients with controlled LDL-C but elevated remnant-C (group 2) remained at increased risk (HR 1.07; 95% CI 1.03-1.12; p&lt;0.001), whereas those with elevated LDL-C but low remnant-C (group 3) showed only modest risk elevation (HR 1.05; 95% CI 1.01-1.09; p=0.024). Elevated remnant-C was consistently associated with myocardial infarction, stroke, and repeat revascularization. Conclusions Remnant-C provides incremental prognostic value beyond LDL-C in patients undergoing coronary revascularization. Even when LDL-C is well controlled, elevated remnant-C identifies patients at persistent residual cardiovascular risk.Cubic Spline CurvesMACCEs
title: Clinical impact of combined LDL cholesterol and remnant cholesterol phenotypes after coronary revascularization: insights from a nationwide cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Early aggressive LDL-C lowering after acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is recommended to reduce recurrent events. Upfront triple oral lipid-lowering therapy is increasingly used to rapidly achieve LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL. Whether achieving an LDL-C target translates into early normalization of biological risk remains uncertain. Purpose To characterize ApoB–corrected LDL discordance and multidomain residual atherogenic and inflammatory risk one month after ACS treated with PCI and universal high-intensity rosuvastatin–ezetimibe–bempedoic acid therapy. Methods In a prospective single-centre cohort of 426 consecutive ACS patients undergoing PCI, all received triple oral lipid-lowering therapy from index hospitalization. At 1 month, corrected LDL-C, ApoB, triglycerides, remnant cholesterol, Lp(a), and hsCRP were assessed. ApoB–LDL discordance was defined using a 2×2 framework (corrected LDL &lt;55 vs ≥55 mg/dL; ApoB ≤65 vs &gt;65 mg/dL). Residual risk domains included LDL non-response, non-HDL-C ≥85 mg/dL, ApoB ≥65 mg/dL, triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL, remnant cholesterol ≥30 mg/dL, Lp(a) &gt;50 mg/dL, and hsCRP ≥2 mg/L. A residual risk burden index was constructed (0, 1, 2, ≥3 domains). Results Corrected LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL was achieved in 350 patients (82%). However, among LDL achievers, 86 patients (23.8%) demonstrated ApoB &gt;65 mg/dL despite target LDL-C. This discordant group exhibited higher triglycerides (149 vs 121 mg/dL), higher remnant cholesterol (21 vs 16 mg/dL), and a higher median hsCRP (0.72 vs 0.48 mg/L) than concordant-low patients. Strikingly, Lp(a) &gt;50 mg/dL was present in 94.2% of discordant patients versus 50.8% of concordant-low individuals. Across the entire cohort, complete residual risk normalization was uncommon. Only 19% of patients had zero risk domains at 1 month, whereas 52% exhibited ≥2 domains and 33% had ≥3 domains, indicating substantial clustering of atherogenic and inflammatory risk despite maximal oral therapy. Conclusions In 426 ACS patients treated with upfront triple oral lipid therapy, achieving LDL-C targets did not equate to biological risk resolution. Nearly one-quarter of LDL achievers demonstrated ApoB discordance with marked enrichment of elevated Lp(a), remnant lipoproteins, and inflammatory activity. Residual risk was multidimensional and frequently clustered early after ACS. These findings support moving beyond LDL-centric assessment toward particle-based phenotyping and provide a mechanistic rationale for early Lp(a)-targeted and anti-inflammatory therapeutic strategies.Figure 1Figure 2
title: LDL-C target achievement does not equal risk resolution after ACS: residual atherogenic and inflammatory burden despite maximal oral triple lipid therapy

abstract: Abstract Background The relationship between triglyceride (TG) levels and adverse events in coronary heart disease (CHD) patients is debated, and the modifying role of genetic background (TG-PRS) is unclear. Aim This study investigated the non-linear relationship between TG and all-cause mortality across TG-PRS strata to inform personalized risk management. Methods 4304 CHD patients undergoing PCI were enrolled. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) Cox regression analyzed the non-linear TG-mortality association in the overall population, adjusted for confounders (age, sex, BMI, hypertension, diabetes, prior PCI/CABG, COPD, PAD, CVD, hs-CRP, ACS). The population was stratified by TG-PRS tertiles (low, medium, high), with RCS repeated per stratum. Further stratified Cox regression was conducted within each PRS stratum, categorizing participants into low- and high-TG subgroups based on stratum-specific inflection points to examine differences in TG's continuous effect on mortality. Results Among 4304 CHD patients (mean age 57.45 ± 10.14 years, 83% male), 496 (11.5%) died after 10-year follow-up. In the overall population, TG showed an L-shaped association with mortality (P=0.0016) before adjustment, shifting to a non-significant U-shaped pattern after multivariable adjustment (P=0.1965). A significant TG and TG-PRS interaction was identified (P=0.031). Stratified RCS analyses revealed: 1. High TG-PRS: marginally significant U-shape (overall P=0.0548, non-linearity P=0.0386, inflection 1.67 mmol/L; red in Figure2); 2. Medium TG-PRS: significant U-shape (overall P=0.0191, non-linearity P=0.0112, inflection 1.44 mmol/L; orange in Figure2); 3. Low TG-PRS: no significant association (overall P=0.5504, non-linearity P=0.4773; blue in Figure2). Further interaction analyses confirmed: In high TG-PRS (P-interaction=0.0107), each 1 mmol/L TG increment reduced mortality by 48.5% in low-TG subgroups (TG&lt;1.67 mmol/L; HR=0.515, P=0.0133), but not in high-TG subgroups (TG≥1.67 mmol/L; HR=1.057, P=0.5147). A similar pattern was seen in medium TG-PRS (P-interaction=0.0061): significant inverse association in low-TG (TG&lt;1.44 mmol/L; HR=0.461, P=0.0258), but not high-TG (TG≥1.44 mmol/L; HR=1.275, P=0.0644). No significant interaction was found in low TG-PRS (P-interaction=0.2981). Conclusion TG is non-linearly associated with all-cause mortality, modified by TG-PRS. A U-shaped TG-mortality relationship was observed in medium and high TG-PRS groups. TG's protective effect in high-genetic-risk patients was confined to low-TG subgroups, highlighting that TG's clinical relevance depends on genetic background and baseline TG status. The observed association between lower TG and poorer prognosis may reflect reverse causation or disease-related factors (e.g., malnutrition, inflammation). Our findings support stratified, personalized TG management over a universal cutoff, especially for high-genetic-risk individuals.Figure1Figure2
title: Genetic modifiers of triglyceride-mediated mortality in coronary heart disease: a large cohort study of polygenic risk and circulating triglyceride level interaction

abstract: Abstract Background Patients with malignancy frequently have concurrent cardiovascular risk factors and undergo percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). European registries have documented substantial treatment gaps in lipid management, but data specifically addressing oncological patients after PCI are lacking (1,2). Aim To compare lipid profiles, LLT strategies, treatment intensification during hospitalization, and LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C) goal attainment between oncological and non-oncological patients undergoing PCI, stratified by a history of high-risk atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (prior ASCVD). Methods In this single-centre retrospective study, consecutive patients undergoing PCI with stent implantation (2022-2023) were stratified by oncological history (active malignancy or history of oncologic diagnosis) and prior ASCVD. LDL-C target was defined as &lt;55 mg/dL per 2019 ESC/EAS guidelines. In the prior ASCVD subgroup, equivalence of lipid target non-achievement was assessed using risk difference (RD) with Newcombe 90% confidence intervals (CI) and a predefined margin of +/-10 percentage points. Baseline LLT was compared within each stratum. As all post-PCI patients qualify as very high-risk ASCVD, LLT intensification and combination therapy at discharge were analysed in the entire cohort. Group comparisons used Fisher’s exact test. Exploratory logistic regression adjusted for age and high-intensity statin therapy. Results Among 1314 consecutive patients, 647 had prior ASCVD. In the ASCVD subgroup with available LDL-C (n=465), lipid target non-achievement did not differ significantly between oncological (19/56, 33.9%) and non-oncological patients (118/409, 28.9%; RD +5.1 percentage points, Newcombe 90% CI −5.1 to +16.6, p=0.811 after adjustment). Oncological patients with prior ASCVD were less frequently treated with high-intensity statins at baseline (9/53, 17.0% vs 128/359, 35.7%; p=0.007). Among patients without prior ASCVD, oncological patients had significantly lower baseline LDL-C (64.2±44.4 vs 104.6±31.6 mg/dL, p&lt;0.001). In the entire post-PCI cohort, LLT intensification during hospitalization was comparable between oncological and non-oncological patients (105/128, 82.0% vs 779/1024, 76.1%; p=0.149). However, oncological patients were discharged with significantly less combination therapy (31/150, 20.7% vs 404/1145, 35.3%; p&lt;0.001) and showed a trend toward lower high-intensity statin use at discharge (90/142, 63.4% vs 796/1121, 71.0%; p=0.065). Conclusion(s) Despite comparable rates of LLT intensification during hospitalization, oncological patients undergoing PCI were discharged with significantly less combination lipid-lowering therapy (p&lt;0.001). These findings suggest therapeutic inertia specifically regarding combination therapy at the cardio-oncology interface, highlighting an actionable treatment gap in secondary prevention.Table.LDL-c values, Lipid lowering therapy
title: Lipid goal attainment and treatment intensification in oncological versus non-oncological patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Achievement of recommended low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) targets remains suboptimal among individuals with or at risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), despite the availability of lipid-lowering therapies. However, contemporary data quantifying this discrepancy between guideline recommendations and real-world practice remain limited. Purpose To evaluate real-world attainment of LDL-C goal attainment in Denmark and to estimate the potential clinical and economic benefits of full implementation of the 2020 Danish and 2019/2025 European lipid guidelines. Methods In this nationwide registry-based cohort study, we included all Danish residents aged 30–85 years with established ASCVD (secondary prevention) or classified as high- or very-high-risk of ASCVD (primary prevention), with LDL-C measurements between January 2022 and December 2023 and repeat measurements 6–15 months later. LDL-C goal attainment were assessed according to the 2020 Danish and 2019/2025 European lipid guidelines. A patient-level Monte Carlo simulation estimated the impact of full implementation of the recommended lipid-lowering treatment algorithms on LDL-C goal attainment, preventable cardiovascular events, and clinical cost savings. Results Among 487,962 individuals (336,705 at high- or very-high-risk of ASCVD and 151,257 with established ASCVD), LDL-C goal attainment at follow-up in the primary prevention group was 39.8% under the 2020 Danish guideline (LDL-C &lt;2.6 mmol/L for high-risk and &lt;1.8 mmol/L for very-high-risk individuals) and 15.1% under the 2019/2025 European guideline (LDL-C &lt;1.8 mmol/L for high-risk and &lt;1.4 mmol/L for very-high-risk individuals). Among adults with established ASCVD, LDL-C goal attainment was 18.8% under both guidelines (LDL-C &lt;1.4 mmol/L). Under optimal implementation, attainment increased to 91.7% (primary) and 63.3% (secondary) for the Danish guideline, and to 75.9% (primary) and 96.6% (secondary) under the European guideline. Compared with real-world outcomes, implementation of the Danish guideline could annually prevent 488 strokes, 411 myocardial infarctions, 485 revascularizations, and 162 cardiovascular deaths. Implementation of the European guideline would avert an additional 168 strokes, 140 myocardial infarctions, 156 revascularizations, and 60 cardiovascular deaths, corresponding to annual clinical cost savings exceeding €14.4 million. In the rapid-intensification simulations, adding PCSK9 inhibitors for all patients above target after high-intensity statin therapy achieved near-universal goal attainment in primary prevention (98.7% Danish; 96.4% ESC/EAS) and 93.6% in secondary prevention. Conclusion Early and broader adoption of combination lipid-lowering therapy, as advocated in the focused updated 2025 European lipid guideline, could substantially improve LDL-C goal attainment, reduce cardiovascular events, and generate meaningful clinical cost savings.Figure 1.Simulation algorithmFigure 2.Simulated LDL-C goal attainment
title: Improving LDL-C goal attainment: real-world outcomes and the impact of guideline optimization

abstract: Abstract Background Statins are central to cardiovascular prevention, yet women and older adults appear less likely to receive guideline-recommended therapy, potentially contributing to outcome disparities. Long-term trends in prescription of statins before acute myocardial infarction (AMI) provide a useful lens to assess equity in prevention. Purpose To examine sex- and age-related differences in statin prescription prior to admission for AMI in France and to evaluate how these evolved over 20 years, alongside changes in lipid-lowering therapy (LLT) use. Methods We pooled data from the nationwide FAST-MI periodic surveys (2005, 2010, 2015) and the FRENCHIE cohort (2019–2022), which enrolled AMI patients admitted to PCI-capable 24/7 centres across France. Pre-admission statin and LLT use were recorded on admission. Patients were stratified by prior atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD: coronary artery disease, peripheral arterial disease, or ischaemic stroke). Multivariable models estimated the association of sex and age with pre-AMI statin use and assessed temporal changes. Results Overall LLT consumption increased over time, particularly statin–ezetimibe combination therapy, with a marked shift after 2019. Marked differences persisted, with distinct patterns according to presence or absence of prior ASCVD. In patients without known ASCVD (n=19,696), statin use prior to admission increased with age (18.1% in ≥80 years vs 5.8% in &lt;50 years), mirroring LLT (21.7% vs 6.6%). Age remained associated with higher treatment probability (≥80 vs &lt;50: aOR 2.48, 95% CI 2.01–3.06; p&lt;0.001). Among patients under 50 with ≥3 risk factors, only 20.8% received statin therapy. Women showed higher unadjusted statin (14.8% vs 12.1%) and LLT use (18.0% vs 14.3%) than men, including across most risk-factor strata and with increasing risk-factor burden (notably ≥3 risk factors: 37.3% vs 34.2%). However, after adjustment women were less likely to receive statins than men (aOR 0.86, 95% CI 0.77–0.96; p=0.01), with no improvement over time. Among patients with established ASCVD (n=7,765), women were less frequently treated than men (51.8% vs 58.6%). Statin use rose with age to 70–79 years but declined after ≥80 years. In adjusted analyses, female sex and older age were associated with lower statin use (aOR 0.79, 95% CI 0.70–0.91; p&lt;0.001 ; ≥80 vs &lt;50 years: aOR 0.54, 95% CI 0.42–0.70; p&lt;0.001 respectively). Conclusion Over two decades in France, women were and have remained less likely to receive statins than men before AMI, regardless of prior ASCVD. Among patients without ASCVD, statin use increased with age, yet the highest-risk younger patients remained markedly undertreated. Statin use paradoxically decreased with age in those with established CVD. Targeted efforts are needed to close these dramatic and persistent sex- and age-related gaps in guideline implementation.Figure Without AtheromaFigure With Atheroma
title: Sex- and age-based disparities in statin use in patients admitted for acute myocardial infarction in France: two decades of failure ?

abstract: Abstract Background Retinal vessel analysis is a non-invasive tool to assess microvascular function (1). Retinal venular widening in static analysis and an impaired flicker light induced dilation (FID) of retinal vessels in dynamic analysis is known to be associated with higher cardiovascular risk (2-4). The course of microvascular dysfunction assessed by retinal vessel analysis in patients with acute myocardial infarction and during follow up on optimal lipid-lowering therapy is so far unknown. Therefore, the aim of the present study was to investigate retinal vessel analysis in patients during the hospital stay of the index event and during long term follow up on optimal lipid-lowering therapy. Methods We performed static retinal vessel analysis (SVA) and dynamic retinal vessel analysis (DVA 3.0) applying flicker light stimuli in 15 patients post STEMI (median within 3 days) and 5 years after the index event. At baseline all patients received a combination of high dose statin therapy (atorvastatin 80 mg) and ezetimibe. We obtained cardiovascular risk status at baseline and during follow up including smoking status, diabetes mellitus, blood pressure, lipid lowering therapy and lipid profile. One patient was excluded due to relevant retinal abnormalities with influence on retinal vessels. In two patients the quality of the measurements was insufficient. We included 12 patients in the final analysis. Results Five years post STEMI all except for two patients still were treated with a combination of statin and ezetimibe. Two patients were on triple lipid lowering with a high intensity statin, ezetimibe and PCSK9-I. Most patients had a previous diagnosis of arterial hypertension, but presented with well-controlled blood pressure (mean 128 ± 4.5 mmHg) at 5 year follow up. The majority of patients reached an LDL cholesterol &lt;1.4 mmol/l for the high-risk group according to the current ESC guidelines for dyslipidemias (LDL-C at baseline median 3.66 mmol/l IQR 1.56 mmol/l, LDL-C at follow up median 1.32 mmol/l IQR 0.58 mmol/l). As expected, static retinal vessel analysis (SVA) revealed lower values for central retinal venular equivalents (CRVE) (one-sided p &lt; 0.036) during follow up compared to baseline. Dynamic retinal vessel analysis (DVA 3.0) showed higher values for FID of retinal arteries (one-sided p = 0.027) and veins (one-sided p = 0.043) during follow up (see figure 1 and figure 2). Conclusion In patients after ST-elevation myocardial infarction optimal lipid-lowering therapy reduces LDL-C and is associated with improved microvascular dysfunction assessed by retinal vessel analysis during long term follow up. Further studies are needed to assess retinal vessel analysis as a tool to improve cardiovascular risk prediction in high risk patients.
title: Intensive lipid lowering therapy improves microvascular function assessed by retinal vessel analysis in patients after ST-elevation myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background After a coronary event, patients are at markedly elevated risk of recurrent cardiovascular events, with low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) representing an important component of residual risk. However, guideline-recommended LDL-C targets are not achieved in a considerable number of patients. Furthermore, in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS), early initiation of intensive lipid-lowering therapy (LLT) during hospitalisation has been shown to result in greater LDL-C reduction compared with more gradual up-titration. However, it remains unclear whether hospitalisation for elective coronary revascularisation represents a similar ‘window of opportunity’ to optimise lipid management. Purpose To compare LDL-C management during hospitalisation for ACS versus elective coronary revascularisation. Methods We included consecutive patients hospitalised for ACS (ST- or non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction [STEMI/NSTEMI], or unstable angina pectoris [uAP]) or elective coronary revascularisation (percutaneous coronary intervention [PCI] or coronary artery bypass grafting [CABG]) in 26 hospitals in the Netherlands between June 2024 and February 2026. Patient characteristics, laboratory data (collected during index hospitalisation or within 6 months prior) and discharge medication prescriptions were extracted from electronic health records. LDL-C targets of &lt;1.8 mmol/L (Dutch guideline) and &lt;1.4 mmol/L (2019 ESC/EAS guideline) were evaluated. Adequate LLT was defined as treatment with a potency equivalent to or greater than a high-intensity statin combined with ezetimibe (i.e. ~ 60% LDL-C reduction). To account for baseline differences, elective coronary revascularisation patients were matched to ACS patients on age, sex, LDL-C at admission, and cardiovascular history. Results In 1,985 patients (27% female; median age 68 years [IQR 60–76]); 76% had ACS and 24% underwent elective coronary revascularisation. LDL-C at admission was &lt;1.8 mmol/L in 19% of ACS patients and 24% of elective coronary revascularisation patients (Table 1). At discharge, adequate LLT was prescribed in 27% of ACS patients compared to 16% of elective coronary revascularisation patients (p&lt;0.001). After matching (n=330 per group, 99% of elective patients with complete data) this LLT disparity remained (27% vs. 15%, p&lt;0.001) (Figure 1). Conclusion In a contemporary large multicentre cohort, lipid management during hospitalisation for a coronary event remains suboptimal, with particular potential for improvement in elective coronary revascularisation patients. Strategies to improve adequate LLT during hospitalisation regardless of ACS or elective coronary revascularisation are urgently needed to improve secondary prevention.Patient characteristicsFigure 1 Adequate LLT
title: Elective coronary revascularisation represents an unutilised opportunity to optimise lipid management: results from a multicentre observational cohort

abstract: Abstract Background Aspirin may be considered for primary prevention in selected patients with diabetes mellitus (DM). Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an independent cardiovascular risk factor linked to myocardial infarction and stroke and may promote thrombogenicity. Whether the association between aspirin use and cardiovascular outcomes differs according to Lp(a) levels remains uncertain. Purpose To evaluate the association between aspirin use and cardiovascular outcomes in primary prevention among patients with DM according to Lp(a) levels. Methods Retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX database. Adults with DM and Lp(a) measurements were included. Individuals with prior atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) were excluded to restrict the analysis to primary prevention. Patients were stratified according to Lp(a) levels as normal (Lp(a) &lt;50 mg/dL) or elevated (Lp(a) ≥50 mg/dL) and categorized as aspirin users or non-users based on prescription records within the first year after DM diagnosis. Follow-up started 366 days after DM diagnosis and continued for up to 5 years. Propensity score matching (1:1) balanced baseline characteristics between aspirin users and non-users in each group. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke. Secondary outcomes included individual components of primary outcome and major bleeding. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Interaction analysis assessed effect modification by Lp(a) levels. Results After matching, among patients with normal Lp(a), aspirin use was associated with a higher risk of the composite outcome (HR 1.31, 95%CI 1.05–1.63) and ischemic stroke (HR 1.53, 95%CI 1.14–2.05), with no significant differences in myocardial infarction, major bleeding, or all-cause death (Figure 1). Among patients with elevated Lp(a), no significant differences were found between aspirin use and non-use in the composite outcome or individual components (Figure 1). A higher risk of major bleeding (HR 1.70, 95% CI 1.11–2.62) was found in aspirin users compared to non-users. No significant interaction was observed between aspirin use and Lp(a) levels for the composite outcome (p-interaction = 0.33), myocardial infarction (p-interaction = 0.67), major bleeding (p-interaction = 0.37), or all-cause death (p-interaction = 0.85). A borderline interaction was observed for ischemic stroke (p-interaction = 0.05), with an increased risk among aspirin users in the normal Lp(a) group but not in those with elevated Lp(a) (Figure 1). Conclusion In this large real-world cohort of patients with DM, no significant interaction between Lp(a) status and aspirin use was observed for the primary outcome. These findings do not support a differential benefit of aspirin according to Lp(a) levels in patients with DM in the primary prevention settings.
title: Aspirin for primary prevention in patients with diabetes according to lipoprotein(a) levels: a real-world propensity-matched analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an established causal risk factor for the development and progression of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Multiple phase 3 trials are currently evaluating targeted Lp(a)-lowering therapies using high entry thresholds. However, real-world eligibility in secondary prevention remains limited, and no universally accepted cut-offs exist. The 2025 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and European Atherosclerosis Society (EAS) guidelines recommend considering Lp(a) ≥105 nmol/L as a cardiovascular risk-enhancing factor. [1] Purpose To evaluate real-world eligibility for emerging Lp(a)-lowering therapies and apheresis in patients with chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) and acute coronary syndrome (ACS), and to determine the association between Lp(a) levels and 5-year cardiovascular outcomes. Methods Consecutive patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) at a tertiary care centre between 2010 and 2021 with Lp(a) measured in nmol/L were analysed. Eligibility was assessed according to trial-aligned thresholds (≥150, ≥175, ≥200 nmol/L) and the guideline-recommended risk-enhancing cut-off (≥105 nmol/L). Lp(a) apheresis eligibility was evaluated using national Central European criteria (Austria: Lp(a) &gt;250 nmol/L plus prior revascularization; Germany: Lp(a) &gt;120 nmol/L plus prior revascularization and LDL cholesterol &lt;130 mg/dL). Five-year major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and target lesion failure (TLF) were endpoints. Results Among 5,942 PCI patients, median Lp(a) was 26.0 [IQR 9.0 – 106.0] nmol/L and 1,498 (25.2%) patients had Lp(a) levels ≥105 nmol/L. Eligibility decreased at higher trial-aligned thresholds: 1,094 (18.4%) ≥150 nmol/L, 881 (14.8%) ≥175 nmol/L, and 688 (11.6%) ≥200 nmol/L (Figure 1). Lp(a) levels were similar in chronic coronary syndrome (CCS; median 28.0 [IQR 9.0 – 118.5] nmol/L) and acute coronary syndrome (ACS; median 25.0 [IQR 9.0 – 96.5] nmol/L), with modestly higher values in CCS. National apheresis criteria were fulfilled by 1.8% (Austria) and 6.1% (German) of patients. Over five years, higher Lp(a) was independently associated with an increased risk of MACE (adjusted HR per 1 SD 1.07 [95% CI 1.02 – 1.12]; p = 0.008) and TLF (adjusted HR per 1 SD 1.06 [95% CI 1.01 – 1.11]; p = 0.020), with pronounced associations observed in ACS. Conclusion Elevated Lp(a) is highly prevalent in PCI patients and independently associated with adverse 5-year outcomes. While a substantial proportion of patients met thresholds for emerging Lp(a)-lowering therapies, few fulfilled composite apheresis criteria. Systematic Lp(a) testing after PCI may improve risk stratification, identify candidates for emerging therapies, and guide implementation of targeted secondary prevention strategies in routine cardiovascular practice.Figure 1
title: Bridging the gap: real-world eligibility for lipoprotein(a)-targeted therapies in chronic and acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type-9 (PCSK9) inhibitors reduce cardiovascular events in secondary prevention. However, real-world evidence comparing statin-free PCSK9 inhibitor therapy with high-intensity statins in primary prevention remains limited. Purpose To evaluate the comparative effectiveness of statin-free PCSK9 inhibitor therapy versus high-intensity atorvastatin for cardiovascular outcomes in individuals without established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Methods We conducted a target trial emulation study using the TriNetX global federated electronic health record network. Adults aged &gt;40 years with dyslipidaemia and no prior ASCVD, heart failure, or cancer (2013–2024) were included. Patients initiating PCSK9 inhibitor monotherapy were compared with those initiating high-intensity atorvastatin (40–80 mg). A 3-month washout period was applied. One-to-one propensity score matching balanced demographics, comorbidities, lipid levels, and concomitant medications. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: all-cause mortality, acute coronary syndrome, stroke, or heart failure) at 1 year. Cox proportional hazards models were used under an intention-to-treat framework. Results Among 308,286 eligible patients, 5,715 received PCSK9 inhibitors and 302,571 received atorvastatin. After matching, 5,570 patients were included in each group. At 1 year, MACE occurred in 2.9% of the PCSK9 group versus 4.2% of the atorvastatin group (hazard ratio [HR] 0.71; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.58–0.86), corresponding to a number needed to treat of 82. PCSK9 inhibitors were associated with lower risks of all-cause mortality (HR 0.51; 95% CI 0.31–0.86), ischaemic stroke (HR 0.63; 95% CI 0.41–0.97), and all-cause hospitalisation (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.77–0.92). Results were consistent across multiple sensitivity analyses and prespecified subgroups, with greater benefit observed in patients with baseline LDL cholesterol ≥190 mg/dL. No association was observed in falsification analyses. Conclusions In this large real-world target trial emulation, statin-free PCSK9 inhibitor therapy was associated with significantly lower cardiovascular event rates compared with high-intensity atorvastatin in individuals without prior ASCVD. These findings suggest potential applicability of PCSK9 inhibitors for primary prevention in clinical scenarios where patients are unable to tolerate statins or require alternative lipid-lowering strategies.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Statin-free PCSK9 inhibitor therapy versus high-intensity atorvastatin for primary prevention: a target trial emulation study

abstract: Abstract Background Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a well-established, genetically determined risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Contemporary consensus guidelines from the ESC and ACC/AHA recommend at least one lifetime Lp(a) measurement; however, interpretation of Lp(a) in the setting of acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) remains challenging. Prior studies suggest that acute myocardial infarction may transiently alter Lp(a) levels, and as a result, a single Lp(a) measurement obtained at the time of STEMI may underestimate a patient’s baseline Lp(a)-related risk. It also remains uncertain whether post-STEMI Lp(a) elevations reflect true biological change or rebound from acute-phase suppression. Purpose We aimed to evaluate longitudinal changes in Lp(a) levels after STEMI in younger patients and to assess whether specific LLTs were associated with changes in Lp(a) at time of follow-up visit. Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis among STEMI patients aged ≤65 years from 13 regional hospitals between January 2016 and December 2022. The primary objective was to determine changes in Lp(a) levels: the inclusion criteria included those with Lp(a) values measured at or shortly following STEMI hospitalization and at follow-up visit (defined as Lp(a) level obtained greater than at least 6 months following baseline measurement). A significant Lp(a) rise was defined as ≥40 nmol/L, based on prior studies (1). The secondary objective was to determine any association in Lp(a) change with LLTs, such as statins, ezetimibe, and PCSK9 inhibitors. Results Among 1262 STEMI patients, 110 patients had two or more Lp(a) values and 78 met inclusion criteria. The baseline Lp(a) was measured during STEMI hospitalization in 15/78 (19%) and shortly after discharge in 63/78 (81%; median 3 [IQR: 1,7] months). The average change in Lp(a) was 7.3 ± 44 nmol/L with median time to follow-up of 13 (IQR 10, 20) months (Figure 1). Compared to baseline Lp(a) at time of STEMI, at median time of 13 months (IQR 10, 20) follow-up, 8/78 patients (10%) experienced Lp(a) increase ≥40 nmol/L (median 73 [IQR: 46, 177]), while 41/78 (53%) had an increase 0-39 nmol/L and 29/78 (37%) had a lower Lp(a) (median -13 [IQR: -20, -7]) (Figure 2). Among this cohort, 76/78 (97%) were on a statin, 16/78 (21%) were on ezetimibe, and 1/78 (1%) were on a PCSK9 inhibitor at time of follow-up measurement. There were no association in changes of Lp(a) levels with specific LLTs, though this was likely underpowered. Conclusion Lp(a) trends following STEMI in younger patients demonstrate substantial heterogeneity, with a small proportion experiencing a significant rise over time. These findings may reflect variable recovery from acute-phase Lp(a) perturbation and/or true longitudinal biological variation. Larger studies are needed to identify determinants of significant Lp(a) changes and to establish their prognostic implications after STEMI.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Changes in lipoprotein(a) levels in younger patients following ST-elevation myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background High cardiovascular (CV) risk patients with no previous stroke could benefit from an intensive lipid-lowering strategy beyond statins alone. However, the comparative efficacy of non-statin treatments in this population remains unclear. Purpose To investigate the efficacy and safety of non-statin treatments—including evolocumab, alirocumab, enlicitide, inclisiran, evinacumab, omega-3 fatty acids, and ezetimibe—in high CV risk patients without previous stroke. Method A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library from inception through January 2026. High CV risk was defined according to standard guidelines. Only studies in which fewer than 10% of patients had a documented history of stroke were eligible. The primary endpoints included major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)—defined as the composite endpoint of CV mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, and coronary revascularization—along with CV mortality and stroke incidence evaluated independently. The secondary endpoints were changes in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels (mg/dL) and lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] levels (%). Results A total of 15 RCTs comprising 78,146 patients (23,626 females [30.2%]; mean age 63.7± 9.2 years) were included. Among the non-statin options, evolocumab demonstrated the greatest reduction in MACE, CV mortality, and stroke incidence, with ORs of 0.75 (95% CI 0.64–0.88, p &lt;0.001), 0.79 (95% CI 0.64–0.98, p = 0.030), and 0.79 (95% CI 0.62–1.01, p = 0.058), respectively, and the highest P-scores of 0.98, 0.91, and 0.84. The top three treatments for LDL-C reduction were evolocumab (MD −55.1 mg/dL, 95% CI −80.3 to −30.0, p &lt;0.001; P-score 0.86), inclisiran (MD −54.1 mg/dL, 95% CI −89.4 to −18.8, p = 0.002; P-score 0.84), and alirocumab (MD −46.3 mg/dL, 95% CI −66.8 to −25.8, p &lt;0.001; P-score 0.76). For Lp(a) reduction, evolocumab ranked highest (MD −26.9%, 95% CI −27.0 to −26.8, p &lt;0.001; P-score 0.91), followed by enlicitide (MD −27.5%, 95% CI −34.4 to −20.7, p &lt;0.001; P-score 0.87) and alirocumab (MD −26.1%, 95% CI −26.5 to −25.7, p &lt;0.001; P-score 0.72). Conclusions Evolocumab had the potential to be the first-line non-statin option for high CV risk patients without previous stroke due to its efficacy in reducing MACE, CV mortality, LDL-C, and Lp(a).Figure 1Figure 2
title: Evolocumab for high cardiovascular risk patients without previous stroke: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

abstract: Abstract Introduction It has been suggested that GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) could offer additional benefits for smoking cessation due to their modulation of reward pathways and anti-craving effects, in addition to their established cardiovascular benefits. Purpose Our aim was to evaluate the impact of GLP-1 RAs on smoking cessation following admission for acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Methods A prospective observational study was conducted in a cohort of active smokers hospitalized for ACS at our center, with angiographically proven coronary artery disease. After one year of follow-up, self-reported smoking abstinence and its associated factors were analyzed, with a focus on GLP-1 RAs prescription at discharge. Appropriate comparison tests and binary logistic regression analysis were used for this purpose. Results A total of 200 patients were included (mean age: 58.2 ± 10.0 years; 16.5% women). At 1-year follow-up, only 61% had successfully quit smoking. No significant differences in smoking cessation were observed according to age, sex, cardiovascular risk factors, ACS presentation, Killip class, or previous cardiovascular disease (Table). Notably, cumulative tobacco exposure (pack-years) was not significantly associated with cessation success. Regarding conventional smoking cessation pharmacotherapies, detailed in Figure (nicotine replacement therapy, bupropion, or varenicline—the latter unavailable for most of the study period), these were infrequently prescribed (23%) and were not significantly associated with smoking cessation. Prescription of GLP-1 RAs at discharge (14.5% of patients, all with diabetes; 96.6% receiving semaglutide) was associated with a remarkably high abstinence rate (89.7% vs. 56.1% in the non-GLP-1 RA group; p=0.001). Specifically, within the diabetic subgroup, patients on GLP-1 RAs achieved significantly higher cessation rates compared to those on other glucose-lowering therapies (86.4% vs. 56.9%; p=0.014). In the multivariable model, GLP-1 RAs emerged as an independent predictor of smoking cessation (OR 5.844; 95% CI 1.620-21.079; p=0.007), alongside participation in cardiac rehabilitation (OR 2.108; 95% CI 1.072-4.144; p=0.031). Conclusions In our cohort, nearly 40% of patients continued smoking one year after an acute coronary syndrome. In addition to the well-established benefits of cardiac rehabilitation, prescription of GLP-1 RAs at discharge was independently associated with smoking cessation. These findings support the need for randomized clinical trials to confirm this potential benefit of GLP-1 RAs, which could have relevant implications for post-ACS management.TableFigure
title: GLP-1 receptor agonists for smoking cessation after acute coronary syndrome: from biological plausibility to clinical impact.

abstract: Abstract Background Smoking cessation after an acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is crucial for secondary prevention, yet early relapse is frequent. Identifying determinants of persistent smoking and evaluating the use of pharmacological cessation therapies may help refine targeted interventions. Methods Consecutive patients admitted with ACS to a tertiary center (2023–2024) who were active smokers at presentation and alive at 12 months were screened. Participants completed a structured telephone questionnaire assessing smoking behavior during the year after discharge, including use of cessation pharmacotherapy. Clinical, behavioral, environmental, therapeutic, and outcome variables were analyzed to identify predictors of persistent smoking at 12 months. Results Among 861 ACS admissions, 254 were active smokers; 236 survived to 12 months, and 184 participated. At one year, 85 patients (46%) remained active smokers. Persistent smokers had higher nicotine dependence (Fagerström score, p&lt;0.001), greater pre-event cigarette consumption (p=0.002), and more frequent household smoking exposure (72% vs 33%; p&lt;0.001). Early relapse strongly predicted long-term persistence: 57% of persistent smokers resumed within 7 days versus 5% of those abstinent at one year (p&lt;0.001). Pharmacological support after discharge was reported by 38% of patients: nicotine replacement therapy (24%), cytisinicline (9%), and bupropion (5%). Structured pharmacotherapy—particularly when initiated during hospitalization—was associated with lower early relapse rates compared with no pharmacological support (29% vs 61%, p&lt;0.001). Nevertheless, nearly two-thirds received no evidence-based pharmacological treatment. Persistent smokers more frequently required unplanned cardiac evaluations or rehospitalizations (20% vs 12%; p=0.048) and repeat coronary assessment (15% vs 8%; p=0.041). No differences were observed in 12-month mortality (p=0.72) or left ventricular function recovery (p=0.31). Multivariable analysis identified smoking within 7 days post-discharge (OR 14.37; 95% CI 3.46–59.68; p&lt;0.001) and household smoking exposure (OR 11.02; 95% CI 2.64–45.94; p=0.001) as independent predictors of persistent smoking. Conclusion Nearly half of smokers hospitalized with ACS remained active at one year. Early relapse and household exposure were the strongest predictors of persistence and were associated with increased subsequent cardiac evaluations. Despite the availability of effective therapies, pharmacological support was underused. These findings underscore the need for immediate, structured cessation strategies with systematic in-hospital initiation of evidence-based pharmacotherapy and early post-discharge reinforcement, particularly for patients exposed to smoking environments.Central figure
authors: Esculudes Dos Santos Ferrao Gomes R
title: Persistence of smoking following acute coronary syndrome: insights from a two-year single-center study

abstract: Abstract Background Obesity is a global epidemic associated with major cardiovascular (CV) risk factors. While previous studies have suggested an "obesity paradox" in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS), characterized by a protective effect of higher body mass index (BMI), its consistency across different demographics and clinical subtypes remains debated. Purpose To evaluate the association between BMI and in-hospital mortality among Chinese ACS patients and to examine whether this relationship is modified by age, sex, and disease subtype. Methods This retrospective cohort study analyzed ACS patients from the Chinese Cardiovascular Association (CCA) Database – Chest Pain Center between January 2016 and December 2023. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Logistic regression and Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW) were used to adjust for baseline confounders. Restricted cubic splines (RCS) were employed to model potential nonlinear associations, with results stratified by age, sex, and ACS subtype. Results The study included a total of 898,798 patients diagnosed with ACS, of whom 32,357 (3.6%) were underweight, 511,779 (56.9%) were normal weight, 299,709 (33.3%) were overweight, and 54,953 (6.1%) were obese. Patients with obesity or overweight exhibited a higher prevalence of classic CV risk factors, a greater proportion of males, higher rates of PCI, shorter pre-hospital delays, and were generally younger. Conversely, underweight patients had a higher burden of other comorbidities. A U-shaped relationship between BMI and in-hospital mortality was observed across the overall population and both sexes. Notably, among ACS patients under 45 years (premature coronary artery disease), the relationship demonstrated a near-linear increase in mortality with higher BMI. In contrast, the classic U-shaped curve remained evident in patients over 60 years. Conclusions A U-shaped association between BMI and in-hospital mortality exists in Chinese ACS patients, though this relationship transitions to a linear increase in younger cohorts. These findings suggest that body weight control strategies should be more precise and tailored to patient age to improve clinical outcomes.
title: The relationship between BMI and ACS in-hospital mortality: findings from the Chinese Cardiovascular Association-Chest Pain Center Registry

abstract: Abstract Background Body mass index (BMI) is a modifiable prognostic factor in non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI). Investigating the impact of BMI on short- and long-term prognosis in patients with NSTEMI can inform clinical management and improve patient outcomes[1, 2]. Purpose This study aimed to investigate the association between BMI and both in-hospital and 10-year all-cause mortality in critically ill NSTEMI patients admitted to the coronary care unit, and to evaluate the incremental value of C-reactive protein (CRP) in mortality risk stratification. Methods This multinational, multicohort study included 7,815 critically ill NSTEMI patients from three international cohorts (TAMI, MIMIC-IV, and eICU-CRD). BMI was categorized into normal, overweight, obesity I, and obesity II/III groups, based on WHO and Chinese criteria. CRP levels were dichotomized at 2 mg/L. The primary endpoints were in-hospital and 10-year all-cause mortality. Associations between BMI and mortality were evaluated using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models and restricted cubic splines. Results In-hospital all-cause mortality rates were 2.99%, 7.28%, and 5.57%, while 10-year all-cause mortality rates were 12.67% and 21.52% for TAMI and MIMIC-IV, respectively. A significant U-shaped association was observed between BMI and all-cause mortality in critically ill NSTEMI patients. In the TAMI cohort, severe obesity (obesity II/III) was independently associated with increased risks of in-hospital (hazard radio (HR)=1.84; 95% CI, 1.20–2.81) and 10-year (HR=1.85; 95% CI, 1.49–2.32) all-cause mortality. Conversely, overweight and obesity I conferred protective associations with lower all-cause mortality risk. Furthermore, the coexistence of severe obesity and elevated inflammation (CRP≥2 mg/L) demonstrated a synergistic risk, adjusted HRs of 4.57 (95% CI, 2.58–8.08) for in-hospital and 3.07 (95% CI, 2.33–4.06) for 10-year all-cause mortality. Subgroup analysis showed that combined presence of severe obesity, elevated inflammation, and diabetes was associated with the highest all-cause mortality risk, with adjusted HRs reaching 6.21 (95% CI, 2.77–13.89) for in-hospital and 3.66 (95% CI, 2.43–4.92) for 10-year all-cause mortality. The pooled meta-analysis results of the three databases were consistent. Conclusions BMI shows a U-shaped association with mortality in critically ill NSTEMI patients, with severe obesity as an independent risk factor. It establishes the combination of severe obesity and elevated inflammation as a distinct, high-risk clinical phenotype. In clinical practice, integrated ‘metabolic-inflammatory’ management should be prioritized, and targeted strategies combining long-term weight control with anti-inflammatory therapy should be actively explored to improve short- and long-term prognosis.
title: Association between body mass index and all-cause mortality in patients with non-ST-segment-elevation myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Worsening aortic regurgitation (AR) after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is associated with adverse clinical outcomes; however, the underlying hemodynamic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Energy loss (EL), a marker of hemodynamic inefficiency, is known to be elevated in AR. Given the distinct physiological roles of systolic and diastolic flow, we hypothesized that an imbalance favoring systolic over diastolic EL after TAVR may identify high-risk patients with worsening AR. Purpose To investigate peri-procedural changes in EL in patients with worsening AR after TAVR and to evaluate their prognostic and mechanistic implications. Methods We examined 205 consecutive patients who underwent TAVR between May 2018 and August 2025 and completed pre- and post-procedural four-dimensional flow magnetic resonance imaging (4D flow MRI). Systolic and diastolic EL were quantified in the ascending aorta (AAo) and left ventricle (LV). Based on echocardiography, patients were classified into worsening AR (AR-w, n=55) and non-worsening AR (AR-nw, n=150), defined as an increase of at least one grade on a five-grade scale. Patients were further stratified according to the post procedural systolic to diastolic EL ratio (S/D) into higher (&gt;1) and lower (&lt;1) groups. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death and heart failure hospitalization. Results The median age was 83 years and 71 patients were male. Baseline characteristics and valve type were comparable between groups. During a median follow-up of 620 days (IQR 253 to 1123), AR-w patients had a higher incidence of the primary outcome compared with AR-nw patients (P=0.030). Systolic EL in the AAo decreased in all groups, although the reduction was smaller in AR-w (P&lt;0.001) after TAVR. In contrast, left ventricular systolic EL increased significantly in AR-w (P=0.008) but remained unchanged in AR-nw (P=0.60). Diastolic EL in both the AAo and LV decreased in AR-nw, whereas no significant changes were observed in AR-w. When stratified by post-procedural S/D ratio, patients with AR-w and a higher S/D ratio demonstrated the highest cumulative incidence of adverse outcomes (Figure 1). In multivariable analysis, AR-w with a higher S/D ratio remained independently associated with adverse outcomes (HR 3.78 95%CI 1.43-0.99). Detailed flow analysis in this high-risk group demonstrated reduced physiologic vortex formation in the LV, more frequent jet inflow collision at larger angles, and a higher prevalence of posteriorly directed wall hugging jets (Figure 2). Conclusion Worsening AR after TAVR is associated with adverse outcomes, particularly when accompanied by a predominance of systolic over diastolic EL. Hemodynamic inefficiency characterized by jet inflow collision and impaired vortex formation may underlie this association. Quantification of EL using 4D flow MRI may provide incremental risk stratification and insights into procedural optimization.
title: Systolic–diastolic energy loss imbalance and adverse outcomes in patients with worsening aortic regurgitation after TAVR

abstract: Abstract Introduction Abdominal fat distribution (AFD), quantified by the ratio of visceral adipose tissue (VAT) to subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) areas (V/S ratio), may be associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD). Although VAT has traditionally been considered the primary contributor to CVD risk, the role of SAT remains less well understood. Despite the common use of the body mass index (BMI) as an indicator of obesity, the associations of AFD indices (V/S ratio, SAT, and VAT) and BMI-stratified physique with CVD outcomes have not been fully elucidated. Purpose This study aimed to investigate the effect of AFD and BMI-stratified physique on long-term cardiovascular outcomes. Methods In total, 942 consecutive patients (mean age 66.7 years; 42.5% female) with suspected coronary artery disease who underwent coronary computed tomography (CT) angiography were evaluated. Plain abdominal CT was also performed at the umbilical level to quantify SAT and VAT areas, and the V/S ratio was calculated as an AFD index. Patients were stratified into two groups based on the median BMI (23.6 kg/m²) and further categorized into high and low groups according to the median V/S ratio, SAT, and VAT (0.625, 115.1 cm², and 76.9 cm², respectively). Associations between these AFD indices and 5-year clinical outcomes were assessed within each BMI group. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiac events (MACEs), including all-cause death, any coronary revascularization, acute coronary syndrome, and emergent hospitalization for cardiac causes. Results Kaplan–Meier analysis showed significantly lower MACE-free survival rates among patients with low BMI and a high V/S ratio than those with a low V/S ratio. Lower MACE-free survival rates were also observed in both BMI groups among patients with low SAT, whereas no significant differences were seen between VAT groups (Figure). A high V/S ratio and high SAT were associated with a 57% increase and a 46% decrease in the risk of MACEs, among patients with low BMI (hazard ratio [HR], 1.57; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.09–2.27; p = 0.015 for high V/S ratio; HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.33–0.89; p = 0.015 for high SAT) in multivariable Cox regression analysis adjusted for traditional coronary risk factors (Table). Conclusion In patients with low BMI, a higher V/S ratio was associated with an increased risk of MACEs, whereas greater SAT was linked to a reduced risk. VAT alone showed no significant association with cardiovascular events. Although VAT and SAT contribute to the V/S ratio, SAT appears to have a stronger influence on cardiovascular outcomes.
