Thus, SAT may exert a protective effect against CVD progression in individuals with low BMI.Table
title: Subcutaneous adipose tissue is associated with decreased cardiovascular events in patients with a lower body mass index suspected of coronary artery disease

abstract: Abstract Background Body mass index (BMI) is widely used for cardiovascular risk stratification, yet it fails to capture underlying cardiometabolic heterogeneity. Whether metabolic–obesity phenotypes are associated with differences in coronary disease complexity and revascularization risk remains incompletely defined. Objectives To evaluate the association between metabolic–obesity phenotypes and SYNTAX I, SYNTAX II scores, and predicted revascularization-related mortality. Methods In this retrospective single-center cohort study, 270 patients undergoing coronary angiography were classified into four metabolic–obesity phenotypes based on BMI (&lt;30 or ≥30 kg/m²) and the presence of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or dyslipidemia: metabolically healthy non-obese (MHNO), metabolically unhealthy non-obese (MUNO), metabolically healthy obese (MHO), and metabolically unhealthy obese (MUO). Anatomical disease complexity (SYNTAX I), clinically integrated risk assessment (SYNTAX II for PCI and CABG), and predicted 4-year mortality were compared across phenotypes using ANOVA with Tukey-adjusted post-hoc testing. Results Anatomical disease complexity assessed by SYNTAX I did not differ significantly among phenotypes (p=0.13). In contrast, SYNTAX II scores differed significantly for both PCI (p=0.013) and CABG (p=0.043). Predicted 4-year mortality following CABG also varied significantly across metabolic phenotypes (p=0.030), whereas EuroSCORE values were comparable (p=0.44). Tukey-adjusted pairwise analyses demonstrated that MUNO patients exhibited significantly higher SYNTAX II PCI scores and higher predicted PCI- and CABG-related 4-year mortality compared with MHNO patients, while no significant differences were observed among other phenotype pairs. Conclusions Metabolic health status, rather than BMI alone, is a key determinant of clinically integrated revascularization risk. Metabolically unhealthy non-obese patients represent a high-risk phenotype that may be underrecognized by BMI-based stratification. Incorporation of simple comorbidity-defined metabolic status may enhance Heart Team risk assessment and guide revascularization decision-making.
title: Metabolic health modifies SYNTAX II–Based revascularization risk beyond body mass index

abstract: Abstract Background Obesity is a major modifiable predictor of cardiovascular disease. Addressing obesity has been shown to improve cardiovascular outcomes. Despite this, obesity remains inconsistently identified and suboptimally managed in routine cardiovascular care. Methods We conducted a retrospective audit of 500 consecutive inpatients admitted in 2025 for acute coronary syndrome (ACS), heart failure (HF) or atrial fibrillation (AF) across two tertiary Australian hospitals. Electronic medical records (EMR) were individually reviewed for documentation of overweight/obesity diagnosis, provision of lifestyle counselling, institution of pharmacological therapy, and referral for specialist weight management. The prevalence, documentation and treatment of other modifiable risk factors (i.e. hypertension, dyslipidaemia, smoking and diabetes) were also determined for comparison. Given low rates of BMI documentation in standard records, anthropometric measurements from echocardiography were used to validate the recorded prevalence of overweight/obesity. Results 391 ACS, 84 HF and 27 AF admissions were included in the study. Mean age was 66.7 ± 5.1 SD years with 40% being female sex and 9% of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ethnicity. BMI by stratum was: &lt;25kg/m2 = 32.2%; 25-29.9kg/m2 = 31.8%; ³30kg/m2 = 34.0%. Obesity was diagnosed or documented in 17%, and waist circumference wasn’t documented in any of the 500 medical records. In contrast hypertension, dyslipidaemia, smoking and diabetes were routinely identified and treated at much higher rates (figure). Obesity-specific management was uncommon: 13.3% were provided dietary advice, 2% were prescribed anti-obesity pharmacotherapy, 1.5% were referred to a dietician and no patients were referred to obesity services (Figure). Conclusion Overweight and obesity were highly prevalent, but rarely documented as a modifiable risk factor, and notably less frequently treated than other traditional risk factors. Systematic strategies are needed to increase obesity identification, improve BMI documentation and streamline obesity management in routine cardiovascular care.Table
title: Gaps in obesity diagnosis and management among australians admitted with cardiovascular disease: a multi-centre audit

abstract: Abstract Background Diabetes is an important and global health challenge and a risk factor for myocardial infarction (MI), which is associated with adverse outcomes. To support systematic improvements in cardiovascular care, many countries have established national quality registries to monitor patient characteristics, treatments and outcomes. The European Unified Registries on Heart Care Evaluation and Randomised Trials (EuroHeart) initiative provides an infrastructure for continuous prospective collection of harmonised clinical variables to support and improve the quality of cardiovascular care in Europe. Purpose To describe baseline characteristics, comorbidities and treatment patterns among patients with MI, with a focus on those with diabetes, in EuroHeart countries reporting data in 2024. Methods Continuous data on patients admitted with MI were collected in participating hospitals across 13 EuroHeart countries in 2024, using variables defined by the EuroHeart data standards. Data were submitted in aggregated form from England and Wales, Estonia, France, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Norway, Portugal, Romania, Singapore, Sweden and Switzerland. Variables included baseline characteristics, in-hospital care and discharge treatments. Individual patient-level data were aggregated at national level by age group, sex and diabetes status prior to central statistical analysis. Data are presented as proportions and means/medians to facilitate visual comparison. Results A total of 173,050 patients with MI were included in 2024 across 13 countries, of whom nearly 32% were women. Diabetes was present in 28% of patients. Those with diabetes were older (mean age 69 years) than those without diabetes (66 years) and had a substantially higher burden of comorbidities, including hypertension and chronic kidney disease (Figure 1). A high proportion of patients underwent coronary angiography (94%) and percutaneous coronary intervention (76%), irrespective of diabetes status. Similarly, only minor differences were observed in the prescription of antiplatelet agents, lipid-lowering therapy, and ACE inhibitors/ARBs between patients with and without diabetes. Among patients with diabetes, 54% (range 28–81%) received metformin, while cardioprotective glucose-lowering therapies were prescribed at discharge to 9% (2–25%) for glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) and 55% (40–76%) for sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, with variation between countries (Figure 2). Conclusions In 2024, nearly one-third of patients with MI in EuroHeart had diabetes, which was associated with older age and a higher burden of comorbidities. Despite similar use of coronary interventions and standard cardiovascular therapies between patients with and without diabetes, the prescription of GLP-1 RA and SGLT2 inhibitors varied widely across countries, highlighting opportunities to optimise diabetes management in patients with MI.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Contemporary characteristics and management of patients with myocardial infarction and diabetes in Europe: Insights from EuroHeart

abstract: Abstract Background Diabetes is defined by glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) thresholds based on the risk of microvascular complications. However, it remains unclear at which HbA1c level macrovascular risk increases among patients without known diabetes, particularly when comparing patients with and without coronary artery disease (CAD). Purpose To examine whether the HbA1c threshold associated with cardiovascular complications is lower than the conventional diagnostic cut-off for diabetes, and whether this differs according to CAD status. Methods We included patients without previously diagnosed diabetes who underwent coronary angiography in Western Denmark from 2011 to 2021. HbA1c was measured within six months prior to angiography. We examined 10-year rates of non-fatal myocardial infarction, coronary revascularization (percutaneous coronary intervention or coronary artery bypass grafting), cardiovascular death, and all-cause death according to HbA1c level. Hazard ratios were estimated using cause-specific Cox regression analysis adjusted for age, sex, hypertension, peripheral artery disease, previous ischemic stroke, smoking, and CAD. Associations between HbA1c and outcomes were modelled using restricted cubic splines with 38 mmol/mol (5.6%) as reference. Analyses were additionally stratified by CAD status. Results Among 55,570 patients, 39,957 (72%) had CAD, and 1,112 (2.0%) had undiagnosed diabetes [i.e. HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%)]. Median HbA1c was 38 mmol/mol (Q1-Q3: 35-40). Median follow-up was 5.1 years (Q1-Q3: 3.0-7.2). HbA1c showed a U-shaped association with fatal outcomes, namely cardiovascular death and all-cause mortality, while there were broadly more linear associations between HbA1c and the non-fatal outcomes of myocardial infarction and coronary revascularization (Figure 1). Cardiovascular risk increased at glycaemic levels below the diagnostic threshold for diabetes across all outcomes. Associations were strongest in patients with CAD, whereas patterns were similar but attenuated among those without CAD (Figure 2). Conclusions In keeping with prior data, HbA1c demonstrates U-shaped associations with fatal CV outcomes, in those with or without CAD, likely in part due to reverse causality. The association between HbA1c and non-fatal CV outcomes of MI and revascularisation were more linear and were apparent even below 48 mmol/mol, likely reflecting in part risk factors that cluster with rising HbA1c across and beyond the normal range. These findings indicate that macrovascular risk becomes apparent before overt diabetes is diagnosed and may support closer cardiovascular risk assessment and preventive strategies in patients with modestly elevated HbA1c.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Cardiovascular risk emerges below the diagnostic threshold for diabetes: insights from the Western Denmark Heart Registry

abstract: Abstract Abstract Stress hyperglycemia exceeds known diabetes in predicting in-hospital mortality after acute myocardial infarction: An 11-year national study of 13,099 patients Background Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a well-established risk factor for adverse outcomes after acute myocardial infarction (AMI). However, the prognostic impact of stress hyperglycemia in non-diabetic patients remains incompletely characterized, particularly in transitional healthcare systems. Aim To evaluate the clinical profile, management, temporal trends, and in-hospital outcomes of AMI patients according to known diabetes status and admission stress hyperglycemia in a nationwide 11-year cohort. Methods We analyzed 13,099 consecutive AMI patients hospitalized between 2014–2024 at Kosovo’s main tertiary cardiology center. Patients were classified as known diabetes or no known diabetes. Among non-diabetics, stress hyperglycemia was defined as admission glucose &gt;11.1 mmol/L. Clinical characteristics, invasive management, and in-hospital mortality were compared. Annual trends were assessed using logistic regression. Results Known diabetes was present in 36.3% (n=4,759) of patients. Diabetic patients were older, more frequently female, and had higher prevalence of hypertension and reduced LVEF (all p&lt;0.001). They underwent less coronary angiography (67.8% vs 71.9%) and PCI (48.4% vs 55.6%; both p&lt;0.001) and had higher in-hospital mortality (11.0% vs 6.7%; p&lt;0.001). Among non-diabetics (n=8,340), 641 (7.7%) presented with stress hyperglycemia. This group had markedly higher mortality compared with normoglycemic non-diabetics (22.2% vs 4.2%; p&lt;0.001) and even higher than known diabetics (22.2% vs 11.0%). They also had lower LVEF, worse renal function, and underwent less PCI (52.7% vs 60.6%; p&lt;0.001). The proportion of AMI patients with known diabetes increased significantly over time (OR per year 1.032; 95% CI 1.019–1.045; p&lt;0.001). Conclusions In this large real-world AMI cohort, both known diabetes and stress hyperglycemia were associated with worse in-hospital outcomes. Importantly, stress hyperglycemia identified a highest-risk phenotype with mortality exceeding that of established diabetes. These findings highlight the need for systematic glycemic assessment and aggressive metabolic management in all AMI patients, regardless of diabetes history.Figure 1
title: Stress hyperglycemia exceeds known diabetes in predicting in-hospital mortality after acute myocardial infarction: An 11-year national study of 13,099 patients

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Τhe diagnosis of coronary artery disease (CAD) remains challenging, often requiring multi-modality imaging. Dobutamine stress echocardiography (DSE) holds an established position through the assessment of segmental wall motion and contraction disorders and the use of the wall motion score index (WMSI) of the left ventricle (LV). In recent years, the echocardiographic assessment of myocardial strain with the Speckle Tracking technique is increasingly used to assess the resting systolic performance of cardiac cavities. Left ventricular global longitudinal strain (GLS) has been better studied. However, the role of this method in detecting CAD during stress has not been adequately examined. Purpose The aim of the present study was to evaluate the incremental value of GLS changes during DSE in the detection of CAD in addition to WMSI changes. Methods Fifty two (52) subjects with clinical suspicion of CAD were examined. The mean age of the participants was 63 years and 35 (67 %) of them were male. Participants underwent a DSE. Both WMSI and GLS changes of the 18 segments of LV and the 3 segments of the free wall of the right ventricle (RV) were calculated. In order to rule-in / rule-out CAD, individuals with an abnormal DSE (n=27) were subjected to an invasive coronary angiography whereas them with normal DSE (n=25) to a computed tomography coronary angiography. Angiographic stenosis of ≥50% of the left main coronary artery or/and ≥70% of the left anterior descending, the circumflex artery, the right coronary artery or/and their major branches established the diagnosis of CAD. Changes in GLS during DSE were correlated with the presence of CAD. Results CAD was diagnosed in 21 (40 %) subjects. As expected, patients with CAD had significantly higher WMSI changes between rest and peak-dose stress compared to non-CAD individuals: +0.18 (from 1.05 to 1.23) versus +0.03 (from 1.00 to 1.03) (p&lt;0.001 for the differences between the 2 groups) (see also Figure 1). Interestingly, changes in LV-GLS during stress were toward different directions in the CAD versus the non-CAD group: +0.9% (from -25.6% to -24.7%) versus -3.2% (from -24.7% to -27.9%) between rest and low-dose stress and +3.0% (from -25.6% to -22.6%) versus -4.3% (from -24.7% to -29.0%) between rest and peak-dose stress. Moreover, changes in RV-GLS during stress were also toward different directions in the CAD versus the non-CAD group: +0.9% (from -25.0% to -24.1%) versus -3.1% (from -25.0% to -28.1%) between rest and low-dose stress and +2.0% (from -25.0% to -23.0%) versus -6.2% (from -25.0% to -31.2%) between rest and peak-dose stress (p&lt;0.001 for all differences between the 2 groups for LV-GLS and RV-GLS changes between rest and low-dose and between rest and peak-dose stress) (see also Figure 2). Conclusion(s) Both LV-GLS and RV-GLS changes during DSE emerge as promising echocardiographic indices that can contribute in the diagnosis of CAD.Figure 1Diagnostic accuracy of WMSI changes.Figure 2Diagnostic accuracy of GLS changes.
title: Global longitudinal strain (GLS) changes during dobutamine stress echocardiography as an indicator of coronary artery disease

abstract: Abstract Background High-risk plaque (HRP) features on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA)—including positive remodeling, low-attenuation plaque (LAP), the napkin-ring sign (NRS), and spotty calcification—are associated with future coronary events, yet the in vivo microstructural substrate that underpins these radiologic signatures remains incompletely defined. Polarization-sensitive (PS) optical frequency domain imaging (OFDI) enables intracoronary quantification of collagen organization (birefringence) and lipid/inflammatory-related signal randomness (depolarization), offering a potential bridge between CT morphology and plaque tissue architecture. Purpose To evaluate whether PS-OFDI–derived polarimetric signatures are linked to CCTA-defined HRP features and to explore quantitative relationships between polarimetric measures and CT plaque metrics. Methods From a prospective intracoronary PS-OFDI registry, we identified 32 patients (53 lesions) who underwent CCTA prior to hospitalization and subsequently received OFDI-guided percutaneous coronary intervention. HRP was defined as the presence of ≥2 CCTA features (positive remodeling, LAP, NRS, spotty calcification). Conventional OFDI findings (qualitative and quantitative) and polarimetric properties (birefringence and depolarization) were compared between HRP and non-HRP lesions. Plaque-level birefringence and depolarization were computed across the segmented plaque volume, and associations between polarimetric measures and CCTA quantitative parameters (including LAP volume) were explored using unadjusted linear regression. Results We analyzed 53 lesions from 32 patients (median age 74 years; 81% male), with HRP present in 26 lesions (49%). Birefringence was significantly lower in HRP versus non-HRP lesions [0.45 (0.42–0.49)×10⁻³ vs 0.51 (0.48–0.55)×10⁻³; p=0.011], consistent with reduced collagen organization or altered fibrous architecture in HRP. Depolarization did not differ significantly between groups [0.13 (0.11–0.16) vs 0.12 (0.11–0.15); p=0.323; log-transformed −2.05 (−2.18 to −1.79) vs −2.14 (−2.25 to −1.90); p=0.323], although values trended higher in HRP. In unadjusted quantitative analyses, birefringence was inversely associated with LAP volume (β −0.35; 95% CI −19.848 to −2.261; p=0.015), supporting a link between increasing lipid-rich/low-attenuation burden and loss of organized fibrous structure (Figure). Conclusion Intracoronary polarimetry with PS-OFDI identifies a microstructural signature associated with CCTA-defined HRP. Lower birefringence in HRP lesions supports reduced collagen organization as a plausible substrate of CT vulnerability markers, suggesting PS-OFDI may complement CCTA by linking plaque morphology to in vivo tissue architecture and pathobiology.Figure
title: Polarimetry reveals reduced collagen signature in CCTA-defined high-risk coronary plaques

abstract: Abstract Background Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a prevalent comorbidity among patients with chronic total occlusions (CTO) and has been associated with worse outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention (CTO-PCI). The microvascular dysfunction, endothelial impairment, and pro-inflammatory state characteristic of DM contribute to accelerated atherosclerosis, impaired collateral formation, and enhanced neointimal proliferation. Despite advances in drug-eluting stent (DES) technology, the independent effect of DM on procedural safety and long-term prognosis in this population remains incompletely defined. Methods Following PRISMA standards, five databases were systematically searched up to January 2026 for studies comparing outcomes in diabetic versus non-diabetic patients undergoing CTO-PCI in the DES era. The primary endpoint was MACE. Secondary endpoints included all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, MI, and TVR, evaluated in-hospital, at 1 year, and at long-term follow-up (&gt;1 year). Pooled risk ratios (RR) with 95% CIs were calculated using random-effects models, with heterogeneity assessed by I². Results Eleven studies comprising 9,030 patients (3,470 DM; 5,760 non-DM; mean age 63.8 vs. 62.8 years) were included, with follow-up of up to 60 months. In-hospital outcomes were comparable between groups: MACE (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.76–1.54), all-cause mortality (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.42–2.52), and MI (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.67–2.00), indicating a similar procedural risk. At 1 year, diabetic patients experienced higher rates of MACE (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.10–1.55) and TVR (RR 1.46, 95% CI 1.23–1.74), while all-cause mortality (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.89–1.75) and cardiovascular mortality (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.61–1.72) did not reach statistical significance. At long-term follow-up, diabetic patients demonstrated significantly higher all-cause mortality (RR 1.54, 95% CI 1.03–2.30) and MACE (RR 1.38, 95% CI 1.05–1.81), whereas cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.38–2.29), MI (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.77–1.57), and TVR (RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.99–1.60) did not achieve statistical significance. A pooled Kaplan-Meier analysis for MACE, derived from reconstructed individual patient-level data of the included studies, showed a persistently worse event-free survival in diabetic patients throughout follow-up (HR 1.78, 95% CI 1.52–2.09; p&lt;0.001). Heterogeneity was low to moderate (I² 0–57.9%). Conclusion Among patients undergoing CTO-PCI with DES, DM did not increase immediate procedural risk but is associated with significantly worse mid- and long-term outcomes, driven primarily by higher rates of repeat revascularisation and all-cause mortality. Kaplan-Meier curves further confirmed a sustained divergence in event-free survival favoring non-diabetic patients over time. These results identify DM as an important prognostic modifier after CTO-PCI in the contemporary DES era and highlight the need for secondary prevention strategies in this high-risk population.Central Illustration
title: Impact of diabetes mellitus on clinical outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention for chronic total occlusions in the drug-eluting stent era: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Risk stratification in patients with diabetes mellitus (DM) remains challenging. Whether SCORE2-Diabetes, a primary prevention risk score, reflects coronary anatomy and clinical outcomes at first myocardial infarction (MI) is insufficiently explored. Purpose To evaluate the association between SCORE2-Diabetes, coronary disease complexity assessed by SYNTAX score, and 1-year mortality, in diabetic patients presenting with a first MI. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 301 consecutive patients with DM admitted for first MI (either STEMI or NSTEMI) in a tertiary university hospital. Patients with previously known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease were excluded. SCORE2-Diabetes was calculated post-hoc, immediately prior to MI, and categorized as &lt;10%, 10-20%, and &gt;20%. Coronary complexity was assessed using the SYNTAX score (≤22, 23-32, ≥33). One-year all-cause mortality was recorded. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify predictors of high coronary complexity and mortality. Results Higher SCORE2-Diabetes categories were associated with increasing coronary complexity. Patients with SCORE2-Diabetes &gt;20% showed a significantly higher prevalence (48.6% vs 15.1%, p&lt;0.001) of high SYNTAX scores (≥33) compared with lower-risk groups. By multivariable logistic regression, SCORE2-Diabetes ≥20% independently predicted high coronary complexity after adjustment for sex, diabetes duration, and HbA1c at admission (OR 1.14, 95% CI 1.06–1.24; p = 0.009). At 1 year, all-cause mortality was 18.7%. Mortality increased stepwise with coronary complexity; Kaplan–Meier survival analysis (Figure 1) demonstrated a markedly reduced survival probability in the high SYNTAX group score &gt; 33 compared with &lt; 33 (63.4% vs 89.4% at 1 year; log-rank p&lt;0.001). Cox proportional hazards analysis showed that SYNTAX &gt;33 was associated with a 3.4-fold increased risk of all-cause mortality (HR ≈3.4). By multivariable analysis, coronary complexity assessed by SYNTAX score remained an independent predictor of 1-year mortality, together with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction &lt;40% and incomplete revascularization (all p&lt;0.05). Conclusion In diabetic patients presenting with a first MI, SCORE2-Diabetes identifies individuals with more complex coronary anatomy. Coronary complexity, in turn, drives 1-year mortality. Risk assessment in diabetic patients is essential, since it predicts both coronary anatomy and prognosis of first MI.Figure 1
title: SCORE2-diabetes predicts coronary complexity assessed by SYNTAX score in diabetic patients with first myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) is an established marker of early kidney dysfunction and a predictor of chronic kidney disease progression. Beyond renal risk, albuminuria reflects systemic endothelial dysfunction and has been associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes. Purpose To evaluate whether pre-procedural uACR predicts 1-year major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of patients undergoing PCI at a single tertiary center between 2012 and 2023. Individuals with available uACR measurements within 1 year prior to PCI were included. Patients were stratified into three groups: uACR &lt;30 mg/g, 30–&lt;300 mg/g, and ≥300 mg/g. The primary endpoint was 1-year MACE, defined as the composite of all-cause mortality and myocardial infarction (MI). Hazard ratios (HR) were calculated using Cox proportional hazards models. Secondary endpoint was acute kidney injury (AKI) within 48 hours post-PCI as defined by either &gt;0.3mg/dL increase or &gt;50% increase in serum creatinine from baseline. Results Among 1,220 patients, 728 (59.7%) had uACR &lt;30 mg/g, 375 (30.7%) had uACR 30–&lt;300 mg/g, and 117 (9.6%) had uACR ≥300 mg/g. Higher uACR was associated with a greater burden of comorbidities, including chronic kidney disease (35.7% vs. 65.0%) and diabetes mellitus (78.6% vs. 86.3%) across increasing uACR categories (Table 1). At 1 year, there was a stepwise increase in MACE across uACR groups. Compared with the reference group (uACR &lt;30 mg/g), patients with uACR 30–&lt;300 mg/g had a non-significant increase in risk (HR 1.22, 95% CI 0.87–1.72; p=0.25), whereas those with uACR ≥300 mg/g had a significantly higher risk of MACE (HR 1.66, 95% CI 1.04–2.65; p=0.03). A significant trend was observed across categories (p-trend=0.03) (Figure 1). Severe albuminuria was associated with higher rates of peri-procedural AKI, occurring in 14.3% of patients with uACR ≥300 mg/g compared with 7.2% and 6.2% in the lower uACR groups (p=0.011 and p=0.007 for comparisons vs ≥300 mg/g). Conclusion Elevated pre-procedural uACR is associated with a stepwise increase in 1-year MACE following PCI. Severe albuminuria (≥300 mg/g) identifies a high-risk population with significantly worse ischemic outcomes. These findings suggest that uACR may provide incremental risk stratification prior to PCI.Figure 1Table 1
title: Pre-procedural urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and one-year major adverse cardiovascular events following percutaneous coronary intervention

abstract: Abstract Background Diabetes is a significant predictor of adverse cardiovascular events following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). However, comprehensive data on very long-term outcomes in the era of drug-eluting stents (DES) is still limited. Purpose To assess the impact of diabetes on clinical outcomes after PCI with DES over a 10-year period, using individual patient-level data from randomised controlled trials (RCTs). Methods We pooled individual patient data from five RCTs with a 10-year follow-up. Patients were divided into two groups according to their diabetic status at baseline. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality. The secondary endpoints were cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction (MI), definite stent thrombosis (ST), target lesion revascularisation (TLR), target vessel revascularisation (TVR) and non-target vessel revascularisation (nTVR). Results Of the 9,699 patients, 2,298 (31%) had diabetes mellitus at baseline. Over a period of up to 10 years, diabetic patients were found to be at a higher risk than nondiabetic patients regarding all-cause death (41.3% vs. 26.4%; HRadj:1.67 [95% CI, 1.59–1.77]); cardiovascular death, (23.5% vs. 12.9%; HRadj: 1.74 [1.61–1.87]); MI (HRadj: 1.29 [0.92 - 1.80]); definite ST (HRadj: 1.44 [1.11 – 2.14]); TLR (HRadj: 1.35 [1.21 – 1.51]); TVR (HRadj: 1.28 [1.14 – 1.43]) and nTVR (HRadj:1.23 [1.09 – 1.40]). Statistically significant interactions were found for most outcomes between diabetes and age (a stronger impact of diabetes in patients under 75 years old), sex (a stronger impact of diabetes in women), clinical presentation (a stronger impact of diabetes in patients with acute coronary syndromes) and type of DES (a stronger impact of diabetes in patients receiving second-generation DES). Conclusions Having diabetes independently increases the risk of adverse events after DES implantation. Interestingly, however, the impact of diabetes varies depending on patient characteristics and the type of PCI performed.Ten-Year Cumulative Incidence
title: Diabetes mellitus and 10-year outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention with drug eluting stents: insights from the DECADE cooperation

abstract: Abstract Background Rapid progression of non-culprit coronary lesions (NCLs) following acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is an important determinant of recurrent cardiovascular events, yet its clinical predictors remain incompletely defined. Stress hyperglycemia ratio (SHR), reflecting acute glycemic elevation relative to chronic glycemic status, has been associated with adverse outcomes in ACS. Its relationship with rapid NCL progression and long-term clinical events according to diabetes status remains unclear. Purpose To assess whether SHR improves risk stratification for rapid NCL progression and subsequent MACE after ACS, and whether its predictive performance differs between patients with and without diabetes. Methods In this multicenter prospective cohort study, consecutive patients with ACS undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention were enrolled. Among 682 patients with serial coronary angiography demonstrating non-culprit lesions, rapid NCL progression was assessed using prespecified criteria. SHR was calculated using fasting blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c). Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) were defined as a composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and unplanned revascularization. Multivariable logistic and Cox regression analyses were performed separately in patients with and without diabetes mellitus (DM). Results Rapid NCL progression occurred in 165 patients (24.2%). In patients with DM, higher SHR was independently associated with rapid progression when modeled as both a continuous variable (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 3.28, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.10–10.22, p=0.035) and a categorical variable (adjusted OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.01–3.57, p=0.046). No significant association was observed in patients without DM. Over a median follow-up of 2.0 years (interquartile range 1.14–2.13), 251 patients (36.8%) experienced MACE. Rapid NCL progression was strongly associated with subsequent MACE in both diabetic and non-diabetic groups. In patients with DM, the combination of rapid progression and elevated SHR was associated with increased risk of MACE (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 3.12, 95% CI 1.77–5.49, p&lt;0.001). In patients without DM, elevated SHR alone was independently associated with MACE (adjusted HR 1.72, 95% CI 1.12–2.65, p=0.014), and the highest risk was observed in those with both rapid progression and elevated SHR (adjusted HR 5.73, 95% CI 3.46–9.50, p&lt;0.001). Conclusions In this multicenter ACS cohort, rapid progression of non-culprit lesions was strongly associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes. SHR was independently related to angiographic progression among patients with diabetes and identified higher-risk individuals in both diabetic and non-diabetic populations. These findings emphasize the prognostic relevance of non-culprit lesion dynamics and support further evaluation of stress-related glycemic markers in risk stratification following ACS.
title: Associations of stress hyperglycemia ratio with rapid non-culprit lesion progression and clinical outcomes in acute coronary syndrome: a multicenter cohort study according to diabetes status

abstract: Abstract Background Myocardial extracellular volume fraction (ECV) derived from coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) is an established surrogate for myocardial interstitial characterization, including fibrosis, inflammation, and edema. While post-percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) coronary flow velocity reserve (CFVR)—measured via stress transthoracic Doppler echocardiography (S-TDE)—is a pivotal prognostic indicator of microvascular integrity in chronic coronary syndrome (CCS), the mechanistic link between pre-procedural structural remodeling (ECV) and post-procedural functional outcomes (CFVR) remains to be elucidated. Methods We prospectively evaluated CCS patients undergoing CCTA prior to PCI for de novo left anterior descending artery (LAD) lesions, followed by post-PCI S-TDE. The primary objective was to determine the association between pre-PCI ECV within the LAD territory (LAD-ECV) and post-PCI microvascular dysfunction, defined as a CFVR &lt;2.5. Results Of the 43 patients enrolled (mean age 67.6±11.3 years), 52.8% exhibited impaired post-PCI CFVR. Pre-PCI LAD-ECV demonstrated a robust inverse correlation with post-PCI CFVR (R = -0.460, P = 0.002). Multivariable linear regression identified LAD-ECV (β = -0.079, P &lt; 0.001) and estimated glomerular filtration rate (β = 0.014, P = 0.009) as independent predictors of post-PCI CFVR. Notably, LAD-ECV was the sole significant predictor for impaired CFVR in logistic regression analysis (OR: 1.33, P = 0.002). Receiver operating characteristic analysis revealed a superior diagnostic performance for LAD-ECV (AUC 0.854), with an optimal threshold of 31.8%. Patients with LAD-ECV &gt;31.8% had a strikingly higher prevalence of microvascular impairment compared to those below the threshold (80.8% vs. 6.2%, P &lt; 0.001). Conclusion Pre-procedural CCTA-derived ECV serves as a novel and potent predictor of post-PCI microvascular function. This non-invasive structural assessment offers critical insights into the functional recovery of the coronary microvasculature following revascularization in patients with CCS.
title: Predictive value of pre-procedural computed tomography-derived extracellular volume fraction for post-PCI coronary microcirculation in chronic coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Air pollution has emerged as a novel risk factor for atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease (CAD). Both acute and chronic exposure to air pollutants have been associated with adverse cardiovascular events; however, their prognostic impact in patients following ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) remains insufficiently studied. Methods Observational registry including consecutive patients admitted with STEMI between 2020 and 2023, with air pollution exposure data available on the day of the index invasive procedure (acute exposure) and over the preceding two years (chronic exposure). Patients were stratified according to chronic exposure to fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅) using the World Health Organization-recommended cutoff of 15 μg/m³ (&gt;15 μg/m³ vs ≤15 μg/m³). The primary endpoint was the occurrence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as a composite of all-cause death, recurrent acute myocardial infarction (AMI), and hospitalization for heart failure (HF), assessed over a median follow-up of 3 years. Secondary endpoints included: i) in-hospital cardiovascular death, recurrent AMI, and arrhythmias; ii) long-term cardiovascular death, recurrent AMI, and HF hospitalization. Results A total of 312 patients (median age, 64 [IQR:57-74] years, 250 [80.1%] males) were included. Baseline clinical characteristics, cardiovascular risk factors, clinical presentation, in-hospital management, and discharge medical therapy were comparable between groups. Patients with higher PM₂.₅ levels exhibited more often multivessel disease (p=0.015), higher inflammatory markers at admission (p=0.013), and consistently greater exposure to air pollutants both acutely (day of the index event: PM2.5, PM10, O3, NO2, C6H6 p&lt;0.010 for all) and chronically (PM2.5, PM10, NO2, C6H6 p&lt;0.001 for all). In-hospital outcomes did not differ significantly between groups. At 3-year follow-up, Kaplan–Meier analysis showed that patients exposed to PM₂.₅ levels&gt;15 μg/m³ had a significantly lower rate of MACE (Log rank 6.95, p=0.008) and recurrence of myocardial infarction (Log rank 9.62, p=0.002). No differences were observed for all-cause death, cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization. At multivariable Cox regression analysis, chronic PM₂.₅ exposure was independently associated with an increased risk of MACE after adjustment for confounding factors (HR 1.13, 95% CI 1.03-1.23; p=0.008). Conclusions Chronic exposure to fine particulate air pollution is independently associated with worse long-term outcomes after STEMI. These results support air pollution reduction as a public health priority to improve long-term cardiovascular outcomes in patients following STEMI.KM figures
title: Impact of air pollution exposure on short and long-term outcomes in patients with ST-elevation myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Air pollution is increasingly recognized as a modifiable cardiovascular risk factor, given the growing body of evidence supporting its role in cardiovascular disease and its substantial socio-economic and public health implications. Purpose This study aimed to evaluate the impact of air pollution on the clinical presentation of acute myocardial infarction (AMI)—STEMI versus NSTEMI—in order to explore potential pathophysiological mechanisms underlying pollution-related ischemic events. Methods We analyzed data from the AMIPE registry, including patients admitted for AMI to the STEMI Hub hospitals in the province of Bologna (Ospedale Maggiore and Ospedale Sant’Orsola Malpighi) between January 2018 and December 2023. Environmental exposure was assessed using daily mean concentrations of PM2.5, PM10, and NO₂ recorded by the monitoring station closest to each patient’s residence. Average pollutant levels were calculated over multiple time windows (daily, weekly, monthly, bimonthly, and yearly) preceding the index event and scaled per 10 µg/m³ increase. Comparisons were performed between STEMI and NSTEMI presentations. Results The study population included 3974 AMI cases (mean age 69.7 ± 13 years; 68.5% male; NSTEMI 60%; STEMI 40%). Patients presenting with NSTEMI showed significantly higher mean exposure to PM2.5 and PM10 in the two months preceding the acute event compared with STEMI patients (PM2.5: p = 0.007; PM10: p = 0.016). No significant differences were observed for monthly or annual exposure (p &gt; 0.05). In multivariable analysis adjusted for age, sex, smoking status, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), elevated bimonthly exposure to PM2.5 and PM10 emerged as an independent predictor of NSTEMI presentation (PM2.5 [10 µg/m³]: OR 1.10; 95% CI 1.02–1.22; p = 0.022; PM10 [10 µg/m³]: OR 1.008; 95% CI 1.001–1.016; p = 0.028). Conclusions Prolonged exposure to PM2.5 and PM10 is independently associated with NSTEMI rather than STEMI. The exact pathophysiology remains partly unclear, but type II mechanisms (supply–demand mismatch, endothelial dysfunction, microvascular impairment) and diffuse coronary artery disease may act as triggers. Further studies and environmental prevention strategies are warranted.OR PM2.5/PM10
title: Long term air pollution and myocardial infarction: differences between STEMI and NSTEMI

abstract: Abstract Background Micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) are ubiquitous environmental pollutants. Evidence is increasing that they accumulate in human tissues following exposure and are emerging as a risk factor for health. Nonetheless, current knowledge about the burden of MNPs in the coronary circulation across the spectrum of coronary artery disease (CAD), from the acute to the chronic setting, remains limited. Moreover, the association between MNPs, air pollution exposure, and biological pathways underlying inflammation and clinical presentation of CAD has still to be investigated. Purpose To evaluate the burden (presence, concentration and type) of MNPs in the coronary blood of patients undergoing invasive coronary angiography for suspected CAD, stratified according to the clinical presentation into: 1) patients presenting with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI); 2) patients with chronic coronary syndromes (CCS); 3) patients with angiographically normal coronary arteries (control group). We explored associations among coronary burden of MNPs, air pollution exposure and inflammatory biomarkers across the three study groups. Methods Cross-sectional study, including 61 consecutive patients undergoing coronary angiography for suspected CAD, stratified into: STEMI (n=19), CCS (n=20) and controls with normal coronary arteries (n=22). MNPs were quantified in coronary and peripheral blood using pyrolysis-gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and laser direct infrared spectroscopy. Air pollution exposure data were collected on the day of the invasive procedure (acute exposure) and over the preceding two years (chronic exposure). Results MNPs were detected significantly more frequently in STEMI patients (84.2%) than in CCS (40%) and controls (31.8%) (p=0.002), with higher concentration and greater polymer diversity [median of 3 polymers (IQR: 2–4), p&lt;0.001]. Polyethylene was the predominant polymer (97%). The same polymers were consistently identified in peripheral and coronary blood samples from individual patients, with the highest concentrations in coronary blood (p&lt;0.001). STEMI patients showed higher levels of IL-6 and TNF-α (p&lt;0.006) and were exposed to higher levels of PM2.5 (p&lt;0.012). MNP detection was more frequent among smokers and patients exposed to PM2.5&gt;15 µg/m³ (p=0.006), with all patients presenting both factors showing detectable MNPs (p&lt;0.001). In multivariable analysis, smoking history emerged as the only independent predictor of MNP presence (OR 5.69, 95%CI 1.33-26.63, p=0.023). Conclusions STEMI patients exhibited a greater burden of MNPs in coronary blood than CCS and controls. MNPs detection frequently co-occurred with elevated inflammatory biomarkers, greater PM2.5 exposure, and smoking, suggesting a potential association between environmental exposure and CAD.Figure 1
title: Micro and Nano-Plastics in coronary blood and air pollution exposure across the spectrum of coronary artery disease

abstract: Abstract Introduction ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is a life-threatening cardiovascular emergency requiring immediate reperfusion therapy and continuous availability of catheterization facilities. Despite well-established risk factors, the precise triggers determining the timing of acute events remain incompletely understood. Growing evidence suggests that short-term environmental exposures may contribute to the onset of STEMI. Purpose However, the effects of multiple environmental factors have not been sufficiently investigated at the population level. Therefore, the ALERT-ITS project analyses the association between extreme environmental conditions and the incidence of STEMI. Methods We performed a retrospective population-based time-series (2009-2023) analysis of anonymised statutory health insurance data from a German health insurance institute. Daily STEMI cases, defined by ICD-10-GM criteria, were stratified by sex and age (≥60 vs. &lt;60 years) and assigned to nationwide bio-meteorological regions, with a focus on Southeast Germany. Meteorological and air-quality data included daily mean sea-level pressure (SLP), summer days (SD), hot days (HD), tropical nights (TN), cold-wave duration (CD), and ozone (O₃). Associations were estimated using Quasi-Poisson generalized additive models with distributed lags (weather ≤10 days; pollutants ≤7 days), adjusting for seasonality, long-term trends, and weekday effects. Results During the study period, a total of 57,896 confirmed STEMI cases were identified in Southeast Germany. In men ≥60 years, SD (p = 0.044), HD (p = 0.037) and O3 (p = 0.026) were significant predictors. In women ≥60 years, SD (p = 0.001), HD (p = 0.004), CD (p &lt; 0.001), and SLP (p = 0.020) showed significant associations. No predictor reached statistical significance in men &lt;60 years, whereas in women &lt;60 years, SD (p = 0.010) and CD (p = 0.008) were significant. The strongest linear association was observed for SD in women ≥60 years (p = 0.0012), with a relative risk of 0.91 (95% CI 0.85–0.96), corresponding to a 9.3% relative reduction in STEMI incidence on summer days compared with non-summer days. Conclusion In Southeast Germany, specific environmental patterns were associated with short-term changes in STEMI incidence, particularly among older patients. Integrating these insights into planning strategies may enhance proactive resource allocation in acute cardiovascular care.
title: Environmental constellations and STEMI incidence in southeast Germany - a population-based analysis

abstract: Abstract Introduction Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) is a multifactorial cardiovascular condition. In addition to established cardiovascular risk factors, short-term environmental exposures have been proposed as potential triggers of acute coronary events. However, the combined effects of multiple environmental factors at the population level remain insufficiently characterised. Purpose This study aimed to investigate the association between environmental factors and the incidence of NSTEMI within a defined population in Southeast Germany. Methods We conducted a retrospective population-based time-series analysis using anonymised statutory health insurance data provided by a German health insurance institute. Confirmed NSTEMI cases were identified according to ICD-10-GM criteria over the study period (2009–2023) and stratified by sex and age (&lt;60 and ≥60 years). Daily case counts were temporally matched with region-wide environmental and meteorological data derived from a European reanalysis dataset and an atmospheric composition monitoring service. Associations were estimated using generalised additive models with a quasi-Poisson distribution and distributed lag structures (weather ≤10 days; pollutants ≤7 days), adjusting for seasonality, long-term trends, and weekday effects. Results A total of 226,713 NSTEMI cases were identified (63% male, 37% female). Several environmental variables were significantly associated with changes in NSTEMI incidence, including windy days, frost days, heat waves (HW), particulate matter (PM₁₀), the wind chill index (WCI), daily mean air pressure, and heat stress wave duration and intensity. WCI showed consistent positive associations across demographic subgroups (p values ranging from 0.001 to 0.004). Among men aged ≥60 years, both HW (p = 0.007) and WCI (p = 0.004) were significantly associated with increased NSTEMI incidence, whereas HW was not significant in women. In contrast, heat stress wave duration and intensity were primarily associated with NSTEMI incidence in women aged &lt;60 years. The strongest association was observed for windy days in women aged ≥60 years, with a relative risk of 1.07 (95% CI, 1.03–1.11), corresponding to a 6.8% increase in NSTEMI incidence. Conclusion Extreme environmental conditions appear to play a significant role in modulating the incidence of NSTEMI at the population level. The interaction of combined environmental factors may act as risk-enhancing triggers for acute coronary events. Incorporating environmental forecasting into regional healthcare management strategies may therefore contribute to improved preparedness and optimisation of cardiovascular care delivery.
title: Environmental determinants of NSTEMI incidence: a population-based time-series analysis in southeast Germany

abstract: Abstract Background Climate change is increasingly recognized as a major threat to global health. Beyond gradual global warming, climate change manifests through more frequent and intense heat (HW) and cold waves (CW), which can trigger health events. Purpose This study aims to assess the impact of extreme weather events on cause-specific cardiovascular (CV) mortality in the population of Poland in the context of environmental exposure. Methods A geospatial analysis was conducted for the years 2011-23 on the Polish population (Fig 1). Primary endpoints were CV mortality and secondary: case-specific mortality [heart failure (HF), acute coronary syndrome, all-cause and external]. All analyses were conducted using individual-level mortality data. We operationalised temperature extremes at the municipality-day level using the Excess Heat and Cold Factor. Daily air pollutant exposure data at municipality level was obtained using the GEM-AQ model. Individual exposure was assigned based on the place of residence. A Poisson pseudo–maximum likelihood regression with high-dimensional fixed effects was used. Models were adjusted for long-term temporal trends, day of the week, COVID-19, influenza activity, holidays,weather conditions. Results are reported as incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (95%CI). Results Total recorded deaths were 5,386,726 (51.9% male), including 2,084,773 CV deaths (45.9% male). HW exposure was consistently associated with increased mortality across all examined outcomes, with the strongest effects observed at lag 0-2 and a gradual attenuation over the following days. For CV mortality, the risk increased by 9% on the day of exposure (lag 0:1.09; 95%CI: 1.08-1.10) and peaked on lag 1 (1.10; 95%CI:1.09-1.11). Conversely, CW were associated with elevated CV mortality, with effects persisting across multiple lag days and showing a more prolonged temporal pattern (p&lt;0.001) – Fig. 2. The observed associations remained robust in models that accounted for both temperature extremes and air pollution exposure. HW-related mortality was more pronounced among women and older individuals, particularly for CV and HF deaths, whereas CW exerted stronger effects in men (p&lt;0.001). For external-cause mortality, significant associations (more pronounced among men aged &lt;65 years old) were observed only during HW. HW affected mortality more in urban than rural areas, while no significant effect modification was observed based on socioeconomic status. The attributable burden was substantially greater for HW (513,997 years of life lost) than for CW (169,128), which translates into 28,501 and 11,297 deaths, respectively. Conclusions Both heat and cold waves significantly increased CV mortality, with heat effects being more acute and cold effects more prolonged. These findings identify vulnerable subgroups and support the integration of climate-sensitive risk stratification into public health and CV prevention policies.Fig 1.Flow chart of the study design
title: Mortality patterns in the context of climate change: a 14-year nationwide analysis of extreme weather events

abstract: Abstract Background Coronary microvascular dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a contributor to angina in patients without obstructive coronary artery disease (ANOCA). Coronary flow reserve (CFR) and index of microvascular resistance (IMR) are key invasive measures of microvascular function. Effects of environmental factors, including air pollution, noise, temperature, and green space, on chronic and acute coronary syndrome have been recently recognized, but their impact on coronary microvasculature in ANOCA patients remains unclear. Purpose We aimed to investigate associations between high-resolution, residential environmental exposures and coronary microvascular function, as measured by CFR and IMR, in a ANOCA cohort in Belgium, part of the ENACT project. We also explored potential sex-specific differences in these associations. Methods We analyzed 380 patients (mean 64.8 ± 10.8 years, 182 males) undergoing an ANOCA protocol across two centers between October 2019 and November 2024. Environmental exposures at participants’ residential addresses were modeled using high-resolution interpolation, including particulate matter (PM₂.₅, PM₁₀), nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), ozone (O₃), temperature, raodway and aircraft noise, distance to major roads and airports, and neighborhood greenness (NDVI). Linear regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, active smoking, diabetes, hypertension, BMI, personal and family cardiovascular history, chronic kidney disease, obstructive sleep apnea, study centre, and area-level deprivation (BIMD). Analyses were performed in the total population and stratified by sex. Results For CFR, 30-day mean PM₂.₅ was inversely associated with CFR in males (β = −0.342; 95% CI: −0.667 to −0.017; p = 0.039) but not in females. Ozone exposure showed consistent positive associations, particularly the 30-day mean (total population: β = 0.355; 95% CI: 0.041–0.669; p = 0.027; males: β = 0.568; 95% CI: 0.112–1.025; p = 0.015). Mean temperature on the day before the ANOCA protocol was positively associated with CFR in the total population (β = 0.389; 95% CI: 0.103–0.676; p = 0.008) and in males (β = 0.683; 95% CI: 0.267–1.099; p = 0.001). Noise, road proximity, airport distance, and NDVI were not significantly associated. For IMR, associations were generally weaker. Short-term PM₂.₅ exposure was positively associated with IMR in females (β = 2.310; 95% CI: 0.171–4.448; p = 0.034), whereas most other exposures showed no consistent associations. Conclusion In this Belgian multicenter ANOCA cohort, coronary microvascular function showed sex-specific sensitivity to environmental exposures. PM₂.₅ was linked to lower CFR in males and higher IMR in females, while ozone and temperature were positively associated with CFR, especially in males. These findings underscore the relevance of sex differences and high-resolution environmental modeling in understanding microvascular health.Table 1:environmental associations with CFRTable 2:environmental associations with IMR
title: Environmental determinants of coronary flow reserve and microvascular resistance in ANOCA patients

abstract: Abstract Background Short-term exposure to ambient air pollution is associated with acute cardiovascular events, but effects may differ by pollutant type, clinical presentation, and exposure–lag structure. Purpose To evaluate pollutant-specific and lag-dependent associations between air pollution and acute cardiovascular and cerebrovascular admissions. Methods We analysed 50,537 consecutive admissions to a UK cardiac–stroke receiving unit (2015–2025). Daily counts of diagnoses (including ST-elevation myocardial infarction [STEMI], non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, unstable angina, ischaemic stroke, atrial fibrillation [AF], acute heart failure, and total admissions) were linked to daily ambient pollutants (PM₂.₅, PM₁₀, nitrogen dioxide [NO₂], nitric oxide [NO], and ozone) and meteorology. Associations were assessed using single-pollutant quasi-Poisson time-series models adjusted for seasonality, long-term trends, and day-of-week effects. Effect estimates are presented per 10 µg/m³ increase. Distributed lag non-linear models (DLNM) for NO₂ and PM₂.₅ were fitted over 0–7 days. Results Associations differed by pollutant class and clinical phenotype. Traffic-related gaseous pollutants demonstrated consistent harmful effects on acute thrombotic events: NO₂ was associated with increased STEMI admissions (RR 1.09, 95% CI 1.01–1.18), and NO with both STEMI (RR 1.16, 1.02–1.32) and unstable angina (RR 1.15, 1.01–1.31). Similar directional increases were observed for ischaemic stroke, supporting a shared thrombo-inflammatory mechanism across arterial vascular beds. In contrast, associations for non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction and atrial fibrillation were smaller and less consistent, suggesting differential susceptibility of plaque rupture versus demand-mediated or arrhythmic presentations. Particulate pollutants showed divergent patterns. PM₂.₅ was associated with reduced admissions for acute heart failure (RR 0.90, 0.82–0.99) and total admissions (RR 0.92, 0.88–0.97), while ozone showed no significant associations. DLNM clarified these heterogeneous findings. Increased risk for thrombotic events (STEMI, unstable angina, and ischaemic stroke) was concentrated at short lags (0–2 days), consistent with acute triggering. In contrast, inverse associations for acute heart failure were delayed (lags 2–4 days), consistent with short-term displacement or behavioural avoidance rather than a protective effect. NSTEMI and AF showed attenuated or less temporally structured lag responses. Conclusion Ambient air pollution shows heterogeneous, diagnosis-specific effects with distinct lag structures. Traffic-related pollutants are associated with immediate increases in thrombotic events, while delayed inverse associations for heart failure likely reflect displacement or behavioural effects. Incorporating lag structure is essential to avoid misinterpretation of same-day associations.Figure 1
title: Differential associations of ambient air pollutants with acute cardiovascular and cerebrovascular admissions: a 10-year time-series analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Noise from road traffic increases risk of ischemic heart disease whereas evidence of a similar effect of aircraft noise remains limited. ENACT study (EU 2025 Horizon project 101157151) is a 10 year nationwide population based study aiming to assess the effects of different environmental stressors on acute coronary syndrome (ACS), in Belgian population. Purpose To evaluate the association between residential aircraft noise exposure and the incidence of STEMI/NSTEMI between 2012 and 2021, accounting for demographic, socioeconomic, and atmospheric co-pollutants. Methods We conducted a retrospective population-based study including all Belgian citizens admitted to a hospital with STEMI or NSTEMI as primary diagnosis ICD code. Aircraft noise exposure was modelled at the living place using a 4x4 km^2 spatial grid (n=2,098 units) covering the Belgian territory. Air pollution levels were assessed using the previously described RIO geostatistical interpolation model. Concurrently, residential aircraft noise exposure from Belgium’s six major airports was mapped via Geographic Information Systems using official noise contours and spatially aligned with the RIO grid. Grid cells were categorized by noise exposure according into core (Lden &gt; 55 dB; n=50), intermediate (1st RIO cell aside core, n=116) and broad (2nd RIO cell aside core, n=227), and zones, with non-exposed cells (n=1,705) serving as the reference. Negative binomial regression models were fitted to estimate Incidence Rate Ratios (IRR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI), adjusting for RIO cell population density, age, gender, socioeconomic deprivation (Belgian Index of Multiple Deprivation (BIMD)), urbanisation level, PM2.5 and NO2 concentrations (Air Quality). Results We identified 99,611 STEMI and NSTEMI admissions (mean age 69.1±13.8 years, 70% male). In fully adjusted models, residential aircraft noise exposure was consistently associated with a higher incidence of STEMI/NSTEMI across all zones: Broad Area (IRR 1.12, 95% CI 1.05–1.18, p &lt; 0.001), Intermediate Area (IRR 1.15, 95% CI 1.07–1.23, p &lt; 0.001), and Core Area (IRR 1.15, 95% CI 1.04–1.28, p = 0.007). Among environmental co-exposures, PM2.5 concentration was also correlated with increased incidence (IRR 1.02, 95% CI 1.01–1.03, p = 0.003), whereas NO2 levels showed no significant independent association (p = 0.229). Interaction analyses indicated that the association between noise exposure and ACS incidence remained stable across different levels of socioeconomic deprivation and urbanisation Conclusion This national population based study demonstrates for the first time that long term residential aircraft noise exposure is significantly associated with increased STEMI/NSTEMI incidence, independent of air quality and socioeconomic status. Furthermore, this study identifies a dose response gradient across exposure zones, and some associations below WHO standards.
title: Long term residential aircraft noise exposure increases the risk of acute coronary syndromes: results from environmental effect on health care and wellbeing and active interventions (ENACT) study

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction High-risk plaque (HRP) detected by coronary CT angiography (CCTA) may predict future adverse events. Studies showed that plaque rupture is mainly related to fibrous cap (FC) thickness, while clinical events are associated with plaque burden (PB). Purpose To evaluate the association of HRP features with FC thickness and PB using multimodality imaging. Methods Patients undergoing pre-intervention CCTA, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) were included. HRP was defined as a plaque with at least 2 of the following 4 features: positive remodeling (PR), low-attenuation plaque (LAP), napkin-ring sign (NRS), and spotty calcification (SC). FC thickness was assessed by OCT and PB by IVUS. High PB and thin FC were defined using the median values. Results A total of 549 plaques from 305 patients were analyzed (46.6% ACS, 18.7% women). CCTA-defined HRP was associated with both thin FC (OR 2.03, 95% CI 1.30–3.18; P=0.021) and high PB (OR 3.59, 95% CI 2.35–5.49; P&lt;0.001). NRS, LAP, and SC were associated with thin FC (all P&lt;0.05), while NRS, LAP, and PR were associated with high PB (all P&lt;0.05) (Figure, Panel A). When all three HRP features associated with thin FC were present, the predicted probability of thin FC increased to 72% (Figure, Panel B). When all three HRP features associated with PB were present, the predicted probability of high PB increased to 77% (Figure, Panel C). Conclusions NRS, LAP, and SC were associated with thin FC, whereas NRS, LAP, and PR were related to high PB. An increasing number of HRP features was associated with a progressively higher probability of thin FC and high PB. Distinguishing HRP features of thin FC or greater PB may improve prediction of plaque disruption and risk for developing acute coronary syndromes.HRP Features, Thin FC, and High PB
title: Comparison of high-risk plaques on CCTA with fibrous cap thickness measured by OCT and plaque burden assessed by IVUS: a multimodality imaging study

abstract: Abstract Background Risk stratification in non-obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD) remains challenging due to heterogeneity across clinical and imaging data. Multimodal machine learning approaches offer the potential to improve prognostic accuracy. Objective To develop and validate a transformer-based multimodal model that integrates electronic health records (EHR), blood tests, electrocardiography (ECG), and computed tomography coronary angiography (CTCA) features to predict major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with non-obstructive CAD. Methods This retrospective cohort study was conducted at the participating hospital from January 2014 to October 2024. The study included consecutive patients undergoing CTCA, with those requiring revascularization excluded. Across 7940 eligible CTCA assessments, 729 were excluded for prior events, and 452 for revascularization, resulting in 6,759 eligible for analysis. Integrated data modalities included diagnostic codes from EHRs, laboratory tests, digitized ECG signals processed via the DigitHeart pipeline, and CTCA-derived metrics such as plaque volume, tissue composition, stenosis severity, fractional flow reserve, and fat attenuation index. These data were integrated using a transformer architecture featuring multi-level embedding and temporal encoding to fuse the diverse multimodal information. The primary endpoint was a composite of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as cardiovascular death, acute coronary syndrome, heart failure hospitalization, or ventricular arrhythmia. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and risk stratification was assessed with Cox proportional hazards models. Results Single-modal models yielded AUCs of 0.640 for diagnostic codes, 0.690 for blood tests, 0.610 for ECG, and 0.680 for CTCA. Combining CTCA with EHR or blood tests modestly improved performance, yielding AUCs of 0.710 and 0.700, respectively. The full multimodal transformer model achieved a superior AUC of 0.760. Patients classified as high risk by the model demonstrated a significantly increased risk of MACE, with a hazard ratio of 1.40 (95% CI 1.00-1.96; p = 0.049). Conclusions A transformer-based multimodal integration approach significantly improves MACE prediction in non-obstructive CAD compared with single-modality assessments, supporting more precise, personalized risk stratification. Prospective validation in external cohorts is warranted before clinical implementation.Multimodal Transformer fusion modelMultimodal ROC Curve and KM Curve for MACE
title: Transformer-based multimodal data integration for enhanced prediction of major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with non-obstructive coronary artery disease

abstract: Abstract Background Severe coronary calcification remains a major challenge in percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), frequently requiring atherectomy-based debulking devices that increase procedural complexity and periprocedural risk. However, the decision to use atherectomy devices is typically made intra-procedurally, and objective preprocedural tools to predict device necessity are lacking. Purpose We aimed to develop and externally validate a deep learning (DL) model using preprocedural cardiac computed tomography angiography (CCTA) to predict the use of atherectomy devices at the lesion level during PCI and to evaluate the incremental value of clinical variables. Methods The dataset included CCTA images of 498 moderate-to-severely calcified coronary lesions from 415 patients who underwent PCI with preprocedural CCTA in 14 cardiovascular hospitals. The dataset was annotated with clinical data including PCI reports. Data from 12 hospitals (401 lesions) were used for model training and internal validation with stratified four-fold cross-validation, and data from 2 independent hospitals (97 lesions) were used as an external validation cohort. We developed a novel transformer-based DL model incorporating a convolutional neural network (CNN) as a feature extractor in a multi-instance learning (MIL) framework and optimized hyperparameters to maximize the AUC. We integrated clinical variables into a multimodal extension of the DL model. We evaluated the performance of the DL model and compared it with that of human readers, based on majority voting of three general cardiologists and three PCI experts, using the McNemar test in the external validation cohort. Results We found that the CCTA-based model achieved an AUC of 0.79 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.70–0.88) for predicting atherectomy device use at the lesion level in the external validation. The addition of clinical variables resulted in an AUC of 0.80 (95% CI, 0.71–0.89), suggesting the importance of anatomical characteristics to determine the need for atherectomy devices (Figure 1). In a non-clinical competition with blinded human readers, the DL model demonstrated superior accuracy compared with general cardiologists (p=0.005) and comparable accuracy to experts (p=0.093) (Figure 2). Conclusion We demonstrate that a novel DL model enables lesion-level prediction of atherectomy device use in PCI from preprocedural CCTA. This image-based approach may support objective preprocedural risk stratification, facilitate procedural planning, and improve informed decision-making in patients with calcified coronary lesions.Figure 1
title: A deep learning model to predict atherectomy device use during PCI from preprocedural CCTA

abstract: Abstract Background Sex differences in coronary artery disease extend beyond luminal stenosis and include differences in plaque burden and composition. However, women often experience comparable cardiovascular outcomes despite lower quantified plaque. Purpose To evaluate sex differences in quantitative plaque phenotype, coronary anatomy, FFR-CT, and cardiovascular outcomes. Methods 3,771 consecutive patients (1813 women, y men) undergoing clinically indicated coronary CT angiography with quantitative plaque analysis and fractional flow reserve–derived from CT (FFR-CT) had evaluation for total plaque volume (TPV), calcified plaque volume (CPV), non-calcified plaque volume (NCPV), low-attenuation plaque volume (LAPV), and total plaque atheroma volume (TPAV). Total coronary volume was measured as a marker of lumen size. Baseline demographics and clinical cardiovascular (CV) risk factors were recorded and compared between sexes. The primary endpoint was a composite of CV death or myocardial infarction (MI). The secondary endpoint was CV death, MI, or ischemic stroke. Results Women were older (57.8 ± 8.8 vs 55.7 ± 9.5 years, p &lt; 0.0001) and had higher prevalence of diabetes (25.4% vs 19.2%, p &lt; 0.0001) and hypertension (50.1% vs 44.3%, p = 0.0004). Although women had a higher risk[RR1] burden, they exhibited substantially lower plaque burden across subtypes: median TPV 43 mm³ (IQR 8–127) vs 111.5 mm³ (28–340), CPV 2 mm³ (0–15) vs 8 mm³ (0–56), and NCPV 41 mm³ (7–105) vs 99 mm³ (27–277). Total plaque atheroma volume was also lower in women (2.2% [0.4–6.6] vs 4.2% [1.1–13]).Women demonstrated less ischemia by lowest FFR-CT ≤0.80 (31.0% vs 45.9%). Despite lower plaque burden and less frequent ischemia, women experienced similar rates of CV death or MI compared with men (3.4% vs 4.0%, p = 0.32). Similarly, rates of the secondary endpoint (CV death, MI, or ischemic stroke) were comparable between women and men (7.8% vs 8.2%, p = 0.66). Notably, women demonstrated significantly smaller total vessel and lumen volumes (both p &lt; 0.0001), which, in combination with physiologic coronary tapering, may limit effective myocardial perfusion. In multivariable analysis, non-calcified plaque atheroma volume independently predicted CV death or MI (HR 1.053, 95% CI 1.036–1.069, p &lt; 0.0001), whereas sex was not independently associated with outcomes. Conclusions Women exhibit substantially lower plaque burden and less frequent ischemia by FFR-CT compared with men, yet experience comparable CV event rates. Smaller coronary vessel and lumen volumes may represent an alternative anatomical pathway contributing to risk beyond plaque burden alone, suggesting that plaque burden alone does not fully explain sex-specific CV risk.Figure
title: Sex differences beyond stenosis in quantitative plaque phenotype, coronary anatomy, FFR-CT, and cardiovascular outcomes: the BEYOND-PLAQUE study

abstract: Abstract Background Coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD), quantified by reduced myocardial flow reserve (MFR), is a robust predictor of adverse cardiovascular outcomes. Reduced MFR may result from impaired hyperaemic myocardial blood flow (classical CMD) or elevated resting flow (here defined as endogenous CMD), reflecting potentially distinct microvascular phenotypes. Whether these mechanisms carry similar prognostic significance remains unclear. Purpose To investigate the prognostic impact of flow-based CMD phenotypes in patients with suspected coronary artery disease referred for clinical 82Rb-PET and to evaluate the prognostic relevance of resting and hyperaemic myocardial blood flow in patients with preserved MFR. Methods A multicentre cohort from three Danish centres included patients referred for a clinically indicated 82Rb-PET myocardial perfusion imaging between January 2018 and August 2020 (N=7323), with complete follow-up through nationwide registries. Patients with reversible perfusion defects &gt; 4% were excluded. CMD was defined as MFR &lt; 2.0 and subclassified by resting myocardial blood flow (MBF) into ‘classical CMD’ (≤ 1.2 mL/min/g) and elevated resting-flow CMD’ (&gt;1.2 mL/min/g). Patients with preserved MFR (≥ 2) were characterized as true normal or grey-zone based on resting and hyperaemic MBF. The primary outcome was a composite of myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, heart failure, unstable angina, cardiovascular death with follow-up until 14 May 2024. Competing risk and Cox regression models adjusted for age and sex were applied. Results A total of 3,223 patients were included. Patients with classical CMD were older, more often male and had a higher burden of risk factors (table). Using true normal patients as reference, classical CMD showed the strongest association with the composite endpoint (subdistribution hazard ratio (SHR) 3.14, 95% CI: 2.50–3.95), with particularly high risks of heart failure (SHR 4.95, 95% CI: 3.42-7.15), cardiovascular death (SHR 6.18, 95% CI: 2.77-13.75), and all-cause death (HR 2.96, 95% CI: 2.15-4.09) (figure 1). CMD driven by elevated resting myocardial blood flow was also independently associated with the composite endpoint, though with lower effect sizes mainly driven by all-cause death (HR 3.04, 95% CI: 2.23-4.16) and cardiovascular death (SHR 3.35, 95% CI: 1.43-7.81). Among patients with preserved MFR, grey-zone abnormalities were associated with modestly increased risk, primarily for heart failure (SHR 1.74, 95% CI: 1.20-2.54) and all-cause death (HR 1.59, 95% CI: 1.16-2.18. Conclusions CMD driven by impaired hyperaemic flow carries substantially higher cardiovascular risk than CMD driven by elevated resting flow. Even in patients with preserved MFR, abnormalities in resting or hyperaemic MBF identify subgroups at increased risk.Table1_baselineFigure_cummulative
title: Flow-based phenotypes of coronary microvascular dysfunction and cardiovascular risk

abstract: Abstract Background Despite equivalent reperfusion, women experience higher rates of heart failure and mortality after STEMI. Conventional imaging alone cannot explain this disparity. Whether multimodality imaging reveals sex-specific differences in LV remodelling, diastolic function, and tissue characteristics — independent of age — remains unknown. Purpose To evaluate age-adjusted sex differences in LV morphology, diastolic function, and myocardial tissue characteristics using multimodality imaging within a prospective STEMI registry. Methods We analysed 251 consecutive STEMI patients treated with primary percutaneous coronary intervention (196 men [78%], 55 women [22%]), who underwent echocardiography (end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes, global longitudinal strain (GLS), myocardial work indices, and systolic and diastolic parameters) and CMR (indexed LV volumes, myocardial mass, late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), native T1 mapping, extracellular volume fraction (ECV), microvascular obstruction (MVO), and intramyocardial haemorrhage (IMH)). Sex differences were assessed by ANCOVA with age as a continuous covariate; sex-by-age interaction terms were tested to evaluate effect modification. Results Women were significantly older than men (p&lt;0.001). After age adjustment, men demonstrated significantly larger LV volumes (EDV: p&lt;0.001; ESV: p&lt;0.001), left atrial volume (LAV: p=0.003), CMR-derived indexed LV volumes (EDVI: p&lt;0.001; ESVI: p=0.010), and LV myocardial mass (p&lt;0.001). Despite comparable LGE-defined infarct size (p&gt;0.05), women exhibited higher LV filling pressures (E/e′: p=0.015) and elevated remote zone native T1 (p=0.049). Although MVO was more frequent in men on unadjusted analysis (p=0.016), this difference was no longer significant after age adjustment (p=0.116); age was the primary determinant of MVO (p=0.008; sex×age interaction p=0.825). Remote zone native T1 correlated positively with E/e′ average (r=0.297, p=0.036). Conclusions Male sex is associated with larger LV volumes and mass after age adjustment, while excess MVO in men is primarily age-driven rather than sex-specific. Women exhibit elevated remote zone native T1, reflecting diffuse interstitial fibrosis, and higher LV filling pressures independent of age. The positive correlation between remote zone native T1 and E/e′ provides mechanistic evidence of fibrosis-mediated diastolic dysfunction in women after STEMI. These findings support sex-specific myocardial tissue characterisation and early cardioprotective therapy in women after STEMI.
title: The silent scar: remote myocardial fibrosis underlies diastolic dysfunction in women after STEMI-multimodality imaging phenotyping

abstract: Abstract Background The angiographic extent of coronary artery disease (CAD) strongly influences prognosis in patients with acute myocardial infarction (MI). While age, sex, and traditional cardiovascular risk factors are known determinants of atherosclerosis, the independent relationship between habitual physical activity and anatomical CAD burden at the time of MI remains insufficiently defined. Objectives To evaluate age- and sex-related differences in CAD extent and to determine whether preadmission physical activity independently predicts multi-vessel disease beyond traditional cardiometabolic risk factors. Methods We prospectively included 306 consecutive patients with STEMI or NSTEMI who underwent coronary angiography. CAD was classified as single-vessel or multi-vessel disease (≥2 significantly stenosed vessels). Habitual physical activity during the four weeks preceding admission was assessed using a self-reported 10-point effort scale. Hierarchical multivariable logistic regression models were constructed: (1) age and sex; (2) addition of physical activity; (3) addition of traditional risk factors (smoking, hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, BMI); and (4) fully adjusted model. Model discrimination was assessed using area under the ROC curve (AUC). Results Multi-vessel CAD was present in 60.5% of patients. Age was independently associated with multi-vessel disease across all models. Sex was not independently associated after adjustment. In the fully adjusted model, lower physical activity remained a strong independent predictor of multi-vessel CAD (OR 0.567 per 1-point increase; 95% CI 0.494–0.651; p&lt;0.001). Diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia were also independently associated with disease extent.
