Among the admission diagnoses, 21% were NSTEMI and 79% were unstable angina. The median high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T value was 5 nanograms per litre (interquartile range, 3 to 12) for the first troponin sample, and 9 nanograms per litre (interquartile range, 6 to 29) for the second one. In 6% of patients, a CCTA was not obtained due to a high coronary artery calcium score (&gt;400 AU). It was observed that 39% did not have any coronary lesions or plaques. 38% had non-obstructive coronary artery disease (plaques &lt;50%). The rest had significant lesions in at least one vessel (16%) or were nondiagnostic (7%). 23% of the patients included underwent invasive coronary angiography and 11% required revascularisation. Compared to men, women underwent significantly fewer invasive coronary angiographies (23.4% (102/436) vs 45.5% (257/565); RR=0.51; p&lt;0.001) and required fewer revascularizations (11.0% (48/436) vs 32.6%(184/565); RR=0.34; p&lt;0.001). Pearson’s chi-square test confirmed these differences were statistically significant (χ2=51.3 and 63.0 respectively, both p&lt;0.001). Conclusion In this cohort, 77% of women with an NSTE-ACS had no significant obstructive lesions on CCTA. With a CCTA-guided strategy for low- to intermediate-risk NSTE-ACS, women demonstrated a markedly lower need for invasive coronary angiography and revascularization compared with men. This strategy could allow for a more tailored, precision-based and non-invasive approach that improves diagnostic yield while minimizing procedural risks and vascular injury.ICA and revascularization in women and menTable 1
title: CCTA-guided management of NSTE-ACS in women: a tailored diagnostic strategy

abstract: Abstract Background Reduced muscle mass is associated with abnormal cardiorespiratory fitness, decreased quality of life, and worse prognosis in the general population. There are no data on the potential differences in the association between muscle mass and heart failure after myocardial infarction (MI). Fat-free mass (FFM) is considered a surrogate for lean mass, which is regarded as the best surrogate for skeletal muscle mass. Purpose We investigated the association between FFM and congestive heart failure (CHF) as well as all-cause one-year mortality in men and women with MI who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Methods A retrospective study was conducted at a tertiary referral hospital with a 24/7 PCI service. We included 6493 MI patients who underwent PCI. FFM tertiles were created and further divided by sex, resulting in three female and three male groups. These groups were compared by sex and by FFM for CHF and one-year all-cause mortality. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics. Results The lowest incidence of CHF was observed in the high FFM group (third FFM tertile) in both sexes, followed by the second FFM tertile (medium FFM) and the first FFM tertile (low FFM) (7.5%, 10.9%, and 15.1% in men, and 7.9%, 14.5%, and 22.0% in women, respectively; p&lt;0.0001 for both sexes and between sexes) (Figure 1). An inverse relationship between FFM and CHF was found in both sexes. The Spearman correlation coefficient showed a negative correlation between FFM and CHF in both sexes, which was stronger in women (r = -0.91; p&lt;0.0001) than in men (r = -0.71; p&lt;0.0001). A similar inverse relationship was observed between FFM tertiles and one-year mortality. The lowest one-year all-cause mortality occurred in the third FFM tertile (high FFM), followed by the second tertile (medium FFM) and the first tertile (low FFM), with rates of 5.8%, 12.2%, and 22.6% in men, and 6.9%, 16.9%, and 25.5% in women, respectively (p&lt;0.0001 for both sexes and between sexes) (Figure 2). Conclusion In patients with MI treated with PCI, muscle mass was important for both sexes in relation to CHF and one-year mortality. Based on the correlation, low FFM is expected to be more harmful in women than in men. According to our results, women with low muscle mass are particularly at risk for CHF and mortality and should receive special attention after MI.Congestive heart failure in the hospitalOne-year mortality
title: Differential impact of muscle mass in women and men on heart failure and mortality after myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Aims To assess sex-specific temporal changes in prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors (CVRF) in patients admitted for cardiovascular diseases (CVD) in Spain, a high-income country with universal health care, from 2007 to 2022. Methods A retrospective, population-based analysis using the Spanish Minimum Basic Data Set, including all adults (≥18 years) hospitalised with a principal diagnosis of CVD was performed. Analyses focused on acute myocardial infarction (STEMI, NSTEMI), stroke, heart failure (HF), and aortic stenosis (AS). Temporal trends in the prevalence of the CVRF throughout the study period, for CVD in general and for each specific CVD (, both in the overall sample and in men and women, were studied using the join-point jump regression method. Results There were 6,734,967 hospital admissions for CVD, 3,776,811 (56.1%) in men and 2,958,156 (43.9%) in women. Women were older (79; IQR: 70-86 vs. 72; IQR 61-81 years; p&lt;0,001). Hypertension was present in the 43.8%, dyslipidaemia in the 36.9% and diabetes mellitus in the 32% of episodes, without differences clinically relevant between women and men. However, smoking habit (19.8%) and alcohol consumption (4%) were significantly and clinically (standardised difference in means-SDM) relevant more frequent in men (29.5% vs 7.5% and 6.6% vs 0.6%, respectively), and obesity (11.5%) in women (13.7% vs 9.8%) (figure 1). Over time, prevalence of most CVRF increased in both sexes, except for hypertension, which declined in both (figure 2). Notably, particularly concerning increases in obesity, dyslipidaemia and smoking were observed among women (figure 2).The prevalence of CVRFs increased between 2007-2022 for the whole population, except for hypertension which significantly decreased (average annual percent change: -1,9; CI: 2.7; -1.1), and smoking without a statistically significant trend (AAPC: 0,7; CI: -0.2; 1.7). Women showed statistically higher increases than men for alcohol consumption (8,5; CI: 6.5 ; 10.5 vs 4,3; CI: 3.6 ; 5.1); smoking (5,3; CI: 4.8 ; 5.8 vs 0,2; CI: -0.8 ; 1.3) and a more pronounced decline for hypertension (-2,9; CI: -3.9 ; -2.0 vs -1,1; CI: -1.8 ; -0.5). Meanwhile men showed higher increases for obesity (5,7; CI: 5.2; 6.2 vs 3,3; CI: 2.9; 3.8) and diabetes mellitus (1,8; CI: 1.5; 2.2 vs 0,3; CI: 0.0; 0.6). Conclusions Our results underscore persistent current and over the time sex-specific differences in the prevalence of CVRF in Spain from 2007 to 2022. Men consistently exhibited higher rates of smoking and alcohol consumption, while prevalence of obesity/overweight and hypertension was higher in women. Despite women having lower rates of smoking and alcohol consumption than men, adverse trends in obesity, dyslipidaemia, and smoking among women are narrowing historical sex differences. These findings highlight the need for sex-sensitive prevention strategies to reduce cardiovascular burden in ageing populations.CVRF in men and womenCVRF temporal trends
title: Worsening trends in modifiable cardiovascular risk factors among patients hospitalised for cardiovascular disease in Spain (2007–2022): a nationwide sex-specific analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Cardiovascular disease remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in women, yet important sex-related disparities persist in acute coronary syndromes(ACS). Women are frequently underdiagnosed and undertreated, experience higher short-term mortality and present with sex-specific or under-recognised risk factors complicating diagnosis and management. The Gender, Diversity and Inclusion GEDI-ACS registry is the first Italian prospective, multicentre study designed to identify the phenotypic and genetic profiles of women with ACS. Purpose To report preliminary findings from the first 93 women enrolled in the GEDI-ACS registry. Methods Women≥18 years admitted with ACS across Northern and Southern Italy were consecutively enrolled. Comprehensive clinical, imaging, biochemical and molecular phenotyping was performed, including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics. Socioeconomic status, health literacy, quality of life and risk awareness were assessed through standardised questionnaires. All patients were treated according to current ESC guidelines1. Results Mean age was 66.1±12.1years, 97.8% were Caucasian and 94.6% Italian-born. Traditional cardiovascular risk factors were prevalent. From a female-specific perspective, most women(87.1%) were postmenopausal, with 13.9% reporting premature menopause; 30.1% had a history of miscarriage. In 81.7% ACS was the first manifestation of heart disease. Non-cardiac comorbidities were frequent, particularly vascular disorders(12.9%) and cancer(15.1%). Clinically, STEMI and NSTEMI predominated and MINOCA occurred in 38.7%, mainly Takotsubo syndrome and coronary spasm. Mean LVEF was 49.1±11.4. Psychosocial vulnerability was prominent: most women had low education (mean10.4±4.3years) and income, only 37.6% were employed and 41.9% had anxiety/depression. Health literacy was limited, with 69.8% reporting difficulty understanding health information and 70.9% requiring support during medical encounters. At 30 days no deaths, stroke or reinfarction were observed; 8.6% experienced recurrent symptom and therapy adherence was good. Conclusions The GEDI-ACS registry highlights the multidimensional profile of women with ACS, integrating clinical, biological and psychosocial domains. For many, ACS was the first cardiovascular event and frequently coexisted with non-cardiac comorbidities. Female-specific factors and adverse obstetric history support the need for tailored preventive strategies, while psychosocial and socioeconomic barriers, such as low income, anxiety and limited health literacy, may adversely affect recovery and adherence. The high prevalence of MINOCA underscores the importance of precise endotype characterisation through advanced cardiovascular imaging. Despite this complexity, short-term outcomes were favourable. Ongoing enrolment and multiomics integration will deepen the understanding of women’s cardiovascular risk and inform targeted management.GEDI ACS TableGEDI ACS Figure
title: Advancing the understanding of acute coronary syndromes in women: insights from the GEDI-ACS registry

abstract: Abstract Introduction Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in women, yet women are underrepresented in revascularization trials, and treatment decisions are often extrapolated from predominantly male populations. Given established sex-related differences in coronary anatomy, comorbidity burden, and procedural risk, uncertainty persists regarding the comparative effectiveness of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) versus coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) in women. Purpose To perform a comprehensive time-to-event meta-analysis comparing PCI and CABG in women with CAD. Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials for eligible studies. Outcomes included all-cause mortality, repeat revascularization, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), myocardial infarction, and stroke. Hazard ratios (HRs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were pooled using random-effects models to account for between-study variability. Statistical heterogeneity was quantified using the I² statistic. A two-sided P-value of &lt; 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results We included women from 42 studies. The follow-up ranged from 1 to 10 years. Compared with CABG, PCI was associated with a statistically significant higher risk of all-cause mortality (25 studies, 74,292 women; HR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.15-1.38; I² = 56.7%; P &lt; 0.0001), repeat revascularization (12 studies, 22,884 women; HR, 3.13; 95% CI, 2.22-4.41; I² = 87.3%; P &lt; 0.0001), MACE (17 studies, 22,816 women; HR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.00-1.32; I² = 49.7%; P = 0.0483), myocardial infarction (6 studies, 15,140 women; HR, 2.03; 95% CI, 1.52-2.70; I² = 54.5%; P = 0.0015). In contrast, PCI was associated with lower rates of stroke (5 studies, 16,660 women; HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.48-0.97; I² = 47.9%; P = 0.0402). Conclusions In women with CAD, CABG was associated with lower risks of mortality, repeat revascularization, MACE, and myocardial infarction compared with PCI, albeit at the expense of a higher risk of stroke. Overall, these findings indicate a prognostic advantage of surgical revascularization in women and underscore the urgent need for dedicated sex-specific randomized trials to better inform treatment selection.
title: Sex-specific outcomes of percutaneous coronary intervention versus coronary artery bypass grafting in women with coronary artery disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background The burden of cardiovascular diseases among young women is rising despite advancements in pharmacological therapies. Emerging evidence suggests that lifelong atherogenic burden and persistent undertreatment of younger women contribute to this trend. Conventional prediction tools often classify younger women as low risk, resulting in delayed initiation of adequate lipid-lowering therapy (LLT) despite elevated LDL-C levels. Whether these gaps translate into real-world differences at the time of coronary intervention remains insufficiently characterised. Purpose To evaluate age-related differences in LDL burden, LLT utilisation, and temporal trends among women undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Methods We retrospectively analysed women undergoing PCI between 2012 and 2024 from a large contemporary PCI registry. Patients were stratified by age (18–54, 55–65, and 66–85 years). LDL control was defined according to American guideline-recommended targets (LDL-C &lt;70 mg/dL). Age-stratified LDL-C distributions, temporal trends, and LLT utilisation at admission and discharge were assessed. Results Among 6,910 women undergoing PCI, 753 were aged 18-54 (10.9%), 1892 aged 55-65 (27.4%) and 4265 aged 66-85 (61.7%). Younger women had a higher prevalence of family history of coronary artery disease and presentation of myocardial infarction [OA1] (25.4% and 21.4%, respectively). The baseline LDL-C control differed significantly across age groups (p &lt; 0.001) (Figure 1); proportions of LDL-C &lt; 70 mg/dL increased gradually with age, occurring in 28.4% of women aged 18–54 years, 34.0% of those aged 55–65 years, and 39.4% of those aged 66–85 years. Although the prevalence of LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL decreased over time, younger women consistently exhibited the highest rates of uncontrolled LDL throughout the study period. LLT use at admission was significantly lower in younger women (72.6% vs older women 76.4% and 79.0%: p &lt; 0.001). Temporal analyses demonstrated increasing LLT use at admission across age groups, with significant upward trends observed in women aged 55–65 years (p=0.0139) and 66–85 years (p=0.0231) (Figure 2). Despite overall improvement, younger women remained consistently less likely to receive LLT throughout the study period (p=0.9712) (Figure 2). Conclusions Despite improvements in lipid management over time, younger women remain disproportionately undertreated and present with higher uncontrolled LDL-C levels at the time of PCI. These findings underscore persistent prevention gaps and emphasise the need for earlier and more proactive LLT strategies in women.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Age-stratified LDL trends and lipid-lowering therapy gaps in women undergoing cardiac catheterization

abstract: Abstract Background Coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) is a common cause of ischemic symptoms without obstructive coronary disease and is disproportionately observed in women. However, sex-specific patterns linking CMD, coronary calcification and prognosis remain unclear. Purpose To define sex differences in clinical characteristics, coronary calcium phenotype and outcomes in PET-defined CMD. Methods In this prospective cohort study, patients referred for stress myocardial perfusion imaging with 82Rb-Positron Emission Tomography (PET) were enrolled. Perfusion findings were classified as normal perfusion, localized ischemia (summed difference score ≥2) or CMD (reduced global coronary flow reserve (CFR &lt;2.0) without localized ischemia). Multivariable logistic regression models identified independent predictors of CMD. The primary prognostic endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; death, myocardial infarction, or coronary revascularization) within 2 years, analyzed using Cox proportional hazards models. Results Of 3,228 patients, 55.8% had normal perfusion, 36.4% localized ischemia, and 7.8% CMD. The prevalence of CMD was significantly higher in women than in men (11.3% vs 6.1%; OR 1.95 [1.51–2.53], p&lt;0.001). In multivariable analysis, age (aOR 1.73 per 10 years [1.50–2.01], p&lt;0.001) and diabetes (aOR 1.94 [1.42–2.64], p&lt;0.001) were independent predictors of CMD. Within the CMD cohort (n=251), women and men were of similar age (median 72 vs 71 years). Compared with men, women with CMD had less established coronary artery disease (31% vs 45%, p=0.039) and less smoking as a risk factor (43% vs 67%, p&lt;0.001). However, women more often presented with angina pectoris (22% vs 10%, p=0.02) and had a higher prevalence of hypertensive heart disease (17% vs 6.6%, p=0.02). Women with CMD had lower coronary calcium burden than men (median 28 vs 357, p&lt;0.001) and more often had coronary artery calcium (CAC) score of zero (35% vs 5.2%, p&lt;0.001). In multivariable adjusted models, higher CAC was associated with CMD in men (aOR 1.66 [1.24–2.21]) but not in women (aOR 0.98 [0.77–1.23]). A zero-calcium score was associated with lower odds of CMD in men (aOR 0.33 [0.11–0.93] vs 1.19 [0.71–1.99] in women). During 2-year follow-up, both localized ischemia and CMD were associated with increased risk of MACE compared with normal perfusion (localized ischemia: aHR 3.14 [2.17–4.55]; CMD: aHR 2.26 [1.21–4.20]; p&lt;0.001). Within CMD, MACE risk did not differ between women and men (female vs male aHR 0.54 [0.14–2.08]). Conclusions CMD was associated with a two-fold increase in adverse events compared with normal perfusion, underscoring that microvascular ischemia is not benign. CMD was over-represented in women despite lower coronary calcium, whereas in men it was more often accompanied by greater calcified plaque burden and known coronary artery disease. Importantly, a zero-calcium score does not exclude CMD, particularly in women.Kaplan-Meier Curve PET categoriesAdjusted survival curve CMD
title: Sex Differences in Risk Profiles, Coronary Calcium and Outcomes in Coronary Microvascular Dysfunction

abstract: Abstract Background Previous observational studies have shown that women undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) are generally older and have a higher burden of comorbidities than men, and exhibit higher unadjusted rates of adverse events after PCI. Purpose To investigate sex-based differences in clinical outcomes among patients on long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC) undergoing PCI with drug-eluting stent (DES) implantation. Methods The PERSEO registry is a prospective, multicentre, observational study conducted at 25 Italian centres, enrolling consecutive patients on OAC for atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism, left ventricular thrombus, mechanical heart valves, or other indications, undergoing PCI with DES implantation. Pharmacological and interventional management was left to operator discretion. The primary outcome was net adverse clinical events (NACE), defined as the composite of major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE) and major bleeding. MACCE included all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), stent thrombosis, urgent/unplanned target vessel revascularization (TVR), and non-fatal stroke/transient ischaemic attack (TIA). Secondary outcomes, including MACCE, all-cause death, cardiac death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke/TIA, TVR, and major and clinically relevant bleeding were also compared. Multivariable Cox analysis was adjusted for predictors of NACE including Body Mass Index, Charlson score, CHA2DS2VASc, HAS-BLED, chronic kidney disease, anaemia, type of OAC (direct oral anticoagulants/vitamin K-antagonists), and duration of the initial triple antithrombotic therapy. Results Among 1234 enrolled patients, women (n=333, 27%) were older and had higher thromboembolic and bleeding risk profiles, whereas men (n=901) more frequently had prior ischaemic heart disease and smoking history. NACE occurred in 26% of women and 21.3% of men (p=0.084; log-rank p=0.129). Similarly, MACCE rates were comparable(16.2% vs 13.3%, p=0.189). Women had higher rates of all-cause (14.1% vs 9.4%, p=0.020) and cardiac (6.4% vs 3.1%, p=0.010) death, while other ischaemic and bleeding outcomes did not differ significantly. In univariable analysis, male sex was associated with lower all-cause and cardiac mortality; however, after multivariable adjustment, sex was not independently associated with NACE, MACCE, mortality, ischaemic, or bleeding events. Conclusions Among patients on OAC undergoing PCI with DES, women presented with a higher baseline risk profile and higher unadjusted mortality. However, after adjustment for confounding factors, sex was not an independent predictor of ischaemic or bleeding outcomes, suggesting that baseline clinical differences rather than sex per se drive outcome disparities.
title: Sex-based differences in patients on oral anticoagulation undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents: a subgroup analysis of the PERSEO registry

abstract: Abstract Background Sex-related differences in outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) remain debated. Women referred for TAVI tend to be older, have smaller aortic annuli, and present with more comorbidities, yet some studies suggest a long-term survival advantage over men. Understanding sex-specific outcome patterns is essential for refining patient selection and periprocedural management. Purpose To evaluate sex-based differences in baseline characteristics, procedural data, in-hospital complications, and long-term all-cause mortality following TAVI in a large cohort. Methods We analysed consecutive patients (who underwent TAVI in a prospective registry of two tertiary centers. Baseline characteristics, procedural data, and in-hospital outcomes were compared between sexes using chi-square/Fisher’s exact tests for categorical and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality. Long-term survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis with log-rank testing. Outcomes were reported according to the Valve Academic Research Consortium-3 (VARC-3) criteria. Results We analysed 4,331 consecutive patients (2,299 males [53.1%]; 2,032 females [46.9%]). Women were older (83 vs 82 years; p&lt;0.001) and had higher pre-procedural transvalvular gradients (mean gradient 45 vs 43 mmHg; p&lt;0.001), smaller aortic valve area (0.66 vs 0.70 cm²; p&lt;0.001), and better preserved left ventricular function (LVEF ≥50%: 78.8% vs 64.5%; p&lt;0.001). Men had a significantly higher burden of coronary artery disease (prior MI: 17.7% vs 9.2%; prior PCI: 31.7% vs 19.4%; prior CABG: 25.9% vs 14.9%; all p&lt;0.001), diabetes (27.6% vs 23.1%; p&lt;0.001), and atrial fibrillation (28.1% vs 22.3%; p&lt;0.001). Women experienced significantly higher rates of cardiac tamponade (2.2% vs 0.8%; p&lt;0.001), vascular access-site complications (14.4% vs 9.2%; p&lt;0.001), any bleeding (15.0% vs 8.8%; p&lt;0.001), in-hospital cerebrovascular accident (4.0% vs 2.6%; p=0.011), conversion to sternotomy (1.0% vs 0.3%; p=0.010), and in-hospital mortality (3.2% vs 2.0%; p=0.018). Conversely, men had a higher rate of new permanent pacemaker implantation (17.5% vs 13.2%; p&lt;0.001). VARC-3 technical success was achieved in 97.3% of males vs 96.0% of females (p=0.021). Over a median follow-up of 6.4 years, 1,594 deaths occurred (890 males, 704 females). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated significantly better long-term survival for women (median survival: 7.1 vs 6.0 years; log-rank p&lt;0.001). Conclusions Despite a higher incidence of periprocedural complications, including vascular injury, bleeding, tamponade, and in-hospital mortality, women undergoing TAVI demonstrated significantly higher long-term survival compared to men. These findings underscore the need for sex-specific risk stratification, tailored periprocedural management to mitigate the higher early risks in women, and long-term outcome assessment beyond the index hospitalisation.Kaplan Meier analysis
title: Sex-based differences in baseline characteristics, periprocedural outcomes and long-term survival following transcatheter aortic valve implantation

abstract: Abstract Background A clinical dilemma is how we should manage women currently on systemic hormone therapy at the time of a myocardial infarction (MI). Current guidelines generally discourage hormone therapy in women with established cardiovascular disease but provide limited guidance for those already receiving therapy at the time of MI. Contemporary evidence on the safety of continuation versus discontinuation of hormone therapy after MI is limited and inconclusive. Purpose To investigate whether continuation of systemic hormone therapy after MI is associated with increased risk of recurrent cardiovascular events or all-cause mortality within the first two years after discharge, and to evaluate whether cardiovascular risk profile influence this association. Methods This nationwide registry-based study included women aged 40–70 years with first MI recorded in the SWEDEHEART registry between 2006 and 2021. Hormone therapy exposure was obtained from the Swedish Prescribed Drug Register and based on dispensing patterns in relation to the index MI admission. Exposure was defined as at least one dispensed prescription of systemic hormone therapy within four months before admission. Continued use was defined as at least one dispensed prescription within four months after discharge, and women were categorised as discontinuers or continuers accordingly. The primary outcome was 1-year MACE, defined as recurrent MI, heart failure hospitalisation, unplanned coronary angiography or percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), ischaemic stroke, arterial thrombosis, or all-cause death. To reduce misclassification and ensure accurate exposure classification, follow-up for outcomes began four months after discharge. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), adjusted for age, cardiovascular risk factors, and comorbidities. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were constructed and groups were compared using the log-rank test. Results Among 23 675 women (mean age 60.9 ± 7.3 years), 1818 (7.7%) were using hormone therapy prior to MI. Of these, 1139 (62.7%) continued therapy after MI, whereas 679 (37.3%) discontinued. During 1-year follow-up, 150 MACE events occurred, including 52 among discontinuers and 98 among continuers (crude HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.79–1.55, p=0.545). Continuation of hormone therapy was not significantly associated with increased risk of MACE compared with discontinuation (adjusted HR 1.11, 95% CI 0.79–1.56, p=0.540). At 2 years, there were a corresponding trend towards higher risk among continuers that did not reach statistical significance (log-rank p=0.084; adjusted HR 1.25, 95% CI 0.98–1.59, p=0.07). Conclusion Continuation of hormone therapy after MI was not associated with increased risk of recurrent cardiovascular events within the first year. However, a trend towards higher risk emerged beyond one year, suggesting that potential longer-term effects warrant further investigation.
title: Continuation of systemic hormone therapy after myocardial infarction and risk of recurrent cardiovascular events: a SWEDEHEART nationwide cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background Cardiogenic shock remains a leading cause of mortality in acute cardiovascular emergencies, with microaxial flow pump (MAFP) support increasingly used as a haemodynamic rescue strategy. However, sex-based differences in clinical presentation, device utilisation, and outcomes among MAFP-supported patients remain poorly described. Purpose To evaluate sex-based differences among consecutive patients receiving MAFP support at two tertiary cardiovascular centres. Methods We retrospectively analysed 267 consecutive patients, who received MAFP support at two tertiary hospitals between January 2018 and February 2026. Baseline demographics, comorbidities, diagnosis, Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI) shock stage, device type, and outcomes were compared between sexes. Continuous variables are presented as median [interquartile range] and compared using Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables are presented as n (%) and compared using Chi-square or Fisher’s exact test as appropriate. Statistical significance was set at P &lt; 0.05. Results Women comprised 24.0% (64/267) of the cohort. Male patients were significantly older than females (median 56 [46–65] vs 47 [36–61] years; P = 0.004) and had higher body mass index-related anthropometrics (height, weight, body surface area; all P &lt; 0.001). The comorbidity burden was comparable between sexes, with no significant differences in hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, or chronic heart failure. The distribution of underlying diagnoses differed significantly between sexes (P &lt; 0.001). Men more frequently presented with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI; 39.3% vs 28.1%) and dilated cardiomyopathy acute decompensated heart failure (DCM ADHF; 27.4% vs 15.6%), whereas acute myocarditis was significantly more prevalent in women (28.1% vs 5.0%). SCAI shock severity was similar, with 65.0% of males and 73.4% of females presenting in SCAI stage ≥D (P = 0.222). Cardiac arrest rates were non-significantly higher in women (41.0% vs 34.2%; P = 0.337). Despite these differences in presentation, 30-day mortality was comparable between males and females (44.6% vs 49.1%; P = 0.560), as was in-hospital mortality (61.2% vs 64.5%; P = 0.739). Median duration of MAFP support was also similar (5 [1–9] vs 6 [1–10.5] days; P = 0.347). Conclusions In this two-centre cohort of MAFP-supported patients, women represented approximately one quarter of cases and were younger than men. While the underlying aetiologies differed significantly, SCAI shock severity and short-term mortality were comparable between sexes. These findings suggest that, despite differing pathophysiology, MAFP support provides equitable short-term outcomes regardless of sex. Prospective, larger-scale studies are warranted to further delineate sex-specific phenotypes and inform tailored management strategies in mechanical circulatory support.Figure
title: Sex-based differences in baseline characteristics and outcomes among patients treated with microaxial flow pump support for cardiogenic shock

abstract: Abstract Background Anomalous aortic origin of the left coronary artery (L-AAOCA) is a leading cause of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in the young, especially with an interarterial course. L-AAOCA arising from the non-coronary sinus (NS) with a juxtacommissural origin is less well characterized and its risk profile remains incompletely defined. Purpose We aim to report the clinical presentation, evaluation, management and outcomes in L-AAOCA/NS, juxtacommissural in a pediatric cohort. Methods Single institution cohort study of patients &lt;21 years with L-AAOCA/NS, juxtacommissural evaluated following a standardized approach. Coronary anatomy was assessed on retrospective ECG-gated CTA while functional assessment included EST and nuclear stress perfusion imaging (sNPI) or dobutamine stress CMR in patients ≥6 years. Invasive intracoronary flow assessment (iFR, FFR) on cardiac catheterization was performed in selected cases if concerns with symptoms and negative non-invasive studies. For surgical patients, repeat studies were performed at 3 months postoperatively. High-risk features included exertional symptoms, aborted SCD, intramural (IM) course, slit-like ostium, or inducible myocardial ischemia. Results In total, 20 patients (55% male), median age of 10 years (IQR 4.4 - 4.2) presenting with L-AAOCA/NS, juxtacommissural between 12/2012 - 7/2025 were included, compring 15% of all patients presenting with L-AAOCA. Of these, 6/20 (30%) had exertional chest pain or syncope, 1/20 (5%) presented with cardiogenic shock and 1/20 (5%) had aborted SCD (Figure). CTA was performed in 18/20 (90%); 8/20 (40%) had an origin adjacent to L/NS commissure with none having an IM course defined on CTA. EST was performed in 15/20 (75%) patients and was abnormal in 2/15 (13%). Stress perfusion testing was completed in 13/20 (65%) patients and 4/13 (31%) were positive for ischemia. Abnormal iFR/FFR was present in 1 of 2 cases studied. Surgery was indicated and performed in 7/20 (35%) patients, median IM length 2 mm (IQR 1-3): 2/7 (29%) reimplantations, 2/7 (29%) unroofings, 2/7 (29%) osteoplasty, and 1/7 (14%) neo-ostium formation. One patient denied recommended cardiac catheterization, thus recommendation for surgery could not be provided. Post-operative tests indicated resolution of pre-operative inducible ischemia (invasive/non-invasive) in all 5 patients. As of last follow-up (median 3.6 years, IQR 2.3 – 8.1), all patients were alive 20/20 (100%) and all engage in physical activity including recreational 11/20 (55%), school organized 5/20 (25%), and club level 4/20 (20%). Conclusion In this pediatric cohort of L-AAOCA/NS, juxtacommissural, 10% presented with aborted SCD/cardiogenic shock and 1/3 had evidence of inducible ischemia, suggesting a less benign AAOCA subtype in some patients. Following repair, there was resolution of inducible ischemia with excellent post-surgical medium to long-term outcomes with successful return to physical activity.Figure
title: High-risk anomalous aortic origin of a left coronary artery (L-AAOCA) beyond interarterial course: outcomes in a pediatric cohort with L-AAOCA from the noncoronary aortic sinus

abstract: Abstract Background Anomalous aortic origin of a coronary artery (AAOCA) remains a leading cause of sudden cardiac death (SCD) in the young, particularly left-AAOCA. The more common right(R)-AAOCA, albeit rare, can also lead to SCD. Risk stratification remains a challenge, especially in patients with exertional symptoms and negative noninvasive studies under stress. Purpose We report outcomes in a pediatric cohort of R-AAOCA patients undergoing invasive intracoronary flow assessment (ICFA). Methods R-AAOCA patients underwent advanced imaging and functional assessment with non-invasive provocative stress studies (EST, perfusion imaging). Patients with exertional symptoms and negative noninvasive studies had cardiac catheterization for ICFA using coronary angiography (figure 1) and a Verrata pressure guide wire. ICFA was performed at baseline and under dobutamine stress. IVUS was performed in select cases. Instantaneous wave-free ratio (iFR) was considered abnormal if ≤0.85. Fractional flow reserve (FFR) was considered abnormal if &lt;0.8. For patients undergoing surgery, repeat catheterization was performed at 3 months postoperatively. Results Our cohort included 30 patients (figure 2) with R-AAOCA, median age 14 (9-19) years and weight 57 (37-143) kg. Of these, 24 (80%) had an intramural course median length of 6 mm. Eight (27%) patients had abnormal ICFA and surgery was offered, 1 declined. Fourteen (47%) patients had negative ICFA and among these, surgery was not offered in 12/14 (86%) and 2/14 (14%) underwent surgery given exertional symptoms and shared decision making. One (3%) patient had incomplete data and surgery was performed based on shared decision making. In 7/30 (23%) patients, stable wire position in the distal R-AAOCA could not be obtained (most early in our experience); thus ICFA was not completed. No significant complications were encountered during or after cardiac catheterization. At 3 months post-operatively, 9/9 (100%) patients with pre-operative ICFA were scheduled for repeat study: 7 completed and 2 are pending. In those completed, data normalized/improved in 6/7 (86%) and could not be obtained in 1/7 (14%) due to wire position. In medium-term follow-up, 3-5 years after surgery, there is no evidence of ischemia or concerning symptoms. Conclusion Cardiac catheterization with ICFA plays an important role in the management of R-AAOCA, especially in those patients with concerning exertional symptoms and negative noninvasive studies. Of patients with negative ICFA data, most were not offered surgery. These procedures can be technically challenging in children, with a learning curve involved. Multicenter data are warranted to better characterize the role of ICFA in management decision making in R-AAOCA, as the current cut-off values derive from adult studies with coronary artery disease, a distinct condition from (R)-AAOCA in children.figure 1figure 2
title: Invasive intracoronary flow assessment in a pediatric cohort of anomalous aortic origin of the right coronary artery (R-AAOCA): is it time to expand the assessment of coronary ischemia?

abstract: Abstract Background Pediatric heart failure (HF) remains a high-morbidity condition with distinct cellular and clinical profiles compared to adult populations. Energy deficiency and metabolic inflexibility drive myocardial dysfunction in children, where congenital heart disease and cardiomyopathies predominate. Current management relies heavily on adult data extrapolation, creating significant gaps in evidence-based pediatric care. Purpose This study evaluates the comparative effectiveness of emerging pharmacological agents and mechanical circulatory support (MCS) innovations to define an optimized, patient-centered therapeutic hierarchy for children with advanced heart failure. Methods A comprehensive review of recent clinical trials, multicenter registries, and longitudinal studies was conducted. Data were synthesized regarding the efficacy of neurohormonal blockade, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i), and ventricular assist devices (VAD), including the Berlin Heart EXCOR and HeartMate 3. Outcomes focused on ventricular recovery, bridge-to-transplant (BTT) success, and mortality. Results Pharmacological analysis indicates that while angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNI) and SGLT2i show promise in improving left ventricular ejection fraction and NT-proBNP levels, they do not consistently demonstrate superiority over traditional ACE inhibitors in large pediatric cohorts. In mechanical support, registry data confirm a 1-year survival rate of approximately 79%. The Berlin Heart EXCOR remains the definitive support for infants, showing a 38.1% recovery rate in specific myocarditis cases. Conversely, the HeartMate 3 has expanded off-label use in older children, demonstrating reduced pump thrombosis and stroke risk through fully magnetically levitated rotor technology. Successful weaning from MCS is predominantly observed in acute myocardial injury rather than chronic dilated or structural phenotypes. Conclusion Optimal pediatric HF outcomes require a shift from adult-centric protocols toward etiology-specific interventions. Integration of standardized anticoagulation and early referral for MCS are critical for improving survival. While new drug classes offer symptomatic benefits, rigorous pediatric-specific randomized trials remain essential to establish long-term safety and neurodevelopmental outcomes.Figure 1figure 2
title: Comparative effectiveness of different treatment strategies for paediatric heart failure: a narrative review

abstract: Abstract Background The newly introduced high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T generation 6 (hs-cTnT-gen6) is expected to replace hs-cTnT-gen5, but it is unknown whether established ESC diagnostic criteria for perioperative myocardial infarction/injury (PMI) remain valid. Methods Consecutive patients undergoing major non-cardiac surgery were prospectively included, hs-cTnT-gen6 was measured preoperatively and on postoperative days 1 and 2. PMI was centrally adjudicated and defined according to ESC criteria using an absolute hs-cTnT-gen6 increase ≥27 ng/L between two measurements in the PMI-VITAL cohort (one university hospital in Switzerland). Diagnostic endpoints included the incidence and aetiologies of PMI; the prognostic endpoint was a composite of major adverse cardiac events (MACE) and all-cause mortality, analysed using a Royston–Parmar model with time-varying hazard ratios (HRs). Results 451 patients (median age 72 years; 26% women) were included, PMI occurred in 67 (14.86%) patients, including 61 (91.04%) of cardiac and 6 (9.84%) of extracardiac aetiology (Figure 1). MACE occurred in 9% at 30 days and 23.9% at 1 year of patients with PMI versus 1.3% and 6% of patients without PMI, respectively. All-cause mortality was 7.5% at 30 days and 25.4% at 1 year of patients with PMI versus 0.5% and 6% of patients without PMI, respectively (Figure 2). Adjusted HRs of PMI were 3.24 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.38-7.6) at 30 days and 4.88 (95% CI, 1.84-13) at 1 year for MACE and all-cause mortality. Conclusions PMI defined by ESC criteria using hs-cTnT-gen6 was common and strongly associated with adverse short- and long-term endpoints, supporting its use in clinical practice.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Validation of ESC criteria for perioperative myocardial infarction/injury with the new 6th generation high sensitivity cardiac troponin T assay

abstract: Abstract Background Patients undergoing major vascular surgery remain at substantial risk of perioperative cardiac complications despite contemporary management. Preoperative risk stratification is essential to guide optimisation, perioperative monitoring, and postoperative surveillance. Circulating B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), a marker of myocardial wall stress, may provide objective risk assessment beyond conventional clinical predictors. Purpose To quantify the independent prognostic value of preoperative BNP testing for adverse perioperative outcomes in vascular surgery and to assess its incremental contribution to established risk stratification pathways. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library were systematically searched from inception to identify studies evaluating the association between preoperative BNP levels and postoperative outcomes in adult patients undergoing vascular surgery. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials and observational cohorts. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment. Multivariable-adjusted effect estimates were pooled using a random-effects model. Primary outcomes included perioperative cardiac events (myocardial infarction, myocardial injury, cardiac death), stroke, mortality, and length of stay. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. Results Eleven studies including 3,062 patients met inclusion criteria; all were observational cohorts. Across studies, elevated preoperative BNP was consistently associated with increased perioperative cardiac complications, particularly myocardial infarction, myocardial injury, cardiac death, stroke, and longer hospital stay. The direction of effect was concordant across vascular procedures and risk profiles where reported. Evidence for short-term mortality was directionally consistent but limited. Five studies reporting multivariable-adjusted effect estimates were pooled in the primary analysis. Elevated BNP was independently associated with a significantly increased risk of perioperative cardiac events (pooled OR 4.08; 95% CI 3.20–5.20; p&lt;0.001). No evidence of between-study heterogeneity was observed (I² = 0%), indicating highly consistent adjusted effects across studies. Conclusions Preoperative BNP elevation is associated with an approximately fourfold increase in perioperative cardiac risk in patients undergoing vascular surgery. The strength, independence, and consistency of this association support the integration of natriuretic peptide testing into multimodal perioperative risk assessment frameworks. BNP measurement may facilitate risk-directed monitoring intensity and tailored perioperative management strategies in high-risk patients. Prospective studies are warranted to define optimal biomarker thresholds and implementation pathways before routine guideline endorsement.Forest plot: Adj OR for cardiac events vs BNP
title: Preoperative B-type natriuretic peptide independently predicts perioperative cardiac complications in vascular surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Guideline-recommended surveillance for perioperative myocardial infarction/injury (PMI) depends on systematic preoperative identification of cardiovascular diseases and ordering of cardiac troponin tests. Implementation, however, is often limited by resource constraints and labour-intensive manual chart review, creating a need for scalable digital solutions. Purpose To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of manual screening, natural language processing (NLP), and large language model (LLM)-based approaches for preoperative identification of cardiovascular diseases. Methods Consecutive patients scheduled for major non-cardiac surgery were prospectively included. At 4 PM on the preceding working day, experienced clinical staff performed structured manual screening of available medical records. Simultaneously, the complete electronic health record at that time point was extracted and frozen for automated analysis using NLP and LLM-based algorithms. Discrepant classifications between methods were adjudicated by an independent board-certified cardiologist blinded to the source of identification, generating a reference standard. Diagnostic endpoints included sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) for detection of predefined cardiovascular diseases. Results Among 1104 patients (median age 62 years [IQR 46–73]; 47% women), 150 (13.6%) had ≥1 cardiovascular disease according to the reference standard. Manual screening identified cardiovascular disease with a sensitivity of 76.0% (95% CI 68.6–82.1) and specificity of 98.6% (97.7–99.2), yielding a PPV of 89.8% and NPV of 96.3%. NLP-based screening achieved the highest sensitivity at 99.3% (96.3–99.9) with a specificity of 97.3% (96.0–98.1), corresponding to a PPV of 85.1%, NPV of 99.9%, and F1 score of 91.7%. LLM-based screening demonstrated a sensitivity of 90.0% (84.2–93.8) and the highest specificity of 99.5% (98.8–99.8), with a PPV of 96.4%, NPV of 98.4%, and F1 score of 93.1%. Conclusions Both NLP- and LLM-based screening outperformed structured manual chart review by clinical staff. NLP-based screening achieved the highest sensitivity, supporting its use as a rule-out strategy. In contrast, LLM-based screening demonstrated the highest specificity, suggesting utility for rule-in identification.Figure
title: Manual versus natural language processing versus large language model screening for preoperative identification of cardiovascular diseases: a prospective cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background The DOUBLE-CHOICE trial showed that a sedation-free minimalist strategy for transfemoral TAVI is noninferior to standard of care (SoC), but approximately 20% of patients required intra-procedural crossover. The clinical profile and prognostic implications of such conversion are unclear. Purpose To analyze the clinical impact and determinants of crossover from local anesthesia to conscious sedation during transfemoral TAVI. Methods This subanalysis included all 370 patients randomized to the minimalist approach (including local anesthesia only) in DOUBLE-CHOICE. Crossover to SoC was defined as any systemic administration of sedative or anesthetic medication during the procedure. Outcomes at 30 days were compared between patients who completed TAVI under local anesthesia and those undergoing crossover. Multivariable logistic regression assessed the independent association between crossover and the primary composite endpoint (death, vascular and bleeding complications, infections requiring antibiotics, and neurologic events) and identified baseline predictors of crossover. Results Overall, 72 of 370 patients (19.5%) required crossover. Baseline characteristics were generally similar, although prior stroke was more frequent among crossover patients. Crossover was associated with longer procedure times, greater use of invasive adjuncts, and lower technical (83.3% vs 98.0%) and device success (67.2% vs 87.5%; both p&lt;0.001). The primary endpoint occurred in 38.7% of crossover versus 18.9% of non-crossover patients (odds ratio [OR] 2.7; 95% CI 1.5–4.9; p&lt;0.001). Delirium was also more common after crossover (14.3% vs 3.6%; OR 4.5; 95% CI 1.7–12; p=0.003). In multivariable analysis, crossover remained independently associated with the primary endpoint (adjusted OR 3.28; 95% CI 1.60–6.70; p=0.001). Moderate-to-severe frailty and study center were independent predictors of crossover. Conclusions In sedation-free transfemoral TAVI, intra-procedural crossover to SoC occurs in one in five patients and is associated with adverse 30-day outcomes. Crossover should be regarded as a marker of procedural vulnerability rather than a benign deviation from a minimalist strategy.
title: Clinical impact and determinants of crossover from local anesthesia to conscious sedation during transfemoral TAVI: a subanalysis from the randomized DOUBLE-CHOICE Trial

abstract: Abstract Background Cardiovascular complications are the leading cause of death within 30 days after noncardiac surgery. Myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery (MINS) is the most common cardiovascular complication and is independently associated with increased 30-day mortality. Although MINS portends a poor prognosis, patients with MINS have variable outcomes and there is a need for enhanced risk stratification. Purpose We aimed to assess if postoperative N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) improved predicting of death and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) within 30 days among patients with MINS. Methods We conducted a sub-analysis in the VISION Biobank cohort study, restricted to patients who had developed MINS and had a postoperative NT-proBNP assessment on the day of or after the MINS event. We validated the results within the BASEL-PMI study cohort. We hypothesized that a predefined threshold of postoperative NT-proBNP concentrations ≥718 pg/ml predicted a worse outcome. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause mortality and MACE (myocardial infarction on postoperative day 4 or later, acute heart failure, non-fatal cardiac arrest, and cardiac revascularization) at 30-days after surgery. Adjusted cox proportional hazard models were built. Results Among 179 patients with MINS, median age 72.7 years, 36.9% women, the primary outcome occurred in 22 (12%) patients. Patients with postoperative NT-proBNP ≥718 pg/ml exhibited a 30-day outcome rate of 17% (16/93 patients) compared to 7% (6/86 patients) of those with values &lt;718 pg/ml (adjusted Hazard Ratio [aHR] 2.9, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.1-7.6, p=0.026). The validation cohort with 382 patients with MINS, confirmed these findings (30-day aHR 4.2; 95% CI 1.7-10.4, p=0.002). Conclusion In patients with MINS, postoperative NT-proBNP concentrations are predictors of death and MACE and can help in guiding short-term cardiac risk assessment, medical management, and follow-up for patients with MINS.
title: Predictive value of postoperative N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide in patients suffering myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery

abstract: Abstract Background 300 million surgeries are performed worldwide each year. 10% are urgent or emergency surgeries, with a 3-fold higher mortality than elective procedures. Preoperative troponin elevation is a well-established marker of risk in elective surgery, but prognostic value in urgent/emergency surgeries remains poorly defined. Purpose We aimed to determine the relationship between baseline preoperative troponin (elevated or not) and a composite outcome of death, myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery (MINS), heart failure, atrial fibrillation, or non-fatal cardiac arrest, as well as the single components at 30 days. Additionally, we aimed to understand the relationship between time from troponin measurement to surgery and the occurrence of all-cause death and cardiovascular complications, in patients with and without preoperative troponin elevation. Methods We performed a pooled individual participant data analysis of the VISION-1 study and POISE-3 trial, including patients ≥ 45 years-old who had urgent/emergency noncardiac surgery and had at least one preoperative troponin measurement. We used multivariable Cox proportional hazards models to determine if a preoperative troponin measurement was an independent predictor of the primary composite outcome. We assessed time from troponin measurement to surgery based on troponin status (positive vs. negative) only in POISE-3 as physicians were not always aware of preoperative troponin values in VISION-1 to guide clinical decisions. We performed a mediation analysis to assess the role of time from troponin measurement to surgery as mediator of the outcome. Results Among 5,275 patients, 1,080 had preoperative troponin measured, of whom 242 (22.4%, 95% CI 20.1–25%) were elevated. The primary outcome occurred in 47.5% (95% CI 41.3–53.8) of patients with preoperative troponin elevation versus 11.1% (95% CI 9.1–13.4) without (Figure 1). Increasing age (aHR 1.03, 95% CI 1.02-1.05), preoperative troponin elevation (aHR 3.67, 95% CI 2.65-5.09), and vascular surgery (aHR 1.77, 95% CI 1.05–2.97) independently predicted the primary outcome (Figure 2). Analysis restricted to POISE-3 indicated that preoperative troponin elevation was associated with a slightly prolonged time to surgery (median 22 vs. 18.6 hours, absolute difference 3.4, 95% CI 1–7.3 hours). Mediation analysis indicated that the association between preoperative troponin elevation and primary composite outcome was primarily driven by the direct effect, and the proportion mediated by time to surgery was negligible (3.3%, 95% CI 2.5–12.4, P=0.277). Conclusion Preoperative troponin elevation is independently associated with an increased risk of death or cardiovascular complications after urgent or emergency surgery. Although patients with a preoperative troponin elevation had a slightly delayed time to surgery, the delay did not mediate worse cardiovascular outcomes.
title: Prognostic role of a preoperative troponin elevation in patients undergoing urgent or emergency noncardiac surgery: a pooled analysis

abstract: Abstract Background With an ageing population and rising metabolic comorbidities among liver transplant candidates, perioperative cardiovascular risk assessment has become increasingly important. Pre-transplant cardiac evaluation strategies before liver transplantation vary widely across centres. Risk stratification tools include the Cardiovascular Risk in Orthotopic Liver Transplantation (CAR-OLT) score (predicting perioperative major cardiovascular events) and Coronary Artery Disease in Liver Transplantation (CAD-LT) score (predicting significant coronary artery disease). These were developed to estimate perioperative cardiovascular risk, yet their real-world distribution across evaluation strategies and performance for predicting post-transplant events remain incompletely characterised. Purpose To compare CAR-OLT and CAD-LT score distributions between invasive (left heart catheterisation [LHC]-based) and non-invasive strategies and assess discrimination for one-year major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of 637 adults undergoing orthotopic liver transplantation between 1 January 2017 and 31 December 2024. Cardiac evaluation was categorised as LHC-based (invasive) or non-invasive, primarily stress testing. CAR-OLT and CAD-LT scores were calculated for all patients. One-year MACE was defined as myocardial infarction, new or decompensated heart failure, new or worsening pulmonary hypertension, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest, arrhythmia, cardiovascular death, or cerebrovascular accident. Score distributions were compared between strategies using non-parametric testing. Discrimination for one-year MACE was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results Patients undergoing LHC-based evaluation had higher baseline predicted risk. Median CAR-OLT score was 32.0 (IQR 25.0–39.2) in the invasive group versus 23.0 (IQR 16.0–31.0) in the non-invasive group (p&lt;0.001). Median CAD-LT score was 12.0 (IQR 10.0–15.0) versus 8.0 (IQR 6.0–10.0), respectively (p&lt;0.001). When evaluated for the prediction of one-year MACE, discrimination was modest. The AUC was 0.651 for CAR-OLT and 0.565 for CAD-LT, indicating limited ability of either model to differentiate patients who experienced events from those who did not. Conclusion CAR-OLT and CAD-LT scores were higher among patients selected for invasive pre-transplant cardiac evaluation, supporting the presence of risk-based selection. However, both models show only modest discrimination for one-year post-transplant MACE, suggesting a disconnect between preoperative risk prediction and post-transplant cardiovascular outcomes. These findings highlight the need for more accurate, transplant-specific risk stratification approaches to better guide pre-transplant evaluations and optimise outcomes.Figure 1:A/B/C/DFigure 2:ROC Curve
title: Risk score distribution and one-year MACE prediction by CAD-OLT and CAD-LT in liver transplant candidates

abstract: Abstract Background Myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery (MINS) often lacks typical ischemic symptoms and ECG changes, leading to misdiagnosis despite its link to adverse prognosis. Preoperative non-invasive coronary function assessment remains underexplored. This study utilized coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA)-derived parameters, including computed tomography–derived fractional flow reserve (CT-FFR), peri-coronary fat attenuation index (PFAI), transluminal attenuation gradient (TAG), and coronary artery calcium score (CACS). Objective To investigate the correlation and incremental predictive value of preoperative CCTA-derived parameters for MINS. Methods This single-center retrospective study included consecutive patients who underwent non-cardiac surgery (Jan 2013–July 2022) with CCTA performed within six months preoperatively. We excluded patients with missing troponin, emergency surgeries, prior CABG, post-CCTA PCI, poor image quality, specific non-ischemic MINS causes, or elevated preoperative troponin (&gt;99th percentile upper reference limit (99% URL)). The primary outcome was MINS (postoperative cardiac troponin I &gt;99% URL within 3 days). K-means clustering categorized patients based on five CCTA indicators. Stepwise regression determined covariates for a reference model. Incremental value over the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) and the reference model was assessed via area under the curve (AUC), likelihood ratio tests, and net reclassification improvement (NRI). Results Among 702 included patients (median age 69.0 years, 46.3% women), 115 (16.4%) developed MINS. K-means clustering identified two groups; Cluster 2 (better overall coronary function) exhibited a lower risk than Cluster 1 (OR=0.54, 95% CI 0.34–0.87) after adjusting for clinical and perioperative factors. Specifically, CT-FFR showed a stable correlation with MINS: for every 0.1 increase, risk decreased (OR=0.79, 95% CI 0.64–0.99). Using a 0.75 threshold, the CT-FFR ≥0.75 group had significantly lower risk (OR=0.49, 95% CI 0.28–0.86). High TAG (&gt;median) also indicated lower risk (OR=0.55, 95% CI 0.32–0.95), whereas maximum stenosis, CACS, and PFAI showed no consistent independent associations. The clinical reference model had an AUC of 0.781; adding minimum CT-FFR increased this to 0.794 (P=0.031), improving risk reclassification (NRI=0.090). Including all imaging variables further improved the AUC to 0.800 (P=0.023) with an NRI of 0.160. For the RCRI (baseline AUC 0.597), adding minimum CT-FFR significantly increased the AUC to 0.655 (P=0.022). Conclusion From CCTA-derived parameters, patients with better overall coronary function have a lower risk of MINS. Specifically, CT-FFR in this study demonstrated its correlation with MINS and its incremental predictive value beyond clinical and intraoperative information.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Association between preoperative coronary computed tomography angiography-derived parameters and myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery

abstract: Abstract Background The prognostic relevance of perioperative myocardial injury/infarction (PMI) in older patients undergoing major noncardiac surgery remains unclear, as high comorbidity burden may lessen its impact. Methods Older patients (defined as age ≥70 years with ≥3 comorbidities, or ≥80 years) enrolled in a multicentre, prospective study of patients at increased cardiovascular risk undergoing major noncardiac surgery were analysed. The primary endpoint, all-cause mortality at 1 year, was analysed using Cox proportional hazards regression. Secondary endpoints included MACE (cardiovascular death, acute myocardial infarction, life-threatening arrhythmia, and acute heart failure), analysed using Fine–Gray hazard regression. All models were adjusted for prespecified confounders with PMI as a time-varying exposure. Results Among 4634 older patients (median age 80 years; 42.9% women), PMI occurred in 892 patients (19.2%), which was higher than in younger patients (P &lt; 0.0001). The distribution of PMI aetiologies was comparable between groups. At 1 year, all-cause mortality was 26.2% in patients with PMI and 13.2% in patients without PMI, and MACE occurred in 30% versus 13%, respectively. After multivariable adjustment, the hazard ratio of PMI was highest on postoperative day 1 (all-cause mortality: 10.5 [95% CI 4.5–24.5]; MACE: 4.4 [95% CI 3.2–5.9]), declined by day 90 (1.4 [95% CI 1.0–1.9] and 2.2 [95% CI 1.7–2.7], respectively), and persisted through 1 year. Conclusions PMI was very common among older patients and associated with substantially higher 1-year risks of all-cause mortality and MACE, with greatest vulnerability observed during the initial 90 postoperative days.Hazard ratio of 1-year all-cause mortalityCumulative incidence of all-cause mortality

title: Prevalence and prognostic relevance of perioperative myocardial infarction/injury after major noncardiac surgery in older patients

abstract: Abstract Background Octogenarians (≥80 years) with Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) represent a high-risk group due to comorbidities, frailty, and atypical clinical presentations, which pose significant management challenges. There is limited evidence to guide optimal management, especially regarding the choice between conservative and invasive strategies. This study examines the clinical characteristics, treatment approaches, and short-term outcomes in this population. Methods In this multi-center observational study, 197 octogenarian ACS patients were enrolled between January 2022 and August 2024. Patients were categorized into conservative (57.4%) and invasive (42.6%) management groups. Demographics, comorbidities, clinical presentation, and geriatric assessments (Fried Frailty Scale, CAM, GDS) were collected. Outcomes assessed included in-hospital and 30-day mortality, reinfarction, bleeding (BARC ≥3), and target vessel revascularization (TVR). Results The cohort was predominantly NSTE-ACS (88.3%) with high frailty (53.8%). Selection bias was notable: the conservative group had more Peripheral Vascular Disease (38.9% vs. 19.0%, p=0.003) and delirium (42.5% vs. 26.2%, p=0.02), while the invasive group had higher GRACE scores (p=0.039) and BMI (p=0.028). In-hospital (5.9% vs. 7.9%) and 30-day mortality (9.6% vs. 15.9%) were lower in the invasive group, though these differences were not statistically significant. The invasive group had a higher TVR rate (13.1% vs. 0.0%, p&lt;0.001) and a trend toward lower reinfarction (3.5% vs. 10.6%, p=0.12). Major bleeding rates were similar (13.1% vs. 9.7%, p=0.61). Conclusion Geriatric syndromes have a substantial impact on ACS management in octogenarians. Frailty and delirium are associated with a preference for conservative care. In appropriately selected patients, invasive treatment appears safe and may reduce recurrent events without increasing short-term risk. Comprehensive geriatric assessment is essential for individualized treatment planning.
title: Clinical characteristics, treatment strategies, and short-term outcomes in octogenarian patients with acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Blood pressure (BP) control is a cornerstone of secondary prevention in patients with coronary artery disease who underwent catheter revascularization. However, evidence supporting strict BP targets in very elderly patients, particularly those aged ≥80 years, remains limited. Purpose We investigated whether achieving a BP target of &lt;130/80 mmHg, as recommended by major hypertension guidelines, is associated with reduced stroke risk in patients who underwent catheter revascularization, and whether the magnitude of benefit differs between patients aged ≥80 years and those aged &lt;80 years. Methods We analysed data from the Clinical Deep Data Accumulation System (CLIDAS), a multicentred Japanese registry including 8,793 patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (mean age 70.1±11.1 years; 77.9% male). Patients were stratified by age (≥80 vs. &lt;80 years) and by BP level at hospital discharge (&lt;130/80 vs. ≥130/80 mmHg). The primary outcome was the first occurrence of fatal or nonfatal stroke. Given the high mortality rate among very elderly patients, non-stroke death was treated as a competing risk, and hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated using Fine–Gray models. Absolute risk reductions (ARRs) in 3-year stroke risk were additionally calculated to assess clinical relevance. Results Among the study population, 1,731 patients (19.7%) were aged ≥80 years (mean age 83.9±3.3 years; 65.2% male), and 7,062 patients (80.3%) were aged &lt;80 years (mean age 66.7 years; 81.0% male). During a median follow-up of 2.6 years (24,665 person-years), 311 stroke events (3.5%) were observed. In patients aged &lt;80 years, BP &lt;130/80 mmHg was not significantly associated with stroke risk reduction (HR 0.92, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.57 to 1.47). In contrast, among patients aged ≥80 years, BP &lt;130/80 mmHg was associated with a substantially lower risk of stroke (HR 0.34, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.68). Correspondingly, achieving BP &lt;130/80 mmHg was associated with an absolute reduction in 3-year stroke risk of 3.01% (95% CI 0.85% to 5.44%; number needed to treat [NNT] 33.3) in patients aged ≥80 years, whereas the ARR in patients aged &lt;80 years was 0.69% (95% CI −0.03% to 1.37%; NNT 144.3). Conclusions In patients who underwent catheter revascularization, BP control to &lt;130/80 mmHg was associated with a greater reduction in stroke risk among patients aged ≥80 years compared to those aged &lt;80 years. Given the high baseline risk and limited life expectancy in very elderly individuals, this magnitude of absolute stroke risk reduction may be considered clinically meaningful, supporting the potential benefit of strict BP control even in advanced age.
title: Stroke risk reduction associated with strict blood pressure control in patients aged ≥80 years who underwent catheter revascularization

abstract: Abstract Background Pulmonary embolism (PE) complicated by cardiogenic shock (CS) is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. As the population ages, understanding age-related differences in outcomes and management is critical to optimizing care in this high-risk cohort. Methods Using the National Inpatient Sample database, adults hospitalized with PE and CS, stratifying them into elderly (≥80 years) and younger (18–79 years) groups in the U.S. between 2016-2022. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to evaluate age-based differences in in-hospital outcomes and utilization of advanced therapies. Results Among 55,420 patients with PE and CS, 7,780 (14%) were elderly. In-hospital mortality was significantly higher in elderly patients compared with younger patients (47% vs 37%; adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.51, 95% CI 1.43–1.60; p&lt;0.0001). Despite higher mortality, elderly patients were less likely to receive advanced interventions, including mechanical ventilation (30% vs 43%; aOR 0.68, 95% CI 0.64–0.72), extracorporeal membrane oxygenation ECMO (0.2% vs 6%; aOR 0.06, 95% CI 0.04–0.09), Impella support (1% vs 3%; aOR 0.44, 95% CI 0.35–0.56), and intra-aortic balloon pump IABP (3% vs 5%; aOR 0.54, 95% CI 0.46–0.63) (all p&lt;0.0001). Elderly patients also had higher odds of heart block (15% vs. 10%; aOR 1.49; 95% CI: 1.37 - 1.61), permanent pacemaker implantation (2% vs. 1%; aOR 2.28; 95% CI: 1.80 - 2.90) and in-hospital myocardial infarction (29% vs. 23%; aOR 1.32; 95% CI: 1.25 - 1.41); all p&lt;0.0001. Conclusion Elderly patients with PE complicated by CS experience significantly higher in-hospital mortality while receiving fewer advanced mechanical and circulatory support therapies. These findings suggest potential management disparities and underscore the importance of individualized, age-conscious decision-making that balances clinical risk, frailty, and patient preferences to improve outcomes in this vulnerable population.Central IllustrationBar Graph
title: Clinical outcomes and disparities in advanced therapy use among elderly patients with pulmonary embolism complicated with cardiogenic shock: a nationwide analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Accumulating evidence indicates that systemic inflammatory burden increases with advancing age and represents a hallmark of biological aging. However, whether aging amplifies the prognostic impact of inflammatory biomarkers on long-term cardiovascular outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains unclear. Purpose To investigate age-related effect modification in the associations between inflammatory biomarkers and long-term cardiovascular risk among patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) undergoing PCI. Methods This prospective cohort study enrolled 10,724 consecutive CAD patients undergoing PCI between January and December 2013, with follow-up of up to 10 years. Patients were divided into three groups according to age (&lt;60, 60–74, and ≥75 years). Inflammatory burden was assessed using 12 biomarkers, including white blood cell count and subtypes, derived inflammatory indices, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP). All biomarkers were analyzed as continuous variables and by quartiles. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models, ranging from unadjusted (Model 1) to fully adjusted models (Model 6), were performed. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events (MACE, including death, myocardial infarction, and revascularization) and the secondary outcomes were each component of MACE and cardiac death. Results Among 9,570 patients included in the final analysis (mean age 58.6 ± 10.3 years; 22.8% women), 3,551 (37.1%) experienced MACE during 10-year follow-up. Significant age-related effect modification was observed for the associations between multiple inflammatory biomarkers and MACE. Restricted cubic spline analyses showed clear age-related modification of the dose–response relationships between inflammatory biomarkers and MACE, with predominantly non-linear patterns in patients &lt;60 years but more linear risk increases in older patients (Figure 1). In fully adjusted models, higher quartiles of inflammatory biomarkers were associated with increased risks of MACE and mortality, with substantially stronger associations in older patients, particularly for systemic and composite inflammatory markers such as hsCRP, NLR, SII, SIRI, AISI, and PLR (Figure 2). Conclusions In this large-scale real-world cohort with 10-year follow-up, advancing age significantly amplified inflammation-related cardiovascular risk after PCI, with older patients exhibiting stronger associations between inflammatory biomarkers and long-term adverse outcomes, highlighting the importance of age-informed risk stratification and targeted anti-inflammatory strategies in elderly patients.
title: Age-related amplification of inflammatory risk after percutaneous coronary Intervention: a 10-year large-sample prospective cohort study

abstract: Abstract Background Risk stratification in elderly acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients is challenging due to frailty, atypical presentations, and under-representation in derivation cohorts of conventional scores. Traditional tools may not fully capture geriatric vulnerability driving early outcomes. Purpose To compare the discriminative performance of machine learning (ML)-based geriatric risk scores versus traditional clinical and angiographic scores for predicting 30-day mortality, 6-month mortality, and 6-month major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in elderly ACS patients. Methods This prospective cohort included consecutive ACS patients aged ≥75 years admitted between 2024 and 2025 (n=190; mean age 80.1±4.3 years; 43.2% female; NSTEMI 70.5%, STEMI 29.5%). The primary endpoint was 30-day all-cause mortality; secondary endpoints were 6-month all-cause mortality and 6-month MACE (composite of all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, and unplanned revascularization). Four ML-based geriatric scores (FRAIL-ACS-7, GEM-ACS, GERIAT-ACS, GOLDEN-7) were developed as compact point-based tools (7–9 items) from routinely available clinical/laboratory variables (including frailty indicators, renal function, and inflammatory markers) using supervised ML with explainability. They were compared with GRACE, TIMI, HEART, SYNTAX I and SYNTAX II. Discrimination was evaluated using ROC analysis (AUC); AUCs were compared using DeLong’s test (two-sided). Results Thirty-day mortality occurred in 20 patients (10.5%). AUCs for 30-day mortality were: GERIAT-ACS 0.887, GRACE 0.873, FRAIL-ACS-7 0.830, GOLDEN-7 0.821, GEM-ACS 0.818, SYNTAX II 0.751, TIMI 0.743, HEART 0.702, SYNTAX I 0.630. GERIAT-ACS outperformed TIMI (p=0.014), HEART (p=0.003), and SYNTAX I (p=0.001), but not GRACE (p=0.71). For 6-month mortality (8 events), SYNTAX II showed numerically the highest discrimination (AUC 0.798), followed by GRACE (0.781) and GERIAT-ACS (0.744), and results should be interpreted cautiously due to low event numbers. Discrimination for 6-month MACE was limited across scores (AUC range 0.435–0.575; best GEM-ACS 0.575). Conclusion In elderly ACS patients, ML-based geriatric scores demonstrated strong discrimination for 30-day mortality, with GERIAT-ACS showing the best performance and exceeding most traditional scores, while performing similarly to GRACE. For longer-term mortality, angiographic complexity (SYNTAX II) appeared more informative, whereas none of the evaluated scores adequately predicted 6-month MACE, underscoring the need for outcome-specific risk stratification. External validation is warranted.Discriminatory Performance Comparison and ROCScore Details
title: Machine learning-based vs traditional risk scores for 30-day mortality in elderly ACS patients

abstract: Abstract Introduction In elderly and frail patients presenting with acute coronary syndrome (ACS), the benefit of an invasive management strategy has been questioned in the setting of non-ST-segment elevation ACS. However, there is limited evidence regarding the impact of frailty on clinical outcomes following reperfusion via primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), particularly in those at the highest clinical risk. Objectives The objective of this study was to evaluate the association between frailty and in-hospital outcomes in STEMI patients and to determine its influence on the subgroup of patients presenting with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) or cardiogenic shock (CS) undergoing primary PCI as a reperfusion strategy. Methods Observational, prospective, single-centre study. Consecutive patients ≥50 years of age admitted for STEMI with PCI invasive treatment. Frailty was defined as a score ≥4 on the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS). A multivariate binary logistic regression analysis was performed to elucidate the role of frailty, OHCA-CS, and the frailty*OHCA-CS interaction term as predictors of in-hospital MACE (cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and non-fatal stroke). The association between frailty and MACE within the OHCA-CS subgroup was analysed using an age-adjusted model. Results Among the 549 patients included, the mean age was 66.5±10.3 years, 22.0% were female and 23.1% were frail. At admission, 15.1% (n=83) presented with OHCA or CS, while 12.6% (n=69) experienced an in-hospital MACE. MACE rates were significantly higher in frail patients (25.2% vs. 8.6%; p&lt;0.001) and in those with OHCA-CS (43.4% vs. 7.2%; p&lt;0.001). The OHCA-CS group (Table 1) showed higher rates of diabetes mellitus, with no significant differences in other cardiovascular risk factors, sex, or age. Frailty was more prevalent in the OHCA-CS group (34.9% vs. 21.0%; p=0.006), although no differences were found in the Charlson Comorbidity Index. There were no differences regarding the extent of coronary artery disease, although the complete revascularization rate was lower in the OHCA-CS group (Table 1). In the multivariate analysis, both frailty and OHCA-CS were independently associated with MACE, whereas the frailty*OHCA-CS interaction was not. In the OHCA-CS subgroup, the incidence of MACE in frail patients was double that of non-frail patients: 65.5% (n=19) vs. 31.5% (n=17), p&lt;0.001. The independent association between frailty and MACE in this subgroup was confirmed in an age-adjusted model (Figure 1) Conclusions STEMI patients presenting with OHCA or CS experience high mortality and MACE rates despite reperfusion therapy with primary PCI. These adverse outcomes are twice as frequent in frail patients (CFS ≥4). The benefit of a routine invasive strategy in frail patients with STEMI and OHCA-CS might should be investigated in future studies.Population characteristics by OHCA-CSFigure 1.Multivariate analyses
title: The burden of frailty in high-risk STEMI: outcomes in cardiac arrest and cardiogenic shock

abstract: Abstract Background Current guidelines recommend potent P2Y12 inhibitors for patients with acute coronary syndrome to reduce ischemic events.
