title: Antithrombotic therapy in patients with atrial fibrillation after percutaneous coronary intervention: a systematic review and individual patient data network meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Dual antithrombotic therapy (DAT) after short-term triple antithrombotic therapy (TAT) is recommended in patients requiring chronic oral anticoagulation after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Clopidogrel is the preferred P2Y₁₂ inhibitor to reduce bleeding risk, but its pharmacodynamic limitations raise concerns about ischemic protection. Aims This analysis explored the clinical consequences of intensifying platelet inhibition with ticagrelor as part of DAT in anticoagulated patients undergoing PCI. Methods Data were pooled from two prospective multicenter registries including anticoagulated patients undergoing PCI. Patients were classified by discharge medication: ticagrelor-based DAT, clopidogrel-based DAT, or clopidogrel-based TAT. The co-primary endpoints were a composite of all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, definite stent thrombosis (ST), ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (MACCE) and clinically relevant or major bleeding (BARC 2, 3 or 5) at one year. Propensity score matching was used to adjust for baseline differences. Results Among 1713 patients, 5.8% received ticagrelor-based DAT, 61.5% clopidogrel-based DAT, and 32.7% TAT. Ticagrelor-based DAT had similar MACCE rates (11% vs 12.5%), though higher observed rates of definite ST compared to clopidogrel-based DAT which remained significant after matching (4.6% vs 0.4%, p=0.028). MACCE rates were similar in ticagrelor-based DAT and TAT (11.0% vs 10.4%) which sustained after matching. Bleeding rates did not differ significantly between the two DAT strategies (15% vs 14.3%), but bleeding occurred less frequently with ticagrelor-based DAT than with clopidogrel-based TAT (15% vs 21.4%). Conclusions Intensification of platelet inhibition with ticagrelor was not associated with improved ischemic outcomes while bleeding rates were comparable to clopidogrel-based DAT and lower than with TAT.Central illustration
title: Ticagrelor-based dual antithrombotic therapy in anticoagulated patients undergoing PCI: a pooled analysis of two multicenter registries

abstract: Abstract Background In acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), early aspirin withdrawal with P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy after abbreviated dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) may reduce bleeding, but concerns persist regarding ischaemic safety. We synthesised randomised evidence using frequentist and Bayesian methods to quantify probabilities of benefit and harm. Methods Cochrane Library, Embase, PubMed, and Scopus were searched for randomised trials comparing short-term DAPT (1–3 months) followed by P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy versus standard-duration DAPT after PCI for ACS. Frequentist and Bayesian random-effects meta-analyses were performed; Bayesian models were fitted using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. Co-primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and clinically relevant bleeding (trial-defined). Results are reported as odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) or credible intervals (CrI) and Bayesian probabilities of benefit. Results Ten trials (30,873 participants) were included. Short-term DAPT halved clinically relevant bleeding (OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.41 - 0.56; I2 = 0%; Bayesian probability of benefit 100%) and major bleeding (OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.34 - 0.68; I2 = 38.7%). All-cause mortality numerically favoured short-term DAPT but did not reach significance (OR 0.89; 95% CI 0.67 to 1.19; Bayesian probability of benefit 79.5%). No increase was observed in myocardial infarction (OR 1.08; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.39), stent thrombosis (OR 1.09; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.66), or stroke (OR 0.94; 95% CI 0.68 to 1.30). Net adverse clinical events favoured short-term DAPT (OR 0.73; 95% CI 0.58 to 0.93; Bayesian probability of benefit 99.7%). Conclusions Short-term DAPT followed by P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy halves bleeding without significant increase in ischaemic events in ACS patients undergoing PCI. These findings support short-term DAPT as a bleeding avoidance strategy in appropriately selected patients.Outcome1Mortality
title: Short-term DAPT followed by P2Y12 monotherapy versus standard-term DAPT after PCI for ACS: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials

abstract: Abstract Background Antiplatelet therapy after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) plays a central role in preventing graft thrombosis and reducing adverse cardiovascular events. Aspirin is universally recommended as the cornerstone of postoperative antiplatelet therapy; however, the incremental benefit of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with ticagrelor remains uncertain. While some trials have suggested potential improvements in graft patency, concerns persist regarding bleeding risk and the lack of consistent benefit on clinical outcomes. Purpose To systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of ticagrelor-based DAPT following CABG in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) or stable coronary artery disease (CAD). Methods We conducted a systematic search of Embase, MEDLINE, and Cochrane databases from inception to December 2025 to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing ticagrelor plus aspirin versus aspirin monotherapy in patients undergoing CABG for ACS or stable CAD. Binary outcomes were pooled as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) using a Mantel–Haenszel common-effect model, while continuous outcomes were summarized as mean differences (MD). Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochrane’s Q test and Higgins and Thompson’s I² statistic. All analyses were performed using R software (version 4.4.2). Results Following PRISMA guidelines, 2,573 records were screened, and 4 RCTs comprising 3,101 patients were included, of whom 50.1% were allocated to ticagrelor-based DAPT. Using a common-effect model, ticagrelor-based DAPT was associated with a significantly higher risk of all-cause mortality over a follow-up ranging from 1 to 5 years compared with aspirin monotherapy (RR 2.15; 95% CI 1.17–3.94; p = 0.013), with moderate heterogeneity across studies (I² &lt; 50%). At 1 year, DAPT was also associated with significantly increased risks of major bleeding (RR 2.10; 95% CI 1.37–3.21; p &lt; 0.001) and minor bleeding (RR 2.92; 95% CI 1.72–4.96; p &lt; 0.001), both with moderate heterogeneity (I² &lt; 50%). Conclusion In patients undergoing CABG, ticagrelor-based dual antiplatelet therapy was associated with higher risks of all-cause mortality and bleeding. These findings highlight important safety concerns regarding the routine use of ticagrelor-based DAPT after CABG and support a cautious, individualized approach to postoperative antiplatelet management.Major and minor bleending after 1 year.All-cause mortality after 1-5 years.
title: Ticagrelor-based dual antiplatelet therapy versus aspirin monotherapy after CABG: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

abstract: Abstract Background Few data are available on platelet reactivity in patients exposed to potent P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy without aspirin. Methods This study was nested within the NEO-MINDSET trial, a multicenter, randomised trial evaluating potent P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy early after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for acute coronary syndrome (ACS) compared with dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT). In both groups, only prasugrel or ticagrelor were allowed, which were chosen at investigator discretion. This substudy aimed to assess treatment effects on platelet reactivity. Patients recruited at the coordinating site were eligible. Blood samples were collected pre-dose (trough) and 2-hour post-morning-dose (peak) at a single follow-up visit occurring after at least 30 days of exposure to the assigned treatment. Platelet reactivity was assessed by Platelet Function Analyzer-200 (PFA-200), VerifyNow, light transmittance aggregometry, and impedance aggregometry. Antiplatelet effects between study groups were assessed using linear mixed model for repeated measures. Results A total of 44 trial participants were enrolled: 22 assigned to monotherapy and 22 to DAPT. Mean age was 56.5 years and 36.4% were women. In each group, 16 (72.7%) received prasugrel and 6 (27.3%) received ticagrelor. The median time from randomization to platelet analysis was 183 days (interquartile range 36.8 to 202.5). In the monotherapy group, the mean platelet responses to collagen/epinephrine or arachidonic acid were within or close to the normal range at both trough and peak (Figures). In the DAPT group, platelet function was consistently inhibited with collagen/epinephrine or arachidonic acid at pre- and post-dose. In both groups, no significant increment in platelet inhibition was seen between pre-dose and post-dose values. Using collagen/ADP or ADP as agonists, results indicated platelet inhibition at both trough and peak in patients receiving monotherapy or DAPT. In the monotherapy group, greater platelet inhibition was achieved post-dose compared with pre-dose in PFA-200 (128.8 vs 161.7 seconds; p=0.04), VerifyNow (53.5 vs 24.7 PRU; p=0.003), and light transmission aggregometry (21.3% vs 11.9%; p=0.006). In the DAPT group, peak effects were observed in PFA-200 (228.9 vs 275.4 seconds; p=0.005) and VerifyNow (53.6 vs 27.1; p=0.003). Patients receiving monotherapy compared with DAPT had similar antiplatelet responses to ADP and smaller responses to arachidonic acid, collagen/epinephrine and collagen/ADP (all p-values &lt; 0.01). Conclusions Among patients undergoing successful PCI for ACS receiving monotherapy without aspirin, platelet function was inhibited in response to ADP at both pre- and post-dose, which suggests that potent P2Y12 inhibitor effects are preserved at trough. Conversely, platelet inhibition was greater with DAPT than monotherapy when agonists targeted to the cyclooxygenase-1 pathway were used.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Potent P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy without aspirin early after percutaneous coronary intervention: the NEO-MINDSET Platelet Function Substudy

abstract: Abstract Background The antiplatelet therapy following transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) remains controversial; lifelong single antiplatelet therapy (SAPT) is recommended in patients without an indication for oral anticoagulation, although dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) is routinely prescribed in patients at low bleeding risk. Balancing the prevention of thromboembolic events against the risk of bleeding is the cornerstone in the management of patients after TAVI. Purpose To evaluate whether single antiplatelet therapy improves safety and provides comparable ischemic protection to dual antiplatelet therapy following a TAVI in patients without an indication for oral anticoagulation. Methods A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane library databases (inception-February 2026) identified randomized trials and comparative observational studies enrolling post-TAVI patients without an indication for chronic anticoagulation. Studies comparing single antiplatelet therapy versus dual antiplatelet therapy were included. The primary outcomes were major or life-threatening bleeding and any bleeding. Secondary outcomes were stroke, myocardial infarction, all-cause mortality, and cardiovascular mortality. Pooled risk ratios were calculated using random-effects models in Review Manager. Results Eight studies (3 randomized trials and 5 cohort studies), comprising 15,222 patients, were included. Outcomes were analyzed by follow-up duration, with assessments at early (30 days) and mid-term (≥90 days). During mid-term follow-up, SAPT showed a non-significant trend toward lower major bleeding or life-threatening bleeding (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.46 - 1.33) and any bleeding (RR 0.80, 95% CI (0.60 - 1.06) compared with DAPT; no ischemic benefit of DAPT was observed for stroke (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.71 - 1.43) and myocardial infarction (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.62 - 1.50). Mortality outcomes were similar between antiplatelet strategies (All-cause mortality RR 1.40, 95% CI 0.98 - 1.98; CV mortality RR 1.70, 95% CI 0.80 - 3.65). Early outcomes were consistent with mid-term findings. Conclusions Single antiplatelet therapy in post-TAVI patients provides a comparable ischemic protection against dual antiplatelet therapy, with a tendency to lower bleeding events. DAPT does not provide consistent reductions in stroke, myocardial infarction, and mortality at early and mid-term follow-up. Routine use of DAPT after TAVI may not be justified, and treatment strategies should be individualized according to the patient's bleeding-risk profile.Figure 1.Mid-term outcomesFigure 2.Additionally mid-term outcomes
title: Single versus dual antiplatelet therapy after transcatheter aortic valve implantation in patients without an indication for anticoagulation: a systematic review and meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Dual antiplatelet therapy (APT) with aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor is the cornerstone of the pharmacological treatment in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) or undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to reduce the risk of ischemic complications. Abbreviated dual APT reduces bleeding with no increase in ischemic events in high bleeding risk (HBR) patients undergoing PCI. The risk of ischemic and bleeding events after PCI increases with age. Yet, the comparative effectiveness of abbreviated versus standard APT in elderly patients at HBR remains unknown. Purpose To investigate the impact of age on the comparative effectiveness and safety of abbreviated versus standard DAPT in the largest contemporary cohort of HBR patients undergoing PCI. Methods In the multicenter, randomized, open-label MASTER DAPT trial, 4,579 HBR patients were randomized at 1 month after PCI to an abbreviated or standard APT. Coprimary outcomes were net adverse clinical events (NACE), major adverse cardiac and cerebral events (MACCE), and major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding (BARC type 2, 3, or 5 bleeding) at 11 months after randomization. This pre-specified sub-study evaluates the outcomes of abbreviated versus standard DAPT according to patient age (≥ or &lt; 75 years). Results Of the 4579 patients included, 3154 (68.9%) were ≥75 years of age. Elderly patients had a higher cardiovascular risk profile, including arterial hypertension, diabetes mellitus, prior MI or complex PCI compared with patients aged less than 75 years. At 11-month follow-up, NACE did not differ with abbreviated and standard APT among patients aged ≥75 years (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.89; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.70-1.14) and &lt; 75 years (HR: 1.06; 95% CI: 0.72-1.56, Pinteraction= 0.47) (Figure 1). Similarly, MACCE did not differ in patients aged ≥75 years (HR: 0.90; 95% CI: 0.68-1.19) and &lt; 75 years (HR: 1.27; 95% CI:0.81- 1.99; Pinteraction= 0.21) (Figure 1). Abbreviated APT was associated with consistently lower BARC 2,3 or 5 bleeding in patients aged ≥75 years (HR: 0.66; 95% CI: 0.51-0.84) and &lt;75 years (HR: 0.76; 95% CI: 0.51-1.15; Pinteraction=0.53) (Figure 2).Cubic splines showed that the absolute risk reduction in bleeding with abbreviated APT progressively increased as a function of age. The rate of myocardial infarction was numerically higher with abbreviated versus standard APT in younger (2.7% vs 1.4%), but not in elderly patients (2.6% vs 2.5%). Conclusions Among HBR patients undergoing PCI, abbreviated APT was associated with comparable rates of NACE and MACCE and significantly reduced bleeding irrespective of age. These findings support an abbreviated APT regimen in HBR patients undergoing PCI, particularly in elderly patients who may derive greater bleeding benefit without increased ischemic risk compared with younger patients.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Impact of age on comparative outcomes of abbreviated versus standard antiplatelet therapy in patients at high bleeding risk: a pre-specified analysis from the MASTER-DAPT trial

abstract: Abstract Introduction The optimal P2Y12 inhibitor for long-term single antiplatelet therapy (SAPT) after acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remains uncertain. Evidence directly comparing the long-term efficacy and safety of prasugrel and clopidogrel as SAPT after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains limited. Purpose To compare the efficacy and safety of clopidogrel versus prasugrel monotherapy in patients with ACS after PCI. Methods This single-center observational study included consecutive ACS patients who underwent PCI between January 2019 and December 2021 (N=963). Follow-up was initiated only after both 6 months had elapsed since PCI and patients had transitioned to SAPT. Patients received clopidogrel 75 mg once daily or adjusted-dose prasugrel 3.75 mg once daily as monotherapy. The primary endpoint was net adverse clinical events (NACE), defined as a composite of all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, non-fatal cerebral infarction, stent thrombosis, and clinically relevant bleeding (BARC type 2, 3 and 5). The secondary endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and non-fatal cerebral infarction. Results A total of 283 patients were included in the final analysis, with 160 receiving clopidogrel and 123 receiving prasugrel (Figure 1). Compared with the prasugrel group, patients receiving clopidogrel were older, more frequently female, and had lower body weight. Furthermore, the proportion of patients meeting the Academic Research Consortium for High Bleeding Risk (ARC-HBR) criteria was higher in the clopidogrel monotherapy group. NACE occurred in 21.3% of patients in the clopidogrel group and 8.9% in the prasugrel group (P =0.005). MACE occurred in 17.5% and 4.9%, respectively (P=0.001) (Table 1). Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated a significantly higher cumulative incidence of NACE in the clopidogrel group compared with the prasugrel group (log-rank P=0.036; Figure 2A). Similarly, MACE was also more frequent in the clopidogrel group (log-rank P=0.024; Figure 2B). In multivariable analysis, clopidogrel monotherapy (OR 2.17, 95% CI 1.04–4.82; P=0.039) and ARC-defined high bleeding risk (OR 2.65, 95% CI 1.19–6.16; P=0.017) were independently associated with NACE (Table 2). Conclusion Among stabilized ACS patients in whom follow-up began at the later of 6 months after PCI and transition to SAPT, adjusted-dose prasugrel monotherapy was associated with lower ischemic and net adverse clinical events compared with clopidogrel monotherapy. Large-scale randomized controlled trials are warranted to confirm these findings.Picture 1Picture 2
title: Efficacy and safety of prasugrel monotherapy compared with clopidogrel in Japanese patients with acute coronary syndrome after percutaneous coronary intervention

abstract: Abstract introduction Risk prediction scores for bleeding such as ARC-HBR (Academic Research Consortium, HBR=high bleeding risk) and PRECISE-HBR have been developed for patients undergoing coronary stenting with dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT). Most validation studies are from clinical trials but their performance in real world populations of acute coronary syndrome treated with DAPT has seldom been explored. Methods We used a previously defined cohort of consecutive ACS patients treated with DAPT for 1 year in 5 English hospitals (ROBOT-ACS). Clinical outcomes were identified from the national Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) Admitted Patient Care database. All readmissions with a code for any form of bleeding underwent centrally coordinated adjudication using two experienced clinicians. Bleeding events were categorised using BARC (Bleeding Academic Research consortium) 3-5 criteria and PLATO (Platelet inhibition and Patient outcomes). ARC-HBR and precise-HBR bleeding risk scores were determined from covariates in the database and additional information from HES ICD-10 codes. Predicted versus actual major bleeding events and c-statistics (Reciever operator curves) for BARC 3-5 major bleeding event were determined for the total population and for ACS patients with potent DAPT (aspirin and ticagrelor) versus standard DAPT (aspirin and clopidogrel) Results 5116 patients formed the total study population. The median age was 68 and 34% were female. 52% of patients underwent coronary revascularisation (39% percutaneous coronary intervention, 13% coronary artery bypass surgery). Equal numbers of patients were prescribed ticagrelor versus clopidogrel (allied to aspirin) 1194 Bleeding events were tracked to 11 different English institutions. Clinical outcome data was 100% complete for bleeding. A total of 213 (4.2%) patients were adjudicated as suffering a BARC 3-5 major bleeding or PLATO major bleeding in the year following ACS. 26.6% (1302/4902) and 33.8% (1730/5116) of patients were categorised as high bleeding risk according to Precise-HBR and ARC-HBR scores respectively. Of those assigned very HBR by Precise-HBR, 6.3% had a BARC 3-5 bleed. The corresponding figure was 5.3% for ARC-HBR. Both scores predicted bleeding HBR better when potent antiplatelet (ticagrelor) was prescribed (allied to aspirin) (HBR as determined by Precise HBR: incidence of 1 year major bleed 8.5% vs 2.0% [non-HBR] p&lt;0.001, HBR as determined by ARC-HBR: incidence of 1 year major bleed 6.6% versus 2.0%[non-HBR]. P&lt;0.001 (table) The c-statistic for BARC 3-5 bleeding over 1 year, for all patients, was 0.62 and 0.61 for Precise-HBR and ARC-HBR respectively. Conclusion The performance of both precise-HBR and ARC-HBR bleeding risk scores was modest, but improved when assessing bleeding risk with potent antiplatelet prescription. Further work is required to improve risk tools to predict major bleeding, out with clinical trial populationsPerformance of bleeding risk scores

title: External validation of novel bleeding risk scores, ARC-HBR and PRECISE-HBR, in 5116 consecutive ACS patients in clinical practice

abstract: Abstract Background Aspirin monotherapy is currently recommended as the standard antiplatelet monotherapy for the secondary prevention of ischemic events in patients with established coronary artery disease (CAD). Emerging evidence suggests that, compared with aspirin, clopidogrel is associated with a lower incidence of ischemic events at long-term follow-up, without a concomitant increase in the risk of bleeding. However, it remains unclear whether these effects depend on patient age. Purpose To provide an assessment of the comparative efficacy and safety of clopidogrel versus aspirin monotherapy in patients with established CAD according to patient age. Methods The study represents a prespecified subanalysis of an individual patient data meta-analysis of 7 randomized trials in which patients were stratified according to a prespecified age cut off of 65 years. The main analysis was performed using semi-parametric shared log-normal frailty models (one-stage analysis), including a random intercept to account for differences in the baseline hazard across trials, and a random slope to account for between-trial differences in treatment effects. Secondary analyses included analyses by multivariable frailty models (multivariable one-stage analysis) and two-stage analyses. The primary efficacy endpoint was a composite of major adverse cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events (MACCE) including cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke, assessed at the maximum available follow-up of 5.5 years. The primary safety endpoint was major bleeding at the same follow-up duration. Results A total of 13,980 patients (48.2%) were included in the ≤65 years group (median age: 57 years) and 15,002 patients (51.8%) were included in the &gt;65 years group (median age: 74 years). Baseline characteristics were overall well balanced between treatment groups. At 5.5 years, the significant reduction in MACCE associated with clopidogrel monotherapy over aspirin monotherapy was consistent between age subgroups (≤65 years: hazard ratio [HR] 0.82, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.70-0.96; &gt;65 years: HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.76-1.00), with no significant interaction (Pint=0.577). The results remained unchanged after multivariable adjustment. At 5.5 years, the absence of significant differences in major bleeding between clopidogrel and aspirin monotherapies was consistent between age subgroups (≤65 years: HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.62-1.72; &gt;65 years: HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.72-1.14), with no significant interaction (Pint=0.). The results remained unchanged after multivariable adjustment. The two-stage analysis yielded consistent results for both MACCE and major bleeding. The effects were also consistent across all the secondary endpoints, regardless of the type of analysis. Conclusion Clopidogrel monotherapy is associated with a significant reduction in MACCE without a concomitant increase in major bleeding regardless of the patient age.MACCE
title: Clopidogrel versus aspirin for secondary prevention of coronary artery disease stratified by age: an individual patient data meta-analysis of 28,982 patients from 7 randomized trials

abstract: Abstract Background The clinical superiority between third-generation carvedilol and second-generation bisoprolol remains unclear in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) survivors undergoing contemporary primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). This study aimed to compare the long-term clinical outcomes of these two agents in a strictly defined STEMI cohort. Methods Using the nationwide Korea Acute Myocardial Infarction Registry, we identified 7,774 STEMI survivors who underwent successful primary PCI with second-generation drug-eluting stents. Patients were stratified based on prescription of either carvedilol (n=4,725) or bisoprolol (n=3,049) at discharge. To minimize selection bias, 1:1 propensity-score matching (PSM) was performed. The primary endpoint was 3-year all-cause mortality, and secondary endpoints included major adverse cardiac events (MACE). Results PSM yielded a well-balanced cohort of 5,186 patients, with 2,593 in each group. At 3 years, there was no significant difference in all-cause mortality between the carvedilol and bisoprolol groups (4.3% vs. 4.2%; HR 1.019; 95% CI 0.778-1.333; P=0.945). The incidence of MACE was also comparable (11.0% vs. 11.5%; HR 0.958; 95% CI 0.806-1.138; P=0.660). These neutral findings were consistent across major clinical subgroups, including patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction. Conclusion In STEMI survivors treated with contemporary primary PCI, carvedilol and bisoprolol demonstrated comparable 3-year clinical outcomes. This prognostic parity allows clinicians to individualize beta-blocker selection without compromising long-term survival or ischemic protection.

title: Comparative clinical outcomes of carvedilol versus bisoprolol in STEMI survivors after primary PCI: a propensity-score matched analysis

abstract: Abstract Background β-blockers are a core medication for the secondary prevention of acute coronary syndrome (ACS). However, their long-term benefits in ACS patients with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≥50% remain controversial. Previous studies have mostly focused on static medication status, lacking analyses of dynamic medication adherence trajectories and heterogeneity across ACS subtypes. Purpose This study aimed to identify and classify trajectory patterns of β-blocker use after discharge using Group-Based Trajectory Modeling (GBTM) in ACS patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with LVEF ≥50%, to investigate the association between different adherence trajectory groups and 5-year clinical outcomes, and to clarify potential heterogeneity of this association across different clinical subtypes. Methods We enrolled patients who were prescribed β-blockers at discharge and had no adverse events within 1 year after discharge. GBTM was used to characterize β-blocker adherence trajectories during the first year after PCI, and the correlation between different trajectory groups and clinical outcomes was further evaluated. Stratified analyses were performed according to ACS type to explore subtype-specific differences in this correlation. The primary endpoint was defined as major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCE) within 5 years after PCI, a composite endpoint consisting of all-cause death, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and any revascularization. Secondary endpoints were the individual components of the primary endpoint. Results A total of 3552 patients on β-blocker therapy with no adverse events (death, MI, stroke, revascularization, rehospitalization) within 1 year were included. Based on 1-year post-discharge β-blocker adherence trajectories, patients were divided into three groups: consistent adherence (n=1645), fluctuating adherence (n=965), and rapid discontinuation (n=942). The incidence of MACCE was significantly lower in the consistent adherence group (10.6% vs 13.5% vs 14.4%, P=0.010). However, multivariate Cox regression showed no significant difference in 5-year MACCE risk between the other two groups and the consistent adherence group. Subgroup analysis by ACS type demonstrated that in the AMI subgroup, rapid discontinuation was associated with a significantly higher MACCE risk (adjusted HR: 1.747, 95%CI: 1.212–2.518, P=0.003), whereas no significant difference was observed in the unstable angina subgroup. Conclusions In ACS patients with LVEF ≥50%, the long-term impact of β-blockers on clinical outcomes depends on medication adherence and disease subtype. Among AMI patients, good post-discharge β-blocker adherence significantly reduces the risk of adverse cardiovascular events. Thus, β-blocker use should be individually evaluated in these ACS patients, and enhanced adherence management in AMI patients may improve long-term prognosis.
title: β-blocker adherence trajectories and 5-year clinical outcomes in PCI-treated ACS patients with LVEF ≥50%: a group-based trajectory modeling analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Sexual dysfunction is common after myocardial infarction (MI), but the role of beta-blockers on these disturbances remains unclear. Purpose To evaluate the presence of beta-blocker induced sexual dysfunction in post-MI patients without a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF ≥40%) enrolled in the BETAMI-DANBLOCK trial. Methods A prespecified analysis of data from BETAMI-DANBLOCK which randomly assigned patients with a recent MI and an LVEF ≥40% to open-label beta-blocker therapy (median treatment dose metoprolol 50mg/day) or no beta-blocker therapy. For patients reporting sexual activity within the past 12 months, sexual function during the past 4 weeks was assessed at baseline and follow-up (3, 12, and 21 months) with the 5-item International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF, men) and the 6-item Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI, women). Sum scores for IIEF (range 5–25) and FSFI (6–30) provides measures of sexual function increasing with higher sexual function; thresholds for dysfunction were IIEF ≤21 and FSFI ≤19. Beta-blocker effects on IIEF and FSFI scores were analysed as between-group differences in change using linear mixed models (negative estimates indicating worse sexual function with beta-blockers). Odds ratios (ORs) for sexual dysfunction were estimated with multivariable logistic regression adjusting for randomisation stratification variables LVEF and study site. Results Among 5574 patients in BETAMI-DANBLOCK, 2850 stated sexual activity within past year at baseline. Of these, 2332/2850 (82%) responded to IIEF or FSFI at least once during the trial period. Among men, baseline median IIEF score was 23 (IQR: 19-24) in the beta-blocker group and 23 (IQR: 19-25) in the no beta-blocker group, with 39% reporting scores indicating erectile dysfunction and 12% in DANBLOCK dispensing sildenafil. We found no statistically significant effect of beta-blockers on the total IIEF score during follow-up (Table). However, the odds of erectile dysfunction was slightly higher in the beta-blocker group at the first follow-up (3 months OR: 1.58, 95% CI: 1.02, 2.42), but not on the subsequent timepoints. The proportion of filled sildenafil prescriptions was similar in the beta-blocker and no beta-blocker group (18% vs 17%) during follow-up in DANBLOCK. Among women, median FSFI score at baseline was 24 (IQR: 20-27) and 24 (IQR: 18-27), with 24% and 31% of patients having a score indicating sexual dysfunction for the beta-blocker group and the no beta-blocker group, respectively. We found no effect of beta-blocker therapy on FSFI scores during follow-up, but effect estimates were uncertain. Conclusions In the BETAMI-DANBLOCK trial, beta-blocker therapy after MI was associated with a small transient increase in erectile dysfunction among men, but no long-term effects were observed.
title: Beta-blocker therapy and sexual dysfunction after myocardial infarction: a sub-study of the BETAMI-DANBLOCK trial

abstract: Abstract Introduction Beta-blockers have long been recommended after myocardial infarction (MI) based on evidence from the pre- reperfusion era. However, in the contemporary era of routine percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and guideline-directed medical therapy, the benefit of long-term beta-blocker use in patients with preserved or mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) remains uncertain. This meta- analysis evaluated whether beta-blocker therapy, compared with no therapy or treatment discontinuation, reduces major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in this population. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled and comparative trials published from January 2000 to October 2025 was conducted using major medical databases. Eligible studies enrolled adult post-MI patients with preserved or mildly reduced LVEF and compared beta-blocker therapy with no therapy or interruption. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality, with secondary outcomes including cardiovascular death, recurrent MI, heart failure hospitalization, and stroke. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-effects models. Results Five randomized controlled trials—REBOOT CNIC, BETAMI, DANBLOCK, REDUCE-AMI, CAPITAL RCT, and the ABYSS trial—comprising a total of 23,524 patients were included in the analysis. Overall, participants were predominantly male, in their early to mid-60s, had preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, and underwent PCI with high use of contemporary guideline-directed medical therapy. Beta-blocker therapy was associated with a modest but statistically significant reduction in all-cause mortality (RR 0.92; 95% CI 0.85–0.99). However, no significant differences were observed in cardiovascular death, recurrent myocardial infarction, hospitalization for heart failure, or stroke. Heterogeneity across the evaluated outcomes was low. Conclusion In the contemporary PCI era, beta-blocker therapy after MI confers a small survival benefit but does not significantly reduce specific cardiovascular events in patients with preserved or mildly reduced LVEF, supporting an individualized approach to long-term therapy.
title: Beta-blocker therapy after myocardial infarction in the PCI Era: an updated meta-analysis

abstract: Abstract Background The multinational registry-based pragmatic randomised trial REDUCE-AMI showed that initiation of beta-blocker treatment in individuals with myocardial infarction and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF ≥ 50%) did not reduce the risk of death or recurrent myocardial infarction compared with no beta-blockers in an intention-to-treat analysis (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% confidence interval 0.79, 1.16) (1). However, among participants in Sweden who attended follow-up visits, 18.1% of those assigned to beta-blockers were reported to have discontinued treatment by 11–13 months, while 14.3% of those assigned to no beta-blockers were reported to have initiated beta-blockers. A secondary analysis of the trial is required to assess the per-protocol effect of beta-blockers compared with no beta-blockers under full adherence to the treatment strategies. Methods We restricted the per protocol analysis to the Swedish participants of the REDUCE-AMI trial for whom linked longitudinal data were available. All dispensation data relating to the beta-blockers metoprolol succinate and bisoprolol (the treatment strategies defined in the trial protocol) were manually extracted. Individuals were censored if and when they deviated from their assigned treatment strategy, taking into consideration time varying indications and contraindications (2). Risks were estimated using pooled logistic regression models with adjustment via inverse probability weighting for baseline and time-varying covariates associated with non-adherence to account for selection bias introduced by informative censoring. Results The study population was composed of 4,786 individuals. The median follow up was 30 months in the beta-blocker group and 38 months in the no beta-blocker group. Adherence was 71.8% in the beta-blocker group, and 89.7% in the no beta-blocker group. The estimated 5-year adjusted risk of the composite outcome of death or recurrent myocardial infarction was 10.2% (8.5%, 12.0%) in the beta-blocker group and 11.7% (10.1%, 13.4%) in the no beta-blocker group, corresponding to a risk difference of -1.5% (-3.9%, 1.0%), a risk ratio of 0.87 (0.70, 1.10), and an average hazard ratio by 5 years of 0.87 (0.70, 1.10). Discussion This per protocol analysis found little evidence of a large effect of beta-blockers on the composite outcome of death or myocardial infarction in individuals with myocardial infarction and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, consistent with intention-to-treat estimates.Estimated risk of death or MI
title: Long-term effect of beta-blockers after myocardial infarction with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction in a per protocol analysis of the REDUCE-AMI trial

abstract: Abstract Background The benefit of beta-blocker therapy in elderly patients without left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVSD) following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for acute myocardial infarction (MI) remains unclear. Moreover, data regarding the long-term clinical outcomes associated with beta-blocker use in this specific population are limited. Purpose This study aimed to evaluate the long-term clinical impact of beta-blocker therapy in elderly patients who underwent PCI for acute MI and had no evidence of LVSD. Methods Among 13,104 patients with acute MI who underwent PCI and were enrolled in a nationwide, prospective, real-world registry, 2,566 elderly patients (defined as ≥70 years) without LVSD (defined as EF ≥50%) were included in the analysis. Of these, 2,063 patients received beta-blockers, whereas 503 did not. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiac events (MACE), defined as a composite of cardiac death, recurrent MI, any revascularization, readmission due to heart failure (HF), stroke, or definite/probable stent thrombosis (ST). MACE and its individual components were compared using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models, propensity score (PS) matching, and PS-adjusted analyses. Results Over a median follow-up duration of 998 days, MACE, all-cause mortality, and cardiac mortality occurred in 560 (21.8%), 374 (14.6%), and 224 (8.7%) patients, respectively. The beta-blocker group demonstrated significantly lower rates of MACE (entire cohort: 20.9% vs. 25.4%, hazard ratio [HR] 0.66, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.58–0.76, p=0.03; PS-matched cohort: n=986, 20.3% vs. 25.8%, HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.61–0.78, p&lt;0.001), all-cause mortality (entire cohort: 12.9% vs. 21.5%, HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.44–0.69, p&lt;0.001; PS-matched cohort: 11.8% vs. 20.9%, HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.47–0.72, p&lt;0.001), and cardiac mortality (entire cohort: 7.7% vs. 13.1%, HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.41–0.72, p&lt;0.001; PS-matched cohort: 7.3% vs. 13.5%, HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.43–0.79, p&lt;0.001) compared with the no beta-blocker group. There were no significant differences between the two groups in the risks of recurrent MI, any revascularization, readmission due to HF, stroke, or definite/probable ST. The reduced risk of MACE associated with beta-blocker use was consistently observed across predefined subgroups. In patients aged ≥80 years, beta-blocker therapy was associated with numerically lower rates of MACE, all-cause death, cardiac death, recurrent MI, any revascularization, readmission due to HF, stroke, and definite/probable ST compared with no beta-blocker therapy, but insignificantly. Conclusions In this nationwide registry, beta-blocker therapy was associated with improved long-term clinical outcomes compared with no beta-blocker use in elderly patients without LVSD following PCI for acute MI.BB for old pEF AMI PCI
title: Long-term clinical outcomes of beta-blocker therapy in elderly patients with preserved left ventricular function after percutaneous coronary intervention for acute myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background While proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitors (PCSK9i) effectively lower low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels and reduce the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with STEMI, the anti-inflammatory effects and impact on early cardiac remodeling of PCSK9i remain unclear. Purpose This study aims to investigate the effects of PCSK9i on early inflammatory factors[interleukin (IL)-1β , IL-18, IL-17A, and CC chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2)] and left ventricular (LV) function in ST-elevation-myocardial infarction(STEMI) patients. Methods Totally 257 STEMI participants were divided into 2 groups based on their real-world prescriptions: those treated with statin only (statin group) and those treated with statin in addition to the evolocumab (evolocumab group). Serum levels of IL-1β , IL-18, IL-17A, and CCR2 were measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay at baseline, 1 week, and 4 weeks. LV function was assessed by echocardiography at baseline, 4 weeks and 12 weeks. Results At 4 weeks, the evolocumab group exhibited a greater reduction in IL-1β (−29.35% ± 12.08%, from 16.95 to 11.96mmol/L) compared to statin alone (-25.27% ± 10.89%, from 16.64 to 12.48 mmol/L), with a mean between-group difference of -4.08% (95% CI: -7.24% to -0.91%, p= 0.012). Similarly, IL-17A decreased more significantly with evolocumab (-30.22% ± 15.91%, from 5.64 to 3.88 mmol/L) than with statin therapy (-25.35% ± 15.91%, from 5.73 to 4.21 mmol/L), with a mean between-group difference of -4.88% (95% CI: -9.06% to -0.69%, p = 0.023). By 12 weeks, evolocumab significantly improved LV ejection fraction (7.53% ± 7.44% vs 5.07% ± 8.05%, p=0.007) , especially in the patients with LVEF&lt;50% at baseline (11.36% vs. 7.40%, p = 0.014) and increased the incidence of LV global function improvement (ΔEF≥ 5%: 78.2% vs 55.1%, p&lt;0.001) compared to statin alone. Multivariate analysis identified the use of evolocumab (OR= 4.36, 95% CI = 1.16-16.23, p=0.029), reductions in IL-1β (OR= 1.49, 95% CI= 1.10-2.02, p=0.011) and IL-17A (OR= 1.47, 95% CI =1.02-2.11, p=0.037) at 4 weeks as independent predictors of ΔEF≥ 5% at 12 weeks adjusted for the change in LDL-C. Mediation analysis showed that 8.74% and 9.60% of LV functional improvement were attributable to reductions in IL-1β and IL-17A respectively. Conclusions Early evolocumab therapy in STEMI rapidly attenuates inflammation and improves left ventricular function, with partially mediated by IL-1β/IL-17A axis. Our findings support evolocumab's role beyond lipid-lowering, suggesting that early PCSK9 inhibition as a potential strategy to mitigate early inflammation-driven cardiac dysfunction in STEMI management.
title: Evolocumab early reduces Interleukin-1β/Interleukin-17A and improves left ventricular function in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: an observational study in the real world

abstract: Abstract Background Despite strong recommendations from the European Society of Cardiology / European Atherosclerosis Society for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) &lt;55 mg/dL after acute coronary syndrome (ACS), real-world attainment remains suboptimal. Whether systematic early reassessment, combined with the predominant use of oral combination lipid-lowering therapy (LLT), can achieve durable target control is uncertain. Purpose To evaluate longitudinal LDL-C goal attainment and the impact of sustained combination therapy in a consecutive post-ACS percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) cohort managed under a structured intensive lipid strategy. Methods All consecutive ACS patients undergoing PCI between October 2022 and January 2026 were included. Institutional policy mandated intensive LLT at discharge, favouring dual or predominantly triple oral therapy targeting LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL, with repeat lipid testing encouraged every 3–6 months. Predefined follow-up intervals were analysed up to 36 months. The proportions achieving LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL and receiving combination therapy were assessed longitudinally. Results At 1 month, 93.8% of patients received combination therapy, and 78.6% achieved LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL. Goal attainment remained high during the first year (77–79%) while combination therapy use exceeded 86%. Beyond 12 months, a progressive reduction in combination therapy (to ~74% at 18–24 months) was paralleled by declining LDL-C target achievement (74.4% at 18 months; 67.7% at 24 months). At 36 months, LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL was achieved in 51.1% of patients. Temporal reductions in treatment intensity were consistently associated with a decline in LDL-C target durability. Conclusion In a real-world ACS population, structured early reassessment combined with predominant oral combination therapy achieved high guideline-recommended initial LDL-C goal attainment. However, therapeutic de-intensification beyond the first year undermined long-term maintenance of lipid targets. Sustained combination therapy and systematic follow-up are essential to prevent late loss of control.Table
title: Sustained combination lipid-lowering therapy determines durability of LDL-C &lt;55 mg/dL after ACS: a structured implementation study (2022–2026)

abstract: Abstract Background Alirocumab, a PCSK9 inhibitor, is widely used in Hong Kong for managing dyslipidaemia in high-risk patients. However, real-world data comparing different dosing intervals are limited. Understanding whether dosing frequency influences lipid outcomes, medication adherence, and cardiovascular events may inform clinical practice and healthcare planning. Purpose This study aimed to evaluate the clinical and lipid outcomes of patients prescribed biweekly versus monthly alirocumab across Hong Kong, with a subgroup analysis focusing on patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Methods A retrospective territory-wide cohort study was conducted, including all adults prescribed alirocumab between June 1, 2020, and December 31, 2025. Patients were categorized according to dosing frequency (biweekly or monthly). The primary outcome was 12-month major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), comprising myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularization (PCI/CABG), or cardiovascular death. Secondary outcomes included compliance (defined as discontinuation of therapy) and achievement of LDL-cholesterol (LDL-C) goals: &lt;1.4 mmol/L, &lt;1.8 mmol/L, and &gt;50% reduction from baseline. Subgroup analyses were performed for patients with ACS. Statistical comparisons were conducted using appropriate inferential tests. Results A total of 2012 patients were included, with 72.0% receiving biweekly and 28.0% monthly dosing. At 12 months, there was no statistically significant difference in the incidence of MACE between groups (8.6% vs. 8.9%; p=0.829). Monthly dosing was associated with superior treatment persistence (83.7% vs. 77.2%; p=0.001) and higher proportions achieving LDL-C targets at all thresholds: &lt;1.4 mmol/L (64.8% vs. 54.0%; p=&lt;0.001), &lt;1.8 mmol/L (75.5% vs. 66.2%; p=0.002), and &gt;50% LDL reduction (56.6% vs. 48.0%; p=0.007). In the ACS subgroup (n=404), both regimens demonstrated comparable rates of MACE and lipid control (all p&gt;0.05). Conclusions In this real-world Hong Kong cohort, monthly alirocumab dosing led to better adherence and LDL target attainment but similar cardiovascular outcomes compared with biweekly dosing. Among ACS patients, efficacy was comparable. Monthly dosing appears to be a convenient and effective option for maintaining lipid control without compromising safety.
title: Real-world outcomes of biweekly and monthly alirocumab regimens: a population-based analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Observational data have suggested an inverse relationship between lipoprotein [Lp](a) and risk of bleeding, including cerebral hemorrhage. This is a potential safety concern for investigational Lp(a)-lowering agents. In a post hoc analysis of the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial, we evaluated the association of Lp(a) and bleeding events. The trial population with recent acute coronary syndromes (ACS) was opportune due to high prevalent use of potent antiplatelet therapy. Methods ODYSSEY OUTCOMES enrolled 18924 patients 1-12 months post ACS and elevated atherogenic lipoproteins despite optimized statin therapy, randomized to PCSK9 inhibitor alirocumab (ALI) or placebo, and followed for median 2.8 years. Lp(a) was measured by mass assay at baseline, months 4 and 12. Investigator-reported serious bleeding events were identified from serious adverse events lists, blinded to treatment assignment. An adjusted analysis accounted for study treatment, baseline use of antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents, systolic blood pressure, and history of hypertension or diabetes. Because arterial revascularization occurred more often after randomization in patients with higher Lp(a) and often leads to intensified antiplatelet therapy (and thus risk of bleeding), it was accounted for as a time-varying covariate. Results At baseline, median (Q1, Q3) Lp(a) was 21.3 (6.7, 59.6) mg/dL; 89% of patients were treated with at least one antiplatelet agent. Alirocumab reduced time-weighted Lp(a) by a mean 25%. There were 334 first serious bleeding events (including adjudicated hemorrhagic strokes). The adjusted analysis showed a non-significant trend to higher serious bleeding risk with higher baseline Lp(a) quartile (Figure, Ptrend across Lp(a) quartiles 0.10). There was also no relation between 55 intracranial bleedings and Lp(a) quartiles (Ptrend 0.67) Overall, there were numerically fewer serious bleeding events with ALI than with placebo: HR (95% CI) = 0.810 (0.653, 1.005), p=0.056. This treatment effect was consistent across quartile of baseline Lp(a) (Ptrend =0.64). Finally, in the ALI group with 150 serious bleeding events, there was a lower risk of bleeding with time-weighted decreases of log2(Lp(a)) from baseline (adjusted p=0.01): for the mean decrease in Lp(a), the HR for bleeding (95% CI) was 0.86 (0.77, 0.97). Conclusion In this post hoc analysis, there was no evidence of an inverse association of Lp(a) levels with serious bleeding or with cerebral hemorrhage. There was no indication that treatment with ALI or decreases in Lp(a) on ALI increased bleeding; to the contrary, decreases in Lp(a) on ALI were associated with decreased bleeding risk, a finding that might be related to ALI prevention of ischemic events and therefore intensity or duration of antiplatelet therapy. These reassuring findings require confirmation in ongoing randomized trials evaluating targeted Lp(a)-lowering agents.Figure
title: Association of lipoprotein(a) levels with risk of serious bleeding : findings from the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial

abstract: Abstract Background ODYSSEY OUTCOMES demonstrated that alirocumab reduces cardiovascular event rates after acute coronary syndrome. VESALIUS-CV recently showed that evolocumab lowers cardiovascular event rates in patients without prior myocardial infarction (MI) or stroke. Data on alirocumab effectiveness in patients without prior ischemic events are limited. Aim To evaluate 4-year absolute and relative risk reductions in major adverse cardiovascular events after initiation of alirocumab in patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) without prior MI, unstable angina, or ischemic stroke. Methods OPTIMUS-EPIC (Outcomes and PrevenTIon program with PCSK9i Monoclonal antibodies in ASCVD PopUlation without prior iSchemic events) is an observational comparative-effectiveness study using the PHARMO Data Network. Using this population-based network of linked electronic healthcare databases in the Netherlands (2016-2024), adults with established ASCVD and no prior MI, unstable angina, or ischemic stroke were identified. New users of alirocumab (75 mg Q2W, 150 mg Q2W, or 300 mg Q4W) were propensity-score matched (1:3) to patients not receiving a PCSK9 inhibitor. The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause death, MI, or ischemic stroke. Four-year cumulative incidence was evaluated using observed rates in the matched cohort and using target-trial emulation with g-computation, both under an intention-to-treat framework. The confounder set for g-computation comprised all baseline characteristics (Table). Results A total of 4,008 patients were included in the study (1,008 alirocumab users and 3,000 matched comparators). Median (IQR) age was 66 (59-72) years in the alirocumab group and 66 (59-73) years in the comparator group, and 62% of alirocumab users versus 63% of comparators were male. Baseline median (IQR) LDL-C levels were 3.4 (2.6-4.3) mmol/L in the alirocumab group and 3.3 (2.5-4.4) mmol/L in the comparator group. Use of lipid-lowering therapy, including statin+ ezetimibe combination, was high in both groups (Table). At 4 years, the observed primary endpoint rate (95%CI) was 9.5% (7.0-12.0%) with alirocumab versus 15.5% (13.8-17.0%) without a PCSK9 inhibitor, with an absolute risk reduction (ARR) of 6.0% (3.0-9.0%; p&lt;0.001) and relative risk reduction (RRR) of 38.7% (18.7-58.7%; p&lt;0.001); (Figure 1A). Using g-computation, the 4-year primary endpoint rate (95%CI) was 9.4% (7.6-11.5%) with alirocumab versus 15.3% (13.9-17.0%) without a PCSK9 inhibitor, with ARR of 5.9% (3.3%-8.2%; p&lt;0.001) and RRR of 38.6% (21.0-50.7%; p&lt;0.001); (Figure 1B). Conclusions In this population-based cohort of patients with ASCVD without prior acute ischemic events, alirocumab was associated with lower 4-year risk of all-cause death, MI, or ischemic stroke, supporting the clinical value of alirocumab in these patients and complementing recent randomized trial evidence.KM
title: Alirocumab and cardiovascular outcomes in patients without a prior ischemic event

abstract: Abstract Introduction Repeated testing of lipoprotein(a) (Lp(a)) levels is generally viewed as unnecessary for most individuals since concentrations are largely genetically determined. Given that Lp(a)-targeting therapeutics under development are focused on concentrations above certain thresholds, there is a need to determine whether there are characteristics associated with greater variability in Lp(a) measurements over time, which might impact eligibility for these emerging treatments and therefore warrant repeated testing. Purpose To document predictors of variability in Lp(a) measurements in a cohort of high-risk participants on optimized statin therapy following an acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Methods The analysis cohort comprised participants from the placebo arm of the ODYSSEY OUTCOMES study with measurements of Lp(a) mass concentration at randomization, month 4, and month 12. Participants were randomized 1-12 (median 2.6) months after qualifying ACS; accordingly, baseline values were not expected to be influenced by an acute phase response resulting from ACS. A plot of the per-participant mean versus the maximum difference of the three measurements relative to the mean was generated to summarize variability in the measurements. The range of measurements was related to participant characteristics in linear regression models, overall and for subsets above the LLQ and with averages above clinically relevant thresholds. Results Among 9462 participants, 9212 (97.3%) had baseline, month 4, and month 12 Lp(a) assessments; none initiated PCSK9i therapy prior to 12 months, and median (IQR) was 21.6 (6.6, 60.1), 20.0 (6.1, 58.4), and 20.3 (6.1, 59.4) mg/dL, respectively. The measurements were strongly correlated (all pairwise Spearman r&gt;0.95); absolute but not relative variability increased with average concentration (Figure). Of 27,636 Lp(a) measurements, 7286 (26.4%) deviated from the per-participant means by more than ±20%, and 1180 (4.3%) deviated from the per-participant means by more than ±20 mg/dL. Furthermore, 8.6% of 1181 participants with baseline Lp(a) 30 to &lt;50 mg/dL had at least one subsequent measurement &gt;=70mg/dL, whereas 5.8% of 1923 participants with baseline Lp(a) &gt;=70mg/dL had at least one subsequent measurement &lt;50 mg/dL. While several characteristics were related to range, only baseline and average Lp(a) explained a meaningful proportion of the variance in this outcome (Table). Conclusion Over 12 months, material fractions of individuals at high risk for cardiovascular events but unselected for Lp(a) shifted in and out of ranges studied in Lp(a)-targeting outcomes studies. Baseline and average concentration explained a meaningful proportion of variability, suggesting repeated testing of those with relatively high Lp(a) may be warranted to determine eligibility for treatment if these therapeutics are ultimately indicated for individuals with elevated levels.
title: Variability in lipoprotein(a) measurements in ODYSSEY OUTCOMES: is one-and-done testing sufficient?

abstract: Abstract Background Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease driven by dyslipidemia and activation of immune system. Scavenger receptors CD16+, CD36+ and CD45+ on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) are involved in foam cell formation and endothelial dysfunction, promoting atherosclerosis. Although protein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors (PCSK9i) effectively lower lipid concentration and reduce cardiovascular events, their impact on above mentioned scavenger receptors remains poorly understood. Purpose We aimed to examine the impact of PCSK9i treatment on the expression of scavender receptors CD16+, CD36+ and CD45+ on PBMC, and their association with lipoprotein levels in patients with stable coronary disease and significantly elevated lipoprotein (a) (Lp(a)) levels. Methods In randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial we included 100 statin-treated patients in stable phase after myocardial infarction elevated Lp(a) values. The patients received PCSK9i or placebo every two weeks for 6 months. Biochemical and cell analysis at baseline and after 6 months were performed. Results Treatment with PCSK9i significantly decreased concentration of PBMCs expressing CD16+ and CD45+ (p=0.046 and p&lt;0.001, respectively), and non-classical monocytes (NCM) expressing CD36+ (p=0.019), while no differences were observed among classical (CM) or intermediate monocytes (IM) expressing CD36+, neither in the placebo group. After treatment with PCSK9i, expression of IM CD36+ was associated with changes in Lp(a) (ρ=-0.276, p=0.029), total cholesterol (ρ=-0.306, p=0.014), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (ρ=-0.276, p=0.027) and apolipoprotein B (ρ=-0.400, p=0.001). Additionally, expression of NCM CD36+ was associated with changes in Lp(a) (ρ=-0.252, p=0.046). No significant associations were observed between lipid parameters and monocyte subsets in the placebo group. Conclusion In patients with stable coronary disease and elevated Lp(a) levels, treatment with PCSK9i significantly decreases expression of scavenger receptors CD16+, CD36+ and CD45+ on PBMCs.
title: Treatment with PCSK9 inhibitors reduces the expression of scavenger receptors CD16, CD36 and CD45 in patients with stable coronary artery disease and elevated Lp(a) levels

abstract: Abstract Background Current European Society of Cardiology/European Atherosclerosis Society (ESC/EAS) guidelines recommend aggressive low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) targets of &lt;55 mg/dL for acute coronary syndrome (ACS) patients, with a more stringent target of &lt;40 mg/dL for recurrent events. However, real-world achievement rates across different lipid-lowering regimens remain poorly characterized. Methods We analyzed 298 ACS patients with valid baseline LDL-C measurements (mean 99.7 ± 40.8 mg/dL) from a tertiary care cohort. We performed McNemar's tests to account for the paired nature of the data.We simulated LDL-C reduction with seven treatment regimens: low-intensity statin (25% reduction), moderate-intensity statin (35%), high-intensity statin (50%), low-intensity statin plus ezetimibe (40%), moderate-intensity statin plus ezetimibe (48%), high-intensity statin plus ezetimibe (65%), and triple therapy with high-intensity statin, ezetimibe, and PCSK9 inhibitor (85%). Target achievement rates were calculated for both &lt;55 mg/dL and &lt;40 mg/dL thresholds, with statistical comparisons performed using chi-squared and pairwise tests. Results The distribution of baseline LDL-C categories was as follows: 81 patients (27.2%) had baseline LDL-C &lt;70 mg/dL, 76 patients (25.5%) had LDL-C 70-100 mg/dL, 63 patients (21.1%) had LDL-C 100-130 mg/dL, 43 patients (14.4%) had LDL-C 130-160 mg/dL, and 35 patients (11.7%) had LDL-C ≥160 mg/dL (Table 1). This distribution indicates substantial heterogeneity in baseline lipid profiles, with approximately one-quarter of patients having relatively well-controlled LDL-C at baseline and another quarter having markedly elevated levels requiring intensive therapy.High-intensity statin monotherapy achieved the &lt;55 mg/dL target in 61.9% of patients, while the addition of ezetimibe increased achievement to 88.1% (χ² = 29.03, p &lt; 0.0001). Triple therapy achieved 100% target attainment for &lt;55 mg/dL (χ² = 12.07, p = 0.0005 vs. high-intensity statin plus ezetimibe). For the &lt;40 mg/dL target, achievement rates were 38.1%, 65.3%, and 100% for high-intensity statin, high-intensity statin plus ezetimibe, and triple therapy, respectively (Figure 1). Baseline LDL-C category analysis revealed that patients with baseline LDL-C ≥160 mg/dL required triple therapy to reach guideline targets, while those with baseline LDL-C &lt;100 mg/dL achieved targets with high-intensity statin monotherapy. Conclusions High-intensity statin monotherapy is insufficient for most ACS patients to achieve ESC/EAS LDL-C targets. To bridge the gap between guidelines and clinical practice, early initiation of combination therapy is essential, particularly for patients with baseline LDL-C 160 mg/dL who necessitate a "triple therapy" approach from the outset.Figure 1:Target achievementTable :Baseline LDL levels
title: Comparative effectiveness of lipid-lowering regimens for achieving ESC LDL-cholesterol targets in acute coronary syndrome: a real-world cohort analysis

abstract: Abstract Introduction The persistence of coronary events in statin-treated patients highlights residual risk mechanisms beyond low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), with lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] playing a pivotal role. Treatment with statins has been suggested to be associated with an elevation in plasma Lp(a) levels, though the clinical significance remains uncertain. Purpose This study analyzes Lp(a) levels and their relationship with prior statin therapy, as well as their association with a diagnosis of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) prior to admission in patients hospitalized for acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Methods This observational study included 729 patients admitted for ACS with available Lp(a) measurements. Clinical variables, lipid profile, prior statin therapy, and adherence assessed by the 8-item Morisky Medication Adherence Scale were recorded. The association between prior statin therapy and log-transformed Lp(a) levels was evaluated using multivariable linear regression adjusted for confounding factors. Additionally, propensity score matching (1:1 nearest neighbor, caliper 0.2) was performed as a sensitivity analysis, yielding 117 matched pairs. Sample size was estimated a priori to ensure 80% power (α=0.05) to detect a small effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.20). Based on an estimated standard deviation of 1.33, a minimum of 722 participants was required; thus, the final cohort of 729 patients (361 on statins and 368 statin-naive) provided adequate statistical power. Results Prior statin therapy was present in 49.5% of patients. These subjects exhibited lower LDL-C and apoB, but higher Lp(a) levels (77 [26–181] vs. 56 [26–133] nmol/L; p = 0.009) (figure). However, this association lost significance after multivariable adjustment (B = 0.025; 95% CI −0.204 to 0.255; p = 0.829) and propensity score adjustment (p = 0.686). Neither statin intensity [84 (29–187) vs. 71 (31–174) nmol/L; p = 0.644] nor treatment adherence [78 (29–192) vs. 79 (31–178) nmol/L; p = 0.749] influenced Lp(a) levels. Female sex was the only independent predictor of Lp(a) levels (table). Conversely, elevated Lp(a) was independently associated with prior ASCVD (OR 1.638; 95% CI 1.115–2.405; p = 0.012), indicating that higher Lp(a) levels are more prevalent in patients with recurrent cardiovascular events. Conclusion In ACS patients, Lp(a) remains a marker of residual cardiovascular risk independent of statin therapy. The observed association between elevated Lp(a) levels and statin use is primarily driven by confounding by indication, reflecting the patients' higher baseline risk profile rather than a direct biological effect of the medication.FigureTable
title: Lipoprotein(a) levels in patients hospitalized for acute coronary syndrome according to prior statin therapy

abstract: Abstract Background Many patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) do not reach LDL-C goals. Despite their established clinical benefits, access to PCSK9i in the UK remains limited, with a stepwise approach requiring clinicians to use ezetimibe before PCSK9i can be prescribed to patients who need lipid-lowering therapy intensification. While the clinical and economic benefits of adding PCSK9i to standard of care was previously demonstrated (1.14 life years (LYs) gained and a number needed to treat (NNT) of 4.5 to prevent a cardiovascular (CV) death), the clinical benefits of immediate PCSK9i use versus this stepwise approach for patients with established ASCVD in the UK have not been quantified. Purpose To assess the clinical benefits of immediate PCSK9i use versus delayed use (ezetimibe first, with PCSK9i added 3 years later) in patients with established ASCVD in the UK whose LDL-C goal is not reached with maximally tolerated statin therapy. Methods A cohort state-transition Markov model was used to estimate cardiovascular outcomes for immediate versus delayed PCSK9i use in patients with established ASCVD whose LDL-C goal is not reached with maximally tolerated statin therapy in the UK over a lifetime horizon. The model includes the following states/events: ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, acute limb ischemia or amputation, unstable angina, revascularization, CV and non-CV death. The model tracks first versus subsequent events and time since last event. Transition probabilities were derived from UK real-world ASCVD risks using CPRD-HES-ONS. LDL-C efficacy data for PCSK9i, ezetimibe, and PCSK9i plus ezetimibe were obtained from the literature. The association between LDL-C reduction and CV event risk was based on Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' studies, with time-dependent risk reduction incorporated. LYs and CV events were not discounted. Results Among patients with ASCVD, immediate versus delayed PCSK9i use led to an increase of 0.31 LYs per patient over a lifetime. The estimated non-fatal, fatal, and total CV events avoided per 1,000 patients were 16, 7, and 23, respectively. NNT to prevent one non-fatal, fatal, or any CV event were 61, 147, and 43, respectively, over a lifetime (35 years; mean starting age 65). For the 1.3 million eligible UK patients, total estimated non-fatal, fatal, and all CV events avoided over a lifetime were 21,408, 8,848, and 30,256, respectively. Conclusions Providing clinicians the option for immediate PCSK9i use increases LYs and prevents tens of thousands of CV events among ASCVD patients not at LDL-C goal with maximally tolerated statin therapy in the UK. These findings suggest that a stepwise approach through ezetimibe delays effective care and increases CV events. Guidelines and policymakers should consider earlier, more intensive LDL-C lowering strategies to maximize cardiovascular health outcomes.Table for abstract
title: The clinical benefits of immediate versus delayed use of PCSK9 inhibitors for patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease in the UK

abstract: Abstract Background Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of triglyceride (TG)-lowering therapies show inconsistent benefits on major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Because TGs poorly reflect atherogenic particle burden, apolipoprotein B (ApoB) may be a better marker of treatment effect. It remains unclear how often ApoB is reported in these trials or weather data are sufficient for pooled analyses. Aim To systematically assess how fully ApoB is reported in TG-lowering RCTs and weather ApoB reduction correlates with MACE reduction. Methods We performed a systematic review of RCTs evaluating TG-lowering therapies (EPA and/or DHA, fibrates, and niacin/nicotinic acid) in high-risk populations reporting MACE. MEDLINE, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were searched. After screening and inclusion, we performed an exploratory meta-regression assessing the association between absolute ApoB reduction and risk ratio (RR) for a composite and individual outcome of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and coronary revascularization. Results Twenty-nine RCTs met inclusion criteria, but only 8 adequately reported ApoB values at baseline and end of study, or provided absolute ApoB change, allowing quantitative analysis. These trials included 86,216 participants and 10,285 MACE. ApoB reduction was associated with a lower risk of MACE (RR 0.90 per 10 mg/dL reduction; 95% CI [0.80-1.01]; p = 0.084; I² = 61%), although this did not reach statistical significance – Figure 1A. ApoB reduction significantly correlated with a reduced risk of MI (RR 0.84; 95% CI [0.71-1.00]; p=0.048; I²=42%) – Figure 1B. For coronary revascularization, there was a trend toward risk reduction (RR 0.87; 95% CI [0.75-1.00]; p=0.057; I²=42%). No significant associations were observed for CV death (RR 1.07; 95% CI [0.91-1.26]; p=0.42; I²=61%) or stroke (RR 0.96; 95% CI [0.83-1.11]; p=0.57; I²=60%). Conclusions ApoB reporting in TG-lowering RCTs was limited, constraining evaluation of effects on atherogenic particle burden. Still, available data suggest greater ApoB reduction aligns with lower CV risk, especially MI, highlighting ApoB potential to reveal benefits not captured by TG levels. Larger trials with consistent ApoB reporting are needed to define the true cardioprotective impact of TG-lowering therapies.
title: Effect of apolipoprotein B reduction on major adverse cardiovascular events in randomized controlled trials of triglyceride-lowering therapies: systematic review and exploratory meta-regression

abstract: Abstract Background Non-ischemic acute myocardial injury (NI-AMInj) carries substantial long-term mortality, yet no evidence-based pharmacotherapy exists. Statins possess pleiotropic anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and endothelial-protective properties beyond lipid lowering, but their role in NI-AMInj remains unknown. Purpose To evaluate the association between in-hospital statin initiation and 1-year all-cause and cause-specific mortality in NI-AMInj patients, and to explore the influence of statin type, intensity, and timing. Methods This retrospective cohort study included NI-AMInj patients from a regional multi-center platform (development cohort, 2013–2022) and a critical care database (external validation, 2008–2022). Patients with prior statin use were excluded from the development cohort. The exposure was in-hospital statin initiation. The primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes included cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular death. Multivariable Cox regression models with stepwise covariate adjustment were used. Sensitivity analyses included propensity score matching (PSM), inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and exclusion of early deaths and high-risk subgroups. Results The development cohort included 50,670 statin-naive patients (statin group: 25,135; non-statin group: 25,535; 1-year mortality: 11.5% vs 27.5%). The external validation cohort included 10,893 patients (statin: 5,819; non-statin: 5,074; 1-year mortality: 29.1% vs 41.1%). In fully adjusted models, statin use was independently associated with lower 1-year all-cause mortality in both cohorts (development: HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.75–0.84; validation: HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.69–0.80; both P&lt;0.001). In the development cohort, statin use was also associated with reduced cardiovascular death (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.82–0.96), non-cardiovascular death (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.61–0.72), cancer-related death (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.51–0.79), and respiratory death (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.51–0.69). The benefit was consistent across different statin types (class effect). Moderate-to-high intensity therapy showed the clearest benefit. Both early (≤48h) and late (&gt;48h) initiation were associated with significant mortality reduction. Subgroup analyses showed no significant interaction by sex, diabetes, coronary artery disease, or baseline LDL-C level. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of the findings. Conclusions In-hospital statin therapy is independently associated with significantly lower 1-year all-cause and cause-specific mortality in NI-AMInj patients across different populations and healthcare settings. The benefit extends beyond cardiovascular death, exhibits a class effect across statin types, and persists regardless of initiation timing. These findings support consideration of statin therapy in NI-AMInj, a population currently lacking specific pharmacological recommendations.Association of Statin Use with Mortality Risk
