title: Engulfed or enriched? illness identity and mental health among Canadian and Australian patients after SCAD

abstract: Abstract Background Early post–myocardial infarction (MI) cardiac rehabilitation (CR) represents a critical window for secondary prevention. Dietary counselling is routinely implemented, however, data describing concurrent changes in diet quality and body composition during early post-MI CR remain limited. Purpose To evaluate changes in body composition and dietary habits during early post-MI CR, and to explore associations between nutritional knowledge and dietary habits after MI. Methods 50 post-MI patients, undergoing a 3 month CR programme including dietary counselling, were enrolled in this prospective study. Baseline and final assessments included body composition (BMI, fat mass, fat-free mass proportions) and dietary information including Mediterranean diet adherence, overall diet quality and nutritional knowledge assessed with validated questionaries. Results In patients undergoing CR BMI decreased from 27.17 [25.46; 29.41] to 26.81 [24.77; 28.73] (p&lt;0.001), body fat percentage decreased from 38.23 [33.09; 41.18] to 36.90 [32.81; 38.75] % (p&lt;0.001), and fat free mass percentage increased from 61.77 [58.82; 66.91] to 63.10 [61.25; 67.19] % (p&lt;0.001). Dietary habits improved, with Mediterranean diet adherence increasing from 5.00 [4.00; 7.00] to 7.00 [6.00; 8.00] points (p&lt;0.001) and overall diet quality index increasing from 5.87 [−0.04; 17.39] to 15.21 [5.61; 23.70] points (p=0.005). The nutritional knowledge score did not change significantly (13.50 [11.00; 16.00] vs 15.00 [12.00; 18.00] points; p=0.110). At follow-up, nutritional knowledge correlated with Mediterranean diet adherence (R=0.441; p=0.001) and overall diet quality (R=0.286; p=0.044). Conclusion During early post-MI CR with dietary counselling, patients demonstrated significant improvements in dietary habits alongside favourable body composition changes. Despite not significant changes in nutritional knowledge itself, the final knowledge score was associated with better dietary adherence and quality, supporting the clinical relevance of educational components within CR programmes.
title: Dietary counselling in early post-myocardial infarction cardiac rehabilitation is associated with improved dietary habits and favourable body composition changes

abstract: Abstract Background The 2024 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines on Chronic Coronary Syndrome (CCS) recommend low risk chest pain assessment pathway. This can help to streamline patient flow, reduce hospital admissions, and minimise outpatient clinic workload while maintaining clinical safety. Aim To evaluate the effectiveness of 2024 ESC guidelines on CCS by nurse led low risk chest pain pathway within the cardiology department of a busy district general hospital Methods A retrospective review was conducted of patients presenting with chest pain to the Emergency Department of a district general hospital, between October 2024 and October 2025. Of 316 patients referred for pathway consideration, criteria eligible individuals were assessed by a team of Cardiology Advanced Nurse Practitioners (ANPs) through clinical evaluation and followed by targeted investigations, including treadmill exercise tolerance testing (ETT), transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE), computed tomography coronary angiography (CTCA), invasive coronary angiography (ICA), Dobutamine Stress echocardiography (DSE) or nuclear myocardial perfusion study (NMPS), when indicated. Results Of the 316 referred patients, 88.2% met the pathway eligibility criteria. The mean age of the patients was 59 years. 53% were women and 47% were men. Following the first visit for ANP assessment, 22.1% did not require any cardiac investigations as they met very low pretest probability for obstructive CAD and 78.6% were fit for discharge to primary care with lifestyle and risk factor modification advice combined with disease-modifying and if necessary anti-anginal medications for the management of CCS. ETT was the most frequently used initial investigation (71%), with most performed on the same day of first ANP assessment. 4.3% of eligible patients needed TTE. 22% patients needed added cardiac investigations after their first ANP visit. Overall, 17% patients underwent coronary angiographic assessment (77% of these angiography assessments were CTCA and 23% had ICA). 3.2% of total patients assessed in this pathway (as 19% of patients who had coronary angiography) needed revascularisation procedure. 78% of these revascularisation procedures were percutaneous coronary interventions and 22% were coronary artery bypass grafts and required further Consultant led clinic follow up. Conclusion The Cardiology Nurse led low risk chest pain pathway reduced demand on outpatient services and inpatient beds while maintaining patient safety. These findings support the continued use of the 2024 ESC guidelines for the management of chronic coronary syndrome.
title: Effectiveness of nurse-led low risk chest pain assessment pathway in a District General Hospital in West of Scotland: a retrospective study

abstract: Abstract Background Acute myocardial infarction (MI) is one of the deadliest cardiovascular diseases (CVD), and leading causes of cardiac-related morbidity. Excess mortality and morbidity observed following MI is largely attributed to the development of subsequent cardiovascular complications, most notably heart failure (HF) and atrial fibrillation (AF), which occur in up to 18% and 21% of patients, respectively. The electrocardiogram (ECG) is a low-cost, non-invasive method to measure cardiac electrical activity, routinely acquired at the time of MI. AI has shown promise in ECG-based diagnosis and prognosis, however no established approach currently predicts the development of HF or AF following acute MI. Aim This study aims to establish a proof of concept for the application of AI, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs), to predict development of HF and AF in post-MI patients based on 12-lead ECG, which can facilitate early detection and timely treatment. Methods Patient ECG data were obtained from the MIMIC-IV database for 1066 MI patients, 688 of whom developed AF and 552 developed HF. ECGs recorded within the first week following MI treated with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) were considered. These were labelled HF or AF if the patient developed the respective condition after 3 months post-MI. The CNN model learned subtle morphological waveform variations from the labelled ECG data, leveraging its ability to extract temporal and spatial features from time-series data. The model consisted of a pre-trained ResNet-style encoder, previously trained on 800,035 ECGs from 161,352 unique patients, which was fine-tuned on the study cohort, followed by a multilayer perceptron (MLP) decoder trained to map extracted features to clinical outcomes. Class imbalance was addressed using a weighted sampling strategy during the model training. The model performance was evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation. Results The trained CNN was applied to predict HF and AF from patient ECG post-MI. For HF prediction, the model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.78 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.75–0.81) and an F1-score of 0.75 (95% CI 0.72–0.78). For AF prediction, the AUC was 0.78 (95% CI 0.75–0.81) with an F1-score of 0.76 (95% CI 0.73–0.78). These findings suggest that early, post-PCI ECGs contain predictive morphological signatures associated with subsequent CVD complications. Conclusion This study demonstrates the potential of AI to predict post-MI outcomes from early ECGs. The results suggest that routinely acquired ECGs may contain prognostic information for subsequent HF and AF, highlighting the promise of AI-based ECG analysis for improving post-MI patient management.AI-ECG workflow for prediction post-MI.
title: AI-ECG prediction of long-term adverse cardiovascular outcomes in post myocardial infarction patients

abstract: Abstract Background Cardiac index (CI) is a key hemodynamic parameter guiding revascularization and mechanical circulatory support decisions. However, CI assessment requires right heart catheterization, which is underutilized in routine practice. Whether CI can be inferred directly from coronary angiography (CAG) videos using artificial intelligence remains unknown. Purpose To develop and validate a three-dimensional convolutional neural network (3D-CNN) model to predict reduced CI from routine CAG videos. Methods We retrospectively included adult patients undergoing CAG with simultaneous CI measurement during the same catheterization session. A 3D-CNN based on the X3D architecture was trained to classify CI as normal (≥2.2 L/min/m²) or reduced (&lt;2.2 L/min/m²). Data were split at the patient level into training (70%), validation (15%), and test (15%) sets. All available angiographic videos per study were analyzed. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score. Calibration and decision-curve analyses were performed. Results A total of 11,475 angiographic studies from 9,103 patients were analyzed; 25.2% had reduced CI. On the test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.83, a sensitivity of 0.72, a specificity of 0.78, and an F1 score of 0.62. Calibration was acceptable (Brier score 0.148), and decision-curve analysis demonstrated net clinical benefit across threshold probabilities ranging from 0.1 to 0.5. Performance remained stable across age, sex, body surface area, and comorbidity subgroups (all AUC &gt;0.80). Restricting input to predefined two-, three-, or four-view combinations yielded similar performance (AUC 0.81–0.82). Conclusion A 3D-CNN model can predict the reduced CI index directly from routine CAG videos with strong discriminative ability and consistent subgroup performance. This method may offer real-time hemodynamic insights without extra invasive procedures; however, prospective validation is still necessary.Figure 1
title: Predicting cardiac index from routine coronary angiography videos using a 3d convolutional neural network

abstract: Abstract Abstract Prompt recognition of acute coronary artery occlusion (ACO) is critical for myocardial salvage and cath-lab activation in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) but ECG patterns interpretation remains challenging. Artificial intelligence (AI) has shown promise, but direct comparisons with first-line clinicians in routine practice are needed. To compare the diagnostic performance of an AI-based ECG algorithm detection of ACO in ACS with that of human readers. Methods This retrospective bicentric study included consecutive patients admitted for ACS and planned to invasive strategy. 12 lead-ECGs recorded prior to angiography were independently classified as suggestive of ACO or not by 32 clinicians (senior cardiologists, cardiology residents, senior emergency physicians, and emergency residents) blinded to all clinical and angiographic data. The AI algorithm provided a binary output for ACO detection. Coronary angiography reviewed by two experienced practitioners served as the reference to define ACO using two prespecified definitions: strict ACO (TIMI flow ≤1) and an extended definition (TIMI flow ≤2). Standard ESC STEMI criteria for ECG analysis, reviewed by three independent cardiologists were also used to define ACO. The primary endpoint was the sensitivity for strict ACO detection comparing AI and human readers. Secondary endpoints included accuracy, AI performance assessed by receiver operating curves, intra-observer agreement among clinicians and AI reproducibility using Cohen’s κ. Results Among the 194 patients included, the prevalence of strict ACO (TIMI ≤1) after coronary angiography was 39.7% (77/194) and 45.4% (88/194) for the extended definition (TIMI ≤2). AI reclassified 11 of 88 ACO (TIMI ≤2) patients (12.5%) not identified by physician reviewers. The left circumflex was the culprit vessel in 45%. AI demonstrated higher sensitivity than clinicians under both predefined definitions of ACO: 68.8% for AI versus 59.7% for clinicians (p = 0.035) for TIMI ≤1 and 68.2% vs. 58.0% for TIMI ≤2, (p=0.013) with similar specificity (78% vs. 79% and 82.1% vs. 81.1%, respectively). Intra-observer agreement was markedly higher for AI (κ = 0.89) than for clinicians (κ = 0.44). ESC ECG STEMI criteria were observed in only 22.2% of the patients (43/194) and demonstrated a lower sensitivity (37% across both definitions) than AI and human readers. Across clinician specialties, diagnostic accuracy was not significantly different and ranged from 66.5% for emergency residents to 69.1% for senior cardiologists, but remained lower than AI (75.8%). Conclusion AI-assisted ECG analysis significantly improves sensitivity for detecting acute coronary artery occlusion compared with human readers and standard ESC STEMI ECG criteria, without compromising specificity, and by reducing interpretative variability. These findings support the integration of AI as a robust decision-support tool to optimise triage and early management in acute coronary syndromes.visual abstract 1/2visual abstract 2/2
title: Human versus artificial intelligence–assisted ECG analysis for the detection of acute coronary occlusion in acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) patients are usually revascularized within 120 minutes, whereas fewer than one-third of non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) occlusions are treated this quickly [1], potentially contributing to worse long-term outcomes [2]. Purpose We aimed to fine-tune and validate a foundation model to detect occluded myocardial infarction (OMI) from 12-lead ECGs. Methods This study included digital ECGs recorded at a tertiary PCI center and affiliated ambulances between 2016 and 2022. ECGs were linked to data from the catheterization laboratory as well as troponin (TnT) measurements. The primary outcome was OMI, defined as an acute culprit lesion, qualitatively determined to be &lt;3 months old, with TIMI flow 0–2 and treated with PCI. To be eligible, ECGs had to be recorded &lt;72 hours prior to the acute invasive procedure. A foundation model was fine-tuned on our dataset using asymmetric focal loss and Muon optimizer. The data were split at the patient level and stratified by outcome into 80% development and 20% test sets, with performance evaluated on the held-out test set. Results We included 16 346 ECGs from 10 880 patients. In the test set, 254 (12%) cases were classified as OMI, of which 93 (37%) were NSTEMIs. As shown in the Figure, the fine-tuned OMI model achieved an area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.91 (95% CI, 0.88-0.93) and an Area Under the Precision–Recall Curve (AUPRC) of 0.73 (95% CI, 0.66-0.79) for detecting all OMI cases. For ST-elevation OMI, performance improved to an AUROC 0.98 (95% CI, 0.96-0.99) and an AUPRC 0.87 (95% CI, 0.77-0.94), whereas for OMI without visible ST-elevations the AUROC was 0.85 (95% CI, 0.81-0.89) and the AUPRC 0.34 (95% CI, 0.25-0.47). A prediction threshold of 0.181 was selected to obtain a positive predictive value (PPV) of =0.5 for NSTEMIs. The model's sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and negative predictive value (NPV) for all OMI cases, STEMIs and NSTEMIs are presented in the Table. Of the OMI cases with door-to-balloon time &gt;120 minutes (n=120), the model flagged 56 cases (47%), of whom 88% had NSTEMI, and a median TnT of 1213 (IQR, 104-12373) ng/L. In contrast, the remaining 64 OMI cases (53%) with door-to-balloon time &gt;120 minutes that were not flagged by the model (98 % NSTEMIs), TnT levels were significantly lower (400 ng/L; IQR, 42–4 123; p = 0.05). This difference may partly be explained by a higher prevalence of collateral circulation in the unflagged group (p &lt; 0.05). Conclusion The fine-tuned foundation model shows performance within the range of state-of-the-art in detecting OMI from ECGs [3], including NSTEMIs with occlusions. Notably, the model identified almost half of OMIs currently receiving PCI later than 120 minutes upon hospital arrival, underscoring the model’s potential to enhance early diagnosis and timely management of under-recognized, but high-risk OMIs.Figure.ROC & PRC for OMI detectionTable.Model performance at threshold=0.181
title: Artificial intelligence for detecting acute occluded myocardial infarction: fine-tuning and evaluation of an ECG foundation model

abstract: Abstract Background In-stent restenosis (ISR) remains the principal long-term complication of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), affecting 5–10% of drug-eluting stent recipients. All existing prediction models require post-hoc structured data unavailable during the procedure, precluding real-time intra-procedural risk stratification. Deep learning (DL) has transformed cardiovascular image analysis, yet no framework has attempted to predict ISR directly from routine angiographic video. Purpose We aimed to develop and temporally validate an end-to-end DL framework that predicts ISR risk directly from coronary angiographic video at two peri-procedural time points, without any structured clinical input. Methods This retrospective study enrolled 431 patients (518 target lesions) from a tertiary cardiovascular centre. Lesions were divided into a training set (n=278, ISR 110 [39.6%]; 2017–2019), a development set (n=120, ISR 32 [26.7%]; same period) and a temporally independent external-validation set (n=120, ISR 60 [50.0%]; 2021–2022). An attention-based global–local feature-extraction architecture operating on coronary digital subtraction angiography video was used to build two models: pre-PCI video and post-PCI video. Discrimination was assessed by AUC with DeLong 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Three-level head-to-head comparisons were conducted: (1) alternative DL architectures (DenseNet-121, ResNet-50, Swin Transformer) under identical protocols; (2) five clinical models built from clinical structured variables; and (3) six board-certified interventional cardiologists scoring ISR risk from identical video under blinded conditions. Model interpretability was assessed by gradient-weighted class-activation mapping (Grad-CAM). Results In the temporal external-validation set, pre-PCI achieved an AUC of 0.856 (95% CI 0.782–0.920) and post-PCI 0.870 (0.807–0.929). Conventional DL backbones achieved AUCs of only 0.611–0.682 (all P&lt;0.001). The best clinical tabular model reached 0.655 (all P&lt;0.001 vs. our model). In blinded evaluation, the model significantly outperformed pooled expert cardiologists: pre-PCI 0.856 vs. 0.683 (P=0.023) and post-PCI 0.870 vs. 0.723 (P=0.035), with substantially higher sensitivity (0.917 vs. 0.567). Risk stratification yielded odds ratios of 8.27 (95% CI 3.67–19.94; P &lt; 0.001) for pre-PCI and 20.43 (7.65–65.73; P &lt; 0.001) for post-PCI. Grad-CAM revealed model attention concentrated on vessel and stent zones. Conclusion An end-to-end DL model operating on routine coronary angiographic video predicts ISR with clinically meaningful accuracy, significantly outperforming conventional architectures and expert cardiologists. The dual-time-window design enables real-time intra-procedural risk stratification and may guide stent optimisation decisions at the point of care.Figure 1Figure 2
title: End-to-end deep learning on coronary angiographic video predicts in-stent restenosis at dual peri-procedural time points

abstract: Abstract Background Current artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) prediction models for myocardial infarction (MI) use a single 10s ECG. Whether model performance changes across serial ECGs or longer recordings is poorly understood. We aimed to investigate the impact of intra-patient variability on model prediction for MI. Purpose To predict Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) type 1 using three AI and ML models, quantify prediction variability, and evaluate the impact on MI diagnosis and clinical risk assessment. Methods Logistic Regression (LR) and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) models, and a Deep Learning (DL) Residual Neural Network were derived to predict NSTEMI Type 1. The DL model was pretrained on 180,522 hospitalized patients matched with ICD-10 codes. All models were derived on a prospective cohort comprising 7,591 patients presenting with suspected MI to the Emergency Department (ED). Evaluation was conducted on a separate prospective cohort of 1,409 patients where 5-minute resting ECGs were available at presentation to the ED. Final diagnoses for the derivation and evaluation cohorts were centrally adjudicated by two independent cardiologists according to the Fourth Universal Definition of MI. Continuous 5-minute ECGs were partitioned into 10s segments, yielding 30 probabilities per patient. The intra-patient variability was defined as the 95% prediction interval across 5 minutes. The impact of intra-patient variability on MI diagnosis and clinical risk assessment was evaluated by comparing the first segment to the 5-minute min/max probabilities, quantifying reclassification across high-risk (predefined positive predictive value 70%) and low-risk (predefined sensitivity 99.5%, negative predictive value 99.0%) thresholds. Results Area under the curves of the models were 0.75 [95%-CI 0.74–0.75] for LR, 0.75 [0.74–0.76] for XGBoost, and 0.79 [0.78–0.80] for DL. Higher patient median probability correlated with larger intra-patient variability (Spearman’s: LR 0.75, XGBoost 0.85, DL 0.84; all p&lt;0.001). Intra-patient variability significantly affected MI diagnosis and clinical risk assessment within the 5min ECG. Comparing the first segment to the minimum probability segment: the low-risk cohort increased from 3.0% to 5.9% for LR, 12.3% to 20.8% for XGBoost, and 14.4% to 24.4% for DL. Comparing the first segment to the maximum probability segment: the high-risk cohort increased from 0.1% to 0.4% (LR), 1.0% to 3.2% (XGBoost), and 0.6% to 2.3% (DL). Conclusion Model predictions for NSTEMI Type 1 exhibit significant intra-patient variability across serial ECGs. Higher patient median probability correlated with increased intra-patient variability, leading to frequent reclassification of clinical risk. These findings highlight a key limitation of current ECG-based MI-prediction models as clinicians cannot rely on a single 10s ECG prediction for diagnostic certainty.Central IllustrationResults
title: Impact of intra-patient variability of artificial intelligence and machine learning models on the diagnosis of myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background In the occlusion myocardial infarction (OMI) paradigm, the focus shifts from rigid electrocardiogram (ECG) criteria to the underlying pathology of acute coronary occlusion requiring urgent reperfusion. Direct comparison of an ordinal AI-ECG model against an ordinal troponin-based logistic regression model for OMI/NOMI detection in unselected emergency department (ED) patients at presentation is lacking. Methods This study fine-tuned an ordinal AI-ECG model from a foundation model (pre-trained on pooled cohorts n=10.7 million), with preliminary fine-tuning on retrospective cohorts (n=338’580) using ICD-10 codes and final fine-tuning on pooled cohorts (n=13’879) with ordinal OMI/NOMI outcomes. An ordinal logistic regression model using hs-cTnT (LR-Trop) as predictor was fitted in parallel. Models were externally validated and compared in a prospective multicenter study of unselected ED patients with chest pain (validation n=4728), with ECG and hs-cTnT at presentation. Diagnoses were centrally adjudicated. Primary outcome was Occlusion Myocardial infarction (angiographic culprit with TIMI 0–1, or TIMI 2–3 with peak hs-cTnT ≥1000 ng/L). TIMI flow was assessed by two cardiologists. Performance was evaluated by receiver operating characteristic curves (ROC) and precision-recall curves (PR). A sensitivity analysis was performed in the combined group of patients with NSTEMI-OMI and those without MI. Results Among 4728 patients, occlusion myocardial infarction (OMI) was the final diagnosis in 300 (6.3%), of whom 122 (41%) had STEMI. Model discrimination for OMI was high (AI-ECG AUC 0.89 [0.87-0.90] vs LR-Trop 0.93 [0.92-0.95]). For a threshold with PPV of 0.7, the proportion of patients with OMI identified was similar (AI-ECG 0.35 [0.30-0.41] vs LR-Trop 0.41 [0.35-0.47], p &gt;0.05) (Figures A and C). In patients with NSTEMI-OMI or no MI, model discrimination dropped for AI-ECG while it remained high for LR-Trop (AI-ECG AUC 0.84 [0.81-0.87] vs LR-Trop 0.93 [0.91-0.95]). For a threshold with PPV of 0.7, the proportion of patients with NSTEMI-OMI identified was significantly lower for AI-ECG compared to LR-Trop (0.07 [0.04-0.11] vs 0.26 [0.20-0.33], p &lt; 0.05) (Figures B and D). Conclusions & clinical implications In this prospective multicenter validation of unselected emergency department patients with chest pain, the fine-tuned ordinal AI-ECG model demonstrated strong discrimination for OMI and identified a comparable proportion of cases to the hs-cTnT-based LR-Trop. While the performance of AI-ECG was high for OMI, it was inferior to ordinal logistic regression with cardiac troponin testing in patients with NSTEMI-OMI, highlighting the need for optimised models in this vulnerable population.Figures A-DGraphical Abstract
title: Comparison of ordinal AI-ECG versus ordinal hs-cTnT logistic regression for diagnosis of occlusion myocardial infarction: a prospective multicenter validation study

abstract: Abstract Background Coronary artery disease (CAD) is highly prevalent among patients undergoing vascular surgery. False-negative referral decisions for coronary angiography (CA) expose high-risk vascular patients to potentially preventable adverse cardiac events. Conventional clinical judgment is associated with substantial false-negative rates. Machine learning (ML) models optimised to constrain false negatives may improve patient safety while maintaining acceptable overall performance. Methods A retrospective cohort of 7464 vascular patients referred for CA at a tertiary care centre was analysed, with angiographic findings serving as the reference standard. After preprocessing, feature selection, and standardisation, ML models were trained for binary classification (positive vs. negative CA findings). To prioritise patient safety, models were optimised using decision thresholds explicitly constrained to maintain a false-negative rate (FNR) ≤10% (α_FNR=0.1). Random Forest and CatBoost classifiers were identified as best-performing architectures. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix analysis. Results were compared to physician-based decision-making reported in prior analyses. Results A Random Forest model using four routinely available clinical variables (hyperlipidemia, prior myocardial infarction, prior PCI, and ejection fraction) achieved an FNR of 6.9%, with accuracy 68.2%, precision 69.3%, recall 93%, and F1-score 0.64. A CatBoost model incorporating a broader clinical feature set (age, diabetes, smoking status, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, sex, atrial fibrillation, prior myocardial infarction, prior PCI, angina pectoris, ejection fraction, and aneurysmatic disease) achieved an FNR of 10.0%, accuracy 71.1%, precision 71.4%, recall 90%, and F1-score 0.69. Both ML approaches substantially reduced false-negative referrals compared with physician decision-making, while maintaining balanced overall classification performance. High recall values indicate effective identification of patients with true positive angiographic findings. Conclusion ML models optimised with false-negative constraints can reduce missed coronary disease to below 10% using simple clinical variables. Such safety-oriented ML decision support systems have the potential to substantially improve coronary angiography referral strategies in vascular patients, minimising underdiagnosis while preserving acceptable diagnostic efficiency.
title: False-negative constrained machine learning for coronary angiography referral in vascular patients

abstract: Abstract Background Type 2 myocardial infarction (T2MI) is frequently perceived as a secondary clinical entity compared to type 1 myocardial infarction (T1MI), often leading to a conservative "wait-and-watch" approach. However, this clinical assumption may overlook patients with extreme physiological vulnerability. Purpose We utilized an explainable machine learning (ML) framework to characterize the distinct phenotypic features of T2MI and evaluate its associated long-term mortality in a large-scale real-world population. Methods A multicenter registry of 163,335 patients was screened to identify individuals with acute myocardial injury. After excluding estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) &lt; 15 ml/min/1.73m2, dialysis, or non-ischemic etiologies, a final cohort of 37,251 patients was established. T2MI was defined as acute myocardial injury triggered by supply-demand mismatch without coronary revascularization. An eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) algorithm was trained on 17 clinical variables, with model decision-making decoded using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values to ensure diagnostic transparency. Results The final cohort included 35,197 patients with T1MI and 2,054 patients with T2MI. The ML model achieved a high discriminative performance with a validation area under the curve (AUC) of 0.870 (95% CI 0.820–0.920) (Figure 1A). Hemoglobin emerged as the most critical predictor for T2MI identification (gain: 0.399), followed by log-transformed N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (log-NT-proBNP) and serum glucose (Figure 1C).SHAP analysis confirmed a consistent clinical logic where lower hemoglobin levels and increased hemodynamic stress strongly influenced T2MI diagnosis (Figure 2A), with a non-linear risk increase observed when hemoglobin fell below approximately 120 g/L (Figure 2B). Longitudinal follow-up over 3,500 days revealed a profound survival gap, as AI-defined T2MI patients exhibited significantly higher cumulative mortality compared to T1MI patients (log-rank p &lt; 0.0001) (Figure 2C). Conclusion Machine learning effectively identifies T2MI by quantifying the complex interplay between anemia and cardiac load. While the calibration slope of 3.34 reflects a systematic overestimation of probabilities, this outcome is a deliberate consequence of a high-sensitivity diagnostic strategy designed to prioritize the detection of a high-risk minority class within clinical screening. The significantly higher mortality observed in the AI-defined T2MI group underscores that these patients represent a vulnerable phenotype currently under-recognized in clinical practice, warranting earlier risk stratification and targeted intervention.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Prognostic significance of explainable machine learning-defined type 2 myocardial infarction: unmasking a high-risk phenotype in multicenter data

abstract: Abstract Background ​ In-stent restenosis (ISR) remains a significant adverse event following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Quantitative flow ratio (QFR) and radial wall strain (RWS) provide functional and mechanical assessments of coronary lesions. Machine learning (ML) offers advantages in integrating multi-dimensional features to improve the accuracy of ISR risk stratification. Purpose ​ To develop and validate ML-based survival models for predicting the risk of ISR following PCI, and to compare their performance. Methods ​ Consecutive adult patients who underwent PCI were enrolled. The primary endpoint was angiographically confirmed ISR during follow-up. Clinical, laboratory, lesion characteristics, and procedural variables were recorded. Key variables included pre-stent and post-stent QFR measurements (e.g., QFR, △QFR, △QFR/stent length (mm), maximum percentage diameter stenosis (Max%DS)), the Lu-index (residual QFR/residual length), and QFR and RWS measurements (e.g., distal △QFR, distal Max%DS, distal RWS, distal RWS%) within 5 mm from the stent edges. Eleven machine learning algorithms (including AKE, random survival forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and DeepSurv) and a Cox proportional hazards (CoxPH) model were employed. The dataset was randomly split into training (70%) and testing (30%) sets. Model performance was evaluated using the concordance index (C-index), integrated Brier score, and time-dependent receiver operating characteristic curves (time-ROC). Time-dependent feature importance plots were used to interpret predictor contributions over time. Results ​ A total of 363 patients (mean age 63.5 years, 63.74% male) were included. During a median follow-up of 1.44 years, 131 cases (36.09%) of ISR were observed. Following feature selection, eight key predictors were retained, namely post-stent QFR, △QFR, stent length, Max%DS, distal RWS, distal RWS%, △QFR/stent length (mm), and the Lu-index. In the testing set, the AKE model demonstrated superior discriminative performance (C-index: 0.730, 95% CI: 0.680-0.780) compared to the CoxPH model (C-index: 0.645, 95% CI: 0.595-0.695). The AKE model also achieved a lower integrated Brier score (0.256 vs. 0.274) and a time-dependent AUC of 0.741 (95% CI: 0.639-0.840) at 3 years. Time-dependent analysis identified distal RWS%, stent length, and the Lu-index as the most consistently important predictors for ISR risk. Conclusion ​ The AKE machine learning model effectively predicts the risk of ISR in post-PCI patients and outperforms the conventional Cox regression model. This model shows potential as a precise risk stratification tool to support clinical decision-making.C-index and ROCfeature importance and KM curves
title: Machine learning-based survival models integrating quantitative flow ratio to predict in-stent restenosis after percutaneous coronary intervention

abstract: Abstract Background Post-cardiotomy low cardiac output syndrome (PC-LCOS) complicates ~10% of cardiac surgeries and is associated with increased mortality, prolonged ICU stay and greater need for mechanical circulatory support. It is characterised by refractory haemodynamic instability requiring inotropes, vasopressors and/or mechanical support, although diagnostic criteria remain heterogeneous. Current risk stratification relies on clinical assessment and perioperative scores with limited predictive performance. Supervised machine learning (ML) may improve prediction by integrating complex perioperative and early postoperative data. Although high discrimination (AUC &gt;0.89) has been reported, most models are retrospective and single-centre, and externally validated tools for early PC-LCOS prediction are lacking. Purpose To develop and validate supervised ML models for early prediction of PC-LCOS in adults admitted to a postoperative cardiac ICU using routinely available perioperative and early ICU data. Methods This retrospective study included adults undergoing cardiac surgery at a tertiary centre and admitted to the postoperative cardiac ICU. PC-LCOS during ICU stay was the binary primary outcome, defined as clinician-diagnosed low cardiac output syndrome and/or escalation of inotropic or mechanical circulatory support beyond routine care. Demographic, perioperative, haemodynamic and laboratory variables available within an early postoperative window were analysed. Logistic regression, random forest and gradient boosting models were trained using random training/testing split with cross-validation. Performance was assessed by AUROC, sensitivity and specificity. Results Among 1,041 patients, 173 (16.6%) developed PC-LCOS. Affected patients had higher EuroSCORE II, longer cross-clamp and cardiopulmonary bypass times (all p &lt; 0.001), and more frequent previous cardiac surgery, heart failure and atrial fibrillation (all p ≤ 0.016). Logistic regression achieved AUC 0.83 (95% CI 0.77–0.89), sensitivity 75% and specificity 81% (accuracy 80%, NPV 94%). Random forest showed similar discrimination (AUC 0.83, 95% CI 0.76–0.89) with higher sensitivity (81%), specificity (83%) and NPV (96%) (accuracy 82%). Gradient boosting yielded AUC 0.76 (95% CI 0.69–0.83). Key predictors were operative complexity (bypass and cross-clamp duration), EuroSCORE II and early haemodynamic markers (cardiac index, lactate, central venous pressure). Conclusions Supervised ML demonstrated good discrimination for early PC-LCOS prediction using routinely collected perioperative and ICU data. Random forest achieved comparable AUROC to logistic regression with improved sensitivity and NPV. Operative complexity and early haemodynamic instability were dominant predictors. ML-based tools may support early risk stratification in postoperative cardiac ICU populations.ROC Curves Comparison
title: Early prediction of low cardiac output syndrome in post-cardiotomy patients using supervised machine learning

abstract: Abstract Background Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of death globally. While X-ray coronary angiography (XCA) guides diagnosis and percutaneous coronary intervention, interpretation remains expert-dependent.1 Ongoing digitalization introduces opportunities to embed data-driven and AI-supported intelligence into the catheterization laboratories workflow. Purpose This systematic review evaluates deep learning (DL) applications to XCA, focusing on methods, validation strategies, and indicators of translational feasibility. Methods We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review, searching PubMed, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore (2014–2025) for peer-reviewed studies developing deep learning (DL) models for X-ray coronary angiography (XCA). Database searches were supplemented by forward/backward citation chasing via Lens.org. Two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts using Rayyan, resolving conflicts with a third reviewer; full-text assessment followed identical procedures. Studies were quality-rated using CLAIM checklist.2 Translational feasibility was evaluated through external validation evidence, reference standard agreement, real-time performance metrics, generalizability across populations/equipment, and CLAIM reporting transparency. Results We included 118 studies (2016-2025), observing a surge in research output after 2020. Most studies (86%) focused on a single task, mainly vessel segmentation and CAD detection (Figure 1). While 91% specified the target vessel, population demographics were reported in 14% and patient presentation in 23%. Methodological robustness was limited: 25% of studies included external validation, 20% used multi-centre data, and none employed a prospective design. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were the most frequently utilized models. Nine studies employed self-/semi-supervised learning to address limited annotations. Transfer learning saw a steady increase (from 2% in 2019 to 11% in 2025), yet no foundational models were used. Annotator expertise was described in 77%, 29% used ≥2 experts. Reporting quality (CLAIM 2024; median = 48.8%) was moderate, with sparse reporting on ground truth (5% reported the inter/intra-rater variability) and missing data (2%). Translational feasibility indicators revealed systematic limitations across all domains (Figure 2B). Real-time feasibility was demonstrated in 19% and inference time reported in 28% of the papers. Reproducibility remained low (availability of code 28%, data 21%, models &lt;1%). Conclusion DL for XCA is advancing rapidly, reflected in growing research output and increasing methodological sophistication, yet a clear path from technical innovation to clinical translation remains to be established. With the adoption of standardized benchmarking, open science practices, and clinically grounded frameworks such as CLAIM and FUTURE-AI, the field is well-positioned to bridge this gap.Figure 1:Field of application and taskFigure 2:Clinical readiness indicators
title: Deep learning for x-ray coronary angiography: a systematic review of methods, validation, and clinical readiness

abstract: Abstract Background Takotsubo syndrome (TTS) almost always presents with a pathological electrocardiogram (ECG) that initially is indistinguishable from myocardial infarction (MI). Studies have tried to develop an ECG-criteria to diagnose TTS but have been hampered by heterogeneity and small sample size. Previously machine learning (ML) classification of TTS from MI, using neural networks, have been limited by the black-box nature of the method and by low precision-recall, and low positive predictive value. Purpose Our aim was to apply generative machine-learning to the dynamical clustering of heartbeat morphologies to distinguish between TTS and MI, improving previous classification results, and emphasising visualisation of potentially new ECG features for takotsubo syndrome. Methods 507 TTS cases and 14,978 controls, from a database of takotsubo syndrome and myocardial infarction subjects, admitted to hospital between 2010 -2019 with a suspicion of MI and an indication for coronary angiography, were identified from the Swedish SCAAR register. The main outcome of the study was the ability of ML to identify (1) TTS from suspected MI, (2) TTS from ST-elevation MI (STEMI), (3) TTS from non-ST-elevation MI (NSTEMI), (4) TTS from verified MI, and (5) apical TTS from anteriorSTEMI. Bayesian non-parametric clustering was applied to the sequence of heartbeats, identifying relevant features, and classified recordings by logistic regression. 10-fold cross-validation was performed to emphasize the robustness of our results. Results ML differentiated TTS from MI: 1) TTS from suspected MI with area under the curve (AUC) of 0.89 (95% CI 0.88-0.91); 2) TTS from verified MI with 0.92 (0.90-0.93); 3) TTS from ST-elevation MI (STEMI) with 0.94 (0.93-0.95); 4) TTS from non-ST-elevation MI with 0.91 (0.89-0.92); and 5) apical TTS from anterior STEMI with 0.90 (0.88-0.92). In each scenario the model characterized electrocardiographic patterns for classification. Pointing towards a combination of heterogenic features, including ST-elevations/depression, inverted T-waves, QT-prolongation associated with takotsubo syndrome. As a novel finding atrial activation disturbances was found to be associated with TTS and important for classification. Conclusion In the present approach ML could discriminate TTS against suspected and verified MI with good to excellent performance. The study shed light on new ECG features for takotsubo syndrome. Providing evidence for a heterogenic pattern of the ECG features and supporting criteria previously recognised in the literature. For the first time atrial activation disturbances were found to be associated with TTS and important for classification.Table over performance of ML models
title: Generative machine learning applied to the electrocardiogram (ECG) to uncover relevant ECG features in distinguishing takotsubo syndrome from myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Introduction Therapeutic management after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) requires precise rhythm risk stratification. While prior studies have described arrhythmias either before or after TAVI, intra-individual data quantifying qualitative and quantitative rhythm changes across the intervention remain limited. Purpose We aimed to characterize paired arrhythmia dynamics using extended ambulatory ECG monitoring before and after TAVI. Methods Consecutive patients undergoing TAVI were prospectively enrolled if 14-day ambulatory ECG patch monitoring was available both before and after the procedure. Paired intra-individual analyses were performed to evaluate changes in arrhythmia incidence as well as quantitative parameters, including arrhythmia burden, longest episode duration, and daily episode rate. Results Paired 14-day ECG monitoring was available in 100 patients (median age 82 years [78–85], 43% female), with comparable analyzable durations before and after TAVI. Following TAVI, the incidence of high-degree atrioventricular block (HAVB) increased from 0% to 9.1% (p=0.004), accompanied by significant increases in HAVB episode rate and burden (both p=0.009). Atrial fibrillation (AF) occurrence increased from 16% to 25% (p=0.035). Among patients with AF pre- or post-TAVI, AF burden increased significantly (median 0.4% vs. 18.3%, p=0.026). However, in patients with pre-existing AF (n=16), the longest AF episode was significantly shorter after TAVI (median 179.5 h vs. 50.8 h, p=0.041), with no significant change in AF burden. In contrast, ventricular arrhythmias showed improvement in patients with pre-existing non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT, n=55). Daily NSVT episode rate decreased (median 0.2 vs. 0.1 episodes/24h, p&lt;0.001), together with a reduction in longest NSVT episode duration (median 3.0 s vs. 2.6 s, p=0.012). Supraventricular or ventricular ectopy did not change significantly in paired analyses. Conclusion Paired extended ECG monitoring reveals divergent electrophysiological effects of TAVI. While conduction disturbances and AF increase post-procedure, NSVT frequency and arrhythmia persistence decrease in patients with pre-existing tachyarrhythmias. These findings suggest simultaneous pro-arrhythmic effects on the conduction system and potentially anti-arrhythmic effects through hemodynamic unloading, underscoring the need for individualized rhythm surveillance after TAVI.Graphical Abstract
title: Paired 14-day ECG monitoring reveals divergent arrhythmia dynamics before and after transcatheter aortic valve implantation

abstract: Abstract Introduction Unwitnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) has poor survival rates, due to the delayed recognition. Wearable technologies offer a promising approach to automatically detect and alert for cardiac arrest, potentially improving survival by faster emergency response. Purpose In the DETECT-studies, a wristband-based photoplethysmography (PPG) algorithm for cardiac arrest detection has been developed. Since left ventricular function influences the PPG signal, this study evaluates algorithm performance in relation to the left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). Methods This post hoc analysis included patients previously enrolled in the DETECT-1a and DETECT-1b studies, comprising of individuals undergoing ventricular tachycardia (VT) ablation, transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI), and S-ICD implantation. Patients without known calculated LVEF were excluded. Cardiac arrest events included pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT) during VT ablation, rapid ventricular pacing (RVP) with aortic balloon inflation during TAVI, and ventricular fibrillation (VF) induction during S-ICD implantation. During the procedures, patients wore a PPG-based wristband. Cardiac arrest was confirmed using continuous ECG monitoring and invasive arterial blood pressure measurements. All recorded PPG data were analysed using the previously developed cardiac arrest detection algorithm. Patients were categorized into poor/moderately reduced LVEF (LVEF &lt;40%) and mildly reduced/normal LVEF (LVEF ≥40%). Sensitivity for cardiac arrest detection and false-positive rates were assessed. Results A total of 219 patients were included, of whom 42 had an LVEF &lt;40% and 177 had an LVEF ≥40%. The median LVEF was 30% (IQR 23–35%) and 55% (IQR 49–60%) respectively. Patients in the LVEF &lt;40% group more frequently underwent VT ablation and S-ICD procedures than in the LVEF&gt;40% group. In the LVEF &lt;40% group, 45 cardiac arrests were induced; 25 pVT, 3 VF, and 17 RVP events. In the LVEF ≥40% group, a total of 184 CAs occurred; 10 pVT, 7 VF, and 167 RVP events. In patients with LVEF &lt;40%, the algorithm correctly identified 40 CAs, corresponding to a sensitivity of 89% (95% CI 80–95%). In the LVEF ≥40% group, 181 CAs were correctly identified, yielding a sensitivity of 98% (95% CI 97-100%), see Figure 1 (p=0.028 for comparison between LVEF groups). Four false-positive alarms occurred during 107 hours of PPG monitoring in patients with LVEF &lt;40%, compared with 12 false positives during 346 hours in the LVEF ≥40% group. Conclusions Sensitivity for detecting cardiac arrest was lower in patients with LVEF &lt;40%, although performance in this group remained clinically acceptable. Missed cardiac arrest events were primarily VTs, which may explain the lower sensitivity. Future studies should validate performance in real-life cardiac arrests and aim to reduce false-positive alarms during daily-life use.Sensitivity in LVEF groups
title: Wristband-based automated cardiac arrest detection and alerting: Algorithm performance in relation to the left ventricular function

abstract: Abstract Background Wearable ambulatory electrocardiography (aECG) monitors are commonly used to detect arrhythmia, with an array of devices marketed directly to the consumer. Their widespread availability and ease of use make them an attractive option for detecting transient ischemia but their accuracy has not been systematically compared thus far. Purpose To compare the diagnostic accuracy of three aECG devices in detecting myocardial ischaemia: the Apple Watch, Kardia ‘6-lead’ (6L) and Cardiostat patch. These devices represent a spectrum of aECG technologies, ranging from user-triggered to continuous monitors, as well as single to multi-lead devices. Methods Patients presenting with confirmed ST elevation myocardial infarction on 12-lead ECG and scheduled for primary PCI were eligible, if they were older than 18 years and provided verbal assent followed by formal post-hoc consent. Recruitment is ongoing with a target of 50 participants. Those in cardiogenic shock or presenting with cardiac arrest were excluded. De-identified ECGs were recorded on each device at two time points: at presentation and after revascularisation, defined either as the point when the ST segment became isoelectric or after 72 hours of convalescence, whichever occurred first. The degree of ST elevation visible was adjudicated by researchers blinded to clinical and 12-lead ECG data. Accuracy was judged against time-matched 12 lead ECGs. Results 46 patients were recruited from a single tertiary cardiac centre, between December 2023 and January 2026. Paired (12-lead and aECG) data were available for 32 participants using the Apple Watch, 32 using the Kardia 6L and 20 using the Cardiostat patch. Not all participants completed recordings with all devices due to logistical constraints. The Kardia 6L demonstrated moderate diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.81) with 81% sensitivity and 54% specificity at detecting STEMI at a threshold of 1mm of ST elevation. Discriminatory performance improved further within the inferior STEMI subgroup (AUC = 0.90). Conversely, both the Apple Watch and Cardiostat performed poorly (AUC = 0.64 and 0.57 respectively). All three devices systematically underestimated STE compared to the 12-lead ECG; mean differences on Bland-Altman analysis were -0.55mm (95% CI -0.82 to -0.29) for the Kardia 6L, -1.52mm (95% CI -1.96 to -1.08) for the Apple watch and -1.36 mm (95% CI -1.99 to -0.73) for the Cardiostat. The Kardia demonstrated significantly less underestimation than both the Apple Watch (p &lt; 0.01) and Cardiostat (p &lt; 0.05). Conclusion aECG devices do not have comparable accuracy at detecting ischemia. The Kardia 6L performed best, possibly related to its additional limb leads. The clinical utility of multi-lead aECG devices needs to be assessed in prospective studies of patients prone to transient ischemia.AECG Figure
title: Assessing the diagnostic accuracy of wearable ECG monitors in detecting ischaemia

abstract: Abstract Background Wearable ECG patches used after transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) enable continuous rhythm monitoring and allow patients to report symptoms via trigger buttons and diary entries. However, the correlation between triggered events and clinically relevant arrhythmias after TAVI remains uncertain. Purpose We aimed to systematically analyze patient-triggered events and their corresponding rhythm findings during 14-day ECG patch monitoring after TAVI. Methods Adult patients undergoing TAVI at a Swiss tertiary centre were prospectively enrolled and monitored with a 14-day ECG patch before discharge. Patients were instructed to record any cardiac-related symptoms using the patch trigger button and/or diary function. Results A total of 307 patients (median age 82 years [78–86], 43% female) underwent ECG patch monitoring. Median monitoring duration was 13 days [11 –14]. At least one patient-triggered event was recorded by 100 patients (33%), with a median of 2 triggered events per patient [1–5]. In 27 patients (9%) triggered events occurred exclusively during sinus rhythm without any associated arrhythmia. Atrial fibrillation was detected by continuous monitoring in 82 patients (27%), newly detected in 15 patients (5%). Among AF-patients, 22 (27%) reported symptoms during AF episodes. Pauses were identified in 59 patients (19%) and high-grade atrioventricular (AV) block in 33 patients (11%), with no triggered events during pauses and only one patient (3%) reporting associated symptoms during high-grade AV block. Ventricular tachycardia (≥3 beats) occurred in 154 patients (50%) and was not associated with any patient-triggered events. Supraventricular and ventricular ectopy (PACs, PVCs) were frequently detected and prompted patient activation in 14% and 10% of cases, respectively. On a per-event analysis 404 events were recorded. 53 (13%) were unevaluable due to imprecise diary entries. Of all symptom-reported events, 141 (35%) were not associated with any arrhythmia. The most frequent arrhythmias were PACs (89, 22%) and PVCs (77, 19%), followed by atrial fibrillation (67, 17%). Notably, 34 (8%) events were associated with more than one arrhythmia. Conclusions After TAVI, patient-triggered events during ECG patch monitoring poorly reflect objectively detected arrhythmias and substantially underestimate the burden of clinically relevant rhythm disturbances. This highlights the importance of continuous ECG monitoring after TAVI for accurate and safe arrhythmia detection in this high-risk population.Graphical Abstract
title: Diagnostic yield of patient-triggered events during 14-days-electrocardiographic monitoring after transcatheter aortic valve implantation

abstract: Abstract Background Women presenting to the emergency department (ED) with suspected acute coronary syndrome (ACS) experience higher rates of misdiagnosis and adverse outcomes than men. Existing clinical decision aids improve risk stratification but have sex-specific limitations that may disadvantage women. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based clinical decision support at the point of care has the potential to reduce this inequity, though its real-world impact remains uncertain. Purpose To determine whether AI-based decision support narrows sex-based disparities in care and outcomes among patients with suspected cardiac chest pain. Methods We conducted a sex-specific subgroup analysis of a multicentre cluster-randomised controlled trial across 12 South Australian EDs which deployed real-time AI-based clinical decision support in the ED for suspected ACS. Analyses were conducted both on the overall cohort, and among those with a predicted 30-day risk of death or myocardial infarction (MI) of &gt;1%. The primary outcome was 12-month cardiovascular (CV) death, MI and unplanned CV readmission. Time-to-event outcomes were analysed with Cox proportional hazards models, adjusted for clustering. Results Among 14,131 participants (49% women), AI-based decision support reduced the 12-month primary composite endpoint in women (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.70-0.92; p = 0.001), with the greatest effect in the elevated-risk group (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.69–0.85; p &lt; 0.001). No significant benefit was observed in men, suggesting that the intervention did not impact the cohort uniformly. Conclusion AI-based decision support reduced major CV events in women presenting to the ED with suspected cardiac chest pain, with effects most evident in those at higher baseline risk. This may represent a novel strategy to address sex-based inequities in ACS care.
title: Artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support may reduce sex disparities in suspected ACS: sub-analysis of a multicentre cluster-randomised trial

abstract: Abstract Background Around 400,000 people die annually from cardiovascular diseases in Brazil. The state of Maranhao, which has an area of ​​similar size to Italy, has one of the highest mortality from ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). Only the state capital offers percutaneous coronary intervention, and no other city has a thrombolysis protocol, leaving 7 million people without assistance. We propose a strategic model to allocate STEMI thrombolysis services in high-demand areas of Maranhao. Purpose We used the Location-Allocation Model (LAM) as an automated tool to decide the best allocation of resources and optimize the distribution of thrombolysis services for STEMI in a low-resource region with the highest mortality rate from cardiovascular diseases in Brazil. This project can support future evidence that aims to reduce the time to access treatment for cardiovascular diseases in low- and middle-income countries, where choosing the best health facilities is based on population demand using open-source data to perform the analyses. Methods Ecological study using the LAM and the following parameters: population density and distribution (demand), location of health facilities (supply), and transportation network (mobility). The demand was estimated by dasymetric gridding from WorldPop, corresponding to 5,072,506 people in Maranhao. The supply points corresponded to the coordinates of the emergency public hospitals that are candidates to implement thrombolysis services, totaling 362 services across the state. The mobility was set with the roads available on OpenStreetMap. We used ArcGIS Pro 2.9 with the Maximize Attendance algorithm to set a 30-minute cutoff time for demand to reach the facilities using the mobility network. The optimal number of chosen facilities was defined as the plateau point at which additional facilities yield no significant increase in population coverage. Results The plateau point was 45 health facilities allocated in the regions of Maranhao with the highest population demand. Together, these hospitals could cover 94.56% of the population (about 4.8 million people) to perform thrombolysis in 30 minutes in the case of STEMI. Conclusion This automated, low-cost approach indicates that more strategic hospitals in low-resource settings are needed to improve timely access to acute care for STEMI, decentralize acute treatment for STEMI, and reduce cardiovascular disease mortality.
title: Increasing access to thrombolytic treatment for ST-elevation myocardial infarction using the Location-Allocation Model in a low-income state in Brazil

abstract: Abstract Background Accurate identification of baseline cardiovascular conditions is essential for clinical registries and trials but relies on labor-intensive manual abstraction. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential solution, yet their real-world performance and reliability remain uncertain. Purpose We evaluated LLM accuracy, model confidence, and areas of disagreement with registry classifications for common cardiovascular conditions. Methods Data were obtained from patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) at a tertiary academic center who were entered into a regional cardiovascular registry in 2024. Among 889 patients, analyses were restricted to 279 with available linked admission notes after excluding repeat admissions and those without note linkage. Registry comorbidities were entered by a nurse overseeing data quality. A locally hosted LLM (Llama 3.3 70B) identified hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and heart failure, while also assigning high or low confidence based on admission notes. Performance was evaluated overall and by confidence, with review of disagreements by a board-certified cardiologist. Results The prevalence of baseline conditions was high, including hypertension (85.3%), diabetes (44.8%), dyslipidemia (86.7%), and heart failure (42.7%). AI demonstrated high overall accuracy in identifying cardiovascular conditions: hypertension 87.5% (95% CI 83.0–91.1), diabetes 96.1% (95% CI 93.1–98.0), dyslipidemia 90.7% (95% CI 86.6–93.8), and heart failure 87.1% (95% CI 82.6–90.8). Sensitivity and specificity were as follows: hypertension 89.1%/78.1%, diabetes 92.0%/99.4%, dyslipidemia 96.3%/54.1%, and heart failure 75.6%/95.6%. Accuracy was higher for high-confidence compared with low-confidence predictions across all conditions, including hypertension (94.6% vs 58.2%), diabetes (99.2% vs 93.7%), dyslipidemia (91.9% vs 55.6%), and heart failure (96.3% vs 83.3%) (Figure 1). Across all condition determinations (n=1116), 108 (9.7%) were discordant between AI and registry classifications. Manual review by a board-certified cardiologist found that the AI classification was correct in 85 (78.7%) discordant cases while original human determination was correct in 23 (21.3%) cases (Figure 2). Conclusion AI accurately identified cardiovascular conditions in this real-world registry cohort, and model-derived uncertainty may help prioritize manual review. Discordance analyses suggest a role for AI in supporting data quality in registries and trials.
title: Artificial intelligence for automated baseline cardiovascular condition identification: accuracy, confidence, and discordance

abstract: Abstract Introduction Translating guideline flowcharts into bedside clinical decision support is frequently delayed by dependence on specialist software engineering, sustaining the evidence–practice gap. Large language model (LLM) coding assistants may enable clinicians to act as software architects; however, bedside deployment demands deterministic behaviour and verifiable pathway completeness. Purpose To demonstrate the feasibility of clinician-led, LLM-assisted development of a deterministic clinical decision support system (CDSS) implementing the ESC 2022 pre-operative cardiovascular assessment workflow for non-cardiac surgery (NCS), and to quantify algorithmic completeness by exhaustive state-space enumeration. Methods A cardiology team used an LLM coding assistant to implement the ESC 2022 NCS workflow as a standalone, client-side HTML/JavaScript hard-coded rules engine with no runtime AI. The CDSS encodes 12 conditionally presented decision nodes — surgical urgency, surgical risk category, symptoms/signs, established CVD, patient age, cardiovascular risk factors, family history of genetic cardiomyopathy, functional capacity, frailty, cardiac murmur, prior PCI/CABG, and ischaemia concern — with each node presented only when logically triggered by earlier answers. Completeness testing enumerated all tool-reachable input states (n = 3,313), requiring a structured, non-null recommendation for each. The large state count, despite only 12 nodes, reflects the multiplicative effect of conditional branching: the theoretical Cartesian product of all node values exceeds 31,000, but the conditional logic constrains reachable paths to 3,313. Outputs were then clustered into unique actionable recommendation bundles. Results The CDSS generated deterministic recommendations for all 3,313 reachable input states (100% coverage), collapsing to 67 unique actionable recommendation bundles. This reachable state space arises from the conditional branching structure of the 12 decision nodes, where later nodes are presented only when logically triggered by earlier answers, constraining enumerable paths well below the theoretical Cartesian product of all node values. All outputs were non-null, guideline-concordant, and reproducible, confirming complete pathway coverage with no dead-end or undefined states. Conclusion Physician-as-architect development, accelerated by LLM coding assistance and safeguarded by exhaustive state-space verification, can operationalise ESC guideline workflows into transparent, deterministic, institution-independent CDSS. Prospective evaluation should address usability, clinical governance, version control, and impact on peri-operative testing rates, appropriate escalation, and patient outcomes.Central Illustartion
title: Physician-as-architect: clinician-led LLM-assisted development and deterministic verification of an ESC-aligned peri-operative decision support system

abstract: Abstract Background Systematic outcome modelling in cardiology is limited by the lack of high-quality, scalable extraction of structured variables from heterogeneous clinical documentation. In routine care, key information for phenotyping and risk stratification remains embedded in unstructured narratives, while structured documentation is often difficult to achieve because clinical information is complex and context-dependent; manual review and extraction of relevant data are resource-intensive and difficult to scale. Purpose To develop a privacy-preserving, on-premise hybrid pipeline for multi-document clinical digital fingerprinting to support real-time risk prediction in routine TAVI care. Methods We developed an on-premise workflow integrating: (i) rule-based (regex) extraction for 74 deterministic standardised parameters, (ii) a locally hosted LLM ensemble consisting of 3 general-purpose foundation models for 43 context-dependent procedural and narrative variables across echocardiography, TAVI, and discharge documentation, (iii) an LLM verifier for post-extraction consistency checks, and (iv) selective human-in-the-loop (HITL) assessment in case of ensemble disagreement. Extracted variables were harmonised into a patient-level digital fingerprint (117 structured variables) covering cardiac structure/function, valvular haemodynamics, and procedural/peri-procedural domains. The pipeline was evaluated in 240 consecutive TAVI patients using routine TAVI pathway documentation. Performance was assessed against a manually corrected gold standard annotated by two clinical reviewers, with discrepancies resolved through discussion. Results Rule-based modules achieved 100% value agreement for all standardised parameters. The selectively assessed LLM ensemble achieved 97.2% accuracy for context-dependent variables extracted from narrative clinical documentation. Integration of the LLM verifier improved ensemble accuracy from 89% to 97% by flagging inconsistent outputs. Selective HITL assessment was required in 8% of ensemble outputs. Fingerprints were complete in 87% of patients; incompleteness was driven by absent source documentation rather than extraction errors (manual abstraction ceiling: 87%). Multiple clinical scores could be calculated, with completeness primarily limited by source documentation; (e.g., CHA₂DS₂-VASc 91% and EuroSCORE 89% of patients). Conclusion A reliable and scalable hybrid extraction pipeline combining rule-based and LLM-based extraction with selective HITL assessment enables high-quality structuring of multi-document cardiology text into clinically meaningful digital fingerprints. This supports privacy-preserving, on-premise phenotyping in routine care and provides a practical foundation for real-time clinical risk prediction and decision support.Figure ESC Abstract.png
title: Reliable and scalable hybrid extraction pipeline with selective human-in-the-loop assessment for clinical digital fingerprinting enabling real-time prediction in cardiology

abstract: Abstract Background Digital cardiac rehabilitation (CR) has been suggested as an innovative approach to increase participation in CR. However, few programmes are comprehensive, assess physical/mental functioning and quality of life, and are not restricted by age and comorbidity burden. Purpose We tested application user-friendliness, recruitment, and attrition of the multicentre, comprehensive 12-week eCardiacRehab programme including physical tests and goal setting in an outpatient setting 2-4 weeks after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Methods Patients were consecutively recruited following guideline-based inclusion criteria from January to October 2025 into three arms; i) eCardiacRehab allowing for tailored solutions according to patients’ functional abilities and needs, ii) Control group 1: usual care, iii) Control group 2: usual care and physical tests (e.g. cardiopulmonary exercise test, bioimpedance, and hand grip strength). All patients completed questionnaires, and all arms had pre-planned oversampling of women. Core components, health registrations, definition of personalised goals, and communication with the interdisciplinary CR team was key (Figure 1). User-friendliness was assessed with the Post-Study System Usability Questionnaire (PSSUQ). Programme metrics on engagement were established. Detailed flowcharts were developed for each arm. Results In total, 159 patients were included: 52 (38% women) in the intervention group, and 57 patients (44% women) in Control group 2. Median age was 66 (range 39-87) across the two groups, and the attrition rate was 25% at 12 weeks. Those lost to follow-up were older and living alone. Selected clinical variables are presented in Table 1. Pre-specified success criteria for inclusion (55%) and attrition rates (≤ 20%) were approached but not fully achieved. Success criteria were achieved on engagement with the programme and user-friendliness. Most modules were completed by 65-80% of patients, and reported as ‘Very useful’ or ‘Useful’. The overall PSSUQ score was 1.9, indicating high user satisfaction and excellent system usability. Notably, difficultly logging in was frequently reported. eCardiacRehab helped achieve goals on lifestyle changes (71%), and provided satisfactory support from clinicians (93%). Conclusion eCardiacRehab is both feasible and acceptable to patients after PCI, warranting further evaluation of clinical outcomes and cost-effectiveness in a larger efficacy trial. Refinements are required on recruitment strategies and technical barriers.Patient journey and contentTable 1Variables on completers/drop-out
title: Digital cardiac rehabilitation – feasibility of the interdisciplinary, comprehensive 12-week eCardiacRehab programme

abstract: Abstract Background While invasive angiography and quantitative flow ratio (QFR) are gold standards for diagnosing coronary functional ischemia, they primarily reflect focal anatomical hemodynamics and fail to capture the systemic metabolic vulnerability of the patient. We aimed to develop and rigorously validate a noninvasive predictive framework using integrated lipidomics and machine learning (ML) for functional stenosis and multivessel disease. Methods High-throughput plasma lipidomic profiling (LC-MS/MS) was performed on a cohort of 441 patients with confirmed acute coronary syndrome. We integrated high-dimensional lipid data with clinical features to construct and optimize ML models (including Support Vector Machine [SVM], Random Forest, and XGBoost). To evaluate real-world robustness against data drift, the optimal models underwent rigorous prospective temporal validation based on a chronological enrollment cutoff. Results The SVM model demonstrated superior performance, achieving cross-validated area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.81 for functional stenosis and 0.79 for multivessel disease, significantly outperforming conventional clinical models. Crucially, prospective temporal validation confirmed the models' robust generalizability (AUC 0.66 with high positive predictive value). Explainable AI (SHAP analysis) successfully pinpointed specific atherogenic lipid drivers: ether-linked phosphatidylinositol (ePI 38:4) emerged as the dominant predictor for general stenosis, reflecting intense oxidative stress, whereas specific sphingomyelins (SM 38:5) and phosphatidylserines (PS 36:1) characterized the multivessel phenotype, biologically mirroring macrophage foam cell formation and the expansion of the apoptotic necrotic core. Conclusion This ML-driven lipidomic framework enables robust, noninvasive systemic risk stratification for functional ischemia and multivessel disease. By uncovering specific atherogenic lipid signatures, it not only optimizes pre-catheterization triage but also identifies potential novel lipid targets for future precision cardiovascular therapeutics.Figure 2.Temporal Validation of ML Models.Figure 1.Abstract
title: Noninvasive prediction of functional coronary stenosis and multivessel disease in acute coronary syndrome using integrated lipidomics and machine learning

abstract: Abstract Background Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) accounts for nearly 20% of acute hospital admissions (1). While validated risk tools (GRACE and HEART scores) can effectively stratify low-risk patients (2), acute inpatient management remains resource-intensive. Our retrospective feasibility study (3) showed a favourable safety outcome and potential financial benefits, including reduced acute-bed days, from streaming these patients into the chest pain virtual ward (CPVW). Purpose In this prospective analysis, we envisaged CPVW as an alternative model of care for low-risk patients with ACS, whilst offering safe remote monitoring and timely elective interventions, enabling early discharge and improving patient flow. Methods This study compared a prospective cohort of low-risk ACS patients managed via a dedicated CPVW (March 2025–February 2026, n=30) with a retrospective inpatient cohort identified from the Myocardial Ischaemia National Audit Project (MINAP) registry (March 2022–April 2023, n=55). Low-risk ACS was defined by a GRACE score &lt;140, HEART score &lt;4, non-dynamic ECGs, down-trending troponins, and absence of ongoing chest pain. The primary endpoints were 30-day readmission and all-cause mortality, along with evaluation of total inpatient length of stay (LOS) and time to elective coronary angiography. Results Baseline demographics and cardiovascular risk factors were comparable between groups (Figure 1). Median in-hospital stay was significantly shorter in the CPVW cohort (2 [IQR 1–4] vs 4 [IQR 2–7] days; p=0.003), demonstrating a mean reduction of 2.00 days (95% CI 0.73–3.27; p=0.0026). While the CPVW cohort experienced a longer overall wait to angiography (9 [IQR 7–14] vs 3 [IQR 0–4] days; p&lt;0.001; mean difference 7.67 days, 95% CI 5.59–9.74), this was safely managed in the outpatient virtual setting. Consequently, their post-angiography inpatient stay was significantly reduced (0 [IQR 0–0] vs 1 [IQR 0–3] days; p&lt;0.001; mean reduction 1.33 days, 95% CI 0.72–1.95). Angiography revealed a greater burden of coronary disease in the CPVW group compared to the retrospective cohort, with fewer unobstructed arteries (33% vs 94%; p&lt;0.001) and higher rates of multi-vessel disease requiring intervention (27% vs 4%; p=0.02). No CPVW patients experienced 30-day readmission or mortality, compared with a 9% readmission rate in the retrospective cohort (p&gt;0.05). The mean LOS reduction of 2.00 days for the 30 CPVW patients equates to 60 acute bed days saved, translating to a potential cost saving of £19,200 (assuming £320/bed day). Conclusion Management of low-risk ACS patients via CPVW is effective and associated with a significant reduction in acute-bed days and healthcare costs, without adverse outcomes. Interestingly, while risk-stratification tools effectively ensured safety across both cohorts, our prospective CPVW group had a higher burden of angiographic disease, emphasising the need for timely elective intervention.CPVW Baseline Comparison ChartCPVW Cost Divergence Graph
title: Chest pain virtual ward (CPVW): a prospective analysis of a novel care model for low-risk acute coronary syndrome

abstract: Abstract Background Clinical trials are usually analyzed using frequentist methods and interpreted through p-values, which are often poorly understood. In contrast, Bayesian analyses yield probabilistic statements that offer a more intuitive interpretation of treatment effects and uncertainty. Purpose To demonstrate the utility of probabilistic statements, we conducted Bayesian analyses in two settings: (i) published randomized controlled trials conventionally considered "negative" (p&gt;0.05); (ii) a meta-analysis of percutaneous coronary interventions in elderly patients with NSTEMI. Methods We considered 169 primary outcomes in 130 negative trials published in high impact general medical journals during a single year (2021). For each outcome, we extracted the treatment effect and corresponding standard error. We re-analysed data using Bayesian methods to obtain posterior probabilities that the experimental treatment is better than control, and that the effect is above specific thresholds for clinical significance. For the case example of meta-analysis, we used Bayesian random-effects models with minimally informative priors to summarize the available evidence and produce probabilistic statements regarding the treatment effect of an invasive compared to a conservative strategy. Results Among the 169 outcomes of the negative trials, 113 (70%) reported the treatment effect using ratios, while 56 (33%) reported it as differences. Although all ratios were formally statistical "non-significant", for 23/113 (20%) of the outcomes there was &gt;90% probability that the treatment is superior to control. For 10/113 (9%), this probability was &gt;95%. In 3/56 (5%) of the differences, the probability that the experimental treatment is better than control was ≥90%. In the meta-analysis of invasive strategy in elderly with NSTEMI, for the composite of all-cause mortality or myocardial infarction, we found weak evidence for superiority of the invasive strategy (HR 0.89, 95%CrI 0.68–1.14; 86% probability of benefit). While there was strong evidence that invasive treatment reduces myocardial infarction risk (HR 0.70, 95%CrI 0.56–0.86; ~100% probability of benefit), there was weak evidence of increased all-cause and cardiovascular mortality compared with conservative management (posterior probabilities of 91% and 67%, respectively). Conclusions We illustrated how Bayesian methods can be used to derive probabilistic statements for treatment effects. Such statements can provide a nuanced understanding of scientific findings, improve interpretation, and greatly enhance communication between researchers, clinicians, patients, and guideline developers. Relying solely on statistical significance, without considering clinical importance, can mislead decision-making and potentially deprive patients of beneficial therapies. To facilitate the uptake of the method, we developed a web-app that can be used to produce probabilistic statements.
