title: Probabilistic interpretation of clinical trial results to improve interpretation and communication of findings

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Early postoperative pneumonia and sepsis (ePOPS) remain serious complications following cardiac surgery, yet ePOPS risk stratification is lacking. Supervised approaches may overlook latent patient subgroups. Purpose To identify clinically meaningful phenogroups among cardiac surgery patients using unsupervised clustering and to evaluate whether these phenogroups demonstrate a graded association with ePOPS and early mortality. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 916 adult cardiac surgery patients (excluding heart transplantation) at a single centre between January 2014 and April 2024. After excluding 354 patients with missing values in the prespecified variables, 562 patients were analysed. Fifteen variables including age, comorbidities, preoperative infection, preoperative mechanical circulatory support (MCS), surgical urgency, redo sternotomy, operative time, deep hypothermic circulatory arrest time and transfusion volume were standardised and reduced via principal component analysis. K-means clustering was applied to the principal components, and cluster number (K=2–5) was evaluated by silhouette analysis. To assess the impact of exclusions, the same clustering was repeated on all 916 patients using 11 non-missing variables, and cluster concordance was evaluated using the adjusted Rand index (ARI). The Cochran–Armitage test and logistic regression estimated odds ratios (OR) for trend; Fisher's exact test evaluated the ePOPS–early death association. Sensitivity analyses assessed the ePOPS trend across specifications varying principal components (3–10), clustering algorithm (K-means, Gaussian mixture model, agglomerative), and cluster number (3–5). Results Silhouette analysis indicated K=3–4 as optimal; K=3 was selected to ensure adequate subgroup sizes. Three phenogroups emerged: "standard elective" (Group A, n=310, 55.2%), characterised by low surgical complexity and minimal mechanical support; "acute aortic" (Group B, n=170, 30.2%), distinguished by deep hypothermic circulatory arrest and emergent surgery; and "MCS/high-acuity" (Group C, n=82, 14.6%), marked by preoperative MCS, redo sternotomy, and preoperative infection. Re-clustering on all 916 patients yielded ARI 0.89. ePOPS incidence increased monotonically across groups (0.3%, 1.8%, and 6.1%; trend OR 4.22, 95% CI 1.66–10.70, p&lt;0.001). In-hospital mortality similarly rose (1.3%, 4.7%, and 12.2%; trend OR 3.19, 95% CI 1.82–5.59, p&lt;0.001). ePOPS was associated with in-hospital death (OR 7.60, 95% CI 1.50–39.00, p=0.045). In sensitivity analyses, the primary specification ranked second in silhouette among all configurations, and the ePOPS trend remained in 70/72 (97.2%). Conclusions Unsupervised phenogrouping identified clinically distinct phenogroups with graded ePOPS and early mortality risk. This data-driven approach may complement existing risk models and guide perioperative strategies for high-risk phenogroups.Figure 1Figure 2
title: Unsupervised phenogrouping identifies a graded risk of early postoperative pneumonia and sepsis after cardiac surgery

abstract: Abstract Background Standardisation of cardiovascular data across Europe remains limited despite a high disease burden. The ESC EuroHeart initiative addresses this gap by implementing harmonised clinical data standards and real-time quality metrics to enable benchmarking and continuous improvement. Estonia (population 1.3 million) has a digitally mature publicly financed healthcare system and a national myocardial infarction registry ensuring complete case capture since 2012. Estonia was designated as the EuroHeart pilot country in 2020. Purpose To implement the ESC EuroHeart registry nationally, evaluate feasibility and coverage, assess adherence to selected acute coronary syndrome (ACS) quality indicators, and establish infrastructure for registry-based research and collaborative scientific activities. Methods Implementation was conducted through collaboration between the ESC, Uppsala Clinical Research Centre, the Estonian Society of Cardiology, both national tertiary cardiac centres and a local IT partner, with a university hospital serving as the central IT hub. Legal, data protection and ethical assessments were completed. The QReg5 platform was localised and launched for web-based data collection in ACS, PCI, TAVI and heart failure. ACS data collection began stepwise in two tertiary centres (first patient May 2021; second centre January 2023). Institutional coverage and selected ESC ACS quality indicators were analysed and contextualised using the national myocardial infarction registry. Results A national standardised dataset and IT platform were implemented within two years despite the COVID-19 pandemic. By 2024, national coverage reached 61% for STEMI and 38% for NSTEMI, with institutional inclusion rates of 90% and 63%, respectively. Most inpatient ACS quality indicators demonstrated consistent adherence across centres; however, marked variation was observed in early invasive management of NSTE-ACS (angiography within 24 h: 17% vs 57%), identifying actionable performance gaps. Aggregated national data contributed to three ESC EuroHeart annual reports enabling international benchmarking. Conclusion National implementation of ESC EuroHeart in a digitally mature health system is feasible and delivers high institutional coverage with measurable benchmarking outputs. Embedding EuroHeart within tertiary care while retaining the established national myocardial infarction registry as a comprehensive backbone enabled real-time, contextualised quality feedback without compromising complete population coverage. EuroHeart national architecture represents a scalable model for European cardiovascular quality infrastructure and provides a platform for real-world evidence generation and registry-based trials.
title: Building a national real-time cardiovascular quality infrastructure: five years of ESC EuroHeart implementation in Estonia

abstract: Abstract Background Cardiology is a dynamic field, constantly evolving through innovations that have the potential to revolutionize patient care. Historically the process of incorporating these innovations into the reimbursed healthcare system in the Netherlands lacked coordination and was driven by individual hospitals and companies with a slow bottom-up acceptance. In 2022, the Netherlands Society of Cardiology (NVVC) took decisive action to address this barrier by establishing a streamlined, coordinated approach to prioritize and guide promising cardiological innovations towards inclusion in reimbursed healthcare. Purpose To provide an overview of the NVVC's innovative, coordinated approach to guiding groundbreaking cardiology innovations towards reimbursed healthcare. Methods The NVVC's Science & Innovation Committee, established in 2019, is responsible for overseeing the implementation of a structured innovation procedure. This bottom-up process is driven by contributions from specialized subspecialities Working Groups which help shape the “Innovation Agenda”. For each innovation, expert panels provide recommendations regarding the most appropriate pathway towards reimbursement. In 2022, the NVVC formalized a streamlined approach to guide promising cardiological innovations towards reimbursement, navigating six distinct pathways. Innovations are assessed for inclusion in the basic insurance package, either through open or closed pathways, with stakeholders such as, health insurers, the governmental Dutch Health Care Institute (ZINL), and the Dutch Healthcare Authority (NZa) each fulfilling specific regulatory and advisory roles in this collaborative effort. Results The first Innovation Agenda (2022) prioritized nine innovations not yet covered by reimbursed healthcare (Fig 1). Updates in 2024 and 2026 led to the addition of four new innovations. From the 13 innovations enlisted, two were accepted by the Government as reimbursed care: 1) pulmonary artery pressure monitoring, and 2) percutaneous mitral annuloplasty. One innovation, (cerebral protection during TAVI) was excluded from reimbursed care. Of the remaining 10 innovations, three are under governmental review for "Promising Care patwhay", while four are still in scientific research phases. By appeal of the NVVC, ZINL is currently re-evaluating new evidence for renal denervation. The two innovations added in 2026 are now undergoing the process to define the appropriate route to become reimbursed care. Conclusion The NVVC's structured approach has enabled optimal prioritization of innovations with a high potential to become reimbursed healthcare, thereby reducing ad hoc requests with a low priority. This collaborative strategy has led to significant progress and may serve as blueprint for other countries. The next step will be to focus on the integration of e-health and AI into clinical practice.Fig. 1:NVVC Innovation Flow
title: Implementation of a novel, coordinated innovation policy of a National Society of Cardiology

abstract: Abstract Background Switzerland and Germany share a comparable epidemiological burden of coronary artery disease (CAD), yet their interventional practices differ substantially. According to the latest ESC Atlas in Interventional Cardiology, the rate of diagnostic coronary angiography (CA) in Switzerland is approximately two thirds of that reported per million inhabitants in Germany.1 Both countries provide annual national procedural insights - through SwissCaRe and the German Heart Report - enabling surveillance of CAD and revascularisation practices.2,3 Aim To compare CAD-related hospitalisation and mortality, procedural volumes, use of intravascular imaging and physiology in Germany and Switzerland. Methods We conducted a descriptive comparative analysis of publicly available national datasets using SwissCaRe 2023 and the German Heart Report 2025, both reflecting procedural activity in 2023. Results In 2023, interventional activity was substantially higher in Germany than in Switzerland, with more than one million procedures reported nationally compared with approximately 19,000 procedures in SwissCaRe (Table 2). In Switzerland, data are derived from a voluntary registry and may therefore not capture all procedures nationwide. Percutaneous coronary interventions (PCI) accounted for roughly one third of procedures in Germany and nearly 40% in Switzerland. Non-invasive ischaemia testing prior to CA was documented in approximately two thirds of cases in both countries. Use of coronary physiology during CA was comparable, whereas intravascular imaging during PCI was reported more frequently in Switzerland, with marked centre-level variability. Outcome reporting differed structurally. Switzerland reports procedural MACCE and mortality, whereas Germany provides 7-day, 30-day, and 1-year outcome metrics. Accordingly, MACCE rates were higher in Germany (Table 2). Age distribution was comparable, peaking in the eighth decade. SwissCaRe additionally reported procedural metrics such as door-to-balloon time and post-procedural pharmacotherapy, which are not aggregated in the German Heart Report. The relatively low statin utilisation rates (69% in ACS, 63% in CCS) likely reflect immediate post-procedural data capture rather than discharge medication. In 2023, the median door-to-balloon time was 80 minutes in Switzerland versus 46 minutes in Germany, possibly reflecting differences in networks, triage protocols, and in-hospital workflow structures.4 Conclusions Germany and Switzerland exemplify two high-quality interventional systems with complementary paradigms in interventional cardiology governance. Germany is characterised by volume-oriented, population-based surveillance, whereas Switzerland reflects quality-driven procedural benchmarking with higher reported adoption of adjunctive technologies. Integrating the strengths of both models may enhance transparency, comparability, and patient-centred cardiovascular care at a European level.
title: A tale of two systems: interventional cardiology practices in Germany and Switzerland in 2023

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. In Thailand, healthcare access is provided by three main public insurance schemes: the Universal Coverage Scheme (UCS), the Social Security Scheme (SSS), and the Civil Servant Medical Benefit Scheme (CSMBS). Although UCS has improved access to essential care, it remains to be determined whether insurance scheme is associated with long-term survival after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Purpose To assess the impact of a patient's health insurance scheme on their long-term mortality risk for patients undergoing PCI for ACS. Using a nationwide registry, we hope these real-world findings can guide policies to improve healthcare equity. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort study of patients treated for ACS between May 2018 and August 2020. To evaluate long-term survival, we connected clinical data to the Department of Provincial Administration, which enabled us to monitor all-cause mortality through 2026. Since baseline health is significantly dependent on insurance type, we used inverse probability weighting (IPW) to balance the groups (keeping standardised mean differences under 0.2 and aligning variance ratios close to 1). Subsequently, we estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HR) for all-cause mortality using a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model to control for clinical and procedural risk factors. Results The study included 12,280 patients (8,612 UCS; 2,820 CSMBS; 848 SSS). Baseline disease severity varied significantly; with UCS (50.66%) presenting with a higher ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) rate than CSMBS (37.41%). After balancing the groups using propensity score weighting, the survival curves show a clear difference. Compared with CSMBS, UCS was associated with higher long-term mortality (HR 1.32; 95% CI 1.18–1.46; p&lt;0.001). Mortality risk was similar between SSS and CSMBS (HR 0.81; 95% CI 0.55–1.20; p=0.296). New requirement for dialysis was the strongest predictor of death (HR 2.83; 95% CI 1.66–4.80; p&lt;0.001), followed by heart failure (HR 2.31; 95% CI 1.57–3.40; p&lt;0.001). We also observed an obesity paradox: underweight status increased mortality risk (HR 1.44; 95% CI 1.01, 2.06; p=0.042), while obesity (Body mass index ≥ 25.0 kg/m2) appeared protective (HR 0.62; 95% CI 0.50, 0.77; p&lt;0.001). Finally, the use of statins (HR 0.57; 95% CI 0.40, 0.80; p=0.001) or beta-blockers (HR 0.60; 95% CI 0.46, 0.77; p&lt;0.001) was strongly associated with improved long-term survival. Conclusion(s) UCS patients had significantly higher long-term mortality after PCI for ACS after adjusting for baseline clinical and procedural differences relative to patients with CSMBS. This disparity highlights a need for targeted health policies to ensure equitable chances of survival for all patients, regardless of their insurance coverage.Health scheme_kaplan meier curveFactors association with all cause of death
title: Impact of health insurance on long-term mortality after percutaneous coronary intervention in acute coronary syndrome patients: a nationwide propensity-weighted analysis

abstract: Abstract Abstract The SHARE TAVI registry provides data of all TAVIs in South Africa for local quality improvement initiatives in the face of high healthcare resource constraints. The ESC 2021 Guidelines for VHD moved from using solely surgical risk scores to determine intervention, focusing more on age (&lt;75 vs. &gt;_75) and anatomical factors, with TAVR preferred for patients &gt;75 years age, or High Risk (STS &gt;8%) or unsuitable for SAVR based on clinical, anatomical and procedural factors at the decision of the Heart Team, and SAVR recommended for those at low surgical risk (age &lt;75 years and STS &lt;4%). Between Jan 2022 and Dec 2025, 1868 patients with TAVI implants were entered into SHARE TAVI, at 31 sites nationally. 1531 (81.96%) met clear criteria for TAVI, 1459 were &gt;75 years and 72 others were STS&gt;8% but &lt;75 years. 337 patients aged &lt;75 years and had low to intermediate STS scores as seen in TABLE 1. As seen in TABLE 2, of the 337 patients aged &lt;75 years, 184 had low STS scores but very severe or severe AS gradient, adhering to Class IB guideline criteria for individual clinical characteristics of suitability for TAVI rather than surgery, at the decision of the Heart Team, and 85 patients had Intermediate STS Scores with moderate to very severe gradients, again within evidence category IB of the guidelines. The 68/1868 remaining patients aged &lt;75 years were individually analysed here for any further specified contraindications to surgery. 15 had no recorded STS Scores or Echo criteria recorded, or additional clinical notes, and could not be evaluated further for adherence to guideline criteria. 16/53 remaining low risk, moderate gradient patients had no recorded specified contraindications to surgery, the other 37 had clearly listed specific comorbidities or contraindications to surgery, thus fulfilling guideline criteria for inclusion in the TAVI program by Heart Team Decision according to Class IB evidence. Conclusion 31/1868 (1.66%) patients over 3 years following publication of the ESC 2021 VHD treatment guidelines received TAVI without clearly recorded indications that TAVI would be more appropriate than SAVR according to Class IB evidence. Measurable criteria shared through local registries allow for quality improvement initiatives in patient selection given the economic restraints in healthcare, but this shows the great majority of TAVI patients in South Africa are being appropriately selected and there was excellent guideline uptake and adherence to the 2021 ESC guidelines.ESC 2026 Tables SHARE TAVI
title: South African TAVI Program adherence to ESC 2021 VHD Treatment Guidelines between 2022-2024

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Lower socioeconomic status (SES) is consistently associated with a higher incidence and mortality of acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Patients with lower SES experience worse outcomes following AMI, including higher rates of recurrent AMI, stroke and heart failure. Longer hospital stay is associated with more comorbidities, higher rates of complications such as cardiogenic shock and vascular complications, readmission for AMI and unplanned revascularization, need for intensive care, heart failure, and increased short-term and long-term mortality. It is unknown whether lower SES is associated with longer hospital stay following AMI. Purpose To evaluate whether SES is associated with length of hospital stay in total as well as length of stay on an intensive care unit or intermediate care unit in a recent German cohort of patients hospitalized for AMI and enrolled in a myocardial infarction registry. Methods We analyzed data of 802 patients admitted with an AMI between April 2019 and December 2024 with available information on the highest level of education and occupational qualification acheived which were used as indicators of SES. Only patients who were discharged alive from the hospital were included. Differences in days of hospital stay in total, days on an Intensive Care Unit or Intermediate Care Unit were analyzed. Statistical significance was tested with analysis of variance. Results Mean age of the cohort was 69.7 years and 70.8% were men. Regarding the level of education, 38.5% had a low, 43.0% had a medium, and 18.5% had a high level of education. Regarding occupational qualification, 7.5% had a low, 74.2% had a medium, and 18.3% had a high occupational qualification. Length of hospital stay was higher among patients with a low level of education (mean 8.1 days) compared to patients with a medium level of education (6.7 days) or high level of education (7.1 days) (P=0.007). Differences according to a low (8.5 days), medium (7.4 days), and high (6.8 days) occupational qualification were not statistically significant (P=0.14). Patients with a low occupational qualification had a higher mean length of stay on an Intermediate Care Unit (low occupational qualification: 2.1 days; medium: 1.7 days; high 1.5 days) (P=0.03), whereas there were no differences with regard to the level of education, and no differences in the length of stay on an Intensive Care Unit according to the occupational qualification or the level of education. Conclusion(s) Using the level of education and occupational qualification as indicators of SES, we show that a lower level of education is associated with longer hospital stay in total and lower occupational qualification is associated with longer length of stay on an Intermediate Care Unit following AMI, reflecting higher healthcare resource utilization and costs associated with lower SES in patients with AMI.
title: Associations of socioeconomic status with length of hospital stay in a recent german myocardial infarction registry

abstract: Abstract Background Mechanical circulatory support with a microaxial flow pump (mAFP, Impella CP) improved 180-day survival in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (STEMI-CS) in the Danger Shock trial, but was associated with higher complication rates and longer hospitalisation. Purpose To evaluate the cost consequences of routine Impella CP therapy in STEMI-CS, including in-hospital costs, intensive care utilisation, and post-discharge resource consumption through 180 days. Methods This prespecified within-trial detailed cost analysis was conducted alongside the international, multicentre, open-label, randomised DanGer Shock trial. The cost analysis was performed from a hospital perspective with a 180-day time horizon using an intention-to-treat approach. Index hospitalisation costs were estimated using a micro-costing approach based on prospectively collected patient-level resource utilization and follow-up data, whereas post-discharge hospital contacts within 180 days were valued using national diagnosis-related group tariffs. Costs were compared between mAFP plus standard care and standard care alone, and incremental cost differences were estimated with non-parametric bootstrapping (10,000 replications) to derive 95 % confidence intervals (CI). Results A total of 355 patients with STEMI-CS were randomised to mAFP plus standard care (n=179) or standard care alone (n=176). Patients in the mAFP group had longer median intensive care unit (ICU) stay (6 days, interquartile range (IQR) 2-15 vs 3 IQR 0-10), longer general ward stay (3 days IQR 0-11 vs 1 IQR 0-8), and received more advanced respiratory and monitoring interventions (Figure 1). Patients in the mAFP group further received more blood transfusions, but fewer additional PCI procedures before discharge and fewer heart-failure-related rehospitalisations within 180 days. Mean total index hospitalisation costs were €84,842 (SD ±96,296) in the mAFP group and €46,003 (SD ±75,516) in the standard-care group (Δ €38,839; 95 % CI 21,586-56,896). The difference was primarily driven by higher costs of mechanical circulatory support devices and procedures (Δ €20,768; 95 % CI 13,102-28,947), hospital admission including ICU (Δ €16,121; 95 % CI 4,351-28,065), and in-hospital events and complications (Δ €1,247; 95 % CI 126-2,334). During 180-day follow-up, post-discharge costs did not differ significantly between groups: mean €2,059 (SD ±12,300) in the mAFP group vs €3,384 (SD ±28,594) in the standard-care group (Δ −€1,324; 95 % CI -6,585-2, 406). Conclusion Routine use of mAFP in STEMI-CS was associated with significantly higher index hospitalisation costs, primarily driven by ICU stays and device-related resource use. Post-discharge 180-day costs were similar between groups. These findings inform implementation of Impella therapy in publicly funded healthcare systems.Figure 1Cost breakdown by treatment group

title: Cost analysis of microaxial flow pump (Impella) versus standard care in cardiogenic shock: findings from the danger shock trial

abstract: Abstract Background Recent trial data support the use of the Impella® heart pump for the management of patients with cardiogenic shock (CS). However, questions regarding the cost-effectiveness of Impella® compared with alternative mechanical circulatory support (MCS), such as venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO), effect adoption. In this study, we evaluated the cost-effectiveness of Impella® versus VA-ECMO among patients requiring MCS for CS, from the perspective of the mixed private-public Australian healthcare system. Methods A survival analysis was constructed to estimate cost-effectiveness. Survivors were assigned costs and outcomes over a lifetime time horizon. Clinical inputs were derived from a meta-analysis of propensity score–adjusted studies comparing Impella® with VA-ECMO. Health care resource use and unit costs were included consistent with the Australian health care system perspective. Utility weights were applied to surviving patients to calculate quality-adjusted life years (QALY), and both costs and outcomes were discounted at an annual rate of 5%. Results In the base case, Impella® was associated with cost savings of Australian dollars (AUD) $30,157 per person, 2.798 additional life-years, and 1.206 additional QALYs compared with VA-ECMO. At a willingness-to-pay threshold of AUD $50,000 per QALY, the estimated net monetary benefit was AUD $90,450. Sensitivity analyses demonstrated that results were most influenced by short-term mortality, daily hospital costs, and length of stay. Conclusion Based on this cost-effectiveness analysis and economic modelling, this study offers preliminary evidence that Impella® represents a cost-effective and cost-saving alternative to VA-ECMO for patients presenting with CS in a mixed public-private healthcare system.
title: Economic evaluation of Impella versus VA-ECMO in acute myocardial infarction cardiogenic shock

abstract: Abstract Background Atrial fibrillation (AF) often coexists with an unfavorable lifestyle profile and cardiometabolic comorbidities. However, how these factors interact to shape risk stratification and outcomes in contemporary AF patients remains poorly defined. Purpose To evaluate associations between lifestyle profile and the risk of adverse events in AF patients. Methods Post-hoc analysis of two prospective registries from Europe and Asia. Lifestyle profile was assessed at baseline using a modified Life’s Simple 7 (LS7) score (range 0–14), based on seven domains: body mass index, blood pressure, total cholesterol, glucose metabolism, smoking status, physical activity, and alcohol consumption. Each metric was graded 0–2 points; patients were categorized as Ideal (10–14), Intermediate (5–9), or Poor (0–4), with non-ideal defined as Intermediate/Poor. Logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with non-ideal lifestyle. Cox regression estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs for adverse outcomes according to lifestyle profile. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death (ACD) and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). Secondary outcomes were individual components and major bleeding. Exploratory analyses evaluated individual MACE components (CV death, acute coronary syndrome, and thromboembolic events). Mediation analyses assessed the contribution of CHA2DS2-VASc-related comorbidities, and interaction analyses explored differences between European and Asian cohorts. Results We included 4,052 AF patients, of whom 1,151 (28.4%) had an ideal, 2,727 (67.3%) an intermediate, and 174 (4.3%) a poor LS7 lifestyle profile. Compared with the ideal group, patients with intermediate/poor lifestyle were younger, less often female, and had higher cardiometabolic burden. On multivariable logistic regression, younger age, heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, and vascular disease were associated with non-ideal LS7 lifestyle, whereas prior thromboembolism was inversely associated. After a median follow-up of 721 (IQR 377–740) days, 425 primary outcomes occurred. Compared with the intermediate group, ideal LS7 lifestyle was associated with lower incidence of the composite outcome and ACD (Table 1). On univariable analysis, ideal lifestyle showed a lower risk of the composite outcome (HR 0.69, 95%CI 0.54–0.87) (Figure 1) and ACD (HR 0.58, 95%CI 0.42–0.79); these associations remained significant after age- and sex-adjustment but not after full adjustment. Mediation analyses showed that 53.5% of the association between non-ideal lifestyle and the primary outcome was explained by comorbidity burden. No significant interaction by cohort was observed. Conclusions In AF patients, a non-ideal LS7 lifestyle profile was associated with increased risk of adverse events, largely mediated by cardiometabolic comorbidities. These findings highlight the role of lifestyle optimization in modulating risk in AF patients.
title: Lifestyle profile and adverse outcomes in atrial fibrillation: a modified life’s simple 7 (LS7) analysis from two prospective observational registries from europe and east Asia

abstract: Abstract Background Mitochondrial dysfunction is a central driver of myocardial injury following myocardial infarction (MI). Our previous work demonstrated that macrophage-specific knockout of a disintegrin and metalloproteinase 8 (ADAM8), a membrane-anchored metalloproteinase upregulated post-MI, markedly improved cardiac function, yet no small-molecule inhibitor has been identified and the downstream mitochondrial mechanisms remain undefined. Objective To identify an ADAM8 small-molecule inhibitor and elucidate its cardioprotective mechanisms with a focus on OPA1-mediated mitochondrial fusion dynamics. Methods High-throughput structure-based virtual screening and molecular docking targeted the catalytic domain of human ADAM8. Binding affinity of the lead compound, isoacteoside, was determined by surface plasmon resonance (SPR). Cardioprotective effects were evaluated in a murine MI model and an in vitro hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) model. Cardiac function was assessed by echocardiography; mitochondrial ultrastructure was visualised by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and fluorescent probes; OPA1 cleavage was quantified by immunoblotting. Transcriptomic and metabolomic profiles were integrated via multi-omics analysis. Results (1) SPR confirmed that isoacteoside binds ADAM8 with high affinity (KD=0.938 μM). (2) Isoacteoside-treated MI mice showed reduced infarct size and attenuated myocardial fibrosis, with left ventricular ejection fraction and fractional shortening markedly preserved on echocardiography, recapitulating the cardioprotective phenotype of macrophage-specific ADAM8 knockout. (3) TEM revealed that isoacteoside reversed the extensive mitochondrial fragmentation and ruptured cristae seen in vehicle groups, restoring elongated, interconnected mitochondria with tightly stacked lamellar cristae; fluorescent probes confirmed restoration of mitochondrial membrane potential. (4) Mechanistically, ischaemic stress induced ADAM8 to cleave long-OPA1 (L-OPA1) to short-OPA1 (S-OPA1) on the inner mitochondrial membrane. This reduction in the L-OPA1/S-OPA1 ratio abolished inner membrane fusion capacity. Isoacteoside blocked this cleavage, restoring the L-OPA1 pool, GTPase-driven inner membrane tethering activity, and mitochondrial fusion competence. (5) Multi-omics analyses revealed upregulation of purine transporters Slc43a3 and Aqp9, replenishing the mitochondrial GTP pool for OPA1-dependent fusion, alongside enhanced cardiolipin biosynthesis, consolidating the lipid scaffold essential for OPA1-mediated inner membrane curvature and tubular network formation. Conclusion Isoacteoside is a novel ADAM8 inhibitor that protects against ischaemic cardiac injury by blocking ADAM8-mediated L-OPA1 cleavage and providing sustained metabolic support for OPA1-dependent mitochondrial fusion, highlighting ADAM8 inhibition as a promising translational strategy for MI therapy.Schematic diagram
title: Therapeutic targeting of ADAM8 with isoacteoside mitigates myocardial infarction injury via OPA1-mediated mitochondrial fusion dynamics

abstract: Abstract Background Disruption of mitochondrial calcium homeostasis drives post-myocardial infarction (MI) heart failure by impairing excitation-contraction coupling . However, the critical upstream molecular mechanisms remain unclear, necessitating novel interventional targets. Objective To elucidate the core mechanisms driving cardiomyocyte mitochondrial calcium imbalance in ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) and evaluate targeted therapeutic strategies for post-MI remodeling. Methods Human ICM single-nucleus transcriptome data combined with high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA) were utilized to identify core genes regulating cardiomyocyte calcium homeostasis. Using an oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) model in rat cardiomyocytes (H9c2) and a murine MI model, myocardium-specific gene knockdown and overexpression were achieved via AAV9 vectors. The mechanisms governing mitochondrial function by the identified core molecule were elucidated through co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), tandem ubiquitin-binding entity (TUBE) pull-down assays, mitochondrial functional assessments, and the IonOptix single-cell contractility system. Furthermore, CellChat was applied to map pathological cell-cell communication networks within the myocardial microenvironment. Results Bioinformatics analysis identified the transmembrane protein 65 (TMEM65) as the core factor regulating myocardial calcium homeostasis, which was significantly downregulated in ICM and during the ultra-early phase of ischemia. In vitro and in vivo mechanistic studies demonstrated that TMEM65 physically interacts with the mitochondrial Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger (NCLX) , thereby inhibiting its polyubiquitination-mediated degradation. Ischemia-induced loss of TMEM65 triggered NCLX degradation and hindered mitochondrial calcium efflux, culminating in the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, reactive oxygen species (ROS) bursts, diminished oxygen consumption rate (OCR), and the failure of excitation-contraction coupling. Myocardium-specific knockdown of TMEM65 exacerbated mitochondrial calcium overload in MI mice, significantly worsening cardiac function and ventricular remodeling. Conversely, targeted overexpression of TMEM65 effectively preserved NCLX stability and mitochondrial calcium efflux, dramatically reducing infarct size and fibrotic area, thereby rescuing heart failure. Conclusion The early and abrupt ischemia-induced downregulation of TMEM65 is a pivotal upstream event that triggers mitochondrial calcium overload and ventricular failure in cardiomyocytes. TMEM65 sustains mitochondrial calcium homeostasis and energy metabolism by preventing the ubiquitin-dependent degradation of NCLX. Targeted restoration of TMEM65 expression in cardiomyocytes can effectively reverse mitochondrial dysfunction and halt pathological remodeling, offering a highly promising novel therapeutic strategy for ischemic heart disease and heart failure.MI
title: TMEM65 ameliorates post-myocardial infarction heart failure by maintaining mitochondrial calcium homeostasis via inhibiting NCLX ubiquitination

abstract: Abstract Background Mitochondrial dysfunction drives metabolic disturbances in cardiac diseases. Mitochondrial transplantation can replace damaged mitochondria and restore cellular metabolism and cardiac function. Although preclinical studies have validated this concept, practical challenges persist. A critical but underexplored question is whether mitochondria from different tissues are equally effective, or whether their tissue-specific metabolic programming influences therapeutic efficacy in the unique metabolic environment of cardiomyocytes. Methods Mitochondria were isolated from heart, liver, and skeletal muscle of 6–8 week C57BL/6 mice using tissue-specific centrifugation. Protein concentration was quantified via Bradford assay for standardized dosing. Isolated mitochondria were injected intramyocardially into mouse models of acute or chronic cardiac disease. Cardiac function was assessed by echocardiography. Mitochondrial metabolic patterns and capacity were evaluated using proteomics, flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, and O2K respirometry. Results Mitochondria were successfully isolated from heart, liver, and skeletal muscle with high yield and purity. Mitochondrial content per tissue mass was higher in heart and skeletal muscle than in liver. Heart-derived mitochondria exhibited significantly greater glucose and fatty acid oxidation (FAO) capacity, as well as higher FAO-related protein expression, compared to liver- or muscle-derived mitochondria. While intramyocardial injection of mitochondria from all three sources restored cardiac function following ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury and heart failure, heart-derived mitochondria were most effective. They demonstrated superior restoration of oxidative respiratory capacity, ATP production, and mitigation of oxidative stress in MIRI, leading to reduced infarct size and greater improvement in cardiac function. Conclusions In conclusion, mitochondria from different tissues exhibit distinct metabolic patterns. The heart relies heavily on fatty acid oxidation (FAO), and heart-derived mitochondria possess the inherent enzymatic machinery to meet this demand. Upon transplantation, they integrate structurally and are metabolically "pre-adapted" to utilize fatty acids efficiently, resulting in sustained ATP production, reduced oxidative stress and cell death, and superior cardiac preservation. In contrast, liver- and muscle-derived mitochondria lack this specific optimization. Therefore, achieving optimal cardioprotection requires "donor/recipient metabolic compliance." For acute injuries like ischemia-reperfusion, autologous mitochondria from healthy cardiac tissue offer the most prominent protection. This highlights the importance of donor source selection and supports further investigation of heart-derived mitochondrial transplantation. Future research should focus on optimizing delivery methods, timing, and ex vivo preconditioning to enhance efficacy.
title: Optimal cardioprotection effects of mitochondria transplantation requires donor/recipient metabolic compliances

abstract: Abstract Background Aging is an independent risk factor for exacerbating myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury, yet the pathological role of aged circulating extracellular vesicles and their key molecular mechanisms remain elusive. This study integrates single-cell transcriptome sequencing and quantitative proteomics to systematically elucidate the mechanism by which aged EVs regulate myocardial energy metabolism and redox homeostasis. Methods Circulating EVs were isolated from the peripheral blood of young and aged rats, characterized by NTA, Western blot, and transmission electron microscopy, and validated for uptake by cardiomyocytes. A rat model of myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury was established, and young/aged EVs were administered via intramyocardial injection to assess their effects on myocardial injury. Single-cell transcriptome sequencing was performed on heart tissues to analyze cellular subpopulations and energy metabolism pathways. Quantitative proteomics was employed to screen differentially expressed proteins between young and aged EVs, and the findings were validated in plasma EVs from elderly coronary heart disease patients. Co-immunoprecipitation was used to identify the interaction between PTX3 and thioredoxin 1. Rescue experiments with PTX3 overexpression and TXN1 silencing were conducted to verify the causal relationship. Results Aged EVs were efficiently internalized by cardiomyocytes and significantly aggravated myocardial injury, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and energy metabolism disorder in I/R rats. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed downregulated mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in cardiomyocytes. Proteomic analysis and clinical sample validation confirmed that PTX3 was significantly downregulated in aged rat EVs and plasma EVs from elderly patients. Mechanistically, PTX3 directly interacted with TXN1 to maintain redox balance and mitochondrial function. PTX3 overexpression ameliorated myocardial injury induced by aged EVs, whereas TXN1 silencing abolished the protective effects of PTX3. Conclusion Aged circulating EVs exacerbate myocardial I/R injury by downregulating PTX3 and disrupting its interaction with TXN1, leading to mitochondrial energy metabolism disorder and oxidative stress. The EV–PTX3–TXN1 axis serves as a novel mechanism and potential therapeutic target for age-related cardiovascular diseases.
title: Aged extracellular vesicles exacerbate myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury via PTX3

abstract: Abstract Background Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) modulates coronary atherosclerosis via paracrine signalling. We aimed to define the cellular heterogeneity and extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated crosstalk within human EAT during acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Methods We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and EV transcriptomic profiling of EAT from patients with AMI , unstable angina (UA), and non-coronary artery disease (non-CAD). Analyses included clustering, pseudotime trajectory inference, cell-cell communication (CellChat), and computational deconvolution of EV cellular origins. Results scRNA-seq revealed a dramatic shift in EAT cellularity during AMI, characterised by a 3.3-fold expansion of fibroblasts (dominated by profibrotic SPSB1+ and IGLC2+ subsets) and significant infiltration of myeloid cells, alongside a marked reduction in endothelial cells. Pseudotime analysis indicated inflammatory reprogramming of these key populations. Cell-cell communication analysis identified significantly reinforced fibroblast-macrophage crosstalk in AMI, primarily mediated by ECM ligand-receptor pairs FN1-CD44 and COL1A2-CD44. EV cargo analysis showed enrichment for TNF, mTOR, and IL-17 signalling pathways in AMI. Bioinformatic deconvolution suggested a shift in the predominant EV source from immune cells in UA to activated fibroblasts (~68% contribution) in AMI, with their cargo enriched for lipid metabolism and oxidative stress genes. Conclusion This study unveils an AMI-specific cellular and vesicular axis within EAT, featuring expanded profibrotic fibroblasts engaging reinforced crosstalk with macrophages. The concomitant shift towards a fibroblast-dominated EV profile suggests a novel paracrine mechanism. These findings highlight potential diagnostic and therapeutic targets within the EAT microenvironment for post-infarction remodelling.ScRNA-seq analyses of EATCellular origin analysis of EVs
title: Single-cell and extracellular vesicle profiling reveals fibroblast-macrophage crosstalk in epicardial adipose tissue during acute myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Lipid droplet-mitochondria (LD-Mito) crosstalk is a core hub for cellular lipid metabolism and energy homeostasis, and its dysregulation drives acute myocardial infarction (AMI)-induced cardiac remodeling and mitochondrial dysfunction. Perilipin 5 (Plin5), a cardiac-enriched LD-localized protein, maintains organelle physical contact and metabolic balance. However, the molecular mechanism by which Plin5 downregulation reshapes organelle interaction networks to regulate AMI progression and post-infarction remodeling remains unclear. Purpose This study investigated the function and mechanism of Plin5 downregulation in AMI via multi-omics and in vivo/in vitro experiments, explored its role in mediating cardiomyocyte LD-Mito crosstalk under ischemia, and identified Plin5 as a potential therapeutic target for AMI by restoring its expression. Methods Metabolomic and proteomic analyses were performed on myocardial tissues from AMI C57BL/6J mice to screen Plin5 as a key target related to AMI and LD-Mito crosstalk. AAV-mediated Plin5-overexpressing mice were used to establish the AMI model, with infarct severity evaluated at 3 days post-AMI. Adenovirus-mediated Plin5 overexpression models were constructed in adult/neonatal mouse cardiomyocytes (ACM/NMCM) and HL1 cells to explore Plin5 function under ischemic stress. Results Multi-omics identified Plin5 as a core protein associated with AMI and LD-Mito crosstalk, with its expression negatively correlated with AMI severity. Public database analysis confirmed Plin5 downregulation in human AMI cardiomyocytes, linking Plin5 downregulation to AMI pathogenesis. In vivo, Plin5 overexpression reduced AMI infarct size, attenuated ischemic injury and inhibited cardiomyocyte death, and enhanced cardiomyocyte LD-Mito colocalization and contact site integrity. In vitro, Plin5 overexpression alleviated ischemic injury in ACM, NMCM and HL1 cells, reduced ROS production, restored mitochondrial function and ATP levels, normalized lipid metabolism, and maintained lipid and energy homeostasis by improving mitochondrial FAO activity. Mechanistically, Plin5 overexpression strengthened LD-Mito crosstalk to promote lipid substrate transfer for FAO, alleviating mitochondrial lipotoxicity and dysfunction, and ultimately inhibiting cardiomyocyte death to exert cardioprotection against AMI. Conclusions Plin5 is a key regulator of AMI, and its downregulation disrupts LD-Mito crosstalk to exacerbate myocardial injury. Plin5 overexpression restores organelle interaction, improves mitochondrial lipid and energy homeostasis, and protects against ischemic cardiomyocyte death, highlighting Plin5 as a promising therapeutic target for AMI.ResearchFlow
title: Multi-omics and functional analyses reveal Plin5-mediated organelle crosstalk as a pivotal regulator of acute myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Emerging evidence suggests that B lymphocytes play a crucial role in the progression of myocardial infraction. However, the existence, unique phenotype and function of B lymphocytes in response to physical exercise after MI remain poorly understood. Objective This study aimed to investigate the mechanism underlying exercise training-induced mobilization of B lymphocytes to the myocardium after myocardial infraction and to examine the activation, cytokine secretion, and autoantibody production of B lymphocytes in response to exercise training. Additionally, we sought to determine whether this mechanism contributes to the protective effects against MI. Methods and Results An 8-week-old C57BL/6J mouse model was used, with mice randomly assigned to sedentary control or exercise training groups. After 2 months of training, MI was induced by permanent left coronary artery ligation, and parameters were assessed at 3 and 21 days post-MI. Sedentary mice showed reduced left ventricular function, increased cardiomyocyte apoptosis, and leukocyte infiltration, whereas exercise-trained mice exhibited significant improvement in these measures. Further experiments revealed that exercise-driven B lymphocytes mediated the cardioprotective effects of exercise. Exercise reduced myocardial CXCL13 expression and CXCR5 levels on B cells, leading to decreased B-cell infiltration. Transfer of CXCR5-deficient or exercise-derived B cells into μMT⁻/⁻ mice reduced cardiac fibrosis and inflammation and improved cardiac function after MI. Moreover, B cells lacking granzyme B alleviated post-MI remodeling, and transfer of anti-CD19-CAR-NK cells protected cardiac function by inhibiting B cells. Conclusions Physical exercise exerted a protective effect against MI by regulating B lymphocytes infiltration in the heart. This protection is mediated through the downregulation of CXCL13 expression in the myocardium and reduced CXCR5 levels on B lymphocytes, thereby limiting B-cell recruitment after MI. In addition, exercise training decreases granzyme B release from B cells, attenuating myocardial injury and improves heart function. These findings highlight therapeutic potential of targeting B lymphocytes and their receptors to enhance the cardioprotective benefits of exercise following MI.
title: Exercise training protects against myocardial infarction by regulating B cell infiltration and function

abstract: Abstract Background Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury remains a major clinical challenge. Ferroptosis, a form of regulated cell death characterized by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, has emerged as a critical mechanism underlying cardiomyocyte loss following I/R. Coenzyme A (CoA) is essential for energy metabolism; however, its specific role in modulating ferroptosis during I/R injury remains poorly understood. Purpose This study aims to characterize the alteration of CoA metabolism during myocardial I/R injury, identify CoA-binding proteins that regulate ferroptotic signaling, and establish the CoA-IGFBP2 axis as a target to attenuate cardiomyocyte loss and preserve cardiac function following I/R. Methods Ferroptosis was induced in neonatal mouse cardiomyocytes (NMCMs) via cystine deprivation and assessed by cell viability and lipid peroxidation assays. Multi-modal metabolomics (untargeted, spatial, and targeted) profiled CoA alterations in vitro and in vivo. The functional role of CoA was determined via CoA supplementation and genetic modulation of PANK1 (the rate-limiting CoA biosynthetic enzyme) or NUDT8 (a key enzyme in CoA catabolism). CoA-binding proteins were screened by limited proteolysis-mass spectrometry (LIP-MS) and validated via SPR, CETSA and pull down assays. The function of the lead candidate, IGFBP2, was confirmed using siRNA and cardiomyocyte-specific knockout (IGFBP2-cKO) mice. Furthermore, mass spectrometry was employed to characterize oxidative conformational changes and disulfide bond remodeling in IGFBP2. Results Cystine deprivation induced significant ferroptosis in NMCMs, accompanied by marked downregulation of the CoA biosynthetic pathway. Restoring CoA levels either through supplementation or genetic modulation of PANK1/NUDT8 successfully rescued NMCMs from ferroptosis. In murine I/R hearts, spatial and targeted metabolomics revealed significant collapse in free CoA and multiple acyl-CoA species. Consequently, PANK1 overexpression or NUDT8 knockdown significantly reduced infarct size and improved cardiac function. Mechanistically, LiP-MS identified IGFBP2 as a intracellular CoA-binding protein. Cystine deprivation triggered oxidative disulfide bond remodeling of IGFBP2 and suppressed the BRCA1-associated DNA damage response, thereby amplifying ferroptosis. Conversely, CoA binding prevented this deleterious conformational change and inhibited this pro-ferroptosis cascade. Finally, IGFBP2-cKO mice exhibited reduced ferroptosis and improved cardiac function following I/R. Conclusions This study delineates dynamic CoA depletion during myocardial I/R and identifies IGFBP2 as an intracellular CoA-binding protein. By preventing IGFBP2 oxidative disulfide remodeling, CoA acts as a critical endogenous suppressor of ferroptosis. The CoA-IGFBP2 axis represents a promising therapeutic target for mitigating myocardial I/R injury.
title: IGFBP2 serves as a coenzyme A sensor to regulate cardiomyocyte ferroptosis in cardiac ischemia-reperfusion injury

abstract: Abstract Background The safety of atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation during rapid procedural dissemination remains controversial, with clinical registries reporting extremely low mortality compared with administrative databases suggesting 10-fold higher rates with worsening trends. (Ref 1, 2) Moreover, as observed in percutaneous coronary intervention (3) and transcatheter aortic valve replacement, (4) the widespread dissemination of complex cardiovascular technologies is historically associated with a transient deterioration in outcomes driven by the widening "efficacy-effectiveness gap" as procedures migrate from specialized centers to general practice: a phenomenon we refer to as a "diffusion penalty". We investigated whether this phenomenon occurred during the rapid nationwide expansion of elective catheter ablation for AF. Methods We utilized the JROAD-DPC nationwide database (Fiscal Years 2012–2022), which captures the vast majority of AF ablation in Japan, covering the rapid diffusion phase from "early adopters" to the "early majority". A major strength of this study is the strict reimbursement-linked verification of procedure codes, admission type (scheduled vs. emergency), and discharge status (survival vs. death). Leveraging this high-fidelity data, the cohort was restricted to scheduled elective admissions for transseptal AF ablation, systematically excluding emergency cases. The primary and secondary endpoints were mortality during index hospitalization and 30-day mortality during readmission, respectively. Results We analyzed 412,947 procedures. Consistent with the transition to the early majority phase, annual volume increased &gt;5-fold (10,969 to 63,014), and participating centers expanded from 198 to 515. Patient complexity rose significantly: median age increased from 64 to 70 years, and patients with a Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) ≥3 increased from 2.5% to 5.9%. Despite this expansion, in-hospital mortality remained exceptionally low at 0.029% (119 deaths) and exhibited a statistically significant downward trend (P=0.037). (Figure 1) Thirty-day deaths during readmission were also rare (0.017%), indicating minimal uncaptured mortality risk. (Figure 2) Among deaths during the index hospitalization, the most frequent concurrent complications were cardiac tamponade (21.8%), pneumothorax/hemothorax (14.3%), and stroke (9.2%). In multivariable analysis, independent predictors of mortality included CCI ≥3 (OR 4.59; 95%CI 2.59–8.14) and low institutional volume (≤50 cases/year; OR 1.84; 95%CI 1.02–3.33), whereas age showed a modest association. Conclusion Rapid nationwide expansion of elective AF ablation was achieved while maintaining exceptionally low mortality despite increasing patient complexity. These findings demonstrate the absence of a "diffusion penalty" during the transition to general practice and establish a contemporary global safety benchmark for this complex cardiovascular therapy.Figure 1.Trends in In-Hospital MortalityFigure 2.Trends in 30-Day Outcomes
title: Achieving low mortality without a 'diffusion penalty': nationwide analysis of 412,947 elective atrial fibrillation ablations

abstract: Abstract Background/Introduction Ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury is a critical determinant of prognosis in myocardial infarction patients undergoing revascularization. Macrophage-mediated inflammation plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of cardiac I/R injury. Mincle, a pattern recognition receptor (PRR), mediates immune responses through recognition of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). However, its role in cardiac I/R injury remains largely unknown. Purpose To investigate the role of macrophage Mincle in myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury. Methods Transcriptomics, single-cell sequencing, genetic ablation, and bone marrow transfer chimeric models were used to determine the functional significance of macrophage Mincle in myocardial I/R injury. Immune cell infiltration and inflammatory responses were examined by western blot, quantitative real-time PCR, and immunohistochemistry. Co-immunoprecipitation coupled with mass spectrometry, surface plasmon resonance, and mutant plasmid constructs were employed to identify the key domain of RTN4 binding to Mincle. RTN4 activation of Mincle-related pathways was validated through multiple cell biology experiments. Endothelial-specific RTN4 knockdown via AAV was performed to validate the functional relevance of this interaction in vivo. Results Following I/R injury, Mincle expression was rapidly upregulated on bone marrow-derived macrophages infiltrating the heart. Myeloid-specific Mincle deficiency significantly improved cardiac function and reduced cardiomyocyte apoptosis, which was associated with downregulation of CXCL1 and GCSF, decreased Ly-6G⁺ neutrophil infiltration and suppressed inflammatory responses. Mechanistically, we identified endothelial RTN4 as a potential ligand for Mincle, with its N-terminal 1-185aa fragment being the critical domain for activating the Mincle/Syk pathway and promoting inflammation. Notably, endothelial cell-specific knockout of RTN4 recapitulated the protective effects against I/R injury, whereas exogenous administration of the RTN4 1-185aa peptide abolished this protection, underscoring the functional relevance of this ligand-receptor interaction in intercellular crosstalk. Conclusion(s) Our results reveal a pivotal role of Mincle-RTN4 interaction in driving myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury. Targeting this ligand-receptor interaction represents a novel and viable therapeutic strategy to limit cardiac damage.
title: Macrophage Mincle drives myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury by recognizing coronary endothelial RTN4

abstract: Abstract Background Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury is still a lack of effective therapeutic drugs. Recently, gut microbiota-derived metabolites have been associated with various cardiovascular diseases. However the specific role of shikimic acid (SA) in the context of I/R injury remains unclear. Objective This study aims to investigate the protective role of shikimic acid, a gut microbial metabolite, against myocardial I/R injury and its potential mechanism. Methods We established an in vivo mouse model of myocardial I/R and an in vitro hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) model using neonatal rat cardiomyocytes (NRCMs). Myocardial tissues underwent untargeted metabolomics to assess metabolic changes. Cardiac function, infarct size, fibrotic area, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels were assessed using echocardiography, TTC/Evans blue staining, Masson staining and biochemical assays, respectively. Markers relevant to ferroptosis, including glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH1), and ROS levels were assessed by Western blotting and immunofluorescence. Results Metabolomic analysis revealed a significant depletion of SA in I/R-injured myocardial tissues. Exogenous SA supplementation markedly restored cardiac systolic function, including left ventricular ejection fraction and fractional shortening and reduced both infarct size and fibrotic area. Mechanistically, SA treatment suppressed I/R-induced ferroptosis by increased GPX4 expression. These findings were confirmed in vitro, where SA treatment enhanced cardiomyocyte viability and mitigated ROS by maintaining GPX4 and FTH1 expression under H/R conditions. Conclusion The gut microbial metabolite SA alleviates myocardial I/R injury by inhibiting ferroptosis through preservation of GPX4 and FTH1. These data suggest that SA may represent a novel therapeutic candidate to alleviate reperfusion injury in ischemia heart disease.Figure 1
title: Shikimic acid, a gut microbiota-derived metabolite, alleviates myocardial ischaemia–reperfusion injury by suppressing ferroptosis

abstract: Abstract Background Programmed cell death is a major contributor to myocardial infarct expansion following cardiac ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury. Acute inhibition of apoptosis and ferroptosis prior to ischemia has been shown to reduce cardiac I/R injury. However, the effects of chronic inhibition of apoptosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis during cardiac I/R injury have not yet been investigated. Purpose To investigate whether pharmacological inhibition of apoptosis, ferroptosis, and pyroptosis can alleviate infarct size, cardiac dysfunction, and mitochondrial dysfunction in prediabetic rats subjected to I/R injury. Methods Male rats were fed either a high-fat diet (HFD) to induce prediabetes or a normal diet (ND) as a control for 24 weeks. Subsequently, HFD-fed rats were divided into four subgroups: (1) vehicle (normal saline solution, subcutaneous injection), (2) apoptosis inhibitor (Z-VAD, 1 mg/kg, subcutaneous injection), (3) ferroptosis inhibitor (Fer-1, 1 mg/kg, subcutaneous injection), and (4) pyroptosis inhibitor (disulfiram, 50 mg/kg, oral gavage). Rats received their assigned intervention for an additional 2 weeks before being subjected to 30 minutes of LAD ligation to induce ischemia followed by 2 hours of reperfusion. Left ventricular function, arrhythmia score, infarct size, and mitochondrial function were assessed. Results HFD-fed rats exhibited more severe cardiac I/R injury than ND-fed rats, as indicated by a larger infarct size, greater left ventricular (LV) dysfunction, and more pronounced mitochondrial dysfunction. Treatment with programmed cell death inhibitors significantly reduced infarct size to a similar extent across groups (Fig 1A). However, treatment with apoptosis and pyroptosis inhibitors provided greater improvement in LV function, as evidenced by a greater reduction in LV end-diastolic pressure and a higher LV ejection fraction, compared with ferroptosis inhibition (Fig 1B). Mitochondrial function analysis showed that although all programmed cell death inhibitors similarly attenuated mitochondrial oxidative stress, apoptosis and pyroptosis inhibitors greater attenuated mitochondrial depolarization (Fig 1C) and mitochondrial swelling. Arrhythmia scores were comparable among groups regardless of diet or programmed cell death intervention (Fig 1D). Conclusion Although programmed cell death inhibitors effectively reduced infarct size in prediabetic rats with cardiac I/R injury, apoptosis and pyroptosis inhibition provided superior cardioprotection compared with ferroptosis inhibition, as demonstrated by greater improvements in mitochondrial and LV function.
title: Apoptosis and pyroptosis inhibitors exerted greater cardioprotection against cardiac I/R injury than ferroptosis inhibitor in prediabetic rats via an improvement of mitochondrial membrane potential

abstract: Abstract Background Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury impairs the efficacy of reperfusion therapy for acute myocardial infarction[1]. Evidence has confirmed that Lactobacillus can ameliorate, myocardial I/R injury by inhibiting apoptosis, inflammation, oxidative stress, and ferroptosis[2]. However, the roles of microbiota-metabolite interactions in myocardial I/R injury have not been explored. Purpose This study aimed to elucidate the effects of Lactobacillus on the gut microbiota composition and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production in I/R rats, and to investigate the therapeutic potential of short-chain fatty acids in I/R-induced cardiac damage. Methods Following Lactobacillus gavage for 4 weeks, I/R was induced in Sprague-Dawley rats. The diversity, composition and abundance of gut microbiota were detected by 16S rRNA sequencing. Targeted metabolomics of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in serum was determined by liquid chromatographytandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Furthermore, sodium butyrate was administered to rats for 21 days before myocardial I/R injury was induced. The protective efficacy of sodium butyrate against I/R injury was assessed by Evans-TTC staining, echocardiographic detection, HE staining and immunofluorescent staining. Results Lactobacillus significantly reshaped the composition of gut microbiota according to the PCoA of β-diversity, and remodeled gut microbiota at both phylum and genus levels. Linear discriminant analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) analysis identified Desulfovibrionales enrichment as a hallmark of I/R-induced dysbiosis, which was reversed by Lactobacillus. Through the detection of targeted metabolomics, butyric acid and other SCFAs, were found to be upregulated by Lactobacillus gavage, compared with the IR group. Similarly, the abundance of several butyrate-producing bacteria was upregulated under the influence of Lactobacillus. Notably, butyrate supplementation significantly improved cardiac function, as evidenced by increased left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and fractional shortening (LVFS), along with decreased left ventricular end-diastolic diameter (LVIDs) and end-systolic volume (LVESV), and attenuated myocardial infarct size compared with the I/R group. HE staining also demonstrated that butyrate treatment markedly attenuated myocardial structural damage, preserved myofibrillar arrangement, and reduced inflammatory infiltration, while immunofluorescence staining confirmed a concomitant reduction in myocardial macrophage infiltration. Conclusions Administration of Lactobacillus altered the composition, abundance of gut microbiota and the production of butyrate in rats with myocardial I/R injury. The Lactobacillus-butyrate axis is associated with the pathogenesis of myocardial I/R injury, and exogenous butyrate exerts cardioprotective effects by improving cardiac function and reducing infarct size, offering a novel microbiota-targeted therapy for I/R injury.
title: Lactobacillus ameliorates myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury by regulating butyrate production

abstract: Abstract Background and Purpose Anemia is frequently observed in patients with cardiovascular diseases (CVD) such as acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Anemia, either alone or in combination with other morbid conditions, leads to a poor prognosis in AMI. Studies using anemic mouse models and clinical patient data have demonstrated that anemia is associated with an unchanged infarct size but increased mortality. However, the underlying mechanisms are not clear. We hypothesize that an energy imbalance in the heart contributes to left ventricular dysfunction in AMI, leading to a worse prognosis in anemia. Methods STEMI (ST-elevation myocardial infarction) patients with and without anemia were analyzed by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) to assess cardiac contractile function. Acute blood loss anemia was induced by repeated blood withdrawal for three consecutive days in male C57BL/6J mice with and without left anterior descending artery (LAD) ligation. Heart function was assessed using CMRI at baseline, after three days of anemia, and 24 hours post-AMI. Proteomic and respirometry analyses were performed on isolated LV tissues from anemic and sham mice after AMI. Flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry were used to analyse immune cell infiltration. Mitochondrial respiration was analyzed in LV biopsies from anemic ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) patients. Results Anemia in STEMI patients was associated with significantly worse infarct-region contractile function as assessed by CMRI-derived global longitudinal strain. In a mouse model, anemia did not affect baseline or pre-infarction regional function but led to a marked reduction in fractional shortening within the infarct region after AMI. This dysfunction was accompanied by ischemic myocardial energetic imbalance, evidenced by depletion of the phosphocreatine/ATP ratio, and altered mitochondrial respiration. These findings were validated in LV biopsies from anemic ICM patients. Mechanistically, anemia was associated with increased neutrophil infiltration, myeloperoxidase elevation, and oxidative stress, while anemic red blood cells (RBCs) directly impaired mitochondrial respiration in human cardiomyocytes. Importantly, antioxidant treatment with N-acetylcysteine fully restored mitochondrial coupling, demonstrating therapeutic reversibility. Conclusion Anemia worsens infarct-region LV dysfunction due to increased oxidative stress from dysfunctional RBCs and neutrophil infiltration, leading to altered mitochondrial respiration and contractile impairment. Antioxidant therapy emerges as a promising strategy to protect the anemic heart after AMI.
title: Anemia exacerbates regional left ventricular functional impairment and energetic imbalance in acute myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background The restoration of coronary blood flow, or called “reperfusion”, is a goal for treatment of acute myocardial infarction. Unfortunately, reperfusion commonly results in increased mortality via increased infarct size, which is defined as “myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury”. Probiotic Lactobacillus Reuteri KUB-AC5 has been found to exert a protective effect against obesity-induced cardiac dysfunction by ameliorating cardiac mitochondrial impairment. However, the effect of this probiotic on cardiac mitochondria in a model of myocardial I/R injury has never been determined. Purpose To examine the effect of probiotic Lactobacillus Reuteri KUB-AC5 on cardiac mitochondria and cardiac function in a rat model of myocardial I/R injury. Methods Male Wistar rats were divided into 4 groups (n=8 per group), including Sham, myocardial I/R treated with vehicle (IR), myocardial I/R treated with live form of probiotic Lactobacillus Reuteri KUB-AC5 (IRL), and myocardial I/R treated with heat-killed form of probiotic Lactobacillus Reuteri KUB-AC5 (IRH). Sham and IR groups were treated with 1 mL per day of normal saline solution as a vehicle, while IRL and IRH groups were treated with 1 x 108 colony forming unit (cfu) per day of live form and heat-killed form of Lactobacillus Reuteri KUB-AC5, respectively. All treatments were administered via oral gavage. After 12 weeks of treatment, the Sham group received sham surgery, while the other 3 groups received ligation of left anterior descending coronary artery for 30 min (ischemic period) followed by 120 min of reperfusion. Pressure-volume loop was recorded during the operation. After 120 min of reperfusion, the rats were euthanized. Cardiac tissue was then collected for mitochondrial isolation studies and infarct size analysis. Results The IR group exhibited left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction, as indicated by a reduction in LV ejection fraction, when compared to the Sham group (Fig. 1A). Regarding cardiac mitochondria, increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (Fig. 2A), mitochondrial membrane depolarization (Fig. 2B), and mitochondrial swelling (Fig. 2C) were found in the IR group. In addition, the IR group had decreased expressions of a mitochondrial antioxidant-related protein (SOD2) and a mitochondrial fusion-related protein (MFN2), while the expressions of a mitochondrial fission-related protein (DRP1) and a mitophagy-related protein (PINK1/parkin ratio) were increased in this group (Fig. 2D). Treatment with Lactobacillus Reuteri KUB-AC5, both live and heat-killed forms, ameliorated LV systolic dysfunction (Fig. 1A), diminished infarct area (Fig. 1B), and improved mitochondrial-related parameters (Fig. 2A-D) in the heart of rats with myocardial I/R injury. Conclusion Probiotic Lactobacillus Reuteri KUB-AC5, both live and heat-killed forms, alleviates myocardial I/R injury by mitigating cardiac mitochondrial dysfunction.
title: Probiotic Lactobacillus Reuteri KUB-AC5 attenuates myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury by mitigating cardiac mitochondrial dysfunction

abstract: Abstract Introduction Coronary artery disease (CAD) is classically viewed as a vascular disorder, yet systemic inflammation may extend beyond the coronary circulation to the myocardium and adjacent adipose depots. Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) is increasingly recognized as an active modulator of cardiovascular pathology, but the cellular architecture and signaling programs of myocardial-associated EAT (mEAT) in CAD remain poorly defined. We previously identified two inflammatory mEAT cell states enriched in CAD, marked by transcriptional signatures of immune activation, metabolic stress, extracellular-matrix remodeling, and impaired adipogenesis: inflammatory adipogenic cells (IAC) and inflammatory stromal cells (ISC). Purpose We aim to define mEAT–myocardial crosstalk in CAD at single-cell resolution, with a focus on inflammatory mEAT cell populations and their impact on cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells. Methods Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) was performed on paired mEAT and right atrial (RA) myocardium from 9 individuals (18 samples): CAD patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (n=4), non-CAD surgical controls with aortic disease (n=3), and forensic controls without cardiovascular disease (n=2). Batch-corrected integration (Harmony) yielded 124,000 nuclei. Putative ligand–receptor interactions were inferred using CellPhoneDB. Findings were complemented by functional assays using conditioned media from mEAT-derived adipocytes (including IAC) applied to human iPSC-derived cardiomyocyte microtissues and primary endothelial cells. Results Integrated analysis of paired mEAT and RA myocardium revealed prominent mEAT-to-myocardium signaling, with cardiomyocytes, stromal cells, endothelial cells, and macrophages receiving THBS1- and semaphorin-mediated inputs, particularly from inflammatory mEAT populations. Interaction analysis prioritized THBS1–CD36 and SEMA4A/SEMA3C–NRP1/PLXNA2/PLXNA4 axes as candidate mediators linking mEAT inflammation to cardiomyocyte stress responses and microvascular dysfunction, suggesting pathogenic adipose–myocardial communication even in the absence of overt myocardial injury. Functionally, conditioned media from CAD-mEAT adipocytes and inflammatory adipogenic fractions induced structural remodeling, altered contractile dynamics, and activated inflammatory gene programs in cardiomyocyte microtissues, while also impairing endothelial tube formation and migration, supporting a paracrine mechanism of myocardial and microvascular impairment. Conclusions We provide a high-resolution map of mEAT–myocardial cellular interactions in CAD and identify candidate disease-driving signaling pathways. Our findings position inflammatory mEAT cell states as key mediators of adipose–myocardial crosstalk and support mEAT as a potential therapeutic target for risk stratification and intervention in CAD.
title: Inflammatory epicardial adipose tissue–myocardial crosstalk in coronary artery disease: a single-cell analysis

abstract: Abstract Background Activation of the sympathetic nervous system following myocardial infarction (MI) contributes to adverse cardiac remodelling, ventricular dysfunction, heart failure, and ventricular arrhythmias. Catheter-based renal sympathetic denervation (RDN) lowers systemic sympathetic activity by ablating renal nerves and is currently indicated only for patients with arterial hypertension that remains uncontrolled despite pharmacological treatment. Purpose This study aimed to evaluate the effect of early RDN on cardiac function, arrhythmic substrate, and myocardial scar characteristics in a porcine model of MI. Methods Ten pigs with MI were randomized to a Control group or an RDN-treated group (n=5 per group). RDN was performed immediately after MI induction by radiofrequency ablation. Cardiac function was assessed by magnetic resonance imaging at days 2 and 29 post-MI. On day 30, an electrophysiological study with programmed electrical stimulation and high-density mapping was performed to evaluate electrophysiological properties and ventricular tachycardia (VT) inducibility. Myocardial samples from infarcted and remote regions were collected for histological and immunohistochemical analysis of fibrosis and vascularization, as well as RNA-seq evaluation. Results At day 2 post-MI, the RDN group showed an attenuated left ventricular systolic dysfunction without differences in scar size compared to controls. By day 29, LVEF was similar between groups, but total and dense scar mass was significantly smaller in RDN-treated animals. At 30 days, the RDN group tended to have fewer deceleration zones and exhibited markedly reduced VT inducibility (0% vs. 60% in controls). Analyses of myocardial infarcted tissue showed no differences in type I or III collagen content, whereas vascular density within the scar was higher in the RDN group. RNA-seq of infarcted tissue identified 143 differentially expressed genes between groups, revealing broad down-regulation of inflammatory pathways, including those related to lymphocyte activation and migration in the RDN group. Conclusions Early RDN after MI down-regulates inflammatory and lymphocyte-related pathways, which is associated with a smaller and more vascularized myocardial scar, and reduced arrhythmic susceptibility, suggesting a protective effect on post-infarction remodelling.
title: Effect of renal denervation in a porcine model of myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Progression in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) to the inflammatory, profibrotic subphenotype metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is linked with increased mortality and incidence of heart failure post-myocardial infarction. Currently, the mechanisms underlying this apparent accelerated progression to heart failure are poorly defined. We hypothesise that pre-existing MASH dysregulates post-MI wound healing, leading to aberrant collagen deposition and worsened cardiac function. Here, we developed a combined Western-style diet-induced MASH (WD) and isoprenaline-induced myocardial injury/infarction (MI) model in Sprague-Dawley rats. Concurrently, we conducted a systems-level bioinformatics analysis of heart and liver global transcriptomic data from ~100 mouse strains in the Hybrid Mouse Diversity Panel (HMDP) and a preclinical model of heart failure with preserved-ejection fraction (HFpEF). Acute myocardial injury, assessed by plasma cardiac troponin I (cTnI), did not differ between WD and control diet groups post-isoprenaline administration (mean±SEM; WD – 6009±1224 ng/L; Control – 4405±670 ng/L; Mann-Whitney test; p=0.57). By day 7 post-MI, the WD group had greater histological myocardial collagen deposition than controls (WD – 5.88±1.09%; Control – 3.90±0.18%; Mann-Whitney test; p=0.04). At 12-weeks, the WD group had impaired systolic function on echocardiography, indicated by reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) (WD – 54.78±2.86%; Control – 63.31±1.34%; Mann-Whitney test; p=0.01). Our bioinformatics analysis ranked genes encoding liver-secreted proteins by their cross-tissue correlations with cardiac genes and pathways, leveraging natural variation across the HMDP and changes observed in HFpEF1,2. To explore the translational relevance, we analysed a publicly available plasma proteomics dataset from patients with MASLD and MASH3, identifying several liver-derived factors potentially implicated in adverse myocardial remodelling, including afamin, lumican, and orosomucoid 2. Using the SteatoSite patient cohort (n=707) with histologically staged MASLD fibrosis and bulk RNA-sequencing data4, we assessed whether hepatic gene expression correlates with fibrosis severity and are now investigating whether these secreted factors are associated with major adverse cardiovascular events. Collectively, these data support that pre-existing MASH exacerbates post-MI collagen deposition and cardiac dysfunction, despite comparable initial injury. We are now characterising myocardial remodelling with whole-heart clearing and 3D imaging, and validating hepatic gene expression and plasma levels of candidate liver-secreted factors implicated in adverse remodelling.
title: Investigating the heart-liver-axis in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and acute myocardial infarction

abstract: Abstract Background Scar formation during myocardial remodelling after ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) is tightly regulated by the immune system and its effector cells.
